units.la: Quippe traduntur hic Regulæ Iuris. Tametsi autem generali & lata significatione leges quoque appellatione Regulæ continentur: sic n.l.2.in sin.D.de ll. Lex definitur iustorum & iniustorum regula: speciali tamen & huic loco convenienti significatione Regulæ Iuris sunt variæ ex omnibus iuris partibus excerptæ sententiæ; seu maximæ & axiomata variarum rerum, quæ eodem se modo habent, eodemque iure censentur: adeoque breues comprehensiones iuris, omnibus eiusdem generis rebus subiectis, quo ad æquitatem, in thesi competentis. Cuiusmodi regulæ & Aphorismi (ut Hippocratea phrasi utar) summam in omni scientiarum genere utilitatem præstant.
units.tr: Here are presented the Rules of Law. Although in a general and broad sense laws are also comprised under the name of rules, as in l. 2 in fine D. de legibus, where law is defined as the rule of the just and the unjust, in a special sense, and one suited to this place, the Rules of Law are various maxims and axioms drawn from all parts of the law, that is, statements of various matters which stand in the same way and are judged under the same law. They are brief summaries of the law, applicable in principle, with regard to equity, to all matters of the same kind that fall under them. Such rules and aphorisms (to use the Hippocratic phrase) are of the greatest usefulness in every branch of learning.

units.tr: which elsewhere, in the other parts of the law, are scattered and dispersed far and wide, are here gathered together as in a kind of summary. These rules greatly illustrate and confirm the law of nature and natural equity. In courts and the noise of the forum, the material of this title is most useful both to the judge and to the litigating parties.

units.la: Etenim Iudex in sententia ferenda temere à regula discedere non debet, l. ab ea parte. ff. de probat. l. suos quoq; 4. §. puto recte. de hered. inst. litigantibus vero tantopere seruit, ut, si regulam Iuris pro se habeant & adducant, intentionem suam fundatam habeant: Ideoque in aduersarium, qui exceptionem aliquam regulæ prætexit, onus probandi transferant; quæ probatio si ipsum defecerit, Regula palmam ferre debet, arg. l. 4. §. 1. ibi, Propter quæ ad ge-
units.tr: For a judge ought not to depart rashly from the rule in pronouncing sentence, l. ab ea parte. ff. de probat. l. suos quoque 4. §. puto recte. de hered. inst. but to litigants it is of such service that, if they hold and bring forward a rule of law in their favour, they have their claim well founded. Therefore they shift the burden of proof onto the adversary who puts forward some exception to the rule; and if that proof fails him, the rule ought to carry the palm, arg. l. 4. §. 1. there, On account of which matters, to ge-

units.la: Nec obstat, quod omnis regula suam quandā patiatur exceptionem: Etenim exceptio firmat regulam, eiusque naturam & generalitatem tuetur, in casibus non exceptis. Proinde exceptio regulæ, non est vitium regulæ; sed potius secretum quid ac remotum à regula, in unico forte casu. Et in Politicis regula universalis, est universale practicum, quod ob admirabilem casuum, factorum, & circumstantiarum varietatem, facile exceptionem quandam, in casu forsan uno vel altero, admittit, regula interim ipsa semper salua.
units.tr: Nor does it stand in the way that every rule suffers some exception of its own. For an exception confirms the rule and preserves its nature and generality in the cases not excepted. Hence an exception to a rule is not a defect in the rule, but rather something set apart and remote from the rule, perhaps in one single case. And in political matters a universal rule is a universal practical principle, which, on account of the wonderful variety of cases, facts and circumstances, readily admits some exception, perhaps in one or another case, while the rule itself always remains safe.

units.la: Ut autem istiusmodi maximarum seu

units.la: DEDICATIO.

units.la: seu axiomatum in iudiciis utilitas tanto plenius percipiatur, attendere conuenit, duo causarum genera in iudicia deduci. Unum earum, quæ non nisi ex speciali legum authoritate veniunt decidendæ, in quibus iudex non aliter iudicare potest, quam legibus, constitutionibus, aut moribus proditum est. Inst. de offic. iudic. in princ. quas ordinarias appellamus. Alterum earum causarum est, in quibus ob defectum legum, ius arbitrio iudicantis permittitur definiendum: quas nunc extraordinarias, nunc arbitrarias causas nuncupamus. Et hoc est, quod c. vnaquæque. §. sin. 13. quæst. 2. dicitur: Quæ legibus definita sunt, mutare non licet. quæ autem legibus expressa non sunt, arbitrium sequuntur humanæ voluntatis. Pro hac causarum varietate, præcepta quo-que
units.tr: In order that the usefulness of such axioms in judgments may be grasped all the more fully, it is fitting to note that cases brought to trial are of two kinds. One kind is that which can be decided only by the special authority of the laws, in which the judge cannot rule otherwise than as it has been handed down by laws, constitutions or customs, Inst. de offic. iudic. in princ., and these we call ordinary. The other kind is that in which, because of a lack of laws, the law is left to the judgment of the judge to determine; these we now call extraordinary, now arbitrary cases. And this is what is said in c. vnaquæque, §. sin., 13. quæst. 2: What has been defined by laws it is not permitted to change; but what is not expressed by laws follows the discretion of human will. In keeping with this variety of cases, the precepts also

units.la: DEDICATIO:
units.tr: DEDICATION:

units.la: que iuris distinguuntur, ut alia leges sint, alia regulæ & rationes. Leges ordinariis potissimum causis decidendis ser-uiunt. Regulæ arbitrium iudicis instruunt; ideoque præcipuus harum vsus est in causis & iudiciis extraordinariis & arbitrariis. Non tamen nullus etiam in ordinariis: nam rationes legum nil aliud sunt, quàm regulæ iuris, quæ mentem legum explicant. Quocirca non est par legum ac regularum authoritas; siquidem legum authoritas necessaria est, à qua iudici recedere non licet: regularum probabilis tantum, à qua iudex causa cognita recedere potest.
units.tr: There are also rules of law, which are distinguished from laws, so that some are laws and others are rules and reasons. Laws serve chiefly for deciding ordinary cases; rules furnish the judge with discretion, and so their principal use is in extraordinary and arbitrary cases and trials. Yet they are not without use even in ordinary cases: for the reasons of the laws are nothing other than rules of law which explain the mind of the laws. Hence the authority of laws and of rules is not equal. The authority of laws is binding, and a judge may not depart from it; the authority of rules is only probable, and a judge may depart from it when he has considered the case.

units.la: Ad Rubricam. De diuersis regulis Iuris antiqui.
units.tr: On the rubric. Concerning the various rules of ancient law.

units.la: EX omnibus partibus Iuris, variæ sententiæ & Regulæ hoc titulo proponuntur, id est multarum rerum, quæ eodem se habent modo, comprehensiones breues; vel ex eo quod plerumque fit, rerum definitiones breues. Paci hic in princ. vel, vt alii, ἀξιώματα, petita, postulata. Cuiusmodi regulæ magnā vtilitate in omni scientiarum genere adferūt. Hinc Vegetius 3. cap. 26. recenset regulas quasdam generales bellorum. Idem medicis præstant Aphorismi Hippocratis. Eodem fine Anniaeus ex Pauli sententiis quasdam Gothis suis selegit, quæ hodie receptæ Pauli sententiæ dicuntur.Gothofr.hic lit.e.&c. ¶ Lex autem a regula in eo differt, quod illa dicitur, quam populus certo & cognito omnibus iure constituit: Regula vero, quam Iurisconsulti ex pluribus legum capitibus notatis, inter seque comparatis, elicuerunt: vt non omnino incommode dicere possimus, leges esse tanquam voces, & sonos singulos: Regulam vero esse tanquam harmoniam & concentum. Hotom.2.observ.4. Pac.hic lit.a. Hoc tamen notandum; quasdam leges in hoc titulo proponi, quæ neque regulam constituunt, neque ad has regulas pertinent. vti sunt l.dinus 23. l. hereditas.62. l. ea est natura 65. l. vbi lex.191. l. Neratius 101. quæ omnes ab hoc titulo alienissimæ sunt. Nam quod est in l.28. Constitutio est D. Pij, non regula Iuris: aut si ea constitutio est regula, & quælibet igitur alia Constitutio. Eadem causa est constitutionis relatæ in l.vbi lex.101.& in l. Neratius.191. Lex hereditas 62. definitio est hereditatis: & l.ea est natura 65. definitio est cauillationis vel soritis. Hæ ergo duæ leges melius fuissent positæ in titulo præcedente: aut, si hereditatis, vel soritis definitio est regula, omnis quoque alia definitio erit regula. Paci. hic in fine. Cuia. in recitat. posthum. ad rubric. h.t. §.3. Denique consequens erit, has leges alio remittendas: secus omnes Constitutiones & Definitiones, omnia responsa, erunt regulæ: quod multo absurdius est, quam affirmare, Tribonianum hic errasse, vt aliâs sæpe: nec tam festinanter tam magnum opus à Triboniano confici ita potuit, vt in eo nihil reprehendi possit. Cuiac. in d. §. 3. in fine.
units.tr: From all parts of the law, various sayings and rules are set out under this title, that is, brief summaries of many things that stand in the same relation, or brief definitions of things as they commonly happen. Pacius here at the beginning. Or, as others say, they are axioms, assumptions, postulates (ἀξιώματα, petita, postulata). Rules of this kind are very useful in every field of learning. So Vegetius, book 3, chapter 26, lists certain general rules of war. The aphorisms of Hippocrates serve physicians in the same way. With the same aim, Annianus chose certain sentences from the Opinions of Paul for his Goths, which are today called the received Opinions of Paul. Gothofredus here, letter e, etc. ¶ A law differs from a rule in this respect: a law is what the people have established by a certain and known right for all to see, whereas a rule is what the jurists have drawn out from several chapters of the laws, noted and compared with one another. So we may not unreasonably say that laws are like single voices and sounds, while a rule is like a harmony and concord. Hotman, Observations 2, 4. Pacius here, letter a. It should be noted, however, that some laws are set out under this title which neither establish a rule nor belong to these rules, such as l. Dinus 23, l. hereditas 62, l. ea est natura 65, l. ubi lex 191, l. Neratius 101, all of which are quite foreign to this title. For what is in l. 28 is a constitution of the divine Pius, not a rule of law; or, if that constitution is a rule, then every other constitution will be a rule too. The same reason applies to the constitution cited in l. ubi lex 101 and in l. Neratius 191. Law hereditas 62 is a definition of inheritance, and l. ea est natura 65 is a definition of a sophistical quibble or sorites. These two laws would have been better placed in the preceding title. Or, if the definition of inheritance or of the sorites is a rule, then every other definition will also be a rule. Pacius here at the end. Cujas, in the posthumous Recitations on the rubric of this title, §3. Finally, it follows that these laws should be referred elsewhere; otherwise all constitutions and definitions, all responses, will be rules, which is far more absurd than to say that Tribonian erred here, as he often did elsewhere. Nor could so great a work have been completed so hastily by Tribonian that nothing in it could be found fault with. Cujas, on the same §3, at the end.

units.la: Iuris antiqui Ius antiquum hîc non vocat id, quod antiquatum seu abrogatum est iure novo: neque quod leges introduxerunt aut Constitutiones, sed antiquam prudentiam iuris Auctorum, vt est in leg. 21. Cod. de furt. & consonam Iurisconsultorum definitionem in l. vlt. C. Theod. de diuerf. rescrip. qualis est regula Catoniana, quæ dicitur regula iuris antiqui, l. vlt. de regul. Caton. & argumento l. qui soluendo 42. de hared. instituend. l. 29. & pen. h. t. Cuiusmodi etiam est hæc, Ex delicto defuncti, hæres poenali actione non tenetur, quæ est hîc 38. & 44. & dicitur certissima regula §. non autem. Instit. de perpet. & tempor. act. Deterior nostra conditio per seruos fieri non potest. l. vlt. C. de adquir. possess. quæ antiqua est regula. l. 66. hic, sicut & iuri nouo opponitur in §. si vero, Instit. de satisdationib. In ambiguis contra vendentem respondendum est, l. in contrahenda. 172. hoc titul. & l. veteribus 39. de pactis. Omnibus iis, quæ pro se introducta sunt, potest renuntiari, l. 156. hîc, quæ dicitur regula Iuris antiqui, l. penult. C. de pact. Hæreditate non adita, soluitur omnis vis Testamenti.l.181.hic,quod tradit l.eam qua. 14.C.de fideicommiss. Hæres hæredis, hæres est testatoris,l.194.hic: quæ dicitur antiqua in leg. vlt.C.de hered.instituend. Seruum à domino & hæredem & liberum scriptum, ei necessarium hæredem esse.l.4.C.de necess.ser.hered.instit. Ea animalia quæ redire solent ad locum, tam diu nostra sunt, quamdiu reuertendi animum & consuetudinem habent.l.3.de acquir.rer.dom. Cuiac. in recitat. hic in fine. Pacius hic ante sin. Quia ergo iam constat, regulas iuris, quibus derogatum est iure nouo, nullas hoc titulo proponi: etiam hoc non omittendum, non omnes receptas regulas iuris antiqui hoc titulo contineri. Sunt enim omissæ plures. vt, Noxa caput sequitur : quæ non est in hoc titulo; est tamen regula iuris antiqui.L.1,in sin. de priuat.delict. Pacta contra bonos mores non valent, leg.vlt.C. de pact. Ius publicum priuatis pactionibus non infirmatur. l.ius publicum 38. ff.eod. Falsa demonstratione legatum non perimitur. §. huic. Instit.de legat. Per seruum hæreditas non acquiritur, l.1.§.veteres.de acquir.possess. Petitori incumbit necessitas probandi. l.1.C.Theodos.de fide instrum. In exceptionibus reus probat. leg. cum de indebito.25.de probat. Ex pacto nudo non nascitur actio,l.8.de pactis. Facti ignorantia non nocet, iuris nocet. leg.1. de iur. & facti ignor. Quibus dominis legari potest, eorum etiam iam seruis potest. l. si mihi & tibi 12. §. regula. 2. de leg. 1. In rem suam auctor tutor esse non potest. l. 5. de auctor. tutorum. Libertas adimi non potest, si liber hæres scriptus sit, l. si ita scriptum 13. §. regula. de lib. & posthum. Furtum non committit, qui rem voluntate domini contrectat, l. si quis seruo 20. C. de furtis. Is, qui habet aduersus alios actionem furti, ea teneri non potest, l. apud antiquos 21. C. de furtis. Is tenetur petitione hæreditatis, qui pro hærede vel possessore possidet. l. regulariter. 9. de hæred. pet. Cuiac. in Recitationib. posthumis hic. §. 1. Cui adstipulatur Paci. hic circa principium.
units.tr: Of ancient law. By "ancient law" the title does not mean what has been abolished or repealed by newer law, nor what laws or constitutions have introduced, but the ancient prudence of the jurists' law, as in l. 21, Cod., de furtis, and the definition of the jurists agreeing with it in l. ult., C. Theod., de diversis rescriptis. Such is the rule of Cato, which is called a rule of ancient law, l. ult., de regulis Catonianis, and by inference l. qui solvendo 42, de heredibus instituendis, l. 29 and the last law of this title. Of this kind also is the following: an heir is not bound by a penal action on account of the deceased's wrongdoing. This is found here at 38 and 44, and it is called a most certain rule in §non autem, Institutes, de perpetuis et temporalibus actionibus. Our condition cannot be made worse through slaves. l. ult., C. de acquirenda possessione, which is an ancient rule. l. 66 here, and it is set against newer law in §si vero, Institutes, de satisdationibus. In ambiguous matters the response must be given against the seller, l. in contrahenda 172, this title, and l. veteribus 39, de pactis. Anything introduced for someone's benefit may be renounced, l. 156 here, which is called a rule of ancient law, l. penult., C. de pactis. When an inheritance has not been entered upon, all force of a will is dissolved. l. 181 here, which l. eam quae 14, C. de fideicommissis lays down. An heir of an heir is the heir of the testator, l. 194 here, which is called ancient in l. ult., C. de heredibus instituendis. If a slave is written by his master as both heir and free, he must be a necessary heir to him. l. 4, C. de necessario herede instituendo. Those animals which are accustomed to return to a place remain ours for as long as they keep the intention and habit of returning. l. 3, de acquirendo rerum dominio. Cujas, in the Recitations, here at the end. Pacius here before the end. Since it is now clear that rules of law which have been overturned by newer law are not set out under this title, it must also not be overlooked that not all accepted rules of ancient law are contained in this title. For many have been omitted, for example: "The noxal liability follows the person." This is not in this title, yet it is a rule of ancient law. l. 1, at the end, de privatis delictis. Pacts against good morals are not valid. l. ult., C. de pactis. Public law is not weakened by private agreements. l. ius publicum 38, ff. eodem. A legacy is not destroyed by a false demonstration. §huic, Institutes, de legatis. An inheritance is not acquired through a slave. l. 1, §veteres, de acquirenda possessione. The necessity of proof lies upon the claimant. l. 1, C. Theod., de fide instrumentorum. In exceptions the defendant proves. l. cum de indebito 25, de probationibus. No action arises from a bare pact. l. 8, de pactis. Ignorance of fact does not harm, ignorance of law does. l. 1, de iuris et facti ignorantia. A legacy may be made to slaves of those to whom it may be made as masters. l. si mihi et tibi 12, §regula 2, de legatis 1. No one can be guardian or tutor in his own affair. l. 5, de auctoribus tutorum. Freedom cannot be taken away if a free man is written as heir. l. si ita scriptum 13, §regula, de liberis et posthumis. One who handles a thing with the owner's consent does not commit theft. l. si quis servo 20, C. de furtis. One who has an action of theft against others cannot be bound by it. l. apud antiquos 21, C. de furtis. One is bound by the petition for inheritance who possesses as heir or possessor. l. regulariter 9, de petitione hereditatis. Cujas, in the posthumous Recitations here, §1. Pacius here near the beginning agrees with this.

units.tr: On law 1, beginning "Regula."

units.la: REgula est, quæ rem, quæ est, breuiter enarrat. non ex regula ius sumatur, sed ex iure quod est regula fiat. Per regulam igitur breuis rerum narratio traditur: &, vt ait Sabinus, quasi causæ coniectio est; quæ simul cum in aliquo vitiata est, perdit officium suum.
units.tr: A rule is that which briefly sets out the matter as it stands. Law is not to be drawn from a rule; rather, the rule is made from the law that exists. Through a rule, then, a brief account of things is handed down, and, as Sabinus says, it is a kind of summary of the case. Once it is faulty in any respect, it loses its function.

units.la: Rem quæ est ] id est, ius quod in ipsa re controuersa sequi oportet: vel causam generalem, qua moti sunt prudentes. Nam regulæ de facto non respondent, sed de iure, vt infra Goth. h.
units.tr: The matter as it stands means the law that must be followed in the very matter in dispute, or the general reason by which the jurists were moved. For rules answer not to fact but to law, as below, Gothofredus here.

units.la: Breuiter ] id est generaliter: idque ex iure in variis partibus iuris constituto ac recepto (Dytus ad cap. 1. in sexto eo.) & plurium legum consensione, Hotom. ibi ita ut nihil sit superfluum, nec tamen obscuritas inducatur: Id si contingat, breuitas est laudanda v. l. 37. C. de donat. etiamsi difficile sit regulas ita componere, ut omnino absolutae sint ac perfectae. l. 202. ƒ eod. Est igitur regulae proprium, non ut semper significnum habeat vniuersale affirmatiuum, vel negatiuum, aut indefinitum, ut Dynus putat, sed ut breuiter primaria consilia, primariam rationem iuris controuersi decidendi praebeat. Exempla huius breuitatis varia extant in hoc titulo. Gothofred. in notis hic lit. g.
units.tr: Briefly means generally, and this drawn from law established and received in various parts of the law, and from the agreement of several laws (Dynus on chapter 1 in sexto, de eo; Hotomanus there), so that nothing is superfluous and yet no obscurity is introduced. If this happens, brevity is to be praised (see law 37, C. de donationibus), even though it is difficult to frame rules so that they are wholly complete and perfect (law 202, § eod.). It is therefore the nature of a rule not that it always has a universal affirmative, negative or indefinite form, as Dynus thinks, but that it briefly supplies the primary counsels and the primary reasoning for deciding the disputed law. Examples of this brevity occur in many places in this title. Gothofredus in his notes here, letter g.

units.la: Non ex ] Non ut ex, Pacius legendum esse dicit, & Gothof. h.
units.tr: Not from should, according to Pacius, be read as not as from, and so Gothofredus, on this passage.

units.la: Non ut ex ] Ius antiquius est regula, cum ex eo regula nascatur. Ius, ipsa est aequitatis materia: regula est eius quasi forma, & adaptatio: sicut aliud aedificium, aliud architectonice. ex aedibus immediate habitatio percipitur, mediate ex ipso artificio: ita dici quoque potest, ex regula ius sumi. Gothofred. hic lit. i. Quod sine exemplo haud facile potest intelligi. Regula est: Inuito beneficium non datur; Libertas est beneficium. An ergo non dabitur inuito? Sic sane, si videl. ex illa regula ius sumatur. Et tamen constat, dari inuito. l. vlt. C. de manum. testam. Non est igitur ius sumendum ex regula, sed videndum ex quo iure sumpta sit. Inscriptio autem hic indicat, ad assignationem libertorum bertorum pertinere eam legem. Item regula est, Deteriorem conditionem nostram per seruos fieri non posse l. melior. 133. cod. paciscendo scilicet, vel iusiurandum deferendo. Atqui delinquendo potest; quia dominus seruum noxæ dedere cogitur, l. 1. §. quod igitur. de vi & vi arm. Ergo ex illa regula ius non est sumendum, sed ex quo iure (proximo scilicet immediate) regula sumta sit, videndum, & ad illud ius solum referenda est. Ius enim prius regula, sicut sermo prior est regula, & studio loquendi. Proinde regulæ iuris, quæ in hac disciplina interuenerunt, ius non constituunt, sed ad suum ius referendæ sunt. Itaque leuia sunt argumenta, quæ deducuntur ex regula iuris, & perniciosa: Deniq; ex his non est facile argumentandum. Cuiac. in recitat. posthum. ad hanc l. 1. in sin.
units.tr: Not as from: law is older than the rule, since the rule arises out of it. Law is the very matter of equity; the rule is, as it were, its form and adaptation, just as one thing is the building and another the architecture: from the house we perceive the dwelling immediately, and from the craft itself only mediately. So it may also be said that a rule is drawn from law. Gothofredus here, letter i. This can hardly be grasped without an example. The rule is: a benefit is not conferred on one who is unwilling; liberty is a benefit. Is liberty then not conferred on the unwilling? Certainly it is, if indeed the law were drawn from that rule. Yet it is established that it is conferred on the unwilling (law last, C. de manumissis testamento). Therefore the law is not to be drawn from the rule, but one must see from what law the rule was taken. The heading here indicates that this law concerns the assignment of freedmen. Again, the rule is: our condition cannot be made worse through our slaves (law "melior," 133, cod.), namely by making a pact or by deferring an oath. Yet a condition can be made worse through a slave's wrongdoing, since the master is compelled to surrender the slave for noxal action (law 1, § quod igitur, de vi et vi armata). Therefore the law is not to be drawn from that rule, but one must see from which law (namely the nearest one immediately) the rule was taken, and it must be referred to that law alone. For law is prior to the rule, just as speech is prior to the rule of speaking and to the study of it. Accordingly, the rules of law that have arisen in this discipline do not establish law but must be referred back to their own law. Hence arguments deduced from a rule of law are weak, and dangerous; in short, one should not argue easily from them. Cuiacius in his posthumous Recitations on this law 1, at the end.

units.la: Sed ex iure ] Id est regula, nisi ius aliquod præiacens habeat, regula esse non potest. Ius autem illud est vel strictum, vel æquum ac bonum. Æqui obiecta sunt, honestum, natura, utile. Vtile vero aliquid sæpius est fictione, repræsentatione (sic dolus possessionem, rem, conditionem, factum: culpa rem: factum seu persona, factum aliud, rem aliam, alia persona, repræsentat) præsumptione, coniectura seu interpretatione, non captiosa nimirum, sed ciuili. Hinc interpretatio sumitur ex natura rerum ipsarum, puta genere, specie, toto, partibus, tibus, ab eo quod plus est, & minus, principali, accessorio, priuatione, habitu, signis, verbis, & mente, id est obscuro, seu ambiguo; quo in genere praesumtio sumitur pro authore, pro eo quod verisimilius est, pro rei praesentis oportunitate, pro consuetudine, pro eo quod est benignius, vel fauorabilius; idque maxime cum agitur de libertate, dote, Testamento, iudiciis, contractibus, poenis, lucro, onere, maiori parte, inter fiscum, & priuatos, de tacito & expresso, vbi agitur de actus conseruatione, de coniunctis & disiunctis, de odio & fauore, de duobus malis, de initio vtili, vel inu-tili, de iure nouo. Gothofr. hic lit. a ex Iohan. Ramo.
units.tr: But from law: that is, a rule cannot exist unless it has some underlying law. That law is either strict or equitable and good. The objects of equity are the honourable, the natural and the useful. The useful is often effected by fiction, by representation (thus fraud represents possession, a thing, a condition or an act; fault represents a thing, an act or a person, another act, another thing, another person), by presumption, by conjecture or by interpretation, not of a captious kind but a civil one. Hence interpretation is drawn from the nature of things themselves: from genus, species, whole and parts; from what is more and what is less; from principal and accessory; from privation and possession; from signs, words and intention; that is, from what is obscure or ambiguous. In this category presumption is taken from the author; from what is more probable; from the convenience of the present matter; from custom; from what is more kindly or favourable. This applies especially when liberty, dowry, testament, judgments, contracts, penalties, gain, burden, the greater part is at issue, or disputes between the fisc and private persons, the tacit and the express, the preservation of an act, the conjoined and the disjoined, hatred and favour, two evils, an initial act that is useful or useless, and new law. Gothofredus here, letter a, from Johannes Ramus.

units.la: Quod est] Ne dicas negotij, sed (quia rei vocabulum latissime patet) iuris.
units.tr: Which is: do not say "of the business," but (since the word "thing" extends very widely) "of the law."

units.la: Rerum] quae iure constitutae sunt. Paci. hic.
units.tr: Of things: those which are constituted by law. Pacius here.

units.la: Narratio] Haec erat breuis explicatio caulae, ac veluti summa comprehensio, quam actor in iudicio faciebat, antequam ad aduocatos, & ampliorem disceptationem deueniretur. Paci. hic.
units.tr: Narration: this was the brief explanation of the case, and, as it were, the summary comprehension that the plaintiff gave in court before the matter came to the advocates and a fuller dispute. Pacius here.

units.la: Conjectio] id est, iuris in breue coactio, quod fit a litigantibus, qui per indicem iudici litem exponunt. Cuiac. in Recitat. hic. Nam causam coniicere, est argumentum rei breuiter & summatim iudici exponere. Cic. ad Heren. lib. 2. Gell. lib. 17. c. 5. & lib. 5. c. 10. & Asconius Ped.
units.tr: Conjecture: that is, a compressing of law into brief form, which is done by the litigants who set out the suit before the judge through a summary. Cuiacius in his Recitations here. For to "conjecture a case" is to state the argument of the matter briefly and summarily to the judge. Cicero, Ad Herennium, book 2; Gellius, book 17, chapter 5, and book 5, chapter 10; and Asconius Pedianus on the Verrines.

units.la: Verr. Vt igitur coniectio, causæ summam continet: ita regulæ earum rerum, quæ iure constitutæ sunt, breuiaria atque summas complectuntur. Paci.hic. Alias vulgata lecto habet coniunctio, sed male. Est enim metaphora sumpta ab oratoribus, qui vel in principio cbirer summam totius causæ coniiciunt, vt attentiorem faciant auditorem, vel in fine, vt cum memorem dimittant. Iohannes Ramus. Est igitur ea legis huius sententia; quod est causæ coniectio inter Rhetores, id regula est inter Iurisconsultos. Illa, iura omnia litigatorum in summam aliquam contrahit, hæc (vt sic loquamur) succum elicit, & (vt Alchymistæ loquuntur) quintam essentiam exprimit. Hæc Hotom. 2. obseru. 3. Coniectio igitur vocatur; quia ex regula æquum coniicitur, non aliter quam ex signis factum.
units.tr: Verrines. Thus, just as a conjecture contains the summary of a case, so rules embrace the brief summaries of those things that are established by law. Pacius here. Other editions read coniunctio (conjunction), but wrongly. The word is a metaphor taken from orators, who either at the beginning set out the summary of the whole case, to make the hearer more attentive, or at the end, so that they may send him away mindful of it. Johannes Ramus. The meaning of this law is therefore this: what the conjecture of a case is among the rhetoricians, that the rule is among the jurisconsults. The one gathers all the rights of litigants into some summary; the other, so to speak, draws out the juice and, as the alchemists say, expresses the quintessence. Hotomanus, Observations 2, chapter 3. It is called a conjecture because the equitable is conjectured from a rule, no differently than the fact is conjectured from signs.

units.la: puta, quia male & perperam est cōcepta, non quia exceptiones habet. Nec enim exceptio vitiosum quid continet, sed quid potius secretum, aut remotum à regula, quam exceptio declarat, & in ea declaranda officium suum facit. Hotom. ibid.
units.tr: For example, because it is badly and wrongly conceived, not because it has exceptions. An exception does not contain anything faulty; it sets out something rather separated from or remote from the rule, which the exception declares, and in declaring it performs its function. Hotomanus, ibid.

units.la: vt in fabrica, si praua est regula prima, omnia mendose fieri, atque obstipa necesse est. Lucretius: Hotom. ibid. Perdit igitur officium suum, atque energiam, qua rem, quæ est, enarrat, siue eius enarratione rem ( hoc est, substantiam rei, de qua quæritur) perstringit. Deinde regulariter enarrandi ossicium præstat. Irrita enim fit sæpissime regula ob diuersitatem circumstantiarum, vt elegantER Iauolenus in l. omnis definitio. cod. docet. quæ lex regulam vocat definitionem. Omnis ergo regula lubrica est, non certa, non perpetua, quia facile subuertitur. Ius quidem est, lata significatione; nam scientia procedit ex necessariis. Iuris definitio nulla est perpetua. Accursius tamen in dicta l. omnis. quasdam exceptiones ponit, quas referit esse certas, vt impuberem Testamentum facere non posse: ast ea subuertitur: si impuberes, tribuni militum fuerint, l. vlt. C. de Testam. milit. Item, si viram cœlibem elegerint, constitutione Constantini, quæ est apud Sozomenum. Aliud. Liberum hominem non posse vsucapi: subuertitur, si vxor sit; & ante anni finem tres noctes à marito non abfuerit. Nam vsucapietur. Caeterarum regularum, quas affert Accurs. non est melior conditio. Denique omnis regula iuris cum periculo enuntiatur: modica enim obiectione aut circumstantia destruitur: qua de causa modeste enuntiare quidam solent; mihi videtur, plerumque, fere. Imperiti longe aliter: nam omnia temere affirmant. Cuiac. in Recitat. posth. hic circ. med.
units.tr: As in building: if the first rule is crooked, everything made by it must necessarily be faulty and askew. Lucretius; Hotomanus, ibid. A rule therefore loses its function and its energy, by which it narrates the matter as it stands, or by its narration it touches the matter itself (that is, the substance of the thing in question), and in general it fails to perform the office of narrating. For a rule is very often rendered void by the diversity of circumstances, as Javolenus teaches elegantly in law "omnis definitio," C. This law calls the rule a definition. Every rule is therefore slippery, not certain, not perpetual, because it is easily overturned. Law, in the broad sense, is indeed a science, for science proceeds from necessary things; but no definition of law is perpetual. Accursius, however, in the said law "omnis," sets down certain exceptions, which he reports as settled: for instance, that a minor under puberty cannot make a testament. Yet this is overturned if the under-age persons were military tribunes (law last, C. de testamento militis). Likewise, if they chose a celibate woman, by a constitution of Constantine found in Sozomen. Another: a free man cannot be acquired by usucapion. This is overturned if he is a wife, and if she has not been absent from her husband for three nights before the end of the year, for then she will be acquired by usucapion. The other rules that Accursius brings forward are no better. Finally, every rule of law is stated at risk, for it is destroyed by the slightest objection or circumstance. For this reason some people are accustomed to speak modestly: "it seems to me, for the most part, nearly." The unskilled do quite otherwise, for they affirm everything rashly.

units.la: Ad leg. 2. De fæminis. 1. De impubere.
units.tr: On the Law 2, Concerning Women, 1, Concerning the Impubes.

units.la: FOeminæ ab omnibus officiis ciuilibus vel publicis remotæ sunt: & ideo nec iudices esse possunt, nec magistratum gerere, nec postulare, nec pro alio interuenire, nec procuratores existere. Item impubes omnibus officiis ciuilibus debet abstinere.
units.tr: Women are excluded from all civil and public offices, and so they cannot be judges, hold a magistracy, bring a suit, intervene for another, or act as procurators. Likewise, a minor who has not reached puberty must abstain from all civil offices.

units.la: Officiis ] id est functionibus. Fœminæ enim neque publicis neque ciuilibus officiis fungi possunt: & sic est receptum moribus. l. cum prætor. 12. §. vlt. de iudiciis. l. 1. ad SC. Vell. Officiorum autem vel publicorum vel ciuilium significatio latissime patet. Nam & ad munera pertinet, veluti iudicandi potestatem, hoc est iudicis munus. l. vltim. §. iudicandi. de muner. & honor. Et ad honores reip. velut magistratus, operas, & ministeria omnia Reip. utilia, vt officia argentariorum vel numulariorum. leg. argentarius §. 1. de edendo. Cuiac. in recitat. hic in princ.
units.tr: Officiis] that is, functions. For women can perform neither public nor civil offices, and this has been accepted by custom. l. cum prætor. 12. §. vlt. de iudiciis. l. 1. ad SC. Vell. The meaning of public or civil offices, however, extends very widely. For it covers also duties, such as the power of judging, that is, the duty of a judge. l. vltim. §. iudicandi. de muner. & honor. And it covers the honours of the commonwealth, such as the magistracies, and all the services and ministries useful to the commonwealth, such as the duties of bankers or money-changers. leg. argentarius §. 1. de edendo. Cuiac. in recitat. hic in princ.

units.la: Ciuilibus ] id est, virilibus, l. 1. §. 5. de postulando. l. 18. C. de procuratoribus. in quibus opera & ministerium requiritur. l. 12. §. 2. ff. de iudiciis. l. 1. §. 1. ff. ad Vell. l. 13. de vacat. muner. Goth. b.
units.tr: Ciuilibus] that is, manly, l. 1. §. 5. de postulando. l. 18. C. de procuratoribus. in which labour and service are required. l. 12. §. 2. ff. de iudiciis. l. 1. §. 1. ff. ad Vell. l. 13. de vacat. muner. Goth. b.

units.la: Publicis ] id est, honoribus & muneribus publicis, l. 6. ff. de cap. minutis. l. 78. de iudiciis. aut personalibus. l. 3. §. 3. ff. de muneribus. aut corporalibus, l. 18. ibi, tertio officium. de verb. signif. Aliud est in nudis dignitatibus. Nobilitatem enim vel a patre, vel a maritis, accipiunt. l. 8. de Senatoribus. Gothof. hic. Differentia ergo est inter publicum & ciuile officium, argum. tutelae, quae dicitur ciuile munus, in pr. l. vlt. de mun. & hon. & publicum munus. §. 1. Institut. de excusat. tut. Item postulandi officium tam ciuile, quā publicum dici potest, improprie tamen. Nam munus tam ciuile, quam publicum trifariam dicitur: proprie, improprie, non improprie; quae tria sunt diuersa, sicut doctus, indoctus, non indoctus. Munus Reip. veluti annonae subleuandae causa proprie est munus publicum: tutela, non improprie; postulandi, improprie: sicut argentaria, & procuratio, & arbitrium, quae officia non nisi volentes subeunt. Munera autem quae proprie & non improprie publica sunt, inuitis deferuntur, si non sit excusatio iusta. Verum ab officiis etiam voluntariis foeminae remouentur, quia remouentur ab omnibus, & cuiuscunque generis, officiis publicis, vel ciuilibus: quod scilicet fas non sit, eas in publicum procurrere, & contra pudicitiam generis muliebris se alienis negotiis immiscere. Sic licet mas domo ab apparitoribus extrahi possit; mulier tamen non potest educi, l. 1. C. de offic. diuers. ind. cum proprium sit mulieris in domo se continere.
units.tr: Publicis] that is, public honours and duties, l. 6. ff. de cap. minutis. l. 78. de iudiciis. whether personal, l. 3. §. 3. ff. de muneribus. or corporal, l. 18, where it says "thirdly, office", de verb. signif. It is different with mere dignities, for they receive their nobility either from their father or from their husbands. l. 8. de Senatoribus. Gothof. hic. There is therefore a difference between a public and a civil office, by argument from guardianship, which is called a civil duty, in pr. l. vlt. de mun. & hon., and a public duty, §. 1. Institut. de excusat. tut. Likewise the office of pleading can be called civil as well as public, though improperly. For a duty, whether civil or public, is said in three ways: properly, improperly, and not improperly; and these three are different, just as learned, unlearned, and not unlearned are different. A duty of the commonwealth, such as the relief of the grain supply, is properly a public duty; guardianship is not improperly so; pleading is improperly so; just as banking, procuratorship, and arbitration are, which offices are undertaken only by those who are willing. Those duties, however, which are properly and not improperly public are imposed on the unwilling, unless there is a just excuse. But women are removed even from voluntary offices, because they are removed from all public or civil offices of every kind; for it is evidently not right for them to rush forward into public life and mix themselves in other people's affairs, contrary to the modesty of the female sex. Thus a man may be dragged from his house by the officers, but a woman cannot be led out, l. 1. C. de offic. diuers. ind., since it is the proper task of a woman to keep herself within the house.

units.la: Huius autem remotionis duplex est causa. Vna leuitas, mobilitas, & infirmitas sexus: & plerumque ipsos homines mobiles faciunt; modo placent, modo displicent. In leg. 3. C. Theodos. de raptu virginum, est elegans locus, quem notat Græcus Interpres apud Harmenopulum, dum ait, Iudicium earum esse fragile & captioni expositum. Altera ratio est: quia officium mulierum est domum curare, & liberos. l. quæritur 14. §. 1. de adilit. edict. vbi ait, eas non posse saluo pudore in publicum procedere, foro, concionibus, vel consiliis interesse: qua de causa etiam olim arrogare non poterant. Vlp. tit. 12. Gell. lib. 4. c. 10. Hodie secus: quia non fit in comitiis. l. Nam & fœmina. de Adoptionib. Cuiac. in Recitat. hic.
units.tr: There are two causes of this removal. One is the lightness, fickleness, and weakness of the sex, which often make women themselves fickle: they are pleased one moment and displeased the next. In leg. 3. C. Theodos. de raptu virginum there is an elegant passage, which the Greek interpreter cited by Harmenopulus notes, when he says that their judgement is fragile and open to deception. The other reason is that the duty of women is to care for the household and the children. l. quæritur 14. §. 1. de adilit. edict. where it says that they cannot, without loss of modesty, come forward into public, appear at the forum, the assemblies, or councils; for this reason they could not even adopt in former times. Ulp. tit. 12. Gell. lib. 4. c. 10. Today it is otherwise, because adoption does not take place in the assemblies. l. Nam & fœmina. de Adoptionib. Cuiac. in Recitat. hic.

units.la: Remota sunt ] Non quia non habent iudicium, sed ipso sexu d. §. 3. & l. 1. §. 5. de postlando; iure Romano præsertim & moribus l. 12. §. 2. de indiciis. l. 1. §. 1. ad Velleianum; remouentur. Gothof. hic.
units.tr: Remota sunt] Not because they lack judgement, but by reason of their sex itself, d. §. 3. & l. 1. §. 5. de postulando; they are removed, especially by Roman law and custom, l. 12. §. 2. de iudiciis. l. 1. §. 1. ad Velleianum. Gothof. hic.

units.la: Iudices ] quia est publicum officium. l. 12. §. 2. de iudiciis. l. 18. §. 14. de muneribus. Hodie usu & consuetudine, statuto, Principis priuilegio, hereditaria iurisdictione mulier fungi potest. Decius hic. Econtrario quædam causæ esse possunt, vt masculus à iudicando aliquando excusetur. l. 13. de vacatione mun.
units.tr: Iudices] because it is a public office. l. 12. §. 2. de iudiciis. l. 18. §. 14. de muneribus. Today, by usage and custom, by statute, by the privilege of the Prince, or by hereditary jurisdiction, a woman may hold the office of judge. Decius hic. On the other hand, there may be certain causes by which a man is sometimes excused from judging. l. 13. de vacatione mun.

units.la: Magistratum ] quia est publicus honor, non munus : adde leg. 4. §. 2. de officio proconsul.
units.tr: Magistratum] because it is a public honour, not a duty; add leg. 4. §. 2. de officio proconsul.

units.la: Postulare ] cui edicto Calphurnia causam dedit, vt legitur Florentiae in l. 1. §. sexum. de postulan. Sicut Gaia Afrania apud Sueton. Cuiac. in Recitat. posthum. hic.
units.tr: Postulare] the edict of Calphurnia gave occasion for this, as is read at Florence in l. 1. §. sexum. de postulan. Like Gaia Afrania, mentioned by Suetonius. Cuiac. in Recitat. posthum. hic.

units.la: Interuenire ] id est, fideiubere, constituere, compromittere. quod est Senatusconsulto Velleiano comprehensum l. 2. ad SC. Vell. Cuiac. hic.
units.tr: Interuenire] that is, to act as surety, to make a contract, or to submit to arbitration; this is covered by the Senatusconsultum Velleianum. l. 2. ad SC. Vell. Cuiac. hic.

units.la: Procuratores ] l. alienum 18. C. de procuratoribus. Sed haec regula non est prorsus generaliter vera : ergo periculosa. Nam sunt quae competant mulieribus, l. pen. (. de his qui num. lib. excusat. merentur; lib. 10. & licet pro alio postulare non possint: alii tamen petere bonorum possessionem impune possunt. l. seruus 7. de bonor. possessionib. quae omnino huic legi secundae est coniungenda. Foeminarum testimonia in plerisque causis hodie admittuntur, l. qui Testam. 20. de his qui Testamen. fac. poss. Item, foeminae pro parentibus procuratrices esse possunt. l. foeminas 41. de Procuratorib. Adiicit hic Placentinus : id multo fortius esse in filiis; quod Accursius negat, quia iis tutorem debeant petere, tum quidem si filii sint impuberes. Sed si non egeant tutore vel curatore, cur non mater praestabit filiis operam? Nam & olim foeminae filiorum tutelam facile impetrabant a Principe. l. vlt. de tut. Hodie ipso iure
units.tr: Procuratores] l. alienum 18. C. de procuratoribus. But this rule is not wholly true in general, and so it is risky. For there are things that belong to women, l. pen. (. de his qui num. lib. excusat. merentur; lib. 10; and although they cannot plead on behalf of another, they may still seek possession of goods without penalty. l. seruus 7. de bonor. possessionib. which must be joined entirely to this second law. Women's testimony is admitted today in most cases, l. qui Testam. 20. de his qui Testamen. fac. poss. Likewise, women can act as procurators for their parents. l. foeminas 41. de Procuratorib. Placentinus adds here that this holds much more strongly for children, which Accursius denies, because they must ask for a guardian, at least if the children are below puberty. But if they do not need a guardian or curator, why should the mother not render her children this service? For in former times women also readily obtained the guardianship of their children from the Prince. l. vlt. de tut. Today, by the law itself,

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters] sunt tutrices filiorum, nepotumve, si sint expertes secundarum Nuptiarum: quia de re multae sunt Novellae Constitutiones tot. tit. Cod. quando mul. tut. off. fung. Sed quae iterum nupserunt, non gerunt tutelam filiorum. Similiter impuberes non semper removentur ab officiis publicis. Nam honores militares gerere possunt. l. ult. C. de Testam. militar. sicut & hodie fit. Ergo & in iis, quae exposui, regula vitiatur, quae ex iis, quae ut plurimum eveniunt, facta est. Non autem ad omnia existimandum dirigi regulam. Fieri enim non potest, ut rerum humanarum constituatur regula certa. Vulgo existimatur huc pertinere quod tradit l. in multis. de statu homin. Sed detracta mentione publici officii potest commode sumi exemplum ex l. 15. §. liberti. 8. de excusat. tut. Libertus, qui patrono suo senatorio procurat negotia, excusationem habet; secus in patrona. Ergo in hoc deterior est conditio mulieris. Cuiac. in recitat. h. in sin.
units.tr: [illegible] are guardians of their children or grandchildren, if they are free from second marriages; on this matter there are many Novel Constitutions, tot. tit. Cod. quando mul. tut. off. fung. But women who have married again do not hold the guardianship of their children. Similarly, minors are not always removed from public offices. For they can hold military honours, l. ult. C. de Testam. militar. as is also done today. Therefore the rule is also undermined in the cases I have set out, a rule which was made from what happens for the most part. But the rule cannot be thought to apply to everything, for a certain rule cannot be laid down for human affairs. It is commonly thought that what l. in multis. de statu homin. teaches belongs here; but, with mention of public office set aside, a suitable example can be taken from l. 15. §. liberti. 8. de excusat. tut. A freedman who manages the affairs of his patron, a senator, has an excuse; it is otherwise for a freedwoman. Therefore in this matter the condition of a woman is worse. Cuiac. in recitat. h. in sin.

units.la: Lex 3. Non nolle. Velle.
units.tr: Law 3. Not to be unwilling. To be willing.

units.la: EIus est non nolle, qui potest velle.
units.tr: It is the mark of one who can will that he does not refuse.

units.la: Eius ] Coniunge l. 4. de acq. hered. ex qua potest cognosci vera lectio. Pacius hic.
units.tr: Eius] Join this with law 4, de acquirenda hereditate, from which the true reading can be known. Pacius here.

units.la: Non nolle ] Eius est nolle, vulgata lectio. Hugo à Porta. Eius est non velle: quam lectionem defendit Cuiacius 6. obs. 39. & 15. obs. 23. reprehensus à Roberto 2. recept. 26. & 1. animadnimaduer. 30. defensus ab Antonio Mercatore 1. Notat. 30. Velle autem proprie dicitur, qui sciens l. 1. §. 3. ff. de tribut. nec coactus l. 4. J eod. iubet, mandat, & imperat, aut expressim approbat. Nolle dicitur, qui sciens nec coactus, expressim vel palam vetat, aut refragatur. Non nolle is videtur, qui tacite approbat, qui sciens patitur, nec expressim fieri iubet; estque inter velle & nolle medium. Quod medium non est velle, quia palam non iubet: non est nolle; quia non refragatur, sed tamen probat. Non velle, non est expressim refragari, sed factum tacite reprobare. Non est velle, quia non iubet. Non est nolle, quia palam non vetat. Non nolle, non est iubere, sed approbando pati: (vel tacere ac pati. Cuiac. in recit. h. t. ad l. 4. in sin.) Non velle, non est vetare, sed tamen reprobando pati. Velle igitur & nolle, est iussio & prohibitio expressa: nō nolle & nō velle, tacita. Huc res redit, Velle potes? potes ergo nolle, vt hic, secundū vulgatam: potes etiam non velle, secundum Haloandrum, & Graecos, & non nolle secundum Florentinam. Econtrario non potes cum effectu velle? non videris ergo nolle, l. 4. ff. de acquir. hared. huc adde l. 37. J eodem. Nolle non dicimur; quoties velle contrarium vtiliter non possumus. l. 101. de condit. & demonstrat. Nolle dicimur, cum contrarium possumus l. 17. §. 7. de adil. edict. Gothof. hic adde omnino Cuia. in recit. h. tit. ad l. 4. circ. sin. Non dicitur noluisse, qui errans facit, nec corrigit factum, cum potest; sed dicitur non voluisse quia errans facit. At noluisse dicitur, qui errans facit, & corrigit factum. Cuiac. ibid. quia scilicet cum poenitet facti ex errore admissi. Cuia. 5. obs. 39. in pr. Tandem haec lex pertinet ad adquisitionem hereditatis. Et sicuti, qui potest adire hereditatem, potest & nolle adire; quod proponitur in l. 3. h. tit. ita e contrario, quod proponitur in l. 4. de acquir. hered. qui non potest adire, non videtur adire nolle & repudiare. Accurs. scribit esse diversa in l. 16. & 18. de acquir. hared. nolle adire, & recusare. Male. Nam repudiare & recusare diversa sunt: Repudiatio fit solenniter in iure l. sicut. C. de repud. hared. Recusatio fit quoquo modo & quoquo iure. l. recusare 6. ad Trebell. l. recusari 95. de acquir. hared. Repudiat solus heres: recusat solus fideicommissarius l. cogi. 16. §. si quis heres ad Trebell. Praeterea filiusfam. aut seruus, nolle adire aut recusare potest l. filiusfam. de auro & argent. legat. l. 3. C. de hared. instituend. Repudiare autem non potest Hereditatem, & repudiando nihil agit l. 13. §. vlt. de acquir. hared. Et licet aliud sit, nolle adire, aliud repudiare: tamen de repudiatione, aditione, & recusatione, eaedem proponuntur regulae l. qui potest facere. 174. h. tit. quia qui potuit adire, potuit repudiare. l. 18. de acq. hared. quod maxime obtinet in iis, qui hæc suo nomine exsequuntur. Nam tutor, qui rem gerit pupilli nomine, non suo, infantis nomine hereditatem adire potest, repudiare non potest: cuius etiam pupilli, & qui maior est infante, nomine petere bonorum possessionem potest, repudiare non potest. Quia petere, tutori permissum est, non repudiare l. tutor. 8. de bonor. possess. Tutor potest administrate negotia pupilli, potest nouare, soluere, solutum accipere, transigere decidendi causa; spoliare, perdere, repudiare non potest. Nam ei tutela commissa est, non ius spoliandi datum. At in iis, qui suo nomine agunt, si quæratur, an possint repudiare: videndum est, an possint adire; si adire non possunt, nec repudiare poterunt. Exemplo est heres, qui sub conditione scriptus, ante conditionem non potest adire. Ergo nihil agit, si ante conditionem repudiet: cuius rei exempla proferri multa possunt ex tit. de acquir. hared. Cuia. h.
units.tr: Non nolle] The vulgate reading is "Eius est nolle" (it belongs to one who is unwilling). Hugo à Porta. "Eius est non velle" (it belongs to one who does not will) is the reading defended by Cuiacius, 6. obs. 39. and 15. obs. 23., though he is criticised by Robert, 2. recept. 26. and 1. animadv. 30., and defended by Antonius Mercator, 1. Notat. 30. A person is properly said to will when, knowingly and not under compulsion, he orders, commands or expressly approves, l. 1. §. 3. ff. de tribut. and l. 4. eod. A person is said to be unwilling when, knowingly and not under compulsion, he expressly or openly forbids or objects. A person is seen to be not unwilling when he tacitly approves, that is, when he knowingly allows a thing and does not order it expressly; and this lies between willing and being unwilling. It is not willing, because he does not openly order; it is not unwilling, because he does not object, but nonetheless he approves. Not willing is not to object expressly, but to disapprove tacitly. Not to be unwilling is not to order but to allow by approving (or to be silent and allow, Cuiac. in recit. h. t. on l. 4, at the end). Not to be willing is not to forbid, but still to allow while disapproving. To will and to be unwilling are therefore express command and express prohibition; not to be unwilling and not to be willing are tacit. The matter comes to this: can you will? If so, you can be unwilling, as here, according to the vulgate; you can also be not willing, according to Haloander and the Greeks, and not be unwilling according to the Florentine manuscript. Conversely, if you cannot will with effect, you do not seem to be unwilling, l. 4. ff. de acquir. hered.; add l. 37. eodem. We are not said to be unwilling whenever we cannot usefully will the contrary, l. 101. de condit. et demonstr. We are said to be unwilling when we can do the contrary, l. 17. §. 7. de aedil. edicto. Here add also Cuiacius, in recit. h. tit. on l. 4, near the end. A person is not said to have been unwilling if, acting in error, he does not correct what he did when he could; he is said not to have willed, because he acted in error. But a person is said to have been unwilling if, acting in error, he corrects what he did. Cuiac. ibid., namely because he regrets an act done through error. Cuiac. 5. obs. 39, at the beginning. Finally, this law concerns the acquisition of an inheritance. Just as one who can enter upon an inheritance can also be unwilling to enter, which is set out in l. 3. h. tit., so conversely, what is set out in l. 4. de acquir. hered.: one who cannot enter is not seen to be unwilling or to renounce. Accursius writes that in l. 16 and 18, de acquir. hered. to be unwilling to enter and to refuse are different things. He is wrong. For to renounce and to refuse are different: renunciation is made solemnly before the court, l. sicut C. de repud. hered.; refusal is made in any manner and by any right, l. recusare 6. ad Trebell., l. recusari 95. de acquir. hered. Only the heir renounces; only the fideicommissary refuses, l. cogi 16. §. si quis heres ad Trebell. Moreover, a son under power or a slave can be unwilling to enter or can refuse, l. filiusfam. de auro et argento legato; l. 3. C. de hered. instituendis. But one cannot renounce an inheritance, and by renouncing accomplishes nothing, l. 13. §. ult. de acquir. hered. And although being unwilling to enter is one thing and renouncing another, yet the same rules concerning renunciation, entry and refusal are laid down in l. qui potest, 174. h. tit., because one who could enter could also renounce, l. 18. de acquir. hered. This holds especially for those who carry out these acts in their own name. For a guardian who manages the affairs of a ward in the ward's name, not his own, can enter upon an inheritance for an infant but cannot renounce it; likewise, in the name of a ward, and of one who is older than an infant, he can ask for possession of the goods but cannot renounce it. For it is permitted to the guardian to seek, not to renounce, l. tutor 8. de bonor. possess. A guardian can administer the ward's affairs, can novate, pay, accept payment, settle a matter by agreement to end a dispute; but he cannot despoil, waste or renounce. For the guardianship was entrusted to him, not a right to despoil given. But with those who act in their own name, if it is asked whether they can renounce, one must see whether they can enter; if they cannot enter, neither can they renounce. An example is an heir who is instituted under a condition: before the condition is fulfilled he cannot enter, so if he renounces before the condition he accomplishes nothing. Many examples of this matter can be cited from the title de acquir. hered. Cuiac. h.

units.la: Lex 4.
units.tr: Law 4.

units.la: VELle non creditur, qui obsequitur imperio patris vel domini.
units.tr: He is not thought to be willing who obeys the command of his father or master.

units.la: Non creditur] imo creditur, l. 26. §. 8. in sin. de pignorib. l. 12. de sponsalib. l. 22. de ritu nuptiarum.
units.tr: Not "is not believed": rather, he is believed. See Dig. 26, §8 at the end, de pignoribus; Dig. 12, de sponsalibus; Dig. 22, de ritu nuptiarum.

units.la: Obsequitur] vide l. 4. C. de adulteriis. Eius qui obsequitur, an actus voluntarius, & spontaneus sit dicendus: an, & quomodo, voluntas coacta, voluntas dicatur, vide Decium hic. An iussus superioris excuseᴛ à delicto, v. l. 20. de oblig. An velle dicatur, qui cogitur, v. Caiacium 16. obs. vlt. adde l. 142. inf. eod.
units.tr: "Obeys": see l. 4. C. de adulteriis. Whether the act of one who obeys is to be called voluntary and spontaneous; whether and how a coerced will is called a will, see Decius here. Whether the order of a superior excuses from a delict, see l. 20. de oblig. Whether one who is compelled is said to will, see Caiacius 16. obs. vlt.; add l. 142. inf. eod.

units.la: Huius regulæ exemplum sumamus de seruis & filiisfamilias, qui sunt alieni iuris: nam ad eos hæc lex pertinet, & recte in libris Græcorum ponitur sub titulo de his, qui sunt sui vel alieni iuris. Seruus hereditatem Testamento delatam adire velle non videtur, quia suo arbitrio eam adire non potest, dum paret domini sui imperio, vel filiusfam. imperio patris, iubentis adire: nec enim seruus aliter adire potest, vt nec filius sine iussu patris. l. qui filio. 38. §. si quis seruum, de hered. instit. Denique adire velle seruus non videtur, qui adit imperio domini, l. 4. de acquir. hered. Itaque hic est vsus acquirendæ hereditatis, si seruus adierit iussu domini, expirat substitutio vulgaris, l. 3. in sin. de hered. instit. quia falsum est, eum inuitum tum adiisse & non adiisse: vt: ille seruus heres esto; si noluerit, Caius heres esto. Seruus coactus adiit Hereditatem iussu domini: si liber fuisset, non adiisset; sed vt Domino morem gereret, necesse habuit adire. Finita est substitutio vulgaris, quia non potest dici noluisse adire hereditatem, vt qui non videtur etiam voluisse.
units.tr: Let us take as an example of this rule slaves and children under power of the household, who are under another's authority. For this law applies to them, and it is rightly placed in the books of the Greeks under the title on those who are under their own or another's authority. A slave is not thought to be willing to enter upon an inheritance left to him by will, because he cannot enter upon it by his own choice, while he obeys the command of his master, or the son under power obeys the command of his father, who orders him to enter; for a slave cannot enter upon an inheritance otherwise than a son cannot without his father's order. l. qui filio. 38. §. si quis seruum, de hered. instit. Finally, a slave is not thought to be willing to enter who enters at his master's command, l. 4. de acquir. hered. Hence the use of this rule is this: if a slave enters at his master's command, the ordinary substitution lapses, l. 3. in sin. de hered. instit. because it is false that he both entered and did not enter against his will, as in: "let that slave be heir; if he refuses, let Gaius be heir." A slave compelled to enter upon the inheritance at his master's command would not have entered had he been free; but he had to enter in order to humour his master. The ordinary substitution is ended, because it cannot be said that he was unwilling to enter the inheritance, since he is not seen to have been willing either.

units.la: Respondeo : voluisse quis videtur dupliciter: si velit ultro & sua sponte, quæ voluntas est integra. Voluisse item videtur, si velit cogente Domino, quæ voluntas remissa est. Potest autem cogi seruus, vt adeat. l.1. §. quid ergo. si quis omiss. caus. test. l. Diuus §. & quatenus. ad L. Cornel. de fals. Hoc modo voluisse videtur seruus, qui adiit coactus, & heredem dominum facit, & substitutum excludit. l. si mulier 21. §. vlt. de eo, quod met. caus. l. si patre 22. de ritu N. Noluisse similiter duobus modis dicitur, & qui vltro noluit, & qui coactus. l. si seruus. 58. de adquir. hered. Sic igitur fit, vt diuersa quis ratione, & voluisse & noluisse dicatur. Nam seruus qui coactus adiit, & voluisse & noluisse videtur. Et quatenus dicitur voluisse, expirat substitutio vulgaris: quatenus noluisse: non expirat: nam vulgarem tam remissa voluntas, quam integra excludit. Quod si seruus non pareat iubenti domino, nec cogatur adire, non expirat substitutio vulgaris. l.3. de hered. inst. Cuiac. in Recitat. posthum. hic.
units.tr: I answer: one is seen to have been willing in two ways: if he is willing of his own accord and spontaneously, which is a whole will; and one is also seen to have been willing if he is willing under compulsion from his master, which is a diminished will. A slave, moreover, can be compelled to enter. l. 1. §. quid ergo. si quis omiss. caus. test. l. Diuus §. & quatenus. ad L. Cornel. de fals. In this way the slave who entered under compulsion, and makes his master heir and excludes the substitute, is seen to have been willing. l. si mulier 21. §. vlt. de eo, quod met. caus. l. si patre 22. de ritu N. In the same way one is said to have been unwilling in two ways: both he who was unwilling of his own accord and he who was unwilling under compulsion. l. si seruus. 58. de adquir. hered. Thus it comes about that one may be said both to have been willing and to have been unwilling, for different reasons. For a slave who entered under compulsion is seen both to have been willing and to have been unwilling. And insofar as he is said to have been willing, the ordinary substitution lapses; insofar as he is said to have been unwilling, it does not lapse, for a diminished will excludes the ordinary heir just as a whole will does. But if the slave does not obey his master's command and is not compelled to enter, the ordinary substitution does not lapse. l. 3. de hered. inst. Cuiac. in Recitat. posthum. hic.

units.la: Ad Leg.5. De furioso, & pupillo.
units.tr: On Law 5. On the madman and the ward.

units.la: IN negotiis contrahendis alia causa habita est furiosorum, alia eorum qui fari possunt, quamuis actum rei non intelligerent. Nam furiosus nullum negotium contrahere potest: pupillus omnia tutore auctore agere potest.
units.tr: In contracting business, one kind of case has been held for madmen and another for those who can speak, even though they do not understand the nature of the act. For a madman can make no contract at all; a ward can do everything with his guardian's authority.

units.la: Furiosus] vid. l. 1. §. 12. de obligat.
units.tr: The madman] see l. 1. §. 12. de obligat.

units.la: Pupillus] vid. l. 43. ff. eodem.
units.tr: The ward] see l. 43. ff. eodem.

units.la: Hæc lex etiam est ex tractatu de acquirenda Hereditate, vt patet ex inscriptione & coniunctione l. pupillus. 9. de acquir. hered. quæ ex eodem Pauli libro sumpta.
units.tr: This law also comes from the treatise on acquiring an inheritance, as is evident from its inscription and from its connection with l. pupillus 9 de acquir. hered., which is taken from the same book of Paul.

units.la: Est autem in adquirenda hereditate magna differentia inter furiosum & pupillum. Neuter quidem intelligit adquirendæ Hereditatis causam, vtrum deferatur ex Testamento, an ab intestato, agnationis, patronatus, peculii, an hereditatis iure; quod tamen requiritur in adquirenda hereditate, l. sciis. 22. de acquir. hered. Decernere etiam neuter potest, d. l. pupillus. 9. quod tamen requiritur. Inde nomen cretionis. Ad re hereditarem est suscipere, & quasi aditum in eam facere. l. filius. §. vlt. de lib. & posth. Cernere est decernere se heredem esse velle intra tempora deliberationis. l. is qui heres. 13. §. 1. de acquir. hered. & d. l. pupillus. Et antequam heres decernat de hereditate, adire non potest: (vulgus male legit discernere.) Vterque est actus legitimus: vterque fit pure tantum sine die & conditione, l. actus. 77. hoc tit. & semel tantum l. si solus. 80. §. vlt. de acquir. heredit. Et fit verbis conceptis. l. eum qui 51. §. vlt. eod. titul. Et per se, non per alium; nec per procuratorem adire vel adquirere potest. l. per procuratorem 90. de acquir. hered. Et fit testibus præsentibus Cic. ad Attic. lib. 10. Et vtriusque symbolum est digitorum percussio. Omnes fere actus legitimi olim habebant symbola quaedam: vt: Immissionis erat palmae datio, ductio, ictus, colaphus alternatiuus: attrectatio aurium in testium rogationibus, cognitionibus: aditionis, digitorum percussio. Hinc Cicero; digitis concrepuerunt. Et petere & adire bona dicitur. l. 1. C. de Testam. milit. Cuiac. in Recitat. posthum. hic in pr.
units.tr: In acquiring an inheritance, however, there is a great difference between a madman and a ward. Neither indeed understands the cause of entering upon the inheritance, whether it is deferred by will or on intestacy, by agnation, by patronage, by peculium, or by the right of inheritance; yet this is required in acquiring an inheritance. l. sciis. 22. de acquir. hered. Neither can make a decision either, d. l. pupillus 9. though this is required. Hence the name cretion. To take up the inheritance is to take it up and, as it were, make an approach into it. l. filius. §. vlt. de lib. & posth. To cern is to decide that one wishes to be heir within the time allowed for deliberation. l. is qui heres. 13. §. 1. de acquir. hered. & d. l. pupillus. And before the heir makes his decision about the inheritance, he cannot enter upon it (the common people wrongly read "discern"). Both acts are lawful; both are made purely, without a day or condition, l. actus. 77. hoc tit. and only once, l. si solus. 80. §. vlt. de acquir. heredit. and both are made in set words, l. eum qui 51. §. vlt. eod. titul. and in person, not through another; nor can one enter or acquire through a procurator, l. per procuratorem 90. de acquir. hered. and it is made with witnesses present, Cic. ad Attic. lib. 10. And the symbol of both is the snapping of the fingers. Almost all lawful acts formerly had certain symbols: for the taking of possession there was the giving of a palm, a leading, a blow, an alternating cuff; for the summoning and examining of witnesses, a tugging of the ears; for entering upon an inheritance, the snapping of the fingers. Hence Cicero: "they snapped their fingers." And to seek and to enter upon the goods is said. l. 1. C. de Testam. milit. Cuiac. in Recitat. posthum. hic in pr.

units.la: Quamuis actum rei non intelligerent] intelligant vulgar. lect. Neque pupillus, neque furiosus intelligit causam adeundae hereditatis: magna tamen cum differentia. Nam pupillo propter aetatem praestatur fauorabiliter, vt, si infans non sit, possit adire Hereditatem tutore autore, etiam honorario. d. l. pupillus. Nam aditio non est administrationis, sed animi & consilii potius, quam facti: & in adeunda hereditate honorarii tutoris autoritas sufficit. Furiosus autem nec curatore quidem autore adire potest hereditatem. Pupillo defertur hereditas, non furioso, etiamsi sit scriptus. l. r. §. furiosi. de success. edict. Per tutorem adquiri infanti hereditas potest, pupillo non potest, hoc est, maiori infanti, sed ei peti potest bonorum possessio. Furiosio non potest adquiri hereditas per procuratorem, nec peti bonorum possessio edictalis: datur tamen decretalis. l. 15. §. ult. vlt. de curat. furiof. dat. Generaliter autem, vt in l. f. proponitur, pupillus, qui excessit infantiam, omnia contrahere potest negotia tutore auctore; furiosus non potest. §. furiosus. Instit. de inutilib. stipulat. Est etiam differentia inter eos in acquirenda possessione: eam infans autore tutore acquirere potest. maior infante, etiam sine tutore autore potest: furiosus nullo modo potest. Vid Cuiac. ibid.
units.tr: "Although they did not understand the nature of the act": the common reading is "understand." Neither the ward nor the madman understands the cause of entering upon the inheritance, but with a great difference. For the ward, on account of his age, is favoured, so that, if he is not an infant, he can enter upon an inheritance with his tutor's authority, even that of an honorary tutor. d. l. pupillus. For entering is not an act of administration, but rather of mind and judgement rather than of deed; and in entering upon an inheritance the authority of an honorary tutor suffices. A madman, however, cannot enter upon an inheritance even with the authority of a curator. An inheritance is deferred to a ward, not to a madman, even if he is named as heir. l. 1. §. furiosi. de success. edict. An inheritance can be acquired for an infant through a tutor, but not for a ward, that is, a older infant; yet possession of goods can be sought for him. An inheritance cannot be acquired for a madman through a procurator, nor can possession of goods by edict be sought; yet possession by decree is given. l. 15. §. ult. vlt. de curat. furiof. dat. In general, however, as is set out in the law, a ward who has passed infancy can make all contracts with his tutor's authority; a madman cannot. §. furiosus. Instit. de inutilib. stipulat. There is also a difference between them in acquiring possession: an infant can acquire it with his tutor's authority; a greater infant can do so even without his tutor's authority; a madman cannot do so in any way. See Cuiac. ibid.

units.la: In negotiis contrahendis] Negotii contrahendi appellatione aditio hic comprehenditur. Nam qui adit hereditatem, contrahere videtur. Cuiac. d. loc. circ. med.
units.tr: "In contracting business": under the term of contracting business, entering upon an inheritance is included here. For he who enters upon an inheritance is seen to contract. Cuiac. d. loc. circ. med.

units.la: Lex 6. De eo qui ad alium vult transfer- re hereditatem.
units.tr: Lex 6. On the one who wishes to transfer an inheritance to another.

units.la: NON vult heres esse, qui ad alium transferre voluit hereditatem.
units.tr: He who has wished to transfer an inheritance to another does not wish to be heir.

units.la: Coniunge l. fuit quaest. de acquir. hered.
units.tr: Compare the law Fuit quaestionis, de acquirenda hereditate.

units.la: Heres esse] Ex testamento, vel ab intestato.
units.tr: To be heir] either by testament or from intestacy.

units.la: Voluit] id est, qui re ipsa transtulit, vel transferri passus est. l. 88. in sin. ff. de hered. instituen. Nam, velle, multis casibus cum effectu intelligendum est. Gothofr. hic.
units.tr: Wished] that is, he who has transferred it by the act itself, or has allowed it to be transferred. l. 88. in sin. ff. de hered. instituen. For to wish must in many cases be understood as having effect. Gothofr. hic.

units.la: Vt regulam hanc melius intelligamus, eam in hanc speciem redigamus. Scriptus heres omisit hereditatem, accepto a substituto suo, vel legitimo coherede, pretio, quaeritur an videatur pro herede se gerere? Et placet non videri. Nam quod agit pro contraria voluntate, monstrat, eum illud non videri capere iure hereditario, sed mortis causa. l. qui pretio. 8. de mort. caus. donationib. Veruntamen is qui ita omisit hereditatem, accepto pretio: tenebitur ex edicto, si quis omissa causa testamenti, legatariis, ut prior possessor, dum est ipse excutiendus. Denique non videtur pro herede se gerere, sed praetorio iure perinde exsequi tenetur voluntatem defuncti, ac si heres esset l. si duo 18. si quis omiss. caus. testam. Cuiac. in Recitat. posth. h.
units.tr: To understand this rule better, let us reduce it to this case. A instituted heir has let go of the inheritance, having taken a price from his substitute or from a co-heir at law, and the question is whether he is to be regarded as having acted as heir. The answer is that he is not so regarded. For what he does against his own will shows that he is not taken to hold the estate by hereditary right but as a gift in view of death. l. qui pretio. 8. de mort. caus. donationib. Nevertheless, the one who has thus let go of the inheritance for a price will be liable under the edict, if anyone, with the testamentary bequest left out, is to be sued by the legatees, as the prior possessor, while he himself is still to be pursued. In short, he is not regarded as having acted as heir, but by praetorian law he is bound to carry out the will of the deceased just as if he were heir. l. si duo 18. si quis omiss. caus. testam. Cuiac. in Recitat. posth. h.

units.la: Lex 7. De testato & intestato.
units.tr: Lex 7. On the testate and the intestate.

units.la: IVS nostrum non patitur, eundem in paganis & testato & intestato decessisse: earumque rerum naturaliter inter se pugna est, Testatus, & intestatus.
units.tr: Our law does not allow the same person to die in respect of pagan goods both testate and intestate; and between these two, testate and intestate, there is by nature a conflict.

units.la: Patitur ] Imo patitur l. 15. in sin. de inofficioso.
units.tr: Allows] Indeed it allows it. l. 15. in sin. de inofficioso.

units.la: Paganis ] rebus sc. paganis, id est non militis, secundum Gothof. hic. Quamuis Cuiac. in Recitat. posth. reprehendat Accursium, quod In paganis, id est, bonis paganis, acceperit. Nam, ait, de castrensibus bonis veterani non poterant pro parte testari, pro parte non, l. 13. in pr. de milit. testam. Intelligendum igitur de paganis hominibus, idque dicitur ad differentiam militum, qui possunt pro parte testari, & pro parte non. Imo si vnum heredem miles scripserit ex fundo, reliqua bona pertinent ad legitimum heredem l. 6. de Testam. milit. Et si miles duos heredes scripserit, vnum ex semisse & alterum ex semisse, primo repudiante, pars eius venit ad legitimum, nec accedit secundo. l. si duobus 37. de milit. Testam. atque ita ex parte habet testamentarium heredem, ex parte legitimum. Sicut etiam, si miles ex parte heredem instituerit, non prohibetur alium ex altera parte, & altero Testamento heredem facere l. quaerebatur 19. de milit. testam. Plane diuersum est in paganis. Nam si paganus aliquis vnum heredem scripserit ex certa parte: is heres erit ex asse. Causa enim Testamenti in paganis retrahit causam intestati: Item: si paganus duos heredes scripserit ex partibus, vno deficiente, altera pars eius adcrescit. Rursus si paganus duo Testamenta fecerit, prius tollitur posteriore. Nam sicut vnius dum viuit, non possunt esse duo patrimonia. l. Iurisperitos 39. §. 1. de excusat. tut. ita etiam mortui duae hereditates esse non possunt, vna testamentaria, altera regularis. Hereditas autem vicem defuncti sustinet. l. legatum 116. §. seruo, de legat. 1. Cuiac. in pr. huius R. in Recitat. posthum.
units.tr: Pagan] that is, with reference to things of a pagan, that is, of a non-soldier, according to Gothofredus here. Although Cuiacius in the posthumous Recitations criticises Accursius for having taken it as "in pagan things," that is, in pagan goods. For, he says, the goods of a veteran acquired as military property could not be bequeathed partly by will and partly not. l. 13. in pr. de milit. testam. It must therefore be understood of pagan persons, and this is said in contrast to soldiers, who can make a will for part and not for the rest. Indeed, if a soldier has instituted one heir to a farm, the remaining goods go to the heir at law. l. 6. de Testam. milit. And if a soldier has instituted two heirs, one to half and the other to half, and the first renounces, his share passes to the heir at law and does not accrue to the second. l. si duobus 37. de milit. Testam. Thus he has in part a testamentary heir and in part an heir at law. Likewise, if a soldier has instituted an heir for part, he is not prevented from appointing another heir to the other part, by another will. l. quaerebatur 19. de milit. testam. It is quite different with pagans. For if a pagan has instituted one heir to a certain part, that heir will be heir to the whole estate. For the testamentary cause in pagans draws back the cause of intestacy with it. Likewise, if a pagan has instituted two heirs to shares, and one fails, his share accrues to the other. Again, if a pagan has made two wills, the earlier is annulled by the later. For just as while one person is alive there cannot be two patrimonies, l. Iurisperitos 39. §. 1. de excusat. tut. so also a dead person cannot have two inheritances, one testamentary and the other by regular succession. But an inheritance takes the place of the deceased. l. legatum 116. §. seruo, de legat. 1. Cuiac. in pr. huius R. in Recitat. posthum.

units.la: Testato] v. l. 6. in sin. de Testam. milit. §. 5. Instit. de haered. instit. alias & testatum & intestatum hic legitur.
units.tr: Testato] See law 6, at the end, de testamento militis, and §5 of the Institutes, de heredibus instituendis. Elsewhere here one reads "testatum" and "intestatum".

units.la: Decessisse ] Decedimus pro parte intestati, si vniuersalis heres pro parte hereditatem potest repudiare, l. 1. l. 2. de acquir. hered. Item, si portio repudiantis heredis, reliquis scriptis heredibus non adcrescit. l. 63. de hered. instit. Ideoque, ne id fiat, ius adcrescendi introductum est. Quid si testator partes omisit? Idem ius erit, siquidem tacite vult eas scriptis adcrescere. Quid si voluit scriptos heredes adcrescendi iure uti? Hic Gothof. Dynum improbat, & alios, dicentes, nihilominus ius adcrescendi competere, cum id testator vetuerit. Nec probat Bartoli opinionem in l. 9. §. si duo. de hered. instit. tota rem ad causam intestati reduci. Neq; probat id quod Clarus ait 3. sentent. §. testamentum. quaest. 74. Testamentum corruere, cum actui, id est Testamento, sit faciendum, ut valeat. Placet ipsi media sententia, in partem non scriptam, heredes ab intestato ex praesumpta & collecta voluntate testatoris admitti, ne alioquin actus pereat. l. 12. ff. de reb. dub. Nam qui vetat scriptos heredes iure adcrescendi uti, tali prohibitione & Testamentarios confirmat heredes, & ad alias partes vacantes, heredes ab intestato satis expresse vocat, ut iam non ab intestato succedatur, sed ex Testamento. Idem dicendum, si mandauit distinctis & expressis verbis, ut partes non scriptorum heredum ad heredes ab intestato deferrentur: tunc enim huc successio non erit ab intestato, sed ex testamento. Statuto tamen aliud constitui poterit; quod notauit Decius in l. 27. num. 7. ĩ h. t. Gothofred. in notis hic & ad l. vlt. de iurisd.
units.tr: To die] A person dies in part intestate if a universal heir can renounce the inheritance for part. l. 1. l. 2. de acquir. hered. Likewise, if the share of a renouncing heir does not accrue to the other instituted heirs. l. 63. de hered. instit. Therefore, to prevent this, the right of accrual was introduced. What if the testator has left out shares? The same right will apply, since he tacitly wishes those shares to accrue to the instituted heirs. What if he has wished the instituted heirs to use the right of accrual? Here Gothofredus disapproves of Dynus and others, who say that the right of accrual nevertheless applies, since the testator has forbidden it. Nor does he approve the opinion of Bartolus in l. 9. §. si duo. de hered. instit. that the whole matter is reduced to the cause of intestacy. Nor does he approve what Clarus says, Sent. 3, §. testamentum, quaest. 74, that the will collapses, since the act, that is the will, must be made so that it may be valid.
