He himself prefers the middle opinion: that heirs at law are admitted to the part not written in, on the presumed and gathered will of the testator, lest otherwise the act should perish. l. 12. ff. de reb. dub. For he who forbids the instituted heirs to use the right of accrual, by such a prohibition both confirms the testamentary heirs and calls the heirs at law, quite expressly, to the vacant shares, so that the succession is no longer from intestacy but from the will. The same is to be said if he has commanded, in distinct and express words, that the shares of the non-written heirs be deferred to the heirs at law; for then this succession will not be from intestacy but from the testament. A statute, however, may establish otherwise, as Decius noted in l. 27. num. 7. in h. t. and Gothofredus in the notes here and on l. vlt. de iurisd.

units.la: Pugna ] Constitutiones tamen Principum hanc pugnam admittunt in milite, fictione quadam, duorum quasi hominum hereditatibus factis. l. si certarum 17. §. 1. de test. milit. l. duorum 49. de oper. libert. Venia enim datur imperitiæ militum, & ponunt hæ Constitutiones quasi duas personarum duarum hereditates. At si vnum fecit Testamentum castrense, alterum reliquorum bonorum, an possit inter heredes iudicium familiæ herciscundæ reddi? Minime: quia hic sunt duæ hereditates, Militaris & Pagana. Diuisio fit ipso iure: qua de causa si hereditas tantum constat in nominibus, cessat familiæ herciscundæ actio. Fit enim diuisio ex l. 12. tab. Quia igitur fit, quod duæ hereditates sint in bonis militum? Id constitutionibus est inductum fictione quadam. Recte autem l. C. in l. hereditates 19. §. 2. de castrens. pecul. ait: militem ab initio pro parte testatum, pro parte intestatum decedere posse. Ab initio: Nam per querelam inofficiosi Testamentum pro parte rescindi non potest. Itaque ex diuerso in pagano ita constitutum est, paganum Ab initio non posse pro parte testatum & pro parte intestatum decedere. Nam paganus per querelam inofficiosi Testamenti pro parte testatus, pro parte intestatus fieri potest: ita vt vnus idemque sit heres ex Testamento & ab intestato l. 19. de inoff. Test. Verum ipse heres scriptus non potest repudiare hereditatem pro parte, sed per alium querela inofficiosi Testamenti agentem potest fieri intestatus pro parte. Nam initio ei accrescit portio l. un. §. in his 10. C. de caduc. tollend.
units.tr: Conflict] Yet the constitutions of the princes admit this conflict in the case of a soldier, by a certain fiction, as if two persons' inheritances were made. l. si certarum 17. §. 1. de test. milit. l. duorum 49. de oper. libert. For indulgence is granted to the inexperience of soldiers, and these constitutions treat it as if there were two inheritances of two persons. But if he has made one military will and another for the rest of his goods, can a suit for partition of the family estate (iudicium familiae herciscundae) be brought between the heirs? Not at all, because here there are two inheritances, military and pagan. Division takes place by the law itself, so that if the inheritance consists only in debts, the action for partition of the family estate ceases. For division takes place by the Twelve Tables. Why then does it happen that there are two inheritances among the goods of soldiers? This has been introduced by the constitutions through a certain fiction. Rightly, however, the Code, in l. hereditates 19. §. 2. de castrens. pecul., says that a soldier can die, from the beginning, partly testate and partly intestate. From the beginning: for a will cannot be rescinded in part by the complaint of an undutiful will. Thus, conversely, for a pagan it has been established that a pagan cannot die, from the beginning, partly testate and partly intestate. For a pagan can become partly testate and partly intestate through the complaint of an undutiful will, so that one and the same person is heir both by will and from intestacy. l. 19. de inoff. Test. But the instituted heir himself cannot renounce the inheritance in part; yet through another person bringing the complaint of an undutiful will he can become intestate in part. For at the beginning the portion accrues to him. l. un. §. in his 10. C. de caduc. tollend.

units.la: Ad leg. 8. De iure sanguinis.
units.tr: On law 8, On the rights of blood.

units.la: IVra sanguinis nullo iure Ciuili dirimi possunt.
units.tr: The rights of blood cannot be dissolved by any civil law.

units.la: Coniunge l. 4. de suis & legit.
units.tr: Compare law 4, On heirs of one's own and legitimate heirs.

units.la: Cuiacius h. in Recitat. posthum. Iura sanguinis vocant iura cognationis, & proximitatis: nec abutitur hac significatione l. quis in adoptionem 23. de adoptionibus, cum ait: adoptio affert ius agnationis, non sanguinis, hoc est cognationis. l. vel si sanguine 12. de manum. vind. Et merito. Nam cognatos vocat sola ratione sanguinis l. 2. unde cognati. Agnatis etiam idem nomen, eadem familia, eaedem imagines; & agnati sunt, etiamsi ex eodem non sunt sanguine vel familia. Et haec quidem iura agnationis tolli possunt iure Ciuili: vt filius, dum est in potestate mea, agnatus mihi est, quia suus: sed si emancipetur, desinit esse agnatus: non tamen desinit esse cognatus: desinit esse filiusfamilias, non tamen filius: quoniam iura sanguinis tolli emancipatione non possunt, sicut nec adoptione. Ac similiter frater meus, qui in eiusdem patris potestate est, mihi cognatus est, & agnatus: sed si emancipatus, sui iuris fiat, vel transeat in alienam familiam, non desinit esse frater & cognatus, desinit tamen esse consanguineus. Nam consanguineus non dicitur, nisi qui est eiusdem familiæ l. 4. unde cognati, quæ huic legi iungenda est. Denique minima capitis diminutione non tollitur cognatio; agnatio tollitur: quia ciuilis iuris agnatio est, cognatio naturalis. l. iurisconsultus 10. §. inter agnatos de grad. & affin. Ac quo modo naturaliter cognati sunt, siue per mares, siue per fœminas descendant, omnes ex æquo vocantur ad successionem pro ratione graduum: Iure autem ciuili non omnes admittuntur. Nam ii tantum qui per mares descendunt, admittuntur, & ideo proprio nomine notantur, quo vocantur agnati, hæc enim appellatio est ciuilis, hoc est, ex l. 12. tab. Secundum naturam Cognatos appellamus; secundum ius Agnatos, ad differentiam eorum, qui per fœminas coniuncti sunt. Denique quia ius agnatorum ciuile est, ideo iure ciuili corrumpitur facile. Nam lex legem tollit. At ius Ciuile non potest corrumpere iura naturalia. Triplex est capitis deminutio: maxima, media, & minima. Maxima aufert ius Gentium & Ciuile: Media priuat ciuitate: Minima affert aliam familiam. Iure Ciuili minima capitis deminutione non tollitur cognatio: media & maxima tollitur. Nam videmus iura sanguinis corrumpi per ius Ciuile. Et ita fit, vt me seruo effecto vel peregrino, mater mea cesset mater mea esse. l. 2. §. 1. ad Tertyll. Ratio est: quia maxima & media capitis deminutione videtur amitti libertas; vtraque enim morti assimilatur: atque ideo cognatio tam ciuiliter quam naturaliter amittitur. Seruitus & peregrinatio mors est; neq; semel perempta cognatio recipitur manumissione l. Is qui 7. unde cognati. Restitutione tamen recipitur cognatio, vt, si peregrinus recipiatur l. 1. §. filio 4. ad Tertyll. Restitutio plenior est manumissione. Manumissio non restituit cognationem: ea enim libertatem tantum facit, non aliud. Accursius hic male iura sanguinis vocat iura consanguinitatis. Nam ius consanguinitatis est fraternitas. Species agnationis sunt fraternitas, suitas, consanguinitas, agnatio. Suitas liberorum est: Consanguinitas fratrum vel sororum. Agnatio eorum, qui sunt ex transuerso. Cuiac. in Recitat. posth. hic.
units.tr: Cuiacius, on the posthumous Recitations here, says that the rights of blood are called the rights of kinship and proximity. He does not misuse this sense in law "Quis in adoptionem," 23, On adoptions, where he says that adoption confers the right of agnation, not of blood, that is, of kinship. Law "Vel si sanguine," 12, On manumission by vindication. And rightly so. For he calls men cognates by the sole reason of blood law 2, Unde cognati. The name agnates is also the same, the same family, the same images; and they are agnates even if they are not of the same blood or family. These rights of agnation can indeed be annulled by civil law: for example, a son, while he is in my power, is my agnate, because he is my heir; but if he is emancipated, he ceases to be an agnate, yet he does not cease to be a cognate. He ceases to be a son under power, but not a son; because the rights of blood cannot be removed by emancipation, any more than by adoption. Likewise my brother, who is under the same father's power, is my cognate and agnate; but if he is emancipated, becomes his own master, or passes into another family, he does not cease to be my brother and cognate, but he does cease to be a consanguine. For a person is not called a consanguine unless he belongs to the same family law 4, Unde cognati, which must be joined to this law. Finally, cognation is not destroyed by the smallest loss of status; agnation is destroyed, because agnation is of civil law and cognation is natural. Law "Iurisconsultus," 10, §. "Inter agnatos," On degrees and affinity. And just as men are natural cognates, whether they descend through males or through females, so all are called to succession equally according to the degree of relationship; but by civil law not all are admitted. For only those who descend through males are admitted, and so they are marked by their own name, by which they are called agnates; for this appellation is civil, that is, from the law of the Twelve Tables. We call cognates according to nature, and agnates according to law, to distinguish those who are joined through females. Finally, because the right of agnates is civil, it is easily corrupted by civil law. For a law overturns a law. But civil law cannot corrupt the natural rights. There are three kinds of loss of status: greatest, middle, and least. The greatest takes away the law of nations and the civil law; the middle deprives one of citizenship; the least brings one into another family. By civil law cognation is not destroyed by the least loss of status; by the middle and greatest it is destroyed. For we see that the rights of blood are corrupted by civil law. And so it happens that when I am made a slave or a foreigner, my mother ceases to be my mother law 2, §. 1, Ad Tertullianum. The reason is this: by the greatest and middle loss of status liberty seems to be lost, for both are likened to death; and therefore cognation is lost both civilly and naturally. Slavery and foreign status are a kind of death, and cognation once destroyed is not restored by manumission law "Is qui," 7, Unde cognati. Yet cognation is restored by restitution, as when a foreigner is received back law 1, §. "Filio," 4, Ad Tertullianum. Restitution is fuller than manumission. Manumission does not restore cognation, for it makes only liberty, and nothing else. Accursius here wrongly calls the rights of blood the rights of consanguinity. For the right of consanguinity is fraternity. The kinds of agnation are fraternity, the condition of a child under power, consanguinity, and agnation. The filial condition is that of children; consanguinity is that of brothers or sisters; agnation is that of those who are related sideways. Cuiacius, on the posthumous Recitations here.

units.la: Lex 9. De obscuris.
units.tr: Law 9. Concerning unclear matters.

units.la: SEmper in obscuris quod minimum est sequimur.
units.tr: In unclear matters we always follow what is the lesser.

units.la: Ex l. si ita scriptum 14. de legat. 1.
units.tr: From law 14, "si ita scriptum", De legatis 1.

units.la: Obscuris ] Pertinet ad quaestionem legatorum, l. si ita scriptum 14. in fi. de legat 1. Sic si fundus Cornelianus legatus sit, si sint duo eiusdem nominis, nec appareat, de quo testator senserit, minor praestatur. l. cum servus 39. §. scio ex facto. de leg. 1. Sic si legavit decem aut quindecim, decem tantum videntur legata. l. si ita relictum 43. §. vlt. de leg. 2. Cuiac. h. in Recitat.
units.tr: Obscuris] This pertains to the question of legacies, law 14, at the end, De legatis 1. Thus if the Cornelian farm is bequeathed, and there are two of the same name, and it does not appear which one the testator meant, the lesser is given. Law 39, §. scio ex facto, De legatis 1. Likewise, if he bequeathed ten or fifteen, only ten are considered bequeathed. Law 43, §. last, De legatis 2. Cuiacius here, in Recitationes.

units.la: In obscuris ] scilicet legatorum; item contractuum, poenarum, non iudiciorum. Attenditur enim in his, quod melius esse potest actori: vide Decium hic. Gothof. in not. hic De obscuro v. l. 22. inf. ff. de fideicom. libertat. De ambiguo v. l. 80. ff. de verb. obligat.
units.tr: In obscuris] that is, of legacies; likewise of contracts and penalties, but not of judgments. For in these one considers what can be better for the plaintiff. See Decius here. Gothofredus in his notes here. On the word obscuro, see law 22 below, De fideicommissaria libertate. On the word ambiguo, see law 80, De verborum obligationibus.

units.la: Minimum ] l. 14. in sin. l. 39. §. 6. ff. de legat. 1. l. 43. in fine ff. de legat. 2. l. 29. §. 1. l. 75. ff. de legat. 3. l. 83. §. 3. l. 109. ff. de verb. obligat. & quod benignius l. 56. ff eod. verisimilius, aut quod plerumque fieri solet l. 114. ff eod. quod mitius l. 4. §. 3. ff. de suspectis tutoribus. l. 32. in sin. l. 42. ff. de poenis. quod levius l. 51. ff. de conditionib. & demonstrationibus. quod utilius dicenti. l 66. ff. de indic. heredi, l. 8. §. 3. ff. de legat. 2. reo & debitori. l. 11. ff. de iure dot.
units.tr: Minimum] law 14 at the end; law 39, §. 6, De legatis 1; law 43 at the end, De legatis 2; law 29, §. 1; law 75, De legatis 3; law 83, §. 3; law 109, De verborum obligationibus. and what is more lenient law 56, same title. more probable, or what usually happens law 114, same title. what is milder law 4, §. 3, De suspectis tutoribus; law 32 at the end, De poenis. what is lighter law 51, De conditionibus et demonstrationibus. what is more useful to the one speaking law 66, De iudiciis; to the heir law 8, §. 3, De legatis 2; to the defendant and the debtor law 11, De iure dotium.

units.la: Sequimur ] nisi de legato ad pias causas agatur l. 38. in f. ff. de auro. & nisi restatoris voluntas l. 13. ff. de reb dub. aut actus contrahentium repugnet l. 39. ff. de pact. l. 25. l. 34. §. 6. ff. de contrah. empt. nisi obscurum a iudice declarari oporteat l. 69. §. 1. ff. de l. dot. nisi id quod minimum est nullius sit momenti. l. 37. ff. de legat. 1.
units.tr: Sequimur] unless the matter concerns a legacy for pious causes, law 38 at the end, De auro; and unless the will of the testator law 13, De rebus dubiis, or the act of the contracting parties, is opposed law 39, De pactis; law 25; law 34, §. 6, De contrahenda emptione. unless the unclear matter ought to be declared by a judge law 69, §. 1, De iure dotium; unless what is the least has no weight at all. Law 37, De legatis 1.

units.la: Lex 10. De commodis & incommodis.
units.tr: Law 10. On benefits and burdens.

units.la: Secundum naturam est, commoda cuiusque rei eum sequi, quem sequuntur incommoda.
units.tr: It is according to nature that the benefits of any thing follow the one whom its burdens follow.

units.la: Secundum ] Terent. in Hecyr. act. 5. scen. pen.
units.tr: Secundum] Terence, Hecyra, act 5, next-to-last scene.

units.la: Commoda ] v. l. ult. §. 3. C. de furtis. adde 2. Eclog. 3. cap. 11. l. 65. in fine ff. pro socio l. 13. §. 1. ff. de acquir. possess.
units.tr: Commoda] see the last law, §. 3, C. de furtis. Add 2 Eclogae, chapter 11, title 3; law 65 at the end, Pro socio; law 13, §. 1, De acquirenda possessione.

units.la: Sequi ] Consequi.
units.tr: Sequi] to attain (consequi).

units.la: Referenda videtur haec regula ad fructuarium l. usufruct. 7. §. 1. de usufruct. ad hereditatem. l. 1. de bon. possess. ad fideicommissarium universalem, cui & in quem omnes transeunt actiones; sicut ad emptorem pertinet commodum & incommodum l. id quod 7. de peric. & comm. rei vend. Sic ex facto institoris sentire debemus commodum & incommodum l. 1. de instit. act. Cuiac. in Recitat. h.
units.tr: This rule seems to apply to the usufructuary, law usufructus 7, §. 1, De usufructu; to the inheritance, law 1, De bonorum possessione; to the universal fideicommissary, to whom and against whom all actions pass; just as the benefit and burden belong to the buyer, law id quod 7, De periculo et commodo rei venditae. So too, from the act of the institor we ought to feel the benefit and the burden, law 1, De institoria actione. Cuiacius here, in Recitationes.

units.la: Lex II. De translatione Dominii.
units.tr: Law II. On the transfer of ownership.

units.la: ID quod nostrum est, sine facto nostro ad alium transferri non potest.
units.tr: What is ours cannot be transferred to another without some act of ours.

units.la: Pertinet ad tractatum de vsufr. l. velinutilem 69. & l. seq. de vsufr. Fœtus pecorum sunt fructuarii, hoc est, eius qui fructus gregis habet, quia fœtus est in fructu. Ceterū fructuarius tenebitur ex agnaris pecoribus supplere siue summittere capita gregis, quæ mortua sunt, atq; ita redintegrare gregem. Submissa pecora fructuarii esse desinunt, inq; proprietariū transferuntur, quia gregis fiunt. Igitur vt proprietarii fiant, opus est facto fructuarii, hoc est submissione. Submissio illa non fit iure ipso, sed est facti. Itaque fœtus non desinunt esse fructuarii, nisi ex ipsis suppleuerit. Denique sine facto domini dominum non transfertur. Neque enim nuda voluntate dominium transfertur. l. traditionib. 19. C. de pactis. Et sic non nuda conuentione sed traditione dominium transfertur. Vt emptio, quæ solo consensu perficitur, emptorem dominum non facit: traditio autem facit. Itaque id quod venditur sine facto meo, hoc est traditione, ad emprorem non transfertur. Interdum tamen nuda voluntate transfertur dominium. §. interdum. Instit. de rer. diuis. Item legatum sine facto heredis vel domini ipso iure ex l. 12. tab. adquiritur. Vlp. in fragm. tit. de dominiis l. Legatum ita 80. de legat. 2. Nunquā factum heredis recta via transit. Imo & sine facto & sine voluntate domini, interdum transfertur dominium, scilicet vsucapione & adiudicatione, vt videre est apud Vlp. d. t. in fragm. Item in distractione pignoris sine facto & voluntate domini dominium transfertur. In his omnibus regula vitiatur.
units.tr: This belongs to the treatise on usufruct: l. velinutilem 69. & l. seq. de vsufr. The young of a flock belong to the usufructuary, that is, to the one who has the produce of the flock, because the young are part of the produce. However, the usufructuary is bound to make good from the lambs the animals of the flock that have died, and so restore the flock. The animals substituted cease to belong to the usufructuary and pass to the owner, because they become part of the flock. So, for them to become the owner's, an act of the usufructuary is needed, namely the substitution. That substitution does not happen by law itself, but by an act. Accordingly, the young do not cease to belong to the usufructuary unless he has made good the losses from them. In short, ownership is not transferred without an act of the owner. For ownership is not transferred by a bare will: l. traditionib. 19. C. de pactis. Thus ownership is transferred not by a bare agreement but by delivery. Just as a sale, which is completed by consent alone, does not make the buyer owner, but delivery does, so what is sold is not transferred to the buyer without my act, that is, delivery. Sometimes, however, ownership is transferred by bare will: §. interdum. Instit. de rer. diuis. Likewise, a legacy is acquired by operation of law without an act of the heir or the owner, from the Twelve Tables: Vlp. in fragm. tit. de dominiis l. Legatum ita 80. de legat. 2. The act of an heir never passes directly. Indeed, even without any act or will of the owner, ownership sometimes passes, namely by usucapion and adjudication, as may be seen in Ulpian, d. t. in fragm. Likewise, in the sale of a pledge, ownership passes without any act or will of the owner. In all these cases the rule is violated.

units.la: Lex 12. De interpretatione testa- mentorum.
units.tr: Law 12. On the interpretation of wills.

units.la: INtestamentis plenius voluntates testantium interpretantur.
units.tr: In wills, the intentions of those making them are interpreted more fully.

units.la: Coniunge l. fundi. de vsu & habit.
units.tr: Join l. fundi. de vsu & habit.

units.la: Plenius] vide l. 7. C. de fideicom.
units.tr: More fully] see l. 7. C. de fideicom.

units.la: Interpretantur] Interpretamur legit Pac. Alias verbum Interpretandi habet hic patiendi significationem: cuiusmodi multa sunt deponentia, vt l. à diuo Pio. 15. §. sed utrum 9. de re iudicat. Cuiac. in Recitat. b.
units.tr: Are interpreted] the reading of Pacius is "we interpret." Otherwise, the verb "to interpret" here has a passive sense, as many deponent verbs do: l. à diuo Pio. 15. §. sed utrum 9. de re iudicat. Cuiac. in Recitat. b.

units.la: Praesens regula videtur falsa. Nam dictum est supra l. 9. quod minimum est, in obscuris sequimur. Videamus itaque quo sit referenda. Est desumpta ex Pauli lib. 3. ad Sabinum, in quo tractatur de vsufructu legato.
units.tr: This rule seems false. For it was said above, l. 9., that in obscure matters we follow the lesser sense. Let us see, then, to what it should be referred. It is taken from Paul, book 3 on Sabinus, where usufruct bequeathed by legacy is discussed.

units.la: Plenius ICTus non dixit, facta comparatione ad contractus, quasi dicat, Plenius, quam in contractibus, vt falso putat Accursius, sed pleplenius, hoc est, non admodum stricte, vel paulo æquius quam stricta ratio fert. Cuiac. in Recit. posthum. Spectemus igitur hic vsum legatorum: nec statuamus perpetuo defunctorum voluntates plenissime interpretandas esse Cuiac. ibid. in fi.
units.tr: The jurist did not say "more fully" by comparison with contracts, as if he meant "more fully than in contracts," as Accursius wrongly supposes, but "pleniusque," that is, not very strictly, or somewhat more equitably than strict reason requires. Cuiac. in Recit. posthum. Let us therefore consider here the practice concerning legacies, and not lay down that the wills of the dead are always to be interpreted most fully. Cuiac. ibid. in fi.

units.la: Lex 13. De effectu Exceptionis.
units.tr: Law 13. On the effect of an exception.

units.la: NOn videtur cepisse, qui per Exceptionem à petitione remouetur.
units.tr: He does not seem to have received who is repelled from the claim by an exception.

units.la: Exceptionem] v. l. 115. in f. infr. h. t. & ibi Cuiac. v. l. 7. §. 8. ff. de dolo.
units.tr: Exception] see l. 115. at the end below, this title, and there Cuiac.; see l. 7. §. 8. ff. de dolo.

units.la: Regulam hanc referri posse arbitramur ad querelam inofficiosi, vt intelligatur quis proprie dicatur cepisse. Qui legatum cepit, repellitur à querela inofficioli Testamenti, à bonorum possessione contra tabulas. Legatum autem capitur non tantum præstatione, sed etiam adquisitione. Capere est adquirere. Sed an videatur legatum capere is, qui id totum alii administrauit? Minime, & ideo non repellitur à querela. l. nihil 12. §. pennult. de inoff. test. quæ lex loquitur de eo, cui ademtum erat legatum, quem constat repelli plerumque ab exceptione doli, vt Accurs. notauit rectè. Sed huic legi locus est in edicto de calumniatoribus, vt constat ex l. 115. Si quis obligatione liberatus sit, eum videri cepisse: non tantum eum qui pecuniam acceperat, sed etiam qui obligatione liberatus est. Cuiac. in Recit. b. in pr. & in sin. ibid. Non dicemus, eum habere actionem, qui exceptione repellitur, si essectum spectemus. Nil interest, an ipsum ius excludat, an exceptio.
units.tr: We think this rule may be referred to the querela of an undutiful will, so that it may be understood who is properly said to have received. One who has received a legacy is barred from the querela of an undutiful will, and from possession of goods against the tablets. A legacy is received not only by payment but also by acquisition, for to receive is to acquire. But does one seem to have received a legacy if he has wholly administered it for another? Not at all, and so he is not barred from the querela: l. nihil 12. §. pennult. de inoff. test., which law speaks of one from whom the legacy had been taken away, who is commonly, as Accursius rightly noted, barred by the exception of fraud. But this law applies to the edict on calumny, as is clear from l. 115. If anyone has been freed from an obligation, he is considered to have received: not only one who had accepted money, but also one who has been freed from an obligation. Cuiac. in Recit. b. in pr. & in sin. ibid. We will not say that the one repelled by an exception has an action, if we look at the effect. It makes no difference whether the law itself excludes him or an exception does.

units.la: Lex 14. De die obligationis.
units.tr: Law 14. On the day of the obligation.

units.la: IN omnibus obligationibus, in quibus dies non ponitur, præsenti die debetur.
units.tr: In all obligations in which no day is fixed, the debt is due on the present day.

units.la: Ponitur ] alias apponitur.
units.tr: Fixed] otherwise "added."

units.la: Præsenti ] v. l. 41. §. 1. ff. de verb. obligat.
units.tr: Present] see l. 41. §. 1. ff. de verb. obligat.

units.la: Hæc lex est Pomponij lib. 5. ad Sabinum: Sed hæc sententia aperta est; ex stipulatione pura scilicet deberi; nisi locus, modus, conditio, vel ius diem trahat. Nam ut debitum sit efficax, non tantum ex die, sed etiam ex loco datur dilatio: etiam ex modo, & ex reipsa, ut si promittatur partus futurus. l. 29. l. nemo 55. de legat. 1. l. interdum. 73. de verb. oblig. Sunt autem valde notanda hæc verba, præsenti die debetur; quibus statuitur, præsenti die non esse soluendum. Nam agi potest confestim, nec vllum datur legis laxamentum. Nam non exspectatur, quod dies prætereat, sed statim agitur. l. liber homo. 118. §. 1. de verb. oblig. Sed si res promissa non sit in manu, hoc est, in abrupto, à Prætore dabitur eius comparandæ spatium. §. vlt. Inst. de inutil. stipul. Citatur in hanc rem l. quod dicimus 105. de folut. quæ coniungenda est cum l. 1. §. item si ita ad L. Falcid. testator aliquid præstare iussit, statim ab adita hereditate id est accipiendum, inquit, non sine aliquo spatio: alioqui cogeretur heres adire cum sacco & folle, ex quo statim numeraret pecuniam. Sed id spatium est permodicum & incertum, daturque pro modo necessitatis. Citatur male in eandem rem l. cum militi 16. in f. de compens. Nam ea lex non loquitur de hoc permodico spatio: sed de tempore iudicati, legibus definito, quod olim dabatur humanitatis causa. Cuiac. in Recitat, h.
units.tr: This law is from Pomponius, book 5 on Sabinus: but this opinion is plain, namely that a pure stipulation is due at once, unless place, condition, or law defers the day. For that a debt may be effective, a delay is given not only by the day but also by the place; also by the manner and by the thing itself, as when what is promised is a future birth: l. 29. l. nemo 55. de legat. 1. l. interdum. 73. de verb. oblig. But these words "is due on the present day" are to be carefully noted, for by them it is laid down that payment is not to be made on the present day. For action may be brought at once, and no relief of the law is given, since one does not wait for the day to pass but sues at once: l. liber homo. 118. §. 1. de verb. oblig. But if the promised thing is not in one's hand, that is, is not immediately available, the Praetor will give time to procure it: §. vlt. Inst. de inutil. stipul. Cited for this matter is l. quod dicimus 105. de folut., which must be joined with l. 1. §. item si ita ad L. Falcid., where a testator orders something to be given, and it is to be understood, it says, as taken from the moment of accepting the inheritance, yet not without some interval; otherwise the heir would be forced to enter with a sack and purse, from which he would at once count out the money. But that interval is very short and uncertain, and it is granted according to the need. It is wrongly cited for the same point l. cum militi 16. in f. de compens., for that law does not speak of this very short interval, but of the time after judgment, fixed by the laws, which was formerly given for reasons of humanity. Cuiac. in Recitat, h.

units.la: Lex 15. De effectu actionis.
units.tr: Law 15. On the effect of an action.

units.la: ISqui actionem habet ad rem recuperandam, ipsam rem habere videtur.
units.tr: A person who has an action to recover a thing is considered to have the thing itself.

units.la: Coniunge l. eandem 72. ff. de legat. 3.
units.tr: Compare l. eandem 72. ff. de legat. 3.

units.la: Actionem] v. l. 52. ff. de acquir. rer. dom. leg. 143. ff. de verb. oblig. Actio in rem, vice rei est.
units.tr: Actionem] see l. 52. ff. de acquir. rer. dom.; l. 143. ff. de verb. oblig. An action in rem stands in place of the thing.

units.la: Videtur] repræsentatione, non reipsa l. 204. eod. l. 15. §. 3. & 4. ff. qui satisdare. vid. l. 13. sup. & l. 115. inf. eod. & ibi Cuiac. hanc legem explicantem.
units.tr: Videtur] by representation, not in fact; see l. 204. eod.; l. 15. §. 3 & 4. ff. qui satisdare; see also l. 13 above and l. 115 below, and there Cuiacius explaining this law.

units.la: Lex 16. De Imaginaria venditione,
units.tr: Law 16. On imaginary sale.

units.la: IMaginaria venditio non est, precio accedente.
units.tr: A sale is not imaginary when a price is attached to it.

units.la: Imaginaria venditio dicitur duobus modis.
units.tr: An imaginary sale is spoken of in two ways.

units.la: Si quis vendat vno nummo; quod vere non est vendere. Neq; enim pretium esse existimatur. Imo pretium opponitur nummo l. si quis 10. §. vlt. de acquir. poss. Deinde nullo pretio accedente. Vt sit venditio, non est necesse, vt pretium soluatur: Potest enim remitti: sed est necesse vt conueniatur de pretio certo. Itaque si conuenit, imaginaria non est. Imaginatiae venditiones nullae sunt. l. nuda. 55. de contrah. emt. l. contractus 54. de oblig. & act. l. 1. §. diui fratres 6. de quaest. Et plerumque fiunt in fraudem legis, donationis causa. Vt, lex est, ne vir donet vxori. Itaque venditionem faciunt imaginariā; quae improbatur. Nam aliud agitur, aliud simulatur. Sic etiam filii dimittebantur per imaginariam venditionem. §. praeterea. Instit. quib. mod. ius pat. pot. solu. Hereditates vendebantur venditione imaginaria. §. 1. Instit. de test. ordin. Vxores ducebantur specie venditionis, qui modus seruatur quodammodo in hac vrbe. Nam nummos aliquot numerat vxori maritus, & ita fit imaginaria venditio, nummo intercedente. Imaginaria etiam venditio est, si quis nomen suum alienae venditioni emtioni accommodet. l. 10. C. de distrah. pign. Contraria tamen causa plus valet, quod agitur, quam quod simulatur. Interdum tamen hac venditione vtimur. l. 4. §. si ab ignoto. de manumiss. Regulariter imaginarii contractus nulli sunt; imaginariæ apochæ nullæ sunt.l.13 C.de solut.l.1. C.Theodos.de annon. & tribut.Cuia.in recit.h.
units.tr: If someone sells for a single coin, that is not really a sale, for the coin is not considered a price. Indeed, the price is set against the coin; see l. si quis 10. §. vlt. de acquir. poss. Next, when no price is attached. For there to be a sale, it is not necessary that the price be paid, for it may be remitted; but it is necessary that a definite price be agreed. So if a price is agreed, the sale is not imaginary. Imaginary sales are void: l. nuda 55. de contrah. emt.; l. contractus 54. de oblig. & act.; l. 1. §. diui fratres 6. de quaest. They are commonly made in fraud of the law, for the sake of a gift, as when the law forbids a husband to give to his wife. So they make an imaginary sale, which is disapproved, for one thing is done and another is pretended. In the same way sons were released by an imaginary sale; see §. praeterea. Instit. quib. mod. ius pat. pot. solu. Inheritances were sold by imaginary sale; see §. 1. Instit. de test. ordin. Wives were taken in the form of a sale, a practice which in some measure is kept in this city. For the husband counts out some coins to the wife, and so an imaginary sale is made, with a coin intervening. An imaginary sale also occurs if someone lends his name to another's sale or purchase; see l. 10. C. de distrah. pign. Yet in a contrary case what is done counts for more than what is pretended. Sometimes, however, we use this kind of sale; see l. 4. §. si ab ignoto. de manumiss. As a rule imaginary contracts are void; imaginary receipts are void; see l. 13 C. de solut.; l. 1. C. Theodos. de annon. & tribut.; Cuiac. in Recitat. h.

units.la: Lex 17. De tempore.
units.tr: Law 17. On time.

units.la: CVm tempus in testamento adiicitur, credendum est pro herede adiectum, nisi alia mens fuerit testatoris: sicut in stipulationibus promissoris gratia tempus adiicitur.
units.tr: When a time is added in a will, it is to be believed that it was added for the heir, unless the testator's intention was otherwise, just as in stipulations a time is added for the sake of the promisor.

units.la: Pendet haec tota regula ex l.14. de verb. oblig. Est autem talis regula: in stipulatione dies adiectus videtur pro promissore. Item, solutio differtur promissoris causa. In testamentis autem diei adiectio pro herede est. Vbique igitur pro promissore, id est, debitore est. Quamobrem etiam interpretes adiiciunt: debitor ad diem, ante diem recte soluit. Nam cum dies eius gratia adiectus sit, quare non liceat ei hunc diem negligere? Non tantum soluit recte, sed & debitum offert recte nolenti, aut recusanti accipere. Non liberatur tamen pecunia oblata perempta; quoniam creditor moram facere non videtur, cum suo die non offertur pecunia.
units.tr: This whole rule depends on l. 14. de verb. oblig. The rule is this: in a stipulation a day added is regarded as for the promisor. Likewise, payment is deferred for the sake of the promisor. In wills, however, the addition of a day is for the heir. Thus everywhere it is for the promisor, that is, the debtor. Hence the commentators also add: a debtor may rightly pay before the day. For since the day was added for his sake, why should he not be allowed to forgo this day? He not only pays rightly, but also rightly offers the debt to a creditor who is unwilling or refuses to accept it. Yet money offered is not released if it perishes, since the creditor does not seem to cause delay when the money is not offered on its day.

units.la: Cum igitur creditor, qui ante diem pecuniam accipere non vult, moram non faciat, consequens est, vt non liberetur debitor, etiamsi res perimatur, argumento l. item illa. 18. de constitu. pecun. Interdum diei adiectio pro stipulatore est: regulariter pro promissore. Interdum pro legatario. l. sita. 43. §. Pegasus. de legat. 2. l. eum qui. 15. de ann. leg. vt verbi gratia: si testator ei, qui rem familiarem tueri non potest, in eum diem legauerit, quo tueri poterit, adiectio erit non heredis gratia, sed legatarii. Cuiac. in Recitat. posth. h. Nec videtur donasse, qui ante diem soluit. ibid.
units.tr: Therefore, since a creditor who refuses to accept money before the day does not cause delay, it follows that the debtor is not released even if the thing perishes; by the argument of l. item illa. 18. de constitu. pecun. Sometimes the addition of a day is for the stipulator, but as a rule for the promisor, and sometimes for the legatee: l. sita. 43. §. Pegasus. de legat. 2.; l. eum qui. 15. de ann. leg. For example, if a testator bequeaths to one who cannot manage his own property a legacy payable on the day when he will be able to manage it, the addition is made not for the heir's sake but for the legatee's. Cuiacius in Recitat. posth. h. And one who pays before the day is not seen to have made a gift; ibid.

units.la: Lex 18. De acquisitione.
units.tr: Law 18. On acquisition.

units.la: QVæ legata mortuis nobis ad heredem nostrum transeunt, eorum commodum per nos his, quorum in potestate sumus, acquirimus, aliter atque quod stipulati sumus. Nam & sub conditione stipulantes, omnimodo eis acquirimus, etiamsi nobis potestate domini li- beratis conditio existat.
units.tr: Legacies that pass to our heir after our death are acquired through us by those in whose power we are, in a different way from what we have stipulated. For even when we stipulate under a condition, we acquire it for them in every case, even if the condition is fulfilled after we have been freed from the power of our lord.

units.la: Coniunge l. 78. de verb. obligat. & v. Hotom. 5. obser. 3.
units.tr: Compare l. 78. de verb. obligat. and Hotomanus, 5. obser. 3.

units.la: Heredem nostrum] alias heredes nostros.
units.tr: Heredem nostrum] other manuscripts read heredes nostros.

units.la: Omnimodo ] id est, etiamsi conditio existat post emancipationem filii. In eo differt legatum à stipulatione. Ex hac adquiritur patri, etiamsi conditio existat post emancipatum filium. Ex illa nō item. Gothofr. in notis hic: quem & vid. ad l. 78. de verb. obl.
units.tr: Omnimodo] that is, even if the condition is fulfilled after the son's emancipation. In this the legacy differs from the stipulation. Through the latter the father acquires even if the condition is fulfilled after the son has been emancipated; through the former he does not. Gothofredus in his notes here, which see also on l. 78. de verb. obl.

units.la: Liberatis] Pac. legit, libertate praestita à dominis, &c.
units.tr: Liberatis] Pacius reads libertate praestita à dominis, etc., with freedom granted by the masters.

units.la: Domini] Hanc vocem domini, Horomannus expungit. observation. 2. in sin.
units.tr: Domini] Horomannus deletes this word domini; see his observation 2 at the end.

units.la: In hac l. differentiae duae inter legata & stipulationes proponuntur. Vulgus vnam tantum proponi dicit. Prima est. Legatum, quod in heredem transmittitur, patri vel domino legatarii acquiritur iure potestatis. Stipulatio autem, quae in heredem transmittitur, non adquiritur semper patri vel domino, vt stipulatio ire agere licere. Hae stipulationes patri vel domino non adquiruntur, quae personae filii, &c. cohaerent, & factum comprehendunt. §. sed cum factum 2. Inst. de seru. stipul. Ex hac stipulatione soli seruo, non domino, & heredibus eius, ire agere licet. Huiusmodi est & electionis stipulatio, qua sibi electionem recipit stipulator. Nam si stipulator prius non elegerit rem in stipulationem deductam, licebit heredi eius eligere, & ita certum condicere: idem licclicebit ei etiam, cui ipse cesserit actione l. si sic. 75. §. penult. de legat. Patri tamen eius vel domino non datur facultas eligendi. Atque ita quæ electio datur heredi stipulatoris, patri vel domino non datur. Sic fit vt differentia constituatur inter stipulationem & legatum in hoc. Per stipulationem collatum factum in meam persona, facilius transfertur in heredem, quam vt per potestatem patri adquiratur. Et hæc est prima differentia quæ proponitur in hac lege. Nam quo casu stipulati fuimus, in heredem transmittimus, non eodem semper in patrem vel dominum transmittitur. Sed hæc prima differentia ne videatur noua, subiicit aliam, nempe hanc: Nam & sub conditione stipulantes omnino iis adquirimus: secus etiam in legatis. Conditionalis stipulatio patri adquiritur, etsi quando post mortem vel emancipationem extiterit. Legatum conditionale non adquiritur, si eius præstandi dies post mortem, vel emancipationem legatarii extiterit. l. 78. de verb. oblig. Ex qua l. repetita est pars l. non omne. 144. infra h.t. Filiusfamilias stipulatur sub conditione, emancipatur, deinde existit conditio, actio ex stipulatu patri competit, quia in stipulationibus id tempus spectamus, quo contrahitur. Tempore autem stipulationis stipulator fuit in potestate. In legatis spectatur tempus cessionis, quo dies cedit, hoc est, quo existit conditio. Hoc scripsit Paulus lib.62. ad edictum. Ex quibus ambæ hæ sunt leges. Vtraq; autem lex loquitur tantum de stipulatione. Sed secus esse in legatis, idem Paulus ibidem scripsit, vt apparet ex l.4. de ann.leg. Stipulatio conditionalis, si conditio existat, post emancipationem patri competit: filio sub conditione legatum, non competit patri. l.legata 41. de condit. & demonstr. ostendit legato relicto sub conditione, heredem heredis teneri pendente conditione: contra tamen legatarii heredi non tenetur heres. Atque ita magna differentia est inter legata & stipulationes.
units.tr: In this law two differences between legacies and stipulations are set out. The common view says only one is set out. The first is this: a legacy that passes to the heir is acquired for the legatee's father or master by right of power. A stipulation that passes to the heir is not always acquired for the father or master, as in a stipulation that one may go and act. Those stipulations which are bound to the person of the son, and which cover a deed, are not acquired for the father or master; see §. sed cum factum 2. Inst. de seru. stipul. By such a stipulation the slave alone, not the master, and his heirs, may go and act. Of this kind is also a stipulation of choice, by which the stipulator receives the choice for himself. For if the stipulator has not first chosen the thing brought into the stipulation, his heir may choose, and so sue for a definite thing; and the same holds for anyone to whom he has ceded the action; see l. si sic. 75. §. penult. de legat. But no power of choice is given to his father or master. So the choice given to the heir of the stipulator is not given to the father or master. Thus a difference is established between stipulation and legacy in this respect: what is conferred by stipulation in my person passes more easily to my heir than it is acquired for my father by power. This is the first difference proposed in this law. For in the case where we have stipulated, we transmit it to our heir, but it does not always pass in the same way to the father or master. But lest this first difference seem new, the law adds another, namely this: those who stipulate under a condition acquire for them in every case, but the position is otherwise with legacies. A conditional stipulation is acquired for the father even if the condition is fulfilled after death or emancipation; a conditional legacy is not acquired if the day of its payment falls after the legatee's death or emancipation; l. 78. de verb. oblig. From this law a part of l. non omne. 144. infra h.t. is repeated. A son under power stipulates under a condition; he is emancipated; then the condition is fulfilled; the action on the stipulation belongs to the father, because in stipulations we look to the time when the contract is made, and at the time of the stipulation the stipulator was under power. In legacies, however, the time of vesting is considered, on which the day falls due, that is, when the condition is fulfilled. Paulus wrote this in book 62 on the Edict. From these two laws come both differences. Yet both laws speak only of stipulation. That the position is different with legacies, Paulus wrote in the same place, as appears from l. 4. de ann. leg. A conditional stipulation, if the condition is fulfilled, belongs to the father after emancipation; a legacy left to a son under a condition does not belong to the father; l. legata 41. de condit. & demonstr. shows that when a legacy is left under a condition, the heir of the heir is bound while the condition is pending, but conversely the heir is not bound to the legatee's heir. And so there is a great difference between legacies and stipulations.

units.la: Ex quo efficitur: stipulationem cedere ex die contractus: legatum autem ex euentu conditionis: in stipulatione spectari tempus contractus, conditionem vero legati non retrotrahi ad tempus mortis. Ratio differentiæ nondum demonstrata, hæc est. Stipulatio siue pure, siue conditionaliter interponitur obligationis contrahendæ causa statim ita, vt non liceat inuito altero ei ab illa recedere. In legatis autem ambulatoria voluntas. Igitur non statim conficit obligationem. Et stipulationem interponimus etiam non tantum vt nobis consulamus, sed & posteris. l.9. de probat. Verum facta stipulatione cum conditione, etsi contrahentes non hoc assequuntur, heredibus tamen proficiet hic contractus, si statuamus eius vires statim consistere ab initio, etiamsi conditio non extiterit. Alia est differentia adhuc inter stipulationem & legatum. Seruus hereditarius frustra vsumfructum stipulatur sub conditione.l. vsusfructus 26. de stipul. seruor. Seruus hereditarius scilicet, qui dominum non habet, hoc est, iacente hereditate. Iam serui hereditarii, neque ipsi personam habent. Vsusfructus autem sine persona constitui nequit. Igitur talis seruus inutiliter stipulatur vsumfructum. Legari tamen ei vsusfructus recte poterit, quia cedente die legati, adita erit hereditas. Seruus ad prædium domini seruitutem recte stipulatur l. si vnus. 19. ff. de seru. rust. præd. at non recte legatur seruo seruitus ad prædium domini, quia forte cedente die legati, erit liber, atque ita inutile legatum deprehendetur. Præterea stipulatio conditionalis ad tempus contractus retrotrahitur. l. 2. §. id quoque. de coll. bon. Pater vero de eo, quod promissum est filiofamilias, pacisci non potest, quia ex eo nihil sperat. l. & heredi. 21. §. item filiusfam. 4. de pact. Itaque hoc est certissimum, in stipulationibus spectari tempus contractus; in legatis, conditionis. Vnus est casus, quo prout in legatis, ita in stipulationibus, tempus conditionis spectatur, vt est regula Caroniana. In stipulationibus conditionalibus cessat regula Caroniana. Finge: Rem meam stipulor sub conditione: si spectas præpræsens tempus, non valet stipulatio. Spectare præsens tempus regula Catoniana exigit. Tamen stipulatio valet, si modo tempore conditionis alia na esse deprehendatur.l. Sirem meam. 31. de verb. oblig. Cuiac. in Recit. b.
units.tr: From this it follows that a stipulation takes effect from the day of the contract, but a legacy takes effect only on the occurrence of the condition. In a stipulation the time of the contract is what counts; the condition of a legacy does not relate back to the time of death. The reason for this difference, not yet explained, is as follows. A stipulation, whether pure or conditional, is entered into at once in order to create an obligation, so that neither party may withdraw from it without the other's consent. A will, however, is a revocable intention, so it does not create an obligation at once. We also enter into stipulations not only for our own benefit but for that of our successors (l.9. de probat.). But when a stipulation is made under a condition, even if the contracting parties do not themselves obtain its benefit, this contract will still profit the heirs, provided we hold that its force exists from the beginning, even if the condition never occurs. There is yet another difference between a stipulation and a legacy. A slave belonging to an inheritance stipulates for a usufruct under a condition to no effect (l. vsusfructus 26. de stipul. seruor.). That is, a slave of an inheritance, who has no owner, since the inheritance is lying vacant, has no legal personality, and a usufruct cannot be established without a person. Therefore such a slave stipulates for a usufruct ineffectually. Yet a usufruct may validly be left to him, because when the day of the legacy arrives, the inheritance will have been accepted. A slave validly stipulates for a servitude over his master's estate (l. si vnus. 19. ff. de seru. rust. præd.), but a servitude over his master's estate cannot validly be bequeathed to a slave, because perhaps when the day of the legacy arrives he will be free, and so the legacy will prove void. Moreover, a conditional stipulation relates back to the time of the contract (l. 2. §. id quoque. de coll. bon.). A father, however, cannot make an agreement about what has been promised to his son under his power, because he gains nothing from it (l. & heredi. 21. §. item filiusfam. 4. de pact.). Hence it is most certain that in stipulations the time of the contract is what counts, and in legacies the time of the condition. There is one case in which, as in legacies, so in stipulations the time of the condition is considered, namely the Catonian rule. In conditional stipulations the Catonian rule does not apply. Suppose I stipulate for my own property under a condition: if one looks at the present time, the stipulation is not valid, since the Catonian rule requires attention to the present time. Yet the stipulation is valid if, at the time of the condition, it turns out that the thing is otherwise (l. Sirem meam. 31. de verb. oblig. Cuiac. in Recit. b.).

units.la: PAVLVS.
units.tr: PAUL.

units.la: Si filiusfamilias sub conditione stipulatus, emancipatus fuerit: deinde exstiterit conditio, patri actio competit: quia in stipulationibus id tempus spectatur, quo contrahimus.
units.tr: If a son under power stipulated under a condition and was then emancipated, and the condition is afterwards fulfilled, the action belongs to the father, because in stipulations the time at which we contract is the time that is considered.

units.la: Emancipatus ]
units.tr: Emancipated.

units.la: Lex 19. de conditione contrahentis vel legatarii. De doli exce- ptione.
units.tr: Law 19. On the condition of the contracting party or of the legatee. On the exception of fraud.

units.la: QVI cum alio contrahit, vel est, vel esse debet non ignarus conditionis eius: heredi autem imputari hoc non potest, cum non sponte cum legatariis contrahit. §. 1. Non solet exceptio doli nocere his, quibus voluntas testatoris non refragatur.
units.tr: One who contracts with another either is, or ought to be, not ignorant of that person's condition. But this cannot be imputed to the heir, since he does not contract with legatees of his own accord. §1. The exception of fraud does not usually harm those to whom the will of the testator does not object.

units.la: Debet ] Excusat tamen iusta ignorantia l. 3. ff. de Macedon.
units.tr: Ought: yet a reasonable ignorance excuses. Law 3, Digest, on the Macedonian decree.

units.la: Ignarus ] In iis quae scire possumus, & ignorare non debemus, factum nocet. leg. pen ff. de Macedon. l. 48. ff. de fideiussor.
units.tr: Not ignorant: where we can know a thing and ought not to be ignorant of it, the fact does harm. Last law, Digest, on the Macedonian decree; law 48, Digest, on sureties.

units.la: Conditionis ] id est status, an sit paterfamilias, vel filiusfamilias, seruus vel dominus. Cuiac. 7. observ. 36. Hotom. 5. obser. 8. haec legis verba porrigit ad eos, qui vel contrahendi vel distrahendi ius non habent. Superioribus adde illud Senecae, nomina facturi, diligenter in patrimonium, & vasa debitoris inquirimus. 1. de beneficiis in princip. Notandum tamen, quod conditio etiam significet aetatem, mores, fortunam, valetudinem. l. post. legatum 5. §. 1. in f. de his, quibus ut indig. auf. l. 1. §. cuius 4. de exer. act. & alibi saepe. Hic & illud notandum, quod heres soluens legatum seruo, liberetur, si ignorat conditionem: alioquin debuit soluere domino. At non recte heres soluens furioso vel prodigo vel pupillo, liberatur. Pupillo non recte soluitur sine tutore, furioso sine curatore. Itaque qui soluit, non liberatur: quod si ignoret heres, videtur non liberari: quia earum personarum tutor tutelaque exigit, ne liberetur. Interdum vbi cessat conditio indebiti, hae personae faciunt, vt comperat condictio l. interdum 29. de condict. indeb. Et hoc ita, si furiosus aut prodigus perdiderunt legalegatum. Nam potius fauendum iis personis, quam ignorantiae heredis: earum quippe personarum publica est causa, heredum non aeque. Cuiac. in Recit. posth.
units.tr: Condition: that is, status, whether one is a head of household or a son under power, a slave or a master. Cuiacius, Observations 7, 36; Hotomanus, Observations 5, 8. The words of this law extend to those who have no right to contract or to alienate. To the above add that saying of Seneca: when we are about to make contracts, we make careful inquiry into a debtor's estate and effects. Seneca, On Benefits, at the beginning. It must be noted, however, that condition also signifies age, character, fortune and health. Law "Post legatum" 5, §1, at the end, On those to whom, as unworthy, ...; law 1, §"cuius", 4, On the exercise of actions; and often elsewhere. Here it must also be noted that an heir who pays a legacy to a slave is discharged if he is ignorant of the slave's condition; otherwise he ought to have paid the master. But an heir who pays a madman, a spendthrift or a ward is not rightly discharged. Payment to a ward is not valid without a guardian, nor to a madman without a curator. So one who pays is not discharged; but if the heir is ignorant of this, he is held not to be discharged, because the guardian of these persons and their guardianship insists that he not be discharged. Sometimes, where the condition of an undue payment is lacking, these persons bring it about that the condition is brought in; Law "Interdum" 29, On the condition of undue payment. And this holds if a madman or a spendthrift has lost the legacy. For it is rather to be favoured for these persons than the heir's ignorance; the cause of such persons is a public one, that of heirs is not equally so. Cuiacius, posthumous Recitations.

units.la: Postremo sciendum est, ad superiores duas differentias interstipulationem & legatum, de quibus in l. 18. proponi in hac lege aliam. Prior sentensententia huius legis accipienda est de debito=re. Ait, qui cum alio contrahit, hoc est, reus promittendi. Huic confertur heres, qui reus est debendi. Reus ergo debendi ex contractu, vel qui stipulanti promisit, ignorare non debet conditionem stipulatoris. Imo, si quis stipulanti filiofam. promiserit, soluere debet patri: quia patris propria est actio, non filii; idemque est in domino. Sed quaeritur, si quis stipulanti filiofam. promisit, cum ignoraret eum esse filiumfam: an liberetur? Et placet, non liberari. Haec ignorantia non vacat culpa: itaque ei soluendo non liberatur, & patri est actio integra. Soluendo igitur filiofam. non liberatur per ignorantiam: quia debuit & hoc despicere. Fateor, nonnunquam eam ignorantiam iustam esse, l. 1. de exerc. act. Potest quis iuste ignorare aliquem esse filiumfam. si sic muneribus fungebatur, vt paterfamilias. Quamobrem is, qui tali pecuniam dedit, Senatusconsulto Macedoniano non tenetur. Sed hoc regulariter non procedit. Similiter vero, si filiofam. legatum sit, heres soluere debet legatum patri: nec potest soluere, nec recte soluit legatum filio, nisi nominatim iusserit testator filiofam. solui; quod eleganter ostenditur in l. si vsusfr. 13. §. sed ita 2. quando dies legat. cedat. Ceterum si id non iusserit testator, & sciuerit heres, eum esse filiumfamilias: ei male soluit. Quid fiet, si testator id non iusserit, & heres ignorauerit eum esse filiumfamilias ? Liberabitur. Ita & hac re distat ab herede promissor. Cum non sponte contrahit cum legatariis, ipse heres sibi legatarios non facit, sed incidit in eos aditione: atque ita non potest dispicere de conditione eorum. Ergo si heres probauerit, se ignorasse, legatarium esse filiumfam. liberabitur, & pater repelletur exceptione. Ita hæc l. est aptanda l. si vsusfr. 13. quand. dies legat. ced. Cuiac. in recit. h.
units.tr: Finally, it must be known that the earlier two differences, between a stipulation and a legacy, of which the eighteenth law speaks, are proposed in this law as another. The first sentence of this law is to be understood of the debtor: "one who contracts with another", that is, the party promising. To this is compared the heir, who is the party owing. Therefore the party owing under a contract, or one who has promised to the stipulator, ought not to be ignorant of the stipulator's condition. Indeed, if someone has promised to a son under power, he must pay the father, because the action is the father's own, not the son's; and it is the same with a master. But the question is raised: if someone has promised to a son under power, being ignorant that he was under power, is he discharged? The answer given is that he is not discharged. This ignorance is not free of fault; therefore by paying the son he is not discharged, and the father's action remains whole. By paying the son under power, then, he is not discharged on account of ignorance, because he ought to have looked into this too. I grant that sometimes such ignorance is reasonable: Law 1, On the exercise of actions. A person may reasonably be ignorant that someone is under power if that person was discharging duties as if he were a head of household. Hence one who gave money to such a person is not bound by the Macedonian senatus consultum. But this does not hold as a general rule. Likewise, if a legacy has been left to a son under power, the heir ought to pay the legacy to the father; he cannot pay it, nor does he rightly pay the legacy to the son, unless the testator has expressly ordered that it be paid to the son under power. This is elegantly shown in the law "Si usufructus" 13, §"sed ita" 2, On when the day of a legacy falls due. Otherwise, if the testator has not so ordered and the heir knew that the legatee was under power, he pays him wrongly. What will happen if the testator has not so ordered and the heir was ignorant that the legatee was under power? He will be discharged. In this respect, too, the heir differs from the promisor. Since he does not contract with the legatees of his own accord, the heir does not make the legatees for himself, but falls into them by acceptance of the inheritance; and so he cannot be expected to know their condition. Therefore if the heir proves that he was ignorant that the legatee was a son under power, he will be discharged, and the father will be repelled by the exception. This law is to be applied in this way: law "Si usufructus" 13, On when the day of a legacy falls due. Cuiacius, posthumous Recitations.

units.la: Lex 20. De fauore libertatis.
units.tr: Law 20. On favour toward liberty.

units.la: QVoties dubia interpretatio libertatis est, secundum libertatem respondendum erit.
units.tr: Whenever the interpretation of liberty is doubtful, the answer must be given in favour of liberty.

units.la: Libertatis ] voluntatis. Petrus Faber.
units.tr: Liberty: of intention. Petrus Faber.

units.la: Secundum ] l. 179. inf. eod. l. 13. ff. de probat. l. vlt. §. 1. ff. de vulgari. leg. 3. in f. ff. de his quæ in Testamento delentur. l. 24. ff. de manumiss. l. 10. inf. ff. de manumiss. testam.
units.tr: In favour: law 179, below, same title; law 13, Digest, On proofs; last law §1, Digest, On the vulgar substitution; law 3 at the end, Digest, On those things which are cancelled in a will; law 24, Digest, On manumission; law 10, below, Digest, On testamentary manumission.

units.la: Libertatem ] cuius causa pia dicitur l. 1. §. penult. C. de communi seruo. legitimæ anteponenda: deductis enim libertatibus, quarta initur l. 8. §. 9. ff. de inofficioso. Gothofr.
units.tr: Liberty: whose cause is called pious: law 1, §penultimate, Code, On the common slave. It is to be preferred to the legitim, for once liberties are deducted, the fourth is taken: law 8, §9, Digest, On the inofficious will. Gothofredus.

units.la: Finge: libertas directo est relicta seruo pignorato. Inutilis est libertas: per fideicommissum tamen manumitti potest. Interpretabimur pro libertate fideicommissum. l. generaliter 24. ter 24. §. si quis seruo 10. de fideicom. libert. Eo-dem pertinet l. cum in Testamento 48. de fidei-com. libert. Quidam manumisit quod est in utero ancillae, & singulari verbo visus est. At plures sunt editi? An omnibus competet liber-tas? ita docuit l. in obscuris sup. h.t. Et libertas omnibus rebus fauorabilior est: ideo fit, ut, si seruo libertas relinquatur, simulque legetur sub conditione, pereat legatum, seruetur li-bertas. Cuiac. in Recitat. h.
units.tr: Suppose liberty is directly bequeathed to a slave who has been pledged. The liberty is void, but he can still be manumitted through a trust. We shall interpret the trust in favour of liberty. Law "Generaliter" 24; §"si quis servo" 10, On trusts for liberty. To the same point belongs the law "Cum in testamento" 48, On trusts for liberty. A certain man manumitted what was in the womb of his female slave, and he seemed to have done so by a single word. But are there several editions? Will liberty belong to all? So the law "In obscuris" above, under this title, teaches. And liberty is more favoured than all things; hence it comes about that, if liberty is left to a slave and at the same time a legacy is made to him under a condition, the legacy perishes but the liberty is preserved. Cuiacius, Recitations on this title.

units.la: Lex 21. De eo quod plus vel minus est.
units.tr: Law 21. Concerning what is more or less.

units.la: Non debet, cui plus licet, quod minus est, non licere.
units.tr: He to whom the greater is permitted ought not to be denied the lesser.

units.la: Coniunge l. si legato 11. de man. test.
units.tr: Compare the law "si legato," 11, de manumissis testamento.

units.la: Cui] cui quod plus. Pac.
units.tr: Cui: read "cui quod plus" (to whom what is more). Pacius.

units.la: Plus] adde l. 26. inf. eod. l. 110: l. 163. l. 165. inf. eod. cap. cui licet 53. de regulis in 6. minor poteist restitui, ergo appellare. l. 43. ff. de minoribus. potuit iudex non deferre iuramentum; poterit igitur iuraturo certam summam definire, intra quam iuret. l. 76 ff. de rei vind. l. 5. §. 1. ff. de in litem iurando. De argumento a maiori ad minus affirmatiue concepto vide l. 11. in f. ff. de liberis. adde l. 22. §. 3. ff. de adulter. 12. C. ne fideiussores dotium. nisi id quod maius est, alicui specialiter & stricte sit concessum, vel ex iustis causis, minoribus, ut l. 61. inf. ff. de iudiciis. l. 7. §. 3. ff. de reb. eor. quod in dispensatione, ne, he, delegatione, decreto, & mandato perspicitur. Goth.
units.tr: Plus: add law 26 below, same title; laws 110, 163 and 165 below; the chapter "cui licet," 53, de regulis iuris in Sexto. A minor may be restored, therefore he may appeal. Law 43, Digest, de minoribus. A judge could decline to defer the oath; therefore he may fix for the one swearing a certain sum within which he must swear. Law 76, Digest, de rei vindicatione. Law 5, §1, Digest, de in litem iurando. On the argument from the greater to the lesser, stated affirmatively, see law 11, at the end, Digest, de liberis; add law 22, §3, Digest, de adulteriis; 12, Code, ne fideiussores dotium. Unless what is greater has been granted to someone specially and strictly, or for just causes, to minors, as in law 61 below, Digest, de iudiciis; law 7, §3, Digest, de rebus eorum, which is evident in dispensation, in delegation, in decree and in mandate. Gothofred.

units.la: Licere ] Econtrario valet argumentum à maiori ad minus negatiue conceptum. l. 4. ff. de Senatoribus. l. 5. ff. de seruis exportandis. l. 7. in f. ff. de interdict. & relegat. l. 7. in f. C. de renocand. donationibus. l. vlt. C. de decurionibus. v. Nov. 89. c. 11. Gothofred. Vt si mortis causa donare non potest, multo minus Testamentum facere: firma est ratio. Sed fallunt aliquando hæ argumentationes, vt in Præside Prouinciæ. Si Præses deportare non potest, multo minus gladio punire: quod vitiosum est. Collectio est à maiori. Negandum est tamen consequens propter legem, ex cuius præscripto id ei conceditur specialiter, quod est meri imperii. Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: Licere (to be permitted): conversely, the argument from the greater to the lesser, stated negatively, holds. Law 4, Digest, de senatoribus; law 5, Digest, de seruis exportandis; law 7, at the end, Digest, de interdictis et relegatis; law 7, at the end, Code, de revocandis donationibus; last law, Code, de decurionibus; Novel 89, chapter 11. Gothofred. For example, if one cannot make a gift in view of death, much less can one make a will: the reasoning is sound. But such arguments sometimes fail, as in the case of a provincial governor. If a governor cannot banish, much less can he punish with the sword: which is faulty. The inference is from the greater. Yet the consequence must be denied, on account of the law by whose prescription this is granted to him specially, which belongs to mere imperium. Cujas, in Recitationes.

units.la: CORONIS.
units.tr: Appendix

units.la: Ab hac regula ducuntur argumenta illa: Si donare potest, ergo vendere. Si vendere. Ergo & vendenti consentire. Si donare causa mortis. Ergo donationi consentire. Quæ argumenta sunt Aristotelia à minori, hoc est, minus probabili. Minus probabile est quod possit quis donare. Magis vero, quod possit vendere aut venditioni consentire. Minus probabile est, vt quis alienet. Magis vero, vt alienationi consentiat. Vnde argumentari licet, si id quod minus est, probabile est. Igitur & id, quod magis est. Sunt autem hæc argumenta nonnunquam fallacia: & ideo hæc regula non semper quadrat. Vt, si Decurio prædium suum donare potest. Ergo & vendere; quod falsum est. Nam verum est, posse quidem decurionem donare, sed non vendere. l. 3. C. de præd. decur. Nouella Constit. 38. certam rationem induxit, cur non possit Decurio sua prædia vendere: ne scilicet minus reddatur idoneus gerendis ciuilibus muneribus. Cur igitur donatio non inhibetur? quia facilius quis vendit, quam donat. Id quod facilius quis facit, lex inhibet. Igitur interdicitur venditio. Sic Senatusconf. Velleiano succurritur mulieri obliganti, non donanti, quia facilius obligat se, quam donat. Non tam prompti sunt homines ad donandum, quam ad obligandum. Argumenta à minori plerumque ad affirmandum valent, non ad negandum. Ergo male infertur: Non potest vendere vel manumittere, ergo nec vendenti, vel manumittenti consentire. Argumenta à maiori valent ad negandum. Mortis causa donare non potest. Ergo multo minus testamentum facere: firma est ratio. Interdum non valent. Præses deportare non potest: Ergo multo minus gladio punire. Male. Ad affirmandum non valent. Cuia. in Recit hic.
units.tr: From this rule come those arguments: if he can give, then he can sell; if he can sell, then he can also consent to a sale; if he can give in view of death, then he can consent to a gift. These arguments are Aristotelian arguments from the lesser, that is, from the less probable. It is less probable that someone may give, and more probable that he may sell or consent to a sale. It is less probable that someone may alienate, and more probable that he may consent to an alienation. Hence one may argue that if the lesser is probable, then the greater is too. But these arguments are sometimes fallacious, and so this rule does not always hold. For example, if a decurion may give his estate, then he may also sell it; this is false. For it is true that a decurion may give, but may not sell. l. 3. C. de præd. decur. Nouella Constit. 38. set out a clear reason why a decurion may not sell his estates: namely, so that he does not become less fit to discharge civic duties. Why, then, is giving not forbidden? Because it is easier to sell than to give, and the law forbids what is easier to do. So sale is forbidden. Likewise, the Velleian Senatusconsultum comes to the aid of a woman who binds herself, not one who gives, because people are less ready to give than to bind themselves. Arguments from the lesser generally hold for affirming, not for denying. So it is wrongly inferred: he may not sell or manumit, therefore he may not consent to a seller or manumitter. Arguments from the greater hold for denying: he cannot give in view of death, therefore much less can he make a will; the reasoning is sound. Sometimes they do not hold: a governor cannot banish, therefore much less can he put to death by the sword. That is wrong; such arguments do not hold for affirming. Cuia. in Recit hic.

units.la: Lex 22 De seruis. De conditione in arbitrium domini, vel procuratoris eius collata.
units.tr: Law 22, On slaves. On a condition placed at the discretion of the master or his agent.

units.la: IN personam seruilem nulla cadit obligatio. §. 1. Generaliter probandum est, vbicunque in bonæ fidei iudiciis confertur in arbitrium domini, vel procuratoris eius, conditio, pro boni viri arbitrio hoc habendum esse.
units.tr: IN no obligation arises from a slave's person. §1. It must be generally proved that wherever, in actions of good faith, a condition is placed at the discretion of the master or of his agent, it is to be held that it is to be judged by the discretion of a good man.

units.la: Coniunge l. 8. hæc venditio de contrah. empt. Nulla ] ex contractu ciuili scilicet; alias ex delicto, & naturali, cadit. v. l. 14. ff. de oblig. adde l. 33. Gothofr. Loquitur enim hæc lex de obligatione ex contractu: ex delicto enim seruus obligatur, & ciuiliter & naturaliter. Ex contractu non ciuiliter, sed naturaliter tantum: non est necessitas soluendi, sed duntaxat tenetur de peculio prætorio iure. l. serui. 14. de oblig. & act. Excipiuntur certi casus: si interuenerit pro alio extra rem peculiarem, vel si forte condemnatus sit, si compromiserit. Si actor in iudicio iusiurandum obtulerit. Lex 107. cum seruo inf. eod. videtur scripta de seruo proprio. Domino cum seruo nulla est actio, vel ex contractu, l. lis nulla 4. de iudic. vel ex delicto. Nam licet ex delicto seruus extraneo naturaliter & ciuiliter obligetur: domino tamen naturaliter tantum obligatur, & ob id peculii deductio fit. l. 9. §. sine autem 6. de pecul.
units.tr: Connect l. 8. hæc venditio de contrah. empt. Nulla: that is, from a civil contract; otherwise it does arise from a delict or from natural law. v. l. 14. ff. de oblig. adde l. 33. Gothofr. For this law speaks of obligation from contract. From a delict a slave is bound both civilly and naturally. From contract he is bound not civilly but only naturally: there is no necessity of paying, but he is bound only to the extent of the peculium under praetorian law. l. serui. 14. de oblig. & act. Certain cases are excepted: if he has intervened for another outside the peculiar property, or if he has perhaps been condemned, or if he has compromised. If the plaintiff has offered an oath in court. Law 107, cum seruo, below in the same title, seems written of a slave one owns. Between master and slave there is no action, either from contract, l. lis nulla 4. de iudic. or from delict. For although a slave is bound naturally and civilly to an outsider for a delict, he is bound to the master only naturally, and for that reason a deduction from the peculium is made. l. 9. §. sine autem 6. de pecul.

units.la: Ceterum verum est regulariter cum seruo alieno nullam actionem esse neque ex contractu, neque ex delicto. Nam ex delicto alieno obligatur extraneo seruus, verum non agitur cum eo, sed cum domino: vel cum eo manumisso agi poterit ex delicto. Nam est ex eo delicto ciuilis quam sequitur actio. Cuiac. in Recitat. posth.
units.tr: Moreover, it is true that, as a rule, there is no action with another's slave, neither from contract nor from delict. For a slave is bound to an outsider for another's delict, but the action is not brought against him but against the master; or, once he is manumitted, an action can be brought against him for the delict. For there is a civil action that follows that delict. Cuiac. in Recitat. posth.

units.la: qui consentit in arbitrum, bonum virum intelligit.
units.tr: He who consents to an arbiter understands a good man.

units.la: Generaliter] Ad §. hunc potest videri l. 7. de contrah. empt. ex qua sumatur exemplum, cuius sententia hæc est: Venditio serui ita facta est: seruus venditus esto, si arbitrio meo rationes reddideris. Hæc venditio est conditionalis, sed conditionis verba sunt ambigua; quod arbitrium dupliciter accipiatur: pro pleno, mero & libero: & pro boni viri arbitrio, modo in personam certam, modo in incertam. Item, arbitrio mero adstringuntur, qui se ei adstrinxerunt, etiam iniquo: Boni viri arbitrio non adstringuntur, nisi sit æquum. Nam quod iniquum est, non est boni viri. l. societatem 76. pro socio. Meri arbitrii iniquitas non corrigitur, nisi dolus interuenerit: boni viri arbitrium corrigitur l. 3. C. de recept. arbitr. Præterea, arbitrium merum personam nō egreditur: Nam is solus potest arbitrari, qui nominatus est. l. in compromissis 45. de recept. arbit. Arbitrium boni viri personam egredi potest, etiamsi sit collatum in certam personam. Cum inseritur nomen certæ personæ, non persona, sed æquitas inseri videtur. Igitur si hic æquum non statuerit, licet alium adire. Sed si sit merum arbitrium, non licet alium adire, sed standum est, licet sit iniquum. l. vlt. §. sed etsi quis (. Commun. de legat. Nunc in ea specie, quam posui, si accipias arbitrium pro mero, nulla est venditio. Sicut nec valet venditio, ita facta: Seruus venditus esto, si voluerit. Sic etiam si venditus fit, si arbitrio meo rationes reddiderit: sed accipimus eam conditionem pro arbitrio boni viri: quo casu vtilis est venditio, adeoque, si venditor nolit rationes accipere, vel etiam si rationes ex bona fide redditas nolit probare, venditio valebit. Quoniam cum is in ea re ita versatur, non versatur modo viri boni. Cur enim non accepit rationes, nec subscripsit? Ergo ea conditio pro completa habetur d. l. 7.
units.tr: Generaliter: for this paragraph one may consult l. 7. de contrah. empt., from which an example may be taken, whose sense is this: a sale of a slave was made thus: let the slave be sold, if you render accounts at my discretion. This sale is conditional, but the words of the condition are ambiguous, since discretion may be taken in two ways: as full, mere and free, or as the discretion of a good man, sometimes in a certain person, sometimes in an uncertain one. Likewise, those who have bound themselves to a mere discretion are bound even if it is unfair; those are not bound to a good man's discretion unless it is fair. For what is unfair is not that of a good man. l. societatem 76. pro socio. The unfairness of a mere discretion is not corrected unless fraud intervenes; the discretion of a good man is corrected. l. 3. C. de recept. arbitr. Moreover, a mere discretion does not go beyond the person, for only he can judge who has been named. l. in compromissis 45. de recept. arbit. The discretion of a good man can go beyond the person, even if it has been conferred on a certain person. When the name of a certain person is inserted, it is not the person but equity that is seen to be inserted. Therefore, if this one does not decide what is fair, one may go to another. But if it is a mere discretion, one may not go to another, but must abide by it, even if it is unfair. l. vlt. §. sed etsi quis (. Commun. de legat. Now in the case I have put, if you take the discretion as mere, there is no sale, just as a sale made thus does not stand: let the slave be sold, if he wishes. So too, if he is sold if he renders accounts at my discretion, but we take that condition as the discretion of a good man, in which case the sale is valid. Hence, if the seller is unwilling to accept the accounts, or even if he is unwilling to prove accounts rendered in good faith, the sale will stand. For since he behaves in this matter in such a way, he is not acting merely as a good man would. Why did he not accept the accounts, nor sign them? Therefore that condition is held to be fulfilled. d. l. 7.

units.la: Ad leg. 23. De dolo, culpa, diligentia, & casu.
units.tr: On law 23, On fraud, fault, diligence, and chance.

units.la: COntractus quidam dolum malum duntaxat recipiunt: quidam & dolum & culpam. Dolum tantum, Depositum & precarium: Dolum & culpam, mandatum, commodatum, venditum, pignori acceptum, locatum, item dotis datio, tutelæ, negotia gesta. In his quidem & diligentiam societas, & rerum communio, & dolum & culpam recipit. Sed hæc ita, nisi quid nominatim convenit, vel plus vel minus, in singulis contractibus: Nam hoc seruabitur quod initio convenit. Legem enim contractus dedit; excepto eo quod Celsus putat, non valere si convenerit, ne dolus præstetur; hoc enim bonæ fidei iudicio contrarium est. & ita vtimur. Animalium vero casus, mortes, quæque sine culpa accedunt, fugæ seruorum qui custodiri non solent, rapinæ, tumultus, incendia, aquarum magnitudines, impetus prædonum, à nullo præstantur.
units.tr: Some contracts admit only wilful fraud; some admit both fraud and fault. Only fraud: deposit and precarium. Both fraud and fault: mandate, loan for use, sale, pledge received, lease; likewise the giving of a dowry, guardianship, and managed affairs. In these, partnership and communion of goods also admit diligence, and both fraud and fault. But this holds unless something has been expressly agreed, more or less, in individual contracts, for what was agreed at the outset will be observed. For the contract gives the law, except for what Celsus holds: that it is not valid if it was agreed that fraud should not be answered for, since this is contrary to the judgment of good faith. And so we practise. But the chances of animals, deaths, and whatever occurs without fault, the flight of slaves who are not usually guarded, robberies, tumults, fires, floods of waters, and attacks of pirates are answered for by no one.

units.la: Haec lex valde notanda est de bonae fidei contractibus, & comprehendit etiam obligationes ex quasi contractibus. Contractus sunt, inu[?] manmandatum, venditum, locatum, commodatum, societas, depositum, pignoris datio: & adiicit lex dotis dationem, quod probat l. exigere 65. de iudic. Item arrharum dario est contractus: item diuortium. Sed de his duobus nihil est in h. l. Quasi contractus est tutela, negotiorum gestio, precarium, rerum communio: hi enim sunt contractus, qui recensentur hic. Societas voluntaria est contractus: rerum communio societas necessaria, velut hereditaria, est quasi contractus. Precarium quoque non est contractus, sed donatio potius est, ideo reuocato precario non datur actio ciuilis, sed praetoria. l. secund. de precar. Igitur haec lex est tam de contractibus, quam de quasi contractibus. Ex his contractibus aliis inest tantum doli praestatio, veluti depositro, & precario. Nam qui rem depositam suscepit, dolum tantum praestat, non culpam, quia utilitas eius nulla hic versatur. l. si ut certo. §. nunc videndum. commod. Similiter is, qui precario rogaut, dolum praestat, non culpam: quia scilicet totum pendet ex liberalitate eius, qui dedit. Nam precarium soluitur nuda voluntate dantis; commodatum non soluitur. Est enim satis in precario, in re tam infirma dolum praestari. Nam nulla eius utilitas spectari videtur, cum ex voluntate dantis pendeat. l. quaesitum 8. de precar. In commodato utrumque præstatur. Obligat enim vltro citroque: non possum reuocare rem commodatam, antequam eius vsum compleueris. Merito igitur in precario dolus tantum venit, in aliis contractibus doli præstatio inest, & culpa, minimum in iis, in quibus vtriusque vtilitas versatur, vt in vendito, locato, pignori dato, & societate. Et vnus est contractus tantum, in quo vtilitas eius versatur, qui accepit, vt in commodato. Nam est gratuitum, nec reuocatur quandocunque. Prius enim huius vsum expleat necesse est. Quia demum plus inest huic contractui, quod cæteris, ideo exactissima & extrema diligentia præstatur in eo, vt docet hoc d. l. si vt certo. commodati. In deposito & precario dolus tantum præstatur: in vendito, vel locato, vel societate, vel pignore, dolus & culpa: in commodato etiam diligentia præter culpam & dolum.
