Eiusdem naturæ est negotiorum gestio, tutelæ, mandatum. Præstatur enim & culpa, & exactissima diligentia, opera, & custodia. Fateor quidem in negotio gesto, tutelis, & mandato, nullam versari vtilitatem gestoris, tutoris, procuratoris; sed gestor vltro se ingerit, suscipit absentium negotia non rogatus: tutor autem suscipit rem pupilli, cuius ætas maxime defensorem exigit. Procurator suscipit negotia mandantis: summam autem operam requirimus amicis præstari. stari. Denique in aliis contractibus præstatur dolus & culpa, in iisautem, scilicet, mandato, commodato, negotiis gestis, tutelis,etiam diligentia exactissima, vt accipitur in l. hoc ita 2. de peric. & com. rei. vend. l si vt certo §. custodiam. commod. l. cum seruo de leg. 1. Et hoc vt planius intelligatur, considerandum, dolo ex aduerso opponi bonam fidem; culpæ custodiam & diligentiam, §. socius sicio Inst. de societ. Culpa igitur est negligentia, & alia consistit in faciendo, alia in non faciendo.l. si seruum 91.de verb. oblig. l. 1. de tut. & ration. distrahen. Vtraque præstari intelligitur. Nam & culpa, quæ est in faciendo, negligentia est. Nam facere dicitur, qui facit, quod facere non debet: sicut non facere, qui, quod facere debet, non facit. l. qui non facit 121. h. t. Merito igitur culpa opponitur diligentiæ. Nam nihil aliud est culpa quam negligentia. Igitur quot sunt diligentiæ gradus, tot & culpæ erunt. 1. Est diligentia exactissima ac delatoria curiositas: & hæc sane est scrupulosa inquisitio.l. nec supina 6. de iur. & fact. ign. Et ex aduerso ei opponitur culpa leuissima l. in lege. 44.adl. Aquil. 2. Est diligentia quædam media: ex aduerso culpa leuis. 3. Præterea est diligentia minima: & ex aduerso culpa lata, scilicet quæ est dolo proxima, & dolo comparatur; quam depositarius præstat, perinde ac dolum, sicut & precarii possessor.
units.tr: This law is to be noted carefully concerning contracts of good faith, and it also covers obligations arising from quasi-contracts. The contracts are: mandate, sale, letting, loan for use, partnership, deposit, and the giving of a pledge. The law also adds the giving of a dowry, which l. exigere 65. de iudic. proves. Likewise, the giving of earnest money is a contract, and so is divorce, but the present law says nothing about these two. Quasi-contracts are guardianship, the management of another's affairs, precarium, and the common ownership of things; these are the contracts listed here. Voluntary partnership is a contract, whereas the common ownership of things, or necessary partnership such as that among heirs, is a quasi-contract. Precarium is also not a contract but is rather a gift, so when a precarium is revoked no civil action is given, only a praetorian one; l. secund. de precar. Therefore this law concerns contracts and quasi-contracts alike. In some of these contracts only fraud is answerable, as in deposit and precarium. For the one who has received a thing on deposit answers only for fraud, not for fault, because no advantage to himself is involved here; l. si ut certo. §. nunc videndum. commod. Likewise, the one who receives something by precarium answers only for fraud, not for fault, because clearly everything depends on the generosity of the one who gave. For precarium is ended by the mere will of the giver, whereas a loan for use is not. In precarium it is enough that fraud alone is answered for in a thing so unstable; for no advantage of the borrower seems to be considered, since the arrangement depends on the will of the giver; l. quaesitum 8. de precar. In a loan for use both are answered for, for it binds on both sides: I cannot recall a loaned thing before you have finished its use. Rightly, then, in precarium only fraud is at issue, while in other contracts answerability for fraud is present along with fault, least of all in those in which the advantage of both parties is involved, as in sale, letting, pledge, and partnership. And there is only one contract in which the advantage lies with the one who receives, namely the loan for use: it is gratuitous, and it cannot be revoked at any time, for the borrower must first finish its use. Because this contract has more in it than the others, the most exact and utmost diligence is owed in it, as d. l. si ut certo. commodati. teaches. In deposit and precarium only fraud is answered for; in sale, letting, partnership, or pledge, fraud and fault; in a loan for use, even diligence beyond fault and fraud. Of the same nature are the management of another's affairs, guardianship, and mandate. For fault and the most exact diligence, labour, and care are answered for in them. I grant that in the management of another's affairs, in guardianship, and in mandate there is no advantage to the manager, guardian, or agent; but the manager thrusts himself in, taking up the affairs of absent persons without being asked, while the guardian takes up the property of a ward, whose age especially demands a defender; and the agent takes up the affairs of the one who gave the mandate. Yet we require that the greatest care be shown to friends. In sum, in other contracts fraud and fault are answered for, but in these, namely mandate, loan for use, management of affairs, and guardianship, even the most exact diligence is owed, as is understood from l. hoc ita 2. de peric. & com. rei. vend. l. si ut certo §. custodiam. commod. l. cum seruo de leg. 1. So that this may be understood more plainly, it must be considered that fraud is opposed to good faith, while care and diligence are opposed to fault; §. socius sicio Inst. de societ. Fault, then, is negligence, and it consists in one way in doing and in another in not doing; l. si seruum 91. de verb. oblig. l. 1. de tut. & ration. distrahen. Both are understood to be answered for. For fault that lies in doing is also negligence, since he is said to do who does what he ought not to do, just as he fails to do who does not do what he ought to do; l. qui non facit 121. h. t. Rightly, then, fault is opposed to diligence, for fault is nothing other than negligence. Therefore as many degrees of diligence as there are, so many degrees of fault there will be. (1) There is the most exact diligence and the meticulous curiosity of an informer, which is truly a scrupulous inquiry; l. nec supina 6. de iur. & fact. ign. and opposed to it is the very slightest fault; l. in lege. 44. ad l. Aquil. (2) There is a certain middling diligence, and opposed to it is slight fault. (3) Moreover, there is the least diligence, and opposed to it is gross fault, namely that which is closest to fraud and is compared with fraud, which the depositary answers for just as for fraud, as also the holder of a precarium does.

units.la: Hæc culpa non tam est culpa, quam dolus: vt, si quis nesciat, quod sciunt omnes; nimia est negligentia; d. l. 8. §. quæsitum. de precario. leg. quod Nerua. 31. depos. dicitur culpa lata & magna. l. cedere 213. l. magna 236. de verb. signif. Nunc sic statuamus; in tutela, mandato, gesto, commodato, leuissimam culpam venire. Nam exigitur exactissima diligentia. leg. 10. l. 11. 13. commod. §. vlt. Inst. de oblig. ex quasi contract. leg. vt tutor. de admin. tut. l. si vt certo 5. §. quod etiam commod. In aliis contractibus venit tantum culpa leuis, excepto precario & depositο. Verum potest quis ita arguere. Eadem causa videtur esse tutoris & socii. Itaque non videtur facienda differentia. Socius in seruanda re communi debet præstare dolum & culpam, & diligentiam tantam, quantam in rebus suis adhibet l. 1. de tut. & rat. distr. tamen plus tutorem teneri dicemus, quam socium. Nam separamus tutelam, commodatum, gestum, ab aliis. Sic respondetur ad l. 1. quæ dicit, tutorem præstare culpam & dolum, & diligentiam, quantam in rebus suis: Adiiciendum est, quod Græci adiiciunt in l. à tutoribus 33. de administr. & peric. tut. quid si tutor sit in sua re negligens, an excusabitur tutor? Non. Rursus posset quis dicere: socius debet diligentiam præstare tantam, quantam in suis rebus adhibet; eandemque etiam depositarius. Igitur non plus præstat socius, quam depositarius d.l. quod Nerua depos. Nos tamen diximus, depositarium dolum tantum præstare, sed si suum negligat, culpa vacat: tamen hæc lata est in socio. Nam cuilibet in re sua negligenti esse licet, & in commune est vnusquisque rei suæ arbiter. Hoc ita explicandum est. Depositarius præstat dolum & culpam latam: quæ in depositario culpa lata est, ea in socio est leuis. Lata est in depositario, si non æque sit attentus in re aliena, quemadmodum in sua: In socio secus est, hoc est in re communi, cum sit ex parte mea, & liceat mihi rem meam curare, aliam negligere. Itaque si socius non æque seruet rem communem, ac rem suam, non est lata culpa. (Nam rem suam negligit:) sed est culpa leuis, nec præstatur: similiter in depositario culpa leuis est, si non seruet rem alienam diligentius, quam suam: in re communi est culpa leuissima, si non præstet maiorem diligentiam quam in suis. Sic quæ leuis est in depositario, in socio est leuissima, si non seruet rem communem diligentius quam suam. Leui culpæ opponitur accuratio. Denique vera est definitio sup. expolita. In aliis dolum & culpam præstari. Nunc generaliter definiendum est, in nullis præstari damna fatalia, casusq; fortuitos; & hoc est, quod ait in f.l. animalium casus, mortesque quæ sine culpa accedunt, vt l. in reb. 16. Commod. Conuentio facit, vt culpa præstetur in precario, deposito: vt non præstetur in reliquis, si initio conuenerit, hoc est in ingressu contractus, siue in continenti. Nam ea tantum pacta formant pariuntque actionem, quæ ex continenti fiunt. Itaque ex pacto petes culpam à depositario: alioquin exceptionem tantum pariunt. l. 7. §. quin imo ff. de pact. Igitur pacto fieri potest, vt casus fortuiti præstentur, item culpa præsteatur, vt in precario. Sed non potest pactum fieri, ne dolus præstetur: quia est contra bonos mores, & bonam fidem. l. si vnus. §. illud. de pact. Posteaquam dolo aliquid fecisti, pacto actionem recte remitto: sed non caueo in futurum, vt dolum impune committas.
units.tr: This fault is not so much fault as fraud: for example, if someone does not know what everyone knows, that is excessive negligence; d. l. 8. §. quaesitum. de precario. leg. quod Nerua. 31. depos. it is called gross and great fault. l. cedere 213. l. magna 236. de verb. signif. Now let us establish this: in guardianship, mandate, management of affairs, and loan for use, even the very slightest fault is answered for, for the most exact diligence is required. leg. 10. l. 11. 13. commod. §. vlt. Inst. de oblig. ex quasi contract. leg. vt tutor. de admin. tut. l. si vt certo 5. §. quod etiam commod. In other contracts only slight fault comes into account, except for precarium and deposit. But someone may argue thus: the reason seems to be the same for a guardian and a partner, and so no difference ought to be made. A partner, in preserving the common property, ought to answer for fraud and fault, and for as much diligence as he applies to his own affairs; l. 1. de tut. & rat. distr. yet we shall say that a guardian is bound more than a partner. For we set guardianship, loan for use, and management of affairs apart from the others. Thus it is answered to l. 1., which says that a guardian answers for fault and fraud and for as much diligence as in his own affairs: one must add what the Greeks add in l. à tutoribus 33. de administr. & peric. tut., namely: what if a guardian is negligent in his own affair, will the guardian be excused? No. Again, someone could say: a partner ought to show as much diligence as he applies to his own affairs; and the depositary likewise. Therefore the partner does not answer for more than the depositary; d. l. quod Nerua depos. We nevertheless said that the depositary answers only for fraud, but if he neglects his own property he is free of fault; yet this gross negligence is found in a partner. For it is permitted to anyone to be negligent in his own affair, and in common affairs each one is the judge of his own property. This must be explained thus. The depositary answers for fraud and gross fault: what is slight fault in a depositary is, in a partner, slight fault. It is gross in a depositary if he is not as attentive to another's property as to his own; in a partner it is otherwise, that is, in common property, since it is partly mine, and it is lawful for me to care for my own property and to neglect another's. Thus if a partner does not preserve the common property as carefully as his own, it is not gross fault (for he neglects his own property), but it is slight fault, and it is not answered for. Similarly, in a depositary it is slight fault if he does not keep another's property more diligently than his own; in common property it is the very slightest fault if he does not show greater diligence than in his own affairs. Thus what is slight fault in a depositary is the very slightest in a partner, if he does not keep the common property more diligently than his own. Accuracy is opposed to slight fault. Finally, the definition set out above is true: in other contracts fraud and fault are answered for. Now it must be defined in general that fatal losses and fortuitous accidents are answered for in none; and this is what the law means in f.l. animalium, when it says: "accidents and deaths that occur without fault." l. in reb. 16. Commod. Agreement makes it so that fault is answered for in precarium and in deposit, and not in the rest, if it was agreed at the beginning, that is, at the entering into the contract or immediately. For only those agreements that are made at once form and give rise to an action. Thus by a pact you may demand fault from the depositary; otherwise such pacts give only an exception. l. 7. §. quin imo ff. de pact. Therefore by a pact it can be arranged that fortuitous accidents are answered for, and likewise that fault is answered for, as in precarium. But a pact cannot be made that fraud is not answered for, because it is contrary to good morals and good faith; l. si vnus. §. illud. de pact. After you have done something by fraud, I rightly remit the action by a pact; but I do not guard against your committing fraud with impunity in future.

units.la: Lex 24. De eo quod interest.
units.tr: Lex 24. Concerning that which is of interest.

units.la: QVatenus cuius interest, in facto, non in iure consistit.
units.tr: Insofar as a person's interest lies in the fact and not in law.

units.la: Cuius]cuiusque Hal.
units.tr: "Cuius" is read as "cuiusque" in Haloander.

units.la: Facto]In facto consistunt, de quibus ex facto iudicium est. Potest enim ex eodem facto pro ratione personarum, locorum, temporum l. 15. ff. de negotiis. l. 72. de Iudiciis. l. 16. de pœnis: alias pluris, alias minoris interesse: interdum ne interesse quidem. Ideo nulla iuris definitione id comprehendi potest. Hugo Donell. in libr. de eo quod interest c. 2. in sin. de facti quæstionibus adde l. 16. in sin. de stat. l. 79. §. 1. de indiciis. l. 52. §. 2. ad L. ad L. Aquil. l. 13. qui potiores. l. 8 §. 13. quib. mod. pign. l. 32. de usuris. l. 30. in f. de Testam. tut.
units.tr: Facto: Those things consist in fact about which judgment is made on the basis of the facts. For from the same fact, according to the circumstances of persons, places and times, the interest may sometimes be greater and sometimes less, and sometimes there is no interest at all, l. 15. ff. de negotiis. l. 72. de Iudiciis. l. 16. de poenis. Therefore no legal definition can cover it. Hugo Donell. in libr. de eo quod interest c. 2. in sin. For questions of fact, add l. 16. in sin. de stat. l. 79. §. 1. de indiciis. l. 52. §. 2. ad L. Aquil. l. 13. qui potiores. l. 8 §. 13. quib. mod. pign. l. 32. de usuris. l. 30. in f. de Testam. tut.

units.la: Iure] In iure ea consistunt, in quibus cum quid inciderit, constat, quidnam id, aut quale sit. Sunt haec huiusmodi, ut hominum prudentia æstimari & diiudicari possint. Donell. ibid.
units.tr: Iure: Those things consist in law in which, when something has occurred, it is agreed what it is, or of what kind it is. Such things are of a kind that can be estimated and judged by human prudence. Donell. ibid.

units.la: Obscurum est, quando cuius quid interest, cum in facto, non in iure consistat. Ius est certum, facti plerumque interpretatio prudentissimos fallit. l. 2. de iur. & fact. ignor. Quanti ergo cuiusque interest, obscurum est: plus, aliàs minus interest. Et hac ratione etiam morae definitio difficilis esse dicitur. l. mora 32. de usur. quia, si quæratur, an mora facta sit, de facto quæritur, non de iure; nec certa auctorum sententia confirmari potest. Denique hoc tantum facti est, non iuris: aliàs mora fit ex re, aliàs ex persona: aliàs interpellatio requiritur; interdum duplex, interdum nulla. Sicut etiam quod interest dicimus absolute definiri non posse, cum sit facti, non iuris. Denique obscura est definitio eius quod interest. In iis quæ obscura sunt, sequimur id quod minimum est. l. 9. sup. h. Longe gravior enim est excessus quam defectus, & ob id illud, quod interest, in dubio ad exiguum & minimum redigitur d. l. 9. arbitrio sc. iudicis l. 1. §. in hoc interdicto. Quod vi aut clam. Et generaliter ea quæ sunt facti, in arbitrio sunt iudicis. Et ea de causa commodius est etiam eriam stipulari certam summam & quantitatem, quam generaliter id quod interest, quod ad exiguam summam redigitur. §. vlt. Inst. de verbor. oblig. Melius est certam summam stipulari, quam quanti interest per se. Fieri enim plerumque non potest, v. certus modus definiatur eius, quod interest. Ideo Iustinianus in l. vnic. C. de sentent. quae pro eo, quod interest prof. dicit, se definuisse pro eo ac fieri potuit, vt in casibus, qui habent certam summam, vel naturam certam, hoc est certum corpus, vt in venditione, locatione, in quibus est pretium certum, & omnibus contractibus. Denique in casibus certis constitutur, ne aestimatio eius quod interest, excedat summam dupli. & id probatur etiam l. Titius. 43. cum l. seq. de act. emt. In casibus autem incertis non potest constitui certus modus eius, quod interest. Itaque necessario standum est sententiae iudicis. Cuiac. in Recitat. posth. Iudex autem non spectat multas allegationes & exaggerationes partis, sed veritatem & aequitatem.
units.tr: It is unclear how much a person's interest is, since it consists in fact and not in law. Law is certain; the interpretation of fact often deceives even the most prudent. l. 2. de iur. & fact. ignor. Therefore, how much each person's interest is remains unclear: it is sometimes more and sometimes less. For this reason the definition of delay (mora) is also said to be difficult, l. mora 32. de usur., because if one asks whether delay has occurred, the question is one of fact, not of law, and the opinion of the authorities cannot be confirmed with certainty. In short, this is a matter of fact and not of law: otherwise delay arises sometimes from the thing and sometimes from the person; sometimes a demand is required, sometimes twofold, sometimes none. Just so, we say that what is of interest cannot be defined absolutely, since it is a matter of fact and not of law. In short, the definition of what is of interest is obscure. In obscure matters we follow what is least, l. 9. sup. h., for excess is far more serious than deficiency, and so in doubt that which is of interest is reduced to a small and minimal amount, d. l. 9., to the discretion, namely, of the judge, l. 1. §. in hoc interdicto. Quod vi aut clam. And generally, those matters which are of fact lie within the judge's discretion. For this reason it is more convenient to stipulate a certain sum and quantity, rather than generally that which is of interest, which is reduced to a small sum, §. vlt. Inst. de verbor. oblig. It is better to stipulate a certain sum than the interest itself, for it often cannot be done unless a certain measure of that interest is fixed. Therefore Justinian, in l. unic. C. de sentent. quae pro eo quod interest prof., says that he has defined it as far as could be done, namely in cases which have a certain sum or a certain nature, that is, a certain thing, as in sale and lease, where there is a fixed price, and in all contracts. Finally, in certain cases it is established that the estimate of what is of interest may not exceed the sum of double, and this is also proved by l. Titius 43. cum l. seq. de act. emt. In uncertain cases, however, a certain measure of what is of interest cannot be fixed, and so one must necessarily abide by the judge's opinion. Cuiac. in Recitat. posth. The judge, moreover, does not look to the many allegations and exaggerations of the party, but to the truth and equity.

units.la: Lex 25. De cautione.
units.tr: Lex 25. Concerning security.

units.la: PLus cautionis in re est, quam in persona. Plus Imo tantundem. l. 4. §. 8. ff. de fidecom. libertat. Imo minus, Reales minore tempore, & re extincta tolluntur: Personales ad genus, quod nunnunquam erit, competunt; realis non competit in quadruplum. In reali probandum est dominium, quod est difficile, solue; Plus cautionis est rem habere apud se, quam contra alium agere.v. Bellonum 1. suppatat.8.
units.tr: There is more security in a thing than in a person. Plus: Indeed, the same amount. l. 4. §. 8. ff. de fidecom. libertat. Indeed, less: real (security) is extinguished in a shorter time and when the thing perishes, while personal (security) extends to the kind, which will sometimes be lacking; a real action does not extend to the fourfold. In a real action ownership must be proved, which is difficult; solve this. Having a thing in one's own possession is more security than acting against another. v. Bellonum 1. suppatat. 8.

units.la: In re] In rem vulgata Haloand. id est, in pignore, §. 4. Inst. de oblig. quæ ex delicto, in pactis. l. 21. in sin. ff. de pactis, actionibus, quæ id quod deest personalibus, supplent. l. 16. §. 3. de pignoribus. & priuilegiis realibus. l. 3. in sin. l. 4. §. 3. de censibus.
units.tr: In re: "In rem" in the common edition of Haloander, that is, in pledge, §. 4. Inst. de oblig. quae ex delicto, in pacts, l. 21. in sin. ff. de pactis, in actions which supply what is lacking in personal ones, l. 16. §. 3. de pignoribus, and in real privileges, l. 3. in sin. l. 4. §. 3. de censibus.

units.la: In persona] in personam. Pac. nisi lex personalium præcise mentionem faciat. l. 7. supra de stipulat. prætor.
units.tr: In persona: "In personam." Pac. Unless the law makes express mention of personal (actions), l. 7. supra de stipulat. prætor.

units.la: Lex 26.
units.tr: Law 26.

units.la: Qui potest inuitis alienare, multo magis & ignorantibus & absentibus potest.
units.tr: He who can alienate against the will of others can much more do so even when they are unaware and absent.

units.la: Inuitis] inuitis aliquibus. Pac. qui difficilius, idem facilius præstare potest l. 4. §. 3. de fideicom. libertat. adde l. 6. de tutor. datis. Hinc colligunt neminem cogi ad eum citandum, quo inuito actus exerceri potest: Decius.
units.tr: Against the will] against the will of some. Pac. He who can do the more difficult thing can do the easier one. l. 4. §. 3. de fideicom. libertat. add l. 6. de tutor. datis. From this they conclude that no one is to be summoned when an act can be carried out without his consent: Decius.

units.la: Absentibus] non debet expectari præsentia quæ nihil operatur. l. 13. in sin. ad Velleianum.
units.tr: Absent] one should not wait for a presence that accomplishes nothing. l. 13. in sin. ad Velleianum.

units.la: Potest] nisi ratio sit diuersa, vt in arbitro l. 18. ff. de arbitris: & in iudicibus, quorum præsentia alios potest in suam sententiam trahere. l. 39. de re iudicata. Hæc argumenta à minori sæpe fallunt. Creditor pignus vendere potest inuito debitore. E. & ignorante & absente. Negatur. Debitor priusdenunciabit, vt pignus luat. Cuia.h.v.sup. ad l.21.
units.tr: Can] unless the reason is different, as with an arbiter, l. 18. ff. de arbitris; and with judges, whose presence can draw others to their opinion, l. 39. de re iudicata. These arguments from the lesser often fail. A creditor can sell a pledge against the debtor's will; therefore also when the debtor is unaware and absent. This is denied: the debtor must first be notified, so that he may redeem the pledge. Cuia, h.v. sup. ad l.21.

units.la: Lex 27. De pactis. De causis obligationum. De modo actionum.
units.tr: Lex 27. On pacts. On the causes of obligations. On the manner of actions.

units.la: NEc ex prætorio nec ex solenni Iure priuatorum conuentione quidquam immutandum est: Quamuis obligationum causæ pactione possint immutari & ipso iure; & per pacti conuenti exceptionem: Quia actionum modus vel lege, vel per prætorem introductus, priuatorum pactionibus non infirmatur, nisi tunc, cum inchoatur actio, inter eos conuenit.
units.tr: Neither by the praetorian nor by the solemn law may private persons' agreements change anything, although the causes of obligations can be changed by agreement, both by the law itself and through the exception of an agreed pact. For the manner of an action, whether introduced by statute or by the praetor, is not weakened by private agreements, unless the parties agree on this at the moment the action is begun.

units.la: Prætorio ] Idem de publico. l.45. in sin. infr. eod. l.38. de pactis: de communi l.7. §.18. de pactis: de regulis iuris Ciuilis l.28. de pactis. de legibus, l.55. de legatis 1. de iure Reip. l.2. §.8. de administratione rer. de iurisdictione & forma iuris publici l.13. C. de Testamentis, de iure naturæ, de quo v. l.9. ff. eod.
units.tr: Praetorian: the same applies to public law. See l. 45 in fine, below, same title; l. 38, de pactis; on the common law, l. 7 §18, de pactis; on the rules of civil law, l. 28, de pactis; on laws, l. 55, de legatis; 1, de iure reipublicae; l. 2 §8, de administratione rerum; on jurisdiction and the form of public law, l. 13 C., de testamentis; on natural law, see l. 9 ff., same title.

units.la: Priuatorum ] aliud in consuetudine & statuto, quibus derogari potest iuri publico. vid. Gothof. not. ad l.9. C. de testamen.
units.tr: Private: other than custom and statute, which can derogate from public law. See Gothofredus's note on l. 9 C., de testamentis.

units.la: Nisi] nec si tunc. Graeci ita legisse videntur; quam lectionem interpretationi Bulgari anteponit Gothofr. qua fingitur, modo competituræ actioni praetoriae, vel legali resisti non posse: iam competenti posse vel ante exordium causæ, vel in ingressu iudicii.
units.tr: Unless: or not even if then. The Greeks seem to have read it so, and Gothofredus prefers this reading to the Bulgarus interpretation, on which it is supposed that one cannot resist an action that is about to be brought, either praetorian or statutory, but can resist one already brought, either before the start of the case or at the beginning of the trial.

units.la: Actio] pactio vulg. Pacto, Hugo à Porta. Rectius actio Cuia. h.
units.tr: Action: the Vulgate has pactio, "pact"; Hugo à Porta reads "pact." Cujas reads actio more correctly.

units.la: Ius Praetorium & solemne, hoc est civile, privatorum pactionibus sive conventionibus immutari vel tolli non potest; Sicut neque ius publicum: quod etiā proponitur in l. ius publicum. de pactis. Filia de iure succedit. E. non potest fieri pacto, ut non succedat. Testator facere non potest, ne lex Falcidia locum habeat. Sunt enim ea contra ius publicum. Obligationum tamen causæ mutari possunt; nempe vel ipso iure, vel per exceptionem pacti: ut, si in commodato ab initio convenerit, ne culpa praestetur, culpæ nomine ipso iure non est actio commodati. Nam pactum illud inest contractui: exceptio pacti inest actioni commodati, hoc est eam opponi non est necesse, nam res effectum habet ipso iure. Quod enim paciscimur ab initio, pars contractus esse videtur. Ad Formam sane spectat, & ex eo contractus formatur. Pacto etiam per exceptionem, obligationis causæ mutantur: vt, si ex intervallo conuenerit, ne venditor de evictione naturaliter teneatur, hoc pactum non haberet effectum, nisi per exceptionem opponeretur. l. pactum. 72. de contrahend. empt. Non enim insunt bonæ fidei iudicio. Idemque est in stipulatu, si post stipulationem conuenerit ne pecunia reddatur. leg. si unus 27. §. pactus. de pact. Igitur pacto obligationum causæ, & actiones, vel ipso iure infirmantur, vel ope exceptionis. Cuius sententiæ interpretationem statim subiicit Pomponius, quia actionum modus, &c. hoc est, quia opponi exceptionem necesse est. Nam si quis roget Pomponium: cur dixisti, per pacti conuenti exceptionem; & ipso iure? Respondebit: Actio Prætoria vel civilis ipso iure non tollitur, exceptione enim opposita opus est, nisi initio actionis conueniat. Sic initium actionis tutelæ est pubertas, cum adultus est pupillus. Generatim ergo actiones ipso iure infirmantur, si aliquid in ipso contractus initio conuenit. Et pactum ex intervallo factum, non valet nisi exceptione: ab initio factum, format actionem. Cuiac. in Recit. posth.
units.tr: Praetorian and solemn law, that is civil law, cannot be changed or abolished by private pacts or agreements, just as public law cannot; this is also laid down in l. "Ius publicum", de pactis: a daughter succeeds by law, therefore it cannot be done by pact that she should not succeed. A testator cannot prevent the Falcidian law from taking effect, for such things are against public law. The causes of obligations, however, can be changed, either by the law itself or by the exception of a pact. For example, if in a loan for use it was agreed from the outset that no liability for fault should be owed, then by the law itself there is no action on the loan for use for fault. For that pact is part of the contract; the exception of the pact belongs to the action on the loan for use, that is, it need not be opposed, since the thing takes effect by law itself. For what we agree at the beginning is seen to be part of the contract; it belongs to the form, and the contract is shaped by it. Obligations are also changed by a pact through an exception: for example, if after an interval the seller agreed that he should not be bound naturally to answer for eviction, this pact would have no effect unless it were opposed by way of exception, since it does not belong to the judgment of good faith. l. pactum 72, de contrahenda emptione. The same holds for a stipulation: if after the stipulation it was agreed that the money should not be repaid, l. si unus 27 §pactus, de pactis. Therefore by a pact the causes of obligations and the actions are either weakened by the law itself or by the aid of an exception. Pomponius immediately adds an explanation of this opinion, when he says "the manner of actions," etc., that is, because an exception must be opposed. For if someone asks Pomponius why you said "by the exception of an agreed pact" and "by the law itself," he will answer: a praetorian or civil action is not abolished by the law itself, for an exception must be opposed, unless the agreement is made at the beginning of the action. Thus the beginning of the action on guardianship is puberty, when the ward becomes an adult. Generally, therefore, actions are weakened by the law itself if something is agreed at the very beginning of the contract. A pact made after an interval has no force except by exception; a pact made at the beginning gives rise to the action. Cuiac. in Recit. posth.

units.la: Ad leg. 28. De his qui ex liberalitate conueniuntur.
units.tr: On law 28. Concerning those who are sued on the basis of liberality.

units.la: DIuus Pius rescripsit, eos qui ex liberalitate conueniuntur, in id quod facere possunt, condemnandos.
units.tr: The deified Pius rescripted that those who are sued on the basis of liberality are to be condemned only up to what they are able to pay.

units.la: Sumpta est ex l. si extraneus de Iur. dot. coniunge l. si quis crediderit ff. de pact. & l. maritum ff. solut. matr.
units.tr: The rubric is taken from the law "si extraneus", De iure dotium; join the law "si quis crediderit", De pactis, and the law "maritum", De solutionibus matrimonio.

units.la: Liberalitate ] propria, seu à se facta, non ab altero: mera, seu vera, non ob causam l. 49. in sin. l. 50. de re iudic. sed & ante rem traditam l. 9. de condict. indeb.
units.tr: Liberalitate: of one's own, that is, done by oneself and not by another; pure or true, not on account of a cause, l. 49. in sin. l. 50. de re iudic.; but also before the thing was handed over, l. 9. de condict. indeb.

units.la: In ] v. l. 12. de donationibus.
units.tr: In: see l. 12. de donationibus.

units.la: Possunt ] Facere posse videntur deducto ære alieno l. 19. §. 1. ff. de re indicata: & omnibus ita deductis, ne ipsemet donator egeat. l. 173. infr. eod.
units.tr: Able: they seem able to pay once the debt has been deducted, l. 19. §. 1. ff. de re indicata; and with all such debts deducted, so that the donor himself does not come to want, l. 173. infr. eod.

units.la: Cum quæritur, quantum quis facere possit, prius deducenda sunt alimenta; idque non tantum in donatore locum habet, sed generaliter in omnibus similibus, qui tantum præstare, quantum possunt, quod proponitur in l. in condemnatione 173. h.t. & l. inter. de re indicat. ne egeant, hoc est ne victus vestitusque desit. Nam plus est, egenum esse, quam pauperem. Egenus est, qui ne id quidem habet, quo vitam tueatur, & quod victui sufficiat. Pauper vero etiamsi habet quod victui sufficit. Senec. de benef.
units.tr: When it is asked how much someone can pay, maintenance must first be deducted. This applies not only to the donor but generally in all similar cases, where a person is required to pay only as much as he is able, as is set out in l. in condemnatione 173. h.t. & l. inter. de re indicat., so that he does not come to want, that is, so that food and clothing are not lacking. For it is more to be in want than to be poor. A needy man is one who does not even have what he needs to sustain his life and to suffice for food. A poor man, however, has what suffices for food, even if he has little more. Seneca, de benef.

units.la: Denique in donationibus deducendum est primo æs alienum. Nam plenius succurritur donatori (ne sua liberalitate pauper fiat) quam ei, à quo verum debitum exigitur l. sunt qui 16, l. inter eos 19. de re iudicat. l. qui 1d. 33. de donation. l. maritum 12. solut. matrim. l. verum 63. §. id quod. 3. pro soc. Prior ratio habetur priorum creditorum, quam eius, cui debetur ex donatione. Sed si pluribus ex donatione debeatur, puta, primo, secundo, tertio; agente primo, non deducitur quod debetur secundo aut tertio, sed potior erit causa occupantis, hoc est præuenientis, d. l. inter eos 19. de re iudicat. Et hæc de donationibus. In aliis autem personis similibus quæ in id, quod facere possunt, condemnantur, deducunt quidam alimenta: si conueniuntur ex vera causa debiti, deducetur æs alienum priuilegiatorum, vt sunt Fisc vs, Dos; & id ex cognitione; sed non id, quod debetur eiusdem conditionis creditoribus; quia inter creditores eiusdem conditionis, hoc est non priuilegiatos, melior est causa occupantis & præuenientis. Vigilantibus enim iura scripta sunt, non dormientibus. leg. pupillus 24. qua in fraud. creditor. licet is creditor, qui rem occupauit, sit tempore posterior. Nam ratio temporis obseruatur in hypothecariis tantum; non in actionibus personalibus. L. si pignus. qui potiores in pign. vid. inf. l. 173. ex Cuia. Condemnandos ] nisi tali priuilegio renunciauit donator; quia donationi, (cum habeat originem ex contractu) renunciari potest v. Decium hic n. 8.
units.tr: Finally, in the case of donations, the debt owed must first be deducted. For the donor is more fully helped (so that he does not become poor through his own generosity) than the man to whom a true debt is owed, l. sunt qui 16, l. inter eos 19. de re iudicat., l. qui 1d. 33. de donation., l. maritum 12. solut. matrim., l. verum 63. §. id quod. 3. pro soc. The claim of earlier creditors is taken into account before that of the one to whom a debt arises from the donation. But if a debt arising from the donation is owed to several persons, say first, second, and third: when the first sues, what is owed to the second or third is not deducted, but the cause of the one who has seized first, that is, who has come first, will be the stronger, d. l. inter eos 19. de re iudicat. So much for donations. In other similar persons who are condemned only up to what they can pay, some deduct maintenance. If they are sued on a true cause of debt, the debts of privileged creditors are deducted, such as the Treasury and a dowry; and this by examination. But what is owed to creditors of the same standing is not deducted, because among creditors of the same standing, that is, unprivileged ones, the cause of the one who seized first and came first is better. For written laws are made for the vigilant, not for the sleepers, leg. pupillus 24. qua in fraud. creditor., even if the creditor who seized the thing is later in time. For the order of time is observed only in hypothecary actions, not in personal actions, L. si pignus. qui potiores in pign.; see below l. 173, from Cuiacius. Are to be condemned: unless the donor has renounced such a privilege; for a donation, since it has its origin in a contract, can be renounced, see Decius here, n. 8.

units.la: Lex 29. De eo cuius initium vitios- um est.
units.tr: Law 29. Concerning that whose beginning is faulty.

units.la: Quod ab initio vitiosum est non potest tractu temporis convalescere.
units.tr: What is faulty from the beginning cannot become valid through the passage of time.

units.la: Coniunge l. qui à quolibet. de contrah. empt. & l. 5. de author. tut. & l. pen. h. t.
units.tr: Compare l. qui à quolibet. de contrah. empt. & l. 5. de author. tut. & l. pen. h. t.

units.la: Initio ] v. l. 178. l. 201. l. 210. infr. eod. 2. Eccl. 3. cap. 29. v. l. 1. ff. de regul. Caton. adde l. 27. de obligat. cap. non firmatur 18. de reg. in 6. exemplum erit in sententia l. 19. ff. de appellationibus. institutione l. 210. inf. eod. testamento aut codicillis. v. l. 201. inf. eod. matrimonio cap. 1. de desp. imp. in 6. fideicommisso l. 2. ff. de legat. 2. l. 1. ff. de reg. Caton. stipulatione leg. 83. §. 5. ff. de verb. obligat. adquisitione, laudo, liberatione, confessione, electione, Decius hic: possessione ab initio inutili, Jason in l. iuste possidet. de adquir. possess. Gothof.
units.tr: From the beginning: see l. 178., l. 201., l. 210. infr. eod.; 2. Eccl. 3.; cap. 29.; v. l. 1. ff. de regul. Caton. Add l. 27. de obligat.; cap. non firmatur 18. de reg. in 6. An example will be a sentence, l. 19. ff. de appellationibus.; an institution, l. 210. inf. eod.; a testament or codicils, v. l. 201. inf. eod.; a marriage, cap. 1. de desp. imp. in 6.; a fideicommissum, l. 2. ff. de legat. 2.; l. 1. ff. de reg. Caton.; a stipulation, leg. 83. §. 5. ff. de verb. obligat.; acquisition, approval, release, confession, election, and, as Decius says here, possession that was useless from the beginning, Jason on l. iuste possidet. de adquir. possess.; Gothofredus.

units.la: Tractu ] hoc est, ex post facto, Cuiac.
units.tr: By the passage of time: that is, after the fact, Cuiacius.

units.la: Convalescere ] Nisi duo quae sequuntur concurrant, vitii scilicet cessatio, & novissimus actus, id est, principium ipsius rei utile sequatur, idque verbis, vel aliis actibus extrinsecus declaratis, ratihabitione aliqua, ut in l. 11. ff. ru-fiuor. sticor. l. vlt. comm. pra d. l. 27. de ritu. leg. 6. C. de Nupt. l. 24. §. 1. de legat. 1. l. 1. §. 1. l. 7. de legat. 3. l. 42. de hered. instit. l. 20. §. 1. de condit. instit. L. unica C. de contractib. iudic. l. 1. C. si maior fact. quae leges alioquin contrariae essent. Gothof.
units.tr: Be made valid: unless the two following things concur, namely the cessation of the defect and a final act, that is, a useful beginning of the thing itself follows; and this by words or by other acts declared outwardly, some ratification, as in l. 11. ff. rusticor.; l. vlt. comm.; pra d. l. 27. de ritu.; leg. 6. C. de Nupt.; l. 24. §. 1. de legat. 1.; l. 1. §. 1.; l. 7. de legat. 3.; l. 42. de hered. instit.; l. 20. §. 1. de condit. instit.; L. unica C. de contractib. iudic.; l. 1. C. si maior fact., which laws would otherwise be contrary. Gothofredus.

units.la: Haec regula Catoniana habet locum in legatis, vt constat ex tit. de reg. Caton. & in institutione haeredum, vt constat ex l. penult. eod. In illis autem locum habet, quae cedunt à morte testatoris, non in conditionalibus l. 3. & l. 4. de reg. Caton. l. caetera 41. §. tractari 2. de legat. 1. Neque etiam locum habet in legatis, quae cedunt ab aditione, non morte, vt legatum vsusfructus, vsus, & habitationis, & quaedam alia, quae non transeunt in haeredem, quod ostenditur in tit. quand. dies legat. ced. Legatum relictum seruo manumisso, vel seruo haerede scripto extraneo, cedit ab aditione. Non pertinet etiam ad libertatem, quae ab aditione cedit l. 1. §. libertatem C. de caduc. tollend. excepto vno casu, qui est in l. si alienum 49. de hered. instit. Nec pertinet ad tutelas, quia incipiunt etiam ab aditione: extraneo herede scripto, non etiam necessario, vt Ioan. recte notat in l. 2. de excusat. tut. Nisi, inquit, necessario haerede scripto, vel alio tutore dato. Praeterea non pertinet ad ius nouum, hoc est ad L. Iuliam Papiam, quae hodie sublata est, iure antiquo restituto, hoc est, regula Catoniana l. vlt. de reg. Caton. ton. & l.Iul. Papia non cedunt legata à morte testatoris, sed apertis tabulis. Itemque manifestum, regulam Catonianam non pertinere ad eas leges per l. ultim. de regu. Caton. l. quisoluendo. 42. de hered. instit. Ex his legibus non tantum legata, sed etiam institutiones cedunt ab apertis tabulis: aliae, ex quibus cedunt ab aditione, non imirantur legem Iuliam & Papiam; quod de turore expressum est. l. si is qui. 31. de excusat. tut. Ex aditione cedunt, non ab apertis tabulis. Ergo regula Catoniana pertinet ad Testamenta. Est igitur in ea regula, quod vitiosum est ab initio, hoc est, statim à Testamento, vel Testamenti facti tempore: & haec regula repetitur in l. omnia 201. infr. eod. Sed in stipulationibus etiam habet locum l. inter stipulantem 83. §. sacram 5, de verb. oblig. Fallit haec regula in Testamentis l. 1. de reg. Caton. etiam in contractu. l. cum vir. 24. de usucap. Cuiac. in Recit. posth. vid. infr. l. 210.
units.tr: This Catonian rule holds in legacies, as is clear from the title de reg. Caton., and in the institution of heirs, as is clear from l. penult. eod. It holds, however, for those that vest at the death of the testator, not for conditional ones, l. 3. & l. 4. de reg. Caton.; l. caetera 41. §. tractari 2. de legat. 1. Nor does it hold for legacies that vest on acceptance of the inheritance rather than on death, such as a legacy of usufruct, use, and habitation, and certain others that do not pass to the heir, as is shown in the title quand. dies legat. ced. A legacy left to a slave who is manumitted, or to a slave instituted heir in favour of a stranger, vests on acceptance. Nor does it apply to freedom, which vests on acceptance, l. 1. §. libertatem C. de caduc. tollend., except in one case, which is in l. si alienum 49. de hered. instit. Nor does it apply to tutelages, because these also begin on acceptance, when a stranger is instituted heir and not a necessary heir, as John rightly notes on l. 2. de excusat. tut.: "unless," he says, "a necessary heir is instituted, or another tutor is given." Moreover, it does not apply to the new law, that is, to the Lex Julia Papia, which has today been abolished, the ancient law having been restored, that is, the Catonian rule, l. vlt. de reg. Caton.; and legacies under the Lex Julia Papia do not vest at the death of the testator but on the opening of the tablets. It is likewise clear that the Catonian rule does not apply to those laws, by l. ultim. de regu. Caton.; l. quisoluendo 42. de hered. instit. Under these laws not only legacies but also institutions vest on the opening of the tablets; other institutions, which vest on acceptance, do not imitate the Julian and Papian law, as has been expressed of the tutor, l. si is qui 31. de excusat. tut. They vest on acceptance, not on the opening of the tablets. Therefore the Catonian rule applies to testaments. In that rule, then, what is faulty from the beginning, that is, from the moment of the testament or the time it was made, is void; and this rule is repeated in l. omnia 201. infr. eod. But it also holds in stipulations, l. inter stipulantem 83. §. sacram 5. de verb. oblig. This rule admits an exception in testaments, l. 1. de reg. Caton., and also in contract, l. cum vir 24. de usucap.; Cuiacius, in Recit. posth.; see below l. 210.

units.la: Lex 30. De nuptiis.
units.tr: Law 30. On marriages.

units.la: NUptias non concubitus, sed consensus facit.
units.tr: Not intercourse but consent makes a marriage.

units.la: Coniunge l. 15. de Condit. & Demonstrat.
units.tr: Compare law 15, on Conditions and Demonstrations.

units.la: Consensus ὁμολογίας 2. Eccl. 3. c. 30. affectus. l. 11. C. de repudiis. ἀλλήλοις ἀμοιβαία 22. Novell. 3. An solus consensus? ait Iustinianus Novel. 74. c. 4. ὡς πρὸς γάμος ἐκ μέσης ἱππωδαγ ἀλληλέσεως: adde cap. non locum 14. ibi, solo consensu contrahitur, extra de sponsalib. c. sufficiat, ibi, Solus secundum leges consensus. 22. quaest. 2. adde l. 4. ibi, Nudus consensus. de sponsalib. Horomannus vero 4. obs. 26. negat: ait, praeterea requiri deductionem in domum mariti. l. 5. in sin. de ritu nupt. adde l. 66. in sin. de donat. inter vir, & uxor. Hanc regulam veram esse ait, in muliere in domum deducta, nihil aliud hic innuens, quam Nuptias perfici solo consensu sine tabulis & scriptura. l. 11. Cod. de repud. Gothofr. hic. sic sentit: Nuptias per verba de praesenti contractas, ita esse efficaces, ut secundum matrimonium impediant, & affinitatis causam ipsis coniugibus pariant, cum nihil obsteт eandem virginē esse & uxorem. arg. l. 7. de ritu. Ea vis est semel facti, ut id aliquando fuisse, nunquam possit negari. l. 31. infr. eod. quod accideret, ea negata uxore, quae per verba de praesenti semel fuerit accepta v. l. 15. de condit. & demonstrat. idque evidentissime probatur l. 8. C. de incestis. concubitum non requiri. Deductio tamen mariti in domum requisita fuit, l. 6. Cod. de donat. ante Nupt.
units.tr: Consent [ὁμολογίας, agreement] 2 Eccl. 3, ch. 30, affect. Law 11, C. on divorces. [ἀλλήλοις ἀμοιβαία, mutual to one another] 22 Novell. 3. Is consent alone enough? Justinian says so in Novel. 74, ch. 4 [ὡς πρὸς γάμος ἐκ μέσης ἱππωδαγ ἀλληλέσεως, as to marriage from the middle ... of mutual agreement]. Add ch. 14 non locum, where it says a contract is made by consent alone; extra, on betrothals, ch. sufficiat, where it says consent alone under the laws; 22 q. 2. Add law 4, where it says "bare consent," on betrothals. Horomannus, however, in 4 obs. 26, denies this. He says that a leading of the wife into the husband's house is also required (law 5, at the end, on the rite of marriage; add law 66, at the end, on gifts between husband and wife). He says this rule is true only of a woman led into the husband's house, meaning nothing else here than that marriage is completed by consent alone, without documents and writing (law 11, C. on divorces). Gothofredus here thinks thus: marriages contracted by words in the present tense are so effective that they impede a second marriage and produce the relationship of affinity for the spouses themselves, since nothing prevents the same woman from being both a virgin and a wife (argument from law 7, on the rite). Such is the force of a thing once done that it can never be denied that it once happened (law 31 infra, same title), which would follow if a wife once accepted by words in the present tense were denied (law 15, on conditions and demonstrations). This is most clearly proved by law 8, C. on incests, that intercourse is not required. Yet the husband's leading of the wife into his house was required (law 6, C. on gifts before marriage).

units.la: Lex 31. De factis. De eo quod est impossibile.
units.tr: Law 31. On facts. On what is impossible.

units.la: Verum est, neque pacta, neque stipulationes, factum posse tollere. Quod enim impossibile est, neque pacto neque stipulatione potest comprehendi, ut utilem actionem aut factum efficere possit.
units.tr: It is true that neither pacts nor stipulations can undo a fact. For what is impossible cannot be comprised in a pact or a stipulation, so as to produce a useful action or a fact.

units.la: Conjunge l. 50. ff. de pactis.
units.tr: Join law 50, Digest, on pacts.

units.la: re ipsa. Fictione tamen mortuus dicitur viuere, Instit. de excusat. tut. ut & aliquis bis mori. l. 51. §. 2. ad l. Aquil. & duo possidere l. 13. §. 13. de hereditat. petit.
units.tr: In fact. Yet by fiction a dead man is said to live (Institutes, on excused guardianship), and someone is also said to die twice (law 51, §2, on the Aquilian law), and two people to possess (law 13, §13, on the petition of inheritance).

units.la: v. l. 12. §. 2. ff. de captiuis.
units.tr: See law 12, §2, Digest, on captives.

units.la: v. l. 31. ff. de evict. l. 3. de condit. & demonstrat. l. 35. de verb. obligat.
units.tr: See law 31, Digest, on eviction; law 3, on conditions and demonstrations; law 35, on verbal obligations.

units.la: Ex eo quod est impossibile utile factum nasci non potest: si ita est, nec utilis actio nasci poterit.
units.tr: From what is impossible a useful fact cannot arise. If that is so, a useful action also cannot arise.

units.la: pactum vulgar. sic in manuscripto: & male. Gothofr.
units.tr: "Pactum": the common reading, so it stands in the manuscript, but wrongly. Gothofredus.

units.la: Huic regulæ addi potest l. si ita quis stipulanti 31. de evictionibus. l. aliud est promittere 174. de verb. signif. l. non impossibile. 50. de pact.
units.tr: To this rule can be added law si ita quis stipulanti 31, on evictions; law aliud est promittere 174, on the meaning of words; law non impossibile 50, on pacts.

units.la: Summa hæc est: Pacta & stipulationes factum non posse tollere, & id, quod factum est, extinguere non posse. Sic enim in l. in bello. 12. §. facti 2. de capt. & postlim. reuers. dicitur, quod desiit aliquis possidere, per restitutionem postliminii infectum fieri non posse: hoc est postliminium non posse efficere, ut, qui desiit possidere, possidere non desierit. in pactis factum versatur, in stipulatione ius. l. si unus 27. de pact. Igitur factum illud constituit exceptionem. idem etiam constituit naturalem obligationem.l. nec seruus 41.de pecul. Ergo quia in pacto factum versatur, & quidem solum spectatur, ex pacto exceptio nascitur, & obligatio naturalis. Caeterum quia ius deest pacto, hoc est, quia pactum non est iuris, ideo pactum actionem non constituit, sed exceptionem tantum & naturalem obligationem, quae sunt facti, deficiente Iure Ciuili. Verum rei impossibilis neq; stipulatio vtilem seu efficacem actionem facit, neq; pactum vtile factum, hoc est vtilem exceptionem, vel obligationem naturalem. Hac ratione videtur inutilis stipulatio aedilitia: surem non esse vespillonem, hoc est sepulchri violatorem. Nam vel est fur, vel non est. Si non est, frustra stipulamur: vel si est, impossibile est, vt non sit. Si fecit furtum, impossibile est, vt non fecerit. Item, inutilis videtur stipulatio, ne facias furem, quia non videtur hoc praestari posse, vt, qui sit fur, non sit fur. dict. l. aliud. 174. & qui est fur, fieri non potest, vt non sit. Igitur videtur inutilis ea stipulatio. Verum vtilis fiet, & vtile pactum d. l. si ita quis 31.de euict. & d.l. non impossibile. de pact. quia hac stipulatione non agitur, vt factum infectum fiat, & quod est non fiat, sed quanti interest, furem non esse, praestari, vel quanti interest furem non fieri; atque omnino vtilem actionem efficiet. Cuiac. in Recitat. posth.
units.tr: The sum is this: pacts and stipulations cannot undo a fact, and cannot extinguish what has been done. For thus it is said in law in bello 12, §facti 2, on captives and postliminy reversal, that when someone has ceased to possess, the fact cannot be undone by restoration under postliminy; that is, postliminy cannot bring it about that one who has ceased to possess has not ceased to possess. A pact concerns fact, a stipulation concerns right (law si unus 27, on pacts). Therefore that fact establishes an exception, and the same fact also establishes a natural obligation (law nec servus 41, on the peculium). So because a pact concerns fact, and indeed looks only to the fact, an exception and a natural obligation arise from the pact. Moreover, because a pact lacks right, that is, because a pact is not of right, the pact therefore does not establish an action, but only an exception and a natural obligation, which belong to fact, since civil law is lacking. But neither does a stipulation on an impossible thing make a useful or effective action, nor a pact a useful fact, that is, a useful exception or natural obligation. For this reason the aedilician stipulation seems useless: that a thief is not a grave-robber, that is, a violator of a tomb. For either he is a thief or he is not. If he is not, we stipulate in vain; or if he is, it is impossible that he should not be. If he has committed theft, it is impossible that he should not have committed it. Likewise the stipulation "that you will not make a thief" seems useless, because it does not seem that it can be promised that one who is a thief should not be a thief, and it is impossible for one who is a thief not to be one. Therefore that stipulation seems useless. Yet it will become useful, and the pact useful (said law si ita quis 31, on evictions; and said law non impossibile, on pacts), because by this stipulation it is not sought that a fact be undone and what has been done not be done, but that the interest in his not being a thief be promised, or the interest in his not becoming a thief; and in short it will produce a useful action. Cuiacius, in Recitationes posthumae.

units.la: Lex 32. De seruis. De homin- um æqualitate.
units.tr: Law 32. Concerning slaves. On the equality of men.

units.la: Quod attinet ad Ius ciuile, serui pro nullis habentur, non tamen & Iure naturali: Quia quod ad Ius naturale attinet, omnes homines æquales sunt.
units.tr: As far as civil law is concerned, slaves are regarded as nothing; but not so by the law of nature, because as far as the law of nature is concerned, all men are equal.

units.la: Ciuile ] l. 41. ff. de peculio l. 38. §. 7. de verb. oblig. & quo ad ius quoque prætorium l. 20. §. 7. ff. qui Testam. & extraordinarium leg. 7. de falsis.
units.tr: Civile] see Dig. 15.1.41 (de peculio); Dig. 45.1.38 §7 (de verborum obligationibus); and also as regards the praetorian law, Dig. 28.5.20 §7 (qui testamenta facere possunt), and the extraordinary law, Cod. 9.22.7 (de falsis).

units.la: Pro nullis ] l. 1. de iure deliberandi, id est nullius iuris habentur l. 3. in f. ff. de capite minutis.
units.tr: Regarded as nothing] l. 1. de iure deliberandi, that is, they are held to have no right, l. 3. in f. ff. de capite minutis.

units.la: Habentur ] excipe l. 4. §. 3. de edendo. leg. 53. de iudiciis l. 38. §. 7. de verb. oblig. l. 7. de falsis. vid. Gothofr. ad leg. 3. in sin. de capit. minut. & ad l. 209. inf. eod.
units.tr: Habentur] except Dig. 11.4.3 §3 (de edendo); Dig. 50.17.53 (de iudiciis); Dig. 45.1.38 §7 (de verborum obligationibus); Cod. 9.22.7 (de falsis). See Gothofredus on Dig. 4.5.3 at the end (de capitis minutione), and on Dig. 50.17.209 below in the same title.

units.la: Naturali ] idcoque solutum non repetitur. l. 13. de condict. indeb. l. 83. de solutionibus.
units.tr: Natural law] hence what has been paid is not reclaimed. l. 13. de condict. indeb., l. 83. de solutionibus.

units.la: Æquales ] natura est communis seruis l. 12. inf. de accusat. Iure naturali omnes sunt liberi. Institut. de libert. hinc seruitutem contra naturam esse dicimus l. 4. §. 1. de statu. Senec 4. Epistola 32. Quid est eques Romanus, aut libertinus, aut seruus? nomina ex ambitione, aut ex iniuria nata. Gothofr. hic.
units.tr: Equal] by nature there is a common condition for slaves, l. 12. inf. de accusat. By the law of nature all are free. Institut. de libert. Hence we say that slavery is contrary to nature, l. 4. §. 1. de statu. Seneca, Epistle 32 of Book 4. What is a Roman knight, or a freedman, or a slave? They are names born of ambition or of injury. Gothofred here.

units.la: Seruo instituto oportet dominum adire, l. nullo 7. de leg. Cornel. de fals. Seruus cum domino nullo modo consistere potest. Idem fere est, quod dicitur seruos pro mortuis haberi. l. antepen. C. eod. nulla in eos cadit obligatio: nullum arbitrii ius: ad solemnia testamenti non adhibentur: tabularii esse non possunt. Idem de seruitute receptum est. l. cum hic status 32. §. si donator. 6. de donat. int. vir. & vxor. Si vir mulieri donauerit, non valet donatio regulariter: si vir moriatur, valet eius morte, ex Constitut. Seueri: si seruus fiat, non valet. Denique seruus est in nullo numero & ex persona domini tantum stipulatur. Instit. de stip. seruor. in princip. Cum stipulatur seruus, domino stipulari videtur. Iure tamen naturali, vt subiicit I C. pro nullo non habetur, quia iure naturali omnes homines sunt liberi. Seruitus contra ius naturale est. Hinc vero fit, vt seruus, qui iure naturali incognitus est, obligetur naturaliter tantum, non etiam ciuiliter. l. necessarius. 41. de pecul. cum dicimus Seruum debere, factum demonstramus, non ius, l. eo tempore 50. de pecul. l. atqui natura 19. de negot. gest. Regulariter igitur seruus iure naturali obligatur. Excipiuntur tamen certi casus, quibus etiam naturaliter non obligatur. Iure Gentium non obligatur: si seruus vtroque iure nullus est, neutro obligatur iure, neque Gentium neque Ciuili; etsi ex diuerso liber homo, qui cum seruo contrahit, obligatur naturaliter & Ciuiliter, vt & dominus, non ciuiliter tantum. d. l. necseruus. Nam absurdum esset, si in uno esset naturalis & Ciuilis obligatio, in altero naturalis tantum; & qui debet Iure Gentium, plerumque etiam debet Iure Ciuili. l. 1. de pact. Interdum quod Iure Gentium debetur, non debetur Iure Ciuili, vt pupillus, qui pecuniam mutuam accepit sine tutoris authoritate, si factus sit locupletior ex ea, iure Gentium debet, iure Ciuili non debet, nisi hodie ex Constitutione D. Pii. Qui iure naturali non debet, plerumque etiam non debet Iure Ciuili. Verum vtraque obligatio, Iuris Gentium & Iuris naturæ inhibet condictionem indebiti, hoc est, qui altero iure obligatus soluit, non condicit. Hic est effectus obligationis vtriusque; qui soluit, quod debet iure naturæ vel Gentium, non condicit. Item vtrique obligationi accedunt fideiussio & pignus. l. si pœna 19. l. si non sortem 26. §. libertus 12. de condict. indeb. leg. 2. de fideiussor.
units.tr: An heir instituted as a slave must approach the master, l. nullo 7. de leg. Cornel. de fals. A slave can in no way coexist with his master. It is nearly the same as saying that slaves are held as dead: l. antepen. C. eod. no obligation falls upon them, no right of judgment belongs to them, they are not admitted to the solemnities of a will, and they cannot act as notaries. The same has been received concerning servitude: l. cum hic status 32. §. si donator 6. de donat. int. vir. & vxor. If a husband has given something to his wife, the gift is as a rule not valid; if the husband dies, it becomes valid by his death, by the constitution of Severus; if the wife becomes a slave, it is not valid. Finally, a slave is counted among no one and stipulates only in the person of his master, Instit. de stip. seruor. in princip. When a slave stipulates, he is seen to stipulate for his master. Yet by natural law, as the jurist adds, he is not regarded as nothing, because by natural law all men are free; slavery is against natural law. Hence it comes about that a slave, who is unknown to natural law, is bound only naturally, not also civilly: l. necessarius 41. de pecul. When we say that a slave owes, we demonstrate a fact, not a right: l. eo tempore 50. de pecul., l. atqui natura 19. de negot. gest. As a rule, therefore, a slave is bound by natural law. Certain cases are excepted, however, in which he is not bound even naturally. He is not bound by the law of nations: if a slave is nothing under both laws, he is bound by neither law, neither that of nations nor civil law; although, conversely, a free man who contracts with a slave is bound naturally and civilly, as is the master, and not civilly only, d. l. necseruus. For it would be absurd if there were a natural and civil obligation in one case, and a natural obligation only in the other; and one who owes by the law of nations usually also owes by civil law, l. 1. de pact. Sometimes what is owed by the law of nations is not owed by civil law: for example, a ward who received a loan of money without the authority of his guardian owes by the law of nations if he has become richer from it, but does not owe by civil law, unless today by the constitution of the divine Pius. One who does not owe by natural law usually does not owe by civil law either. But both obligations, that of the law of nations and that of nature, exclude the condictio indebiti; that is, one who pays while bound by the other law cannot sue to recover it. This is the effect of both obligations: one who pays what he owes by natural law or the law of nations cannot reclaim it. Likewise, suretyship and pledge attach to both kinds of obligation, l. si pœna 19. l. si non sortem 26. §. libertus 12. de condict. indeb., leg. 2. de fideiussor.

units.la: Lex 33. De Actore & Reo.
units.tr: Lex 33. On Plaintiff and Defendant

units.la: IN eo quod vel is qui petit, vel is à quo petitur, lucri facturus est; durior causa est petitoris.
units.tr: In a case where either the one who sues or the one from whom he sues will make a gain, the position of the claimant is the harder one.

units.la: Coniunge l.125. & l.128. cum ibi notatis.
units.tr: Join l.125. & l.128. with the notes there.

units.la: Lucri ] lucri causa Pac. Duobus de lucro certantibus, deterior est actoris conditio, 2. Eclog. 3. cap. 33. nisi alterius causa tempore pendeat l. 98. inf. eod. De lucro adde l. 41. in sin. l. unic. versf. lucratiua C. de imponend. lucrat. descript.lib.10.tit.35.
units.tr: Lucri ] of gain; lucri causa Pac. When two parties contend over gain, the position of the claimant is the worse, 2. Eclog. 3. cap. 33. unless the cause of the other party was pending at an earlier time, l. 98 inf. eod. On gain add l. 41 in sin., l. unic. versf. lucratiua C. de imponend. lucrat. descript., lib. 10, tit. 35.

units.la: Peritoris ]l. 154. infr. eod. econtrario melior est possessoris v.l.126.inf.l.128.l.154.inf.eod.l.41. l.48.ff.de re iudic.
units.tr: Petitoris ] l. 154 infr. eod. Conversely, the position of the possessor is the better one: v. l. 126 inf., l. 128, l. 154 inf. eod., l. 41, l. 48 ff. de re iudic.

units.la: Hæc regula est eadem cum ea,quam Vlpian. constituit in l.nemo §. vlt. inf. h. t. Cum de lucro quæritur duorum, hoc est, actoris & rei, melior est causa possidentis l.in pari 128. hoc tit. in pari causa potior possessor habetur. Theoph. in §. æque. Instit. de act. §. retinendæ Instit. de interdict. Petitor probare debet, quod intendit, ideoque est melior causa possidentis; nisi probet, possessio manet in prima causa. Nam possessori non incumbit onus probandi; imo cum est obscurum, quod in iudicium erat deductum, semper iudicatur contra petitorem. Nam debuit secum diligentius considerare, antequam ageret. Qua de causa actio de dolo est temporaria, exceptio perpetua. l. vlt. §. penult. de doli except. l.1. de Saluian. interdict.
units.tr: This rule is the same as the one Ulpian laid down in l. nemo §. vlt. inf. h. t. When a dispute over gain arises between two parties, that is, the claimant and the defendant, the cause of the possessor is the better: l. in pari 128 hoc tit. where two causes are equal, the possessor is held to be stronger. Theoph. in §. æque. Instit. de act. §. retinendæ Instit. de interdict. The claimant must prove what he asserts, and so the cause of the possessor is the better one; unless he proves it, possession remains in its first state. For the possessor is not burdened with the obligation to prove anything; indeed, when a matter that was brought into court is unclear, judgment is always given against the claimant. For he ought to have considered the matter more carefully before he brought the suit. For this reason the action for fraud is temporary, but the exception is perpetual. l. vlt. §. penult. de doli except. l.1. de Saluian. interdict.

units.la: Lex 34. De Interpretatione Contractuum.
units.tr: Lex 34. On the Interpretation of Contracts

units.la: SEmper in stipulationibus & in cæteris contractibus id sequimur quod actum est, aut, si non appareat quod actum est, erit consequens, vt id sequamur quod in regione, in qua actum est, frequentatur. Quid ergo si neque regionis mos appareat, quia varius fuit? ad id quod minimum est, redigenda summa est.
units.tr: In stipulations and in other contracts we always follow what was agreed; or, if what was agreed does not appear, it will follow that we follow what is customary in the region where the transaction took place. What then if the custom of the region does not appear, because it was inconsistent? The sum must be reduced to the smallest amount.

units.la: Semper ] quoties scilicet constat de voluntate. Alias si nullis signis extrinsecis voluntas scripto manifesto contraria declaretur, scripturæ stabitur. l. 19. ff. de vsu. legato. l. 112. l. 126. §. 2. in f. de verb. obligat. l. 68. §. 1. ff. de fide inssoribus. l. vlt. C. comm. utriusque iudicij. Est enim scriptura mentis & animi testimonium ac indicium, eam tamen ex communi vsu interpretamur. l. 7. §. 2. in sin. ff. de supellect. aut certo iudicio prudentum l. 125. ff. de verb. significat.
units.tr: Semper ] that is, whenever the intention is clearly established. Otherwise, if by no external signs the intention is shown to be contrary to a clear writing, the writing will stand. l. 19. ff. de vsu. legato. l. 112. l. 126. §. 2. in f. de verb. obligat. l. 68. §. 1. ff. de fideiussoribus. l. vlt. C. comm. utriusque iudicij. For a writing is a testimony and indication of the mind and spirit; yet we interpret it according to common usage l. 7. §. 2. in sin. ff. de supellect. or by the certain judgment of the learned l. 125. ff. de verb. significat.

units.la: Actum ] v. l. 52. ff. de verb. oblig. 2. Eclog. 3. cap. 34. quod agitur l. 3. ff. de reb. creditis. actum opponitur dicto. l. 6. §. 1. ff. de contrah. empt. Actum igitur est mens contrahentium ac voluntas leg. 219. ff. de verb. signif. l. vlt. C. quæ res pign. Res l. 41. ff. de Iure dotium; Veritas l. 1. & 3. C. plus valere quod agitur.
units.tr: What was done ] see l. 52. ff. de verb. oblig.; Eclog. 3, cap. 34; "what is being done", l. 3. ff. de reb. creditis. What was done is opposed to what was said. See l. 6. §. 1. ff. de contrah. empt. What was done, therefore, is the mind and will of the contracting parties; see leg. 219. ff. de verb. signif.; l. vlt. C. quae res pign. The thing: see l. 41. ff. de Iure dotium; The truth: see l. 1 and 3 C. that what is done has more force.

units.la: Aut ] quod si non apparet: alias, vnde si non apparet. Pac.
units.tr: Aut ] that is, if it does not appear; otherwise, "unde si non apparet." Pac.

units.la: Id ] id est, consuetudinem regionis sequimur Eclog. ib. v. l. 50. in f. de legatis 1. adde l. 3. in sin. ff. de testib. leg. 21. §. 1. in sin. Qui Testament. adde leg. 37. ff. de legib. l. 3. l. 7. §. 2. in sin. ff. de supellect. l. 14. §. 2. de alim. l. 17. §. 1. de aqua plun. & ideo conducere, cocedere, cotrahere, & quidquis agere, pro more regionis in dubio præsumitur: vide Decium hic. Nam sicut natura non separatur à subiecto, ita nec à consueto. Quod est de consuetudine, habetur pro pacto. Gothofr. hic.
units.tr: Id ] that is, we follow the custom of the region. Eclog. ib. v. l. 50. in f. de legatis 1. adde l. 3. in sin. ff. de testib. leg. 21. §. 1. in sin. Qui Testament. adde leg. 37. ff. de legib. l. 3. l. 7. §. 2. in sin. ff. de supellect. l. 14. §. 2. de alim. l. 17. §. 1. de aqua plun. And therefore, in case of doubt, it is presumed that one hires, grants, contracts, and does whatever else is done, according to the custom of the region. See Decium hic. For just as nature is not separated from its subject, so neither is it separated from what is customary. What rests on custom is held to be an agreement. Gothofr. hic.

units.la: In omnibus contractibus in primis id sequimur, quod actum est; vt in bonæ fidei contractibus veniunt vsuræ, de quibus actum est; & si non appareat, quid actum sit, veniunt vsuræ, quæ in ea regione frequentantur, in qua contractum est l. 1. pr. l. 37. de vsur. Et si hic mos varius sit, veniunt vsuræ leviores. In contractibus stricti iuris veniunt hæ, quæ in his constitutæ sunt. Denique nullæ debentur, nisi certæ in stipulationem deductæ sint: vt, Centum & vsuras promittis? Si non appareat conuentio vsurarum, nullæ debentur; l. quod in stipulatione 31. l. tutor. 41. §. vlt. de vsur. In contractibus vero bonæ fidei veniunt ex officio iudicis. Potest etiam exemplum poni de emptione, venditione, & euictione l. 6. de euict. Vt rursus, si incertus sit mos regionis, dicamus potius conuentum esse de simpla, quam de dupla, de qua non cauetur, nisi ex conuentione vel more regionis. Si conuentio desit, simplum compelletur venditor exsoluere: sic et-iam iam si mos non appareat, simpla tantum præstatur. Itaque semper in obscuris sequimur, non quod minimum est, sed primo, quod actum est: deinde consuetudinem: tertio demum quod est minimum. Sed hoc extremum fit non tantum in contractibus; sed etiam in aliis rebus & causis æstimatio eius, quod interest, ad exiguam summam reducitur l. vlt. de prætor. stipul. Et si iudices plures damnauerint diversis summis, nullam sententiam spectamus: sed id quod minimum est, sequimur. l. inter pares 38. de re iud. Nam inter pares sententias potior est sententia, quæ pro reo pronuntiatur, quod ius est vetustissimum, vt apparet ex Augustino lib.7. de Ciuitat. Dei. Hodie non pronunciatur pro reo in pari causa, sed assumuntur alii iudices, qui hanc diversitatem dirimant. Hoc etiam quod dicitur in hac l. Accurs. transfert ad nummos promissos indistincte, & ita vtimur, vt exiguiores debeantur. Cuiac. in Recit. posth.
units.tr: In all contracts we first follow what was agreed: thus in contracts of good faith the interest is due which was agreed upon; and if it does not appear what was agreed, the interest is due which is customary in the region where the contract was made. l. 1. pr. l. 37. de vsur. And if this custom is varied, the lighter interest is due. In contracts of strict law, those interests are due which have been established for them. Finally, none is owed unless a certain sum has been brought into the stipulation, as in: "Do you promise a hundred and interest?" If no agreement on interest appears, none is owed; l. quod in stipulatione 31. l. tutor. 41. §. vlt. de vsur. In contracts of good faith, however, interest is awarded by the office of the judge. An example may also be given from purchase, sale, and eviction l. 6. de euict. Conversely, if the custom of the region is uncertain, we should say that what was agreed was the single rather than the double amount, since the double is not guaranteed unless by agreement or by the custom of the region. If there is no agreement, the seller is compelled to pay only the single amount; so too, if the custom does not appear, only the single amount is owed. Thus in unclear matters we always follow, not the smallest amount, but first what was agreed; then custom; and third, finally, the smallest amount. But this last rule applies not only to contracts; in other matters and causes too, the estimate of the interest involved is reduced to a small sum. l. vlt. de prætor. stipul. And if judges have condemned in different sums, we look to no one sentence, but follow the smallest sum. l. inter pares 38. de re iud. For among equal sentences the sentence pronounced in favour of the defendant prevails, which is the most ancient law, as appears from Augustine, lib. 7, de Ciuitat. Dei. Today judgment is not pronounced for the defendant in an equal case, but other judges are summoned to resolve the disagreement. What is said in this law Accursius transfers to promised money without distinction, and we use it so that the smaller sums are owed. Cuiac. in Recit. posth.

units.la: Ad Leg. 35. Quibus modis tollitur obligatio.
units.tr: On Law 35. By what means an obligation is dissolved.

units.la: NIhil tam naturale est, quam eo genere quicque dissoluere, quo colligatum est. Ideo verborum obligatio verbis tollitur: Nudi consensus obligatio, contrario consensu dissoluitur.
units.tr: Nothing is so natural as for a thing to be dissolved by the same means by which it was bound. Therefore an obligation made by words is dissolved by words, and an obligation arising from bare consent is dissolved by contrary consent.

units.la: Ex l. an inutilis. de accept.
units.tr: From l. an inutilis, de accept.

units.la: hoc fallit in matrimoniis. v.l.8.C. de repud. & bonorum possessione l.vlt.Cod.qui admitti.
units.tr: This does not hold in marriages. See l. 8, C. de repud. and l. ult., Cod. qui admitti, and on possession of goods.

units.la: id est, eadem fide, alio pacto, altero consensu, aliis verbis v.§.1. Inst.quib.mod.toll.oblig.
units.tr: That is, by the same good faith, by another agreement, by a different consent, or by other words; see § 1, Inst. quib. mod. toll. oblig.

units.la: quodque vulgat.Hal.
units.tr: And this is what is commonly taught, Hal.

units.la: l.100.l.153.infr. eod.v.l.80.ff.de solutionib. cap.1. exter.eo. §.vlt. Instit.quib.mod.toll. oblig.l.1.C quando licet ab empt.
units.tr: l.100. l.153. infra eod. v. l.80. ff. de solutionibus; cap. 1. extra eod. §. ult. Instit. quibus modis toll. oblig.; l.1. C. quando licet ab empt.

units.la: ex necessitate scilicet, non ex superfluo. ideo Testamentum ad pias causas factum coram septem testibus, tollitur per secundum factum coram duobus testibus. Decius hic num.5. Gothof. Huic l.iungi potest l.8. §. penult. de acceptil. quae ostendit, obligationem verborum etiam tolli verbis, hoc est acceptilatione, quae & ipsa fit solemnibus verbis. Sic consensus contrario consensu tollitur, res re.l.prout 80. de solutionib. Sed non est existimandum, sic solummodo solui, sed & aliis modis, vt verborum obligatio solutione, nouatione, confusione, & aliis quibusdam. Pacto non tollitur obligatio, nisi per exceptionem. Certis modis contrahitur obligatio & dissoluitur l.exceptiones.7.§.1. de except.l. obligamur.52. de obligat.& act. Pactum semper valet ad exceptionem. Regula haec tantum est de obligatione ex contractu tollenda ipso iure. Cuiac.in Recit.post.
units.tr: That is, of necessity, not by surplus. Hence a testament made for pious causes before seven witnesses is annulled by a later one made before two witnesses. See Decius here, num. 5; Gothofredus. To this law may be joined l. 8, § penult., de acceptil., which shows that an obligation of words is also dissolved by words, that is, by acceptilation, which is itself made in solemn words. So consent is dissolved by contrary consent, and a thing by a thing; see l. prout 80, de solutionib. But it should not be thought that this is the only way it is dissolved; it is also dissolved by other means, as an obligation of words is dissolved by payment, novation, confusion, and certain others. An obligation is not dissolved by a pact, except by way of exception. Obligations are contracted and dissolved in certain fixed ways; see l. exceptiones 7, § 1, de except.; l. obligamur 52, de obligat. & act. A pact always avails as an exception. This rule applies only to an obligation arising from contract, which is dissolved by the law itself. Cuiacius, in Recit. posth.

units.la: Lex 36. De Culpa.
units.tr: Law 36. On Fault.

units.la: Culpa est, imminiscere se rei, ad se non pertinenti.
units.tr: Fault is meddling with a matter that does not pertain to oneself.

units.la: Culpa
units.tr: Fault

units.la: Est
units.tr: is

units.la: Rei id est negotio.
units.tr: of a thing, that is, of a business.

units.la: Nihil pertinenti id est, cuius est ignarus ac imperitus quæ est aliena , in qua nullum ius habet aut interesse l.71. l.181. de verbor. signif. Gothofr. hic Exemplo sit. Cum vellem rem vindicare, quam meam esse existimabam, quidam se obtulit defensioni rei, & litem contestatus est, & causa cecidit: negat se possidere? hic condemnatur omnino, quod est in l. qui se liti 45. de hared. petit. & l.25. de rei vind. quoniam suo nomine rem defendit, nec potest dici gestor, nec voluntarius procurator, aut amicus, ut dicitur apud Cicer. in Brut. Huic regulæ etiam potest esse locus in procuratore voluntario. Nam etsi voluntarii procuratoris officium laudetur, non culpetur, nonnunquam tamen hoc ei imputatur, cur se immiscuerit rei ad se non pertinenti. Nam si minoris 25. annis causam suscepit, & damnatus sit, ipse solus iudicati actione tenetur, nec regressum aduersus minorem habet. l. eum qui. 46. de minorib. l. iam tamen 5. §. nunc videamus. 3. iudicat. solui. Nam hic accessit ad rem ad se non pertinentem. Quidam fideiussit pro alio iudicatum solui, hic promittit quantitatem certam, nec etiam defensionem suscipit. Sed quid si defensionem subeat vltro, & condemnetur? Repeter quidem, quod soluit, à reo principali, sed non sumptu litis. Nam accessit ad defensionem, cui non erat adstrictus. Laus igitur est interdum, immiscere se rei amici, & culpa nonnunquam.
units.tr: Not pertaining to oneself, that is, of which one is ignorant and inexperienced, which belongs to another and in which one has no right or interest: l.71. l.181. de verbor. signif. Gothofredus. Here is an example. When I wished to recover a thing that I believed to be mine, a certain man offered himself to defend the thing, joined issue, and lost the case. He says he is not in possession? He is wholly condemned, as is laid down in l. qui se liti 45. de hared. petit. and l.25. de rei vind., since he defended the thing in his own name. He cannot be called a manager of affairs, nor a voluntary agent, nor a friend, as is said in Cicero, in Brut. This rule can also apply to a voluntary agent. For although the office of a voluntary agent is praised and not blamed, nevertheless it is sometimes imputed to him that he meddled with a matter not pertaining to himself. For if he undertook the case while under twenty-five years of age, and was condemned, he alone is bound by the action on the judgment, and has no recourse against the minor: l. eum qui. 46. de minorib. l. iam tamen 5. §. nunc videamus. 3. iudicat. solui. For here he came to a matter not pertaining to himself. Someone stood surety for another that the judgment be paid; he promises a certain sum but does not take up the defence. But what if he voluntarily undertakes the defence and is condemned? He may indeed recover what he paid from the principal debtor, but not the cost of the suit, for he came to a defence to which he was not bound. Meddling in a friend's affair is therefore sometimes praiseworthy, and sometimes blameworthy.

units.la: Ad leg. 37. De condemnatione & absolutione.
units.tr: On law 37. On condemnation and acquittal.

units.la: NEmo qui condemnare potest, absoluere non potest.
units.tr: No one who can condemn can acquit.
