units.tr: More right: but the same, for example the same ownership (l. 11. §. 2. ff. de act. empt.), the same servitudes, causes and rights, the same burdens and defects (l. 1. C. sine censu). The law, however, says more right; l. nemo, 120. h.t.: more advantage. No one gives more right than he has; l. 59. h.t. An heir has the action which the deceased had, and sometimes a fuller one: l. reperitur 84. ad L. Falcid.; leg. si per imprudentiam 51. §. non mirum 3. de evictionibus. The heir has the same right. But sometimes more is sold than would have been sold while the testator lived, because of accidents.

units.la: Eadem igitur est actio: sed aliquanto est plenior. Excipiuntur actiones, quæ defuncto, non hæredi, competunt: actio de calumniatoribus, actiones populares, & actio iniuriarum, & quæ vindictæ, non pecuniæ habent persecutionem, de quibus in l. 38. Excipiuntur etiam visus, visusfructus, habitatio, privilegia personalia, quæ hæres non habet. Iura autem hereditaria sequuntur hæredem, nempe omnia incommoda & commoda; & actio quæ cœpit in defunctum, in hæredem transit: leviort tamen nonnunquam l. 4. de magistr. conveniend. leg. 1. C. de hared. tut. Et quod dicitur, heredem succedere in omne ius defuncti, tam actiue quam passiue accipitur: ut hæredi prosit, quod defuncto profuit: & noceat, quod defuncto nocuit. leg. cum heres 11. de diuers. & temp. prescript. Mala fides, quæ obstat defuncto ne vsucapiat, obstat etiam hæredi eius; & est successor vitii defuncti: succedit etiam in malam fidem defuncti, licet sit bonæ fidei possessor. Diuersa causa est eorum, qui in rem succedunt: quoniam hi certo iure non habent actiones, nisi illis cedantur. Non etiam succedunt in vitia l. an vitium 5. de diuers. & tempor. prescript. cuiusmodi sunt legatarii, emptores, &c. Emptor bonæ fidei potest vsucapere rem emptam, licet venditor non potuerit. Eadem causa est legatarii & donatarii dict. l. an vitium.
units.tr: The action is therefore the same, though somewhat fuller. Excepted are actions which belong to the deceased but not to the heir: the action against calumniators, popular actions, and the action for injury, and those which aim at vengeance rather than money, of which see l. 38. Excepted too are usufruct, use, habitation, and personal privileges, which the heir does not have. But hereditary rights follow the heir, namely all burdens and benefits; and an action which began against the deceased passes to the heir, though sometimes in a lighter form: l. 4. de magistr. conveniend.; leg. 1. C. de hared. tut. And when it is said that the heir succeeds to all the right of the deceased, this is taken in both active and passive senses: so that what profited the deceased profits the heir, and what harmed the deceased harms the heir. leg. cum heres 11. de diuers. & temp. prescript. Bad faith, which prevents the deceased from acquiring by usucaption, also prevents his heir; the heir is successor to the defect of the deceased, and succeeds even to the deceased's bad faith, although he himself may be a possessor in good faith. The case is different for those who succeed to a thing, since these have no actions by sure right unless these are assigned to them. Nor do they succeed to defects: l. an vitium 5. de diuers. & tempor. prescript.; such are legatees, buyers, and so on. A buyer in good faith can acquire by usucaption the thing bought, even though the seller could not. The same reasoning applies to a legatee and a donee: dict. l. an vitium.

units.la: In hæredibus ratio diuersitatis est manifesta, quia sunt vniuersi iuris successores, & vicem defuncti sustinent. Sed quod ad hanc regulam attinet, pertinet ea ad quosuis successores. Siis qui vendidit & tradidit, dominus fuerit, transferet dominium: si dominus non fuerit, non transferet dominium in emptorem, sed possessionem solum transferet l. traditio 20. de acquir. rer. dom. l. aliud est vendere 160. h. t. Id tamen vitiatur nonnunquam. Nam creditor distrahendo pignus, dominium transfert pignoris, quod non habet. l. non est novum 46. de acquir rer. dom. Cuius rei rationem adfert Iustinianus, quia distrahit ex voluntate debitoris, atque adeo nihil mirum, si transferatur dominium, distrahente eo. Sed creditor potest pignus distrahere contra conuentionem: scilicet debitore admonito, & non luente pignus. Verum hoc casu videtur distrahere ex tacita voluntate debitoris, cum debitor pignus non luat, quando ei denunciatum est. De omnibus tam rei quam iuris successoribus etiam est, quod dicitur l. iniussu 156. §. cum quis 2. h. t. Plerumque emtoris eadem esse causa debet circa petendum & defendendum, quæ fuit auctoris. Et quod proponitur in l. qui in ius 177. h. t. qui in ius dominiumve alterius succedit, iure eius uti debet. In ius, ut si à non domino; in dominium, ut si à domino, no, vel potius, in ius, hoc est nomen: in dominium, vt si rem emerit, leg. sicut 37. de actionem emt. Lex ait, dolum emptori non nocere, nec prodesse: quia non succedit in vitia venditoris. Eodem ergo iure non vtitur emtor; nec nocet emtori, quod venditori. Non eodem iure est emtor, scilicet passiue: quia non patitur dolum venditoris; succedit tamen emtor in ius & conditionem, quae rei adhaeret. l. apud 4. §. de auctoris 27. de doli exceptio. vt si res sit furtiua, emptor non vsucapiet: si res sit pignori obligata, emtor tenebitur actione hypothecaria: si res sit aliena, emptor tenebitur vindicatione: & si peruenerit ad dominum res, & velit agere Publiciana, repellitur l. pennult. de Publ. in rem act. Beneficium venditoris prodest emptori: dolus si non prodest venditori, & emptori non prodest; atque ita cum emtor lucrum capiat ex dolo venditoris, eodem iure vtimur: submouetur enim, vt si emptor velit accessione temporis, & persona venditoris ad vsucapiendum vti, sane vtetur cum sua causa, eiusque vitiis. Si initium sit vitiosum in persona auctoris, erit etiam in persona emptoris. d. §. de auctoris. l. Pomponius 13. §. 1. de adquir. possess. atq; ita mala fides venditoris non prodest emptori. Sed si emptor nolit eo tempore vti, hoc est, accessione temporis, & velit tunc primum vsucapere, iure vsucapit, nec obe rit vitium auctoris,
units.tr: The reason for the difference among heirs is plain, since they are successors in the whole of right and stand in the place of the deceased. But as far as this rule is concerned, it applies to all successors. If the one who sold and delivered was the owner, he transfers ownership; if he was not the owner, he does not transfer ownership to the buyer, but only transfers possession: l. traditio 20. de acquir. rer. dom.; l. aliud est vendere 160. h.t. Yet this is sometimes overridden. For a creditor, by selling a pledge, transfers ownership of the pledge, which he does not have: l. non est novum 46. de acquir. rer. dom. Justinian gives the reason for this, namely that he sells by the will of the debtor, so that it is no wonder if ownership is transferred when the debtor is the one who sells. But a creditor may sell a pledge contrary to agreement, namely when the debtor has been warned and does not redeem the pledge. In this case, however, he seems to sell by the tacit will of the debtor, since the debtor, having been notified, does not redeem the pledge. What is said in l. iniussu 156. §. cum quis 2. h.t. applies to all successors, both to things and to rights. In general, the buyer's position in seeking and defending should be the same as that of his author. And what is laid down in l. qui in ius 177. h.t.: whoever succeeds into the right or ownership of another must use his right. "Into the right" as when one buys from a non-owner; "into the ownership" as when one buys from an owner; or rather, "into the right" refers to a name, "into the ownership" to one who has bought a thing: leg. sicut 37. de actionem emt. The law says that the buyer's fraud neither harms nor benefits him, since he does not succeed to the defects of the seller. The buyer therefore does not use the same right, nor is he harmed by what harms the seller. The buyer is not in the same position with respect to liability, since he does not suffer the seller's fraud; yet the buyer succeeds to the right and to the condition which adheres to the thing: l. apud 4. §. de auctoris 27. de doli exceptio. Thus if the thing is stolen, the buyer will not acquire it by usucaption; if the thing is pledged, the buyer will be liable to the hypothecary action; if the thing belongs to another, the buyer will be liable to the action of vindication; and if the thing comes to its owner and he wishes to sue by the Publician action, he is repelled: l. pennult. de Publ. in rem act. The seller's benefit profits the buyer; the seller's fraud does not profit the seller, and does not profit the buyer. And so, since the buyer gains from the seller's fraud, we use the same right: for it is set aside, so that if the buyer wishes to use, for usucaption, the accession of time and the person of the seller, he will certainly use it with its own cause and its defects. If the beginning of possession is defective in the person of the author, it will also be defective in the person of the buyer: d. §. de auctoris. l. Pomponius 13. §. 1. de adquir. possess. And so the seller's bad faith does not profit the buyer. But if the buyer does not wish to use the accession at that time, that is, the accession of time, and wishes then for the first time to acquire by usucaption, he acquires by right, and the defect of the author does not stand in his way, if he himself was a buyer in good faith. The same distinction must be applied in l. in his 175. §. ultim. h.t. I ought not to be in a better position than my author, from whom the right passed to me. A woman who guarantees for another is protected by the Senatusconsult...

units.la: H ris, si ipse bonæ fidei emptor fuerit. Eadem distinctio adhibenda est l. in his 175. §. ultim. h. t. Non debeo melioris esse conditionis, quam autor meus à quo ius in me transiit. Mulier intercedit pro alio, munitur Senatusconsulto Velleiano. Intercedit varie fideiubendo, pignora dando. Finge; pignus dedit creditori, & is vendidit pignus bonæ fidei emptori: mulieri datur repetitio rei suæ etiam aduersus bonæ fidei emptorem, ne melioris sit conditionis: & venditur res cum sua causa. Sic igitur dicemus: in eo iure quod transit ab autore in emptorem, non est melior conditio emptoris, eodem igitur iure vti debet. Potest eadem causa esse, & tamen melior potest esse conditio emptoris in eo, quod sibi parat: vt bonæ fidei emptor potest sibi vsucapere, quod venditor propter malam fidem non potuit. Nam hoc ius vsucapiendi non transit ab autore in emptorem, vel vt Accurs. recte ait, emptor non à venditore, sed à se ius vsucapiendi habet. Nam non ab autore, sed à legibus vsucapio requiritur. Igitur mala fides autoris non perfringit bonam fidem emptoris: qua in re emptor, & cæteri, qui huiusmodi ius habent, distant à donatariis & legatariis, qui lucratiuam tantum causam habent. Hi exceptionem doli patiuntur ex persona donatoris vel testatoris, non emptor ex persona venditoris. d. l. apud 4. §. ff §. si quis. de dolo except. In vsucapiendo nulla est differentia inter eos. Nam & emptor & legatarius bona fide vsucapiunt, quod defunctus vel autor non potuit. Sed in exceptione doli, quae illis agentibus obiicitur, est differentia inter eos, qui succedunt ex causa lucrativa, & eos qui succedunt ex causa non lucrativa. Cuia, in Recitat. posth.
units.tr: ...if the buyer himself was a bona fide purchaser. The same distinction must be applied in l. in his 175, §. ultim. h. t. I ought not to be in a better position than my author, from whom the right has passed to me. A woman who stands surety for another is protected by the Senatusconsultum Velleianum. She stands surety in various ways, by guaranteeing a debt and by giving pledges. Suppose she gave a pledge to a creditor, and he sold it to a bona fide buyer. The woman is granted recovery of her property even against the bona fide buyer, so that he is not in a better position, and the thing is sold together with its defect. So we shall say: in the right that passes from author to buyer, the buyer's position is no better, so he must use the same right. The cause may be the same, and yet the buyer's position may be better in what he acquires for himself. A bona fide buyer can acquire by usucaption what the seller could not acquire because of his bad faith. For this right of usucaption does not pass from author to buyer; or, as Accurs. rightly says, the buyer has the right of usucaption not from the seller but from himself. Usucaption is required not by the author but by the laws. So the bad faith of the author does not destroy the good faith of the buyer. In this respect the buyer and others who hold such a right differ from donees and legatees, who have only a gratuitous cause. These suffer the exception of fraud on account of the person of the donor or testator, whereas the buyer does not suffer it on account of the person of the seller. d. l. apud 4, §. ff §. si quis, de dolo except. In usucaption there is no difference between them, for both the buyer and the legatee usucapt in good faith what the deceased or the author could not. But in the exception of fraud that is raised against them when they sue, there is a difference between those who succeed from a gratuitous cause and those who succeed from a non-gratuitous cause. Cuia, in Recitat. posth.

units.la: Ad Leg.55. De eo qui suo iure utitur.
units.tr: On law 55: concerning one who uses his own right.

units.la: NVllus videtur dolo facere, qui iure suo utitur.
units.tr: No one seems to act with fraud when he uses his own right.

units.la: Ex titul. si quis omiss. caus. testament. Paci.
units.tr: From the title "si quis omissa causa testamenti", Pacius.

units.la: Suo iure ] v.l.129.h.t l.26 ff. de damno. & leg. 3. §. 7. ff. de incendio. adde l. 9. §. 1. ff. de condict. caus. data. l. 13. §. 1. ff. de iniuriis: & ita tollendo aedes vicini quis potest obscurare intermisso legitimo spatio. l. 9. l. 14. ff. de seruitut. vrb. l.26. ff. de damno l.8. C. de seruitutibus: nisi sola malitia (cui non est indulgendum) id fiat. l. 61. h.t. l. 38. ff. de rei vindicat. l.1. §. 12. ff. de aqua plun. 2. Eclog. 3. c. 60. Gothofr. hic.
units.tr: "Suo iure": see l. 26 ff. de damno, and l. 3, §. 7 ff. de incendio; add l. 9, §. 1 ff. de condictione causa data, l. 13, §. 1 ff. de iniuriis; and so someone may, by raising his own building and leaving the legal interval, darken his neighbour's house. l. 9, l. 14 ff. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum, l. 26 ff. de damno, l. 8 C. de servitutibus; unless it is done from mere malice, which is not to be indulged. l. 61 h. t., l. 38 ff. de rei vindicatione, l. 1, §. 12 ff. de aqua pluvia. 2. Eclog. 3, c. 60. Gothofredus here.

units.la: Exemplum tale est, Is qui praetermisit causam Testamenti, vel aditionem hereditatis ex causa testari; (qua in re fraudantur legatarii) adit hereditatem ab intestato, quia erat proximus heres, & hoc erat in eius potestate. Hic incidit in edictum; Si quis omissa causa Testamenti: proinde tenetur legatariis, atq; sradi-isset isset ex Testamento, quia dolo id facit. Sed non videtur dolo id facere; & ideo non incidit in edictum illud, si suo iure vratur, vtpote si facultate vtatur à testatore sibi concessa. Quaeritur si resistitor permiserit electionem, hoc est, vt si haeres esse nollet ex Testamento, veniret ab intestato, iure suo vtitur l. 1. §. si proponatur. l. quia 6. §. plane 1. si quis omiss. caus. testam. Et ad hanc speciem haec lex proprie pertinere videtur, vt argumento est inscriptio. Sed potrigi etiam posset ad aliam vt l. 3. §. is qui 6. de lib. homin. exhib. vbi non videtur dolo malo facere, qui suo iure vtitur. Species est aperta. Eadem est regula l. nihil dolo 129. h. t. Sed alio pertinet, maxime ad edictum, quae in fraudem creditorum, siue actionem Paulianam, qua tenentur, qui fraudant. Sed finge. Quidam creditor sibi vigilauit, & occupauit suum petere: non videtur fraudare ceteros, nec fraudat qui suum colligit, hoc est repetit, exigit l. 6. §. apud. quae in fraud. cred. Creditores accipe, quibus ex quacunque causa actio in fraudatorem competit, etiamsi sub conditione competat; dummodo conditionis euentus exspectetur, leg. si cum fideicommissa 16. §. ne quis 2. & §. ponuli. qui & à quibus manam. Adiungenda etiam est l. factum cuique suum 155. h. t. Haec lex nostra, in qua versamur, est de iure, l. factum 155. pertinet ad interdictum Vnde vi; cum quaequædam vis fiebat, ex veteri formula agebatur, vindicabatur, adhibebatur vis quædam ciuilis, quæ non coërcetur interdicto unde vi. Qui manum conserit ex iure, non videtur vim facere: sed interdicto unde vi coërcetur vis, quæ fit contra ius. Cuiac. h.
units.tr: Such is the example: a man who has omitted the cause of a will, or the acceptance of an inheritance, by reason of a testament (in which respect legatees are defrauded), takes the inheritance on intestacy, because he was the nearest heir and this was in his power. Here he falls under the edict "Si quis omissa causa testamenti", and therefore he is liable to the legatees just as if he had accepted the inheritance under the will, because he does this by fraud. But he does not seem to act by fraud, and so he does not fall under that edict if he uses his own right, for instance if he uses a faculty granted to him by the testator. It is asked whether, if the testator allowed the choice, that is, that if the heir were unwilling to be heir under the will he might come in on intestacy, he uses his own right. l. 1, §. si proponatur; l. quia 6, §. plane 1, si quis omissa causa testamenti. This law seems properly to pertain to this type of case, as the inscription indicates. But it could also be applied to another, as in l. 3, §. is qui 6, de libero homine exhibendo, where he does not seem to act with malicious fraud who uses his own right. The case is plain. The same rule is in l. nihil dolo 129, h. t. But it pertains rather to another matter, chiefly to the edict concerning acts done to defraud creditors, or the Pauline action, by which those who defraud are bound. But suppose: a certain creditor has been watchful and has taken care to demand his own. He does not seem to defraud the others, nor does he defraud who collects his own, that is, recovers and exacts it. l. 6, §. apud, quae in fraudem creditorum. Understand "creditors" as those to whom an action lies against the defrauder from whatever cause, even if it lies under a condition; provided the outcome of the condition is awaited. leg. si cum fideicommissa 16, §. ne quis 2, & §. Pomponius, qui et a quibus manumissi. The law "factum cuique suum" 155, h. t. should also be added. This law of ours, with which we are dealing, concerns right: l. factum 155 pertains to the interdict "unde vi". When a certain violence was done, it was pursued by the old formula; it was claimed and a certain civil force was applied, which is not restrained by the interdict unde vi. He who joins hands in a legal contest does not seem to use force; but force that is done contrary to right is restrained by the interdict unde vi. Cuiac. h.

units.la: Lex 56. De dubiis.
units.tr: Lex 56. On doubtful cases.

units.la: SEmper in dubiis benigniora præferenda sunt.
units.tr: In doubtful cases the more lenient interpretation is always to be preferred.

units.la: Benigniora ] τὸ φιλάνθρωπον 2. Eclog. 2. cap. 57. adde l. 168. h. t. l. 18. ff. de legibus l. 4. ff. mandati l. 24. ff. de reb. dub. leg. 5. in sin. ff. de lega. 1. humanius, l. 3. in sin. ff. de his quæ in testam. quod est minus seuerum. leg. 42. ff. de pœnis: quale est fauere liberationi. l. 47. ff. de oblig. liberati, reo, ei quod minus est. l. 38. ff. de re iudic. Gothofr. hîc.
units.tr: Benigniora (more lenient): τὸ φιλάνθρωπον [the humane course] (Eclog. 2, cap. 57). Add l. 168 h. t., l. 18 ff. de legibus, l. 4 ff. mandati, l. 24 ff. de reb. dub., l. 5 in fin. ff. de legatis, 1 humanius, l. 3 in fin. ff. de his quae in testamento: that is, what is less severe. Leg. 42 ff. de poenis: such as favouring release. L. 47 ff. de oblig.: the freed party, the defendant, what is the lesser. L. 38 ff. de re iudic. Gothofredus here.

units.la: Eadem est regula l. ea quæ in partes 192. §. ult. h. t. & ad eam legem constat apponi exemplum in l. 3. de his quæ in testament. del. Id autem est de legatis: qua de causa exemplum videtur aptandum esse ad hanc regulam: quod tale est. Testator induxit nomina heredum, cetera non delcuit. heredibus succedit fiscus, quia videntur remoti q. indigni. Sed quaeritur, An fiscus præstare debeat legata, quæ non sunt inducta? Et à Fisco eis deberi, in dubio dicimus. Hoc enim est benignius, & benigniorem interpretationem sequi oportet. Et est vsus huius regulae frequens in foro: & sunt similia exemplain l.2.de his quae in test.del.l.cum inter. 14. C.de fideicom.libert. l.5. C. de bon. quae liber. Et generaliter capienda est occasio benignioris responsi l. capienda 168. h.t. In poenalibus causis benigniora praeferenda sunt. leg. factum cuique 155. §. vlt. h.t. quod & ostenditur in poenis l. perspiciendum 11. l. interpretatione 42. l. si praefes. 32. de poenis. Sed ad hanc leg. factum cuique suum, pertinet species leg. si praeses. 32. quae tota est de vi. Itaque ad §. in poenalibus pone exemplum ex l. si praeses. Vim fecisse videris, neque constat, de qua vi senserit iudex. Iam sententiam tacite sequitur ipso iure poena, quae est iure constituta. Quaeritur: Is qui damnatur ita, qua poena est plectendus? Lex ait, mitiore. Itaque priuatam vim fecisse existimabitur. Accurs. ad hanc l. 56. & ad l. nullus, non male posuit exemplum ex l. merito 51. pro socio: cuius species est: socius amouit rem communem, an tenebitur furti? videndum quo animo amoverit. Si amouerit lucri faciendi causa, tenebitur lucri causa; si amouerit dolo, furti tenebitur; si amouit suo iure furtum non facit aut dolum, qui suo iure utitur. In dubio itaque benignior interpretatio recipitur. Si igitur dominus furtum non facit; credendum est potius in re dubia, eum qui partis dominus est, potius suo iure uti voluisse, quam furtum fecisse. In dubio itaque benignior interpretatio recipitur.Cuiac. in Recitat. posth. h.
units.tr: The same rule applies in l. ea quae in partes 192 §. ult. h. t., and it is agreed that an example is given for that law in l. 3 de his quae in testamento del. That concerns legacies, so the example seems to fit this rule as follows. A testator named the heirs but did not strike out the rest of the text. The heirs are succeeded by the treasury, on the ground that they are regarded as removed or unworthy. But the question is whether the treasury ought to pay the legacies that were not written in. We say that in doubt they are owed by the treasury, for this is the more lenient view, and a more lenient interpretation ought to be followed. This rule is frequently used in the courts, and similar examples are found in l. 2 de his quae in test. del., l. cum inter 14 C. de fideicom. libert., l. 5 C. de bon. quae liber. In general, the chance of a more lenient answer is to be taken up, l. capienda 168 h. t. In penal causes the more lenient view is preferred, leg. factum cuique 155 §. vlt. h. t., as is shown in penalties by l. perspiciendum 11, l. interpretatione 42, l. si praefes. 32 de poenis. But the case of leg. si praeses 32, which is wholly about violence, belongs to this law, factum cuique suum. So for the clause in poenalibus, take as an example l. si praeses. You are seen to have used violence, and it is not clear what kind of violence the judge had in mind. Now the penalty fixed by law silently follows from the sentence itself. The question is: by what penalty is the one so condemned to be punished? The law says, by the milder one. Therefore he is deemed to have used private violence. The gloss on this l. 56 and on l. nullus does well to give an example from l. merito 51 pro socio, whose case is this: a partner removed common property; will he be liable for theft? One must consider with what intent he removed it. If he removed it for the sake of gain, he is liable on account of gain; if he removed it by fraud, he is liable for theft; if he removed it by his own right, he commits neither theft nor fraud, since he uses his own right. Therefore in doubt the more lenient interpretation is accepted. So if the owner of a thing commits no theft, it is to be believed in a doubtful matter that the part-owner preferred to use his own right rather than to commit theft. Therefore in doubt the more lenient interpretation is accepted. Cuiac. in Recitat. posth. h.

units.la: Lex 57. Ne bis exigatur.
units.tr: Lex 57. That a debt may not be demanded twice.

units.la: BONA fides non patitur, ut bis idem exigatur.
units.tr: Good faith does not allow the same thing to be demanded twice.

units.la: Bis idem] l. 26. ff. de peculio. l. 51. ff. de re iudic. l. 3. §. 18. ff. de tab. exhib. l. 34. ff. de oblig. v. Hotoman. 5. obs. 18. vid. l. 130. infr. eod.
units.tr: Bis idem] See Dig. 14 (de peculio), l. 26; Dig. 42 (de re iudicata), l. 51; Dig. 10 (de tabulis exhibendis), l. 3 §. 18; Dig. 44 (de obligationibus), l. 34; cf. Hotoman, Observationes 5, obs. 18; see also l. 130 below in the same title.

units.la: Haec sententia non tantum in bonae fidei iudiciis locum habet, sed etiam in strictis. Nam & ibi bona fides locum habet, licet maxime in bonae fidei iudiciis dominetur, quod constat ex multis legib. l. venditor 21. de har. vel act. vend. l. si quis dolo 31. de re iud. Is autem qui iterum exigit, modo repellitur ipso iure, modo per exceptionem doli mali. Plerunque ipso iure, quia solutione tollitur obligatio ipso iure: nonnunquam opposita exceptione doli mali l. pupillo 15. l. 3. §. ult. de tab. exhib. Quidam pupillo soluto sine tutoris auctoritate: salua est pecunia penes pupillum: pupillus si interim petit, non repellitur ipso iure; quia soluta est pecunia tutore absente; sed per exceptionem doli. Interdum tamen soluti recte fit exactio, Nov. 18. cap. 8. coercendae inficiationis causa. Is qui soluerat pecuniam debitam, conuentus ex chirographo, negauit se scripsisse chirographum, & pecuniam accepisse : conuictus est mendacii, an poterit postea allegare se soluisse? Minime. Cur enim verum non statim protulit? Ergo bis exigitur idem; haec est inficiationis poena.
units.tr: This principle holds not only in actions of good faith but also in strict ones. For good faith has a place there too, although it rules chiefly in actions of good faith, as is clear from many laws: l. venditor 21 de har. vel act. vend., l. si quis dolo 31 de re iud. He who demands a second time is repelled, sometimes by the law itself and sometimes by the plea of fraud. Usually he is repelled by the law itself, since the obligation is discharged by payment in law. Sometimes, however, a plea of fraud is raised: l. pupillo 15, l. 3 §. ult. de tab. exhib. When a ward has paid without the authority of his guardian, the money remains in the hands of the ward. If the ward in the meantime sues, he is not repelled by the law itself, because the money was paid while the guardian was absent, but by the plea of fraud. Yet sometimes a payment that was made is rightly demanded again, Nov. 18 cap. 8, for the purpose of restraining denial. A man who had paid a debt, when sued on a bond, denied that he had written the bond and that he had received the money. Convicted of lying, can he afterwards plead that he had paid? Certainly not. For why did he not produce the truth at once? So the same thing is demanded twice; this is the penalty for denial.

units.la: Lex 58. De peculio.
units.tr: Law 58. On the peculium.

units.la: EX poenalibus causis non solet in patrem de peculio actio dari.
units.tr: From penal causes an action on the peculium is not usually given against the father.

units.la: Ex titul. de peculio.
units.tr: From the title on the peculium.

units.la: Ex poenalibus] l. 1. §. 7. ff. de his qui deiecerint. l. 6. §. 2. ff. rer. amotar.
units.tr: From penal causes: l. 1. §. 7. ff. de his qui deiecerint; l. 6. §. 2. ff. rer. amotar.

units.la: Actio de peculio, est in solidum peculium; pater ipse tenetur nonnunquam in solidum pro filio: interdum omnino non tenetur: vt si peculium nullum sit rei iudicatae tempore, omnino non tenetur. Interdum non tenetur in solidum: sed in id tantum, quod versum est in peculium, vel in rem suam: interdum etiam nec de peculio tenetur: ex contractu filii pater tenetur de peculio filii, etiamsi nihil in peculium versum sit. Casus quidam sunt, quibus etiamsi actor tem persequatur; in patrem tamen ea est de peculio: sed pro modo tantum eius, quod in rem patris versum est. Nam clausula de in rem verso, inest actioni de peculio, atq; nonnunquam comprehendit utrumque. Id accidit his casibus, vt: si agatur filii impuberis nomine, nam tunc tenetur tantum de eo, quod versum est in rem patris. Nam nec impubes bes tenetur, nisi quatenus locupletior est factus, & nisi in id, quod versum est in rem eius, l.1. §. si cum impubere 4. de peculio. Item si agatur condictione furtiua, vel rerum amotarum in patrem in solidum. l.3. §. pennlt. de pecul. l.30. de act. empt. Idem est, si repetatur quod filius lucratus est alea: nam eius repetitio est. Itaque si repetatur actione de peculio, petetur tantum de eo, quod versum est in peculium l.1. de aleator. Iam si quæras: cur hæ actiones, condictio nempe furtiua, rerum amotarum, & aleatoria, non dentur in solidum peculium, cum tamen rem persequantur? dicam: etsi rem persequantur, tamen videntur esse ex maleficii causa, & proprie non sunt ex maleficio: nam non sunt noxales. An igitur dicemus; dari in solidum? Minime: sed mediam viam sequemur, & dicemus, actionem dari in id, quod peruenit in peculium. Aliis autem casibus, vt ex causa mutui, nullo modo pater tenetur de peculio. l. vlt. ad SCT. Macedon. Si credatur pecunia filiofam: non tenetur filiusfamilias, nisi habeat castrense: sed nec pater, etiamsi peruenerit. Ex poenalib. etiam causis pater non tenetur de peculio: sed post condemnationem pater tenetur actione iudicati l. & si condemnatus 35. de noxal. actionib. l.3. §. idem scribit. 11. de peculio. Imo vero & post litem contestatam mortuo filio, ex causa poenali transfertur iudicium in patrem de peculio. l. tam ex contractibus. 57. de iudiciis. Id omne mirum videri non debet: nam sit exemplo hæredis, de quo regula est: hæredem non teneri pœna ex delicto defuncti. Eadem regula est de patre. Sed hæres tenetur post condemnationem, hoc est, condemnato defuncto, ex causa peculii hæres tenetur iudicatum facere. Sic etiam post litem contestatam pater tenetur de peculio l. omnes. 26. & l. constitutionib. 33. de oblig. & act. Similiter hæres non tenetur mera actione pœnali, nisi de in rem verso. Hæres tenetur actione mixta, vel rei persecutoria in id, quod peruenit. Sic pater tenetur actione, quæ rem persequitur in id, quod peruenit. Idem in noxali actione tenendum est, & in l. Aquilia, quæ sunt mixtæ, & pater tenetur actione mixta in id, quod peruenit. Deniq; eadem est causa hæredis & patris. Cuiac. h.
units.tr: An action on the peculium is for the whole peculium. The father himself is sometimes liable for the whole amount on behalf of his son, and sometimes not liable at all: for example, if there is no peculium at the time of the judgment, he is not liable at all. Sometimes he is not liable for the whole amount, but only for what has been turned to the peculium or into his own property. Sometimes he is not even liable on the peculium: the father is liable on the peculium of his son for a contract entered into by the son, even if nothing has been turned to the peculium. There are certain cases in which, even though the plaintiff pursues the thing itself, the action against the father is still on the peculium, but only to the extent of what has been turned into the father's property. For the clause de in rem verso is contained in the action de peculio, and sometimes includes both. This happens in these cases: if the action is brought in the name of a son below the age of puberty, for then he is liable only for what has been turned into the father's property. For a minor below puberty is not liable except insofar as he has been enriched, and only for what has been turned into his property: l. 1. §. si cum impubere 4. de peculio. Likewise, if the action is a condictio for theft, or for goods carried off, against the father, it is for the whole amount: l. 3. §. pennlt. de pecul.; l. 30. de act. empt. The same holds if what the son has won by gambling is claimed: for that is a claim for recovery. So if it is claimed by an action de peculio, only what has been turned into the peculium is claimed: l. 1. de aleator. Now if you ask why these actions, namely the condictio for theft, for goods carried off, and the action for gambling winnings, are not given for the whole peculium, although they pursue the thing itself, I answer: although they pursue the thing, they seem to arise from a wrongful act, and properly they do not arise from a wrongful act, for they are not noxal actions. Shall we then say that they are given for the whole amount? By no means. Rather we shall follow a middle course and say that the action is given for what has come into the peculium. In other cases, however, as for a loan, the father is in no way liable on the peculium: l. vlt. ad SCT. Macedon. If money is lent to a son under power, the son is not liable unless he has castrense property, and neither is the father, even if it has come into his hands. In penal causes too the father is not liable on the peculium, but after condemnation the father is liable by the action on the judgment: l. & si condemnatus 35. de noxal. actionib.; l. 3. §. idem scribit. 11. de peculio. Indeed, even after litis contestatio, if the son has died, the case is transferred in a penal cause to the father on the peculium: l. tam ex contractibus. 57. de iudiciis. None of this ought to seem surprising, for it follows the example of the heir, concerning whom the rule is that an heir is not liable to the penalty for the dead man's delict. The same rule holds for the father. But the heir is liable after condemnation, that is, when the deceased has been condemned, the heir is bound to satisfy the judgment on the ground of the peculium. So also after litis contestatio the father is liable on the peculium: l. omnes. 26. and l. constitutionib. 33. de oblig. et act. Similarly, the heir is not liable by a purely penal action, except for what has been turned to his use. The heir is liable by a mixed action, or by a real action of pursuit, for what has come into his hands. So the father is liable by an action which pursues the thing, for what has come into his hands. The same must be held of a noxal action, and of the lex Aquilia, which are mixed actions, and the father is liable by a mixed action for what has come into his hands. Finally, the reason for the heir and for the father is the same. Cuiacius, h.

units.la: Lex 59. De hærede.
units.tr: Law 59. On the heir.

units.la: HÆredem eiusdem potestatis iurisque esse cuius fuit defunctus, constat.
units.tr: It is established that the heir is of the same power and right as the deceased whose heir he is.

units.la: Hæc lex 5 in l. 54. expositæ est.
units.tr: This law has been explained under law 54.

units.la: Haeredem ]priorem, non hæredem hæredis. Castr. Consil. 197. Decius hîc num. 7. in sin. & quidem adita hæreditate cum effectu: alias improprie est hæres l. 3. §. 2. ff. de hared. instit. l. 23. ff. de vulg. l. 4. ff. de condit. & demonstr. l. 3. §. 11. ff. de statuliber. l. 18. ff. de stipul. serv.
units.tr: Haeredem: the earlier one, not the heir of an heir. See Castr. Consil. 197, and Decius here, num. 7, at the end; and indeed only with effect once the inheritance has been accepted, since otherwise he is improperly called heir: see l. 3 §. 2 ff. de hered. instit.; l. 23 ff. de vulg.; l. 4 ff. de condit. et demonstr.; l. 3 §. 11 ff. de statuliber.; l. 18 ff. de stipul. serv.

units.la: Eiusdem ]: interdum deterioris, necin eum transit potestas revocandi, infirmandi, & similium
units.tr: Eiusdem: sometimes of a worse one, nor does the power of revoking, invalidating, and the like pass to him.

units.la: Defunctus ] cum testaretur, cum contraheret, cum pacisceretur l. 9. in sin. ff. de probat. aut quid tale faceret l. 14. C. de rei vindicat. Decius hic. num. 34. adde Dynum cap. 9. de regulis in 6. num. 19. 20. Gothofr. hic.
units.tr: Defunctus: when he made a will, when he contracted, when he entered into a pact, or did something of that kind; l. 9 in sin. ff. de probat., or l. 14 C. de rei vindicat. Decius here, num. 34. Add Dynus, ch. 9 de regulis in 6, num. 19, 20; Gothofredus here.

units.la: Ad Leg. 60. Mandati.
units.tr: On Law 60, Mandati.

units.la: SEmper qui non prohibet pro se interuenire, mandare creditur: sed & si quis ratum habuerit quod gestum est, obstringitur mandati actione.
units.tr: Whoever, being present, does not forbid another to act on his behalf is always believed to have given a mandate. And if someone ratifies what has been done, he is bound by the action on mandate.

units.la: Qui non ] qui praesens patitur suo nomine aliquid fieri, necid prohibet, mandare videtur l. 156. in sin. h. t. leg. 1. §. 5. ff. de exercit. leg. 6. §. 2. l. 18. ff. mandati l. 2. in sin. C. de adquir. possess.
units.tr: Qui non] he who, being present, allows something to be done in his name and does not forbid it, seems to have given a mandate l. 156. in sin. h. t. leg. 1. §. 5. ff. de exercit. leg. 6. §. 2. l. 18. ff. mandati l. 2. in sin. C. de adquir. possess.

units.la: Ratum ] v. l. 16. §. 1. ff. de pignoribus. leg. 12. in sin. ff. de solutionibus. cap. ratihabitione 10. de regulis in 6.
units.tr: Ratum] see l. 16. §. 1. ff. de pignoribus. leg. 12. in sin. ff. de solutionibus. cap. ratihabitione 10. de regulis in 6.

units.la: Habuerit ] agnouerit, comprobauerit, l. 12. §. 1. §. 1. ff. ratam rem: verbis vel facto l. 5. C. ratam rem. intra legitimum tempus leg. 24. ff. ratam rem: sic qui fructus percipit, possessionem: qui censum contractu: vt & is qui agit ex contractu, ipsum contractum approbare intelligitur. Item, qui ratione administrationis exigit, gestionem approbat: & breuiter, per ratihabitionem actus attribuitur ratum habenti Dec. hic num. 10. Gothofr. Actus tamen ipso iure nullus, ratus quidem haberi potest, sed nunquam retrotrahitur; cum tantum valeat ab ipso ratihabitionis tempore. Dec. h. n. 16. Si mandatum pro forma a lege vel statuto requiratur, ratihabitio non sufficit. Deci. h. numer. 17. Gothofr.
units.tr: Habuerit] that is, approves, confirms, l. 12. §. 1. §. 1. ff. ratam rem: by words or by deed l. 5. C. ratam rem, within the lawful time leg. 24. ff. ratam rem. Thus he who takes the fruits approves the possession, and he who collects the rent under a contract approves the contract. So too, he who sues on a contract is understood to approve the contract itself. Likewise, he who demands an account by reason of administration approves the management; and in short, by ratification the act is attributed to the one who ratifies. Dec. here num. 10. Gothofr. An act that is void in law itself may indeed be ratified, but it is never carried back in time, since it takes effect only from the moment of ratification. Dec. h. n. 16. If a mandate in a prescribed form is required by law or statute, ratification is not enough. Deci. h. numer. 17. Gothofr.

units.la: Is qui pro alio fideiussit, habet aduersus eum pro quo fideiussit, actionem mandati, & hoc, si eo mandante fideiusserit. Idem est si eo praesente & tacente. Nam taciturnitas imitatur mandatum; atque ita mandatum contrahitur tacito consensu. l. si remunerandi 6. §. si passus 2. l. qui fide 53. mandati l. 6. C. mandati. Is demum non tenetur mandati, pro quo inuito fideiussit quis vel ignorante. Inuitum accipimus eum, qui contradixerit, non qui latet. Non tenetur actione mandati is, pro quo alter fideiussit donandi animo: item, pro quo absente fideiussum est, non tenetur: at pro quo praesente, nec prohibente, fideiussum est, contra cum est actio mandati. Ratihabitio etiam hic mandato comparatur: vt si quis pro Titio absente fideiusserit & ignorante; is vero postea ratum habuerit, tenetur mandati fideiussori. Denique mandati actione tenetur, qui racuit aut ratum habuit. Posui exempla hîc in fideiussore: sed patet latius hæc regula. Nam interuenire dicitur non tantum qui fideiubet, sed etiam qui intercedit, qui rem obligat pro alio, vel iudicium suscipit; quod ostenditur in Velleiano. Igitur quod dicitur de fideiussore, idem dicatur de omnibus interuenientibus. Sed obstat huic sententiæ l. si pupilli 6. §. item quæritur 9. & §. seq. de neg gest. Species hæc est, Quidam accepit meo nomine pecuniam à Titio, quam mihi non debebat, sed alii, itaque alienum negotium gessit proprie, sed non retenetur mei contemplatione: Quæritur, an sit vltro citroque actio negotiorum gestorum, & possim petere pecuniam eam? videtur non esse: quia alienum est negotium. Ratihabitio tamen facit, vt videatur negotium meum gestum, & erit mutua actio negotiorum gestorum. Verum est, esse negotiorum gestorum actionem, si ratum habuero: sed tentari potest, esse etiam mandati actionem. Nam ratihabitio duplicem vim habet: vt alienum negotium eius faciat, & habeat etiam vim mandati: & hæ actiones ambæ sæpe etiam concurrunt; & ager aget ex contractu & quasi contractu. In hac specie actionem mandati habet, quia ratam rem habuit gestam à praesenti, quia praesentia facit, vt ratihabitio sit mandatum. At in l.6. res gesta ab absente rata habita est; haec simplex ratihabitio eandem vim non habet. Itaque si res est gesta ab absente, vt alienum negotium faciat nostrum, non habet mandati actionem. His addatur l.hoc iure.152.§.in maleficio 2. h.t. quae tamen pertinent ad aliam speciem, nempe ad id quod est scriptum in l.1.§. deiecisse.12.de vi & viarm. Videtur deiecisse is, qui ratum habuit. Qui pro tacente fideiussit, tenetur quoque mandati: quia ratihabitio tum pro mandato habetur. Opponit Accursi. l.si cum pecuniam.3.C.de contrah.stipul. vbi ex ratihabitione datur actio negotiorum gestorum: cum tamen hic detur mandati. Non sunt leges hae contrariae. Nam quae dat negotiorum gestorum actionem, non denegat mandati: & contra. Et qui tenetur ratihabitione, tenetur mandati: quia eadem de re alterutra competit. l.5.de exceptt.rei iudic. leg.cum mancipium. de adil.edict. Nam ratihabitio maxime per Sabinum comparatur mandato. l.1.§.deiecisse.12.& §.seq.de vi & viarm. Ideoque, vt ait Vlpianus, recte in maleficiis ratihabitio mandato comparatur, scilicet, si meo nomine aliquid commissum sit, & rem eam ratam postea habuero: vt si quis vicinum meo nomine deiecerit, idque ratum habeam, ipse videor mandasse d. §. deiecisse: quia alter deiecit meo nomine, & in rem meam d. l. hoc iure, 152. h.t. Certum est, mandatorem caedis puniri aeque, atque eum qui fecit. tit. de sicariis. Sed si quis occiderit, non mandato meo, nec postea ratum habuero, an teneor? minime: at si in rem meam factum est, & postea ratum habuero, teneor d. l. hoc iure §. deiicit. h.t. in illa specie. Idem etiam Vlp. admisit in aliis multis: ut exemplum est in l. verum 12. in sin. de solut. cui iunge l. licet 56. de iudic. Species haec est. Si non vero procuratori meo pecuniam soluat debitor mihi debiram, & ratum habuero, debitor liberabitur; nam ratihabitio videtur mandatum. Diuersum exemplum adducit Vlp. in l. quid ergo. 12. de his qui not. infam. vbi ratihabitio non comparatur mandato. Cuiac. in Recitat. h.
units.tr: One who has given surety for another has an action on mandate against the person for whom he gave surety, and this holds if he gave surety at that person's instruction. It is the same if he did so in his presence and in silence, for silence imitates a mandate, and so a mandate is contracted by tacit consent. l. si remunerandi 6. §. si passus 2. l. qui fide 53. mandati l. 6. C. mandati. He who gave surety for another against that person's will, or without his knowledge, is not bound by the action on mandate in the end. By "against his will" we understand one who has objected, not one who is merely hidden. He for whom another gave surety with the intention of making a gift is not bound by the action on mandate; likewise, if surety was given for someone who was absent, that person is not bound. But for whom surety was given in his presence and without his forbidding it, the action on mandate lies against him. Ratification is also here compared to a mandate: so if someone gave surety for Titius, who was absent and unaware, and Titius afterwards ratifies it, Titius is bound to the surety by the action on mandate. In short, one is bound by the action on mandate who has kept silent or has ratified. I have given examples here in the case of a surety, but the rule applies more widely. For one is said to intervene not only when he gives surety, but also when he becomes liable for another, pledges a thing for another, or takes up a lawsuit; as is shown in the Velleian senatus consultum. Therefore what is said of a surety should be said of all intervenors. But this view is opposed by l. si pupilli 6. §. item quaeritur 9. & §. seq. de neg. gest. The case is this: someone received money from Titius in my name, money which he did not owe me but another, and so he managed another's business, properly speaking, but not with a view to me. The question is whether there is a mutual action for management of affairs, and whether I can claim that money. It seems not, because the business is another's. Yet ratification makes it appear that my business was managed, and there will be a mutual action for management of affairs. It is true that there is an action for management of affairs if I ratify; but it may be argued that there is also an action on mandate. For ratification has a twofold force: it makes another's business his own, and it also has the force of a mandate; and these actions often both arise together, so that the principal sues both on contract and on quasi-contract. In this case he has the action on mandate, because he ratified an act done by a present person, since presence makes ratification equivalent to a mandate. But in l. 6, a thing done by an absent person was ratified; this simple ratification does not have the same force. Thus if the thing was done by an absent person so as to make another's business our own, we do not have the action on mandate. To these may be added l. hoc iure 152. §. in maleficio 2. h. t., which, however, pertains to another case, namely to what is written in l. 1. §. deiecisse 12. de vi et vi armata. He who ratified is considered to have dispossessed. He who gave surety for a silent person is also bound on mandate, because ratification is then held to be in place of a mandate. Accursius objects with l. si cum pecuniam 3. C. de contrah. stipul., where an action for management of affairs is given from ratification, whereas here an action on mandate is given. These laws are not contrary. For the law that gives the action for management of affairs does not deny the action on mandate, and conversely. And he who is bound by ratification is bound on mandate, because on the same matter one or the other lies. l. 5. de exceptt. rei iudicatae; l. cum mancipium, de aedilicio edicto. For ratification is compared to a mandate chiefly by Sabinus. l. 1. §. deiecisse 12. & §. seq. de vi et vi armata. Therefore, as Ulpian says, rightly in cases of wrongdoing ratification is compared to a mandate: namely, if something was committed in my name and I afterwards ratify that thing; for example, if someone dispossessed my neighbour in my name and I ratify it, I am seen to have ordered it, d. §. deiecisse, because the other dispossessed in my name and against my property, d. l. hoc iure, 152. h. t. It is certain that the one who orders a killing is punished just as much as the one who did it. tit. de sicariis. But if someone killed without my mandate, and I afterwards did not ratify it, am I bound? Not at all. But if it was done against my property and I afterwards ratified it, I am bound, d. l. hoc iure §. deiicit. h. t., in that case. Ulpian also admitted the same in many other cases, as in l. verum 12. in sin. de solutionibus, to which add l. licet 56. de iudiciis. The case is this: if a debtor who owes me money pays it not to my true agent but to someone else, and I ratify it, the debtor is freed; for ratification is treated as a mandate. Ulpian gives a different example in l. quid ergo 12. de his qui notantur infamia, where ratification is not compared to a mandate. Cuiac. in Recitat. h.

units.la: Ad Leg. 61. De refectione domus.
units.tr: On Law 61. On the Repair of a House.

units.la: DOmum suam vnicuique reficere licet, dum non officiat inuito alteri, in quo ius non habet.
units.tr: Anyone may repair his own house, provided he does not hinder another person against his will, over whom he has no right.

units.la: Coniunge l. 2. de ope publ.
units.tr: Join l. 2. de ope publ.

units.la: Reficere] & sic aliud est reficere, & ad pristinam formam reducere, aliud de nouo facere. l. 3. §. 15. ff. de itin. actuq; priuato: iuste tamen agere posšum. Nam si reficiendo officere vicino inuito non licet, multo minus nouum opus inchoando.
units.tr: Reficere: so it is one thing to repair (reficere), that is, to restore to its former form, and another thing to build anew. l. 3. §. 15. ff. de itin. actuq; priuato: yet one may act lawfully. For if it is not permitted to hinder a neighbour against his will by repairing, much less is it permitted by beginning a new work.

units.la: Officiat] ideo officere non intelligitur, qui iure seruitutis sibi adquisito vtitur, aut qui citra seruitutem iusto spatio, aut altitudine legitima aedificat, id est, qui soli & coeli mensuram analogicam seruat. l.21. §.2 ff. quod vi.
units.tr: Officiat: therefore one is not understood to hinder when he uses a right of servitude acquired to him, or when he builds without servitude at a lawful distance or height, that is, when he keeps the proportional measure of ground and sky. l.21. §.2 ff. quod vi.

units.la: Iunge l.7. de offic. Præf. Haec verba non sunt pro regula. Nam non tantum licet, sed etiam interdum cogitur. Igitur haec regula est: ita quis debet domum reficere, ne vicino noceat. Præses cogit dominos reficere domos, quia ruinæ aedificiorum ciuitatem deformant, & aduersus detrectantem, competenti iudicio deformitati remedium adfert, at, vt ait lex, causa cognita. Nam interdum non cogor lapsas aedes reaedificare: licet aream in hortum commutare secundum morem ciuitatis, si talis sit mos l.3. C. de aedif. priua. Refectio aedium pertinet ad curatorem reip. l. ad curatoris 46. de dam. infect. Scribunt de Vespasiano, eum vicinas areas occupare & aedificare, si domini cessassent, cuique permisisse. Ita coercentur cunctatores. l. vlt. C. de Iur. Reip. l. 11. Lex autem haec scribit, quomodo refectio fieri debeat; vt ne quid noceat vicino. Itaque cauere debet vicino, ne quid immittat, si non habet ius, l. sicut 8. §. Aristo. s. si seruit. vind. Idem est, cum in publico aliquid fieri permittitur: id enim faciendum dum est sine iniuria. l. 2. §. merito. ne quid in loco publ. Unde quaeritur: an qui suas aedes reficit, possit luminibus officere, aut prospectui vicini? Distinctio haec habetur: qui reficit, si servat priorem formam aedificii, potest officere, sicut antea; at non servata pristina forma; si aedes altiores faciat, non poterit obscurare lumina. l. qui luminibus. ii. de servitut. urb. praed. & in Constit. Zenonis C. de aedific. privat. ubi nominatim utitur ea distinctione Iustinianus, & secundum hanc Constitutionem, nisi servet & intermittat spatium duodecim pedum, offecerit luminibus: at si velit impedire prospectum maris, debet intermittere centum pedes. Nov. 63. quod Harmenop. etiam producit ad prospectum montium li. 2. Epitom. & citat ex Papin. lib. 3. quaest. haec verba: prospectum in montes meos prohibere potes: qui locus Papiniani notandus est; alibi enim non invenitur. Cuiac. in Recitat. posth.
units.tr: Join l.7. de offic. Praef. These words are not a rule. For one is not only permitted, but sometimes compelled. The rule, therefore, is this: one must repair a house in such a way as not to harm the neighbour. The praeses compels owners to repair their houses, because collapsed buildings disfigure the city, and against a refractory owner, by a competent judgment, he provides a remedy for the deformity; but, as the law says, only after the cause has been heard. For sometimes I am not compelled to rebuild a fallen house: one may turn the site into a garden according to the custom of the city, if such is the custom. l.3. C. de aedif. priua. The repair of buildings pertains to the curator of the commonwealth. l. ad curatoris 46. de dam. infect. They write of Vespasian that he occupied neighbouring sites and built on them if the owners had been idle, and that he allowed this to each person. Thus the dawdlers are restrained. l. vlt. C. de Iur. Reip. l. 11. But this law writes how the repair ought to be done, so that nothing harms the neighbour. Hence one must take care not to send anything onto a neighbour if one has no right. l. sicut 8. §. Aristo. s. si seruit. vind. The same holds when something is permitted in a public place, for it must be done without injury. l. 2. §. merito. ne quid in loco publ. Hence the question: may one who repairs his own house obstruct the lights or the view of a neighbour? The following distinction is made: one who repairs, if he keeps the earlier form of the building, may obstruct as before; but if he does not keep the former form, and makes the houses higher, he will not be able to darken the lights. l. qui luminibus. ii. de servitut. urb. praed. & in Constit. Zenonis C. de aedific. privat. where Justinian expressly uses this distinction; and according to this Constitution, unless he keeps and leaves a space of twelve feet, he will have obstructed the lights; but if he wishes to block the view of the sea, he must leave a hundred feet. Nov. 63. Harmenopulus also brings this forward for the view of mountains, li. 2. Epitom. and cites from Papinian, lib. 3. quaest. these words: prospectum in montes meos prohibere potes: "you may forbid the view of my mountains." This passage of Papinian is to be noted, for it is found nowhere else. Cuiac. in Recitat. posth.

units.la: Ad Leg. 62. De hereditate.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 62. De hereditate.

units.la: HEreditas nihil aliud est, quam successio in universum ius, quod defunctus habuit.
units.tr: An inheritance is nothing other than succession to the whole right which the deceased had.

units.la: Ex titul. de petit. hered. Coniunge l. ei qui eod. tit. & l. 24. de verb. sign.
units.tr: From the title on petitioning an inheritance. Join with the law "to him who under the same title" and law 24, on the meaning of words.

units.la: Nihil aliud quam quam universum ius quod defunctus habuit, & cui succedi potest. haec definitio constat suo genere, & tribus differentiis. Antequam autem quis succedat, hereditas est quasi domina, & vicem, locum, ac personam defuncti repræsentat. v. l. 31. in sin. ff. de hered. instit. l. 13. §. 5. in fi. ff. quod vi. l. 1. §. 1. ff. si is qui testam. Respectu heredis, vacua, iacens, & vacans dicitur. l. 1. ff. de successorio: nullius l. 13. §. 5. ff. quod vi: Adita, iuncta est heredi. l. 10. §. 12. ff. de vulga. l. 59. in sin. ff. de acquir. hered. fitque eius patrimonium d. §. 2. Socinus ad l 1. §. 16. ff. de adquir. possess. Itaque, si filia, patris hereditati renunciauit, non excluditur à fratris hereditate. Dec. hic num. 6. Superiorib. adde quæ tractat Michael Grassus in §. hereditas, quæst. 1.
units.tr: Nothing other than the whole right which the deceased had and to which succession can be made. This definition consists of its genus and three differences. Before anyone succeeds, the inheritance is, as it were, a lady, and represents the place, the role and the person of the deceased. See l. 31. in sin. ff. de hered. instit.; l. 13. §. 5. in fi. ff. quod vi; l. 1. §. 1. ff. si is qui testam. With respect to the heir it is called vacant, lying, and unclaimed. l. 1. ff. de successorio; nullius, l. 13. §. 5. ff. quod vi. Once entered upon, it is joined to the heir. l. 10. §. 12. ff. de vulga. l. 59. in sin. ff. de acquir. hered. and it becomes his patrimony, d. §. 2. Socinus on l. 1. §. 16. ff. de adquir. possess. Therefore, if a daughter has renounced her father's inheritance, she is not excluded from her brother's inheritance. Decius here, num. 6. To the above add what Michael Grassus treats in §. hereditas, quaest. 1.

units.la: Successio] vt l. 2. C. ad L. Iul de vi. Hinc colligunt, hereditatem non deferri, nisi iure successiuo, omnemque defuncto succedentem, heredis locum habere. v. l. 128 in f h.t.
units.tr: Successio: as in l. 2. C. ad L. Iul de vi. Hence they gather that an inheritance is not deferred except by a successive right, and that whoever succeeds the deceased takes the place of an heir. See l. 128. in f. h.t.

units.la: In vniuersum] l. 24. ff. de verb. sig. Eclog. 3. cap. 61. v. l. 9. §. 12. ff. de heredib. instit. adde l. 6. ff. de except. l. 11. ff. de diuers. & tempor. & ita rei particularis non est hereditas. ex l. 7. ff. eod.
units.tr: In universum: law 24, Digest, on the meaning of words. Eclogue 3, chapter 61, verse 9, section 12, Digest, on heirs instituted; add law 6, Digest, on exceptions; law 11, Digest, on diverse and temporary matters; and so an inheritance is not of a particular thing, from law 7 of the same title.

units.la: Defunctus] l. 50. ff. de hered. petit.
units.tr: Defunctus: l. 50. ff. de hered. petit.

units.la: Habuerit [habuerit tempore mortis. Pac.
units.tr: Habuerit [habuerit: he had at the time of death. Pac.

units.la: Hereditas est successio iuris. l. cum heres 11. de diuers. & temp. prescriptio. l. heredes. de acquir. hered. quod scilicet quis cum moritur, habuerit; vel contra, Hereditas est ius vniuersum successionis, verbis immutatis l. hereditas. supra tit. prox. vbi dicitur, Hereditatem significare quandam vniuersitatem. Hereditas igitur est nomen iuris, hoc est, ius significat, l. hereditas de petit.hered. Est res incorporalis, quæ nec tangi nec cerni potest. Instit. de reb.corp. Cic. in Top. definit, esse pecuniam, hoc est, rem corporalem. Non est ita; sed nos pro iure accipimus, & omnia fere vocabula sic accipiuntur. Sic peculium est ius peculii : sic dos est nomen iuris: nonnunquam etiam fundus. l. cogi. 16. §. inde quaeritur. 3. ad Trebell. Hereditas ius est, non corpus. Nam plerumque sunt hereditates sine corpore, vt quæ consistunt in iuribus: quædam damnosæ sunt, quæ damnum adferunt, non lucrum. Et quidem cum dicitur, hereditas esse successio in vniuersum ius, siue vniuersi iuris, accipitur actiue & passiue : hoc est damni & commodi. Id autem aduertendum est, hanc definitionem complecti vim possessionis : & dicitur sæpe in Cicerone possessio hereditatis: plerumque tamen bonorum possessio dicitur. d.l. 3. in princ. Bona etiam solemus dicere, sed hereditatis appellatione continetur bonorum possessio. Videtur etiam fideicommissarias hereditates continere, post Senatusconsultum Pegasianum maxime, quandoquidem Senatusconsulto in heredem fideicommissarium transeunt actiones omnes, & intendit omnes actiones: ante id Senatusconsultum constitutum secus erat. Cuiac. in Recit. posth.
units.tr: An inheritance is succession to a right. l. cum heres 11. de diuers. & temp. prescriptio. l. heredes. de acquir. hered. that is, what a person had at the time he died; or, conversely, an inheritance is the universal right of succession, with the words changed. l. hereditas. supra tit. prox. where it is said that the word "inheritance" signifies a certain universality. An inheritance is therefore a name of a right; that is, it signifies a right. l. hereditas de petit.hered. It is an incorporeal thing, which can be neither touched nor seen. Instit. de reb.corp. Cicero in in Top. defines it as money, that is, a corporeal thing. That is not so; rather we take it for a right, and almost all words are so taken. Thus a peculium is a right of peculium; thus a dowry is a name of a right; sometimes even an estate. l. cogi. 16. §. inde quaeritur. 3. ad Trebell. An inheritance is a right, not a body. For inheritances are often without body, consisting as they do in rights; some are burdensome, bringing loss rather than gain. And when it is said that an inheritance is succession to the whole right, or of the whole right, it is taken both actively and passively, that is, of loss and of gain. It must be noted, however, that this definition embraces the force of possession; and in Cicero the possession of an inheritance is often mentioned, though usually it is called possession of goods. d.l. 3. in princ. We also commonly speak of goods, but the possession of goods is included under the name of inheritance. It also seems to include fideicommissary inheritances, especially after the Senatusconsultum Pegasianum, since by that Senatusconsultum all actions pass to the fideicommissary heir, and he brings all actions; before that Senatusconsultum the position was otherwise. Cuiac. in Recit. posth.

units.la: Ad Leg. 63. De Mora.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 63. De Mora.

units.la: QVI sine dolo malo ad iudicium prouocat, non videtur moram facere.
units.tr: He who, without bad faith, appeals to a court is not held to be in default.

units.la: Sine dolo ]id est qui iuste l. 21. & 24. ff. de vsuris. Iuste etiam dicitur prouocare, qui id facit quod communiter fieri solet leg. 16. ff. de rei vind. qui iusta ignoratione ducitur, quod in furE non est l. vlt. ff. de condict. furtiu.
units.tr: Without bad faith means one who acts justly l. 21. & 24. ff. de vsuris. A person is also said to appeal justly when he does what is commonly done leg. 16. ff. de rei vind. and when he is led by a just ignorance, which does not apply to a thief l. vlt. ff. de condict. furtiu.

units.la: Debitor eo ipso, quod non soluit pecuniam, non statim facit moram, etiamsi interpellatus fuerit. Definitio morae incerta est: modo fit sine interpellatione, modo cum interpellatione. Nam qui dicit, se paratum esse actionem suscipere, is non est in mora; quia putat se iustam habere causam litigandi. l. si quis solutioni 34. in pr. de vsuris. Si igitur dicat, se non soluturum, quoad sit condemnatus, non facit moram, cum scilicet existimat, se habere iustam causam litigandi: cuius opinionis fur esse non potest. Nam etiamsi paratus sit condictionem furtiuam suscipere, non purgat moram. l. vlt. de condict. furtiu. offerendo rem, purgat: non autem ad iudicem prouocando. Nam scit se non habere iustam causam litigandi. Huc pertinet l. non potest 99. h.t. ad quam regulam recte apponitur exemplum ex leg. residuum. de distra. pign. Quidam petit residuum debiti: debitor ignorat quid sit in residuo, petit arbitrum; qui excutiat rationes, an videatur moram facere, an recte distractum sit pi-gnus? Minime: non potest enim esse in mora, qui perit arbitrum rationibus excutiendis. Cujac. in Recit. posth. h.
units.tr: A debtor does not fall into default at once merely because he does not pay the money, even if he has been called upon to pay. The definition of default is uncertain: sometimes it arises without a demand, sometimes with one. For he who says that he is ready to undertake the lawsuit is not in default, because he thinks he has a just cause for litigating l. si quis solutioni 34. in pr. de vsuris. So if he says that he will not pay until he is condemned, he is not in default, since he evidently thinks he has a just cause for litigating; a thief cannot hold this opinion. For even if he is ready to undergo the action for theft, he does not clear himself of default l. vlt. de condict. furtiu. He clears himself by offering the thing, but not by appealing to the judge, for he knows he has no just cause for litigating. To this belongs l. non potest 99. h.t., to which rightly an example from ex leg. residuum. de distra. pign. is attached. A certain man demands the remainder of a debt. The debtor does not know what is left, and asks for an arbiter to examine the accounts, to see whether he seems to be in default, or whether the pledge was rightly sold? Not at all: for a man cannot be in default who asks for an arbiter to examine the accounts. Cujac. in Recit. posth. h.

units.la: Ad Leg. 64. De raro contin- gentibus.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 64. De raro contingentibus.

units.la: EA quae raro accidunt, non temere in agendis negotiis computantur.
units.tr: Things which happen rarely are not lightly taken into account in transacting business.

units.la: Raro accidunt ] v. l. 114. h. t. l. 4. 5. & 6 ff. de legib. l. 3. in f. ff. si pars. Novell. 94. c. 2.
units.tr: Happen rarely ] v. l. 114. h. t. l. 4. 5. & 6 ff. de legib. l. 3. in f. ff. si pars. Novell. 94. c. 2.

units.la: Non ] quae raro fiunt non sunt sub lege. Quae specialiter cuenire possunt, non attenduntur: Interdum iusta de causa computantur, velut ea quae fiunt a natura, licet raro l. 12. C. de legitim. haered. §. 21. Inst. de rer. divis. Hinc etiam colligunt, temerarium actorem non audiri. leg. 41. ff. de fideiussoribus. Item Raro, & Nunquam, non esse paria. Gothofr. hic.
units.tr: Not ] Things which happen rarely are not under the law. Those which can happen only in particular cases are not regarded; sometimes, for a just reason, they are taken into account, as those things which come about by nature, though rarely l. 12. C. de legitim. haered. §. 21. Inst. de rer. divis. From this they also conclude that a rash plaintiff is not heard leg. 41. ff. de fideiussoribus. Likewise, that "rarely" and "never" are not equivalent. Gothofr. hic.

units.la: Non computantur ] id est non habetur ratio eorum:
units.tr: Are not taken into account ] that is, no account is taken of them:

units.la: Igitur illud primum constat, eorum quae raro accidunt in iure constituendo rationem non haberi. Alioqui nullum ius certum posset constitui: nam obstarent, quae possent accidere. Leges fiunt ex iis, quae saepius fiunt & cueniunt; non habetur autem eorum ratio, quæ fiunt raro, vt in hac specie. Quidam decessit intestatus, relicto filio & vxore prægnante: quæritur, pro qua parte filius sit heres? Id constituere, ne plus petat, difficile est: quia fœtus fortasse sunt in vtero duo, tres, quatuor, vel quinque. Nam tot possunt edi. Vt qubatuor aut quinque nascantur, est rarum; non est rarum, vt tres nascantur. Itaque dicimus, filium interim petitionem quartæ habere. leg. antiqui 3. si pars hered. petat. Exemplum etiam est in Novell. 94. Mulieres quæ iurant se iterum non nuptuias, raro seruant, sed sæpe violant iusiurandum; inspecto eo, quod non fit crebro; melius est non excipere tale iuramentum, ne via periurijs aperiatur. l. 2. §. vlt. C. quand. multit. off. fung. Sciendum autem est, interdum legem fieri de eo quod fit raro. l. si maior. 12. C. de legit. hæred. Fingitur patri heres ex matre quinquagenaria, fiunt leges de successione: ita de incestuoso partu leges sunt scriptæ. Sed obseruandum est, ius commune constitui ex iis, quæ fiunt sæpius. Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: So this first point is established: in framing law, no account is taken of things which happen rarely. Otherwise no certain law could be established, for what could possibly happen would stand in the way. Laws are made from those things which happen more often and commonly; but no account is taken of those which happen rarely, as in this case. A certain man died intestate, leaving a son and a pregnant wife. The question is, in what proportion is the son the heir? It is difficult to settle this so that he does not claim too much, since the foetuses may perhaps be two, three, four or five in the womb, for that many can be born. That four or five are born is rare; that three are born is not rare. Therefore we say that the son meanwhile has a claim to a fourth leg. antiqui 3. si pars hered. petat. There is also an example in in Novell. 94. Women who swear that they will not marry again rarely keep this, but often break the oath; since this is not done often, it is better not to make an exception for such an oath, so that a way is not opened to perjuries. l. 2. §. vlt. C. quand. multit. off. fung. It must be noted, however, that sometimes a law is made concerning what happens rarely. l. si maior. 12. C. de legit. hæred. If a son is imagined to be the heir of his father through a mother aged fifty, laws are made about the succession; thus laws have been written about a child born of incest. But it must be observed that the common law is established from those things which happen more often. Cuiac. in Recit.

units.la: Ad Leg. 65. De Cauillatione.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 65. De Cauillatione.

units.la: EA est natura Cauillationis, quam Græci <bl>ἐρωτήσεις</bl> appellant, vt ab euidenter veris, per breuissimas mutationes ad ea, quæ euidenter falsa sunt, perducatur.
units.tr: This is the nature of cavilling, which the Greeks call questions [ἐρωτήσεις]: that from things evidently true, by the smallest changes, one is led to things which are evidently false.

units.la: Cauil-
units.tr: Cavil-

units.la: Hinc nota subtilitatem nimiam à iure reprobari.
units.tr: Hence note that excessive subtlety is rejected by the law.

units.la: Dec. num. 6. Placet potius quod adire num. 3. subtili responsione, malitiosam interrogationem retundi posse: ideoque, eum qui in veritate mutuum reddidit, posse cum iuramento affirmare, se nihil à creditore habuisse. Placet etiam quod negat, recte eum condemnari, cui confitenti promissa fuerit impunitas. num. 7. 8. Gothofr. hic.
units.tr: Dec. num. 6. It is rather agreed that by a subtle answer a malicious question can be repelled; and therefore, that one who in truth has repaid a loan may affirm on oath that he has received nothing from the creditor. It is also agreed, as he denies, that the one to whom impunity was promised on confessing is rightly condemned. num. 7. 8. Gothofr. hic.

units.la: Definitio est Soritis, ad quam Bulgar. hoc vtitur exemplo: Res sacra nullius est in bonis: quod nullius est in bonis, occupanti conceditur: igitur res sacra occupanti conceditur. Falsa est conclusio. Neque enim res sacra occupanti conceditur. Sic argumentabimur mutato ordine in prima figura.
units.tr: The definition is a sorites, for which Bulgarus uses this example: A sacred thing belongs to no one as property; what belongs to no one as property is granted to the one who takes it; therefore a sacred thing is granted to the one who takes it. The conclusion is false, for a sacred thing is not granted to the one who takes it. We shall argue in this way, with the order changed, in the first figure.

units.la: Quod nullius est in bonis, occupanti conceditur:
units.tr: What belongs to no one as property is granted to the one who takes it:

units.la: At res sacra nullius est in bonis.
units.tr: But a sacred thing belongs to no one as property.

units.la: Ergo res sacra occupanti conceditur.
units.tr: Therefore a sacred thing is granted to the one who takes it.

units.la: Sorites est propter homonymiam vitiosus. Propositio vera est & assumptio. Conclusio falsa. Quia in argumento Bulgari, idem non signisignificat, Nullius, in assumptione, quod in propositione. Itaque est homonymia in propositione: Res sacra nullius est; hoc est non potest in commercio hominum esse. In assumptione vero nullius in bonis est, quod non est quidem extra commercium hominum, sed domino & possessore vacat: Et quod ita nullius est, conceditur occupanti, vt ferae bestiae. Verum de hoc sorite non agitur hoc loco. Nam in exemplo allato nullae fiunt breuissimae mutationes, sed sola homonymia vtrumque corrumpit, syllogismum & soritem: Si nulla fuerit homonymia, necessario res sequitur, valebitque Sorites: vt
units.tr: A sorites is faulty because of an ambiguity. The proposition is true, and the assumption; the conclusion is false. For in Bulgarus's argument the word nullius ("of no one") does not mean the same in the assumption as in the proposition. So there is an ambiguity in the proposition: "A sacred thing belongs to no one", that is, it cannot be in the commerce of men. But in the assumption "belongs to no one as property" means something which is indeed not outside the commerce of men, but is vacant of owner and possessor, and what thus belongs to no one is granted to the one who takes it, like wild beasts. But this kind of sorites is not the matter in hand here. For in the example given no very small changes are made; the ambiguity alone corrupts both the syllogism and the sorites. If there were no ambiguity, the thing would follow of necessity, and the sorites would hold, as here:

units.la: Omnis contractus est obligatio,
units.tr: Every contract is an obligation,

units.la: Omnis obligatio parit actionem,
units.tr: Every obligation produces an action,

units.la: Ergo omnis contractus parit actionem.
units.tr: Therefore every contract produces an action.

units.la: Differentia est in ordine propositionum in syllogismo: etiam differentia est in eo, quod in Sorite vox, à qua desinit propositio, incipit assumptionem: vt in argumento Bulgari propositio desinit in voce nullius, quae eadem vox incipit assumptionem: Hoc vero non cernitur in syllogismo, si enim ita concipias; Quod nullius in bonis est, occupanti conceditur: Nullius in bonis est res sacra.
units.tr: There is a difference in the order of the propositions in the syllogism; there is also a difference in that in the sorites the word with which the proposition ends begins the assumption: as in Bulgarus's argument the proposition ends in the word nullius, which same word begins the assumption. This, however, is not seen in the syllogism, for if you conceive it thus: What belongs to no one as property is granted to the one who takes it: A sacred thing belongs to no one as property.

units.la: Ergo, &c.
units.tr: Therefore, etc.

units.la: Sed de hoc genere Soritis hic non agitur: Id genus, de quo hic agitur, per breuissimas mutatiotationes, & per gradus, & per minutas interrogationes conficitur, vt in hoc exemplo: an duodecim oues gregem faciant? Sic sane. An non etiam vndecim? Sic sane. An decem? Et hoc quoque verum est. l. vlt. de abigeis. Ergo cur nouem gregem non faciunt? Hoc vero est falsum: atque ita rem paulatim disputando deducis à vero ad falsum. Emphyteuticarius si dominus est, sicut superficiarius: cur non imponat seruitutem fundo, vt superficiarius? vel opus nouum non nunciabit? quae omnia verisimilia sunt. Cur non etiam dicam: Emphyteuticarium videri à superficiario distingui non posse. Igitur ad extremum dicam, ne internosci quidem: quod falsum est: & id esse non dicendum, verum est. Igitur haec sententia per breuissimas mutationes, hoc est gradus euidenter veros ad id, quod euidenter falsum est, perducit. Breuissimas mutationes Cicero vocat minutas interrogatiunculas. Et Hieron. aduersus Ruffinum: Soritae sunt q. interrogatiunculae argutae. De ψευδομένῳ etiam tractant ICTi in l. qui quadringenta, 88. ad L. Falcid. quod est argumentario quae seipsam destruit. Species autem legis haec est. Qui habebat in bonis quadringenta, trecenta legauit, & legauit Titio centum, quae restabant, sub conditione, si legi Falcidiae locus non esset. Quaeritur, an valeat legarum Titii? Iureconsultus ait, quæstionem esse τῶν ἀδήλων, hoc est, inexplicabilium. Nam si constituas legatum valere, legi Falcidiæ erit locus: atque imo non valebit legatum deficiente conditione. Si constituas, legatum non valere, legi Falcidiæ non erit locus: atque ita existente conditione, legatum valebit. Huic etiam simile est illud Epimenidis Poetæ, qui scripsit, Cretenses esse mendaces. Si verum est, quod scripsit, esse mendaces, per eandem causam falsum est, Cretenses esse mendaces: quia Epimenides etiam Cretensis, verum dixit. Si dicas, non esse mendaces Cretenses, non est verum: nam Epimenides Cretensis falsum dixit. Hoc modo si quis dicat se mentiri: aut vero mentitur, aut non mentitur: mentitur eo ipso, quod non mentitur. Similes argutiæ occurrunt sæpe. Cur. Ad Cic. in Recit. posth.
units.tr: But this kind of sorites is not the matter here. The kind with which we are concerned here is made by the smallest changes, by steps, and by minute questions, as in this example: do twelve sheep make a flock? Certainly. Do not eleven too? Certainly. Ten? That too is true. l. vlt. de abigeis. Why, then, do nine not make a flock? This is false; and so, by disputing little by little, you lead the matter from truth to falsehood. If the emphyteuta is an owner, like the superficiary, why does he not impose an easement on the land, as the superficiary does? Or will he not announce new work? All these things seem probable. Why should I not also say: the emphyteuta cannot be seen to be distinguished from the superficiary. Therefore at last I will say that he cannot even be told apart; which is false; and that this should not be said is true. Thus this argument, by the smallest changes, that is, by steps evidently true, leads to what is evidently false. Cicero calls the smallest changes "minute little questions", and Jerome, aduersus Ruffinum: the sorites are subtle little questions. The jurists also treat of the liar [ψευδομένῳ] in l. qui quadringenta, 88. ad L. Falcid., which is an argument that destroys itself. The case of the law is this. A man who had four hundred in goods bequeathed three hundred, and bequeathed to Titius a hundred, which remained, under the condition that there should be no room for the Falcidian law. The question is whether the legacy to Titius is valid. The jurist says that the question is one of the undecidable [ἀδήλων], that is, of the inexplicable. For if you hold that the legacy is valid, there will be room for the Falcidian law; and indeed the legacy will not be valid if the condition fails. If you hold that the legacy is not valid, there will be no room for the Falcidian law; and so, if the condition is fulfilled, the legacy will be valid. Similar to this is that saying of the poet Epimenides, who wrote that the Cretans are liars. If what he wrote is true, that they are liars, then by the same reasoning it is false that the Cretans are liars, because Epimenides too was a Cretan and spoke the truth. If you say that the Cretans are not liars, that is not true, for Epimenides, a Cretan, spoke falsely. In the same way, if someone says that he is lying, either he speaks truly and is lying, or he does not lie and therefore is lying. Similar subtleties often occur. Cur. Ad Cic. in Recit. posth.

units.la: Ad Leg. 66. De exceptione.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 66. On the exception.

units.la: MArcellus ait: Definit debitor esse is, qui nactus est exceptionē iustā, nec ab æquitate naturali abhorrentem. (ait) in notis scilicet ad Iulianum. Cuia. h.
units.tr: Marcellus says: The debtor ceases to be a debtor when he has obtained a just exception that does not shrink from natural equity. (He says this) in his notes, that is, on Julian. Cuiacius, on the same passage.

units.la: Definit] id proprie desinere dicitur, quod cœpit. l. 208. h. t.
units.tr: To "cease" (definit) is properly said of what has begun. See law 208, this title.

units.la: Exceptionem] 2. Ecl. 3. cap. 64. Nulla est actio, quæ exceptione repellitur. l. 7. §. 8. ff. de dolo l. 13. ff. h. t. l. 112. 115. in sin. h. t. addel. 118. ff. de verb. signif. Gothofr. ui nactus est exceptionem, iure Ciuili de[?]esse non desinit, iure tamen naturali debitor: & ita accipiendam puto hanc [?]am: vt ad ius naturale respiciat, non ad [?]. Nam falsa est regula, si ius Ciuile spe[?] Qui nactus est exceptionem, legibus & naturali congruentem, vt est pacti, quod [?]t contra bonos mores aut leges. leg. 1. de
units.tr: On the exception: 2 Ecl. 3, chap. 64: "There is no action which is repelled by an exception."
