Law 7, §8, Digest, on fraud; law 13, Digest, this title; laws 112 and 115, at the end, this title; add law 118, Digest, on the meaning of words. Gothofredus. A man who has obtained an exception is not ceasing to be a debtor under civil law, but he does remain a debtor under natural law. I think the phrase should be understood in this way: it refers to natural law, not to civil law [...]. For the rule is false if it is taken to mean that civil law alone decides. He who has obtained an exception that agrees with the laws and with natural law, as in the case of a pact that is not contrary to good morals or the laws. Law 1, on

units.la: Stichum 95. de solutionib. Hanc exce[?]em pacti, qui nactus est iure naturali, [?]uo liberatur ipso iure, & si soluerit, per [?]ionem pacti cum esset tutus, condicit: [?]luerit per errorem, habet condictio[?]quia soluit quod iure & natura non de[?] Denique constat, pactum tollere natu[?] obligationem: ciuilem non ipso iure: [?]c parit actionem. Eadem est causa ex[?] iis iuramenti, doli mali, Senatusconsulti Macedoniani, vt, si filiusfam[?]lleiani. Hæ exceptiones naturali æqui[?]untur: qui has nacti sunt, hi iure natu[?]erantur. Diuersa est causa exceptionis Senatusconsulti Macedoniani, vt, si filiusfam. [?]am acceperit, tam patri quam filio datur [?]o aduersus creditorem, sed non ratio[?] lam naturali, quasi plane non teneatur [?].cui credita est pecunia, sed odio quo[?] generatorum & pœnæ causa: qua de re [?]scuntur sæpe infinita. Et ideo qui hanc [?]nem nactus est, ne iure quidem natu[?] tali liberatur: quia non eius causa datur exceptio, sed odio creditoris. Ac si soluerit per errorem, non repetit, quia soluit natura debitum, l. qui exceptionem 40. l. si pœna 19. de condict. indebiti l. sed etsi pater familias in sin. & l. seq. ad Senatusconsult. Macedon. Exceptio igitur Macedoniani abhorret ab æquitate naturali: Unde consequens est, eum, qui soluit ex causa naturali, non repetere. Eadem est causa exceptionis, quæ datur ex edicto, Quod quisque iuris, &c. ut scilicet, quod ius iniquum per te statutum est, id etiam contra te constituatur l. 3. §. vlt. quod quisque iuris in alter. statu. Creditor agit adversus debitorem: debitor eum potest repellere exceptione ex illo edicto: quoniam forte ille creditor, qui agit cum suo debitore cum esset in magistratu, in iure simili actionem eiusmodi denegauit: qua de causa æquum videtur, ut ei etiam denegetur, si tu creditori actionem in casu simili denegasti, tibi etiam denegari debet. Et finge; debitor unde petebatur, quasi nesciret pactum, non est visus exceptione illa, & soluit. Quæritur: an possit condicere? Et placet, illi condictionem non dari, quia illo edicto non tollitur obligatio naturalis, & exceptio datur non tantum eius causa: Quod quisque iuris, &c. sed & pœnæ causa d. l. 3. §. 1. quod quisque iuris. Datur adversus eum, qui in alium iniquum ius dixit & impetrauit: similis est exceptioni Macedonicedo niani. Vtraque abhorret ab æquitate na-; Itaque & qui hanc & qui illam est natu-rali non liberatur. Eadem est ineratio Bulgari, nisi quod notat, eum exesinere esse debitorem, qui nactus est exonem rei iudicatae. Male. Constat enim, itam rem non tollere naturalem obliga-m, l. Index. §. Iulianus. de condict. indeb. Itaiudicatum soluerit, non condicit. Cuiac. it.
units.tr: Stichus 95, on payments. He who has obtained this exception of a pact under natural law is freed by the law itself, and if he has paid, he may not reclaim the money, since, having the protection of the pact, he was safe. If he paid through error, there is a condiction, because he paid what neither law nor nature owed. Finally, it is established that a pact removes the natural obligation, but not the civil one, which it does not dissolve by the law itself, though it does not give rise to an action. The reason is the same for the exceptions of oath, of fraud, of the Macedonian senatusconsult, and of the Velleian senatusconsult. These exceptions are equal to natural equity; those who have obtained them are not freed under natural law. The reason for the exception of the Macedonian senatusconsult is different: if a son under power has borrowed money, the exception is given both to the father and to the son against the creditor, not on the ground of natural law, as if he were not bound at all to the one to whom the money was lent, but out of hatred for the creditors and as a punishment for them; on this matter there are often endless disputes. And therefore he who has obtained this exception is not freed even under natural law, since the exception is not granted for his sake but out of hatred for the creditor. And if he pays through error, he cannot reclaim, because nature owes the debt; law "qui exceptionem" 40; law "si poena" 19, on the condiction of what is not owed; law "sed etsi pater familias" at the end, and the following law, on the Macedonian senatusconsult. The exception of the Macedonian senatusconsult therefore shrinks from natural equity. Hence it follows that one who pays from a natural cause cannot reclaim. The reason for the exception that is given by the edict "Quod quisque iuris" is the same: namely, that what unjust law has been established by you, the same is to be established against you as well; law 3, §last, "quod quisque iuris" on the other's status. A creditor sues a debtor; the debtor can repel him with an exception from that edict, since perhaps that creditor, when he was in office, had denied such an action in a similar suit. For which reason it seems fair that it should also be denied to him, since you denied the creditor an action in a similar case, so it ought to be denied to you as well. Suppose the debtor, from whom the claim was made, as though he did not know of the pact, did not seem to use that exception, and paid. The question is whether he can bring a condiction. And it is held that no condiction is given to him, since by that edict a natural obligation is not removed, and the exception is given not only for its own sake, "Quod quisque iuris" etc., but also as a punishment, said law 3, §1, "quod quisque iuris". It is given against one who has pronounced and obtained unjust law against another; it is similar to the exception of the Macedonian senatusconsult. Both shrink from natural equity. Therefore he who has the one and he who has the other is not freed under natural law. The reasoning of Bulgarus is the same, except that he notes that he ceases to be a debtor who has obtained the exception of a judgment already rendered. That is wrong. For it is established that a judgment does not remove the natural obligation, law "Index", §"Iulianus", on the condiction of what is not owed. So if he has paid a judgment, he cannot reclaim. Cuiacius, on the same passage.

units.la: Ad Leg. 67. De sermone ambiguo.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 67. On ambiguous speech.

units.la: Vuoties idem sermo duas sententias exprimit, ea potissimum accipietur, quae rei idae aptior est.
units.tr: Whenever the same speech expresses two meanings, the one that is more fitting to the matter in hand is to be taken.

units.la: cipietur ]excipiatur. Gothofr.
units.tr: "Is to be taken": let it be chosen instead. Gothofredus.

units.la: iuri & rei, 2. Eclog. 3. 6. de verbor. obligat.
units.tr: Of right and of the thing; 2 Eclogues 3, 6, on the obligation of words.

units.la: gerende ] puta contractui. l. 15. §. 4. supra Subiectae materiae. l. 4. supra de usur. naturus, iuri communi. l. 30. supra de damno: rum proprietati. Gothofr.
units.tr: "To be carried out": that is, for example, a contract; law 15, §4, above. "The subject matter": law 4, above, on usury. "Will be", under common law; law 30, above, on damage [...] of ownership. Gothofredus.

units.la: idem sermo duas sententias exprimat, ibologia est: si eadem vox duas significahabeat, homonymia est. Itaque restrinis hic totus locus est Accusl. Quae aptior est, quae rem perficit & ad rem pertiet si actor ambigua oratione vtatur, cuius sententia actioni seruiat; altera non, ea accipitur, quæ magis conuenit, l. si quis intentione. 66. de iudic. l. in contrahenda in sin. hoc tit. Cuiac. in recitat.
units.tr: When the same speech expresses two meanings, that is ambiguity; if one and the same word has two meanings, that is homonymy. Accordingly, this whole passage is to be restricted. The one that is more fitting is the one that completes the matter and relates to the matter; if the plaintiff uses ambiguous language whose meaning serves the action, and the other meaning does not, the one that agrees better is taken: law "si quis intentione" 66, on judgments; law "in contrahenda", at the end, this title. Cuiacius, on the passage cited.

units.la: Ad Legem 68. De beneficiis.
units.tr: On Law 68. On Benefits.

units.la: IN omnibus causis id obseruatur, vt, vbi persone conditio locum facit beneficio, ibi deficiente ea, beneficium quoque deficiat: vbi vero genus actionis id desiderat, ibi ad quemuis persecutio eius deuenerit, non deficiat ratio auxilii.
units.tr: In all cases this rule is observed: where the condition of the person gives grounds for a benefit, if that condition is lacking, the benefit lapses too. But where the nature of the action requires it, the ground of aid does not lapse, however far the action has passed to whoever pursues it.

units.la: Vbi persone ] Id est, indiuiduo alicui, non speciei: pura Titio, vt Titio: non Titio, vt minori. hæc enim ad hæredes transeunt l. 6. supra de in integr. l. 18. in sin. sup. de minorib. Idem dicendum in priuilegio dignitati concesso l. vlt. supr. de decurion.
units.tr: Where the person means: for some individual, not for a class. A benefit granted purely to Titius, as Titius, is one thing; a benefit granted to Titius as a minor is another, since the latter passes to heirs. l. 6. supra de in integr. l. 18. in sin. sup. de minorib. The same must be said of a privilege granted to a dignity. l. vlt. supr. de decurion.

units.la: Deficiente ] Persona deficiente, personalia extinguuntur l. 196. inf. eod. 2. Eclog. 3. cap. 66. l. 13. supr. soluto. l. 7. sup. de excep. c. 7. de reg. in 6. l. 28. sup. de legat. 2. l. 1. sup. de iure immunit. Gothofr.
units.tr: Lacking: when the person is lacking, personal rights are extinguished. l. 196. inf. eod. 2. Eclog. 3. cap. 66. l. 13. supr. soluto. l. 7. sup. de excep. c. 7. de reg. in 6. l. 28. sup. de legat. 2. l. 1. sup. de iure immunit. Gothofr.

units.la: Genus ] exemplum est in minorum restitutione. d. l. 6. d. l. 18. dolo. l. 13. sup. de dolo.
units.tr: Nature of the action: the restoration of minors is an example. d. l. 6. d. l. 18. dolo. l. 13. sup. de dolo.

units.la: Primum submoueatur quod Bulg. ait: beneficium vel priuilegium esse, vt vsuræ veniant ex mora, sicut veniunt in actionibus bonæ fidei. Hoc enim non est beneficium, sed ius commune, quod porrigitur etiam ad actiones qualquaedam strictas, ad actionem legatorum & fideicommissorum: nec mirum, si ea actione vexantur heredes. Deinde ponatur exemplum ad hanc legem, quod inscriptioni conueniat, quae est de dotis repetitione. Priuilegium habet mulier, quae dotem repetit, & vir a quo repetitur, priuilegio vtitur: mulier, vt praeferatur omnibus creditoribus: vir, vt in id quod facere potest, condemnetur. Vtrumque personale est, & ideo ad heredem non transit: heres mariti damnatur in solidum: heres vxoris non praeferetur creditoribus l. maritum & seq. 12. & 13. solut. matrim. l. un. C. de priuileg. dot. Igitur actio de dote non est priuilegiata, sed persona mulieris. Idem de actione tutelae est dicendum. Pupillus qui agit actione tutelae, praefertur aliis, sed non heres. Actio igitur tutelae non est priuilegiata, sed persona. l. 1. §. idem 11. de Lege Corn. de falsis. Quaedam sunt actiones priuilegiatae, quae in heredem transeunt cum priuilegio, vt actio funeraria datur heredi eius, qui funus fecit, vt Accursius scribit, sed male hoc probat ex l. si filius; 1. §. vlt. de relig. & sumpt. fun. Lex ait; sunerariam actionem dari heredibus eius, qui funus facit. Is qui funus facit, habet quidem actionem priuilegiatam, sed vt probes, eius heredem quoque habere eiusmodi priuilegium, male colligis: Actio funeraria datur heredi. Ergo & priuilegium. Falsa est consequentia.
units.tr: First, let us set aside what the Bulgarus says: that it is a benefit or privilege that interest should run from delay, just as it runs in actions of good faith. For this is not a benefit but common law, which extends even to certain strict actions, such as the action on legacies and trust-bequests; and it is no wonder that heirs are harassed by that action. Next, let us put forward an example for this law which fits the inscription concerning the recovery of a dowry. The woman who recovers the dowry has a privilege, and the husband from whom it is recovered also enjoys one: the woman so that she is preferred to all creditors, the husband so that he is condemned only to the extent of what he can pay. Both privileges are personal and so do not pass to the heir: the husband's heir is condemned in full, while the wife's heir is not preferred to the creditors. l. maritum & seq. 12. & 13. solut. matrim. l. un. C. de priuileg. dot. So the action on the dowry is not privileged; it is the woman's person that is. The same must be said of the action on guardianship. A ward who sues by the action on guardianship is preferred to others, but his heir is not. So the action on guardianship is not privileged; it is the person. l. 1. §. idem 11. de Lege Corn. de falsis. Some privileged actions do pass to the heir with the privilege, as the funeral action is given to the heir of the one who conducted the funeral, as Accursius writes, though he proves it badly. ex l. si filius; 1. §. vlt. de relig. & sumpt. fun. The law says that the funeral action is given to the heirs of the one who conducts the funeral. He who conducts the funeral indeed has a privileged action, but to prove that his heir also has such a privilege is a bad inference. The action is given to the heir; therefore the privilege too. The consequence is false.

units.la: K Constat tamen, funerariam actionem esse priuilegiatam: non enim persona, sed causa funeris extorsit beneficium: unde sequitur, beneficium in hæredes transfire. Sic etiam seruitutes personales cum persona extinguuntur; at reales manent cum hærede. Eadem in immunitatibus ratio seruatur. l.2. de cens. Eadem distinctio est in iure, quod Princeps dedit. Multum enim interest, an dederit personæ, an prædio l.1.§.permittitur de aqua quotid. & æstiua. verum finge: Princeps concessit ius aquæ personæ, veluti duobus sociis. Vtraque mortua ius extinguitur: quod est personale: at vel vno superstite, integrum ius manet. Frontinus de aquæductu. Itaq; beneficium personale quod duobus datur, non desinit, quamdiu vnus superest. Hæc lex repetitur in l. priuilegia inf. hoc titul. Cuiac. in Repetit.
units.tr: K It is nonetheless agreed that the funeral action is privileged, for it is not the person but the cause of the funeral that won the benefit; hence it follows that the benefit passes to heirs. So too personal servitudes are extinguished with the person, but real servitudes remain with the heir. The same rule is observed in immunities. l.2. de cens. The same distinction holds in the right which the Prince has granted. For it makes a great difference whether he has granted it to a person or to an estate. l.1.§.permittitur de aqua quotid. & æstiua. But suppose the Prince granted a water right to a person, say to two partners. If both die, the right is extinguished, since it is personal; but if one survives, the whole right remains. Frontinus, on aqueducts. Therefore a personal benefit granted to two does not cease so long as one survives. This law is repeated in l. priuilegia inf. hoc titul. Cuiac. in Repetit.

units.la: Ad Leg. 69.
units.tr: On Law 69.

units.la: INuito beneficium non datur.
units.tr: A benefit is not conferred on an unwilling person.

units.la: Inuito] l.156. inf. eod. l. ult. supra de usu & habitat. l.19. §.2. supra de donat. vide l.62. sup. de verb. oblig. Gothof.
units.tr: Invito] law 156 below, same title; the last law above, on use and habitation; law 19, §2 above, on gifts; see law 62 above, on verbal obligations. Gothof.

units.la: Beneficium] l.ult. defensio. d.l.156. donatio. d.§.2. societas l.26. §.4. supr. de condict. indeb. adrogatio. l.5. & 24. sup. de adopt. Sic libertas inuito filio (aliud in seruo. l.ult. C. de testam. manumiss.) non datur. v. l.5. C. de emancip. v. reliqua in l.62. l.62 sup. de verb. oblig. multo minus damno affic etur inuitus l.25. §. 1. in fine sup. soluto: obligabitur, de domo sua extrahetur. l.103. inf. eod. l. 18. sup. de in ius: Sic quæ diuertit, vt inuita ad virum reuertatur, cogi non potest l.7. C. de repud. Gothof.
units.tr: Benefit l.ult. defensio. d.l.156. donatio. d.§.2. societas l.26. §.4. supr. de condict. indeb. adrogatio. l.5. & 24. sup. de adopt. So liberty is not given to an unwilling son (it is otherwise for a slave, l.ult. C. de testam. manumiss.). see l.5. C. de emancip. see the rest in l.62. l.62 sup. de verb. oblig. Much less is a person unwillingly burdened with loss: l.25. §. 1. in fine sup. soluto: he will be bound, he will be dragged out of his own house. l.103. inf. eod. l. 18. sup. de in ius. So too a woman who has left her husband cannot be compelled to return to him against her will. l.7. C. de repud. Gothof.

units.la: Imo datur l.32. sup. de acquir. rer. §.3. Institit. per quas personas cuique. Goth.
units.tr: Indeed it is given: law 32 above, on the acquisition of things, §3; Institutes, "per quas personas cuique." Goth.

units.la: Potest enim quilibet suo iuri renunciare. l.41. sup. de minorib. & suspectus est qui operam inuito ingerit. l.25. de procur. Expolita est quoque hæc l. sup. in l.61.
units.tr: For anyone may renounce his own right. l.41. sup. de minorib. And he is suspect who thrusts his services on an unwilling person. l.25. de procur. This law has also been explained above in l.61.

units.la: Ad Leg.70. De potestate coercitionis.
units.tr: On Law 70. On the power of coercion.

units.la: NEmo potest gladii potestatem sibi datam, vel cuiusuis alterius coercitionis ad alium transferre.
units.tr: No one can transfer to another the power of the sword given to him, or any other power of coercion.

units.la: Coniunge l.solet. de offic. præt.
units.tr: Compare law "solet", on the duties of the praetor.

units.la: l.6. sup. de offic. proconf.
units.tr: Law 6, on the duties of the proconsul.

units.la: animaduertendi in facinorosos. l.5. §. 8. sup. de offic. præf. v. l.3. sup. de iurisd. Gladii potestas est vitæ ac necis authoritas.
units.tr: Of punishing criminals. Law 5, §8, on the duties of the prefect; see also law 3, on jurisdiction. The power of the sword is the authority over life and death.

units.la: Ius puniendi, τὸ δίκαιον τῶν τιμωρειῶν. 2. Eclog.3.c.67.
units.tr: The right to punish, τὸ δίκαιον τῶν τιμωρειῶν [to dikaion tōn timōreiōn]. Eclogues, book 2, title 3, chapter 67.

units.la: Merum imperium, est gladii potestas. l.3. de iurisd.om.iud. Gladii potestas est ius vitæ adimendæ. l. Respiciendum de pæn. quod etiam in illa lege verba illa significant: aut animaduerti in facinorosos, hoc est puniri. Nam animaduerti is dicitur, qui punitur gladio. d. l. Respiciendū & l. seq. Vel animaduerti, hoc est, capite puniri, & lex eos, in quos animaduerti iubet, statuit, seruos fieri poenæ. Sed merum imperiū cōtinet etiam multa alia: nempe ius damnandi ad bestias, cōfiscandi, relegandi, deportandi. l. Merū. de Iurisd. om. iud. l. 1. de offic. eius, cui mand. est iurisd. Datur aūt hæc gladii potestas: non n. eam quisquam, magistratus iure arrogar, sed accipit à lege. Lege igitur conceditur merū imperium, & dicitur ex aduerso mixti. Mixtū sequitur magistratum, & iurisdictioni cohæret. Merum imperium separatur à iurisdictione, hoc est, non cōpetit iure magistratus, sed lege datur, modo magistratui, modo priuato. Præfecto vigilū datum est ius verberandi, non ius gladii. l. 3. §. 1. l. 4. de offic. præf. vigil. Et modo datur merum imperium in omnes personas, modo in certas tātum: vt præfecto vigilum datur ius verberandi incendiarios, fures, effractores, & tales, vt in tit. de offic. præf. vigil. Itaq; priuatus habet merū imperium. Præsidibus prouinciæ datum est ius gladii, non deportandi, nō confiscandi. Nō datur cuilibet magistratui: vt Prætor vrbanus nō habuit merū imperium: & ideo si incidit aliquid apud Prætorē, quod exigit maiorem coercitionem, tunc remitti debet ad Præfectum vrbis, qui sibi vindicat omnia crimina, & cui datum est plene imperium. l. 1. §. Item solent. de offic. præf. urbi. urbi. l. 1. in fine. l. 2. de suspect. tut. Sic praefectus vigilum, cum res superat legem meri imperii, remittit ad Praefectum urbis l. 3. & 4. de offic. praef. vig. Sic olim etiam curatores viarum & regionum, imperium merum habuerunt, & potestatem aliquam, sed non gravissimam coercitionem. Itaque cur omnes magistratus hoc merum imperium non habent? Quia hoc tantum est legis. Quia vero imperium merum lege datur, consequens est, ut id non possit mandari alteri, & ea quae iurisdictionis sunt, non possunt mandari. Nemo tutores dare potest, nemo magistratus, nisi cui lege datum est. Potest tamen privatus dare lege 12. tab. scil. pater: cui hoc lex permisit. Eadem est causa cognitionis, transactionis alimentorum, quae a lege datur l. cum hi. 8. de transact. l. cum alimenta C. cod. & ideo non mandatur d. l. cum hi. §. sed nec mandare. 18. Quaecunque igitur lege dantur, non transferuntur in alium: quae sunt meri imperii, danda sunt nominatim. Merum imperium qui habet, non habet suo iure. Haec sententia reperta est in l. solent 16. de iurisd. Mixtum imperium mandatur & iurisdictio, quia suo iure haec magistratui competunt, nec nominatim aut specialiter haec fuerunt eis concessa. Huic regulae opponitur: Eum cui Proconsul suâ iurisdictione mandavit, custodias audire. l. 6. de offic. proconsul. Videtur igitur mandari imperium merum: quod est negandum. Nam auditio datur ei tantum propterea, ut prasvt præanditos remittat ad Proconsulem, vt ipse puniat aut liberet, aut animaduertat, aut absoluat reū. Hoc genus mandati est extraordinariū. Nam non potest mandari legato, vt animaduertat aut absoluat reum, quia nec reus potest accusari apud legatum, sed apud Proconsulem: at interim audiri potest ante damnationem à legato, voluntate Proconsulis. Rursus obiici solet: legatum Proconsulis, cui mandata est iurisdictio, posse cognoscere de crimine suspecti tutoris. Eundem igitur habere merum imperium. Hoc negatur. Nam cognitio suspecti tutoris non pertinet ad merum imperium, nec ex eo crimine datur grauis coercitio. Infamia est maxima, crimen tamen non semper, sed infamiæ irrogatio non pertinet ad merum imperium. Actio depositi est infamis, an ideo necesse est, eum, qui cognoscit de depósito, merum imperium habere? Minime. Sed causa suspecti interdum exigit grauiorem pœnam l. 1. de suspect. tut. & tū remittitur ad præfectum vrbis puniendus d. l. 1. in fine. Igitur & tunc legatus mittet ad Proconsulem l. si quid erit. 11. de offic. proconf. Præterea verum est, cognitionem suspecti dari lege. Igitur non est existimandum, legatum proconsulis hanc cognitionem habere ex mandato: sed posteaquam ei mandata est generalis iurisdictio; quomodo comprehenduntur tantum ea, quæ possunt mandari.
units.tr: Mere imperium is the power of the sword. Law 3, on the jurisdiction of all judges. The power of the sword is the right to take away life. Law "Respiciendum", on punishments, also shows that in that law the words "or to be punished by death" mean "to be punished": for he is said to be put to death [animadverti] who is punished by the sword. d. l. Respiciendum and the following law. Or "to be punished by death", that is, to be punished by beheading; and the law decrees that those against whom it orders this be made slaves of punishment. But mere imperium also includes many other things: namely, the right to condemn to the beasts, to confiscate, to relegate, and to deport. l. Merum, on the jurisdiction of all judges; l. 1, on the duties of the officer to whom jurisdiction has been entrusted. This power of the sword is given, however, not in such a way that anyone seizes it by the right of his magistracy, but it is received from the law. Mere imperium is therefore granted by law, and is set in contrast to mixed imperium. Mixed imperium follows the magistrate and clings to jurisdiction. Mere imperium is separated from jurisdiction: that is, it does not belong to a magistrate by right of office, but is given by law, sometimes to a magistrate, sometimes to a private person. The prefect of the watch was given the right to flog, but not the right of the sword. l. 3, §1; l. 4, on the duties of the prefect of the watch. And mere imperium is sometimes given over all persons, sometimes over certain persons only: thus the prefect of the watch is given the right to flog arsonists, thieves, burglars, and such people, as in the title on the duties of the prefect of the watch. Thus a private person may hold mere imperium. The governors of provinces were given the right of the sword, but not the right to deport or to confiscate. It is not given to every magistrate: thus the urban praetor did not have mere imperium, and so if some matter arises before the praetor that calls for stronger coercion, it must then be referred to the prefect of the city, who claims for himself all crimes and to whom full imperium has been given. l. 1, §Item solent, on the duties of the city prefect; l. 1, at the end; l. 2, on suspected guardians. So too the prefect of the watch, when the matter exceeds the scope of his law of mere imperium, refers it to the prefect of the city. l. 3 and 4, on the duties of the prefect of the watch. Likewise in former times the overseers of roads and of districts also held mere imperium and some power, but not the most severe coercion. Why, then, do not all magistrates have this mere imperium? Because it belongs to law alone. And because mere imperium is given by law, it follows that it cannot be entrusted to another, and that the things that belong to jurisdiction cannot be entrusted. No one can appoint guardians except one to whom it is given by law, and no magistrate can do so unless it is given to him by law. A private person can, however, appoint one by the law of the Twelve Tables, namely the father, to whom the law has granted this. The same is the case with cognizance, and with the settlement of maintenance, which are given by law: l. cum hi, 8, on settlements; l. cum alimenta, C., same title. And for this reason they are not entrusted: d. l. cum hi, §sed nec mandare. 18. Whatever things are given by law are therefore not transferred to another: those that belong to mere imperium must be given by name. He who has mere imperium does not have it by his own right. This principle is found in l. solent 16, on jurisdiction. Mixed imperium and jurisdiction are entrusted, because these belong to the magistrate by his own right, and were not granted to him by name or specifically. Against this rule is set the case of one to whom the proconsul, by his jurisdiction, entrusted the hearing of prisoners. l. 6, on the duties of the proconsul. It seems, then, that mere imperium is entrusted, but this must be denied. For the hearing is given to him only so that he may send the accused back to the proconsul, so that he himself may punish, or acquit, or put to death, or absolve the defendant. This kind of commission is extraordinary. For it cannot be entrusted to a legate that he should put to death or absolve the defendant, because the accused cannot be prosecuted before a legate, but before the proconsul; yet meanwhile he may be heard by the legate before condemnation, by the proconsul's will. Again it is commonly objected that the legate of the proconsul, to whom jurisdiction has been entrusted, can take cognizance of the crime of a suspected guardian, and therefore has the same mere imperium. This is denied. For cognizance of a suspected guardian does not pertain to mere imperium, nor does such a crime bring on severe coercion. Infamy is the greatest, yet the crime is not always so; but the imposition of infamy does not pertain to mere imperium. The action of deposit is infamous; is it therefore necessary that the one who takes cognizance of a deposit have mere imperium? By no means. But the cause of suspicion sometimes calls for a heavier penalty, l. 1, on suspected guardians, and then the matter is referred to the prefect of the city to be punished, d. l. 1, at the end. Therefore even then the legate will send it to the proconsul. l. si quid erit, 11, on the duties of the proconsul. Moreover, it is true that cognizance of suspicion is given by law. Therefore it should not be thought that the legate of the proconsul has this cognizance by commission, but after general jurisdiction has been entrusted to him; for only those things are included that can be entrusted.

units.la: Cum
units.tr: When

units.la: Cum igitur de suspectis tutoribus possit cognoscere, ex oratione Seueri & Antonini hoc habet.l.1.§.damus.de suspect.tut. Sic legatus potest tutorem dare, non quia ei datur iurisdictio,sed quia ei D. Marcus hoc specialiter dedit.l.1.de tut.& curat. Sic habet ius dandi iudicem ex l. cum prætor. 12. de iudic. non tamen merum imperium. Sed quæcunque lege dantur, non nisi specialiter mandari, & in alium transferri possunt.Cuiac.in Recitat.
units.tr: Since, then, he can take cognizance of suspected guardians, he has this from the speech of Severus and Antoninus, l.1.§.damus.de suspect.tut. So the legate can appoint a guardian, not because jurisdiction is granted to him, but because Divus Marcus gave him this power specifically, l.1.de tut.& curat. So he has the right to appoint a judge from l. cum prætor. 12, de iudic., but not the merum imperium. Yet whatever is given by law can be entrusted only specifically, and cannot be transferred to another, Cuiac. in Recitat.

units.la: Ad Leg.71. Quæ per libellum expe- diri nequeunt.
units.tr: On Law 71: Matters which cannot be dispatched by petition.

units.la: OMnia quæcunque causæ cognitionem desiderant, per libellum expediri non possunt.
units.tr: All matters that require the cognizance of a cause cannot be dispatched by petition.

units.la: Omnia ] coniunge l. Nequicquam, §. ubi decretum de offic.proconsf.
units.tr: Omnia ] join with l. Nequicquam, §. ubi decretum de offic. proconsul.

units.la: Cognitionem ] Aliud in iis, quibus semiplena sufficit.
units.tr: Cognitionem ] It is otherwise in those cases for which a half-finished hearing is sufficient.

units.la: Per libellum ]l. 105.inf. eod. v. l. 9.§ 1.sup. de offic. proconf.
units.tr: Per libellum ] l. 105. inf. eod. cf. l. 9.§ 1. sup. de offic. proconf.

units.la: Sententia haec est: Ea quae desiderant causae cognitionem, siue decretum: per libellum, siue de plano expediri non possunt, sed pro tribunali. Exempla haec sunt: Alienatio praediorum minoris non fit sine decreto Praetoris vel praesidis, quo permittatur alienatio nominatim: nisi causa cognita, etiam secuto decreto, subscriptione ad libellum, non permittitur alienatio. Nam non per libellum, sed pro tribunali expediri debet. l. minorum 6. C. de praed. minor. Sic etiam dilatio litigatoribus non datur de plano, hoc est in transitu extra tribunal, dum magistratus iter facit, dum redit domum, aut abit in forum: quia dilatio exigit causae cognitionem, ideoque petenda est à Iudice sedente pro tribunali, non stante. l. à procedente 4. C. de dilation. Sic etiam bonorum possessio decretalis Carboniana datur non per libellum, aut de plano, sed pro tribunali. l. 3. §. si causa 8. de bon. poss. l. 2. §. dies. quis ordo in bon. possess. seruentur. Idem dicendum est de in integrum restitutione l. omnes 3. de restit. in integ. Idem in abolitione criminum. Haec sententia repetita est ex l. 9. §. 1. de offic. proconf. Cui apte conuenit exemplum l. Excusare 25. de excusat. quae ait: Excusare se tutor per libellum non potest, hoc est; Excusatio tutoris disceptatur & deciditur pro tribunali, quia decreto est opus l. si cum ipse 39. de excus. valde obstare videtur l. 13. §. scire autem 8. & seqq. de excusat. cuius sententia haec est: Tutor debet se excusare intra dies 50. alioqui non recipitur. Potest autem contestari excusationem, ut ait lex, sive speciem excusationis, vel in iure apud tribunal Praetoris, vel de plano per libellum. Igitur tutor se potest excusare per libellum. Dicendum, ad praescriptionem 50. dierum tollendam, contestationem excusationis vel per libellum factam sufficere. Male in d. l. 13. legitur, Supplices libellos, sed interpretandum; de plano. Male Accursius conciliet d. l. 13. cum d. l. excusare, ait, Tutor se non potest excusare per libellum; Tutor absens, inquit, se non potest excusare; praesens potest per libellum, quod falsum est. Nam quid vetat, causam absentis per procuratorem agi, ut in manumissionibus. l. Etiam 15. §. absens 3. de manumiss. vind. De crimine etiam non agitur: de quo tamen constat, absentes audiri per procuratorem. E. & causa excusationis per procuratorem agi potest. Cum vero negatur agi quid posse per libellum, non praesentia exigitur, sed tribunal. Nam pro tribunali, & per libellum, opponuntur l. 2. C. quemadmod. testament. aper. per libellum & in praesentia, non opponuntur. Huc pertinet l. ubicunque 105. ff. hoc tit. Ubicunque causae cognitio est, Praetor tor desideratur, hoc est: Vbi decreto opus est, id debet interponi à Prætore in urbe, à Præside in prouincia, qui tribunal habent: non à Iudice datur, qui de plano iudicat: non à municipali magistratu, qui etiam tribunal non habet. Et est referenda ad edictum de damno infecto, sicut etiam l. Nemo. loquitur de damno infecto, vt constat ex l. 4. in fine de damno infecto, in qua l. vtraque sententia est expressa, sed ab Vlpiano, non à Paulo. Verum est, fateor, quod Vlpianus tractauit lib. 1. ad edict. ex quo sunt dictæ leges, l. nemo & l. vbicunque. Sententia est; vicinus non cauet damni infecti: iubebit Prætor possidere me, quod fit causa cognita. Ergo decretum interponitur à Prætore, non a municipali magistratu. Denique quæ decretum exigunt, debent expediri per Prætorem vel præsidem prouinciæ pro tribunali, non de plano. Quædam tamen sunt, quæ de plano Prætor exequitur, vt seruum de plano manumittit: bonorum possessionem dat de plano: excepta decretali, d. l. 3. de bon. poss. l. 9. de ofsic. proconsl. leg. vnius §. vlt. de quæst. Cuiac. in Recitat.
units.tr: The meaning of this is: those matters which require a hearing of the cause, or a formal decree, cannot be dispatched by petition or summarily, but must be dealt with from the bench. Examples: the alienation of a minor's property is not made without a decree of the praetor or governor, by which the alienation is expressly permitted; unless, after a cause has been heard, and even after a decree has followed, the alienation is not permitted by a subscription to a petition. For it must be dispatched not by petition but from the bench, l. minorum 6. C. de praed. minor. So too a postponement is not granted to litigants summarily, that is, in passing outside the tribunal while the magistrate is on his journey, while he is returning home, or going out to the forum; because a postponement requires the cognizance of the cause, and so must be sought from a judge sitting on the bench, not standing, l. à procedente 4. C. de dilation. So too the decretal Carbonian possession of goods is given not by petition or summarily, but from the bench, l. 3. §. si causa 8. de bon. poss. l. 2. §. dies. quis ordo in bon. possess. seruentur. The same must be said of restitution in integrum, l. omnes 3. de restit. in integ. the same of the abolition of crimes. This opinion is repeated from l. 9. §. 1. de offic. proconf. To it the example of l. Excusare 25. de excusat. fits well, which says: a guardian cannot excuse himself by petition; that is, an excuse of a guardian is argued and decided from the bench, because a decree is needed, l. si cum ipse 39. de excus. The law l. 13. §. scire autem 8. and following, de excusat. seems strongly to oppose this, whose opinion is this: a guardian must excuse himself within fifty days, otherwise he is not admitted. Moreover, as the law says, he may lodge his excuse, or the substance of his excuse, either in court before the praetor's tribunal or summarily by petition. Therefore a guardian can excuse himself by petition. It must be said that to remove the fifty-day limit, a lodging of the excuse made by petition is sufficient. It is wrongly read in d. l. 13. "supplices libellos," but it must be interpreted as "summarily." Accursius wrongly reconciles d. l. 13. with d. l. excusare; he says: a guardian cannot excuse himself by petition; an absent guardian, he says, cannot excuse himself; a present one can by petition, which is false. For what prevents the cause of an absent person from being pursued through a procurator, as in manumissions, l. Etiam 15. §. absens 3. de manumiss. vind. Nor is a criminal matter pursued this way, yet it is established that absent persons are heard through a procurator. Therefore the cause of an excuse can also be pursued through a procurator. When, indeed, it is denied that something can be done by petition, what is required is not presence but the tribunal. For "from the bench" and "by petition" are set against each other, l. 2. C. quemadmod. testament. aper. "by petition" and "in presence" are not set against each other. To this belongs l. ubicunque 105, ff. hoc tit. Wherever there is a cause that requires cognizance, the praetor is required, that is: where a decree is needed, it must be interposed by the praetor in the city, or by the governor in the province, who have a tribunal; not by a judge who judges summarily; not by a municipal magistrate, who does not even have a tribunal. And it refers to the edict on damage not yet done, just as l. Nemo also speaks of damage not yet done, as is clear from l. 4. in fine de damno infecto, in which both opinions are expressed, but by Ulpian, not by Paul. It is true, I admit, that Ulpian treated this in book 1 on the edict, from which the laws l. nemo and l. ubicunque are taken. The opinion is: a neighbour does not give security against damage not yet done; the praetor will order me to possess, which is done after a cause has been heard. Therefore the decree is interposed by the praetor, not by a municipal magistrate. Finally, those matters which require a decree must be dispatched by the praetor or the governor of the province from the bench, not summarily. Yet there are some things which the praetor carries out summarily, as when he manumits a slave summarily, or gives possession of goods summarily, except the decretal possession, d. l. 3. de bon. poss. l. 9. de offic. proconsul. leg. vnius §. vlt. de quaest. Cuiac. in Recitat.

units.la: Ad Leg.72. De iure pignorandi.
units.tr: On Law 72. On the right of pledging.

units.la: FRuctus rei est, vel pignori dare licere.
units.tr: The fruit of a thing is the liberty to give it in pledge.

units.la: Fructus ] Coniunge leg. vlt. supr. de usur.
units.tr: Fruit: join this with the last law above, on usury.

units.la: Eum [?]um fructum mihi is eripit qui impedit, quo [?]nus rem meam pignori dare possim. hinc il[?]d, Non valere pactum, ne creditori liceat pi[?] ora vendere. l. 4. sup. de pignorat. Goth.
units.tr: He takes that fruit from me who prevents me from giving my thing in pledge. Hence the saying that a pact is not valid by which a creditor is forbidden to sell the pledges. l. 4. sup. de pignorat. Goth.

units.la: Repetita est ex l. ult. de usuris. Sententia est. [?]essor cum quo agitur rei vindicatione, in [?]ctus damnatur, & olim in duplos, ob ma[?]n fidem, quod hodie sublatum est. In fru[?]i numerantur multa, & inter caetera, quod [?]re pignori data actor mutuā pecuniam acce[?] ser, si habuisset. Postulat igitur, ut eius ra[?] habeatur. leg. videamus 38. in fine de usuris.
units.tr: This is repeated from l. ult. de usuris. The sense is this: a possessor sued by an action for recovery of a thing is condemned for the fruits, and formerly to double them, on account of bad faith, which has since been abolished. Many things are counted among the fruits, and among other things this: that the claimant could have borrowed money by pledging the thing, had he possessed it. He therefore asks that this be taken into account. leg. videamus 38. in fine de usuris.

units.la: [?]ete igitur Ioannes: si quando in petitione [?]fructuum ratio habenda sit, utilitas, quam [?]or habuisset, si rem pignori dare licuisset, æ[?]nabitur. Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: Hence, then, the view of John: if ever, in a claim for fruits, an account must be taken, the advantage the claimant would have had, had it been lawful to pledge the thing, will be estimated. Cuiac. in Recit.

units.la: Leg. 73. 1. De tutela & hæreditate. 2. De vi & clam. 3. De his quæ in testamento intelligi non possunt. 4. Extra- neo caueri non posse.
units.tr: Law 73. 1. On guardianship and inheritance. 2. On force and stealth. 3. On those things in a will that cannot be understood. 4. That one cannot give security to an outsider.

units.la: Vo tutela redit, eo & hæreditas peruenit, nisi cum fœminæ hæredes intercedunt. 1. Nemo potest tutorem dare cuiquam, nisi cuiquam in suis hæredibus, cum moritur, habituruisve esset, si vixisset. 2. §. Vi fa[?] n id videtur esse, qua de re quis, cum pro[?] hibetur, fecit. Clam, quod quisque, cum controuersiam haberet, habiturum ve se putaret, fecit. 3. §. Quæ in testamento ita sunt scripta, vt intelligi non possint, perinde sunt, ac si scripta non essent. 4. §. Nec paciscendo, nec legem dicendo, nec stipulando, quisquam alteri cauere potest.
units.tr: Where guardianship returns, there the inheritance also comes, unless women intervene as heirs. 1. No one can give a guardian to anyone, unless to one who, when he dies, is or would have been among his own heirs had he lived. 2. §. What someone does with regard to a thing when he is forbidden is considered done by force. What someone does by stealth, while he has a dispute and thinks he will have it, is done secretly. 3. §. Those things written in a will in such a way that they cannot be understood are just as if they had not been written. 4. §. Nor by agreeing, nor by dictating a law, nor by stipulating, can anyone give security to another.

units.la: Quo ] Eo tutela redit, quo hæreditas peruenit, ita restituit Hotom. f. obs. 26. est enim tutela hæreditatis consequentia. l. 3. sup. de legitim. tut. §. 1. Instit. de leg. patron. Hotomanni opinionem confirmat Nouella 118. c. 5. & Graeci 2. Eclog. 3. c. 73. Gothofr.
units.tr: Quo: guardianship returns to where the inheritance comes, as Hotom. f. obs. 26. restores it, for guardianship is a consequence of inheritance. l. 3. sup. de legitim. tut. §. 1. Instit. de leg. patron. The opinion of Hotomannus is confirmed by Novella 118, c. 5, and by the Greeks, Eclog. 3. c. 73. Gothofr.

units.la: Redit ] Redire dicitur, quod lege destinatum est. l. 11. sup. de test. tut.
units.tr: Redit: that is said to return which is assigned by law. l. 11. sup. de test. tut.

In suis ] l. 1. sup. de testam. tut. Habiturusve ] §. vlt. Instit. de tutel. Vi ] v. l. 1. §. 5. sup. quod vi aut clam. Clam ] v. l. 3. §. 7. sup. quod vi aut clam. Vt intelligi ] l. 62. §. 1. sup. de hared. instit. Nec paciscendo ] 2. Eclog. 3. c. 71. l. 38. §. 17. sup. de verb. obligat. Cauere ] multo minus nocere. l. 74. inf. eod. Gothofr.
units.tr: Peruenit: Devolves ] Law 1 above, de legitimis tutelis; and Institutes, de legitima patronorum tutela, at the end. Eclogues 2, 3, c. 73. Why so? See law 65 above, de pro socio. Women ] The law "minores," and the last law, C. de legitimis tutelis. Among their own ] Law 1 above, de testamentaria tutela. Or about to have ] Last §, Institutes, de tutelis. By force ] See law 1, §5 above, quod vi aut clam. By stealth ] See law 3, §7 above, quod vi aut clam. That it be understood ] Law 62, §1 above, de heredibus instituendis. Nor by agreement ] Eclogues 2, 3, c. 71; law 38, §17 above, de verborum obligationibus. To provide against ] much less to harm. Law 74 below, same title. Gothofr.

units.la: In hac lege quinque sunt regulæ. Prima est: Quo tutela redit, eo hereditas peruenit. quæ sedum Placent. ita potius constitui debet; hereditas redit, eo & tutela peruenit. Hæc ... la est de hæreditate legitima & tutela, non a quæ testamento deseritur. Hæreditas m legitima dicitur redire: quia reperit faam. l. 3. si quis omiss. caus. testam. Proinde legi recte subiicitur exceptio, Nisi cum inter hæredes intercedunt. Tunc enim non unt esse tutrices: quoniam hereditates veit ad fœminas, tutelæ non item. l. 1. dele- ut. At neutro loco legitur hæc exceptio: minores 25. annis hæredes intercedant: quia inc non possunt esse tutores. Valde notaest hæc exceptio, & tamen non est addita loco; quia ante testamentum minor ætas excusabat tutelam: seruitus tamen excut. In locum vero minorum 25. annis dair curator, nec desinebant illi esse tutores de tut. & rat. distrah.
units.tr: In this law there are five rules. The first is: where guardianship returns, there the inheritance comes. But as some think, it ought rather to be stated thus: where the inheritance returns, there guardianship also comes. This is said of legitimate inheritance and guardianship, not of that which is left by will. An inheritance is said to return legitimately because it returns to the family. l. 3. si quis omiss. caus. testam. Accordingly, an exception is rightly added to the law: unless women intervene as heirs. For then they cannot be guardians, since inheritances come to women, but guardianships do not. l. 1. dele- ut. But this exception is read in neither place: minors under 25 years who are heirs intervene, because they cannot be guardians. This exception is very noteworthy, and yet it is not added in its place; because before the will, minority excused from guardianship, though slavery excuses too. In place of minors under 25 years a curator is given, and they did not cease to be guardians. de tut. & rat. distrah.

units.la: Ad §. Nemo.
units.tr: On §. Nemo.

units.la: ecunda regula est de testamentaria tutela: no potest testamento tutorem dare, nisi liberis & posthumis: hoc est, iis, qui sunt in vtero, es sint, vt nati videantur. l. 16. de testam. Ergo tutela testamentaria mandatur iure iæ potestatis. leg. impuberi 40. de administ. Pater emancipato filio non dat tutorem te- stamenstamento quia non est suus. Mater filio non potest dare l. peto. 69. §. mater, 2. de leg. 2. quia filius matri non est suus hæres, sed legitimus. Illa est inutilis ratione pupilli: hæc ratione testatricis. l.1. de confirm. tut. Datus tamen à patre emancipato confirmatur sine inquisitione: non idem in matre, sed confirmatus etiam tutor est datiuus d.l.1. de confirm. tut. & l.4. de testam. tut.
units.tr: The second rule concerns testamentary guardianship: no one can appoint a guardian by will except for children and posthumous heirs, that is, those who are in the womb, or who are to be considered born. l. 16. de testam. Therefore testamentary guardianship is given by right of power. leg. impuberi 40. de administ. A father does not appoint a guardian by will for an emancipated son, because he is not his own. A mother cannot appoint one for her son, l. peto. 69. §. mater, 2. de leg. 2. because a son is not his mother's own heir, but her legitimate heir. The former is invalid on account of the ward, the latter on account of the testatrix. l.1. de confirm. tut. Yet a guardian given by an emancipated father is confirmed without inquiry; not so for a mother, but a guardian confirmed is also a dative guardian. d.l.1. de confirm. tut. & l.4. de testam. tut.

units.la: Ad §. Vi factum.
units.tr: On the paragraph Vi factum.

units.la: Regula tertia pertinet ad l. 1. §. quid sit. quod vi aut clam. Opus vi factum videri in solo, quod quis, contra quam prohiberetur, fecit. Iraque si ita fecit, tenetur interdicto, Quod vi aut clam. Tenetur etiam eo interdicto, qui fecit clanculum, cum timeret controuersiam cum vicino aut cum alio: aut iam habet. At contra vi facit, qui, cum prohiberetur, fecit. Alia est definitio eius, qui clam, aut vi fecit. l.3. in princ. & §. 1. de itinere act. priuato. Vbi is, qui prohibetur via vti, & vtitur; clam vtitur. Resp. ex sententia Ioannis: qui prohibenti resistit, hoc est, qui eo verante facit, vi facit. Qui autem prohibenti acquiescit, sed postea ignorante eo, qui prohibuit, pergit opus facere, clam facit: & ita accipe d. l. 3. Quidam prohibiti faciunt, & hi non clam, sed vi faciunt.
units.tr: The third rule belongs to l. 1, §. quid sit, Quod vi aut clam. An act is regarded as done by force (vi) when someone does it contrary to a prohibition. So if he does it in that way, he is liable under the interdict Quod vi aut clam. A person is also liable under that interdict if he acted secretly, because he feared a dispute with his neighbour or someone else, or already has one. But a person acts by force when he acts in spite of a prohibition. The definition of one who acts secretly (clam) or by force is different: l. 3, in princ. and §. 1, De itinere actuque privato. There, a person who is forbidden to use a way and uses it, uses it secretly. According to the opinion of Johannes: one who resists the person forbidding him, that is, who acts while the other objects, acts by force. But one who submits to the prohibition, yet afterwards continues the work when the one who forbade him does not know, acts secretly; and this is how one should understand l. 3 just cited. Some who are forbidden do so openly, and these act by force, not secretly.

units.la: Adj.
units.tr: Add.

units.la: Ad §. Quæ in testamento.
units.tr: On the paragraph Quae in testamento.

units.la: Quod non intelligitur in testamento, non scriptum videtur. l. 2. de his, quæ pro non script. hab. Effectus regulæ est, ut, quod videtur obscurum, apud hæredem sine onere maneat. Ergo incertæ personæ legatum relictum non valet: incertæ rei legatum non valet. l. cum post. 69. §. gener. de iure dot. Ademptio etiam obscura legati nō valet. l. 3. §. si duobus 7. de adim. & transf. leg. Legauit duob. Titiis separatim: postea ademit Titio: quæritur cui ademerit? hoc est incertum utrinque. E. legatum debetur. Huic sententiæ vehementer refragari videtur l. si fuerit 10. de reb. dub. Cuius hæc sententia est. Testatur duobus Sempronii s legatum reliquit; vni ademit: neutri debetur legatum. Resp. si separatim duobus Titiis legatum est: vni cum vellet ademptum inutilis erit ademptio, ut in specie sup. d. l. 3. de adimend. leg. Secus si coniunctim duobus Sempronii s legatum fuerit relictum, vni namque in hac specie adempto legato alteri quoque ademptum censetur, quia quos testator coniunxit in dando, videtur coniunxisse in adimendo.
units.tr: What is not understood in a will is considered not written (l. 2, De his quae pro non scriptis habentur). The effect of the rule is that what appears obscure remains with the heir without burden. Therefore a legacy left to an uncertain person is not valid; a legacy of an uncertain thing is not valid (l. cum post, 69, §. gener., De iure dotium). An obscure revocation of a legacy is also not valid (l. 3, §. si duobus, 7, De adimendis et transferendis legatis). Suppose a legacy is left separately to two named Titii, and afterwards it is revoked from Titius; the question is to whom it was revoked. This is uncertain on both sides, so the legacy is owed. The law si fuerit (10, De rebus dubiis) seems strongly to oppose this view. Its substance is this: a legacy is left to two Sempronii, and it is revoked from one; neither is owed the legacy. Answer: if the legacy was left separately to two Titii, the revocation is ineffective as to one whom the testator wished to be revoked, as in the case of the above-mentioned l. 3, De adimendis legatis. It is otherwise if the legacy was left jointly to two Sempronii, for in this case, when it is revoked from one, it is deemed revoked from the other too, because the testator who joined them in giving is taken to have joined them in revoking.

units.la: Ad §. Nec paciscendo.
units.tr: On the paragraph Nec paciscendo.

units.la: Ultima & quinta regula est: Nemo potest alteri stipulari, pacisci, legem dicere. Vocat autem legem pactionem illam, quæ contractui adiicitur ex continenti. Addit speciale genus pacti, legem dicendo, Hæc lex est pactum, actionem formans, id quod pactorum natura alias non admittit. Pactum enim non solet formare actionem, sed pactio, quæ ex continenti adiicitur, formar actionem, vt lex commissoria, & resoluit contractum, pretio non soluto ad diem, & ita res committitur venditori. Cuiac.in Recit.
units.tr: The last and fifth rule is: No one can stipulate, make a pact, or dictate a law for another. He calls a law that agreement which is added to a contract at once. He adds a special kind of pact, dictating a law: this law is a pact forming an action, which the nature of pacts otherwise does not admit. For a pact does not usually form an action, but an agreement added at once to the contract forms an action, as in a commissory law, which dissolves the contract when the price is not paid on the day, and the thing is thereby forfeited to the seller. Cuiacius, in Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg.74. Ne cui per alterum iniqua conditio inferatur.
units.tr: On Leg. 74. That an unfair condition is not to be imposed on someone through another.

units.la: NOn debet alteri per alterum iniqua conditio inferri.
units.tr: An unfair condition must not be imposed on one person through another.

units.la: Regulæ siue legis huius exemplum sumi potest ex l.1. §. vlt. & leg. 4. quod vi aut clam. cuius hæc species est. Vim facit, qui, cum prohibetur, facit. Quinquam & is vi faciat qui, licet prohibitus non sit, modo à sciente domino se prohibitum iri sciens, quid fecerit, vt, cum te prohibere volentem, quo minus prohibeas, deterreo. Tunc enim pro prohibito censebor, per conseq. vi fecisse videbor. Verum fingamus. Opus aliquod institueram: aduersarius prohibiturus me cum venire vellet, sine dolo malo à Titio fuit detentus, ita, vt me opus facientem prohibere non posset, quaeritur an vim fecisse videar? Respond. quod non, ne sit in potestate alterius meam conditionem deteriorem facere. Hoc vsque adeo verum est, vt ne quidem seruo iniquia conditio inferri per dominum possit. l.5.§.si seruum 4. de his que vt indig. auser. Legatarius qui falsum testimonium dicit, nec obtinet in quaestione falsi, amittit legatum, & redigitur in Fiscum. Nunc seruo alieno relicta est libertas fideicommissaria & legatum ei relictum: dominus falsum testimonium dixit, nec obtinet: an ideo seruus legatum & libertatem fideicommissariam amittet? Minime. Imo seruus à Fisco vindicatur, vt ei restituatur legatum, & obtineat libertatem. Cuia. in Recit.
units.tr: An example of this rule or law can be taken from l. 1, §. ult., and l. 4, Quod vi aut clam, of which this is a case: a person acts by force when he acts while he is forbidden. Indeed, a person also acts by force who, although he is not forbidden, knowingly makes himself liable to be forbidden by the owner, who knows it, as when you deter someone who wants to forbid you, so that he does not forbid you. For then I shall be regarded as forbidden, and consequently I shall be seen to have acted by force. But let us imagine: I had begun some work; my opponent, about to forbid me, wished to come, but without malice was detained by Titius, so that he could not forbid me while I was working. The question is whether I shall be seen to have acted by force. The answer: no, because it must not be in another's power to make my position worse. This is so true that an unfair condition cannot even be imposed on a slave through his master (l. 5, §. si servum, 4, De his quae ut indignis auferuntur). A legatee who gives false testimony, and does not prevail in the inquiry into falsehood, loses the legacy, and it is returned to the Fisc. Now suppose a fideicommissary liberty and a legacy were left to another's slave, and the master gave false testimony and did not prevail: will the slave therefore lose the legacy and the fideicommissary liberty? Not at all. Rather, the slave is claimed from the Fisc, so that the legacy is restored to him and he obtains his liberty. Cuiacius, in Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg. 75. De mutatione consilii.
units.tr: On Leg. 75. On change of intention.

units.la: Nemo Coniunge l. nonnunquam. de collationib. bonorum. Pac. b.
units.tr: Nemo. Join l. nonnunquam, De collationibus bonorum. Pac. b.

units.la: NEmo potest mutare consilium suum in alterius iniuriam.
units.tr: No one can change his intention to another's injury.

units.la: Mutare] c. quod semel placuit 21. cap. mutare consilium 33. dereg. in 6. l. 20. sup. de arbitris. l. 14. sup. de seruit. rustic. praed. Gothofr.
units.tr: Mutare] cf. the chapter "quod semel placuit" (21), the chapter "mutare consilium" (33), De regulis iuris in 6, l. 20; sup. De arbitris, l. 14; sup. De servitutibus rusticorum praediorum. Gothofredus.

units.la: Consilium ] vt & sententiam. v. l. 42. l. 55. 56. sup. de re iudicata. v. l. 1: in sin. sup. de quæstion. l. 27. sup. de pœnis. v. tamen l. 6. C. quomodo & quando Index: confessionem legitime factam v. l. 13. C. de non numerata. contractum. v l. 5. C. de obligat. Electionem. v. l. 20. sup. de opt. vel. elect. leg. adi-tionem hæreditatis v. l. 4. C. de repud. hared. iusiurandum delatum. v. l. 11. C. de reb. cred. actum irrevocabilem. v. tamen l. 27. & quæ ibi dicam de clausula derogatoria. C. de testamentis. Goth.
units.tr: Consilium: also meaning sentence or opinion. Compare l. 42, l. 55, l. 56, supra De re iudicata; compare l. 1, in fine, supra De quaestionibus; l. 27, supra De poenis. But compare l. 6, C. Quomodo et quando iudex: a confession lawfully made (compare l. 13, C. De non numerata pecunia); a contract (compare l. 5, C. De obligationibus); an election (compare l. 20, supra De optione vel electione legata); the acceptance of an inheritance (compare l. 4, C. De repudiis hereditatis); an oath deferred (compare l. 11, C. De rebus creditis); an irrevocable act (compare, however, l. 27, and what I shall say there about the derogatory clause, C. De testamentis). Gothofredus.

units.la: Iniuriam ] quoties sc. ex consilio iam obligati sumus, & alteri aut nobis obligatio est quæsita: tunc enim totum repudiare aut agnoscere teneimur. l. 27. sup. de procurat. l. 11. sup. de usur. l. 16. sup. de administ. tut. l. 7. in sin. sup. de damno, alias re integra, consilium, vt & mentem revocare possumus. l. 22 §. vlt. supr. mandati. vt & in re alternatiue debita. l. 21. in fine. sup. de act. empt. l. 14. sup. rerum amot. l. 28. §. vlt. sup. de liberat. l. 8. sup. de collat. & prius testamentum. l. 6. §. 2. supr. de iure Codicill. l. 12. §. vlt. sup. de leg. 1. l. 22. sup. de leg. 3. Igitur in voluntariis consilia in melius mutare possumus, & ita variauit Papin. l. 6. in fi. sup. de seruis export. l. vlt. C. de furt. variauit & Iulianus l. 19. in fine. sup. ad Vellei. l. 1. C. de emend. serv. variauit Scæuola. l. 23. in fine. sup. de acquir. rer. dom. Mæcianus: quin & ipsi Impp. l. 17. ibi: Sed & cum Maciano, & aliis amicis nostris iu-risperitis adhibitis plenius tractaremus, magis vi-sum m est. supr. de iure patron. adde Cuiacium 4. ad [?] fc.sol.39.in fine. & 2.obs.37. Hinc illud: Sano ntilio vcitur, qui malum consilium reuocat. othof.
units.tr: Iniuriam: whenever, that is, we are already bound by our decision, and an obligation has been acquired by another or by us; for then we are bound to repudiate or acknowledge the whole (l. 27, supra De procuratoribus; l. 11, supra De usuris; l. 16, supra De administratione tutorum; l. 7, in fine, supra De damno). Otherwise, while the matter is still entire, we can revoke our decision, as also our intention (l. 22, §. ult., supra Mandati; likewise in an obligation due in the alternative, l. 21, in fine, supra De actionibus empti; l. 14, supra Rerum amotarum; l. 28, §. ult., supra De liberatione; l. 8, supra De collationibus; and a will made earlier: l. 6, §. 2, supra De iure codicillorum; l. 12, §. ult., supra De legatis 1; l. 22, supra De legatis 3). Therefore in voluntary matters we can change our decisions for the better, and so Papinian changed his view (l. 6, in fine, supra De servis exportandis; l. vlt., C. De furtis). Julian also changed his view (l. 19, in fine, supra ad Velleianum; l. 1, C. De emendatione servorum). Scaevola changed his view (l. 23, in fine, supra De acquirendo rerum dominio). Maecianus too; indeed the emperors themselves (l. 17, where it says: "But when, with Maecianus and other learned friends of ours called in, we discussed the matter more fully, it seemed to us better..." supra De iure patronatus). Add Cuiacius, 4, ad [?], fr. sol. 39, in fine, and 2, Observationes 37. Hence that saying: he is sound of mind who recalls a bad decision. Gothofredus.

units.la: Ex eo libro est l. si filius 32. de minor. in qua tenditur, Filium emancipatum præteritum, gato agnito, non posse in fraudem creditorum hæredum, bonorum possessionem contra b.petere. Eodem modo venditor, quiagit ege commiss. dicens, malle se rem venditam petere, pretio non soluto ad diem: postea into emptore non potest mutare sententiam, pretium repetere. Mutare potest quisque consilium suum, dum non officiat alteri. l. si ndus 4. §. eleganter. de L. Commissoria. Ex eoem lib. est l. nonnunquam 8. de bon.collat. quæ commode huic l. adaptari potest. Certum est, ex illo edicto filium emancipatum præterum concurrere cum fratribus, qui non sunt emancipati, & petere bon. possess. contra tab. scil. si conferat bona propria. Conferuntur rem bona dupliciter, aut re, aut cautione. Quod si igitur filius emancipatus propria sua bona conferre recuset, tunc transfertur pars eius in suos, & aufertur ei beneficium bonorum possessionis contra tab. Nunc fingamus ium emancipatum noluisse conferre: quo su exclusus erit & est à beneficio bonor. possessionis contra tab. nunc vero mutato confi-ssionis contra tab. nunc vero mutato consilio lio vult conferre, oblata cautione, quo beneficio bonor. possess. contra tab. gaudere possit: An audietur? Sic sane. Et hanc, regulæ huius exceptionem, specialis fauor & æquitas, introduxit. Cuia. in Repet.
units.tr: From the same book comes l. si filius, 32, De minoribus, in which it is held that an emancipated son who was passed over, once the will has been acknowledged, cannot seek bonorum possessio contra tabulas to the prejudice of the creditors of the heirs. In the same way, a seller who sues by the commissory action, saying that he prefers to reclaim the sold thing because the price was not paid on the day, cannot afterwards, once the buyer has come forward, change his decision and demand the price. Anyone can change his intention so long as he does not harm another (l. si quidem, 4, §. eleganter, De lege commissoria). From the same book comes l. nonnunquam, 8, De bonorum collationibus, which can fitly be applied to this law. It is certain that under that edict an emancipated son who was passed over concurs with the brothers who are not emancipated, and seeks bonorum possessio contra tabulas, namely if he collates his own goods. Goods are collated in two ways, either in kind or by security. If, therefore, an emancipated son refuses to collate his own goods, then his share passes to his siblings and he loses the benefit of bonorum possessio contra tabulas. Now let us imagine that the emancipated son refused to collate; by that he is excluded and debarred from the benefit of bonorum possessio contra tabulas. But if he afterwards changes his mind and wishes to collate, offering security, so that he may enjoy the benefit of bonorum possessio contra tabulas, will he be heard? Certainly so. And a special favour and equity introduced this exception to the present rule. Cuiacius, in Repetitiones.

units.la: Ad Leg. 76. De his quæ animi destina- tione agenda sunt.
units.tr: On Law 76. Concerning those things which are to be done by intention of mind.

units.la: INtotum omnia, quæ animi destinatione agenda sunt, non nisi vera & certa scientia perfici possunt.
units.tr: In general, all things that are to be done by a determination of the mind can be accomplished only by true and certain knowledge.

units.la: Vera ] Demus aliquid factum à priuato vel principe ex certa scientia: an id reuocari poterit? vtrique. Cum huiusmodi clausula nihil operetur in iis, quæ apparent ignorata. v. l. 57. sup. de oblig. & act. v. Dec. hic num. 7. aliud puto, si quis sciens se non teneri, promiserit. Videtur enim donasse. adde l. 15. sup. de verb. oblig. & quæ notaui ad l. vlt. §. penult. sup. de condict. indeb. Gothofr.
units.tr: True] Suppose something is done by a private person or by the prince with certain knowledge: can it be revoked? By either. Since a clause of this kind has no effect in those matters which are apparently done in ignorance, see law 57 above, de obligationibus et actionibus; see Dec. here, num. 7. I think otherwise if someone, knowing he is not bound, has promised, for he seems to have made a gift. Add law 15 above, de verborum obligationibus, and what I have noted on law last, §penultimate above, de condictione indebiti. Gothofredus.

units.la: In totum ] hoc est generaliter, siue in toto iure. Animi destinatione, hoc est iudicio animi. Quæ animi certo iudicio fiunt, non fiunt, nisi à sciente, ac vere quidem ac certo sciente. Ignarus nihil animi iudicio facere videtur, cum de re ei non liqueat. Exemplum ponunt in hæreditate, & possessione, in hæreditatis aditione, & gestione pro hærede, quæ etiam ipsa est aniest animi potius, quam facti. leg. 20. de acquir. hared. Ita in agnitione bonorum possessionis, quæ quoque fit animi iudicio, scientia exigitur. hoc est, qui hæreditatem amplecti cupit, eum scire oportet, defunctum esse illum, cuius occupare bona cupit, sibique hæreditatem esse delatam: alioqui nihil agit & rem non gerit animi iudicio. l. qui hæreditatem 15. l. si is ad quem 22. de acquir. hæred. Ergo pupillus, cum nihil sciat, adire non potest: tutore tamen auctore adit. Nam quod deest animi iudicio, id suppletur scientia tutoris. Sic quoque in acquirenda possessione requiritur animus. Ergo & scientia eius, cui acquiritur possessio. Nam possessio plurimum animi habet, & animi genere quodam æstimatur. Excipitur tamen causa peculiaris, in qua per servuum ignoranti domino acquiritur possessio. l. peregre 44. §. quæsitum est 1. de acquir. possess. Ex his apparet, ea, quæ fiunt animi iudicio, non perfici nisi à sciente.
units.tr: In general] that is, generally, or in the whole of law. By intention of mind, that is, by judgment of mind. Things done by a certain judgment of mind are not done unless by one who knows, and indeed who knows truly and certainly. The ignorant man seems to do nothing by judgment of mind, since the matter is not clear to him. They give as examples inheritance and possession: in the acceptance of an inheritance and in acting as heir, which is itself a matter of mind rather than of deed, law 20, de acquirenda hereditate. Likewise in the acknowledgment of possession of goods, which is also done by judgment of mind, knowledge is required; that is, he who wishes to embrace an inheritance must know that the one whose goods he wishes to seize is dead, and that the inheritance has been delivered to him. Otherwise he does nothing and does not act by judgment of mind. Law qui hereditatem 15, law si is ad quem 22, de acquirenda hereditate. Therefore a ward, since he knows nothing, cannot enter; yet with his guardian's authority he enters, for what lacks in judgment of mind is supplied by the knowledge of the guardian. So too in acquiring possession, intention is required, and therefore also the knowledge of him to whom possession is acquired, for possession has much of the mind and is judged by a certain kind of mind. Yet a peculiar case is excepted, in which through a slave possession is acquired for an ignorant master: law peregre 44, § quaesitum est 1, de acquirenda possessione. From these things it appears that things done by judgment of mind are not completed unless by one who knows.

units.la: Ad Leg. 77. De actibus legitimis. De tacito & expresso.
units.tr: On Law 77. Concerning legitimate acts. Of the tacit and the express.

units.la: ACtus legitimi, qui recipiunt diem vel conditionem, veluti mancipatio, acceptilatio, hereditatis aditio, servi optio, datio tutoris; in totum vitiantur per temporis vel conditionis adiectionem, nonnunquam tamen actus supra scripti tacite recipiunt quæ aperte comprehensa vitium afferunt. Nam si acceptum feratur ei, qui sub conditione promisit, ita demum egisse aliquid acceptilatio intelligitur, si obligationis conditio exititerit; quæ si verbis nominatim acceptilationis comprehendatur, nullius momenti facit actum.
units.tr: Legitimate acts, which admit a day or a condition, such as mancipation, acceptilation, acceptance of an inheritance, the option of a slave, and the appointment of a guardian, are wholly vitiated by the addition of a time or a condition. Sometimes, however, the acts written above tacitly admit things which, when openly included, bring vitiation. For if an acceptance is made to one who promised under a condition, acceptilation is understood to have effected something only if the condition of the obligation has occurred; but if it is named expressly in the words of acceptilation, the act is of no force.

units.la: Actus ] c. actus legitimi 50. de regul. in 6. An sunt diuersi à legis actionibus? Hotom. ait 32. illustr. sol. 210. liquidem hæ etiam magistratuum communes omnes ex lege; & inter præsentes tantum fieri solent. In actibus legitimis secus. Cuiac. negat dissere 15. obs. 16. Gothofr.
units.tr: Acts] cf. the chapter legitimi actus 50, de regulis iuris in 6. Are these different from the legis actiones? Hotomann says, 32 Illustr. sol. p. 210, that these too are common to all magistrates by law, and are usually done only between those present, whereas in legitimate acts it is otherwise. Cuiacius denies there is a difference, 15 Obs. 16. Gothofredus.

units.la: Actus ] coniunge l. 8. de tut. & rat. distrahendis. Pac.
units.tr: Acts] join law 8, de tutelis et rationibus distrahendis. Pac.

units.la: Legitimi ] An ciuiles & solennes, vt vult Hotom. 32. illust. sol. 219. 220. an à quacunque iuris parte, vt Dynus? add. c. 50. An per legem inuenti, vt Zasius? ad l. eum qui §. qui hominem nunc. 3. sup. de verb. oblig. An qui mero iure radicantur, vt vult idem Zasius ad leg. cum quid mutuum num. 18. sup. de reb. cred. An qui iure finiuntur, vt emptio, locatio, societas, mandatum, stipulatio? An qui ex visu solennis iuris? (Cuiac. 15. obs. 16. in fine. vt sint formulæ rerum à priuatis agendarum extra rerum contrahendarum negotia à ICTis inuentæ, Hotom. ibid. Actum legitimum eadem significatione vlurvsurpari in leg. 21. C. de haret. ait Hotom. 32. illustr. sol. 219. Cuiac. negat 15. observu. 16. in sin. Gothofr.
units.tr: Legitimate] Are they civil and solemn, as Hotomann wills, 32 illust. sol. 219, 220; or from whatever part of law, as Dynus holds? Add c. 50. Or found by law, as Zasius holds? On law eum qui, §qui hominem nunc, 3, de verborum obligationibus. Or which are rooted in pure law, as the same Zasius holds on law cum quid mutuum, num. 18, de rebus creditis? Or which are defined by law, such as sale, lease, partnership, mandate, stipulation? Or which are of the form of solemn law? (Cuiacius 15 obs. 16 at the end.) Or that they are formulas for things to be done by private persons, outside the business of contracting, devised by the jurists, as Hotomann says in the same place. Hotomann says the legitimate act is used in the same sense in law 21 C. de haeredibus; Cuiacius denies this, 15 Observations 16 at the end. Gothofredus.

units.la: Legitimi ] Alciat. l.3. parerg. c.4. & 5.
units.tr: Legitimate] Alciat. law 3, parerg. c. 4 and 5.

units.la: Qui ] qui non recipiunt. vulg. Hal. Hæc particula, inquit Hotom. 32. illustr. sol. 219. suum antecedens restringit, ostenditque, quosdam actus legitimos esse, qui diem vel conditionem recipiunt. Acceptilatio, & optio non recipiunt, vadimonium, comperindinatio, obuagulatio denunciandi testimonii causa, procuratoris datio recipiunt. Cuiac. 15. obs. 16. Florentinam lectionem tuetur. Ideoque hæc verba, qui recipiunt, ita interpretatur, Quibus aperte adiicitur dies vel conditio: alias si tacite adiicitur, non vitiatur Cuiacius ibid. Goth.
units.tr: Who] who do not admit. Vulgate, Hal. This particle, says Hotomann, 32 illustr. sol. 219, restricts its antecedent and shows that some legitimate acts are those which admit a day or a condition. Acceptilation and option do not admit; vadimonium, comperendination, and the summons for the purpose of giving testimony do admit, as does the appointment of a procurator. Cuiacius, 15 Obs. 16, defends the Florentine reading, and so interprets these words, who admit, thus: to which a day or condition is openly added. Otherwise, if it is tacitly added, it is not vitiated. Cuiacius ibid. Gothofredus.

units.la: Mancipatio ] emancipatio vulgo Hal. Hotomannus ibi sol. 214. & 218. vtrumque admittit. Emancipatio actus civilis §. 11. Instit. de hæred. quæ ab intest. inter legis actiones numeratur. Paul. 2. sent. 25. §. 4. Cuiac. 15. obs. 16. mancipationem mancipium dici ait.
units.tr: Mancipation] emancipation in the common editions. Hotomann in the same place, pp. 214 and 218, admits both. Emancipation is a civil act, §11 Institutes, de hereditatibus quae ab intestato, and is counted among the legis actiones. Paul. Sent. 2.25 §4. Cuiacius, 15 Obs. 16, says that mancipation is called mancipium.

units.la: Acceptilatio ] ea per procuratorem fieri non potest. L13. §. 10. sup. de acceptil. v. Hotom. 32. illust. sol. 120. Cuiac. ibi in pr. certis verbis fiebat. L18. sup. de accept. sine die & conditione l.4. & 5. sup. de acceptil. & merito, quia acceptilatio obligationi præsentem interitum affert.
units.tr: Acceptilation] this could not be done through a procurator. Law 13 §10 above, de acceptilatione; see Hotomann, 32 illust. sol. 120. Cuiacius there at the beginning. It was done by fixed words. Law 18 above, de acceptilatione. Without day and condition: laws 4 and 5 above, de acceptilatione; and rightly, because acceptilation brings present extinction to the obligation.

units.la: Aditio ] ea non fiebat per procuratorem leg. 80. §. 80. sup. de acquir. haredit. certis verbis constabat, his puta, Adeo, cernoque. Vlpianus f. 22. §. 28. l. 51. in fine sup. de acquir hered. sine die & conditione fiebat l. 54. sup. de acquir. hared. non iterabatur. l. 80. in fine sup. de acquirenda hered. Hotom. ibi. Gothofr.
units.tr: Aditio] this was not done through a procurator. Law 80 §80 above, de acquirenda hereditate. It consisted in fixed words, such as adeo and cerno. Ulpian f. 22 §28, law 51 in fine above, de acquirenda hereditate. It was done without day and condition. Law 54 above, de acquirenda hereditate. It was not repeated. Law 80 in fine above, de acquirenda hereditate. Hotomann there. Gothofredus.

units.la: Seruio optio ] certis verbis fiebat l. 20. supr. de opt. pure & semel. l. 5. & 8. sup. de opt. l. 5. sup. de leg.
units.tr: Option of a slave] it was done with fixed words. Law 20 above, de optione, pure and once; laws 5 and 8 above, de optione; law 5 above, de legatis.

units.la: 1. An per procuratorem fiebat ? Hotoman. ibi ait sol. 221. arg. l. pen. sup. de opt. quod non admittit Cuiac. 15. obs. 15. Goth.
units.tr: 1. Was it done through a procurator? Hotomann there, p. 221, argues from law penultimate above, de optione, which Cuiacius, 15 obs. 15, does not admit. Gothofredus.

units.la: Datio ] quæ à magistratu fiebat. §. 1. Institut. de Attil. leg. 6. §. 1. supr. de tutelis. non à defuncto leg. 8. §. 1. & 2. supr. de testament. tutela. Gothofr.
units.tr: Appointment] which was made by the magistrate. §1 Institutes, de Attilia tutela; law 6 §1 above, de tutelis. Not by the deceased: law 8 §§1 and 2 above, de testamentaria tutela. Gothofredus.

units.la: Suprascripti ] sunt nè alii actus legitimi praeter suprascriptos? Cuiac. 15. obs. 16. adiicit cessionem in iure & libertatis dationem. Hotom. 32. illust. sol. 218. iudicis addictionem, comperindinationem, vadimonium, denunciationem testimonii causa, quod Cuiacio d. loc. displicet. Idem Hotomannus ibi sol. 218. addit conuentionem in manum; repudium, diuortium ibi sol. 212. numerat inter legis actiones appellationem, vocationem in ius, iusiurandum, tutoris authoritatem: quod eidem Cuiacio displicet. addit idem Hotom. adoptionem, emancipationem, manumissionem vindicta, cessionem in iure, litis contestationem, nonominis in reos relationem, rutelæ cessionem, tutelæ abdicationem, arrogationem, satisdationem, atrestationem, mancipationem, nuncupationem testamenti, aditionem hæreditatis, noxæ deditionem. Quædam etiam Cuiacius d. loco adiicit, ut stipulationem, procuratoris dationem, vsurpationem.
units.tr: Above written] are there other legitimate acts besides those written above? Cuiacius, 15 obs. 16, adds cession in court and the giving of liberty. Hotomann, 32 illust. sol. 218, adds the judge's award, comperendination, vadimonium, and the denunciation for the purpose of testimony, which displeases Cuiacius in the passage cited. The same Hotomann, there at p. 218, adds conventio in manum; at p. 212 he counts among the legis actiones appellation, summons to court, the oath, and the authority of a guardian, which again displeases Cuiacius. Hotomann adds also adoption, emancipation, manumission by the vindicta, cession in court, litis contestation, the relation of a name against defendants, cession of guardianship, abdication of guardianship, arrogation, satisdation, attestation, mancipation, nuncupation of a will, acceptance of an inheritance, and noxal surrender. Cuiacius in the place mentioned adds some others, such as stipulation, appointment of a procurator, and usucaption.

units.la: Tacite ] puta per relationem ad actum aut dispositionem præcedentem. Nam debitum conditionale pure accepto ferri potest inf. eod. & l. 12. sup. de acceptil. Goth.
units.tr: Tacitly] for instance, by reference to a preceding act or disposition. For a conditional debt can be accepted purely and carried over. Below, same title; law 12 above, de acceptilatione. Gothofredus.

units.la: Comprehensa ] expressa nocent, tacita non nocent.
units.tr: Comprehensa: expressed terms do harm, tacit terms do not.

units.la: Vitium afferunt ] quia huiusmodi actus præsens factum continent, ideoq; conditione aut die suspendi non possunt. Goth.
units.tr: Vitium afferunt: because such acts contain a present fact, and therefore cannot be suspended by a condition or a day. Goth.

units.la: Qui sub conditione &c. ] actus legitimus, qui expresse non potest explicari sub conditione, si differtur ad dispositionem præcedentem conditionalem, tacite conditionem recipere potest. Gothofr.
units.tr: Qui sub conditione &c.: a legitimate act, which cannot be expressly explained under a condition, can tacitly receive a condition if it is deferred to a preceding conditional disposition. Gothofr.

units.la: Hoc loco actus legitimi referuntur quinque. Serui optio, intellige etiam, optio vestis, vel alterius rei. Mancipationem accipio generaliter, ut Vlp. in fragm. tit. 19. de dominio. non pro sola emancipatione, per quam liberi exeunt de potestate patris, quæ legis actio est. Novel. 81. Legis autem actio & actus legitimus idem sunt, sed emancipatio etiam fit ex testamento. & ex causa donationis. Omnis mancipatio est legis actio, siue actus legitimus.
