Videamus an alii actus sint legitimi? Ita, adoptio & manumissio.l.2.& 3.de offic.proconf.l.4.de adopt. Idem censeo de diuortio, quod constat fieri, non nisi ex L.Iulia: diuortium est actio L.Iuliæ. Idem censeo de conuentione in manum & cessione in iure, de qua Apulei.lib.2.de asin.aur. Non est eadem ratio depositi & custodiæ. Depositarius est custos, vt vulgo existimatur: Custodiam tamen non præstat & latam culpam. Is, à quo custodia exigitur, præstat leuem culpam: quidam sunt custodes, qui non sunt depositarii. l.1.§. quod autem 33. de vi & vi armat. vt custos domus.l.1.C.de repud.hered. Sic etiam custodiæ illius solennis genus non est depositum, sed actus legitimus. Conditio autem actuum legitimorum hæc est, i. vt fiant certis & solennibus verbis: Sic constat fieri emancipationem, sic aditionem hæreditaris, sic cretionem, sic acceptilationem, diuortium: sic cæteri omnes actus sunt certis verbis. Sed hodie verba solennia non dicuntur, sed vt dicta accipiuntur. l. manumissio 23.de manumiss.vind. Etsi vero lex tantum loquitur de manumissis vindicta: tamen idem putemus dictum de cæteris actibus legitimis. Secundo requiritur, vt legitimi actus fiant testibus præsentibus, quorum plerumq; sunt 7. Sic fit emancipatio, sic diuortium, sic aditio, sic cretio, & cæteri omnes actus legitimi. Tertio fere in omnibus actibus legitimis interueniunt symbola: vt in emancipatione æs & libra: in manumissione, alapæ, siue pulsatio frontis. In aditione, digitorum crepitus & percussio, quo symbolo significatur, hæredem adire hæreditatem. Quarto vt actus legitimi non fiunt per procuratorem, sic aditio hæreditatis non fit per procuratorem. l. 90. de adquir. hared. Sic adoptio l. post mortem 25. de adopt. & vt generaliter definit l. nemo alieno 123. infr. eod. Actus legitimi, h. e. actiones legis, non perficiuntur per procuratorem. Quinto requiritur, vt non iterentur. Sic aditio hæreditatis fit tantum semel. l. si solus 80. de acquir. hared. optio serui fit tantum semel. l. f. de leg. 1. sic adoptio & libertas iusta non reiteratur, Dico Iusta. Nam qui non erant iustam libertatem adepti, poterant iteratione ciues fieri Romani. Sic adoptio non iure facta confirmari potest. l. adoptio 38. de adopt. Testamento non fit adoptio, sed apud Prætorem tantum vel Principem. Ita adoptatur quis testamento, cum nomen testatoris ferre iubetur: at hæc adoptio non valet. Nam confirmari debet à Prætore: si iusta esset, non iteraretur. De optione serui stulte dubitant quidam, an sit actus legitimus, cum nihil sit certius. Nam legata optione serui, ea debet fieri solenniter à legatario, hærede præsente: & ideo non fit rede ante aditam hæreditatem: cum tamen legata ante hæreditatem agnoscantur. l. 10. de leg. 1. l. optione, 16. de opt. leg. hærede inquam præsente & vniuersa familia publice exhibita. l. 3. & 4. de opt. legata. l. 3. §. item si optare 6. ad exhibendum. Sic etiam legata optione vestis, exhibenda est vniuersa synthesis vestium. Igitur verisimile est, optionem fieri testibus præsentibus, cum fiat publice, fit & plerunque ipso prætore diem decernente. l. mancipiorum. 6. de opt. leg. Quæ seruantur in aditione, quæ actio legis, seruantur & in optione. Igitur optio est actus legitimus. Item sicut filiusfam. non potest adire hæreditatem iniussu patris, sic nec optare: cætera legata potest sine iussu patris amplecti, l. 10. de leg. 1. Et hæc est vltima conditio actuum legitimorum, vt omnes fiant pure. Acceptilatio non fit in diem, vel sub conditione. l. 4. & 5. de acceptilat. dilationem non patiuntur, sed protinus exequuntur: sic tutor non datur in diem. l. muto 6. de tutelis. Testamento quidem sub die vel conditione datur tutor: sed ea tantum dario est actus legitimus quæ fit à iudice, inquisitione facta in optimos viros, ex quibus datur vnus; quæ fit testamento non est actus legitimus. Sic emancipatio non recipit diem vel conditionem in l. pen. C. pro socio. dubitatur, an possit societas contrahi sub conditione: quia creditur facile interuenisse mancipatio seu traditio.l.2.pro socio. Atque ideo dominium mutat, aut commutatur, quod non fit in aliis contractibus in quibus facile intelligitur mancipatio interuenire. Mancipatio autem non fit sub conditione, neque societas, ergo. Merito igitur dubitatur: an sub conditione possit fieri societas? Respondeo posse: alia enim est causa expressae, alia tacitae mancipationis. Omnes actus legitimi non recipiunt diem vel conditionem expressam: tacitam recipiunt. Sic acceptilatio expressim non fit in diem vel sub conditione: sed si ego acceptum feram quod tu mihi debes sub conditione, quae nondum extitit, acceptilatio non est quidem pura, sed ei tacite inest conditio, quae tacite obligationi est apposita. Nam acceptilatio non habet vires, priusquam conditio extiterit. Et generaliter, vt ostenditur in l.expressa 195. hoc tit. expressa nocent, non expressa non nocent. Expressi & tacit i non est eadem vis. l. nonnunquam 52. de condit. & demonst. Cuiac. in Rec.
units.tr: Here five legitimate acts are mentioned: the choice of a slave, understood also as the choice of a garment or of another thing. I take mancipation in a general sense, as Ulpian says in the fragments, title 19, de dominio, and not only as emancipation, by which children leave their father's power, which is a legal action. Novel. 81. A legal action and a legitimate act are the same thing, but emancipation also takes place by will and by reason of a gift. Every mancipation is a legal action or a legitimate act. Let us see whether there are other legitimate acts. There are: adoption and manumission. l.2.&3.de offic.proconf. l.4.de adopt. I think the same of divorce, which is known to take place only under the Julian law: divorce is an action under the Julian law. I think the same of conventio in manum and cessio in iure, of which see Apuleius, book 2, de asino aureo. The reason for deposit and custody is not the same. The depositary is a custodian, as is commonly thought, but he does not answer for custody, nor for gross negligence. The one from whom custody is required answers for slight negligence; some are custodians who are not depositaries, l.1.§.quod autem 33. de vi et vi armata, such as the custodian of a house. l.1.C.de repud.hered. So too that solemn kind of custody is not a deposit but a legitimate act. The condition of legitimate acts is this: first, that they are performed in certain solemn words. Thus emancipation is known to be made, thus acceptance of an inheritance, thus cretion, thus acceptilation, divorce; thus all the other acts are done in certain words. But today solemn words are not spoken, but are accepted as if spoken. l. manumissio 23. de manumiss. vind. Although the law speaks only of manumission by the rod, we may think the same was said of the other legitimate acts. Second, it is required that legitimate acts be performed in the presence of witnesses, of whom there are usually seven. So emancipation is done, so divorce, so acceptance, so cretion, and all the other legitimate acts. Third, in almost all legitimate acts symbols intervene: in emancipation, bronze and the scales; in manumission, a slap, or a striking of the forehead; in acceptance, the snapping and striking of the fingers, by which symbol it is signified that the heir enters upon the inheritance. Fourth, legitimate acts are not performed through a proxy; so the acceptance of an inheritance is not made through a proxy. l. 90. de adquir. hared. So too adoption, l. post mortem 25. de adopt. and as the law generally defines it, l. nemo alieno 123. infr. eod. Legitimate acts, that is, legal actions, are not completed through a proxy. Fifth, it is required that they not be repeated. Thus the acceptance of an inheritance takes place only once. l. si solus 80. de acquir. hared. The choice of a slave takes place only once. l. f. de leg. 1. So adoption and lawful freedom are not repeated; I say lawful, for those who had not obtained lawful freedom could become Roman citizens by repetition. So an adoption made not in accordance with law can be confirmed. l. adoptio 38. de adopt. Adoption is not made by will, but only before the praetor or the emperor. Thus a person is adopted by will when he is ordered to bear the name of the testator; but this adoption is not valid. For it must be confirmed by the praetor: if it were lawful, it would not need repeating. Some foolishly doubt whether the choice of a slave is a legitimate act, when nothing is more certain. For when the choice of a slave is bequeathed, it must be made solemnly by the legatee, with the heir present; and therefore it cannot be made before the inheritance is entered upon, although legacies are acknowledged before the inheritance. l. 10. de leg. 1. l. optione 16. de opt. leg. I say, with the heir present and the whole household publicly exhibited. l. 3. & 4. de opt. legata. l. 3. §. item si optare 6. ad exhibendum. So too, when the choice of a garment is bequeathed, the whole stock of garments must be exhibited. It is therefore probable that the choice is made in the presence of witnesses, since it is made publicly, and usually the praetor himself fixes the day. l. mancipiorum 6. de opt. leg. What is observed in acceptance of an inheritance, which is a legal action, is observed also in the choice. Therefore the choice is a legitimate act. Likewise, just as a son under power cannot enter upon an inheritance without his father's command, so he cannot make a choice; but he may accept other legacies without his father's command. l. 10. de leg. 1. And this is the last condition of legitimate acts: that all of them are made purely. Acceptilation is not made for a day or under a condition. l. 4. & 5. de acceptilat. They do not admit delay, but are carried out at once; thus a guardian is not appointed for a day. l. muto 6. de tutelis. Indeed, by will a guardian may be given under a day or a condition; but that giving is a legitimate act only when it is made by a judge, after inquiry among the best men, from whom one is given; what is done by will is not a legitimate act. So emancipation does not admit a day or a condition. l. pen. C. pro socio. It is doubted whether a partnership can be contracted under a condition, because it is easily believed that mancipation or delivery intervenes. l.2. pro socio. And so ownership is transferred or changed, which does not happen in other contracts, in which mancipation is easily understood to intervene. But mancipation is not made under a condition, nor is a partnership; therefore. It is rightly doubted, then, whether a partnership can be made under a condition. I answer that it can: for the cause of an expressed mancipation is one thing, and of a tacit mancipation another. All legitimate acts do not admit an expressed day or condition; they admit a tacit one. Thus acceptilation is not expressly made for a day or under a condition; but if I acquit as received what you owe me under a condition that has not yet arisen, the acceptilation is indeed not pure, but a condition is tacitly present in it, which is tacitly appended to the obligation. For acceptilation has no force before the condition has been fulfilled. And in general, as is shown in l. expressa 195, hoc tit., expressed things do harm, things not expressed do not harm. The force of the expressed and of the tacit is not the same. l. nonnunquam 52. de condit. & demonst. Cuiac. in Rec.

units.la: Ad Leg. 78. De fraude.
units.tr: To Law 78. On fraud.

units.la: GEneraliter, cum de fraude disputatur, non quid habeat actor, sed quid per aduersarium habere non potuerit, considerandum est.
units.tr: In general, when fraud is disputed, we must consider not what the plaintiff has, but what he could not have had through the adversary.

units.la: Non quid] non quid non habeat: Balduinus in comment. ad L. Aquil. & ita Graeci. ὁ πολυπραγμων ὡς οὐκ ἐχει ὁ ἀναγων. 2. Eclog 3. c. 76. 6. Haimenop. 2. in princip. reprehensus à Roberto animad. 15. Vtramque lectionem probat Cuiac. 15. obs. 19. in princ. & Antoninus Mercator, 1. notar. 15. Certe Græcam lectionem antepono, cuius ea sententia est. Id quod actoris interest, non æstimatur tantum ex eo, quod ei decessit, sed ex eo, quod ei adquiri potuit, ut non tantum damni, sed & lucri habeatur ratio. Actor proprie id non habet quod amisit, idque damnum est. Quod habere potuit, nec tamen habet, luctum est proprie, non damnum. Ideoque fructus non tantum percepti, sed & ii qui percipi potuerunt venient. l. 62. in fine supr. de rei vind. l. 39. §. 1. sup. de leg. 1. l. 33. in sin. princ. sup. ad l. Aquil. l. 22. §. 3. sup. de action. empti. l. 10. §. 19. 20. l. 25. §. 4. sup. quæ in fraud. credit l. 13. sup. ratam rem leg. 1. in fine C. de petit. hered. l. 5. C. de rei vind. Goth.
units.tr: Non quid] read "non quid non habeat" (not what he does not have), as Balduinus has it in comment. ad L. Aquil. & ita Graeci. ὁ πολυπραγμων ὡς οὐκ ἐχει ὁ ἀναγων. 2. Eclog 3. c. 76. 6. Haimenop. 2. in princip. He is criticised by Robertus animad. 15. Both readings are approved by Cuiac. 15. obs. 19. in princ. and by Antoninus Mercator, 1. notar. 15. Certainly I prefer the Greek reading, whose meaning is this: what matters to the plaintiff is valued not only by what has been taken from him, but by what could have been gained for him, so that account is taken not only of loss but also of gain. The plaintiff properly does not have what he has lost, and that is a loss. What he could have had and yet does not have is properly a missed gain, not a loss. Hence not only the fruits actually received but also those which could have been received will be taken into account. l. 62. in fine supr. de rei vind. l. 39. §. 1. sup. de leg. 1. l. 33. in sin. princ. sup. ad l. Aquil. l. 22. §. 3. sup. de action. empti. l. 10. §. 19. 20. l. 25. §. 4. sup. quæ in fraud. credit l. 13. sup. ratam rem leg. 1. in fine C. de petit. hered. l. 5. C. de rei vind. Goth.

units.la: - Ait lex; generaliter, cum agitur de actione fraudatoria, non quid habeat actor consideramus, sed quod culpa & fraude aduersarii ei abest: ut cuius rei venditioni creditor consensit, ea fraudatus non videtur, quia non abest ei aduersarii facto, sed sua voluntate l. nemo videtur 145. infr. hoc tit. Græci legunt in hoc loco: Non omne quod habet actor. Vulgaris scriptura nullum idoneum sensum habet. Forsan melius adhuc quam Græci, leges hoc modo: Non quid habeat aduersarius, sed quid actor per aduersarium habere non potuerit, considerandum est. Nam & ita in malæ fidei possessore, cum quæritur de fructibus, Papinianus ait, generaliter non considerari, quid malæ fidei possessor perceperit, sed quid ipse actor non perceperit. l. si navis 62. de rei vindicatione. Idem traditur in interdicto unde vi, fructus venire, non quos prædo percepit, sed quos actor per prædonem non percepit. Ita in fraudatoria actione nō est inspiciendum, quid habeat reus, sed quid rei causa actor non habeat. Fraudatoriæ actiones dantur duabus de causis: Ob fraudatos creditores, qua de causa est actio Pauliana, aut interdictum fraudatorium. Altera causa est ob fraudatum patronum, ex qua est duplex actio, Fabiana & Calusiana. De Pauliana actione tractemus. Hac actione tenetur is, qui sciens aliquid gessit cum fraudatore, idque edicto cauetur de sciente. L. qui in fraud. creditorum l. 10. eod. propositio interdicto fraudatorio, dicitur causa cognita interdum in ignorantem actionem in factum dari, ut in eum, qui à fraudatore rem cepit ex causa lucrativa, est actio in factum, siue Pauliana, qua tenetur, in quantum locupletior factus est. l. 6. §. simili modo 11. d. tit. At is, qui accepit ex causa non lucrativa, ut emptor, Pauliana non tenetur, nisi sciuerit. Tenendum est, actione Pauliana teneri fraudatorem, vulgo quidam putant, id colligi ex l. 12. que in fraud. cred. quod falsum est. Species haec est. Pater dedit filio liberam administrationem peculii; an poterit filius in fraudem creditorum alienare? Minime. Creditores filii, sunt creditores patris. Sed quid si concessit pater alienare in fraudem creditorum? Lex ait, sufficere actiones in patrem competentes. Hoc ita accipiunt quidam: Pater qui fraudavit creditores, tenetur actione Pauliana, dum ait, sufficere. Sed non est necessaria actio Pauliana, cum eius dolo sit diminutum peculium. Hic ergo locus non probat, fraudatorem teneri Pauliana. Pauliana non competit, nisi post venditionem bonorum debitoris. Si ea bona non sufficiant creditoribus, datur eis Pauliana, quia fraudator sive debitor tenetur in quantum facere potest, vel dolo malo fecit, quo minus facere posset. Nam fieri potest, ut aliquid retinuerit, post venditionem bonorum. Ergo non tenetur in solidum: quia inhumanum est, eum qui est exutus bonis, damnari in solidum. § vlt. Instit. de action. Itaque fraudator hic non tenetur, nisi in quantum facere potest: sed non evitat poenam carceris, quam evitat, qui bonis cedit. l. 1. C. qui bonis ced. poss. Ob priuata delicta nemo patitur carcerem. l. 2. C. de exact. tribut. Ergo fraudator, cuius bona distracta sunt, hoc habet priuilegium, ut non teneatur, nisi in quanquantum facere potest: alterum non habet, vt non euitet carcerem L vlt. §. vlt. quæ in fraud. credit. Sententia hæc est. Ait lex: In fraudatorem dari Pauliana m, hoc est verissimum, nam edicto probatur. Mela tamen non probauit. Ratio est, quia sicuti ei nulla datur actio ex ante gesto, hoc est ante venditionem bonorum l. pen. de curat. bon. dand. Ita etiam in eum nunc nulla videtur esse actio danda, posteaquam est exutus bonis omnibus. Sed non datur in eum actio, nisi in id, quod postea incipit facere posse, deductis alimentis: Et res etiam nonnunquam exigit, vt omnino in eum actio detur. Finge enim, cum conscientia fraudis ita quedam dissipasse, vt recuperari non possint. Æquius est, eum teneri Pauliana, licet actor nihil ab eo consequi possit, quam, vt in carcerem includatur. Pauliana autem actione tenentur ambo ex ante gesto. d. l. ait Prætor. 10. §. penult. cod. Nunc sciendum est, si agatur cum debitore siue fraudatore, in actione Pauliana rem & obligationem cum omni causa in restitutionem venire: Deinde non tantum fructus perceptos, sed etiam qui percipi potuerunt à fraudatore. In fraude enim possessor ille est, qui scit, fraudari creditorem. Itaque fructus non veniunt, nisi post litem contestatam: veniunt tamen fructus, qui fundo cohærebant, L vlt. §. non solum 4. cod. Eadem ratio frufructuum habenda est in actione Fabiana & Caluisiana: sed habetur ratio perceptorum & percipiendorum. l. videamus 38. §. in Fabiana 4. de vsuris l. 1. §. vlt. & l. 2. si quid in fraud. credit. quia Prætor omnem fraudem rescindere voluit. Cum agitur fraudatoria actione, vt fraus rescindatur, habenda est ratio fructuum, non tantum eorum quos percepit aduersarius, sed etiam eorum quos aduersarius percipere potuit, nec percepit.
units.tr: The law says: generaliter, when an action for fraud is brought, we consider not what the plaintiff has, but what he has lost through the fault and fraud of the adversary. For example, a creditor who consented to the sale of a thing is not regarded as defrauded of it, because it was not taken from him by the adversary's act but by his own will. l. nemo videtur 145. infr. hoc tit. The Greeks read at this point: "not everything which the plaintiff has." The common text yields no suitable sense. Perhaps one should read it even better than the Greeks do: "not what the adversary has, but what the plaintiff could not have had through the adversary, is to be considered." For Papinian also says that in the case of a possessor in bad faith, when the question is about fruits, it is generally not considered what the possessor in bad faith has received, but what the plaintiff himself has not received. l. si navis 62. de rei vindicatione. The same rule is laid down for the interdict unde vi: the fruits to be brought into account are not those which the robber received, but those which the plaintiff did not receive through the robber. So in an action for fraud we must look not at what the defendant has, but at what the plaintiff does not have because of the fraud. There are two grounds on which fraudulent actions are given: on account of defrauded creditors, which is the ground of the Pauline action or the fraudulent interdict; and on account of a defrauded patron, from which come the double actions, the Fabian and the Calusian. Let us deal with the Pauline action. Under this action is liable the person who knowingly dealt with the fraudulent debtor, and the edict provides for this with the words "about the one who knew." L. qui in fraud. creditorum l. 10. eod. When the fraudulent interdict has been put forward, it is said that, after a hearing of the case, an action in the form of a fact is sometimes given even against one who was ignorant. Thus against one who took a thing from the fraudulent debtor by a gratuitous cause there is an action in the form of a fact, whether Pauline, by which he is bound to the extent that he has been enriched. l. 6. §. simili modo 11. d. tit. But one who received for a non-gratuitous cause, such as a buyer, is not bound by the Pauline action unless he knew. It must be held that the fraudster is bound by the Pauline action; some commonly think this is gathered from l. 12. que in fraud. cred., which is false. The case is this. A father gave his son the free administration of his property. Can the son alienate in fraud of his creditors? Not at all. The creditors of the son are the creditors of the father. But what if the father allowed him to alienate in fraud of creditors? The law says that actions against the father are sufficient. Some take this to mean that the father who defrauded his creditors is bound by the Pauline action, since the law says "sufficient." But the Pauline action is not necessary, since the property was diminished by his deceit. So this passage does not prove that the fraudster is bound by the Pauline action. The Pauline action does not lie except after the sale of the debtor's goods. If those goods are not enough for the creditors, the Pauline action is given to them, because the fraudster, that is the debtor, is bound to the extent that he is able to pay, or to the extent that by his wicked act he has made it impossible for him to pay. For it can happen that he has kept something after the sale of his goods. Therefore he is not bound for the whole, because it is inhuman to condemn for the whole one who has been stripped of his goods. § vlt. Instit. de action. Accordingly the fraudster here is not bound except to the extent that he is able to pay; but he does not escape imprisonment, which the one who makes a cession of goods does escape. l. 1. C. qui bonis ced. poss. No one suffers imprisonment for private offences. l. 2. C. de exact. tribut. Therefore the fraudster whose goods have been sold has this privilege: he is not bound except to the extent he is able to pay; the other privilege, that he escapes imprisonment, he does not have. L vlt. §. vlt. quæ in fraud. credit This is the view. The law says that the Pauline action is given against the fraudster. This is most true, for it is proved by the edict. Mela, however, did not prove it. The reason is that just as no action is given against him for what he did before, that is before the sale of his goods, l. pen. de curat. bon. dand. so now no action seems to be given against him after he has been stripped of all his goods. But an action is not given against him except for what he begins afterwards to be able to pay, after deducting maintenance; and sometimes the matter itself requires that an action be given against him at all. For imagine that, knowing it was fraud, he has squandered certain things so that they cannot be recovered. It is fairer that he be bound by the Pauline action, even though the plaintiff can get nothing from him, than that he be shut up in prison. Both are bound by the Pauline action for what they did before. d. l. ait Prætor. 10. §. penult. cod. Now it must be understood that, if the action is brought against the debtor or fraudster, in the Pauline action both the thing and the obligation, with every cause, come into restitution; then not only the fruits received but also those which could have been received by the fraudster. For in fraud the possessor is one who knows that the creditor is defrauded. Thus fruits do not come into account unless after litis contestatio; yet the fruits which cling to the land do come into account. L vlt. §. non solum 4. cod. The same rule concerning usufructs is to be observed in the Fabian and Calusian actions: the fruits received and the fruits that could be received are taken into account. l. videamus 38. §. in Fabiana 4. de vsuris l. 1. §. vlt. & l. 2. si quid in fraud. credit. because the Praetor wished to rescind all fraud. When an action for fraud is brought, so that the fraud may be rescinded, account must be taken of the fruits, not only of those which the adversary received, but also of those which the adversary could have received and did not.

units.la: Ad Leg. 79.
units.tr: On Leg. 79.

units.la: FRaudis interpretatio semper in iure ciuili, non ex euentu duntaxat, sed ex consilio quoque consideratur.
units.tr: The interpretation of fraud in civil law is always judged not only by the outcome alone but also by the intention.

units.la: Semper ] imo non semper ex consilio, sed ex euentu. l. 10. §, 1. sup. que in fraud.
units.tr: "Always": indeed, not always by intention but by the outcome. L. 10, §1, sup. que in fraud. [Note: "sup. que in fraud." as printed.]

units.la: Ex euentu ] Decipitur, vt ait Poëta, quisquis ab euentu facta noranda putat.
units.tr: "By the outcome": one is deceived, as the poet says, who thinks that deeds must be judged by their result.

units.la: Ex consilio ] Seneca 2. de tranquillitate c. 7. Potest aliquis nocens fieri, quamuis non nocuerit. Venenum dando quis scelere se obligat, etiamsi non nocuit. Non minus latro est, cuius furtum (ita legendum, non, telum, idque confirmari potest l. 6. in fine supr. ad l. Iul. peculatus) opposita veste elusum est. Omnia enim scelera & ante effectum operis, quantum culpae satis est, perfecta sunt, idem 4. controu. 7. Scelera quamuis citra exitum substederunt, puniuntur. addé l. 14. sup. de sicariis l. 18. sup. de pœnis 2. Eclog. 3. c. 77. 6. Harmen. 2. in princ. Goth.
units.tr: "By the intention": Seneca, On Tranquillity, ch. 7. Someone can become guilty even though he has done no harm. By giving poison a man binds himself to crime even if it does no harm. A thief is no less a robber if his theft was foiled by a garment thrown over him (so read, not "telum", which can be confirmed from l. 6 in fine, sup. ad l. Iul. peculatus). For all crimes, so far as the fault goes, are complete even before the work is finished: Seneca, the same, 4 controv. 7. Crimes, though they stopped short of their outcome, are punished. Add l. 14 sup. de sicariis, l. 18 sup. de poenis, 2 Eclog. 3, ch. 77, 6 Harmen. 2 in princ., Goth.

units.la: Fraudasse non videtur, qui fraudauit re ipsa, nisi fraudandi animum habuerit. Duo exigimus: Euentum, & consilium. Ita fraus accipitur in l. Ælia Sentia in edicto Pauliano, & Fabiano l. ait Prætor 10. §. ita demum. 1. & §. illud 7. que in fraud. credit. L. Ælia Sentia cauetur, vt libertates datæ in fraudem creditorum nullæ sint. Idem est in libertatibus datis in fraudem patroni. l. si pariter 9. de lib. causa. Ergo libertates datæ in fraudem creditorum nullæ sunt: cæteræ alienationes valent, non factæ in fraudem creditorum. In omnibus his legibus fraus significat euentum & consilium. Cæterum in legatis & fideicommissis, mortis causa donationibus, & libertatib. fideicommissariis, euentum tantum inspicimus, etiamsi dolus absit l. vlt. C. qui manumittere non poss. l. 4. §. si quid. de fideic. libertat. leg. 1. §. 1. si quid in fraud. patron. Sed hoc fit necessaria ratione. Nam legata & cætera non præstantur ab hærede, nisi deducto ære alieno. l. 1. ad L. Falcid. In alienationibus, quæ fiunt inter viuos, euentus non sufficit: Nam & dolus exigitur: alioquin cessant fraudatoriæ actiones. Est igitur hæc regula accipienda de fraudatoriis actionibus, vt non competant nisi ex euentu & consilio. Fateor, quandoque culpam coërcoërceri, quæ caret dolo, ut ait Accurs. sed hoc nihil ad actionem fraudatoriam. Fateor etiam fraudem, quæ est in reipsa, præterem amouere per exceptionem doli. Sed hoc nihil ad fraudatorias actiones. Fraus significat captionem, quæ est in re ipsa, & dolum ac fraudem habet. Cui. in Recit.
units.tr: He does not seem to have defrauded who defrauded in fact, unless he had the intention to defraud. We require two things: the outcome and the intention. Thus fraud is understood in the Aelian Sentian law, in the Pauline edict and the Fabian edict: l. ait Praetor 10, §ita demum, and §illud 7, que in fraud. credit. The Aelian Sentian law provides that freedoms given in fraud of creditors are void. The same holds for freedoms given in fraud of the patron: l. si pariter 9, de lib. causa. Therefore freedoms given in fraud of creditors are void; other alienations stand valid, unless made in fraud of creditors. In all these laws, fraud signifies both outcome and intention. Moreover, in legacies and fideicommissa, gifts in view of death, and fideicommissary freedoms, we look only at the outcome, even if there is no deceit: l. vlt. C. qui manumittere non poss.; l. 4, §si quid, de fideic. libertat. leg.; l. 1, §1, si quid in fraud. patron. But this is done for a necessary reason. For legacies and other bequests are not paid by the heir unless the debts have first been deducted: l. 1 ad L. Falcid. In alienations made between living persons, the outcome is not enough; deceit is also required, otherwise the fraudulent actions cease. This rule, then, is to be understood of the fraudulent actions: they do not lie unless there is both outcome and intention. I admit that sometimes fault which lacks deceit is restrained, as Accursius says; but this has nothing to do with the fraudulent action. I also admit that fraud which lies in the thing itself can be removed by the exception of deceit; but this has nothing to do with the fraudulent actions. Fraud signifies a deception which lies in the thing itself, and has deceit and cunning in it. Cui. in Recit.

units.la: Ad Leg. 80. De Genere & Specie.
units.tr: On Leg. 80. On Genus and Species.

units.la: IN toto iure generi per speciem derogatur: & illud potissimum habetur, quod ad speciem directum est.
units.tr: In the whole law the genus is derogated by the species, and that is held chiefly which is directed at the species.

units.la: In toto ] in legibus & statutis. l. 15. l. 16. sup. de legibus. poenis l. 41. §. de poenis. legatis v. l. 99. in fine sup. de leg. 3. petitionibus acsententiis. l. 7. sup. de except. rei indic. vltimis voluntatibus l. 41. §. 4. §. 5. sup. de vulg. in laudo, in rescriptis: non in priuilegiis, & mandato fiscali. v. l. 3. C. de commun. fisci deb. libr. 10. tit. 2. & Decium hic num. vlt. Gothofr.
units.tr: "In the whole": in laws and statutes (l. 15, l. 16 sup. de legibus), penalties (l. 41, §de poenis), legacies (cf. l. 99 in fine sup. de leg. 3), petitions and sentences (l. 7 sup. de except. rei indic.), last wills (l. 41, §4, §5, sup. de vulg.), in an award, in rescripts; not in privileges and in a fiscal mandate: cf. l. 3 C. de commun. fisci deb., lib. 10, tit. 2, and Decius here, num. vlt., Gothofr.

units.la: Generi ] cap. generi 34. de reg. in 6. leg. 99. in fine sup. de leg. 3. leg. 41. sup. de poenis 6. Harmenop. 2.
units.tr: "Genus": cap. generi 34, de reg. in 6; l. 99 in fine sup. de leg. 3; l. 41 sup. de poenis; 6 Harmenop. 2.

units.la: Per speciem ] Speciei vocabulo intellige etiam indiuidua, ad quæ significanda, ICti speciei vocabulo abutuntur, vt & generis voce ad species leg. 54. leg. 83. §. 5. sup. de verb. oblig. Gothofr.
units.tr: "By the species": understand by the word species also individuals, which lawyers use the word species to signify, just as they use the word genus for species: l. 54; l. 83, §5, sup. de verb. oblig. Gothofr.

units.la: Derogatur ] siue genus speciem præcedat, siue leue sequatur. arg. l. 6. in fine sup. de nouat. l. 27. C. de pactis l. 1. C. de aedilit. act. Goth.
units.tr: "Is derogated": whether the genus precedes the species or lightly follows it. Cf. l. 6 in fine sup. de nouat.; l. 27 C. de pactis; l. 1 C. de aedilit. act. Goth.

units.la: Et illud ] Idem Cic. lib. 2. de inuent. Rhetorica, dum de contrariis legibus disserit. Pac.
units.tr: "And that": the same Cicero, in book 2 of De inventione rhetorica, where he discusses contrary laws. Pac.

units.la: Vsus huius regulae est frequens in iure. Finge, testator legauit generaliter omne peculium seruo: in peculio continentur vicarii serui, nam ii sunt peculiares serui; at ex iis vnus, liber esse iussus est eodem testamento; an liber erit? Ita; eximetur hic seruus ex generali legato peculii. Species derogauit testamento l. 10. de manumiss. testam. vel finge: Testator mihi legauit seruos vernas, tibi seruos textores, qui etiam vernae erant: sed serui textores, qui tibi legati sunt, eximentur de legato mihi relicto. Tale exemplum est in l. sanctio 41. de poenis. Sanctio est generalis poena, quae solet poni in nouissima parte legis. Nam leges habebant plura capita. Extremum caput erat sanctio. Huic sanctioni derogatur per specialem poenam, si nempe talis alicui capiti legis addita sit. Sic in vniuersum, quae generaliter tracta sunt, eis derogatur per speciem.
units.tr: The use of this rule is frequent in law. Suppose a testator left in general terms the whole peculium to a slave. Among the peculium are included the slave's vicarii, for these are slaves of the peculium; but if one of them is ordered by the same will to be free, will he be free? Yes; this slave will be excluded from the general legacy of the peculium. The species has derogated in the will: l. 10 de manumiss. testam. Or suppose: a testator left me the home-born slaves, and left you the weaving slaves, who were also home-born; but the weaving slaves left to you will be excluded from the legacy left to me. A similar example is in l. sanctio 41 de poenis. The sanctio is the general penalty, which is usually placed in the last part of a law, for laws had several chapters, and the last chapter was the sanctio. This sanctio is derogated by a special penalty, if that is added to some chapter of the law. So, in general, things that are dealt with generally are derogated by the specific.

units.la: Ad Leg. 81. Quae dubitationis tollendae causa inseruntur.
units.tr: On Dig. 81: Clauses inserted to remove doubt

units.la: Quae dubitationis tollendae causa contractibus inseruntur, ius commune non laedunt.
units.tr: Clauses that are inserted in contracts to remove doubt do not impair the common law.

units.la: Qua]
units.tr: Qua]

units.la: Haec regula repetita est in l. qui mutuum 56. mandati. Sciendum est, in creditoris arbitrio esse, quem velit convenire, reum principalem, an fideiussorem, an eius mandatorem; an pignora velit distrahere, & vno electo, si solidum creditor non potuit impetrare, ad alium venire potest. l. grege 13. §. etiam 4. de pignoribus l. 3. §. vlt. de duob. reis. & hoc obtinuit ante Nouell. Iustiniani, ex qua electionem non habet creditor. Nam prius debet excutere reum principalem. Verum loquamur de iure antiquo. Paciscuntur inter se contrahentes, vt creditori liceat convenire mandatorem omisso & inexcusso reo, & pignoribus distractis. Haec conuentio est superuacua. Nam ipso iure hanc electionem habet creditor. Dubitationis tamen tollendae causa haec pactio interuenit. Sed ita conuento reo, potesne redire ad mandatorem pignoribus distractis? Ita sane per hanc nostram regulam. Nam ius commune seruabitur non tantum in casu expresso, sed & omisso. Sumatur aliud exemplum ex leg. 3. C. de fideiussoribus. Sciendum est, si plures sint fideiussores, singulos teneri in solidum: sed habent beneficium diuisionis ex epistola D. Hadriani. Nunc finge: conuenit, ut singuli fideiussores teneantur in solidum: nihil autem adiicitur in conuentione de diuisionis beneficio ex Epistola D. Hadriani: an videbitur renunciatum beneficio diuisionis? Minime. Et sic in superiore specie creditor non videtur renunciasse electioni. Ergo hae conuentiones sunt superuacaneae, nec necessario inseruntur contractibus. Ergo in casibus omissis ius commune non laedunt. Ius commune etiam locum habet, fideiussore iuri communi renuntiante. Non enim dicemus, hac ratione iuri communi renuntiatum videri. Accursius opponit l. inter 26. §. cum inter 2. de pact. dotalibus. & leg. si cum dotem 22. soluto matrim. Sed sciendum est, ex l. inter dotem profectitiam redire ad patrem, mortua in matrimonio filia, siue sua sit, siue emancipata, & siue mortua sit sine liberis, siue superstitibus liberis: Filiae emancipatae soli, diuortio facto, competit repetitio dotis. Si filia sit in potestate, communis est actio, & voluntas utriusque, hoc est patris & filiae exigitur. Ponamus speciem. Pater stipulatus est, dotem sibi reddi, sine liberis mortua in matrimonio filia: hoc ita se habet ipso iure. Ergo secundum hanc regu-lam, etiam superstitibus filiis dos est reddenda patri. Attamen d. l. inter, ait superstitibus liberis, dotem non reddi patri. Sic respondeo: si pater stipuletur dotem sibi reddi, superstitibus filiis, mortua filia huic regulae locus erit. Nam sine liberis mortua filia, dos ad patrem reuertitur, quia manifeste haec conuentio interponitur dubitationis tollendae gratia. Nam de eo magis dubitari poterat, an superstitibus liberis, dos rediret ad patrem, cuius dubii causa interponitur haec conuentio. Sed si conuenerit, dotem reddi sine liberis mortua filia, quod nihil habet dubitationis, haec conuentio non videtur poni, dubitationis tollendae gratia, vt ita dos redeat ad patrem si filia, non extantibus liberis, mortua sit. Itaque liberis extantibus non redit. Quomodo si conuenerit; vt non aliter creditor veniat ad mandatorem, quam pignoribus distractis: vel si conueniat, vt non conueniantur fideiussores in soli-dum, secundum ius D. Hadriani. Sequimur quod actum est, nec derogatur iuri communi, quod permittit, vnumquemque iuri suo renuntiare. Et ita videtur pater renunciasse re-petitioni dotis, d. l. inter de pact. dot. Nam verba, sine liberis, faciunt conditionem in specie d. §. cum inter. Ius commune erat, vt dos reuerteretur ad patrem, vel extantibus, vel non ex-tantikantibus liberis, sic tamen, vt quintæ in singulos liberos retinerentur ex dote vxoris. Vlp. in fragm. tit. de dote 6. Retentio quintarum non est sublata l. unica C. de rei vx. act. Nam in eo §. loquitur tantum de retentione, quæ fit propter liberos diuortio facto, nos non loquimur de diuortio, sed de morte. Itaque quintarum retentio non est sublata. Pactio erat vulgaris olim, vt filiis superstitibus dos tota retineretur à patre, & ita pactum vulgare appellatur in leg. Babius 30. de iure dot. quod vulgo fiebat. Pactio plerisq; locis in ius commune transiit, idq; patet ex multis locis, quibus ostenditur, vulgaria pacta transire in ius commune. Conuentio conditionalis in eo §. facit, vt redear dos ad patrem, quæ erat vulgaris conuentio: ideoque ea verba, sine liberis, accipiuntur pro vulgari pacto. Respondeamus ad leg. si cum dotem. soluto matrim. Sententia l. est. Si pater aut extraneus pacisci tur, sibi dotem reddi in vnum casum: duo sunt casus reddendæ dotis, diuortii & mortis. Si itaque in vnum casum stipuletur tantum, in casum non expressum erit actio propria mulieris. Hoc non pugnat cum hac regula. In extraneo certum est, non pugnare; Nam certum est in extraneo, qui dotem dat, hanc conuentionem non esse superuacuam. Igitur si extraneus in vnum casum pactus est, in casum omissum actio erit mulieris, vel hæredum eius. Illa conuentio non est superuacua: ipso enim iure repetitionem non habet. Hæc autem regula est de superuacuis conuentionibus. In patre etiam nihil aduersatur hæc regula. Nam si ponas, patrem dotem dantem stipulari sibi reddi dotem morte, siue generi, siue filiæ. Hæc conuentio non est supervacua; cum sit iuri dissentanea. Nam in casum mortis filiæ, patris fuisset propria actio dotis. Sed in casum mortis generi hæc conuentio propriam actionem patris facit, quæ aliàs vel communis foret et cum filia sua, vel propria filiæ emancipatæ. Igitur in casum omissum, hoc est diuortii propria erit actio patris, quæ iure communi, foret cum filia communis, detracta nempe conuentione. Et ex contrario: si pater stipulatus sit dotem sibi reddi in casum diuortii, superuacua est actio, nec iuri communi consentanea. Igitur in casu mortis actio erit propria filiæ, vel hæredum. Denique conuentio, quæ à patre interponitur, iuri communi consentanea non est. Verum si generaliter ponas, in mortem tantum filiæ patrem esse stipulatum, superuacua erit pactio, & iuri communi consentanea. In casum igitur omissum actio erit communis.
units.tr: This rule is repeated in l. qui mutuum 56. mandati. It must be understood that it is at the creditor's discretion whom he wishes to sue: the principal debtor, the surety, or the surety's own surety. He may also choose whether to sell the pledges, and if, having chosen one, he cannot obtain the full amount, he may go on to another. l. grege 13. §. etiam 4. de pignoribus l. 3. §. vlt. de duob. reis. This held good before the Novel of Justinian, by which the creditor no longer had this choice, since he had first to exhaust the principal debtor. But let us speak of the older law. The contracting parties agree between themselves that the creditor may proceed against the surety without first pursuing the principal debtor and without exhausting the pledges. This agreement is superfluous, for the creditor already has this choice by law itself. Nevertheless the agreement is made to remove doubt. But if the creditor has sued the principal debtor, may he return to the surety after the pledges have been sold? Certainly, by this rule of ours. For the common law is preserved not only in the case expressly stated but also in the case left out. Let us take another example from l. 3. C. de fideiussoribus. It must be understood that if there are several sureties, each is bound for the whole amount, but they have the benefit of division by the letter of the Emperor Hadrian. Now suppose it is agreed that each surety shall be bound for the whole, and nothing is added in the agreement about the benefit of division under the letter of Hadrian. Will it be thought that the benefit of division has been renounced? Not at all. And so in the earlier case the creditor is not thought to have renounced his choice. Therefore these agreements are superfluous, and are not necessarily inserted into contracts. Therefore in the omitted cases the common law is not impaired. The common law also holds when a surety renounces the common law. For we will not say that by this reasoning a renunciation of the common law is to be inferred. Accursius objects l. inter 26. §. cum inter 2. de pact. dotalibus. & leg. si cum dotem 22. soluto matrim. But it must be understood that from l. inter the dowry given by a father returns to him when a daughter dies during the marriage, whether she is under his power or emancipated, and whether she dies without children or with surviving children. An emancipated daughter alone, once the divorce is made, has the right to reclaim the dowry. If the daughter is under power, the action is shared, and the will of both, that is of the father and the daughter, is required. Let us put a case. A father has stipulated that the dowry be returned to him should his daughter die during the marriage without children. By law itself this stands as it is. Therefore, according to this rule, the dowry must be returned to the father even if children survive. Yet the said l. inter says that with children surviving the dowry is not returned to the father. I answer thus: if the father stipulates that the dowry be returned to him, with children surviving, should the daughter die, this rule will have its place. For when the daughter dies without children, the dowry returns to the father, because this agreement is manifestly interposed to remove doubt. For it could be more doubtful whether, with children surviving, the dowry would return to the father, and it is for the sake of this doubt that the agreement is interposed. But if it was agreed that the dowry be returned when the daughter dies without children, which contains no doubt, this agreement does not seem to have been made to remove doubt, so that the dowry should return to the father if the daughter dies with no children surviving. Thus with children surviving it does not return. The same holds if it was agreed that the creditor should not come to the surety except after the pledges had been sold, or if it was agreed that the sureties should not be sued for the whole amount, according to the law of Hadrian. We follow what was agreed, and the common law is not derogated, which permits each person to renounce what is his by right. And so the father is thought to have renounced the recovery of the dowry, d. l. inter de pact. dot. For the words, without children, make a condition in the case d. §. cum inter. The common law was that the dowry returned to the father whether children survived or not, but in such a way that the fifths were retained from the wife's dowry for each child. Ulpian in the Fragments, title de dote 6. The retention of fifths has not been abolished by l. unica C. de rei uxoriae actione. For in that §. it speaks only of the retention made on account of children when a divorce occurs; we are not speaking of divorce but of death. Therefore the retention of fifths has not been abolished. The agreement was once common, that the whole dowry should be retained by the father when children survived, and so it is called a common agreement in leg. Babius 30. de iure dot. because it was commonly made. The agreement has in many places passed into the common law, as is shown by many passages which show that common agreements pass into the common law. The conditional agreement in that §. makes the dowry return to the father, and this was the common agreement; therefore those words, without children, are taken to mean the common agreement. Let us answer to leg. si cum dotem. soluto matrim. The sense of the law is this: if a father or a stranger stipulates that the dowry be returned to him in one case only, when there are two cases of return of the dowry, divorce and death, then if he stipulates only one case, the wife will have her own action in the case not expressed. This does not conflict with this rule. In the case of a stranger it is certain that it does not conflict, for it is certain that in a stranger who gives the dowry this agreement is not superfluous. Therefore if a stranger has agreed in one case, the action in the omitted case will belong to the wife or to her heirs. That agreement is not superfluous, for by law itself he has no right of recovery. But this rule concerns superfluous agreements. Nor does this rule oppose the case of a father either. For if you suppose that a father who gives the dowry stipulates that it be returned to him on the death of either the son-in-law or the daughter, this agreement is not superfluous, since it is at variance with the law. For in the case of the daughter's death the father would have had his own action for the dowry. But in the case of the son-in-law's death this agreement makes the father's action his own, which otherwise would have been shared with his daughter, or belonged to the emancipated daughter alone. Therefore in the omitted case, that is of divorce, the father's action will be his own, which by common law would have been shared with the daughter, the agreement having been set aside. And conversely: if the father stipulated that the dowry be returned to him in the case of divorce, the action is superfluous and not in accordance with the common law. Therefore in the case of death the action will belong to the daughter or her heirs. Finally, an agreement that is made by the father is not in accordance with the common law. But if you put it generally, that the father stipulated only on the daughter's death, the agreement will be superfluous and in accordance with the common law. In the omitted case, therefore, the action will be the common one.

units.la: Cuiac. in Recitat.
units.tr: Cuiacius, in Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg. 83. De donatione.
units.tr: On Digest Law 83. On gifts.

units.la: DOnari videtur, quod nullo iure cogente conceditur.
units.tr: That is seen as given which is granted by no compelling law.

units.la: Donari ] v. l. 29. sup: de donationib. 2. Eclog. 3. cap. 80.
units.tr: Donari ] see above, law 29, On gifts; Eclog. 2, 3, chap. 80.

units.la: Nullo ] penitus scilicet, si tamen obligati naturaliter quid dederimus, proprie non erit donatio. l.i. sup: de donat.
units.tr: Nullo ] that is, entirely. Yet if we have given something to which we were naturally bound, it will not properly be a gift. Law 1 above, On gifts.

units.la: Exemplum est: si seruus post manumissionem soluat pecuniam sibi creditam in seruitute, nulla est donatio. Soluit quidem quod non debet iure ciuili, sed quod debet naturali iure. Igitur non est donatio: leg. hoc iure 19. de donat.
units.tr: For example: if a slave, after manumission, pays a debt that he contracted while in servitude, there is no gift. He pays what he was not bound to pay by civil law, but what he was bound to pay by natural law. Therefore it is not a gift: law "hoc iure" 19, On gifts.

units.la: Donatio est eius, quod nullo iure cogente conceditur. Sic & contra sententiam Iohan. Bulgari, Accursii & aliorum; si quis aliquem remuneretur, remuneratio non est proprie liberalitas: sed quasi pretium & merces officii. leg. si ut certo §. §nunc videndum ii. commodati l.2.§. & generaliter. vi bonorum raptor. Et naturaliter debetur remuneratio, id est, iure gentium l. sed & si lege. de petit.hared. Ideo quod soluitur ex hac causa non repetitur quasi indebitum.
units.tr: A gift is what is conveyed without any law compelling it. So too, contrary to the opinion of John of Bologna, Accursius and others: if someone rewards another, the reward is not properly generosity, but as it were the price and wage of a service. Law "si ut certo" §. "nunc videndum", ii. commodati; law 2 §. "et generaliter", vi bonorum raptor. And a reward is owed by natural law, that is, by the law of nations: law "sed et si lege", De petitione hereditatis. For that reason what is paid on this ground is not reclaimed as something not owed.

units.la: At vero remunerationem donationem non esse constat ex l.3.§.vlt. & l. hoc iure §.1. de donat, ait lex: officiorum mercedem, esse extra causam donationis, ut, si mihi dones aliquid, quod tibi adfui, vel quod pro te satisfedi, vel quod aliqua in re opera & gratia mea usus fuisti; quae non est proprie donatio, sed remuneratio praecedentis officii. Delenda sunt, quae Accursi scripsit; Nam non intelligit, co §. agi de remuneratione, quæ non est mera liberalitas: donatio vero est mera liberalitas, quæ nullo iure cogente, in alium transfertur. Huius est certus modus; remunerationis non est certus modus. Hæc regula repetita est in l. donari de donationib. sed utraque lege videtur legendum, Papinianus lib. 8. Responsorum. Et ita huic legi coniungetur l. vir vsuras 34. de donat. inter virum, & vx. species est, Mulier promisit dotis vsuras, quod tardius dotem soluerer & præstitit; an præstatio est donatio? Certe non, quia iure cogente dos tribuitur. Sed si vsuras dotis remittat, an donatio est? Sic sane. l. si quis pro uxore l. si uxor. de donat. inter vir. & vx. Finge igitur. Mulier debet dotem, & promisit vsuras dotis, maritus non petit vsuras, tacite remittit vsuras uxori: hæc remissio non valet, nisi morte confirmetur. Finge, maritus dotem uxori prælegauit, & confirmauit, si quid daret uxori, fideicommissum esse: legato dotis vsuræ non continentur: sed titulo donationis confirmantur. Cuiac.
units.tr: Yet it is established that a reward is not a gift, from law 3 §. last, and law "hoc iure" §. 1, On gifts, where the law says that the wage of services lies outside the category of gift: for instance, if you give me something because I helped you, or because I paid on your behalf, or because you have used my work and favour in some matter. This is not properly a gift, but a reward for a service already rendered. What Accursius wrote should be deleted, for he does not grasp that this paragraph treats of a reward, which is not pure generosity; a gift, however, is pure generosity, which is transferred to another without any law compelling it. The gift has a fixed measure; a reward has no fixed measure. This rule is repeated in the law "donari", On gifts, but both laws seem to require reading as Papinian, book 8 of the Responsa. And thus this law is joined to law "vir usuras" 34, On gifts between husband and wife. The case is this: a wife promised interest on her dowry because she would pay the dowry late, and she made good on it. Is the payment a gift? Certainly not, because the dowry is given under compulsion of law. But if he remits the interest on the dowry, is it a gift? Indeed it is: law "si quis pro uxore" and law "si uxor", On gifts between husband and wife. Suppose, then, that the wife owes the dowry and has promised interest on it, and the husband does not demand the interest but tacitly remits it to his wife: this remission is not valid unless it is confirmed by death. Suppose the husband bequeathed the dowry to his wife by legacy, and confirmed that whatever he gave his wife was a trust: the interest on the dowry is not included in the legacy, but is confirmed under the title of gift. Cuiac.

units.la: Ad Leg. 83. De amissione.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 83. De amissione.

units.la: NOn videntur rem amittere, quibus propria non fuit.
units.tr: They do not seem to lose a thing which was never their own.

units.la: Non videntur ] proprie scilicet, alias improprie: amitti etiam dicitur, quod quis consequi non potuit. leg. 33. in fine sup. ad L. Aquiliam. Gothofr.
units.tr: Non videntur] That is, properly speaking; otherwise it is also said improperly that someone loses what he was unable to obtain. Law 33, at the end of the title on the Lex Aquilia. Gothofredus.

units.la: quorum propria Priuatio, habitum: & qualitas subiectum præsupponit leg. 4. sup. de instit. l. 3. in fine sup. de capite minutis l. 1. §. 1. sup. si vsufr. l. 41. verf. quare si nulla sup. de reb. credit l. 4. sup. de act. empti l. 5. sup. de iniusto rupto l. 96. sup. de condit. & demonst. l. 116. sup. de verb. oblig. Gothofr.
units.tr: Privation presupposes a property or habit of which it is the privation, and a quality presupposes a subject: law 4, at the start of the title on institutions; law 3, at the end of the title on loss of status; law 1, §1, at the start of the title on usufruct, "if"; law 41, the passage beginning "why, if there is none", at the start of the title on loans; law 4, at the start of the title on actions of purchase; law 5, at the start of the title on an unjust rupture; law 96, at the start of the title on conditions and demonstrations; law 116, at the start of the title on verbal obligations. Gothofredus.

units.la: Is amittit rem, qui acquisiuit: & ideo Græci apud Harmenop. lib. 3. Epit. tit. 9. hoc solum notant: Casum fortuitum solum dominum agnoscere: vt re pignori tradita creditori, Creditor non videtur rem amittere, sed dominus, cum eius propria nunquam fuerit: Cuiac. in Recitat.
units.tr: He loses a thing who has acquired it. Hence the Greeks, in Harmenopoulos, book 3 of the Epitome, title 9, note only this: that a fortuitous loss affects only the owner. So when a thing is handed over to a creditor as a pledge, the creditor is not seen to lose it, but the owner is, since it was never his own. Cuiacius, in the Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg. 84. De amplius soluto. De natu- ra obligationum.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 84. De amplius soluto. De natura obligationum.

units.la: CVm amplius solutum est, quam debebatur, cuius pars non inuenitur, quæ repeti possit, totum esse indebitum intelligitur, manente pristina obligatione. §. 1. Is natura debet, quem iure gentium dare oportet, cuius fidem secuti sumus.
units.tr: When more has been paid than was owed, and no part of the excess can be found that could be reclaimed, the whole payment is understood to have been not owed, the original obligation remaining. §1. He owes by nature whom it is fitting by the law of nations to give, whose good faith we have followed.

units.la: v. l. 26. §. 4. sup. de condict. indebiti.
units.tr: See law 26, §4, at the start of the title on the condiction of what is not owed.

units.la: Id accidit, quoties res in solutum data diuidi non potest: quia, si indiuiduum est, quod diuidi non potest, nec eius pars aliqua esse poterit: ideoque solutione irrita, totum condicitur, & in solidum erit agendum. leg. 1. §. 9. sup. ad L. Falcid. l. 1. §. 21. sup. si quid in fraud. patron. Gothofr.
units.tr: This happens whenever a thing given in payment in place of what was owed cannot be divided. For if a thing is undivided and cannot be divided, no part of it can exist; therefore, when the payment is void, the whole is recovered by condiction and the action must be brought for the whole. Law 1, §9, at the start of the title on the Falcidian law; law 1, §21, at the start of the title on what was done in fraud of a patron. Gothofredus.

units.la: Is] Coniunge l. Iulianus de condict. indebiti.
units.tr: "He"] Join this with the law of Julian on the condiction of what is not owed.

units.la: Natura] Natura debetur id, quod natura æquum est solui. l. 11. §. 2. sup. de peculio, cuius obligatio solo vinculo æquitatis sustentatur. l. 95. §. 4. sup. soluto. quod tamen per Iudicem peti non potest l. 1. §. 17. sup. ad L. Falcid. leg. 10. in fine sup. de verb. signific. Goth.
units.tr: "By nature"] What is due by nature is what it is fair by nature to pay, an obligation sustained by the bond of equity alone: law 11, §2, at the start of the title on the peculium, law 95, §4, at the start of the title on payment, which nevertheless cannot be claimed before a judge: law 1, §17, at the start of the title on the Falcidian law; law 10, at the end of the title on the meaning of words. Gothofredus.

units.la: Iure gentium] sensus est, Nemo iure gentium debet, quin & natura debeat: nihil iure gentium æquum est, quin & natura quoque sit æquum: at non continuo, qui natura debent, iure gentium debent. Ius enim gentium obligationis actionem magis efficacem facit, quam naturalis Gothofr.
units.tr: "By the law of nations"] The sense is this: no one owes by the law of nations without also owing by nature. Nothing is equitable by the law of nations which is not also equitable by nature; but it does not follow that whoever owes by nature owes by the law of nations. For the law of nations makes the action of an obligation more effective than the natural one does. Gothofredus.

units.la: Fidem] Is naturali æquitate obligatur. l. 1. sup. de pactis. Pertinet hæc lex ad condictionem indebiti. Duæ sunt sententiæ. Ad primam sententiam ponit Accurs. exemplum ex l. si non sortem 26. §. si centum 4. de condict. indeb. Finge: Debeo centum, soluti fundum dignum ducentis: amplius quam debebam solui: non invenitur, quæ pars fundi sit indebita, maxime cum sint confusæ partes. Hoc casu non statuetur communio fundi, sed totus fundus repetetur, manente incorrupta obligatione illorum rum centum. Altera sententia etiam pertinet ad condictionem indebiti, in qua est frequens tractatio de naturali debito : Eum qui natura debet, licet non debeat iure ciuili, eius non habere repetitionem: Is natura debet, cui fidem habuimus, vt qui pacto promisit, se aliquid daturum sine stipulatione, eius verbo fidem habuimus l. in his 5. §. Imperator. de solution. Item; Pupillus, cui pecuniam credidimus, sine tutore authore, ex qua factus sit locupletior, debet natura. l. naturaliter 13. §. 1. & l. seq. de condict. indeb. & ita naturalis obligatio accipitur in l. Stichum 95. §. naturalis 4. de solution. quæ solo vinculo æquitatis sustinetur: Verum sicut natura debet non tantum is, cuius fidem secuti sumus; ita debet non tantum, qui naturali, sed etiam qui iure gentium debet, vt seruus domino, & contra, dominus seruo non debet iure naturali, sed iure gentium, quia seruitus est constitutio iuris gentium; & is qui debet iure naturali, si soluat, non habet condictionem indebiti. Iure gentium condicit. l. indebitum 9. C. de condict. indebiti. Qui autem soluit indebitum iure naturali, vt libertus, qui eo iure est incognitus, non habet condictionem indebiti. Sic operæ non debentur iure naturali, quo est incognitum ius patronatus, sed debentur iure gentium. Nam patronatus est iuris gentium, l. manumissionis 4. de iustit & iure. Ad hanc differentiam puto referri hanc definitionē huius regulae, vt intelligatur, eum, qui iure gentium debet, licet non debeat iure naturali, non habere condictionem indebiti. Cuiac. in Recitat.
units.tr: "Good faith"] He is bound by natural equity. Law 1, at the start of the title on pacts. This law concerns the condiction of what is not owed, and there are two opinions. For the first opinion, Accursius gives the example from law "si non sortem" 26, §"si centum" 4, on the condiction of what is not owed. Suppose: I owe a hundred, and I pay with a farm worth two hundred. More was paid than I owed, and no part of the farm can be found that was not owed, especially since the parts are merged. In this case no joint ownership of the farm is established; the whole farm is reclaimed, while the obligation for those hundred remains intact. The second opinion also concerns the condiction of what is not owed, and in it there is a frequent discussion of natural debt: one who owes by nature, though he does not owe by civil law, has no right of reclaiming what he paid. He owes by nature whose good faith we have trusted, as one who by a pact promised to give something without a stipulation; we trusted his word: law "in his" 5, §"Imperator", on payment. Likewise, a ward to whom we lent money without the authority of a guardian, and who thereby became richer, owes by nature: law "naturaliter" 13, §1, and the following law, on the condiction of what is not owed. And so a natural obligation is understood in law "Stichus" 95, §"naturalis" 4, on payment, which is sustained by the bond of equity alone. Yet just as one owes by nature not only the one whose good faith we have followed, so one owes not only by natural law but also by the law of nations: a slave owes his master, and conversely the master owes the slave, not by natural law but by the law of nations, since slavery is an institution of the law of nations. Whoever owes by natural law, if he pays, has no condiction of what is not owed; whoever owes by the law of nations has one: law "indebitum" 9, C., on the condiction of what is not owed. But one who pays what is not owed under natural law, such as a freedman, who is unknown to that law, has no condiction of what is not owed. So services are not owed by natural law, under which the right of patronage is unknown, but they are owed by the law of nations, for patronage belongs to the law of nations: law "manumissionis" 4, on justice and law. I think this distinction is the reason for the definition of this rule, namely that one who owes by the law of nations, though he does not owe by natural law, has no condiction of what is not owed. Cuiacius, in the Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg. 85. De dote. 1. De his quae ad eum casum peruenerunt, à quo non possunt initium capere. 2. Si æquitate desiderii naturalis ratio aut dubitatio iuris moretur.
units.tr: On Leg. 85, On the dowry. 1. On those things which have come to that event from which they cannot take their beginning. 2. If the reason of natural equity or a doubt of law delays the matter.

units.la: INambiguis pro dotibus respondere melius est. §. 1. Non est nouum, vt quæsemel vtiliter constituta sunt, durent, licet ille casus exciterit, à quo initium capere non potuerunt. §. 2. Quoties æquitate desiderii naturalis ratio, aut dubitatio iuris moratur, iustis decretis tes temperanda est.
units.tr: In doubtful cases it is better to rule in favour of dowries. § 1. It is nothing new that things validly established once should endure, even though that event has happened from which they could not take their beginning. § 2. Whenever the reason of natural equity, or a doubt of law, delays a matter, it is to be tempered by just decisions.

units.la: In ambiguis ] Coniunge l. in ambiguis de iure dot. l. Cuius soluto matrimonio, Pac.
units.tr: In doubtful cases: join this with the law "In doubtful cases" on the right of dowry, and the law "Whose marriage is dissolved," Pacius.

units.la: Pro dotibus ] v. l. 9. §. 1. l. 70. sup. de iure dot. l. 1. sup. soluto 2. Eclog. 3. c. 82. l. vlt. C. ad Vellei. & iis quæ doti comparantur, vt Ecclesia, & fiscus. Dec. hic. De priuilegiis dotalibus vide Oldendorp. in tractat. de iure sing. capite 13. Gothofr.
units.tr: In favour of dowries: see the law 9, § 1, and the law 70 above, on the right of dowry; the law 1 above, "When the marriage is dissolved" (Basilica 2, Ecloga 3, c. 82); and the last law of the Code on the Senatusconsultum Velleianum. And those things which are equated with dowry, as the Church and the fisc. Decius, here. On dotal privileges see Oldendorp in his treatise on singular law, chapter 13. Gothofredus.

units.la: Constituta ] id est, consummata & perfecta. v. Dynum ad c. 73. de reg. in 6. & Dec. hic. Licet] cap. factum legitime 73. de reg. in 6. 2. Eclog. 3. c. 84. sic propter impedimentum superveniens non vitiatur matrimonium, l. 8. sup. de his qui sunt sui: testamentum. l. 18. sup. de his qui est. l. 1. §. 3. sup. secund. tab. lenatorius ordo, iudicandi munus, magistratus. l. 1. §. 5. vers. casum sup. de postul. Sufficit enim, actum ab initio fuisse legitimum. v. l. 29. sup. eod. Tanta est iam facti authoritas, ut interdum, quod prohiberur fieri, factum teneat. leg. 1. §. 5. sup. quando appell. atque ita vrile per inutile non viciatur: inceptum tamen, nec dum perfectum, inutilis aduentu euanescit l. 16. sup. ad L. Aquil. v. Dec. hic. & Dynum d. c. 73. Goth.
units.tr: Established: that is, consummated and perfected; see Dynus on chapter 73 of the rules of the Sixth Book, and Decius here. Although: chapter "Factum legitime," 73 of the rules of the Sixth Book; Basilica 2, Ecloga 3, c. 84. Thus, because of a supervening impediment, a marriage is not vitiated (law 8 above, "On those who are under their own power"; the testament, law 18 above, "On those who are infamous"; law 1, § 3, above, on the second tablet; the senatorial order, the office of judging, the magistracy; law 1, § 5, "the case," above, on postulating). For it is enough that the act was lawful from the beginning; see law 29 above, the same title. So great now is the authority of the deed that sometimes what was forbidden to be done is held to be done (law 1, § 5, above, when appeal may be made). And thus what is useful is not vitiated by what is useless; but what has been begun and not yet completed vanishes when a useless thing supervenes (law 16 above, on the Lex Aquilia). See Decius here, and Dynus on the said chapter 73. Gothofredus.

units.la: Æquitas] æquitatem, vulgo Hal.
units.tr: Equity: equity, commonly "Hal."

units.la: Desiderii] id est, postulantis agentis. Desiderium significat hic libellum. Iraque quoties æquitatem libelli moratur ratio naturalis, aut dubitatio iuris, causa non est iudicanda de plano; sed res est referenda ad diem sessionum, cum sedebit prætor pro tribunali.
units.tr: Of the claimant: that is, of the one petitioning or acting. Here "desire" signifies the petition. Therefore whenever the reason of natural equity or a doubt of law delays the petition, the matter is not to be judged at once; but the affair is to be referred to the day of sessions, when the praetor will sit upon the tribunal.

units.la: Naturaliratio] id est, æquitas iustæ causæ, cui multum à Iudicibus tribui solet. l. 1. in f. l. 26. in sin. sup. ex quib. caus. maior.
units.tr: Natural reason: that is, the equity of a just cause, to which judges are usually accorded great weight (law 1, at the end; law 26, at the end, above, on the causes for restitution by reason of being a minor).

units.la: Dubitatio iuris] quæ oritur ex contrariis legibus.
units.tr: Doubt of law: which arises from contrary laws.

units.la: Moratur] id est, impedimentum affert, quo minus res possit decidi.
units.tr: Delays: that is, brings an obstacle by which the matter cannot be decided.

units.la: Temperanda] Temperare est inter summum mum & nimium indulgens ius, medium lo-cum tenere. l.17. sup. de usur. vt sit sensus. In o-mnibus quidem, maxime tamen in iure æquitas spectatur l.89. inf. eod. 2. Eclog. 3. c. 87.
units.tr: To be tempered: to temper is to hold the middle place between a right granted at its highest and an excessive indulgence, so that the sense is: in all things, but most of all in law, equity is looked to (law 17 above, on usury; law 89 below, the same title; Basilica 2, Ecloga 3, c. 87).

units.la: Prima sententia est: In ambiguis pro dotibus respondere melius est; quæ repetitur in l. in ambiguis 70. de iure dot. Causarum quædam sunt fauorabiles, vt mortuorum illationes, l. sunt persona 43. de relig. & sumpt. fun. & dotes. l. vlt. C. ad SC. Velleian. At in ambiguis, vt pro libertate respondemus, ita pro dote. Sumamus exemplum ex l. Caius Seius 45. soluto matrim. species est: Auus maternus, cum dotem daret pro nepte, stipulatus est, dotem sibi vel nepti reddi soluto matrimonio. An solutionis causa adiecta est nepti, an obligationis causa, & potuitne adiici obligationis causa? Nemo alteri stipulari potest. An hoc dabitur fauori dotium, vt valeat collatio facta in neptem? Air, existimandum, neptem adiectam esse obligationis causa, & vtilem actionem dari. Fauetur dotibus, vt mulieres nubere possint. Igitur in ambiguis doti fauemus. Exemplum aliud est in l. quæsitum 17. de bon. auth. iudic. possid. species est: Certum est, mulierem dotem repetentem habere priuilegium. Sed finge: sponsa dotem dedit, nuptiis renuntiauit postea, an in repetitione dotis habebit sponsa priuilegium? vel finge: minor 12. annis, quasi vxor domum ducta est, ƺta est, & dotem dedit marito: soluitur matrimonium ante pubertatem puellæ, repetit dotem, an habebit priuilegium? Ambigitur, quoniam neutra erat vxor, neque ergo matrimonium, & nec dos. Sed certum est, datam esse dotis speciem, & hoc respectu dos est, & melius est, dicere, dotem esse, & respondere pro muliere. l. si sponsa 74. de iure dot.
units.tr: The first sentence is: in doubtful cases it is better to rule in favour of dowries; which is repeated in the law "In doubtful cases," 70, on the right of dowry. Some causes are favourable, such as the funeral expenses of the dead (law "Such persons," 43, on religious and funeral expenses) and dowries (the last law of the Code on the Senatusconsultum Velleianum). But in doubtful cases, as we rule in favour of liberty, so we rule in favour of the dowry. Let us take an example from the law "Gaius Seius," 45, on dissolved marriage. The case is this: a maternal grandfather, when he gave a dowry for his granddaughter, stipulated that the dowry be returned to him or to the granddaughter once the marriage was dissolved. Was the granddaughter added for the purpose of payment, or for the purpose of obligation, and could she be added for the purpose of obligation? No one can stipulate for another. Shall this be granted in favour of dowries, so that the transfer made in favour of the granddaughter is valid? He says it should be held that the granddaughter was added for the purpose of obligation, and that a useful action is granted. Dowries are favoured, so that women may be able to marry. Therefore in doubtful cases we favour the dowry. Another example is in the law "What is sought," 17, on the goods of the authority of possession. The case is this: it is certain that a woman who demands her dowry has a privilege. But suppose a betrothed woman gave a dowry and afterwards renounced the marriage; will the betrothed woman have a privilege in reclaiming the dowry? Or suppose a girl under twelve years old was led home as if a wife and was married, and gave a dowry to her husband: the marriage is dissolved before the girl reaches puberty, and she reclaims the dowry; will she have a privilege? It is doubtful, since neither was a wife, and therefore there is no marriage, and no dowry. But it is certain that a kind of dowry was given, and in this respect there is a dowry, and it is better to say that there is a dowry and to rule in favour of the woman. The law "If a betrothed woman," 74, on the right of dowry.

units.la: §. Non est nouum.
units.tr: §. It is not new.

units.la: Dum ait in §. 2. Non est nouum, &c. significat regulam non esse. l. non est nouum 46. de acquir. rer. dom. Itaque constitue ita regulam: Ea, quæ initio constiterunt, euanescunt, si in eum casum venerunt, à quo incipere non potuerunt. l. pro parte 11. de seruit. l. 3. §. vlt. de his quæ pro non scripti. Lexistimo 98, l. inter 83. §. sacram. 5. l. pen. & vlt. de verb. oblig. vt in iis exemplis, rem meam inutiliter stipulor, alienam recte. Finge, rem alienam stipulatus sum, recte stipulor: at ea res mea facta est ex aliqua causa, antequam stipulatio facta sit, an rescinditur stipulatio? Ita. Idem est, si stipulatus sum seruitutem ad fundum meum. Nam si acquisiero, & postea vendam partem fundi, stipulatio vitiatur: quia iam non possum seruitutem pro parte acquirere, quia seruitus non acquiritur pro parte. Sic igitur demonstratur, Ea, quæ initio constiterunt, vitiari posse. Sed vt ait ICtus hic vitiatur nonnun-quam, quam, vt in hac specie: Legatus est fundus primo & secundo, à Titio haerede instituto: postea moritur Titius, haeres existit primus Titio, ac idem est haeres & legatarius, quod fieri non potest; quid dicemus? Legatum non accrescere secundo dicemus, sed primo l. plane 34. §. inde dicitur. de leg. i. Idem in hac specie: Vnus ex dominis non potest fundo communi seruitutem acquirere: Dominus autem fundo seruitutem acquirere potest, quia iure acquisiuit Dominus fundi partem eius vendidit, & ita seruitus acquiritur, an seruitus euanescit? Minime. Nam licet seruitus non acquiratur pro parte acquisita, tamen solidum pro parte confirmatur. l. pen. §. vlt. de verb. oblig. His duobus casibus vitiatur stipulatio: vitiatur & in aliis, sed non sine controuersia. Nam singulis in casibus magnae fuerunt controuersiae, an esset admittenda illa regula, an non, dissentiuntque Icti tribus in locis. Ex quo apparet, fallacem esse regulam. Vnum exemplum est; Sciendum est, à filio f. haerede instituto patri legari posse, itemque à seruo haerede instituto, si legatur domino, legatum valere ab initio. Quid fiet, si pater vel dominus haeredes fiant, an extinguetur legatum, quod initio valuit, quia idem legatarius & haeres esse coeperit? Paulus existimat, legatum non vitiari, licet in eam causam peruenerit, à qua incipere non potuit, & imputari in Falcidiam; hoc est, pari Falcidiam. l. à filio de leg. 1. sed Marcianus censet, legatum extingui. l. si à seruo ad L. Falc. Sequitur aliud exemplum: Legatum non valet, si debitor pure legauerit creditori, quod debet pure. Valet tamen legatum, si quod debet in diem, legat pure. Finge, quod debet in diem, legauit pure; viuo testatore venit dies, & iam debet pure: an extinguitur legatum? Papinianus putat non extingui legatum. §. ex contrario Instit. de leg. Paulus secus in l. debitor 82. de legatis. 2.
units.tr: When he says in §. 2. Non est nouum, &c., he means that the rule does not hold. l. non est nouum 46. de acquir. rer. dom. So frame the rule thus: those things which were valid at the outset cease to be valid if they come to a case from which they could not have begun. l. pro parte 11. de seruit. l. 3. §. vlt. de his quæ pro non scripti. Lexistimo 98, l. inter 83. §. sacram. 5. l. pen. & vlt. de verb. oblig. As in these examples: I validly stipulate for my own thing, but ineffectually for another's. Suppose I stipulated for another's thing and I validly stipulate; but that thing has become mine for some cause before the stipulation was made. Is the stipulation rescinded? It is. The same holds if I stipulated for a servitude over my estate. For if I acquire it and afterwards sell part of the estate, the stipulation is vitiated, because I can no longer acquire the servitude in part, since a servitude is not acquired in part. Thus it is shown that things which were valid at the outset can be vitiated. But, as the jurist here says, it is vitiated only sometimes, not always, as in this instance: an estate is bequeathed to a first and a second legatee, with Titius instituted heir. Afterwards Titius dies, and the first legatee becomes heir, so that one person is both heir and legatee, which cannot happen. What shall we say? We shall say that the legacy does not accrue to the second, but lapses to the first. l. plane 34. §. inde dicitur. de leg. i. Likewise in this case: one of several co-owners cannot acquire a servitude over the common estate; yet an owner can acquire a servitude over his estate, because by right he acquired a part of it. If he then sells that part, and so the servitude is acquired, does the servitude cease to exist? Not at all. For although a servitude is not acquired in the part acquired, it is nonetheless confirmed for the whole part. l. pen. §. vlt. de verb. oblig. In these two cases the stipulation is vitiated. It is vitiated in other cases too, but not without controversy. For in each of these cases there have been great disputes whether that rule should be admitted or not, and the jurists disagree in three places. From this it appears that the rule is deceptive. One example: it must be noted that a legacy can be left to a father by a son under power, and likewise to a master by a slave instituted heir; and if it is left to the master, the legacy is valid from the beginning. What happens if the father or master becomes heir? Is the legacy, which was valid at the outset, extinguished because the same person has begun to be both legatee and heir? Paulus holds that the legacy is not vitiated, even though it has come to a state from which it could not begin, and that it is to be charged against the Falcidian portion; that is, it is to be counted toward the Falcidian share. l. à filio de leg. 1. But Marcianus holds that the legacy is extinguished. l. si à seruo ad L. Falc. There follows another example: a legacy is not valid if a debtor purely bequeaths to his creditor what he owes purely. But a legacy is valid if he bequeaths purely what he owes at a future day. Suppose he bequeathed purely what he owed at a future day; while the testator is alive the day comes, and the debt is now pure. Is the legacy extinguished? Papinian thinks the legacy is not extinguished. §. ex contrario Instit. de leg. Paulus holds otherwise in l. debitor 82. de legatis. 2.

units.la: Postremum exemplum est: vnus ex dominis fundo communi seruitutem non potest stipulari. At finge, qui erat dominus in solidum stipulatus est seruitutem fundo suo, & decessit duobus haeredibus relictis, an corrumpitur stipulatio? Ita secundum regulam, quia solus haeres vnus non posset seruitutem sibi stipulari pro parte. Denique res peruenit ad eam causam, vnde incipere non potest. Ergo secundum regulam vitiatur stipulatio. l. 2. §. ex his de verb. oblig. sed diuersa sententia probatur magis, illo loco cessare scil. regulam: Denique stipulationem non corrumpi successione duorum haeredum. Sic igitur videmus superiorem regulam vitiari.
units.tr: The last example: one of several co-owners cannot stipulate for a servitude over the common estate.
