But suppose that a man who was sole owner stipulated for a servitude over his estate, and died leaving two heirs. Is the stipulation corrupted? According to the rule, it is, because a single heir could not stipulate for a servitude to himself in part. Finally the matter has come to that cause from which it cannot begin. Therefore, according to the rule, the stipulation is vitiated. l. 2. §. ex his de verb. oblig. But the contrary opinion is more commonly approved: that the rule ceases to apply in that place, namely that a stipulation is not corrupted by the succession of two heirs. Thus we see the above rule is vitiated.

units.la: §. Quoties æquitate.
units.tr: §. Whenever by equity.

units.la: Postrema est sententia huius legis: Quoties æquitate, &c. Interdum æquitas concurrit cum æquitate, & colliduntur æquitatis rationes. Sæpe quæritur, utrum sit æquius? Duplex est æquitas, Naturalis, & Ciuilis. Confligit sæpe una cum altera. l. siserum 61. §. quod vero 5. de furtis. Species: Ego apud te deposui seruum, quem ego furem esse ignorabam, is tibi surripuit aliquid; an tibi in solidum damnum præstabo, acsi furtum ipse fecissem? an satis erit, seruum noxæ dedere? Æquum esse videtur, ut sufficiat noxæ deditio, ut ne plus damni per seruum eueniat, quam quanti est seruus. At ex contrario æquius etiam est, ut ne depositario officium suum sit damnosum, quod officium suscipit, non sui causa, sed deponentis. Itaque damnum ex asse ei præstare æquum est, quod concludit lex. Sed ad regulam nostram tale proponamus exemplum. Procurator datus est ad litem suscipiendam, & suscipit litem. Itaque dominus pro eo cauit iudicatum solui, restat, ut lis contestetur. Procurator non vult litem contestari. Actor postulat, ut cogatur ad litem contestandam, & iudicium suscipiendum. Hæc postulatio niititur æquitate edicti. At procurator allegat aduersam valetudinem, necessarium munus Reipub. nec se posse exequi mandatum. Hæc excusatio non paruam æquitatem habet. Contra quoque fieri non potest, vt actor admissa hac excusatione lædatur. l. sed etiam 12. de procurat. Itaque instat actor, & vult cogere procuratorem, vt saltem litem contestetur. Res hęc iusto decreto temperabitur. l. sed hac 13. eod. tit. allegatio illa, inquam, non est facile indulgenda, quia non potest culpa esse actoris, & non est etiam stricte, hoc est, præcise deneganda: Sed causa cognita, decreto est res temperanda iusto, hoc est, quod æquius est, & in mediocritate consistit. Sic ex regula generaliter constituendum: quoties quid fieri debet de plano & per libellum, si quo minus id fiat, remouetur ratio naturalis, opus est decreto, & non potest expediri res de plano. Cuiac. in Rec.
units.tr: The last point of this law is: Quoties æquitate, &c. Sometimes equity conflicts with equity, and the reasons of equity collide. It is often asked which is the more equitable. There are two kinds of equity, natural and civil, and they often clash with one another. l. siserum 61. §. quod vero 5. de furtis. Example: I deposited with you a slave whom I did not know to be a thief, and he has stolen something from you. Shall I make good the whole loss to you, as if he had committed the theft himself, or will it be enough to surrender the slave by way of noxal surrender? It seems fair that surrender for noxal liability should suffice, so that the loss caused by the slave does not exceed the slave's value. On the other hand, it is also more equitable that the depositary's office should not be harmful to him, since he undertakes that office not for his own sake but for the depositor's. Therefore it is fair that he should make good the full loss, as the law concludes. But let us put such an example to our rule. A procurator has been appointed to undertake a lawsuit, and he undertakes it. Accordingly his principal has given security for payment of the judgment; it remains only for the suit to be joined. The procurator does not want the suit joined. The plaintiff asks that he be compelled to join the suit and undertake the trial. This demand rests on the equity of the edict. But the procurator pleads ill health, a necessary public duty, and that he cannot carry out the mandate. This excuse has no small equity. Nor can it be that the plaintiff is harmed by admitting this excuse. l. sed etiam 12. de procurat. So the plaintiff presses, and wants to compel the procurator at least to join the suit. This matter will be moderated by a just decree. l. sed hac 13. eod. tit. That plea, I say, is not to be readily indulged, because it cannot be the plaintiff's fault; yet it is not to be strictly, that is, absolutely, refused. But, the cause being examined, the matter is to be moderated by a just decree, that is, by what is more equitable and lies in the middle. Thus the rule must be laid down generally: whenever something ought to be done at once and by a written petition, if it is not done, the natural reason is set aside, a decree is needed, and the matter cannot be settled at once. Cuiac. in Rec.

units.la: Ad Leg.86.De litis contestatione.
units.tr: On Law 86, On joinder of issue.

units.la: NOn solet deterior conditio fieri eorum, qui litem contestati sunt, quam si non, sed plerunque melior.
units.tr: It is not usual for the condition of those who have joined issue to become worse than it would have been had they not done so; rather, it generally becomes better.

units.la: Litem ]v. l. 58. sup. de verb. oblig. adde Hotm. 3. obs. 28.
units.tr: Litem: see l. 58 sup. de verb. oblig.; add Hotman, 3 obs. 28.

units.la: Quam si non ]non essent. vulgat. Hal.
units.tr: Quam si non: the Vulgate reading is "non essent", Hal.

units.la: Ad Leg.87.
units.tr: On Law 87.

units.la: NEmo enim in persequendo deteriorem causam, sed meliorem facit, denique post litem contestatam haeredi quoque prospiceretur, & haeres tenetur ex omnibus causis.
units.tr: For no one, in pursuing his case, makes it worse but better. Finally, after issue is joined, provision is also made for the heir, and the heir is bound by all the causes [of action].

units.la: Primum ait, deteriorem non fieri causam nostram litis contestatione: quia lite contestata, usurae non desinunt currere. leg. 35. de usur. quamuis desinant, novatione facta. Sic etiam lite contestata idem privilegium locum habet. l. aliam causam 29. de novation. Imo litis contestatio actionem nostram facit meliorem: primum actionem nostram prorogat, ut actionem annuam in annos triginta d. leg. aliam & l. ult. de fideiuss. tut. l. nam posteaquam 9. §. sis 3. de iureiur. & triennalem actionem prorogat in annos quadraginta. l. cum C. de praescript. 30. vel 40. annor. similiter litis contestatio facit, ut actio haeredi nostro competat, quae non competeret alias; ut iniuriarum actio, quae non datur, nisi cum defuncto lis contestata fuerit. Similiter in haeredem datur actio lite contestata, quae non contestata non daretur in haeredem rei, ut actiones poenales non dantur in haeredem, nisi post litem contestatam: sic non datur in patrem, nisi lite contestata. l. 58. h. tit. hoc est, quod ostendit l. poenalia 164. inf. quae actio proprie pertinet ad actionem in duplum, qua tenetur qui sciens pro seruo veniit, & non datur in hæredem, nisi post litem contestatam, & est pœnalis. l. vtique 21. & l. seq. §. vlt. de liberali causa. Litis contestatio facit, vt actiones, quæ tempore & morte pereunt, in hæredem transmittantur. Denique per litis contestationem non fit nostra conditio deterior, sed plerunque melior. Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: First, he says that our case is not made worse by joinder of issue, because once issue is joined, interest does not cease to run, leg. 35. de usur. although it does cease when novation has been made. So too, once issue is joined, the same privilege applies, l. aliam causam 29. de novation. Indeed, joinder of issue makes our action better. First, it extends our action: an annual action is extended to thirty years, d. leg. aliam & l. ult. de fideiuss. tut. l. nam posteaquam 9. §. sis 3. de iureiur. and a triennial action is extended to forty years. l. cum C. de praescript. 30. vel 40. annor. Likewise, joinder of issue ensures that an action passes to our heir, which would not otherwise pass to him; for example, the action for injury, which is not given unless issue was joined with the deceased. l. 58. h. tit. Similarly, an action is given against the heir of a defendant once issue is joined, which would not be given against the heir if issue had not been joined; just as penal actions are not given against an heir except after joinder of issue, so too an action is not given against a father except after joinder of issue. l. 58. h. tit. This is what l. poenalia 164. inf. shows, which properly relates to the action for double damages, by which he who knowingly sold a slave for a free man is bound, and which is not given against the heir unless issue has been joined, and which is penal. l. vtique 21. & l. seq. §. vlt. de liberali causa. Joinder of issue causes actions that perish with time and death to pass on to the heir. Finally, by joinder of issue our condition is not made worse, but generally better. Cuiac. in Recit.

units.la: Ad Leg. 88. De mora.
units.tr: On Law 88, On delay.

units.la: NULla intelligitur mora ibi fieri, vbi nulla petitio est.
units.tr: No delay is understood to occur where there is no demand.

units.la: multo minus pœna, quia non debetur pœna sine mora. Goth.
units.tr: much less a penalty, because no penalty is due without delay. Goth.

units.la: Petitio, hoc est, actio: & recte Accursius l. si pupillus 127. de verb. oblig. ex qua hæc regula est repetita. Sententia eius est: Pupillus stipulanti promisit hominem certum sine tutoris authoritate, & fideiussorem dedit, fideiussor obligatur & naturaliter & civiliter, pupillus autem naturaliter tantum. Ex ea obligatione nulla est actio ante rescriptum D. Pii: Sed an tenebitur fideiussor? Sane mora rei solet nocere fideiussori l. mora 88. eod. Sed pupillus non videvidetur moram fecisse. Nam non intelligitur ibi mora fieri, vbi nulla est actio. Itaque si ille homo moriatur ante moram fideiussoris fideiussor liberabitur, nec dici potest mora pupilli, qui non facit moram: non facit quoque moram, qui tenetur actione, sed habet exceptionem l. sciendum 21. de vsuris l. lecta 40. de reb. cred. Opponit Accurs. l. 5. C. de contrahend. stipul. Hæc lex ostendit, eum, qui pactus est, moram facere: ex pacto autem non est actio, & actione non existente aduersus eum, qui stipulatus est, fit mora. Hic respondet Ioh. ex pacto non esse actionem, nisi velit is, qui pactus est. Ergo actio est in volentem & patientem, quod si nolit pati, committitur pœna: at pupillus nec velle, nec pati creditur. Ergo in hac specie incidit in pœnam, qui pactis non paret, quasi mora facta, cum possit parere pacto. Rursus opponitur lex, si ita stipulatus de verb. oblig. Vbi ita proponitur concepta stipulatio: Stichum dabis; si non dederis, decem dabis. Lex ait; moram fieri in non præstando Sticho: sed dicendum, peti potuisse. Mora autem facta, statim desiit Stichus peti posse: quoniam obligatio Stichi transfusa est in obligationem pecuniæ. Cuiac. eod.
units.tr: A demand, that is, an action; and Accursius rightly so, in l. si pupillus 127. de verb. oblig. from which this rule has been repeated. His view is this: a pupil, without the authority of his guardian, promised a certain slave to the one stipulating, and gave a surety; the surety is bound both naturally and civilly, but the pupil only naturally. From that obligation there is no action before the rescript of the divine Pius. But will the surety be bound? Certainly the delay of the principal usually harms the surety, l. mora 88. eod. but the pupil does not seem to have caused delay, for delay is not understood to occur where there is no action. So if that slave dies before the surety's delay, the surety will be released, and it cannot be said that the pupil is in delay, since he does not cause delay; nor does he who is bound by an action but has an exception cause delay. l. sciendum 21. de vsuris l. lecta 40. de reb. cred. Accursius objects, l. 5. C. de contrahend. stipul. This law shows that the one who made the agreement causes delay; but from an agreement there is no action, and when there is no action against the one who stipulated, delay arises. Here Johannes replies that there is no action from an agreement unless he who made the agreement wishes it. So there is an action against one who is willing and submits, and if he is unwilling to submit, a penalty is incurred; but a pupil is believed neither to wish nor to submit. Therefore in this case he who does not obey the agreement incurs the penalty, as if delay had been caused, since he could obey the agreement. Again, the law is objected, si ita stipulatus de verb. oblig. where a stipulation is proposed in this form: "You shall give Stichus; if you do not give him, you shall give ten." The law says that delay arises from not delivering Stichus; but it should be said that he could have been demanded. Yet once delay has arisen, Stichus at once ceases to be demandable, since the obligation to Stichus has been transferred into an obligation to money. Cuiac. eod.

units.la: Ad Leg.89. De successione ex testamento vel ab intestato.
units.tr: On Law 89: On succession by will or on intestacy.

units.la: QVamdiu possit valere testamentum, tamdiu legitimus non admittitur.
units.tr: As long as a will can be valid, a legitimate heir is not admitted.

units.la: Aperta est sententia huius legis, & proponitur l. quam diu 3. l. quam diu 69. leg. illud. 77. de acquir. hæred. l. antequam 8. C. communia de succeff. & ei locus est in tutela. l. si quis sub conditione 11. de testam. tut. Cuiac. in Recitat.
units.tr: The meaning of this law is plain, and it is set out in the laws "quamdiu" (3), "quamdiu" (69), the law "illud" (77) on the acquisition of heirs, the law "antequam" (8) in the Code, "communia de successionibus", and it applies in the case of guardianship: the law "si quis sub conditione" (11) on testamentary guardians. Cujacius, in his Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg.90. De æquitate.
units.tr: On Law 90: On equity.

units.la: IN omnibus quidem, maxime tamen in iure, æquitas spectanda est.
units.tr: In all things, but especially in law, equity is to be regarded.

units.la: Ius strictum est vel ipsa lege scriptum. l.12. sup. qui & a quib. vel ex ipsa lege subtiliter inducta interpretatio. l. 32. in sin. sup. de reb. cred. vt saepius, non est scripta aequitas. leg 14. sup. de diuersis. Sed pro ratione circumstantiarum facto accommodatur: ideoque quae legibus omissa sunt, supplere solent. l. 13. sup. de testib. est igitur aequitas legis scriptae, aequamentum ad utilitatem hominum reductum, vel non scriptae supplementum. Goth.
units.tr: Strict law is either that which is written in the law itself, l. 12 sup. qui & a quib., or an interpretation drawn subtly from the law itself, l. 32 in fin. sup. de reb. cred., as often happens. Equity is not written: leg. 14 sup. de diversis. But it is applied according to the circumstances of the case, and so it is accustomed to supply what the laws have omitted: l. 13 sup. de testib. Equity is therefore either the equity of written law, an equalising brought back to the usefulness of men, or the supplement of unwritten law. Gothofredus.

units.la: Aequitas] 2. Eclog. 3. c. 87. haec est ars boni & aequi l. 1. sup. de Iustit. qua nihil gratius Iureconsulto. l. 57. C. de Episcop. sub cuius tamen authoritate saepissime erratur. l. 91. §. 3. sup. de verb. oblig. Gothofr.
units.tr: Equity] 2 Eclog. 3 c. 87. This is the art of the good and the fair, l. 1 sup. de Iustit., than which nothing is more pleasing to a jurist, l. 57 C. de Episcop., though under its authority very often error is made. l. 91 §. 3 sup. de verb. oblig. Gothofredus.

units.la: Aequitas spectatur potius, quam ius commune & summum. Ait lex: In omnibus: vt in l. placuit 8. C. de Iudiciis. In omnibus, vt in testamentis, iudiciis, contractibus, & pactis. Male Accurs. in iure, hoc est in lege: leges non oportet calumniari, l. pen. ad exhib. Calumniatur leges, qui verba sequitur & literas, reiicit autem aequitatem, vt ait l. scire 17. de legib. vis legum posita est in aequitate, mente & consilio scriptoris. Vetatur calumnia, vetatur fraus legum. Verum si absit calumnia & fraus, sane scriptum sequi debemus. l. prospexit, 12. qui & a quib. manumissi. Sic etiam sequimur testamenti scripturam in l. 16. de condit. & demonst. quae lex ait eleganter, in controversiis, quae pendent ex testamento, sequi nos debere ius scriptum & strictum. Caeterum in iis, quæ sunt citra scripturam testamenti, tum ex æquo & bono interpretationem facimus, cum absit calumnia & fraus. Alias sequimur scriptum, & solius Principis est, duram legem mollire interpretatione. l. 9. C. de legibus. sicut duritiem legis Iuliæ tandem moderati sunt Imperatores. l. quamvis adulterij 30. C. ad L. Iul. de adult. Cuiac. in Recitat.
units.tr: Equity is to be regarded rather than the common and strict law. The law says: In all things, as in l. placuit 8 C. de Iudiciis. In all things, as in wills, judgments, contracts and agreements. Accursius is wrong to read in iure as meaning in lege, "in the law itself": laws ought not to be chicaned, l. pen. ad exhib. He chicanes the laws who follows their words and letters and rejects their equity, as l. scire 17 de legib. says. The force of the laws lies in equity, in the mind and intention of the writer. Chicanery is forbidden, and fraud against the laws is forbidden. But if chicanery and fraud are absent, we must certainly follow what is written: l. prospexit 12 qui & a quib. manumissi. So too we follow the wording of a will, in l. 16 de condit. & demonst., which law elegantly says that in controversies that depend on a will we ought to follow the written and strict law. Otherwise, in matters that lie outside the wording of the will, we interpret according to what is fair and good, when chicanery and fraud are absent. In other cases we follow what is written, and it belongs only to the Prince to soften a harsh law by interpretation, l. 9 C. de legibus, just as the emperors at last moderated the harshness of the Julian law, l. quamvis adulterii 30 C. ad L. Iul. de adult. Cuiacius in Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg. 91. De successione.
units.tr: On Law 91: On succession.

units.la: QVoties duplici iure defertur alicui successio, repudiato novo iure, quod ante defertur, supererit vetus.
units.tr: Whenever a succession is deferred to someone under a double right, and the new right is renounced, the old right, which was deferred earlier, remains.

units.la: Duplici] puta querela inofficiosi (quæ ex iure veteri, secundum Viglium & Cuiacium) & bonorum possessione, unde Legitimi. v. Cuiac. 8. obs. 33. adde l. 17. §. 1. sup. de acquir. hared. l. 1. §. 11. sup. de successorio. l. 2. sup. unde legitimi. Gothof.
units.tr: Double] for example, the complaint of an undutiful will (which under the old law) according to Viglius and Cuiacius, and the possession of goods, whence the legitimate heirs. See Cuiacius 8 obs. 33; add l. 17 §. 1 sup. de acquir. hared.; l. 1 §. 11 sup. de successorio; l. 2 sup. unde legitimi. Gothofredus.

units.la: Defertur. Vel eodem tempore, vel successive. vide Decium hic.
units.tr: Is deferred. Either at the same time or successively. See Decius here.

units.la: Alicui puta parenti Cuiac. ibid.
units.tr: To someone, for example, to a parent. Cuiacius ibid.

units.la: Repudiato novo ac particulari, scil. alias semel repudiata successione, omnibus eius viribus renunciatum videtur, arg. L. 13. §. 2. § 3. sup. de iniur. l. 7. supr. de accept. Sed novi iuris vocabulo hic intelligi satius est, novas causas succedendi. l.17. §.1. sup. de acquirenda haredit. Go-thofr.
units.tr: The new right being renounced, that is, when an inheritance has once been renounced, it is taken to be renounced in all its rights, arg. l. 13 §. 2 §. 3 sup. de iniur.; l. 7 sup. de accept. But it is better to understand here "new right" as new grounds of succession, l. 17 §. 1 sup. de acquirenda haredit. Gothofredus.

units.la: Supererit] Quando vni competunt plura iura, variis temporibus praesertim, & variis de causis: vno repudiato alterum superest. vt hic & l.21. s de seruit. urb. praed. & l.17. s de aquae pluv. imo non superest. l.77. sup. eod. l.17. §.1. l.77. sup. de acquir. hared. solue: Nō superest, si repudiata ipsa sit hæreditas, causa non adiecta, vel si repudiatur vnum, ex quo aliud necessario dependet. v. notata Gothof. ad l.77.
units.tr: It remains] When several rights belong to one person, especially at different times and on different grounds, when one is renounced the other remains: as here, and in l. 21 sup. de servit. urb. praed. and l. 17 sup. de aquae pluv. Indeed it sometimes does not remain: l. 77 sup. eod.; l. 17 §. 1, l. 77 sup. de acquir. hared. The solution: it does not remain if the inheritance itself is renounced without any cause being added, or if one thing is renounced on which another necessarily depends. See the notes of Gothofredus on l. 77.

units.la: Male Bulgarus, Ioan. & Accurs. exemplum ponunt in suis hæredibus, vel agnatis siue legitimis, quibus successio defertur ab intestato, iure ciuili & Praetorio, delata possessione, unde Legitimi: quod est ius nouum: quo repudiato, non prohibentur iure ciuili hæreditatem adire. Fallacia est in eo sita, quod utroque iure nouo & veteri, nullo seruato ordine, defertur successio suis & agnatis, iure ciuili & praetorio. At regula desiderat exemplum, quo successio deferatur simul, non sine ordine, sed iure nouo & veteri. Cum igitur animaduerterent, non valere exemplum: modo interpretantur, quod ante defertur, hoc est, quod deferebatur, iure nouo nondum introducto, quod falsum est. Nam apparet, ius nouum deferre, antequam ius vetus, & superato iure nouo, superesse ius vetus; nam fit comparatio iuris veteris cum nouo. Sed in illo exemplo non perstant, & ita faciunt: Testamento hæres scriptus est, qui ab intestato hæres futurus erat ; repudiato testamento, potest legitimam hæreditatem amplecti, verum tenebitur edicto, Si quis omissa causa testamenti: & inquiunt, si ius testamenti est novum, ius intestati est vetus: & testamenti ius novum defertur prius quam vetus. In quo exemplo duo sunt vitia. Nam intestati ius non est vetustius iure testamenti : utrumq; ius est 12. tabularum. Regula loquitur de eo, cui successio defertur duplici iure. Non autem defertur duplici iure, si legitimus hæres testamento scribatur hæres, quoniam, quamdiu adiri potest hæreditas ex testamento, non aditur ab intestato: sed repudiatur prius testamentum, quam deferatur ab intestato. Regula quærit exemplum ; quo simul duplici iure quæratur successio, seruato tamen ordine. Duo exempla referam. Primum erit de patre testamento filii prætereito, quem pater emancipauerat, cui prætereito datur querela testamenti inofficiosi. Ideo pater, qui acturus est querela, debet agnoscere bonorum possessionem, unde legitimi, ordinandæ litis causa: quoniam facto filio intestato, amplectitur hæreditatem ex bonorum possessione, unde legitimi. Ergo patri datur querela. l. pater. 14. de inof. testam. l. 1. §. vlt. si à patre quis manumiss. Ergo patri prætereito iure duplici post mortem filii defertur hæreditas, id est, ex possessione contra tab. tum ex edicto, unde legitimi: quam potest agnoscere, querelæ & liti de inofficioso testamento ordinandæ gratiâ. Querela est ius antiquum: bonorum possessio contra tabulas est ius nouum. Sed hoc ius nouum defertur prius, quam querela, quæ bonorum possessioni, unde legitimi, locum facit. Ergo repudiato hoc iure, quod ante defertur, superest ius vetus, hoc est, querela siue bonorum possessio, quæ quidem post defertur. Alterum exemplum est ex SCto Officiano & Tertulliano, quæ sunt iura noua. l. tutelas 7 de capite minut. Ex iis Senatusconsultis defertur hæreditas matri & cognatis, & defertur vt legitimis. Ideo datur bonorum possessio, unde legitimi. l 2. §. vlt. unde legitimi. Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: Bulgarus, John and Accursius wrongly give as an example heirs under the will, or agnates or legitimate heirs, to whom succession is deferred on intestacy by civil and praetorian law, possession being deferred, whence the legitimate heirs; this is the new law, and once it is renounced they are not prevented by civil law from taking up the inheritance. Their fallacy lies in this: under both the new and the old law, without any order being kept, succession is deferred to heirs of the body and to agnates, by civil and praetorian law. But the rule requires an example in which succession is deferred at the same time, not without order, but under the new and the old law. Since they noticed that their example would not do, they now interpret "which is deferred earlier" to mean "which was deferred before the new law was introduced", which is false. For it is clear that the new law is deferred before the old, and when the new law is set aside the old remains; for a comparison is made between the old law and the new. But they do not stick to that example, and they do as follows: a man is written as heir under a will, though he would have been heir on intestacy. When the will is renounced he may embrace the legitimate inheritance, but he will be bound by the edict Si quis omissa causa testamenti; and they say that if the right under the will is new, the right on intestacy is old, and the right under the will is deferred before the old. In this example there are two faults. For the right on intestacy is not older than the right under the will: both rights come from the Twelve Tables. The rule speaks of a person to whom succession is deferred under a double right. But succession is not deferred under a double right if a legitimate heir is written as heir under a will, since, as long as the inheritance can be taken up under the will, it is not taken up on intestacy; rather the will is renounced before the inheritance is deferred on intestacy. The rule seeks an example in which succession is claimed under a double right at the same time, yet with order kept. I will give two examples. The first will be that of a father, whose son, whom he had emancipated, was passed over in his will; the passed-over son is given the complaint of an undutiful will. So the father, who is going to bring the complaint, must acknowledge the possession of goods, whence the legitimate heirs, for the sake of ordering the suit, since, when the son has died intestate, he takes up the inheritance under the possession of goods, whence the legitimate heirs. Therefore the father is given the complaint: l. pater 14 de inof. testam.; l. 1 §. vlt. si a patre quis manumiss. Therefore, to the father who was passed over, after the son's death, the inheritance is deferred under a double right, that is, by the possession against the tablets and by the edict, whence the legitimate heirs; he may acknowledge this for the sake of ordering the complaint and the suit on the undutiful will. The complaint is the old right; the possession of goods against the tablets is the new right. But this new right is deferred before the complaint, which gives place to the possession of goods, whence the legitimate heirs. Therefore, when this right, which is deferred earlier, is renounced, the old right remains, that is, the complaint or the possession of goods, which is indeed deferred afterwards. The second example is from the Senatusconsult Officianum and the Tertullianum, which are new rights: l. tutelas 7 de capite minut. By these senatusconsults the inheritance is deferred to the mother and to cognates, and it is deferred as to legitimate heirs. Therefore the possession of goods, whence the legitimate heirs, is given: l. 2 §. vlt. unde legitimi. Cuiacius in Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg. 92. De errore librarii in transcribendo.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 92. On an error of the copyist in transcribing.

units.la: SI librarius in transcribendis stipulationis verbis errasset, nihil nocere, quominus & reus & fideiussor tenerentur.
units.tr: IF a copyist had erred in transcribing the words of a stipulation, this would not prevent both the debtor and the surety from being bound.

units.la: Si forte ex l. 54. de manumiss. testament. nam hic erratum esse videtur.
units.tr: If perhaps (it is taken) from law 54, de manumissis testamento, for here the error seems to lie.

units.la: Librarius] l. 15. §. 1. sup de vsufr. l. 15. §. 5. sup. de excusation. tut. l. 7, §. 5. sup. de oper. libert. Horat. de arte. arte. 2. Et scriptor si peccat, idem librarius, vsq;. Quamuis est monitus venia carer. Librarios Graeci χαρτιγράφος: notarios ταχυγράφος, ὀξυγράφος. Hi notas, illi literas: vt tabularii rationum supputationem tractabant. Gothofr.
units.tr: Copyist: law 15, §1, supra de usufructu; law 15, §5, supra de excusationibus tutorum; law 7, §5, supra de operis libertorum; Horace, De arte (the Art of Poetry). "And if the writer errs, so does the copyist, usque... though he has been warned, he deserves no pardon." The Greeks called copyists chartigraphos [χαρτιγράφος], and notaries tachygraphos [ταχυγράφος] and oxygraphos [ὀξυγράφος]. The latter wrote shorthand notes, the former full letters, just as the clerks of accounts handled the reckoning. Gothofredus.

units.la: Stipulationis ] instrumenti, l.8.sup. de statul. testamenti.v.l.7.C.de tesṫ. precium. v.l.2.C.de errore aduoc. contractus. l.1.C. plus valere quod agitur.
units.tr: Of the stipulation: of the instrument; law 8, supra de statuliberis; see law 7, C. de testamentis, the price; see law 2, C. de errore advocatorum, the contract; law 1, C. plus valere quod agitur.

units.la: Errasset ] citra dolum & falsum, idque in sermone, veluti si scripserit, relictum iure restitutionis pro institutionis: mulierem renunciasse Valeriano pro Velleiano. Titium substitutum procuratorem, pro institutum. In his notarius commissum errorem corrigere potest, cum talis emendatio neminem laedat. Addit Bartolus, ei permissum, indictionem & diem omissum adiicere; nisi dies esset de substantia instrumenti, vt in hypotheca. Si diem permutauit, talem errorem corrigere non potest, nisi de errore testibus constet. Si instrumentum parti traditum est, requiritur sententia Iudicis in errore mutando. Error probari potest authentico, testibus, & partium confessione. v. Decium hic, Gothof. Error librarii non vitiat stipulationem. Librarii, hoc est, scriptoris, tabellionis. Error etiam scriptoris eadem ratione non vitiat testamentum. l.errore 7. C. de testament. non vitiat preces. l.2. Cod.de error. aduoc.
units.tr: Had erred: without fraud or falsehood, and this in the wording, as when someone writes relictum iure restitutionis for institutionis, or mulierem renunciasse Valeriano for Velleiano, or Titium substitutum procuratorem for institutum. In such cases the notary may correct the error committed, since such an emendation harms no one. Bartolus adds that he is also permitted to add an omitted indiction or day; unless the day belongs to the substance of the instrument, as in a mortgage. If he has changed the day, he cannot correct such an error unless the error is attested by witnesses. If the instrument has been handed over to a party, a sentence of the judge is required before the error can be altered. The error may be proved by an authentic document, by witnesses, and by the admission of the parties. See Decius here; Gothofredus. An error of the copyist does not vitiate a stipulation. "Copyist" means a writer or notary. For the same reason an error of the writer does not vitiate a will: law 7, C. de testamentis, "errore". It does not vitiate a petition: law 2, C. de errore advocatorum.

units.la: Summa tituli est: Error aduocati non nocet litigatori absenti, præsenti nocet. Error quoque eius, qui libellum conscripsit, litigatori non nocet, non lædit statum personarum. l. Imperator 8. de stat. hom. Generaliter, in iudiciis veritas rerum erroribus actorum non vitiatur. l. illicitas. 6. §. veritas. 1. de offic. præsid. Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: The sum of the title is this: the advocate's error does not harm an absent litigant, but harms one who is present. The error of the person who drew up the libel likewise does not harm the litigant, since it does not injure the status of persons: law Imperator 8, de statu hominum. In general, in trials the truth of matters is not vitiated by errors of the acts: law Illicitas 6, §veritas, 1, de officio praesidis; Cuiacius, in Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg. 93. De possessione rei pe- culiaris.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 93. On possession of a peculiar thing.

units.la: FIliusfam. neque retinere, neque recuperare, neq; adipisci possessionem rei peculiaris videtur.
units.tr: A son under power seems neither to retain, nor to recover, nor to acquire possession of a peculiar thing.

units.la: Filiusfam. ] Coniunge l. 18. de castrensi peculio.
units.tr: A son under power: join law 18, de castrensi peculio.

units.la: Neque ] id est, filiosfam. interdicta ad retinendam, recuperandam, adipiscendam possessionem non competunt.
units.tr: Neither: that is, the interdicts for retaining, recovering and acquiring possession do not lie for a son under power.

units.la: Videtur ] Nam interdicta dantur pro possessione: filius autem quicquid apprehendit, peculiari nomine, statim pater eius possidet. l. 4. sup. de acquir. possess.
units.tr: Seems: for interdicts are granted on account of possession; but whatever a son takes hold of in the name of his peculium, his father at once possesses. Law 4, supra de acquirenda possessione.

units.la: Tria sunt genera: adipiscendæ, retinendæ, & recuperandæ possessionis, quæ filiusfam. habet ignorans, si cum sit eiectus de possessione fundi peculiaris, & ignorauerit parens, videtur ei nihilominus quæsitum ius, unde vi, l. 1. §. quod seruus. 22. de vi & vi arm. Nam patri ignoranti acquiritur per filium possessio. L. Labeo. 8. de usucap. fucap. Sic filiusf. non potest vsucapere, sed parer potest per filium. l. 4. §. 1. de vsucap. Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: There are three kinds of possession: that of acquiring, retaining and recovering, which a son under power holds without knowing it. If he has been ejected from possession of a peculiar farm, and his parent does not know, the right arising from the interdict unde vi is nonetheless held to have been acquired for the parent. Law 1, §quod servus, D. de vi et vi armata. For possession is acquired through a son for a father who is ignorant of it: law Labeo 8, de usucapionibus. So a son under power cannot usucapt, but the parent can through the son: law 4, §1, de usucapionibus. Cuiacius, in Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg 94. De his quæ abundant.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 94. On those things which are superfluous.

units.la: NOn solent quæ abundant vitiare scriptu- ras.
units.tr: Superfluous matters do not usually vitiate writings.

units.la: Abundant] l.65. sup. de verb. oblig. l.32. §.6. sup. de auro. adde leg. 81. sup. eod. & cap. vtile per inutile. 36. de reg. in 6. l.20. supr. de vsur. l.34. supr. de hæred. instit. l.34. supr. de manumiss. testamento. l. 17. C. de testam. l.34. C. de donat. August. 4. de ciuitate 27. Solet enim à viris peritis dici, superfiua non nocent. Gothof. Vulgo dici solet, falsa demonstratio non vitiat legatum: vt si in legato dixero: seruum vernam Stichum : etiamsi non sit verna sed pretio comparatus, hoc non vitiat legatū. v. l.1. §. si quis uxori 8. de dote pralegata. quæ inquit: Quod rei satis demonstratæ adiicitur, frustra est. Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: Superfluous: law 65, supra de verborum obligationibus; law 32, §6, supra de auro et argento legato; add law 81, supra eodem; and the chapter "utile per inutile", De regulis iuris in 6; law 20, supra de usuris; law 34, supra de haeredibus instituendis; law 34, supra de manumissis testamento; law 17, C. de testamentis; law 34, C. de donationibus; Augustine, De civitate Dei, book 27 (?). For it is commonly said by skilled men that superfluous things do no harm. Gothofredus. It is commonly said that a false demonstration does not vitiate a legacy: for example, if in a legacy I say "my slave Stichus, the home-born", even if he is not home-born but bought for a price, this does not vitiate the legacy. See law 1, §si quis uxori, 8, de dote praelegata, which says: what is added to a thing sufficiently described is idle. Cuiacius, in Recitationes.

units.la: A- d Leg. 95. De eo qui defenditur.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 95. On the one who is defended.

units.la: NEmo dubitat, soluendo videri eum, qui defenditur.
units.tr: No one doubts that he is seen to be solvent who is defended.

units.la: Defenditur] qui fideiussores habet. l. 1. sup. qui satisd. l. 53. sup. de procurat. l. 27. §. 2. supr. de fideiuss. l. 1. sup. de custod. reor. leg. 6. §. 1. sup. de munerib. & ita quis soluendo est per alium. Soluendo est etiam, qui solidum potest soluere v.
units.tr: Defended: that is, who has sureties. Law 1, supra qui satisdare cogantur; law 53, supra de procuratoribus; law 27, §2, supra de fideiussoribus; law 1, supra de custodia reorum; law 6, §1, supra de muneribus. And thus one is solvent through another. He is also solvent who can pay the whole amount.

units.la: {a}l. 114. sup. de verb. signif. qui tei peritæ instar, ab actore, potest consequi l. 28. sup. soluto: non is, cuius bona venduntur. l. 55. in sin. sup. de admin. tut. Goth. Huius regulæ effectus est: Fideicommissi vel crediti causa non distrahi bona eius, qui defenditur vel per se, vel per alium. Vnde titulus, Ex quibus causis, in possess. eatur. Et tit. de rebus authorit. iudic. possid. Cuiac. in Recitat.
units.tr: Law 114, supra de verborum significatione, who by the standard of a skilled man can obtain from the plaintiff; law 28, supra soluto; not he whose goods are being sold. Law 55, at the end, supra de administratione tutorum. Gothofredus. The effect of this rule is that the goods of one who is defended, whether personally or through another, are not sold for the sake of a trust or a debt. Hence the title Ex quibus causis in possessionem eatur, and the title de rebus auctoritate iudicis possidendis. Cuiacius, in Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg 96. De ambiguis orationibus.
units.tr: On Law 96, On Ambiguous Expressions

units.la: IN ambiguis orationibus maxime sententia spectanda est eius, qui protulisset.
units.tr: In ambiguous expressions the intention of the one who uttered them is above all to be considered.

units.la: Sententia ] adde l. 219. sup. de verb. signif.
units.tr: Intention] add law 219 above, On the Meaning of Words.

units.la: Eius ] 2. Eclog. 3. c. 94. adde cap. intelligentia 6. ext. de verb. sign. puta principis legem ferentis. l. vlt. C. de legib. populi aliquid statuentis. l. 46. sup. de re indic. l. 4. §. 1. sup. de acceptilationibus. Prætoris. l. 9. sup. de præt. stipul. testatoris. l. 69. sup. de leg. 3. stipulatoris. l. 94. sup. de verb. oblig. at non venditoris & locatoris. l. 39. sup. de pact. l. 21. l. 33. in sin. l. 134. supr. de contrahenda empt. Gothofr.
units.tr: Of the one] 2 Eclog. 3, c. 94. Add chapter "intelligentia" 6 ext. de verb. sign., as with a prince enacting a law; the last law C. de legib.; of the people establishing something, law 46 sup. de re indic.; law 4 §1 sup. de acceptilationibus; of the praetor, law 9 sup. de praet. stipul.; of the testator, law 69 sup. de leg. 3; of the stipulator, law 94 sup. de verb. oblig.; but not of the seller and the lessor, law 39 sup. de pact.; law 21, law 33 in sin., law 134 supr. de contrahenda empt. Gothofredus.

units.la: Huius regulæ est frequens vsus in materia testamentorum. l. ex facto, 19. de hæred. instit. & est ex libris fideicommissorum. Exemplum est in l. Sempronius 26. de vsu, & vsufr. legato. Sciendum est, Vsumfructum finiri morte vsufructuarii, finitum ita reuerti ad proprietarium. Species est: Testator ab hærede per fideicommissum reliquit fundum Titio post decennium, deducto vsufructu. Ergo ex die reliquit vsumfructum. Fideicommissi dies cedit statim, licet non petatur ante decennium, neque peti possit. Igitur statim debetur fideicommissum, Ideo si fideicommissarius moriatur ante decennium, transmittit fideicommissum in hæredem suum. At finge, Fideicommissarius non est mortuus intra decennium, sed hæres: quæritur, post decennium an hæredis hæres cogatur præstare Titio plenum fundum, an vero possit deducere vsumfructum? Res ambigua est, & dubius videtur esse sermo. Et videtur 1. plenum fundum præstandum esse ab hærede hæredis non deducto vsufructu. Nam hæres primus iam debere id ceperat; dies enim cesserat. Ergo morte primi hæredis finitur vsusfructus. Quod si ita est, ab hærede hæredis non detrahitur vsusfructus: sed plenus fructus solidaque proprietas est præstanda. Contra, non videtur finitus vsusfructus morte hæredis, quia nondum fuit. Nec enim ante est vsusfructus, quam fundum præstiterit, eo deducto, cum retineat semper pleno iure; quia dies nondum venerat. Non potes ergo dicere, finitum vsumfructum morte hæredis: imo dicemus, vsumfructum incipere ab hærede hæredis, & ab eo quoque finiri: ab hærede primo non incepisse. Ergo haeres haeredis non praestabit plenum fundum, sed deducet vsumfructum. Idem dicemus, si sub conditione legatus aut relictus est fundus. Nam, si pendente conditione moriatur haeres, & postea exiltat condicio, haeres haeredis deducet vsumfructum; non tamen finitus videtur in persona primi haeredis. Est igitur quaestio nostra; vtra opinio sit verior? Lex ait, has subtilitates esse praetermittendas; sed sententia testatoris quae fuerit, videndum est. Sententia testatoris inducit priorem opinionem, quae sententia mens vera est. Nam voluit detrahi vsumfructum, qui cohaeret personae haeredis sui: legauit igitur fundum deducto vsufructu, & finitum eum voluit redire ad fideicommissarium: si haeres vsumfructum habere coepisset, in haeredem suum non transmisisset. Ergo etiamsi nondum habere coepit, ideoque haeres haeredis plenum fundum praestabit. Sic igitur in testamentis maxime spectanda testatoris mens: non ita in contractibus, vt apparet ex l.inter 33. de auro & arg. l. & l. si mihi & Titio 110. §. vlt. de verborum oblig. Multum itaque distant contractus a testamentis; distant etiam contractus a iudiciis vel actionibus. Nam in iudiciis spectamus, quid actor senserit. l. inter 83. §. 1. de verb. oblig. Contractus constant ex consensu duorum, actio est vnius. l.continuus 137. §. 1. eod. In contractibus, si ambigua sit contrahentis oratio, sequimur quod vtilius est promissori, &c. exempla sunt in l. Labeo 21. l. si in emptione 34. l. cum in leg. 33. de contrah. empt. l. si arbor 17. §. hæc lex 3. de seruit. vrb. præd. & in actibus ambiguis sequimur quod est vtilius actori, alioqui nullus esset litium exitus l. in contrahenda inf. hoc tit. In contrahenda venditione ambigua lex contra venditorem est interpretanda; ad quam tamen regulam descendendum statim non est. Nam prius spectandum, quid actum sit inter contrahentes, & quid sit verisimile illos contraxisse? l. Insulam 13. qui pot. in pign. l. in leg. 29. l. eadem lege 51. locati deinde spectatur id, quo res, de qua agitur, valeat, l. 80. de verb. oblig. quorum omnium si ratio nulla inuestigari possit; sequimur quod inutilius est venditori aut locatori, quod aperte legem non dixit. Cui. in Recit.
units.tr: This rule is frequently applied in the matter of wills, law "ex facto" 19 de hæred. instit., and it comes from the books on trusts (fideicommissa). An example is in law "Sempronius" 26 de usu et usufr. legato. It must be noted that a usufruct ends with the death of the usufructuary, and once ended it returns to the owner of the property. The case is this: the testator, through his heir by way of trust, left the estate to Titius after ten years, the usufruct being deducted. Therefore the usufruct was left from the day of death. The day of a trust falls due at once, although it is not claimed before the ten years, nor can it be claimed. So the trust is owed at once; hence, if the trustee dies before the ten years, the trust passes to his heir. But suppose the trustee has not died within the ten years, but his heir has. The question is whether, after the ten years, the heir's heir is bound to hand over the whole estate to Titius, or whether he may deduct the usufruct. The matter is ambiguous, and the wording seems doubtful. And it seems, first, that the whole estate must be handed over by the heir's heir without deducting the usufruct. For the first heir had already been under that obligation, since the day had come; therefore the usufruct ended with the death of the first heir. If that is so, the usufruct is not deducted by the heir's heir, but the full fruits and the entire ownership must be delivered. On the other side, the usufruct does not seem to have ended with the death of the heir, because it had not yet begun. For the usufruct does not exist before he has handed over the estate, deducting it, since he always keeps it by full right; the day had not yet come. You cannot therefore say that the usufruct ended with the death of the heir. Rather we shall say that the usufruct began with the heir's heir and also ended with him, and did not begin with the first heir. Therefore the heir's heir will not hand over the whole estate, but will deduct the usufruct. We shall say the same if the estate was left under a condition: if the heir dies while the condition is pending, and the condition is afterwards fulfilled, the heir's heir will deduct the usufruct; yet it does not seem to have ended in the person of the first heir. So our question is: which opinion is the truer? The law says that these subtleties are to be set aside, but one must consider what the testator's intention was. The testator's intention favours the former opinion, and that intention is the true meaning. For he wished the usufruct, which attached to the person of his heir, to be deducted; he therefore left the estate with the usufruct deducted, and wished it, when the usufruct ended, to return to the trustee. If the heir had begun to hold the usufruct, he would not have passed it on to his own heir. Therefore, even if he has not yet begun to hold it, the heir's heir will hand over the whole estate. Thus in wills the intention of the testator is to be considered above all; not so in contracts, as appears from law "inter" 33 de auro et arg. and law "si mihi et Titio" 110 §. vlt. de verborum oblig. Contracts therefore differ much from wills; they also differ from judgments or actions. For in judgments we look at what the plaintiff understood. Law "inter" 83 §1 de verb. oblig. Contracts arise from the consent of two parties; an action belongs to one. Law "continuus" 137 §1 eod. In contracts, if the words of a contracting party are ambiguous, we follow what is more useful to the promisor, etc. Examples are in law "Labeo" 21, law "si in emptione" 34, law "cum in lege" 33 de contrah. empt., law "si arbor" 17 §. "haec lex" 3 de servit. urb. praed.; and in ambiguous acts we follow what is more useful to the plaintiff, otherwise there would be no end to lawsuits, law "in contrahenda" inf. hoc tit. In a contract of sale the ambiguous law is to be interpreted against the seller; yet one must not at once descend to this rule. For first we must look at what was done between the contracting parties and what it is likely they agreed to. Law "Insula" 13 qui pot. in pign.; law "in lege" 29; law "eadem lege" 51 locati; then we look at what makes the thing in question valid, law 80 de verb. oblig. If no reason for all of these can be found, we follow what is less useful to the seller or the lessor, since the law did not state it plainly. Cui. in Recit.

units.la: EA sola deportationis sententia aufert, quæ ad Fiscum perueniunt.
units.tr: Only the sentence of deportation takes away those things which pass to the Fisc.

units.la: Deportationis ] adde l. 8. C. de pœnis l. 1. §. 1. sup. de Iure Fisci.
units.tr: Deportationis ] add l. 8. C. de poenis; l. 1. §. 1. sup. de iure Fisci.

units.la: Sententia est: Pœna deportationis aufert bona liberis, & id sententia sola: nam deportationem sequitur tacite publicatio bonorum, & vt recte ait l. vlt. C. de sent. pass. ipsum per se deportationis nomen bonorum ipoliatio est: qua in re distat a relegatione. Igitur sententia aufert bona liberis. Hodie non aufert, ex Nouella, ut nulli Iudicum, &c. §. ult. collat. 9: Non aufert autem ius agnationis, aut coniunguinitatis. l. ult. C. unde legitimi. l. 8. de interdict. & releg. nam hæc non possunt ad Fiscum transfire. Quæ liberi habent à deportato patre, ea aufert Fiscus: quæ vero à maioribus habent, à genere ipso & gente, ut iura cognationis, non aufert. Itaque sententia deportationis ea sola aufert, quæ ad Fiscum transeunt: ius agnationis non transit ad Fiscum. Cuiin Recit.
units.tr: The meaning is this: the penalty of deportation takes goods away from the children, and it does so by the sentence alone. For confiscation of goods follows tacitly upon deportation, and, as l. vlt. C. de sent. pass. rightly says, the very name of deportation is itself a stripping of goods; in this it differs from relegation. So the sentence takes the goods from the children. Today it does not, by the Novel ut nulli Iudicum, etc., §. ult. collat. 9. Nor does it take away the right of agnation or of kinship, l. ult. C. unde legitimi. l. 8. de interdict. & releg., for these cannot pass to the Fisc. What children have from their deported father, the Fisc takes; but what they have from their forebears, from the kin and the family itself, such as rights of cognation, it does not take. Thus the sentence of deportation takes away only those things which pass to the Fisc: the right of agnation does not pass to the Fisc. Cuiac. in Recit.

Qui prior est tempore 54. de reg. in 6. vide Dynum. prior tempore, prior iure. l 3. Ca qui qui potiores. prior tempore in sorte, prior in vsuris. l.18. sup. qui potiores. G th.
units.tr: Præcedit ] the better position belongs to the one who occupies first, and to the earlier. l. 9. §. 3. sup. de publiciana. l. 10. in fine sup. de peculio. l. 31. in fine sup. de action. empti. l. 33. in fine sup. de legatis 1. l. 19. in princ. & sin. sup. de reb. iudic. And so the one earlier in time is preferred in a cause of gain. c. Qui prior est tempore 54. de reg. in 6. See Dynus. Earlier in time, earlier in right. l. 3. Ca. qui potiores. Earlier in time in the principal, earlier in the interest. l. 18. sup. qui potiores. G th.

units.la: In l. Nemo praedo 126. inf. hoc tit. de qua in l. 33. sup. hoc tit. dixi, Ctus ait: Cum de lucro duorum quæritur, potiorem esse possessorem. In hac l. potior est, qui rem accepit prior. Fieri potest, ut, qui prius initio rem accepit, nunc eam non possideat, cum agitur de eo inter plures. Cum igitur una lex dicat, Potiorem esse possessorem: altera vero, cum qui accepit, & cuius res tradita est, pugnare inter se videntur. Pone exemplum in duobus donatariis, quibus res aliqua donata est, diversis temporibus. Si donata est duobus à diversis, ut mihi ab uno, tibi ab alio donata est, possessoris conditio melior est. Nam in pari causa possessor potior est, & par est causa, cum uterque à non domino accepit: nec dispar est causa propter rationem temporis, quod unus prius acceperit, quam alter: quia tum demum ratio temporis spectatur, cum ab eodem domino acceperunt. Igitur si donatarii à diversis non dominis acceperint, melior est causa possessoris: si igitur ab eodem non domino separatim acceperint, prior potior est; & id seruatur in emptoribus. l.9. §. si duobus de Public. in rem act. Idem est in actione hypothecaria, si ea inter se agant duo creditores, quibus res aliqua pignori, diversis temporibus est obligata.
units.tr: In l. Nemo praedo 126. inf. hoc tit., which I explained under l. 33. sup. hoc tit., the jurist says: when the gain of two persons is in question, the possessor is the stronger. In this law the stronger is the one who first received the thing. It can happen that one who first received the thing at the start no longer possesses it, when the matter is contested between several. Since one law says the possessor is the stronger, and the other says that he who received it and to whom the thing was delivered, the two seem to conflict. Take an example of two donees to whom some thing was given at different times. If the thing was given to two persons by different donors, one to me by one and to you by another, the position of the possessor is the better. For in equal cause the possessor is the stronger, and the cause is equal, since each received from a non-owner. Nor is the cause unequal because of the timing, that one received before the other, since the question of time is considered only when they received from the same owner. So if donees received from different non-owners, the cause of the possessor is the better; if they received separately from the same non-owner, the earlier is the stronger, and this is observed in the case of buyers. l. 9. §. si duobus de Public. in rem act. The same holds in the hypothecary action, if two creditors, to whom some thing was pledged at different times, contest with each other.

units.la: Nam si à diuersis non dominis acceperint pignori diuersis temporibus & contractibus, is potior est, qui pignori accepit prior. l. si non dominus 14. qui pot. in pig. sed his quæ de emptione & d. leg. 9. diximus, obstat l. si ea res 31. de act. empti. quæ l. duobus emcitibus eandem rem separatis contractibus, priorem potiorem facit indistincte, hoc est, siue ab uno non domino, siue ab alio atque alio emerint; semper prior potior est, hoc est qui prior accepit. Resp. cum duo rem eandem emerint separato contractu, neutro rem possidente, si agatur aduersus extraneum rem possidentem, prior potior est, non qui prius emit, sed qui prius rem accepit. At uno ex iis possidente, cum agunt inter se, modo possessor, modo prior potior est, secundum id, quod supra dixi. Sed in specie l. si ea res 31. neuter possidet: in ea igitur non utimur distinctione. Et hæc ita esse diximus, cum duo emunt à non dominis, vel pignori accipiunt: quod si pignori accipiant rem à non domino, diuersis temporibus, separatis contractibus, ex causa venditionis & locationis, tunc siue agant inter se, siue contra extraneum, possessor prior est: prior potior est, hoc est, cui prior res tradita est. l. quoties 15 C. de rei vind. Idem est, si duo à non domino rem eandem accipiant pignori diuersis temporibus. Nam præfertur, qui prius accepit. Quod ita dico; diuersis tem-poriporibus. Nam secus, si non diuersis temporibus, sed simul accipiant. Nam tunc cum omnes agunt in solidum aduersus extraneum actione hypothecaria, inter eos possessor melior est. l. 1. §. 1. de interdict. Salvian. l. si debitor 10. de pignor. sed explicemus l. quoties 15. C. de rei vindic. Species est, Duobus diuersis contractibus & diuersis temporibus res vendita est iure, hoc est, à domino; qui tamen eo nomine coercetur pœna falsi. l. qui duobus 21. ad L. Corn. de fals. Iam in d. leg. quoties 15. quæritur, vter emtor potior sit? item quæri potest, si duobus eadem res diuersis temporibus à non domino sit donata; vter sit potior in rei vindicatione? Lex ait, vtrique rem esse venditam & traditam, vel eodem genere traditionis, vel alio atque alio: potior est is, cui priori tradita fuit. Sed prior emptor habet electionem, vt si rem prius traditam adhuc possideat; si modo pretium soluerit venditori; alioqui traditio non sustulit damnum. l. quod vendidi 19. de contrab. empt. Ergo traditio illa priori non sufficit, nisi damnum transtulero. Quamobrem exigitur prior emptor; hoc est, qui prius rem emptam acceperit, & pretium soluerit. Non est necesse, vt huic emptori traditi sint tituli, hoc est, vt venditor ei tradiderit instrumenta, quo genere sit traditio rei. l. 1. C. de donat. Sed si alio iure res fuerit tradita emptori, frustra exigitur datio instru-
units.tr: For if they received pledges from different non-owners at different times and by different contracts, the one who received the pledge first is the stronger. l. si non dominus 14. qui pot. in pig. But what we said about buyers in the same l. 9. is contradicted by l. si ea res 31. de act. empti., which makes the earlier of two buyers who bought the same thing under separate contracts the stronger without distinction, that is, whether they bought from one non-owner or from different ones; the earlier is always the stronger, that is, the one who first received it. I answer: when two have bought the same thing under separate contracts, and neither holds the thing, if one sues a stranger who holds it, the earlier is the stronger, not he who bought first but he who first received the thing. But when one of them holds it, and they contest with each other, sometimes the possessor and sometimes the earlier is the stronger, according to what I said above. In the case of l. si ea res 31., however, neither holds, so in that case we do not use the distinction. And we have said this holds when two buy from non-owners or take pledges; but if they take a pledge of a thing from a non-owner at different times, by separate contracts, from a cause of sale or of letting, then whether they contest with each other or against a stranger, the possessor is the earlier; the earlier is the stronger, that is, the one to whom the thing was first delivered. l. quoties 15 C. de rei vind. The same holds if two take the same thing in pledge from a non-owner at different times. For the one who received first is preferred. I say this of different times; otherwise, if they receive not at different times but together, then when all sue a stranger in full by the hypothecary action, the possessor is the stronger among them. l. 1. §. 1. de interdict. Salvian. l. si debitor 10. de pignor. But let us explain l. quoties 15. C. de rei vindic. The case is this: a thing was sold on two different contracts at different times, by the owner himself, who nonetheless is punished for forgery. l. qui duobus 21. ad L. Corn. de fals. Now in the said l. quoties 15. the question is which buyer is the stronger. Likewise it may be asked, if the same thing was given to two persons at different times by a non-owner, which is stronger in an action for recovery of the thing? The law says that the thing was sold and delivered to each, whether by the same kind of delivery or by different ones; the one to whom it was first delivered is the stronger. But the earlier buyer has a choice: if he still holds the thing first delivered, provided he has paid the price to the seller; otherwise the delivery did not transfer the loss. l. quod vendidi 19. de contrab. empt. Therefore that earlier delivery does not suffice unless the risk has passed. Hence the earlier buyer is required, that is, the one who first received the thing bought and paid the price. It is not necessary that this buyer be given the titles, that is, that the seller hand over to him the instruments by which the delivery of the thing is made. l. 1. C. de donat. But if the thing was delivered to the buyer by another title, the demand for the delivery of the instru-

units.la: P instrumentorum. Ergo si emptor qui possidet rem aduersus alium emptorem, & nolit restituere possessionem, debet ostendere, rem sibi prius traditam esse, & se pretium soluisse, ideoque dominium acquisiuisse, datio instrumentorum non exigitur: vel etiam hic emptor, si velit, non retinebit possessionem, sed accipiet pretium ab alio emptore cum usuris, habita ratione fructuum & sumptuum, hoc est, meliorationum. Nam forte emptor qui rem traditam prius accepit, magnos sumptus fecit, vel meliorem rem fecit: itaque fructus cum melioratione & usuris compensantur. Igitur hic emptor hanc electionem habet, ut vel rem retineat, vel pretium accipiat de usuris. Si nunc idem emptor rem non possideat, vel rei vindicatione rem ab alio vindicabit, vel sibi cum usuris pecuniam accipiet, habitis rationibus fructuum & sumptuum. Graeci apud Harmenop. lib.3. Epit.tit.3. aliud exemplum ponunt, Duo sunt creditores usurarii, quibus sors est soluta, at usurae non sunt solutae: debitor utrique non est soluendo, & habet tantum unde uni soluat, Cui igitur prius soluetur? Resp. Quoties duobus quid debetur ex simili causa, meliorem esse dico causam eius, qui prior occupauerit agere, hoc est, qui festinauit usuras exigere. l. inter eos 19. de re iudic. Prior erit qui sibi vigilauit, & ius vigilantibus scriptum est; non autem qui prior cum debitore contraxit.Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: ments is pointless. So if a buyer who holds the thing against another buyer is unwilling to restore possession, he must show that the thing was first delivered to him and that he paid the price, and so acquired ownership; then the delivery of instruments is not required. Or this buyer, if he wishes, need not keep possession, but may take the price from the other buyer with interest, after allowance for fruits and expenses, that is, improvements. For perhaps the buyer who first received the thing has made great outlays, or has made the thing better; so the fruits are set off against the improvement and the interest. Therefore this buyer has the choice either to keep the thing or to take the price with interest. If now the same buyer does not hold the thing, he will either recover it from another by an action for recovery, or take his money with interest, after allowance for fruits and expenses. The Greeks, in Harmenopulus, lib. 3. Epit. tit. 3., put forward another example: there are two usurious creditors, to whom the principal has been paid but not the interest, and the debtor is able to pay only one of them, so which one is to be paid first? I answer: whenever something is owed to two persons from a similar cause, I say the better cause is that of the one who first took the initiative in suing, that is, who hastened to demand the interest. l. inter eos 19. de re iudic. He will be first who watched over his own interest, and the law is written for the vigilant; not he who first contracted with the debtor. Cuiac. in Recit.
