units.la: Ad Leg. 100. Quibus modis contractus vel obligatio tollitur.
units.tr: On Law 100. By what modes a contract or obligation is dissolved.

units.la: OMnia, quæ iure contrahuntur, contrario iure pereunt.
units.tr: All things that are contracted under law pass away by the contrary law.

units.la: Contrario] 2. Eclog. 3. c. 98. v. l. 35. supr. eod. l. 153. infr. eod. v. l. 80 sup. de solutionib.
units.tr: Contrario] 2. Eclog. 3. c. 98. v. l. 35. supr. eod. l. 153. infr. eod. v. l. 80 sup. de solutionib.

units.la: Vide quæ notata sunt sup. ad l. 35. & infr. ad l. 153. quæ adiicit, quibus modis quid acquiritur, his etiam modis in contrarium actis amittitur. l. quemadmodum 8. de acquir. vel amit. possess. Sed particulam FERE appoluit propter possessionem. Quoniam verum est, possessionem corpore non solo acquiri, sed exigi etiam animum. Verum etiam, corpore solo non amitti, cum possit retineri solo animo. l. quamvis 46. de acquir. possess. sed animo solo amitti. Igitur non, quibus modis acquiritur possessio, omnino amittitur. Nam acquiritur corpore & animo; solo corpore non amittitur, sed solo animo, etiamsi quis de fundo non discedat. l.3.§. in amittenda. de acquir.poss. Et in d.l.3. Bulgari sententia est: si à corpore incipit, non corpore amitti, sed corpore & animo: si ab animo incipit, solo animo amitti. Et Placentin. hanc sententiam valde notat, & omnes Græci apud Harmen. lib.2. Epit. Bulgarus, hac ratione addiram particulam FERE dicit, ad distinguendum acquisitionem & amissionem possessionis. Ioannes vero, quia, inquit, alius modus liberationis esse potest. Cui non assentior, quia nec ipse in ea sententia perseuerat. Postea enim dicit, FERE ideo adiici, quia pignus nudo pacto contrahitur; nudo pacto non dissoluitur, idque verum quidem est, sed non potest adaptari ad d.l.fere. Duo sunt pignoris genera, pignus & hypotheca: Pignus est contractus; hypotheca pactum. Pignus est contractus re, & re eadem soluitur. Hypotheca pacto constituitur, efficitque actionem vtilem. Sed quemadmodum locum habet pactum in producenda & efficienda hypothecaria actione, ita locum non habet in tollenda. l.sitibi 17. de pignor. l.2. de pact. quia Prætor vtramque vim pacto non dedit. Cur pactum producit hypothecariam actionem? Quia Prætor hanc vim pacto dedit.
units.tr: See what has been noted sup. ad l. 35. & infr. ad l. 153. He adds that by whatever modes something is acquired, it is also lost by the contrary acts. l. quemadmodum 8. de acquir. vel amit. possess. But he has added the particle FERE on account of possession, since it is true that possession is acquired not by bodily act alone but also requires intention. It is also true that it is not lost by bodily act alone, since it can be retained by intention alone, l. quamvis 46. de acquir. possess. but it is lost by intention alone. Therefore not every mode by which possession is acquired causes it to be lost entirely. For it is acquired by body and intention; it is not lost by the body alone, but by intention alone, even if someone does not leave the land. l.3.§. in amittenda. de acquir.poss. And in d.l.3. is the opinion of Bulgarus: if it begins from the body, it is lost not by the body but by body and intention; if it begins from the intention, it is lost by intention alone. Placentinus notes this opinion strongly, and all the Greeks in Harmenopulus lib.2. Epit. Bulgarus says that FERE was added for this reason, to distinguish the acquisition and the loss of possession. John, however, says there may be another mode of release. I do not assent to this, because he himself does not persist in that view. For afterwards he says FERE is added because a pledge is contracted by a bare pact, and is not dissolved by a bare pact; this is indeed true, but it cannot be applied to d.l.fere. There are two kinds of pledge, pignus and hypotheca: pignus is a contract; hypotheca is a pact. A pignus is a contract by the thing, and is dissolved by the same thing. A hypotheca is constituted by pact and produces a utilis action. But just as a pact has a place in bringing about and producing the hypothecary action, so it has no place in dissolving it. l.sitibi 17. de pignor. l.2. de pact. because the Praetor did not give a pact either power. Why does a pact produce the hypothecary action? Because the Praetor gave this power to the pact.

units.la: Cæterum hæc regula non est de pacto, sed de contractu. Non probo etiam, quod Bulgarus ait de articulo FERE, quia, inquit, omnis obligatio verbis potest tolli, aut ipso iure, aut per exceptionem: fateor imprimis, omnem obligationem posse tolli exceptione pacti: sed de hoc genere tollendi non tractamus. Neque hoc proprie est tollere, sed elidere. Nego autem omnem obligationem verbis tolli posse ipso iure. Nam sola obligatio verborum verbis tollitur: sed sola verborum obligatio, non solum erat stipulatio, sed & doli promissio. Dicitur, solam verborum obligationem verbis tolli. l. & per iusiurandum, 13. de acceptil. Verum omnis obligatio novari potest in stipulatione deducta Aquilianam, & deinde acceptilationem tolli verbis. Sic non omnis obligatio tollitur verbis, sed stipulatio vel obligatio novata per stipulationem Aquilianam. Non probo etiam quod Accursius ait, in d.l. fere, cur adiecta sit particula FERE, quia hæ regulæ sunt de obligatione ex contractu, quod obligatio ex delicto contrario modo non solvitur. Tolluntur enim pœnæ solutione, aliæ pacto & iureiurando & dissimulatione: contrario sensu sive actu nulla tollitur, imo & restitutio rei non liberat, ut restitutio rei furtivæ non liberat ab actione furti l. pen. de vi bon. rapt. ad 7. Itaq; harum obligationum longe alia erit conditio. Ergo afgo assentiendum iis, qui ratione possessionis adiectum FERE dicunt. Cui. in Recit.
units.tr: Moreover, this rule is not about pact but about contract. I also do not approve what Bulgarus says about the word FERE, namely that every obligation can be dissolved by words, either by law itself or by exception. I grant first that every obligation can be dissolved by an exception of pact, but we are not treating of this kind of dissolving. Nor is this properly dissolving, but eliding. I deny, however, that every obligation can be dissolved by words by law itself. For only an obligation of words is dissolved by words; but the obligation of words was not only stipulation but also promise of dolus. It is said that only an obligation of words is dissolved by words. l. & per iusiurandum, 13. de acceptil. Yet every obligation can be novated by a stipulation made under the Aquilian stipulation, and then dissolved by acceptilation in words. Thus not every obligation is dissolved by words, but a stipulation, or an obligation novated through the Aquilian stipulation. I also do not approve what Accursius says in d.l. fere, why the particle FERE was added, namely because these rules concern obligation from contract, whereas obligation from delict is not dissolved in the contrary way. For penalties are removed by payment, others by pact, by oath, and by dissimulation; in the contrary sense, nothing is removed by act; indeed even restitution of the thing does not release, as restitution of stolen goods does not release from the action of theft. l. pen. de vi bon. rapt. ad 7. Therefore the condition of these obligations will be quite different. Hence I must assent to those who say FERE was added on account of possession. Cui. in Recit.

units.la: Ad Leg. 101. De duobus mensibus.
units.tr: On Law 101. Concerning two months.

units.la: VBi lex duorum mensium fecit mētionem, & qui sexagesimo & primo die venerit, audiendus est: ita enim & Imperator Antoninus cum diuo patre suo rescripsit. Vt in dilationibus, l. unic. C. Theod. de dilation. ex consensu, lib. 11. tit. 33. compensatione Fisco facienda, l. 46. §. 4. sup. de iure fisci. & aliis. De duobus mensibus vide Nouell. 66. c. 1. & ibi not. Gothofredi.
units.tr: WHERE a law makes mention of two months, one who comes on the sixty-first day is to be heard; for thus the Emperor Antoninus with his divine father rescribed. As in dilations, l. unic. C. Theod. de dilation. ex consensu, lib. 11. tit. 33. in making compensation to the Fisc, l. 46. §. 4. sup. de iure fisci. and in other cases. On two months, see Nov. 66. c. 1. and the note there of Gothofredus.

units.la: Sexagesimo die, sic Græci, ἢ ἐξηκοντα ἡμέρας ἀν τὶ τὰ τῶν προσδέχονται. Sic in l. 30. in sin. supr. de adult. ipse sexagesimus dies comprehenditur, idque probat Cuiacius, c. 13. de præscript. adde l. 132. supr. de verb. sig. Gothfr.
units.tr: On the sixtieth day: thus the Greeks, ἢ ἐξηκοντα ἡμέρας ἀν τὶ τὰ τῶν προσδέχονται. Thus in l. 30. in sin. supr. de adult. the sixtieth day itself is included, and Cuiacius proves this, c. 13. de præscript. add l. 132. supr. de verb. sig. Gothofredus.

units.la: Caracalla scil.
units.tr: Caracalla, namely.

units.la: L. Septimo Seuero scil. quo Imperatore vixit author huius legis, Paulus, coætaneus Mæcii & Triphonini & Tertulliani. vide Cuiac. 7. obserū. 2 vulgata legit, fratre, & male. Gothofr. Lex ait: Eum qui compensatione vtitur aduersus Fiscum, debere probare causam compensationis intra duos menses. Sic duorum mensium mentio fit in l. tutor 7. §. usura 11. de administ. tut. l. aufertur 46. §. qui compensationem 4. de iure Fisci. Hoc est ex lege aliqua. Nam quoties est certum tempus, necesse est, ut id lex aliqua præscripserit. l. v t. qui sine manumiss. In iure nostro menses non computantur ex initio Calendarum, sed ex numero dierum, & 30. dies pro mense. 60. pro duobus mensibus: 90. pro tribus. 270. pro novem mensibus accipiuntur. l. vlt. C. de iure dot. l. 3. §. vlt. de suis & legit. l. 7. C. Theod. de decur. Vno tamen casu menses accipiuntur latius. In causa enim appellationum tres menses accipiuntur pro 93. diebus. l. vlt. C. de temp. appellat. Nunc dicitur: vbi lex duorum mensium facit mentionem, admittitur quis etiam sexagesimo primo die; quod videtur falsum, si mensem accipis pro 30. diebus. Tunc enim qui venit sexagesimo & primo die, venit post duos menses. Vel etiam si vis latius accipere menses, cur no dicit, accipiendum in causis appellationum, qui venit sexagesimo primo die? Hoc enim vel illo modo menses sunt accipiendi semper. In libris Græcorum non legitur, & primo die, sed sexagesimo tantum, quod congruit cum l. 30. ad l. Iul. de adult. vbi sciendum est, diuortio facto mulierem accusari posse intra dies 60. iure mariti, vt præferatur cæteris, & non subscribat in crimen: post dies 6c. est necessario subscribendum. Ait d. l. 30. sexaginta dies a diuortio numerantur, hoc est, duo menses: si venerit extremo die, admittetur. Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: Namely under Septimius Severus, under whose reign lived the author of this law, Paulus, a contemporary of Maecianus, Triphoninus and Tertullian. See Cuiac. 7. observ. 2. The Vulgate reads "fratre" (brother), wrongly. Gothofredus. The law says that one who uses compensation against the Fisc must prove the cause of the compensation within two months. Thus a mention of two months is made in l. tutor 7. §. usura 11. de administ. tut. l. aufertur 46. §. qui compensationem 4. de iure Fisci. This is by some law; for whenever there is a fixed time, it is necessary that some law has prescribed it. l. ut qui sine manumiss. In our law months are not reckoned from the beginning of the Calends, but by the number of days, with thirty days for a month: sixty for two months, ninety for three, two hundred and seventy for nine months. l. ult. C. de iure dot. l. 3. §. ult. de suis & legit. l. 7. C. Theod. de decur. In one case, however, months are taken more broadly. For in the case of appeals three months are taken as ninety-three days. l. ult. C. de temp. appellat. Now it is said: where a law makes mention of two months, one is admitted even on the sixty-first day; which seems false, if you take a month as thirty days. For then one who comes on the sixty-first day comes after two months. Or even if you wish to take months more broadly, why does it not say that in cases of appeal one who comes on the sixty-first day is to be accepted? For months must always be taken in one of these ways. In the books of the Greeks it is not read "and on the first day," but only "on the sixtieth," which agrees with l. 30. ad l. Iul. de adult. where it must be known that, once divorce has taken place, a woman may be accused within sixty days by the right of the husband, so that she is preferred to others and need not subscribe the charge; after sixty days it is necessary to subscribe. d. l. 30. says that sixty days are counted from the divorce, that is, two months: if one comes on the last day, one will be admitted. Cuiac. in Recit.

units.la: Ad Leg. 102. Qui aduersus edictum facere dicatur. 2. De actione deneganda.
units.tr: On Law 102, Who is said to act against the edict. 2. On denying an action.

units.la: QVi vetante Prætore fecit, hic aduersus edictum proprie fecisse dicitur. §. 1. Eius est actionem denegare, qui possit & dare.
units.tr: He who acts against the praetor's prohibition is properly said to have acted against the edict. §1. It belongs to the one who can give an action to also deny it.

units.la: Qui vetante ] adde leg. 121. inf. eod. l. 29. sup. de arbit.
units.tr: The praetor forbidding ] add law 121 below, same title; law 29 above, On arbitrators.

units.la: Aduersus edictum ] eiusdem prætoris scilicet. l. 7. in pr. & §. 2. sup. de iurisdict. l. 4. §. 1. sup. de in ius voc. l. 2. sup. ne quis eum l. 3. sup. de eo per quem. l. vlt. sup. ne quid in loco publ. hic aduersus dictum promissum me facere. l. 17. in sin. sup. de Ædilit. edicto. In legem l. 5. C. de legibus Goth.
units.tr: Against the edict ] of the same praetor, namely law 7 init. and §2 above, On jurisdiction; law 4 §1 above, On summoning to court; law 2 above, That no one...; law 3 above, On him through whom; last law above, That nothing be done in a public place. Here, acting against a dictum or promise: law 17 end above, On the aedile's edict. On the law: law 5 C. On the laws of the Goths.

units.la: Denegare ] qui potest denegare, dare potest l. 3. l. 38. l. 70. l. 100. sup. eod. Est quoddam interdictum, cuius est exceptio, quod aduersus edictum factum sit. l. de pupillo 5. §. si quis forte 4. l. ædibus 18. l. prætor ait 20. §. 1. l. vlt. de noui oper. nunciat. Hoc interdictum datur in eum, qui contra operis noui nunciationem fecit opus, & is tenetur interdicto illo, vt restituat. Nam interdictum illud est restitutorium, non tantum per operis noui nunciationem, sed etiam vetante prætore. l. de pupillo 5. §. meminisse 10. eod. cui si non parebitur, competit idem interdictum. l. si opus 16. eod.
units.tr: Denying ] he who can deny can also give: laws 3, 38, 70, 100 above, same title. There is a certain interdict whose exception is that the act was done against the edict: law On the ward 5 §If anyone perhaps 4; law 18 On buildings; law 20 §1; last law On new work notice. This interdict is given against one who carries on work in contravention of a notice of new work, and he is bound by that interdict to restore matters. For that interdict is restitutory, not only in the case of a notice of new work but also when the praetor forbids. Law On the ward 5 §Remember 10, same title. If one does not obey it, the same interdict lies: law 16 If work, same title.

units.la: Ad §. Eius est, actionem, &c.
units.tr: On §. Eius est, actionem, &c.

units.la: Id referendum est ad formulam Edictorum, quibus Praetor pollicetur se actionem daturum. Ibi enim, vbi dicit; dabo, subintelligitur, vel denegabo. Nam eius est denegare, cuius etiam est dare, & eodem modo explicatur l. nemo 37. sup. h. tit. quam referamus ad formulas iudiciorum, in quibus frequens est, condemna, & ibi supple: vel absolve. Cuiac. in Recitat. posthum.
units.tr: This is to be referred to the formula of the Edicts, by which the praetor promises that he will grant an action. For there, where he says "I will give", it is understood "or deny". For it belongs to deny to one whose it also is to give, and it is explained in the same way in law 37 above, this title. It may also be referred to the formulas of judgments, in which "condemn" is frequent, and there one supplies "or absolve". Cuiacius, in the posthumous Recitations.

units.la: Ad Leg. 103. Neminem de domo sua extrahi.
units.tr: On Law 103. That no one be dragged out of his own house.

units.la: NEMO de domo sua extrahi debet.
units.tr: No one must be dragged out of his own house.

units.la: De domo] l. 18. l. 21. sup. de in ius vocand. l. 4. §. 5. sup. de damno 2. Eclog. 3. c. 101.
units.tr: On his own house: laws 18, 21 above, On summoning to court; law 4 §5 above, On damage; 2. Eclog. 3. c. 101.

units.la: Sua] in qua habitat scilicet non ad tempus, Bart. & Decius hic, quo nomine hortum domui iunctum intelligunt. Eadem ratione volunt, molitori molendinum domus esse loco, & navis navem. Peckius in lib. de Iure sistendi. 6. num. 3. 4. & 5. at non tabernam & apothecam, & quae mercium condendarum causa, non habitationis aedificantur. Idem in porticu ab aedibus separata esse, iudicat idem Peckius ibid. Gothofr.
units.tr: "His own" means the house in which one lives, namely not for a time. Bartolus and Decius here, who under this name understand also a garden joined to the house. By the same reasoning they hold that for a miller his mill counts as his house, and for a ship-owner his ship. Peckius, in the book On the right of summoning, §§3, 4 and 5; but not a shop or a storehouse, nor buildings erected for storing goods rather than for dwelling. The same Peckius judges that a portico separated from the house is likewise excluded, ibid. Gothofredus.

units.la: Extrahi] non potest etiam ibidem arrestari. Peck. ibid. d. numero 3. potest tamen sententia iudiiudicis quis prohiberi, ne domum excedat. l. 7. §. 8. §. 19. l. 9. sup. de interdict. & releg. Goth.
units.tr: "Dragged out": one cannot even be arrested there. Peckius, ibid., the said number 3. Yet by the sentence of a judge a person may be forbidden to leave his house: laws 7 §8 and §19; law 9 above, On interdicts and banishment. Gothofredus.

units.la: Debet ] potest tamen extrahi in criminalibus causis Non 134. c. 3. & fiscalibus Peckius lib. de iure sistendi c. 6. num. 8. sed & quando electus est ad aliquam dignitatem. l. 31. C. de decurionib. Quin huic priuilegio renunciari posse volunt, quod ei accidit, qui omni iuris auxilio renunciat. Peck. ibi. nu. 9. Goth.
units.tr: "Must": yet he may be dragged out in criminal cases, Nov. 134 c. 3, and in fiscal cases, Peckius, book On the right of summoning, c. 6 n. 8. He may also be dragged out when he has been elected to some dignity, law 31 C. On decurions. Indeed they hold that this privilege can be renounced, as happens when one renounces every legal aid. Peckius, ibid., n. 9. Gothofredus.

units.la: Repetita est ex lib. 1. Pauli ad edictum, quo tractat de damno infecto. Ex eodem edicto vicinus, cuius aedes ruinosae sunt, cauere debet, damni infecti, etsi non sit vicinus. Caue re autem debet in iure, hoc est, ad sellam Praetoris. Praetor iubet ei domum denunciari, ut caueat vicino, l. 4. §. Praetor. de damno infecto. non vero debet extrahi de domo: quod ad eundem modum tractauit Paulus l. 18. de damno infect. Ex Vlpiano vero constat in l. 4. eam denuntiationem vel fieri in personam, si domi suae sit: vel si domo abiit, eam fieri ad domum praeconis voce, & libello postibus affixo. Quod etiam fit in plerisque aliis casibus. l. 1. §. 1. de agnosc. lib. l. 5. §. 3. quod vi aut clam. l. 3. de excusat. tut. Adde l. vim 39. §. nuptae ad L. Iul. de adult. Sic etiam denuntiatio siue citatio absentium reorum quae fit per trinuncium, in l. inter 10. de pub. iudic. ea denunciatio potest fieri publice praeconis voce, aut buccina, ut constat ex Plutarcho in Gracchis. & ait, moris esse, vt si non veniat, qui est reus criminis, vocetur ad domum per buccinam. Sic denuntiatio testimonii, hoc est, quoties testes euocantur, si non poterit fieri in persona, fit ad domum testium ex L. XII. tab. in qua ita scriptum est; Cui testimonium defuerit, ternis diebus ob portam obuagulatum ito, hoc est, qui testes requirit, is per triduum testes euocet ob portam ad domum. Puto obuagulatum dici à boatu, quoties testes euocantur amplo boatu præconis. Festus vocat conuitium de iniur. Igitur obuagulatio est testium requisitio, quæ fit magna voce. Sententia igitur legis est, vt is, quites s requirit, per triduum eos euocare debeat ampla voce ad domum. Cuiac. in Recuat. posthum. oper.
units.tr: This is repeated from book 1 of Paul on the Edict, where he treats of damage not yet done. From the same edict, a neighbour whose house is in ruins must give security for damage not yet done, even if he is not a neighbour. He must give security in court, that is, at the praetor's bench. The praetor orders that notice be served on him at his house, so that he may give security to the neighbour: law 4 §The praetor, On damage not yet done. But he must not be dragged out of the house; Paul treated this in the same way in law 18, On damage not yet done. From Ulpian in law 4 it is clear that this notice is given either in person, if he is at home, or, if he has left the house, it is given at his house by the herald's voice and by a notice fixed to the doorposts. This is also done in many other cases: law 1 §1, On acknowledgment; law 5 §3, quod vi aut clam; law 3, On excusing guardians. Add law 39 §nuptae, Julian law on adultery. So too the notice or summons of absent defendants, which is made by three proclamations, law 10, On public trials. This notice can be made publicly by the herald's voice or by trumpet, as is clear from Plutarch in the Life of the Gracchi, who says it was the custom that if the accused, being a defendant, did not come, he was summoned to his house by trumpet. Likewise the notice to witnesses, that is, whenever witnesses are summoned: if this cannot be done in person, it is done at the witnesses' houses, according to the Twelve Tables, in which it is written thus: "Whoever lacks a witness, let him go three days before the gate to obuagulate", that is, whoever seeks witnesses should summon them at the gate, at the house, for three days. I think obuagulatum is so called from the sound (boatus), whenever witnesses are summoned by the herald's loud cry. Festus calls it a shouting. Therefore obuagulatio is the seeking of witnesses, done with a loud voice. The meaning of the law, then, is that whoever seeks witnesses must summon them to the house for three days with a loud voice. Cuiacius, in the posthumous Recitations and Works.

units.la: Ad Leg. 104. De iudiciis famosis & pecuniariis.
units.tr: On Infamous and Pecuniary Trials (Ad Leg. 104)

units.la: SI in duabus actionibus, alibi summa maior, alibi infamia est: præponenda est causa existimationis. Vbi autem æquiparantur famosa iudicia, etsi summam imparem habent, pro paribus accipienda sunt.
units.tr: If in two actions the sum is greater in one and infamy is at stake in the other, the cause affecting reputation is to be preferred. Where infamous trials are equal, they are to be treated as equal even if their sums are unequal.

units.la: Infamia ] l. 36 sup. de obligationib. v. l. 7. l. 97. sup. de solution. l. 10. in fine sup. de pœnis.
units.tr: Infamy: l. 36 sup. de obligationib.; cf. l. 7, l. 97 sup. de solution.; l. 10 in fine sup. de poenis.

units.la: Causa existimationis ] in pari causa, vt infamia vitetur l. 4. §. 2. sup. de suspect.
units.tr: Cause of reputation: in an equal cause, so that infamy may be avoided: l. 4 §2 sup. de suspect.

units.la: Æquiparantur ] Hoc verbū neutraliter accipit Sueton. in Oftauio. c. 94. Virgil. Eclog. 5. Cic. in Tuscul. æquiparantur, vulgat. Halo. Gothofr.
units.tr: The verb æquiparantur is taken intransitively by Suetonius in Octavio c. 94, by Virgil in Eclogue 5, and by Cicero in Tusculanis; the Vulgate reading is æquiparantur. Halo. Gothofr.

units.la: Vulgo ab omnibus hæc ponitur species. Debitor ex pluribus causis soluit pecuniam creditori debitam, nec dixit, in quam causam soluerit. Quæritur, in quam soluta esse videatur? Si debuit ex causa famosa, vt tutela: & non famosa, vt mutuo: id videtur soluisse, quod debebat ex causa famosa. l. 7. & l. cum ex pluribus 97. de solution. Hæc species habet congruentem faciem huic regulæ. At in fine hæc lex definit, quæ iudicia sint maiora & minora, quæ non famosa. Quæ sunt de maiore summa, maiora esse dicit iis, quæ de minore. Famosa autem maiora sunt non famosis: etiamsi non famosa maiorem pecuniæ summam contineant, quia fama præstat omnibus diuitiis. Paria sunt famosa iudicia inter se, licet disparis sint summæ: quia id, quod caput est, spectatur. Caput autem est famæ causa. Iudicia autem famosa ea etiam paria sunt, quæ parem summam habent. Effectus autem regulæ est, vt liqueat in duabus actionibus, vtra earum præponenda sit alteri, idque scitu dignum est, propter iudiciorum ordinem. Minori enim actioni præponitur maior. l. vlt. C. de ord. iudic. Minor actio non mouetur, dum spectatur maior. l. per minorem. 54 de iudio. Quod hoc exemplo planum fiat: Petitio hæreditatis præfertur rei vindicationi, quia in res vniuersas est actio. l. si post litem de except. Eadem ratione fundi vindicatio præponitur vindicationi seruitutis debitæ fundo. l. in fundum de except. Rei vindicatio præfertur communi diuidundo: petitio hæreditatis actioni familiæ erciscundæ. l. 1. famil. ercisc. Ex diuerso: Criminalis actio præfertur ciuili, licet ciuilis sit de summa maiore. d. l. vlt. C. de ordine iud. quia capitis & famæ causa potior est omnibus cæteris. Ideoque criminalis causa ciuili præponitur semper, nec quicquam mutat diuersitas summarum. Eadem ratione actio furti præponitur petitioni hæreditatis, & liberalis causa actioni furti: quia status hominis causa grauior est, quam sit famæ & existimationis. l. pen. §. vlt. C. de ord. iudic. Ita igitur fit comparatio actionum hoc modo. Quoties sub eodem iudicio duæ concurrunt actiones, quæ eidem competunt, & communionem quandam inter se habent, adeo, ut vna præiudicium afferat alteri: præfertur ea, quæ est de summa maiore. Quoties duæ actiones sunt famosæ, licet sint diuersæ summæ, pro paribus accipiuntur, & vna non præponitur alteri. Quo argumento possumus uti ad refellendam speciem, quam vulgo applicant huic regulæ, quæ proposita est initio. Nam in causa solutionis, etiamsi omnia debita sint similia, ut si omnia sint
units.tr: Commonly this case is put forward by everyone: a debtor, owing money to a creditor on several grounds, pays a sum without saying on which account he pays it. The question is, on which account it is taken to have been paid? If he owed on an infamous ground, such as guardianship, and on a non-infamous one, such as a loan, he is taken to have paid what he owed on the infamous ground: l. 7 & l. cum ex pluribus 97 de solution. This case has a fair resemblance to the present rule. But at the end of the law it defines which trials are greater and which lesser, and which are not infamous. Those concerning a larger sum are said to be greater than those concerning a smaller one. Infamous trials, however, rank above non-infamous ones, even if the non-infamous ones involve a larger sum of money, because reputation is worth more than all riches. Infamous trials are equal to one another though their sums are unequal, because what is the head of the matter is what counts, and the head is the cause of reputation. Infamous trials are also equal when their sums are equal. The effect of the rule is that, when two actions are brought, it becomes clear which of them is to be preferred to the other; and this is worth knowing because of the order of trials. For the greater action is preferred to the lesser: l. vlt. C. de ord. iudic. The lesser action is not set in motion while the greater is under consideration: l. per minorem 54 de iudic. To make this plain by an example: the petition for an inheritance is preferred to the action for recovery of a thing, because the action is brought against all the property: l. si post litem de except. By the same reasoning, an action to recover land is preferred to an action for a servitude owed to the land: l. in fundum de except. The action to recover a thing is preferred to the action for partition of common property; the petition for an inheritance to the action for division of an estate: l. 1 famil. ercisc. On the other hand, a criminal action is preferred to a civil one, even if the civil action concerns a greater sum: d. l. vlt. C. de ordine iud. because a case touching life and reputation is stronger than all others. Therefore a criminal case always takes precedence over a civil one, and difference of sums makes no change. By the same reasoning, the action for theft is preferred to the petition for an inheritance, and a case of liberty to the action for theft, because a case concerning a man's status is weightier than one concerning reputation and good name: l. pen. §vlt. C. de ord. iudic. In this way, then, actions are compared. Whenever two actions which belong to the same party come together under one trial, and have some connection with each other, so that one causes prejudice to the other, the one concerning the greater sum is preferred. Whenever two actions are infamous, even if their sums differ, they are taken as equal, and one is not preferred to the other. By this argument we may refute the case which people commonly apply to the rule proposed at the beginning. For in the case of payment, even if all the debts are alike, as when all are on an infamous ground, some order is still observed. For one who pays without specifying, and the creditor who accepts without specifying, is taken to have paid the older debt: l. 5 de solution. d. l. cum ex pluribus 97. But whenever the actions are equal, and the question is about the order of trials, neither is preferred to the other. Cuiac. in Recit. posth. oper.

units.la: . sint ex causa famosa, adhuc seruatur aliquis ordo. Nam qui soluit indefinite, creditore etiam accipiente indefinite, videtur soluisse vetustius debitum. l. 5. de solution. d. l. cum ex pluribus 97. At quoties sunt pares actiones, & quaeritur de ordine iudiciorum, vna alteri non praeponitur. Cuia. in Recit. posth. oper.

units.tr: Wherever there is an examination of the case, there the praetor is required.

units.la: Causae cognitio ] l. 71. sup. eod. l. 9. sup. de offic. proconf. Causae cognitio necessaria est, quoties causa ex iudicis officio & arbitrio definienda est Gothofr.

units.la: Ad Leg. 106. De libertate.
units.tr: On Liberty (Ad Leg. 106)

units.la: LIbertas inaestimabilis res est.
units.tr: Liberty is a thing beyond price.

units.la: vt merito libero homini mini sublata sit à Leone Nouella 59. facultas sui ipsius vendendi Goth.
units.tr: So that, rightly, the power of selling oneself was taken away from a free man by Leo's Novel 59. Goth.

units.la: ideo libertas summum pretium dicitur à Comico in Andria act. 1. scen. 1. nihil ea gratius seruo præstari potest, l. 39. in f. sup. de fideicom. lib. hinc qui liberum acquisiuit, non est factus locupletior l. 126. §. 1. inf. eod.
units.tr: Therefore liberty is called the highest price by the comic poet in the Andria, act 1, scene 1: nothing more welcome can be given to a slave. l. 39 in fine sup. de fideicom. lib. Hence whoever acquires a free person is not made richer. l. 126 §1 inf. eod.

units.la: Libertas inæstimabilis est: hoc est, pecunia æstimari, siue lui non potest, vt ait l. 9. §. pen. de statu lib. Libertas neque minuitur, neque augetur pecunia. Qua de causa, si tibi seruum promisi, & is perductus sit ad libertatem, sine facto meo, puta legis, aut Principis beneficio, obligatio extinguitur: quia res in obligationem deducta dari non potest. Eadem ratione libertates L. Ælia Sentia cohibentur, vt minor 25. annis non possit temere manumittere, nisi causa cognita. §. vlt. Instit. quib. ex caus. manumit. non poss. Sic in leg. non est singulis 176. h. tit. Infinita est (inquit ICTus) æstimatio libertatis & necessitudinis. Exemplum pone ex l. 8. §. si quis à procuratore Rem ratam hab. Procurator nomine alieno facit controversiam status, hoc est eum, qui est in libertate, vocat in seruitutem: qui est procurator, cautere debet, Rem ratam dominum habiturum: cuius quæstionis conclusio est; quanti ea res est, præstiturum procuratorem, nisi dominus ratum habuerit. Verum hoc casu melius est, certam summam comprehendere. Ratio quia libertatis æstimatio infinita. Idemque est; si procurator nomine alieno agat, aliquem non esse, nec fuisse filium, non esse patrem, non patronum, non vxorem, non maritum: melius est, vt procurator cauendo pro mittat certam summam. Et sic etiam in libertate fieri oportet.
units.tr: Liberty is inestimable: that is, it cannot be valued in money, or redeemed, as l. 9 §pen. de statu lib. says. Liberty is neither diminished nor increased by money. For this reason, if I promised you a slave and he has been brought to liberty without any act of mine, say by the law or by the Prince's benefit, the obligation is extinguished, because a thing that has passed into liberty cannot be given. By the same reasoning the freedoms under the Lex Aelia Sentia are restrained, so that a minor of twenty-five years may not rashly manumit unless the case has been examined. §vlt. Instit. quib. ex caus. manumit. non poss. So in leg. non est singulis 176 h. tit. The jurist says: the estimation of liberty and of kinship is infinite. Take an example from l. 8 §si quis a procuratore Rem ratam hab. A procurator, on behalf of another, raises a dispute over status, that is, he calls a man who is free into slavery. The procurator must give security that the owner will ratify the matter; the conclusion of this question is that the procurator will pay whatever the thing is worth, unless the owner ratifies it. But in this case it is better to set down a fixed sum, because the estimation of liberty is infinite. It is the same if a procurator, acting for another, claims that someone is not, and never was, a son, a father, a patron, a wife or a husband: it is better that the procurator, giving security, pay a fixed sum. And so it ought to be done in matters of liberty too.

units.la: Ad Leg. 108. De Iudiciis pœnalibus.
units.tr: On Law 108. Concerning criminal judgments.

units.la: FERE in omnibus pœnalibus iudiciis & ætati & imprudentiæ succurritur.
units.tr: In almost all criminal judgments, relief is given both for age and for lack of judgment.

units.la: Fere] ex tit. de in ius vocando & tit. ne quis eum qui in ius voc.
units.tr: Almost] from the title on summoning to court, and the title that no one should free one who has been summoned to court.

units.la: Ætati] 2. Eclog. 3. c. 106. v. l. 38. §. 7. sup. de adult. l. 16. §. 3. in f. sup. de pœnis. Goth.
units.tr: Age] 2 Eclog. 3, c. 106; see law 38, §7, above, on adults; law 16, §3, at the end, above, on penalties. Goth.

units.la: Imprudentiæ ] l.5. §.4. sup. de obligat. l. vlt. sup. de variis & extraordin. criminib.
units.tr: Lack of judgment] law 5, §4, above, on obligations; the last law above, on various and extraordinary crimes.

units.la: Succurritur ] vt pœna remittatur. l.8. sup. de his, qui not. infam. Male Accursius ætatem pro senili accipit. Nam in pœnalibus actionibus sení non succurritur; licet debeat mitius coërceri. Et constat, in iure nostro, ætatem, cum absolute pronunciatur, accipi pro ætate minoris 25. annis, vel impuberis. Differentia tamen est magna inter impuberes, & inter eos, qui puberes quidem sunt, & tamen adhuc minores sunt annis 25. Duodecim tabulæ iubent puberem verberari, & ita sarciri damnum iubent, quod fecit: at ita de furto non tenetur impubes. Pubes tamen tenetur furti. Rursus impuberi parcitur, si doli mali capax non sit: puberi doli aut culpæ capaci, non parcitur; qualis est is, qui proximus est pubertati; ideo furti, bonorum raptorum, & damni iniuria dati, tenetur. l. impuberem 23. de furt. Huc pertinet l.3. in pr. de sepulch. viol. Illius edicti verba sunt: cum dolo malo violatum est sepulchrum. Ea verba demonstrant; eum tantum teneri, qui dolo malo sepulchrum violauit: Si dolus abfuit, cessabit pœna edicti. Ius iudicium que edicti sequitur personam. Ergo in pœnalibus iudiciis admodum impuberibus parcitur; pubertibus nō, necetiam pubertati proximis. Minoribus etiam 25. annis, in delictis, quæ veniunt animi destinatione, non parcitur, vt in furto. l. si ex causa 9. §. nunc videndum 2. l. auxilium 37. de minorib. Nam inquit d. l. auxilium, vtique in actionibus. Vtique, hoc est, maxime, vt in d. l. si ex causa, §. nunc videndum. At in aliis causis poenalibus, quae sunt extra delicta, saepe minoribus 25. annis parcitur. Mater, quae filiis non petit tutorem, amittit successionem eorum. Excusatur autem, si minor fuerit annis 25. Nam ius forte ignorauit propter aetatem. Et si minor 25. annis falsum testamentum dixerit, in quo sibi legatum erat legatum, nec obtinuerit, legatum tamen consequetur, & venia aetati dabitur. l. 5. §. aetati 9. de his quae vt indign. Sic si minor 25. annis filiofam. pecuniam credidit, non amittit creditum. Verisimile est enim scientem non fecisse contra Senatusconsult. Macedonianum. Et generaliter; vbi non est delictum, sed iuris ignorantia, non laeduntur minores 25. annis l. regula 9. §. 1. de iur. & facti ignor. Ait lex; ignorantiae succurri, hoc est, imperitiae & rusticitati. Quod si quis omnino imperitus homo album Praetoris corruperit, non tenetur. l. si quis id quod 7. de Iurisdict. Idem est, si in ius vocatus aliquis rudis non venerit. l. 2. si quis in ius voc. non venerit. Imprudentiae enim hoc loco succurritur. Sic etiam succurritur casui improuiso, vt imprudentiae teli emissi. l. aut factum. 16. §. euentus 8. de poen. Interdum non parcitur rusticitati.
units.tr: Relief] so that the penalty is remitted. law 8, above, on those who are noted for infamy. Accursius wrongly takes "age" to mean old age. For in criminal actions relief is not given to the old, although they ought to be punished more mildly. And it is established in our law that "age," when stated absolutely, means the age of minors under 25 years, or of those below puberty. There is, however, a great difference between those below puberty and those who are indeed of puberty but still under 25 years. The Twelve Tables order that a pubescent person be beaten and that the damage he caused be made good; but an impubes is not so bound for theft. A pubescent person is nevertheless liable for theft. Again, an impubes is spared if he is not capable of wrongful intent; a pubescent person capable of wrongful intent or fault is not spared, such as one who is close to puberty; therefore he is liable for theft, for goods seized by force, and for damage wrongfully done. law impuberem 23, on theft. Law 3, at the beginning, on violation of tombs pertains here. The words of that edict are: "where a tomb has been violated by wrongful intent." Those words show that only the one who violated the tomb with wrongful intent is liable; if wrongful intent was absent, the penalty of the edict will cease. The right of judgment and of the edict follows the person. Therefore in criminal judgments those who are quite below puberty are spared, but the pubescent are not, nor even those close to puberty. Minors of 25 years are also not spared in offences that arise from a purpose of the mind, as in theft. law si ex causa 9, §nunc videndum; law auxilium 37, on minors. For, as law auxilium says, "certainly in actions." "Certainly," that is, most of all, as in the said law si ex causa, §nunc videndum. But in other penal causes, which lie outside offences, relief is often given to minors of 25 years. A mother who does not ask for a guardian for her sons forfeits their succession. But she is excused if she was under 25 years, for perhaps she did not know the law because of her age. And if a minor of 25 years alleged a forged will, in which a legacy had been left to himself, and did not succeed, he will nevertheless obtain the legacy, and pardon will be given to his age. law 5, §aetati 9, on those things which are unworthy. So too, if a minor of 25 years lent money to a son under his father's power, he does not lose the loan. For it is probable that he did not knowingly act against the Senatusconsultum Macedonianum. And in general: where there is no offence but ignorance of the law, minors of 25 years are not harmed. law regula 9, §1, on ignorance of law and fact. The law says that ignorance is relieved, that is, inexperience and rusticity. But if someone who was wholly inexperienced corrupted the praetor's edict list, he is not liable. law si quis id quod 7, on jurisdiction. The same holds if a rustic man who was summoned to court did not come. law 2, if someone who was summoned to court did not come. For here relief is given to lack of judgment. So too relief is given to an unforeseen event, such as the lack of judgment of one who has let fly a missile. law aut factum 16, §eventus 8, on penalties. Sometimes rusticity is not spared.

units.la: Digitized by Google sticitati. l.2. C. de in ius voc. Si quis parentem vocauerit sine venia, poena proposita est. Sed quid si stultus & rerum omnium ignorans; an tenebitur? Sic sane. Nam nemo est adeo rudis, vt ignoret, parentes honoribus esse afficiendos & patronos. Sic in L. Aquil. imperitia culpae assignatur. l.132. inf. hoc tit. quae est ex l. idem iuris ad L. Aquil. Medicus imperite secuit, Lege Aquilia tenetur. Igitur quod haec regula ait: In omnibus fere: hic articulus, fere, refertur tum ad aetatem, tum ad imprudentiam. Nam & aetati & imprudentiae interdum succurritur, interdum non. Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: Rusticity. law 2, C. on summoning to court. If anyone summoned a parent without permission, a penalty is prescribed. But what if someone was foolish and ignorant of all things; would he be liable? Certainly so. For no one is so rude as not to know that parents and patrons are to be honoured. Thus in the Lex Aquilia, lack of skill is imputed as fault. law 132, below, in this title, which is from the law "the same of right" on the Lex Aquilia. A doctor who cut unskilfully is liable under the Lex Aquilia. Therefore, when this rule says "in almost all," the word "almost" applies both to age and to lack of judgment. For relief is sometimes given to both age and lack of judgment, and sometimes not. Cuiacius, in Recitations.

units.la: Ad Leg. 109. De eo qui non prohibet.
units.tr: On Law 109. Concerning one who does not prohibit.

units.la: NVllum crimen patitur is, qui non prohibet, cum prohibere (non) potest.
units.tr: He suffers no charge who does not prohibit, when he cannot prohibit.

units.la: Nullum] ex tit. de iis qui not. infam. v. l. liberorum & seq. eod. tit.
units.tr: Nullum] from the title On those who are marked with infamy; see the law Liberorum and the following law of the same title.

units.la: Patitur] an hoc significat, extra causam delicti esse, vt Ramus Praeceptor meus interpretatur. l.50. sup. eod. l.1. sup. de noxa, an potius volentem nullam iniuriam pati? l.34. C. de transact. Gothofr.
units.tr: Patitur] Does this mean that he is outside the cause of the offence, as Ramus, my teacher, interprets it, see the law 50 above in the same title, and the law 1 above On noxal actions? Or rather that one who consents suffers no injury? See the law 34 C. On transactions. Gothofredus.

units.la: Cum prohibere] 6. Harmen. 2. cum prohibere possit, ὁ δυνάμενος κωλύειν. 2. Eclog. 3. c. 107. hinc variae sententiae nascuntur. Qui cogitur, proprie non peccat. l.15. sup. de publicanis. Qui patitur, cum possit iniuriam propulsare, de iniuria iuria queri non potest, l.34. C. de transact. Qui patitur alteri iniuriam inferri, cum eam prohibere possit, tenetur. l.45. sup. ad L. Aquil. l.3. sup. de nox. act. l.24. §.6. sup. de damno. Gothof.
units.tr: Cum prohibere] Harmenopulus 6.2: "since he is able to prevent" [ὁ δυνάμενος κωλύειν]; Eclogae 2.3.107. Hence various opinions arise. One who is compelled does not, strictly speaking, sin (law 15 above On publicans). One who suffers, when he could repel the injury, cannot complain of an injury, as an injured party (law 34 C. On transactions). One who allows an injury to be done to another, when he could prevent it, is liable (law 45 above On the Lex Aquilia; law 3 above On noxal actions; law 24 §6 above On damage). Gothofredus.

units.la: Vide quæ dicta sunt sup. ad Leg 50.
units.tr: See what has been said above on Law 50.

units.la: Ad Leg.110. Plus vel minus. Expromissor alie- næ rei. Pupillus. Verba non coniuncta. Mulieres.
units.tr: On Law 110. More or less. A surety for another's thing. A ward. Words not joined. Women.

units.la: IN eo, quod plus sit, semper inest & minus. §.1. Nemo alienæ rei expromissor idoneus videtur, nisi cum satisdatione. §.2. Pupillus pari non posse intelligitur. §.3. vbi verba coniuncta non sunt, sufficit, alterutrum esse factum. §.4. Mulieribus tunc succurrendum est, cum defendantur, non vt facilius calumnientur.
units.tr: In that which is greater, the less is always contained. §1. No one is considered a suitable surety for another's thing unless he gives security (satisdatio). §2. A ward is understood to be unable to consent in the same way as an adult. §3. Where the words are not joined together, it is enough that one of them has been done. §4. Women are to be given aid when they are defended, but not so that they may more easily bring false accusations.

units.la: In eo l.21. sup. eod. l.27. §.5. sup. de pact. l.27. §.3. in sin. sup. de arbitris. l.9. sup. de in lit. iurand. l.9. §.3. supr. de hared. instit. l.15. sup. de legatis. 1. l.3. §.5. sup. de adimend. l.3. §.6. sup. de statulib. l.1. §.4. sup. de verb. oblig. adde l.26. sup. eod. l.163. & 165. infr. eod. adde l.29. sup. de haeredibus instituend. Gothof.
units.tr: In that [case] law 21, above, same title; law 27, §5, above, on pacts; law 27, §3, near the end, above, on arbitrators; law 9, above, on the oath in litem; law 9, §3, above, on inheritances instituted; law 15, above, on legacies; 1. law 3, §5, above, on ademption; law 3, §6, above, on statuliberi; law 1, §4, above, on verbal obligations. Add law 26, above, same title; laws 163 and 165, below, same title; add law 29, above, on instituting heirs. Gothof.

units.la: Inest id est, continetur, vt, qui plus præstet, præstet & minus. At is, qui quid tenetur præstare, minus dando non liberatur. l.120. & 202. sup. de verb. oblig. Gothof.
units.tr: Is contained, that is, is included, so that whoever performs more also performs less. But he who is bound to perform something is not released by giving less. l.120. & 202. sup. de verb. oblig. Gothof.

units.la: Minus non sequitur tamen, vt, cui viginti desunt, desiunt, desint decem, non sequitur quoque, vt fideiussor in maiorem summam datus quam debet principalis, teneatur saltem ratione minoris. l.8. §.7. sup. de fideiuss. vt qui decem locare existimet, Titio quinque condicere existimante, maneat actus in quinque. l.52. sup. locati. Gothof.
units.tr: Less does not, however, follow in this way: if twenty are lacking, it does not follow that ten are lacking as well. Nor does it follow that a guarantor given for a larger sum than the principal debtor owes is bound at least to the extent of the lesser sum. l.8. §.7. sup. de fideiuss. Likewise, one who thinks he is letting out ten, when Titius thinks he is hiring five, the transaction remains effective for five. l.52. sup. locati. Gothof.

units.la: Nemo ] aliud est in eo, qui causam nudæ absentiæ proponit, præsertim in criminalibus. v. l.13. §.1. sup. de public. iudic. Gothof.
units.tr: No one: it is otherwise for one who puts forward a mere absence as his cause, especially in criminal matters. See l.13. §.1. sup. de public. iudic. Gothof.

units.la: Expromissor ] etiam filius, cum is nihil possideat. l.93. sup eod, etiam procurator. l.10. sup. iudicatum solu. l. unica C. de satisdat. etiam defensor; quantumuis possessor immobilium & dives, Decius ex Bartoli sententia hic num.
units.tr: Surety: a son also, since he possesses nothing. l.93. sup. eod. A procurator also. l.10. sup. iudicatum solvi. l. unica C. de satisdat. A defender also, however much he is a possessor of immovables and rich. Decius, following Bartolus's opinion here, no.

units.la: 2. Gothof.
units.tr: 2. Gothof.

units.la: Nisi ] l.46. §.2. sup. de procurat. l.21. in sin. sup. quib. ex caus. maior. l.4. §.3. quib. ex caus. in possess. l.63. sup. de indic. Gothof.
units.tr: Unless ] Law 46, §2, above, on procurators; law 21, near the end, above, on those who claim restitution for minority; law 4, §3, on those who claim possession by reason of the same cause; law 63, above, on judicial inquiry. Gothof.

units.la: Cum satisdatione ] Cur ita? collige ex l.166. infr. eod.
units.tr: With security: Why so? Gather from l.166. infr. eod.

units.la: Pati posse ] sensus est, pupillum in iis, quibus patientia inducit consensum, non obligari. l.33. sup. pro socio. ut in l.4. sup. locati. scientiam eius non sufficere ad negotiationem. l.3. in sin. supr. de tributoria. & tamen iniuriam pati potest. l.3. §.1. sup. de iniuriis. Gothof.
units.tr: Able to suffer: the sense is that a ward is not bound in those matters in which submission induces consent. l.33. sup. pro socio; as in l.4. sup. locati. His knowledge is not sufficient for a transaction. l.3. in sin. supr. de tributoria. Yet he can suffer wrong. l.3. §.1. sup. de iniuriis. Gothof.

units.la: Verba coniuncta ] l.28. in sin. sup. de verb. signif.
units.tr: Words joined: l.28. in sin. sup. de verb. signif.

units.la: Sufficit] in alternatiuis sufficit, alterum impleri. c. in alternatiuis 70. de reg. in 6. l. 10. in fi. sup. de iure dot. l. 5. sup. de condit. instit. l. 13. §. 5. supr. de reb. dub. l. 78. in sin. sup. de condit. & dem. l. 44. sup. de oblig. l. 129. in sin. sup. de verb. oblig. l. 13. ˜s indic. solui. In copulatiua oratione omnes partes veras esse necesse est d. l. 129. l. 5. supr. de condit. instit. l. 13. sup. de reb. dub. Gothof.
units.tr: It suffices: in alternative clauses it suffices that one of the alternatives be fulfilled. c. in alternativis 70. de reg. in 6. l. 10. in fin. sup. de iure dot. l. 5. sup. de condit. instit. l. 13. §. 5. supr. de reb. dub. l. 78. in sin. sup. de condit. & dem. l. 44. sup. de oblig. l. 129. in sin. sup. de verb. oblig. l. 13. de indic. solvi. In a conjunctive statement all parts must be true. d. l. 129. l. 5. supr. de condit. instit. l. 13. sup. de reb. dub. Gothof.

units.la: Mulieribus] & minoribus, in quibus malitia suppler ætatem l. 3. C. si minor se maiorem dix. & quibus denique decipientibus non succurritur. l. 2. C. si res aliena pignori. mitius tamen mulier delinquens punitur. l. 1. in sin. sup. de edendo. l. 2. §. 31. l. 23. l. 30. sup. ad Velleianum. l. 18. C. ad Vellei. l. 1. sup. de iuris & facti. l. 38. §. 7. sup. de adult. l. 1. §. 10. sup. ad Turpil. 2. Eclog. 3. c. 118. §. 5. Gothofr.
units.tr: Women: and minors, in whom malice supplies age. l. 3. C. si minor se maiorem dix. And those who, finally, are not helped when they deceive. l. 2. C. si res aliena pignori. Yet a woman who offends is punished more leniently. l. 1. in sin. sup. de edendo. l. 2. §. 31. l. 23. l. 30. sup. ad Velleianum. l. 18. C. ad Vellei. l. 1. sup. de iuris & facti. l. 38. §. 7. sup. de adult. l. 1. §. 10. sup. ad Turpil. 2. Eclog. 3. c. 118. §. 5. Gothofr.

units.la: Cum defendantur] defendant Vulgat. Haloan. defraudentur, Pacius. Inesse quid dicitur pluribus modis, vt in toto pars. l. 7. de except. rei indic. l. in toto 113. inf. h. t. In maiore summa minor est. l. 1. §. si stipulanti 4. de verb. oblig. l. si quis 3. §. si quis plus. ˜s de adim. leg. sic in contractu pactum inesse dicitur, cum adiectum est. l. 7. §. quin imo. de pact. Qua de causa, si quis adimat plus, quam legauit, ademptio valet: nam ademisse videtur, quod minus est. Item si quis promittat plus, quam stipulatione continetur, valet. Si quis plus petat, ne pro parte quidem valet let stipulatio: cum tamen in eo, quod plus est, inest minus. Si vero quis petierit fundum, & non obtinuerit, secundum hanc regulam partem fundi petere non potest. Est ergo & in toto pars d. l. 7. Contra: inesse dicitur totum in partibus: propterea, quod totum non est sine partibus. Et hoc modo iurisdictio dicitur inesse in imperio mixto, quasi totum in parte. l. 3. de iurisdictione. Nam iurisdictio totum est. Eius sunt partes duae: Iurisdictio, & imperium mixtum. Contra; mixtum imperium dicitur inesse iurisdictioni, sicut pars in toto. l. 1. §. vlt. de offic. eius cui mand. Alio etiam modo dicitur inesse species in genere. l. semper specialia 147. h. t. ut in contractu inest mandatum, vel depositum. Contra etiam genus dicitur inesse in specie: ut in agnatis dicuntur esse cognati. l. pen. unde legitimi. Sed in cognatis non utique sunt agnati, hoc est, non quilibet agnati sunt cognati. In empto dicitur inesse paratum, quod varia sit paratio. l. si quid earum §. 1. de leg. 3. In parato contra non dicitur esse emptum, hoc est, non quodlibet paratum dicitur esse emptum. Genus ad probandam speciem non valet: ut recte non conficies ita. Est actio: ergo conductio. Species tamen valet ad probandum genus. Conductio est: ergo actio est. Sic non valet, si dixeris: Est cognatus: ergo agnatus. Valet tamen hoc modo: Est agnatus: ergo cognatus. Sic Accurs. in l. vlt. de
units.tr: When they are defended: the Vulgate, Haloander, read "defend"; Pacius reads "are defrauded". Something is said to be "contained" in several ways, as the part is in the whole. l. 7. de except. rei indic. l. in toto 113. inf. h. t. In a larger sum there is a smaller. l. 1. §. si stipulanti 4. de verb. oblig. l. si quis 3. §. si quis plus. sup. de adim. leg. So in a contract a pact is said to be contained when it has been added. l. 7. §. quin imo. de pact. For this reason, if someone revokes more than he bequeathed, the revocation is valid, for he is seen to have revoked what is less. Likewise, if someone promises more than is contained in the stipulation, it is valid. If someone demands more, not even in part is the stipulation valid, although the lesser is contained in the greater. If indeed someone claims a farm and does not win it, by this rule he cannot claim part of the farm. So there is also a part in the whole. d. l. 7. On the contrary: the whole is said to be contained in its parts, because the whole is not without parts. And in this way jurisdiction is said to be contained in mixed imperium, as the whole in a part. l. 3. de iurisdictione. For jurisdiction is a whole; its parts are two: jurisdiction and mixed imperium. On the contrary, mixed imperium is said to be contained in jurisdiction, as a part in the whole. l. 1. §. vlt. de offic. eius cui mand. In another way too, a species is said to be contained in a genus: as mandate or deposit is contained in a contract. On the contrary, a genus is also said to be contained in a species: as cognates are said to be in agnates. l. pen. unde legitimi. But not all agnates are cognates; that is, not every agnate is a cognate. In a purchase, the preparation is said to be contained, since preparation may vary. l. si quid earum §. 1. de leg. 3. In a preparation, on the contrary, a purchase is not said to be contained; that is, not every preparation is said to be a purchase. A genus does not prove a species: so you will not correctly conclude, "It is an action; therefore it is a hiring." But a species does prove a genus: "It is a hiring; therefore it is an action." So it is not valid if you say, "He is a cognate; therefore he is an agnate." It is valid, however, in this way: "He is an agnate; therefore he is a cognate." So Accursius on l. vlt. de

units.la: Q in integ. restit. Inesse etiam dicitur in materia forma. Inesse dicuntur in principe facultates subiectorum, Inesse etiam dicuntur propria: inesse etiam accidentia ex quadam parte. Aristot. in Topic. lib. 1.
units.tr: Q in integ. restit. Form is also said to be present in matter. The faculties of subjects are said to be present in a prince. Proper qualities are also said to be present, and accidents are present in some respect. Aristot. in Topic. lib. 1.

units.la: Ad §. Nemo alienae rei. 1.
units.tr: On §. Nemo alienae rei. 1.

units.la: Idoneus, hoc est, locuples. sic in l. qui rem alienam 166. h. t. Qui rem alienam defendit, nunquam locuples habetur. Ergo satisdatione eget, iudicatum solui. Non solet, qui est locupples, satisdare, vt Fiscus leg. 1. §. fiscum. vt legat, nom. cau. Igitur qui rem alienam defendit, non habetur pro locuplete, hoc est, satisdare debet; vt in hac etiam regula; Nemo alienae rei, &c. Interdum vero expromissor pro defensore accipitur in tit. de satisdat. Instit. in l. qui proprio 46. §. qui alium 2. de procur. Nemo ergo recte defendit sine satisdatione. Hoc loco expromissor est, qui iudicium pro alio accipit, nouandi causa: vel etiam promittit pro alio, & ita in libris nostris accipitur saepe. Et hic plane defensor est, qui in se transfert omnem litem. Eadem omnino regula constituit de procuratore, qui satisdare debet de rato, maxime si dubitetur de mandato. Non est enim procurator idoneus sine satisdatione, quod demonstrat l. hac autem 5. §. vlt. quib. ex caus. in possess. eatur. & l. recte 63. de indic. Nam satisdatio exigitur plerunplerunque tantum ab eo, qui rem alienam non suam defendit.
units.tr: Suitable, that is, wealthy. So in l. qui rem alienam 166, h. t. Someone who defends another's property is never considered wealthy. Therefore he needs security, to pay the judgment. A wealthy person does not usually give security, as the Treasury does in l. 1, §. fiscum, ut legat, nom. cau. So one who defends another's property is not regarded as wealthy, that is, he must give security. This is also the point of the rule Nemo alienae rei, etc. Sometimes, however, an expromissor is taken to mean a defender: in tit. de satisdat. Instit.; in l. qui proprio 46, §. qui alium 2, de procur. So no one rightly defends without giving security. Here the expromissor is the one who takes over a suit on behalf of another, for the purpose of novation, or who also promises for another; and in our books the term is often used in this way. The defender here is plainly the one who takes the whole lawsuit upon himself. The same rule applies to a procurator, who must give security for ratification, especially if the mandate is in doubt. A procurator is not a suitable one without security, as l. hac autem 5, §. vlt., quib. ex caus. in possess. eatur, and l. recte 63, de indic. show. For security is usually required only from one who defends property that is not his own.

units.la: Ad §. Pupillus. 2.
units.tr: On §. Pupillus. 2.

units.la: Pupillus vt non creditur nolle, nec velle sine tutoris authoritate: ita etiam non creditur non nolle, aut non velle, quod est pati, vt in specie l.sed no nita de aqua pluu. arcend. Pupilli nulla est voluntas, ne quidem tacita, de hoc diximus l.4. & 5. sup. Patitur quidem iniuriam & vim pupillus: sed non patitur, hoc est, non exercet actionem animae patibilem: non intelligitur quicquam velle, nec expresse, nec tacere.
units.tr: Just as a pupil is not believed to be unwilling or willing without the authority of his guardian, so he is also not believed to be not unwilling or not willing, which is to suffer. See the example in l. sed non ita de aqua pluv. arcend. A pupil has no will, not even a tacit one; we discussed this in l. 4 and 5, sup. A pupil indeed suffers injury and force, but he does not suffer in the sense of exercising a passive act of the mind. He is not understood to will anything, either expressly or by silence.

units.la: Ad §. Vbi verba coniuncta. 3.
units.tr: On §. Ubi verba coniuncta. 3.

units.la: Vbi verba alternatiua sunt, vt sunt duae conditiones non coniunctae, alteram fieri vel impleri sufficit: nisi cum verba non sunt coniuncta; sed pro conuinctis habentur. l. 5. de condit. instit. leg. pupillus §. ult. de condit. & dem. Item si illud aut illud legetur, satis est alterum praestare.
units.tr: Where the words are alternative, as with two conditions not joined together, it is enough to fulfil or perform one of them. This does not hold where the words are not joined, but are treated as joined. l. 5, de condit. instit.; l. pupillus §. ult., de condit. et dem. Likewise, if it is bequeathed that this or that, it is enough to give one of them.

units.la: Ad §. Mulieribus. vlt.
units.tr: On §. Mulieribus. vlt.

units.la: Pertinet ad Velleianum l.2. de SCto Velleiano. Ex hoc SCto mulieribus pro aliis intercedentibus succurritur: sed no, si callide interuenerunt, si deceperunt creditores, si interuenerunt, runt, cum creditores nescierunt, eas interuenisse: cuius rei sunt varia exempla. Cuiac. in Re-citat. posthum.
units.tr: This pertains to the Velleianum, l. 2, de SC. Velleiano. By this senatus consultum women who stand surety for others are given aid, but not if they intervened craftily, or if they deceived the creditors, or if they intervened when the creditors did not know that they had done so. There are various examples of this. Cuiac. in Recitat. posthum.

units.la: Ad Leg. III. De pupillo: heredeque actio-nibus poenalibus.
units.tr: On Leg. III. Concerning the pupil and the heir, and penal actions.

units.la: PVpillum, qui proximus pubertati sit, capacem esse & furandi, & iniuriae faciendae. §.
units.tr: A pupil who is close to puberty is capable of both theft and doing injury. §.

units.la: 1. In haeredem non solent actiones transire, quae poenales sunt ex maleficio, veluti furti, damni iniuriae, vi bonorum raptorum, iniuriarum.
units.tr: 1. Actions that are penal because of a wrong do not usually pass to the heir, such as those for theft, damage under the Aquilian law, violent seizure of goods, and injuries.

units.la: Qui proximus ] In delictis proximus pubertati pro pubere habetur v. l. 23. supr. de furt. 2. Eclog. 3. cap. 109. leg. 14. supr. de Silaniano. At non in testamenti faciendi facultate. Decim hic. Gothofr.
units.tr: Qui proximus: In delicts, one close to puberty is treated as an adult; see l. 23, supr. de furt.; Eclog. 2, 3, cap. 109; l. 14, supr. de Silaniano. But not in the capacity to make a will. Decim hic. Gothofr.

units.la: Iniuriae faciendae ] mitius tamen punitur. l. 108. sup. eod. Gothofr. Pacius addit Faciendae, vocabulo, vocem constat.
units.tr: Iniuriae faciendae: yet he is punished more leniently. l. 108, sup. eod.; Gothofr. Pacius adds faciendae; the word is established by usage.

units.la: In haeredem ] v. l. 1. sup. de priuat. delict. §. 1. Institit. de perpet. v. l. unic. C. ex delict. defuncti.
units.tr: Against the heir ] See l. 1 above, de privatis delictis; §. 1 Institutes, de perpetuis et temporalibus actionibus; l. unic. C. ex delicto defuncti.

units.la: Non solent ] regulariter. Nam lite cum defuncto contestata transmittuntur v. l. 164. inf. eod. Multo magis si defuncto poena ipso iure erat imposita, ut in l. 22. sup. de Silaniano. L. 14. sup. de publicanis. Tenetur etiam haeres ex eo, quod ad eum peruenit. l. 38. sup. eod. l. 5. sup. de calum. l. 26. supr. de dolo. & poena defuncto imposita transftransmittitur in eius hæredes. l. 3. §. 5. sup. quod quisque. Gothofr.
units.tr: Non solent: as a general rule. For once the suit has been joined with the deceased, the actions pass on (see l. 164, inf. eod.). Much more so if a penalty was imposed on the deceased by law itself, as in l. 22, sup. de Silaniano; l. 14, sup. de publicanis. The heir is also liable for what came to him from the wrong, l. 38, sup. eod.; l. 5, sup. de calum.; l. 26, supr. de dolo. A penalty imposed on the deceased is also transmitted to his heirs. l. 3, §. 5, sup. quod quisque. Gothofr.

units.la: Quæ pœnales ] aliud in pecuniariis l. 22. sup. de Silaniano. & condictione furtiva: l. 7. §. 2. sup. de cond. furt. Gothof.
units.tr: Quae poenales: different for pecuniary penalties, l. 22, sup. de Silaniano, and for the condictio furtiva, l. 7, §. 2, sup. de cond. furt. Gothofr.

units.la: Veluti furti ] d. §. 1. Instit. de perpet. & temp. act.
units.tr: Veluti furti: d. §. 1, Instit. de perpet. et temp. act.

units.la: Damni ] l. 23. §. 8. sup. ad L. Aquiliam.
units.tr: Damni: l. 23, §. 8, sup. ad L. Aquiliam.

units.la: Vi ] l. 2. in sin. sup. vi bon. rapt.
units.tr: Vi: l. 2, in sin., sup. vi bon. rapt.

units.la: Iniuriarum ] d. §. 1. Instit. de perp. & temp. act.
units.tr: Iniuriarum: d. §. 1, Instit. de perp. et temp. act.

units.la: Vide sup. in l. 108. item in l. 38.
units.tr: See above on l. 108, and also on l. 38.

units.la: Ad Leg. 112. De actione non compe- tente & exceptione.
units.tr: On Leg. 112: On an action that does not lie, and on exception.

units.la: NIhil interest, ipso iure quis actionem non habeat, aut per exceptionem infirmetur.
units.tr: It makes no difference whether someone lacks an action in law or is defeated by an exception.

units.la: Per exceptionem ] l. 13. §. 1. & 66. sup. eod. l. 7. §. 8. sup. de dolo l. 7. §. 14. inf. sup. quib. ex causs. in possess. l. 1. §. 10. sup. ad Turpil. Goth.
units.tr: By exception: l. 13 §1 and 66 above, same title; l. 7 §8 above, de dolo; l. 7 §14 below, quib. ex causs. in possess.; l. 1 §10 above, ad Turpil. Goth.

units.la: Vide notata supra ad Leg. 13. & inf. ad l. 115.
units.tr: See the notes above on Leg. 13, and below on l. 115.

units.la: Ad Leg. 113. De toto & parte.
units.tr: On Leg. 113: On the whole and the part.

units.la: INtoto & pars continetur.
units.tr: In the whole, the part is contained.

units.la: Intoto ] totum in loco, ut ubique: in tempore, ut semper: in modo, cuius partes sunt accidentales, ut possessio bonæ, malæ fidei, qualitatis, ut omnis, nullus, quilibet, centum: integrale, cuius partes essentiales integræ, græ, vel homogeneæ, vt in aqua, aut heterogeneæ, vt partes totius compoliti, totum quiddam efficiunt, vt ædificium, fundamenta, parietes, & rectum: totum vniuersale est vel personarum, vt ciuitas, collegium, ducatus, comitatus, regnum & similia: vel rerum, vt hæreditas, domus, grex, equitium, armentum: totum naturale vel artificiale, cui nulla pars naturalis aut artificialis deest. Goth.
units.tr: "In the whole": the whole in place, as everywhere; in time, as always; in mode, whose parts are accidental, as good possession, bad faith, quality; as all, none, whoever, a hundred. Integral, whose parts are essential and whole, either homogeneous as in water, or heterogeneous as the parts of a compound whole, which together make up a thing, as a building: foundations, walls and roof. The universal whole is either of persons, as a city, a college, a duchy, a county, a kingdom and the like; or of things, as an inheritance, a house, a flock, a herd of horses or cattle. A natural or artificial whole, lacking no natural or artificial part. Goth.

units.la: Et pars ] l. 21. sup. eod. l. 147. sup. eod. l. 7. sup. de except. rei iudic. c. plus 35. c. in toto 80. de reg. in 6. Gothofr.
units.tr: And the part: l. 21 above, same title; l. 147 above, same title; l. 7 above, de except. rei iudic.; c. plus 35, c. in toto 80, de reg. in 6. Gothofr.

units.la: Vide quæ proxime dicta sunt. ad l. 110.
units.tr: See what was said just before, on l. 110.

units.la: Ad Leg. 114. De ob- scuris.
units.tr: On Leg. 114: On unclear matters.

units.la: IN obscuris inspici solet quod verisimilius est, aut quod plerunque fieri solet.
units.tr: In unclear matters one usually looks to what is more likely, or to what usually happens.

units.la: Inspici solet ] quo gradu? voluntas prius spectatur, tum verisimilius, propria deinde verborum significatio, ab hac id quod minus est. Id si non apparet, actus iudicatur non valere. v. Dynum ad c. 45. de reg. in 6. num. 5. Goth. Pro solet, Pacius solere.
units.tr: One usually looks: by what degree? First the intention is considered, then what is more likely, then the proper meaning of the words, and after that what is less. If this does not appear, the act is judged not to be valid. See Dynus on c. 45, de reg. in 6, n. 5. Goth. For "solet", Pacius has "solere".

units.la: Quod verisimilius ] verisimilius præsumitur. c. inspicimus 45. de reg. in 6. 2. Eclog. 3. c. iii. in dubio scilicet & iudicando, & litibus dicidendis: quod sæpissime faciunt ICti, vt docet Tiraq. in repet. legis si vnquam 8. C. de reuoc. donat. num.37. ad 60. Non verisimile, credibile non est, nec attenditur: pro eo non præsumitur. l. 13. sup. quod metus l. 19. §. 4. sup. de peculio l. 6. sup. de pignorib. leg. 41. sup. de manumiss. testam. imaginem habet falsitatis. Verisimile ducitur ex more, consuetudine, iis quæ fieri solita sunt frequentius, communi opinione, natura, qualitatibus rei, vel personis, tempore, de quib. vide Oldend. in Topic. in loco, à conjectura seu præsumpt. sumitur etiam à pietate l. 41. §. 2. inf. sup. de leg. 3. l. 102. sup. de condit. & demonstrat. l. 30. C. de fideicom. rerum inter se comparatione. l. 1. sup. de rebus dub. & aliis conjecturis l. 13. sup. de prob. l. 50. in sin. sup. de legatis 1. Goth.
units.tr: What is more likely: what is more likely is presumed. c. inspicimus 45, de reg. in 6; Eclog. 2, 3; c. iii. In doubt, that is, in judging and in settling suits, which lawyers do very often, as Tiraquellus teaches on the law si unquam 8, C. de revoc. donat., n. 37, to 60. What is not likely, what is not credible, is neither regarded nor presumed in its favour: l. 13 above, quod metus; l. 19 §4 above, de peculio; l. 6 above, de pignorib.; l. 41 above, de manumiss. testam. It has the appearance of falsehood. What is likely is judged from custom, habit, what usually happens more often, common opinion, nature, the qualities of the thing or of the persons, and time; on which see Oldendorp, Topica, under the heading from conjecture or presumption. It is also taken from piety, l. 41 §2 below, de leg. 3; l. 102 above, de condit. et demonstrat.; l. 30 C. de fideicom.; from comparing things with one another, l. 1 above, de rebus dub., and from other conjectures, l. 13 above, de prob.; l. 50 at the end, above, de legatis 1. Goth.

units.la: Variis modis obscura deciduntur, ut sup. expositi. Inspicitur quod est verisimilius egisse contrahentes. l. qui Insulam qui pot. in pig. Inspicitur quod plerunque fieri solet. l. pactum de probat. & quod in ea regione frequentatur. leg. semper in stipulationibus h. tit. Cuiac. in Recitat. posthum.
units.tr: Obscure matters are settled in various ways, as explained above. One looks at what is more likely to be what the contracting parties intended: l. qui Insulam, qui pot. in pig. One looks at what usually happens: l. pactum de probat. and at what is common in that region: leg. semper in stipulationibus, h. tit.; Cuiacius, in Recitationes posthumae.

units.la: Ad Leg. 115. Qui videntur cepisse seu accepisse.
units.tr: On Leg. 115: Those who are said to have taken, or to have received.

units.la: SI quis obligatione liberatus sit, potest videri cepisse. §. 1. Non potest videri accepisse, qui stipulatus potest exceptione submoveri. St. ex tit. de calum. Coniunge l. 2. eod. tit. quæ idem pene principium habet. Pac.
units.tr: If someone has been freed from an obligation, he may be said to have taken. §1. A man who has been sued cannot be said to have received if he can be turned away by an exception. St., from the title de calumniatoribus. Compare l. 2 of the same title, which has almost the same beginning. Pac.

units.la: Obligatione ] obligatione liberatus, cepisse intelligitur: dare videtur, qui debitum remittit. l.2. l.3. sup. de calumniat. l.10. in sin. sup. de condict. causa. l.41. §. 2. sup. de condict. causa. l.41. §. 2. sup. de iure dot. l.3. §. 10. sup. de don. inter virum & vx. l.81. §. 5. sup. de leg. 1. non tamen litigiosum, poenale & ob aliam causam l.19 sup. de lib. causa. vid. Decium hic. Goth.
units.tr: Freed from an obligation: one who is freed from an obligation is understood to have taken; he who remits a debt is seen to give. l. 2, l. 3 above, de calumniat.; l. 10 at the end above, de condict. causa; l. 41 §2 above, de condict. causa; l. 41 §2 above, de iure dot.; l. 3 §10 above, de don. inter virum et uxorem; l. 81 §5 above, de leg. 1. Not, however, a disputed claim, a penal one, or one owed for another reason: l. 19 above, de lib. causa. See Decius here. Goth.

units.la: Potest videri] vox, videri; nota est fictionis.
units.tr: He may be said: the word "may be said" is a mark of fiction.

units.la: Ideoque proprie aliud est dare, aliud remittere. l.46. sup. de cond. & demonstr. Goth.
units.tr: And so, strictly speaking, to give is one thing and to remit another. l. 46 above, de cond. et demonstr. Goth.

units.la: Cepisse] accepisse.
units.tr: To have taken: that is, to have received.

units.la: Exceptione] l.13. sup. eod. v. l.112. sup. eod. l.24. sup. de nouat. Goth.
units.tr: By exception: l. 13 above, same title; cf. l. 112 above, same title; l. 24 above, de novat. Goth.

units.la: Duae sunt huius L. sententiae: in prima vitur illo verbo Cepisse. Hoc ideo, quia in illo edicto de calumniatoribus utimur promiscue his verbis, Cepisse, & accepisse; vt in edicto: si cui plus, quam per L. Falcid, &c. Et ad illud sunt referenda in l.71. tit. prox. Aliud est capere, aliud accipere: quae lex, quamuis haec verba, capere & accipere, promiscue accipiantur in Edictis: tamen interea ostendit subtilem quandam differentiam: quae est, vt capere sit cum effectu. Capio id, quod omnino mecum remansurum est. Accipio etiam, quod omnino sum restituturus. Sed haec differentia, neque in eo seruatur edicto, neque in edicto de calumniatoribus. Est vero haec sententia longe diuersa ab ea, quam affert Bulg b.l.115. Ca-pitut pitur vel ex nuda obligatione, vel ex vltima voluntate: accipitur ex pacto. Sententia falsa est. Et præterea in hac lege, aliud est capere, quod pertinet ad illud edictum, Si cui plus, quam per L. Falcid. Vltimo loco docet, quemadmodum sint intelligenda verba, His PRÆSTARI RECTE, atque ita commode tota lex hæc ad edictum illud conferetur. Hoc igitur colligamus ex his quæ dicta sunt: Cepisse videri non tantum eum, qui rem habet, sed & eum, qui habet actionem, siue exceptionem, remotionem; nam videtur rem ipsam habere. l.15.h.tit.&ita l.si partem 19.quemadmodum seruitutes. §. si cui fundus Instit. de legat. & l.magis §. fundum 8. de reb. eorum, qui sub tut. ait, legatum acquiri, significans legatorum actionem acquiri ignoranti. l. quæsitum 91. §. penult. de leg.
units.tr: This law has two meanings. The first rests on the word "to take" (capere). This is because in that edict on calumniators we use the words "to take" and "to receive" interchangeably, as in the edict: if anyone receives more than the Falcidian law allows, and so on. And to that edict the matters in l. 71 of the next title refer. To take is one thing, to receive another; this law, though these words, "to take" and "to receive", are used interchangeably in the edicts, nevertheless indicates a certain subtle difference, namely that to take is to take with effect: I take what will certainly remain with me; I receive also what I will certainly have to return. But this difference is observed neither in that edict nor in the edict on calumniators. Indeed this opinion is very different from the one that Bulgarus (b.l. 115) gives: one takes either from the bare obligation or from the last will; one receives from a pact. That opinion is false. Moreover, in this law, to take is one thing, and it relates to that edict: If anyone takes more than the Falcidian law allows. In the last place it teaches how the words "to be paid rightly" (his praestari recte) are to be understood, and so this whole law is conveniently applied to that edict. Let us therefore gather from what has been said: one is seen to have taken not only if he has the thing, but also if he has an action, or an exception, that is, a means of removing (an obstacle); for he is seen to have the thing itself. l. 15 of this title; and so l. si partem 19, quemadmodum servitutes; §si cui fundus, Instit. de legat.; and l. magis, §fundum 8, de reb. eorum qui sub tut. says that a legacy is acquired, meaning that the action for the legacy is acquired by one who does not know of it. l. quaesitum 91, §penult., de leg.

units.la: 1. His verbis, LEGATVM ACQVIRITVR, non significatur dominii acquisitio, sed diei cessio, & recte Interpres ad L. illam 15. inquit, qui legatum agnouit, quia habet actionem, in hoc ipso legatum habere videtur, vt hoc voluntas defuncti complere possit. Denique hæc verba, capere, habere & peruenire, plerunque cum effectu accipimus. d.l. aliud est capere sup. tit. prox. & cepisse videtur, qui actionem habet cum effectu, vt in l.13. sup. hoc tit. sic etiam habere d.l. 15. Sic peruenire in cautione emptæ hæreditatis. l.2. §. peruenisse 3. de hared. vel act. vend.
units.tr: 1. By the words "a legacy is acquired" is not meant the acquisition of ownership, but the transfer of a claim; and the commentator rightly says on the law illam 15 that one who has acknowledged a legacy, because he has an action, is seen to have the legacy in this very fact, so that he can fulfil the will of the deceased. Finally, we ordinarily take the words "to take", "to have" and "to come to" (capere, habere, pervenire) in the sense of taking effect. d.l. aliud est capere, above, the previous title; and one is seen to have taken who has an action with effect, as in l. 13 above, this title; so also to have, as in the same law 15. So too "to come to" in a security for a purchased inheritance. l. 2 §pervenisse 3, de hered. vel act. vend.

units.la: hic sic in cautione, quæ ex L. Iulia à marito præstatur vxori. l. si vero 64 §. Item quicquid. soluto matrim. Denique habere, ad eum peruenisse, cepisse videtur is, qui habet actionem cum effectu, vel quod est idem, sine exceptionis metu, & non tantum is, qui habet ad rem adipiscendam, sed etiam is, qui actionem habet ad rem recuperandam, & ita legito in l. 15. sup. hoc tit. Et hoc propositio actionis nomen est latissime sumptum, quia interdictum & restitutio in integrum sub eo comprehenditur. l. si quis vi 17. de acquirenda possess. Nam qui restitutionem in integrum habet, non videtur exclusus. l. nemo 5. de in integ. restit. Sed non dicemus, eum habere actionem, qui potest exceptione remoueri. Nam vt ait l. nihil interest 112. sup. hoc tit. nihil interest, vtrum ipsum ius te excludat, an exceptio. Ordo tamen iuris & causa est diuersa, ideo in iure maxime disputatur de ipso iure, vtilis, an directa detur. l. actio 47. de negot. gest. quia scilicet idem est effectus, agendi tantum forma & causa est diuersa, & licet effectus sit idem, accidentia tamen sunt diuersa: igitur ad effectum respicientes, dicemus, non habere actionem eum, qui exceptione repelRitur. Cui in Recit. posthum.
units.tr: Thus also in the security which a husband gives to his wife under the Julian law. l. si vero 64 §Item quicquid, soluto matrim. Finally, one who has an action with effect, or what is the same, without fear of an exception, is seen to have, to have come to, or to have taken; and this is said not only of one who has a right to obtain a thing, but also of one who has an action to recover a thing; and so read it in l. 15 above, this title. And this proposition, the name of action is taken very widely, since an interdict and restitution in integrum are included under it. l. si quis vi 17, de acquir. possess. For one who has restitution in integrum is not seen as excluded. l. nemo 5, de in integr. restit. But we shall not say that one has an action if he can be removed by an exception. For, as l. nihil interest 112, above, this title says, it makes no difference whether the law itself shuts you out or an exception does.
