The order and the cause of the law, however, are different; therefore in law the question is chiefly raised about the law itself, whether the action is given as useful or as direct. l. actio 47, de negot. gest. Because, of course, the effect is the same and only the form and cause of the action differ; and although the effect is the same, the circumstances are nevertheless different. Therefore, looking to the effect, we shall say that one who is repelled by an exception does not have an action. Cuiacius, in Recitationes posthumae.

units.la: litur.
units.tr: ...is repelled.

units.la: Ad Leg. 116. De consensu, vi, metu. 2. De eo qui ius publicum sequitur.
units.tr: On Law 116, On consent, force, and fear. 2. On one who follows public law.

units.la: 3. De errore.
units.tr: 3. On error.

units.la: Nihil consensui tam contrarium est, qui bonae fidei iudicia sustinet, quam vis atque metus: quem comprobare contra bonos mores est. §. 1. Non capitur, qui ius publicum sequitur. §. 2. Non videntur, qui errant, consentire.
units.tr: Nothing is so contrary to consent, which upholds actions of good faith, as force and fear. To approve of it is contrary to good morals. §. 1. One who follows public law is not taken in. §. 2. Those who err are not thought to consent.

units.la: Est haec lex ex Vlpiani lib. 11. ad Edict. quo libro tractauit de restitutionibus in integrum. Prima sententia pertinet ad edictum, Quod metus causa. Ex hac regula confirmari potest: quod sicut dolus dans causam contractui bonae fidei, vitiat contractum & infirmat: ita vis & metus. Nam in metu inest dolus: adeo ut concurrat currat actio, Quod metus causa, cum actione de dolo. l. item si cum 14. §. eum qui 13. quod metus causa. In deposito non licet pacisci de dolo. l. 1. §. illud depositi. ita nec de metu. Itaque si convenerit de metu, conventio est contra bonam fidem, & contra bonos mores.
units.tr: This law is from Ulpian, book 11 on the Edict, where he treated of restitution in integrum. The first opinion pertains to the edict "Quod metus causa." From this rule it can be confirmed that just as deceit giving cause to a contract of good faith vitiates and invalidates the contract, so do force and fear. For fear contains deceit, so that the action "Quod metus causa" runs together with the action of deceit. l. item si cum 14. §. eum qui 13. quod metus causa. In a deposit it is not permitted to agree about deceit; l. 1. §. illud depositi. so neither is it permitted about fear. Therefore, if there has been an agreement about fear, the agreement is against good faith and against good morals.

units.la: Ad §. Non capitur.
units.tr: On the paragraph "Non capitur."

units.la: Pertinet & hic §. ad Edictum de minoribus 25. annis, qui capti sunt, hoc est, decepti, & hi restituuntur. At non decipiuntur qui iuris communis sequuntur. Exemplum est in l. inter eos 51. §. pen. de fideiuss. Ius commune est, ut, si sint plures fideiussores, teneantur in solidum singuli. habeant tamen beneficium diuisionis, quod ita habent, si litis contestatae tempore omnes soluendo sint. Caeterum si quidam sint inopes, hoc onerat locupletes. Verum si omnes sint soluendo, diuidatur actio: & si post litem contestatam quidam fiant non soluendo, alii non tenebuntur. Nunc finge: Egit minor 25. annis cum fideiussoribus: diuisa est actio: quidam post litem contestatam facti sunt non soluendo; an succurritur minori ob aetatem? Minime. Nam non succurritur, nisi capto & circumscripto. Non videtur autem deceptus, qui iure communi est usus & diuisit actionem inter fideiussores, qui tempore litis contestatæ soluendo fuerunt. Eadem sententia repetitur in l. vlt. C. de in integ. restit.
units.tr: This paragraph also pertains to the edict concerning those under 25 years of age, de minoribus 25. annis, those who were taken in, that is, deceived, and these are restored. But those who follow the common law are not deceived. An example is found in l. inter eos 51. §. pen. de fideiuss. It is the common law that, if there are several sureties, each is bound for the whole; yet they have the benefit of division, which they have if all are solvent at the time of the litigation. But if some are insolvent, this burdens the wealthy. If, however, all are solvent, the action is divided; and if after the suit has begun some become insolvent, the others are not bound. Now suppose: a minor under 25 sued the sureties; the action was divided; some after the suit became insolvent. Is help given to the minor because of his age? Certainly not. For help is not given unless he was taken in and circumvented. But one is not seen to be deceived who used the common law and divided the action among the sureties who were solvent at the time of the litigation. The same opinion is repeated in l. vlt. C. de in integ. restit.

units.la: Ad §. Non videntur.
units.tr: On the paragraph "Non videntur."

units.la: Pertinet ad causam restitutionis in integrum. Restitutio datur ob metum illatum, ad quam pertinet prima sententia. Restitutio in integrum datur ob ætatem, ad quam pertinet secunda. Datur etiam ob errorem iustum, ad quam sententiam pertinet l. 3. de in integ. restit. l. 1. §. vlt. quod falso tut. aut ad quam pertinet vltima hæc sententia: qui lapsi sunt errore, restituuntur, quia non consenserunt. Cuiac. in Resp. posthum.
units.tr: This pertains to the cause of restitution in integrum. Restitution is given on account of fear inflicted, to which the first opinion pertains. Restitution in integrum is given on account of age, to which the second pertains. It is also given for just error, to which opinion pertains l. 3. de in integ. restit. l. 1. §. vlt. quod falso tut. or to which the last of these opinions pertains: those who have lapsed through error are restored, because they did not consent. Cuiac. in Resp. posthum.

units.la: Ad Leg. 117. De bonorum possessione.
units.tr: On Law 117. Concerning bonorum possessio.

units.la: PRætor bonorum possessionem, hæredis loco, in omni causa habet.
units.tr: The praetor has the bonorum possessio, in the place of the heir, in every case.

units.la: Bonorum possessionem] Alii, bonorum possessorem legunt, & is à Græcis hîc κληρονόμος appellatur, id est, successor. 2. Eclog. 2. c. 115. Goth.
units.tr: Bonorum possessionem] Others read bonorum possessorem, and the Greeks here call him κληρονόμος [klēronomos], that is, successor. 2. Eclog. 2. c. 115. Goth.

units.la: Hæredis loco] l. 25. §. 7. sup. de acquir. hared. v. l. 29. §. 2. sup. de condit. & demonst. l. 2. sup. de bon. possess. Goth.
units.tr: In place of the heir [Hæredis loco]: Dig. 25.7 above, on acquiring heirs; and Dig. 29.2 above, on conditions and demonstrations; Dig. 2 above, on possession of goods. Gothofredus.

units.la: Pertinet etiam hæc lex ad restitutionem in integrum, quæ est Pauli ad Edict. lib. 11. Restitutio in integrum transfertur in hæredem. l. 3. de in integ. restit. An & in bonorum possessorem rem: Ita. Quia praetor illum habet in omni causa haredis vice. l. 2. de bon. possess. Praetor heredem non facit, ut nec dominum. Si quem Praetor iussit possidere, vsucapio competere dicitur, vt sit dominus: alter erit tantum possessor. In omni causa, hoc est, siue agat, siue cum eo agatur: siue experiatur, siue conueniatur vt recte Bulgarus, & sustinet incommodum omne, & commodum hereditatis, perinde ac si heres esset iure ciuili: & restituitur quis aduersus eum, veluti aduersus heredem. Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: This law also bears on restitutio in integrum, as Paul says in book 11 of his commentary on the Edict: "Restitutio in integrum is transferred to the heir." l. 3. de in integ. restit. Does it also extend to the possessor of the goods? Yes, because the praetor has him in every case in the place of the heir. l. 2. de bon. possess. The praetor does not make someone heir, any more than he makes him owner. If the praetor has ordered someone to possess, he is said to have usucapion available, so that he becomes owner; otherwise he will be only a possessor. "In every case" means whether he sues or is sued, whether he brings the action or the action is brought against him, as Bulgarus rightly says; and he bears every burden and enjoys every benefit of the inheritance, just as if he were heir by civil law; and one is restored against him just as against an heir. Cuiac. in Recit.

units.la: Ad Leg. 118. De vsucap- ione. De possessione.
units.tr: On Law 118. On Usucaption. On Possession.

units.la: Qui ... Q Vi in seruitute est, vsucapere non poterit. Nam cum possideatur, possidere non videtur.
units.tr: Qui ... A person who is in servitude cannot acquire by usucaption, for since he is himself possessed, he is not considered to possess.

units.la: Qui ] ex tit. Quib. ex causis maiores, &c. vbi de vsucapione multa. Pac.
units.tr: Qui] from the title Quibus ex causis maiores, &c., where much is said about usucaption. Pac.

units.la: In seruitute ] & in potestate. l. 93. sup. eod.
units.tr: In servitude] and in power (potestas). l. 93 above, same title.

units.la: Vsucapere ] l. 4. §. 4. sup. de vsurpat. 2. Eclog. 3. c. 116.
units.tr: Usucapere] l. 4 §4 above, de usurpationibus; Ecloga 2, 3, c. 116.

units.la: Cum possideatur ] l. 54. sup. de acquir. rerum dom. l. 1. §. 6. sup. de acquir. poss. l. 21. sup. de adult. Gothofr.
units.tr: Cum possideatur] l. 54 above, de acquirendo rerum dominio; l. 1 §6 above, de acquirenda possessione; l. 21 above, de adulteriis. Gothofredus.

units.la: Pertinet haec constitutio ad restitutionem in integrum, eam scil. quae datur ex Edicto; Ex quibus causis maiores. Eo edicto data actione rescissoria, succurritur absentibus metus causa, & Reip. iis qui in vinculis sunt, in seruitute, in hostium potestate. Si quid interim de eorum bonis vsucaptum sit, & propter lapsum temporis actionem amiserint, amissum dominium restituitur, & rescinditur vsucapio, & redditur actio amissa. Hoc comprobat l. ab hostibus 28. de postlim. reuers. l. non quocunq; 82. §. 1. de leg. 1.
units.tr: This constitution pertains to restitution in integrum, namely the kind granted by the Edict, Ex quibus causis maiores. By that edict a rescissory action is granted, and aid is given to those who were absent, to those who acted under fear, and to the commonwealth, and to those who are in chains, in servitude, or in the power of enemies. If anything of their goods has been acquired by usucaption in the meantime, and through the lapse of time they have lost the action, the lost ownership is restored, the usucaption is rescinded, and the lost action is given back. l. ab hostibus 28, de postliminio reversis; l. non quocunque 82 §1, de legatis 1, confirms this.

units.la: Altera parte eiusdem edicti succurritur aduersus absentes non defensos, & qui erant in vinculis, l. 7. quib. ex causs. maior. & aduersus eos, qui in hostium potestate erant. §. rursus. Instit. de action. Et ita si res præsentium non susceperint per se, vel per alias personas, cum ipsi se non defenderent, aut per alium non defenderentur, atque adeo non possent interpellari, vel ipsi, vel alii eorum nomine: quare æquum est, vt aduersus eos succurratur præsentibus, si quid interim de bonis absentium vsucaptum sit. Sed ii qui sunt in seruitute, non continentur hac parte, quia serui vsucapere no possunt. Non fit vsucapio sine possessione: at is possidere non potest, qui per alium possidetur. Igitur serui non vsucapiunt, hoc est, neque inchoare vsucapionem possunt, neque inceptam complere. Possessio bonorum seruitute interrumpitur, non absentia aut vinculis: & absens & qui est in vinculis vsucapere potest. Dices, hac parte Edicti succurritur etiam præsentibus adaduersus captiuos: qui tamen vsucapere non possunt, cum sint serui hostium? Resp. Vsucapere quidem per se non possunt, sed per personas sibi subiectas, ex causa peculiari. l. ait Prætor 23. §. hi plane 3. ex quib. caus. maior. l. pen. de capt. & postlim. reuerf. Quin etiam, licet incepta vsucapio interrumpatur ab iis, vsucapio tamen non interrumpitur, quæ fit per filiumfam. vel seruum, vel personas sibi subiectas. l. si is qui pro emptore 15. de vsucap. quæ fit potestate postliminii, vel fictione L. Corneliæ, si perieris apud hostes. Hæ fictiones locum habent solum in captiuis. Igitur qui in seruitute sunt, nec per se, nec per alias personas sibi acquirunt. l. liber homo 19. de acquir. rer. dom. d. l. ait Prætor. Itaque non continentur secunda parte edicti: prima continentur. In seruitute autem esse, & seruum esse, diuersa sunt: sicut aliud est, in possessione esse, aliud possidere. l. si quis ante 10. §. idem Pomponius, de acquir. poss. In seruitute etiam esse potest liber homo, puta cum detinetur, quasi seruus l. ei quoque 11. ex quib. caus. maior. Seruus est, qui domino alieno subiectus est iure. Quintilianus lib. 5. cap. 10. aliud est seruire, aliud seruum esse: seruire latius patet. Seruiunt serui addicti & nexi, mercenarii, qui operas vendunt: seruiunt liberi homines, qui seruiunt tanquam serui. Proinde in hac regula, In seruitute esse, non est, seruum esse, nec captiuum esse. Verum his verbis, quæ sunt in Edicto, qui sunt in seruitute, possunt contineri captiui. l. item ei succurritur 14. ex quib. caus. maior. Sed hoc ideo; quia reuersi finguntur nunquam fuisse serui, propter fictionem postliminii. Et prima parte, qua succurritur iis, qui in seruitute erant, contineri poterant, qui erant captiui: At in secunda parte, qui sunt in seruitute, & captiui seseparandi sunt. Nam captiui vsucapere possunt: qui sunt in seruitute non possunt. Ad secundam pertinet hæc regula: Quo concesso, sequitur, in hac regula his verbis: in serui-tute, non contineri captiuum, notando Edictum, Ex quibus caus. maior. subueniri absentibus, & aduersus absentes, non tantum data actione rescissoria, sed etiam, ut rem nanciscantur, data exceptione: si non rem meam, me absente, vsucepisti: vel dabitur hæc exceptio, si non, cum esses absens, defendebaris, hoc est, rem meam vsucepisti: Vsucepisti quidem & vindicasti, sed absens. Cui dabimus actionem rescissoriam, multo magis dabimus exceptionem rescissoriam. l. nec non 28. §. exemplo 5. ex quib. caus. maior. Restitutio in integrum potest induci in modum exceptionis. l. Nam posteaquam 9. §. si minor 4. de iureiurand. Dicunt quidam: aduersus absentes non esse opus præsentibus restitutione in integrum: quo nihil est stolidius. Cuiac. in Recit. postb.
units.tr: By the other part of the same edict, aid is given against absent persons who were not defended, and who were in chains, l. 7, quibus ex causis maiores, and against those who were in the power of enemies, §rursus, Institutes, de actionibus. And so, if they did not take up the affairs of present persons, either in person or through other persons, since they did not defend themselves, or were not defended through another, and so could not be called to account, either themselves or others on their behalf, it is therefore fair that aid be given against them to the present, if anything of the goods of absent persons has been acquired by usucaption in the meantime. But those who are in servitude are not included in this part, because slaves cannot acquire by usucaption. Usucaption does not occur without possession, but a person cannot possess who is possessed through another. Therefore slaves do not acquire by usucaption; that is, they can neither begin a usucaption nor complete one that has begun. Possession of goods is interrupted by servitude, not by absence or chains; and an absent person and one who is in chains can acquire by usucaption. You will say: by this part of the Edict aid is also given to present persons against captives, who nevertheless cannot acquire by usucaption, since they are slaves of enemies? I answer: they indeed cannot acquire by usucaption in their own person, but through persons subject to them, by a special cause. l. ait Praetor 23, §hi plane 3, ex quibus causis maiores; l. pen., de captivis et postliminio reversis. Indeed, even though a begun usucaption is interrupted by these persons, usucaption is not interrupted when it is made through a son under power, or a slave, or persons subject to him. l. si is qui pro emptore 15, de usucaptionibus; which occurs by the power of postliminium, or by the fiction of the lex Cornelia, if you have perished among the enemy. These fictions hold only in the case of captives. Therefore those who are in servitude acquire neither in their own person nor through other persons subject to them. l. liber homo 19, de acquirenda rerum dominio; d. l. ait Praetor. Therefore they are not included in the second part of the edict; the first part does include them. Now, being in servitude and being a slave are different things, just as being in possession is one thing and possessing is another. l. si quis ante 10, §idem Pomponius, de acquirenda possessione. A free man too can be in servitude, for instance when he is held as if a slave. l. ei quoque 11, ex quibus causis maiores. A slave is one who is subject by law to the power of another master. Quintilian, book 5, chapter 10: serving is one thing, being a slave is another; serving has a wider sense. Those who serve include bondservants and debtors bound to service, hired workers who sell their labour, and free men who serve as if they were slaves. Accordingly, in this rule, to be in servitude is not the same as to be a slave, nor to be a captive. But by the words of the Edict, who are in servitude, captives may be included. l. item ei succurritur 14, ex quibus causis maiores. But this is so because those who return are feigned never to have been slaves, by the fiction of postliminium. And in the first part, by which aid is given to those who were in servitude, captives could be included; but in the second part, those who are in servitude and captives must be separated. For captives can acquire by usucaption; those who are in servitude cannot. To the second part pertains this rule: which being granted, it follows, under this rule, that by the words in servitude a captive is not included, as is noted in the Edict, Ex quibus causis maiores, that aid is given to the absent, and against the absent, not only by granting a rescissory action, but also, so that they may recover the thing, by granting an exception: "if you acquired my thing by usucaption while I was absent," or this exception will be given: "if, while you were absent, you were not defended," that is, "you acquired my thing." You acquired it and also claimed it, but while absent. To whom we grant a rescissory action, much more shall we grant a rescissory exception. l. nec non 28, §exemplo 5, ex quibus causis maiores. Restitution in integrum can be introduced in the manner of an exception. l. Nam posteaquam 9, §si minor 4, de iureiurando. Some say that against absent persons there is no need for restitution in integrum for those present; nothing is more foolish. Cuiac. in Recit., post.

units.la: Ad Leg. 119. De alienatione.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 119. On alienation.

units.la: NOn alienat, qui duntaxat omittit possessionem.
units.tr: A person does not alienate who merely gives up possession.

units.la: Non] 2. Eclog. 3. c. 117. l. 4. §. 1. sup. de alienat. iudicii mut. caus. &c. & ideo prohibentur donationes. l. 5. §. 10. sup. de donat. inter virum. non prohibentur alienationes possessionis. l. 1. §. 4. sup. de acquir. possess. Gothof.
units.tr: "Does not": see Eclog. 2, 3, c. 117; l. 4, §1, sup. de alienat. iudicii mut. caus., etc. For this reason donations are prohibited (l. 5, §10, sup. de donat. inter virum et uxorem), but alienations of possession are not prohibited (l. 1, §4, sup. de acquir. possess.). Gothof.

units.la: Alienat] proprie sc. secus improprie. l. 4. §. 2. & l. 21. §. 2. sup. quod metus.
units.tr: "Alienates": properly, that is; otherwise, improperly. See l. 4, §2, and l. 21, §2, sup. quod metus.

units.la: Possessionem] est enim alienatio proprie dominii. l. 67. sup. de verb. signific. Goth. Pertinet haec lex ad restitutionem in integrum, quae fit aut datur de alienatione, iudicii mutandi causa facta. l. 4. §. 1. de alien. iudi. mut. caus. fact. Ex illo edicto datur actio rescissoria ei, cuius interest. Finge: Ego rem habeo, cuius nomine mecum actuus est Titius. Ante litem ego rem meam alienaui, non quod habere rem nollem, sed dolo malo, ut duriorem aduersarium Titio opponerem. Teneor eo Edicto in id, quod interest, conditionem duriorem fecisse; & hoc ita, si possessionem vel dominium in alium transtuli. Sed si dominium non transtuli, sed tantum possessionem deserui, dum litem abhorreo, an teneor? Minime: Nam non alienat, qui possessionem transfert in alium, & ut ait l. 4. factum eius non viruperat Praetor, quia mauult uult re carere, quam litigare. Sed qui litem transfert in alium, tenetur. Cuiac. in Recit. posthum.
units.tr: "Possession": for alienation properly concerns ownership (l. 67, sup. de verb. signific.). Goth. This law pertains to restitution in integrum, which is granted or given for an alienation made for the purpose of changing the judge (l. 4, §1, de alien. iudi. mut. caus. fact.). By that edict an action for rescission is given to the person whose interest is involved. Suppose: I have a thing, and Titius has brought suit against me over it. Before the suit I alienate my thing, not because I am unwilling to keep it, but with bad intent, so that I may set a harsher opponent against Titius. By that edict I am liable for the extent of the interest, as having made the condition harder; and this holds if I have transferred the possession or the ownership to another. But if I have not transferred the ownership, and have only given up possession because I shrink from the lawsuit, am I liable? Not at all. For a person does not alienate who transfers possession to another; and, as l. 4 says, the praetor does not condemn the act, because he would rather lack the thing than litigate. But whoever transfers the lawsuit to another is liable. Cuiac. in Recit. posthum.

units.la: Ad Leg.120. De hærede.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 120. On the heir.

units.la: NEmo plus commodi hæredi suo relinquit, quam ipse habuit.
units.tr: No one leaves to his heir more advantage than he himself had.

units.la: Hoc etiam caput pertinet ad restitutionem in integrum: Ex quibus causf.maior. Miles vel alius absens Reip. causa, cum non defenderetur, nec vsucapi res posset à domino, rem alienam cœpit vsucapere: hæres impleuit vsucapionem, non ipse: an scinditur vsucapio, facta per hæredem ? Sic sane. Nam alioqui videretur plus commodi transtulisse in hæredem, quam haberet. Idem seruandum de hærede, qui succedit in vsucapione. De hac regula satis in l.54. sup.hoc tit.Cuiac.in Recit.posthum.
units.tr: This chapter also pertains to restitution in integrum: Ex quibus causis maior. A soldier or another person absent on the public business, while he was not defending the thing, and it could not be acquired by usucapion from its owner, began to usucapt another's thing. The heir completed the usucapion, not he himself. Is the usucapion, made by the heir, divided? Yes, certainly. For otherwise it would seem that more advantage had been transferred to the heir than he himself had. The same is to be observed of an heir who succeeds in usucapion. More on this rule may be found in l. 54, sup. hoc tit. Cuiac. in Recit. posthum.

units.la: Ad Leg. 121. De eo, qui non facit, quod fa- cere debet: vel facit, quod facere non debet.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 121. On one who does not do what he ought to do, or does what he ought not to do.

units.la: QVi non facit quod facere debet, videtur facere aducrsus ea, quia non facit. Et qui facit, quod facere non debet, non videtur facere id, quod facere iussus est.
units.tr: One who does not do what he ought to do is held to act against those things, because he does not do them. And one who does what he ought not to do is not held to do what he was ordered to do.

units.la: Aduersus ea ] in fraudem alterius quis facit, qui id non facit, quod in eius vtilitatem facere debet. l. 4. sup. quae in fraudem creditorum, & ita non facere, est facere: facit igitur interdum, qui non facit, adde l. 102. sup. eod. Goth.
units.tr: Against those things: one acts to the detriment of another when he fails to do what he ought to do for that other's advantage (l. 4, sup. quae in fraudem creditorum). And so not doing is doing; thus sometimes one who does not act does act. Add l. 102, sup. eod. Goth.

units.la: Quia non facit ] quae non faceret. Goth. vel, quae non facit. Pac.
units.tr: Because he does not do: that is, "which he would not do," or "which he does not do." Pac.

units.la: Et qui ] Atqui.
units.tr: And one who: read "But."

units.la: Delenda sunt, quae hic dicit Accurf. pro quibus haec repono: hanc regulam pertinere ad compromissa & constipulationes, quae fiunt in arbitrum, & ita concipiuntur: si aduersus ea factum erit, poena nomine tot dari l. ita demum 31. de recept. arbit. vel sic: Si ita factum non erit, poena nomine tot dari. Et certe, cum quid stipulamur ne fiat, satius est, subiicere poenalem obligationem: si aduersus ea factum erit, tot dari. Expriori formula committitur stipulatio, si quis non fecerit, quod facere debet, l. continuus 137. §. poena de verb. oblig. Sed si quis sit promiscue usus, an ideo minus committitur stipulatio? Minime. Nam cum ita stipulamur, ut quid fiat, ut scilicet sententiae arbitri stetur, si ita subiiciatur poena, si aduersus ea factum erit tot dari: uno ex litigatoribus non obtemperante sententiae arbitri, committitur stipulatio. Nam aduersus ea facere videtur, non tantum qui non facit, quod facere debet: sed etiam qui facit, quod facere non debet: quia hic non facit, quod promisit: promisit autem, se velle non facere. Verum ait Regula, Non videtur facere id, quod iussus est; quod pertinet ad sententiam arbitrorum, qui verant & iubent: quod non facit, hoc facit ut nolit facere: Alioqui non est verum, quod dicunt Stoici: omne peccatum est in actione. Elegantius est, his formulis uti distincte. Caeterum, si quis utatur promiscue, non ideo minus committitur stipulatio, quae est vis & potestas huius regulae. Cui in Recit. posthum.
units.tr: The things Accursius says here should be deleted, and in their place I put the following: this rule applies to compromises and stipulations made before an arbiter, which are worded thus: "if anything is done against these terms, let so much be given as a penalty" (l. ita demum 31, de recept. arbit.), or thus: "If it is not done in this way, let so much be given as a penalty." Indeed, when we stipulate that something not be done, it is better to add a penal obligation: "if anything is done against these terms, let so much be given." In the former form the stipulation is forfeited if someone does not do what he ought to do (l. continuus 137, §poena, de verb. oblig.). But if someone uses the two forms indiscriminately, is the stipulation less forfeited on that account? Not at all. For when we stipulate in such a way that something be done, namely that the decision of the arbiter be obeyed, and the penalty is attached in this form, "if anything is done against these terms, let so much be given," then when one of the litigants does not obey the arbiter's decision, the stipulation is forfeited. For he is held to act against those terms not only who fails to do what he ought to do, but also who does what he ought not to do, since such a one does not do what he promised; and he promised that he would not wish to act. But the rule says, "He is not held to do what he was ordered to do." This pertains to the decision of arbiters who forbid and command: what he does not do, he does in order that he may refuse to do it. Otherwise it is not true, as the Stoics say, that all sin lies in the act. It is more elegant to use these forms distinctly. Otherwise, if someone uses them indiscriminately, the stipulation is not for that reason less forfeited, and this is the force and power of this rule. Cui in Recit. posthum.

units.la: Ad Leg. 122. De libertate.
units.tr: On Law 122. On liberty.

units.la: Libertas omnibus rebus favorabilior est.
units.tr: Liberty is more favourable than anything else.

units.la: Favorabilior] Eclog. 3. c. 119. leg. 20. v. l. 106. sup. eod. l. 176. in sin. inf. eod. l. 16. sup. de manumiss. testam. l. 38. sup. de re iudic.
units.tr: More favourable] Eclog. 3. c. 119. leg. 20. v. l. 106. sup. eod. l. 176. in sin. inf. eod. l. 16. sup. de manumiss. testam. l. 38. sup. de re iudic.

units.la: De liberali causa compromissum fieri non potest. De omnibus causis civilibus adiri arbiter potest, non de libertate. Favor libertatis petit maiores iudices, ut Praetores & Praesides. l. non distinguemus 32. §. de liberali causa 7. de recept. arbit. Est igitur omnibus rebus favorabilior libertas, quae exigit Praetores & Praesides, non arbitros. Praetores in liberali causa, semper faucent libertatibus. l. poenales 32. ad L. Falcid. l. 20 sup. hoc tit, Cui. in Recit.
units.tr: A dispute about a free status cannot be submitted to arbitration. Any civil cause may be referred to an arbiter, but not a cause concerning liberty. The favour shown to liberty calls for higher judges, such as the Praetors and the Presidents. l. non distinguemus 32. §. de liberali causa 7. de recept. arbit. Liberty is therefore more favourable than all other things, and it requires Praetors and Presidents, not arbiters. In a case of liberty, Praetors always favour freedom. l. poenales 32. ad L. Falcid. l. 20 sup. hoc tit, Cui. in Recit.

units.la: Ad Leg. 123. Lege agere. Temporaria permutatio.
units.tr: On Law 123. Bringing an action by law. A temporary exchange.

units.la: NEmo alieno nomine lege agere potest. Temporaria permutatio ius prouinciae non innouat.
units.tr: No one can bring an action by law in another's name. A temporary exchange does not alter the right of a province.

units.la: Lege agere ] lege agere, est in iure agere ex formulis a lege institutis, ex praescripto legis, impetratis solenniter actionibus, apud magistratum experiri: hinc legis actiones, formulae agendi in iure apud eum, qui iuri dicundo praeest l.4. sup. de adopt. l.3. sup. de offic. proconf. l.1. sup. de officio Iudicis. Paulus 2. sentent. 25. §. 4. Goth.
units.tr: Lege agere] To bring an action by law is to plead in court, under the forms laid down by law and in accordance with the law's prescription, by solemnly obtaining actions and pursuing them before a magistrate. Hence the legal actions are the forms of pleading in court before the one who presides over the administration of justice. l.4. sup. de adopt. l.3. sup. de offic. proconf. l.1. sup. de officio Iudicis. Paulus 2. sentent. 25. §. 4. Goth.

units.la: Temporaria ] temporalis, vulgata, sensus est, Momentanea imperium non habent in ea quę iuris sunt: ideoque consuetudo duobus, aut tribus iudiciis contrariis non euertitur. Decius hic. Gothofr.
units.tr: Temporaria] The common reading is temporalis. The sense is that momentary changes have no power over matters of law; so a custom is not overturned by two or three contrary judgments. Decius hic. Gothofr.

units.la: Huius legis initium explicatum est supr. in l. actus 77.
units.tr: The beginning of this law has been explained supr. in l. actus 77.

units.la: Ad §. Temporaria.
units.tr: On the paragraph "Temporaria".

units.la: Prouinciae quaedam sunt Proconsulares, quaedam Praesidiales. Theophil. in §. per traditionem Inst. de rerum diuis. Sed si in Praesidialem prouinciam mittatur quidam non praeses, Proconsulari imperio ad tempus & caeterarum rerum
units.tr: Some provinces are proconsular, others presidial. Theophil. in §. per traditionem Inst. de rerum diuis. But if someone who is not a president is sent into a presidial province, with proconsular authority for a time, and his cause for the other matters is not changed, the right of the province is not thereby altered; the presidial province remains what it was.

units.la: rum sum causa non immutetur, non ideo ius prouincię innouatur: sed prouincia præsidialis manet. Mittuntur sæpe iudices extra ordinem: sed non ideo mutatur vel nouatur ordo iuris. Temporaria permutatio iudicis ordinem iuris non innouat. Cui. in Recit.
units.tr: Judges are often sent out of the ordinary course, but the order of law is not thereby changed or renewed. A temporary change of judge does not alter the order of law. Cui. in Recit.

units.la: Ad Leg. 124. De muto, surdo & furioso.
units.tr: On Law 124. On the mute, the deaf and the insane.

units.la: VBi non voce sed præsentia opus est, mutus, si intellectu habet, potest videri respondere. Idem in surdo, hic quidem & respondere potest. §. Furiosus absentis loco est. & ita Pomp. lib. 1. Epistol. scribit.
units.tr: Where presence rather than speech is needed, a mute person, if he has understanding, may seem to respond. The same holds for a deaf person, who indeed can respond. §. A madman stands in the place of an absent person. Pomponius writes this in the first book of his Epistles.

units.la: Vbi] v. l. 48. sup. de obligationib.
units.tr: Where] see l. 48. sup. de obligationib.

units.la: Præsentia] id est, præsentis consensu & intelligentia opus est, l. 209. sup. de verb. signif.
units.tr: Presence] that is, the consent and understanding of one who is present are needed. l. 209. sup. de verb. signif.

units.la: Respondere] responderi.
units.tr: To respond] to be answered.

units.la: Absentis] v. l. 2. §. 3. sup. de Iure Codicill. l. 17. §. 11. inf. sup. de iniuriis. Idem corpore præsens esse potest, mente absens l. 26. sup. de captiuis. Gothofr. hic.
units.tr: Absent] see l. 2. §. 3. sup. de Iure Codicill. l. 17. §. 11. inf. sup. de iniuriis. One may be physically present and mentally absent, l. 26. sup. de captiuis. Gothofredus here.

units.la: Loco est] imo non est l. 2. §. 1. sup. de procurat.
units.tr: Stands in the place of] nay, it does not; l. 2. §. 1. sup. de procurat.

units.la: In negotiis, in quibus sermone opus est, surdus aut mutus interuenire non potest, vt in stipulatione, aut manumissione vindicta, authoritate præstanda pupillis, vt in testamentis, in quibus verba olim necessaria. In aliis autem negotiis, in quibus præsentia opus est, non sermone, mone, mutus interuenire potest, dummodo intelligat quid agat. Idem est in surdo. Et ideo surdus aut mutus emere, locare, vendere, conducere, possunt. Item; si quis coram Titio iubeatur adire hæreditatem, recte adit coram Titio, etsi Titius sit mutus. Itaque surdus & mutus præsentes esse intelliguntur. In omni iure videtur iudex sententiam dixisse, etiamsi coram muto vel surdo litigatore dixerit; eas vero res non recte peragit, quæ verba desiderant, vt stipulationem. Diuersum est in surioso, qui absentis loco est l. coram 209. de verb. sign. l. si quis mihi 25. §. si coram 10. de acquir. hæred. l. diem 27. de recept. arb. Habetur etiam suriosus pro absente, in l. sed si vnius 17. §. filiofam. 11. de iniuriis. Patris præsentis est actio, vt agat iniuriarum, non filiifam. Sed si pater absit, tum agit filiussam. abesse videtur, si furiosus aut demens sit. Habetur furiosus pro absente in Edicto, Ex quibus causis maiores. Nam vt aduersus absentem, ita aduersus furiosum laso succurritur. l. 22. §. pen. & §. vlt. ex quibus caus. maior. si quid vsuceperit furiosus. Nam vsucapere potest per subiectas suo iuri personas ex causa peculiari. & vsucapio eius furore non interrumpitur. l. 4. §. furiosus 3. l. iusto 44. de vsucap. Ideoque si quid vsu suum fecerit, cum interpellari vsucapio in personam furiosi non possit, succurretur ei, qui vsucapione rem suam amisit, data actione & exceptione rescissoria in furiosum, imo etiam pro furioso, vt traditur in l. 2. §. furiosus de iure Codicil. Furiosus codicillos facere non potest; Nam vbique pro dormiente & quiescente est. Et ait l. per omnia & in omnibus, vt ostendat, furiosum nihil agere posse, neque inter viuos, neque in vltima voluntate l. 5. sup. h. tit. sed si furiosus tutor detur aut curator, cum absens tutor dari possit, an igitur furiosus recte dabitur, cum habeatur pro absente? Minime, Nam quod dicimus, absentem tutorem dari posse, de sano accipiendum est. Male Iohannes existimat, hanc legem non pertinere ad contractus; cum lex dicat, potest videri respondere. Loquitur ergo de his negotiis, in quibus opus est, vt alter interroget, alter respondeat, quo genere contrahuntur omnes stipulationes: alii etiam contractus & pacta fiunt eodem modo per interrogationem & responsionem, vel quod idem est, per rogationem & sponsionem. l. iurisgentium 7. §. quod fere 12. de pact. Ostendit ibi, ambiguum esse sermonem: Rogauit Titius, spopondit Maeuius. Nam haec verba non tantum pro stipulatione accipi possunt, sed etiam pro pacto, & aliis praeter stipulationem contractibus, tacita responsio sufficit. l. 1. de pactis l. in quibuscunque 48. de oblig. & act. In aliis contractibus, praesens, si actum rei intelligat, respondere videtur. Præsentia opus est nostra vel aliena in contractu, sicut in acquirenda possessione corpore opus est nostro, vel alieno, vel eo, quod vice corporis nostri fungitur, & quo æstimantur præsentes, vt Epistolæ, per quas mentis conceptum exprimimus, & quasi contrahimus. Præsentia opus est, vt ostendit l. 2. §. furiosus de iure codicill. vbi ait, Furiosum nihil agere posse, quod absentis loco habeatur. Si desit nuntius, vel epistola, sane non erit contractus, nisi presens cum præsente contraxerit. Hi porro contractus, vbi opus est præsentia, habentur recte cum muto & surdo, non cum furioso. Stipulatio non contrahitur cum ipsis: nam in stipulatione præsentia non sufficit. Verum ei quod diximus, Mutum haberi pro præsente, valde obstat l. vlt. de verb. signif. Proponitur in ea l. quid sit exhibere. Definitio sumitur ex Labeone, qui definit, exhibere esse præsentiam eius, de quo agitur, præstare. Refellitur hæc definitio duplici argumento. Primo, quod communis sit: Nam & is, qui sistit aliquem, præsentiam præstat, si eum sistat, nec tamen eum exhibet. Nam tantum is exhibet, qui denuntiandi potestatem facit, quam non facit, qui tantum sistit. Secundum argumentum est: qui mutum aut furiosum, aut infantem exhibet, exhibet quidem, sed præsentiam non præstat; hoc est, hæ personæ vere præsentes esse, dici non possunt. Sed meo iudicio male comparatur mutus furioso, aut infanti. Cuiac. in Rec. posthum.
units.tr: In transactions that require speech, a deaf or mute person cannot take part, as in a stipulation, a manumission by the rod, the authorising of a ward, or as in wills, in which words were formerly necessary. In other transactions, however, where presence is needed but not speech, a mute person can take part, provided he understands what he is doing. The same holds for a deaf person. And so a deaf or mute person can buy, let, sell and hire. Likewise, if someone is ordered in the presence of Titius to enter upon an inheritance, he enters validly in Titius's presence, even if Titius is mute. Thus deaf and mute persons are understood to be present. In every law, a judge is considered to have pronounced sentence even if he has spoken before a mute or deaf litigant; but those acts which require words, such as a stipulation, are not validly performed. It is otherwise with the insane, who stand in the place of an absent person. l. coram 209. de verb. sign. l. si quis mihi 25. §. si coram 10. de acquir. hæred. l. diem 27. de recept. arb. The insane person is also held to be absent, in l. sed si vnius 17. §. filiofam. 11. de iniuriis. The action for injury belongs to the father, if he is present, to bring, not to the son in the family; but if the father is absent, then the son in the family is regarded as absent. A madman or a demented person is regarded as absent. In the Edict, Ex quibus causis maiores, the insane person is held to be absent. For just as relief is given against an absent person, so it is given against a madman. l. 22. §. pen. & §. vlt. ex quibus caus. maior. If a madman has acquired something by possession, for he can acquire possession through persons subject to his power by a special cause, and the usucapion is not interrupted by his madness. l. 4. §. furiosus 3. l. iusto 44. de vsucap. Therefore, if he has gained something by usucapion, since usucapion cannot be pressed against the person of the madman, relief is given to the one who lost his property by usucapion, by granting an action and an exception of rescission against the madman, or even on behalf of the madman, as is taught in l. 2. §. furiosus de iure Codicil. A madman cannot make codicils, for everywhere he is treated as asleep and at rest. And the law says per omnia & in omnibus, to show that a madman can do nothing, neither between living persons nor in a last will. l. 5. sup. h. tit. But if a madman is appointed guardian or curator, since an absent person can be appointed guardian, will a madman be validly appointed, since he is regarded as absent? By no means. For what we say, that an absent guardian can be appointed, must be understood of a sane person. John is wrong to think that this law does not apply to contracts, since the law says potest videri respondere. It speaks therefore of those transactions in which one party must ask and the other answer, a kind by which all stipulations are made; other contracts and pacts also are made in the same way, by question and answer, or what is the same, by asking and promising. l. iurisgentium 7. §. quod fere 12. de pact. There it shows that the speech is ambiguous: Titius asked, Maevius promised. For these words can be taken not only of a stipulation, but also of a pact and of other contracts besides stipulation, where a tacit response suffices. l. 1. de pactis l. in quibuscunque 48. de oblig. & act. In other contracts, a person present who understands the matter of the transaction is considered to respond. Presence, whether ours or another's, is needed in a contract, just as in acquiring possession bodily presence is needed, whether our own or another's, or that which takes the place of our body, by which persons are judged present, such as letters, through which we express the thought of the mind and as it were contract. Presence is needed, as l. 2. §. furiosus de iure codicill. shows, where it says that a madman can do nothing, since he is regarded as in the place of an absent person. If there is no messenger or letter, there will certainly be no contract, unless a person present contracts with a person present. Moreover, those contracts in which presence is needed are validly made with a mute or deaf person, but not with a madman. A stipulation is not contracted with such persons, for in a stipulation presence does not suffice. Indeed, our statement that a mute person is held to be present is strongly opposed by l. vlt. de verb. signif. In that law it is asked what it is to exhibit. The definition is taken from Labeo, who defines exhibiting as furnishing the presence of that about which the action is brought. This definition is refuted by a double argument. First, because it is too general: for one who brings a man before a court also furnishes presence, if he brings him before the court, and yet does not exhibit him; for only he exhibits who makes it possible to give notice, which one does not do who merely brings him before the court. The second argument is this: one who exhibits a mute, or a madman, or an infant, does exhibit, but does not furnish presence; that is, these persons cannot truly be said to be present. But in my judgement a mute person is wrongly compared with a madman or an infant. Cuiac. in Rec. posthum.

units.la: Ad Leg. 125. De actore & reo.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 125. Concerning the plaintiff and the defendant.

units.la: FAuorabiliores rei potius sunt, quam actores habentur.
units.tr: Defendants are rather to be favoured than plaintiffs are held to be.

units.la: Rei ] l. 41. sup. eod. l. 38. sup. de re iudic. l. 47. sup. de obligat. c. cum sunt paria iura 11. de reg. in 6. 2. Eclog. 3. c. 121: adde Aristot. problem. 18. id est, proniores sumus ad reum absoluendum d. leg. 47. l. 5. in pr. sup. de poenis. l. 4. §. 13. sup. de dolo except. fauetur possidenti v. leg. 128. infr. eod. plus etiam dilationis reo datur: leg. vlt. supr. de feriis l. 6. in f. C. de temporib. in integr. l. 2. C. de dilation. Gothofr.
units.tr: Rei ] see l. 41 above, same title; l. 38 above, concerning the judgment of a thing; l. 47 above, concerning obligations; c. cum sunt paria iura, 11, de regulis iuris in 6; Eclog. 3, c. 121. Add Aristotle, Problems 18, that is, we are more inclined to acquit the defendant: d. l. 47; l. 5 in pr. above, de poenis; l. 4 §13 above, de doli exceptione. The possessor is favoured, see l. 128 below, same title. More delay is also granted to the defendant: l. last above, de feriis; l. 6 in f. C. de temporibus in integrum restitutionibus; l. 2 C. de dilationibus. Gothofredus.

units.la: Actores ] in causae decisione, non tamen in praeparatoriis iudiciorum l. 8. sup. qui satisdare. l. 66. sup. de iudiciis. l. 83. §. 1. sup. de verb. obligat. in medio vero causae, actor reo edere tenetur, non econtra. l. 4. l. 5. C. de edend. ad causae decisionem id pertinet, nam illo non probante, reus absoluitur. Fauorabiliores igitur rei in re dubia & testimoniis, hinc & inde paribus; Aliud est, si pro actore plene sit probatum; tunc enim lis dubia esse desinit cum certa appareat. Gothofr.
units.tr: Actores ] in the decision of the case, but not in preliminary proceedings of trials: l. 8 above, qui satisdare; l. 66 above, de iudiciis; l. 83 §1 above, de verborum obligationibus. In the middle of the case, however, the plaintiff is bound to produce [evidence] for the defendant, not the reverse: l. 4, l. 5 C. de edendo. That pertains to the decision of the case, for if the plaintiff does not prove it, the defendant is acquitted. Therefore defendants are more favoured in a doubtful matter and in testimonies that are equal on both sides. It is otherwise if the case has been fully proved for the plaintiff; for then the dispute ceases to be doubtful, since the matter appears certain. Gothofredus.

units.la: Habentur ] idem Aristot. in probl. sectione 18.
units.tr: Habentur ] the same Aristotle, in Problems, section 18.

units.la: S
particula 12. de his quae ad ius ciuile pertinent. Pacius.
units.tr: Section 12, on those things which pertain to civil law. Pacius.

units.la: Latior est haec lex lege in eo. sup. 33. & l. in pari inf. eod. Pertinet enim ad multa alia, de quibus in illis duabus nihil. Absens actor condemnatur, reus non. l. absentem 5. de pæn. Olim actori dabantur duę horę ad causam agendam, reo tres. Bulgarus ad hanc l. speciem eiusmodi ponit. Quædam res duobus est donata aut legata, vnus eam possidet, alter petit, durior causa est petitoris. Propositá hac specie, Bulg. subiicit hanc rationem. Nam in pari causa est melior conditio occupantis. l. inter 19. de re iudic. Reprehenditur ob eam rem à Ioanne, quem & hic Accursius refert. Ratio est, quia in l. inter 19. is dicitur occupasse, non qui possidet, sed qui prior agit. Hoc mihi demonstrat, Ioannem scripsisse in hunc titulum, qui aliud esse, occupantem præferri, ait, etsi petitor sit, aliud esse possessorem præferri. Sententia hæc est, si duobus sint res donatæ separatim, & neuter possideat, melior est causa eius, qui occupat agendo, verum si vnus possideat, is vincit semper. l. siue autem 9. §. si duobus 4. de Public. in rem act. l. si ea res 31. §. vlt. de act. empt. Itaque merito reprehenditur Bulgarus. Ratio hic, Possessoris semper potior est causa, etiamsi non occupauerit prior, petitoris vero non est potior, nisi is occupauerit. Qua in re lapsus est Accursius. Accurs. Non enim species reprehenditur, sed ratio. Ratio est de eo, qui prior egit, occupationis iure est potior vel prior, & ita potior est causa actoris. Denique occupantis potior est causa, etiamsi petat: possessor prior, etsi non coeperit agere. Cuia in Recit.
units.tr: This law is broader than the law in eo, above, 33, and the law in pari, below, same title. For it pertains to many other matters, of which those two laws say nothing. The absent plaintiff is condemned, the defendant is not: l. absentem 5, de poenis. Formerly the plaintiff was given two hours to bring his case, the defendant three. Bulgarus, on this law, gives the following case of this kind. A certain thing has been given or bequeathed to two persons, one possesses it, the other claims it; the claimant's cause is the harder. Having set out this case, Bulgarus adds this reasoning: for in an equal cause the condition of the one who takes possession is better: l. inter 19, de re iudicata. John rebukes him for this, and Accursius here reports it. The reason is that in l. inter 19 the one said to have taken possession is not the one who possesses but the one who sues first. This shows me that John wrote on this title that it is one thing for the one who takes possession to be preferred, and another for the possessor to be preferred even if he is the claimant. His view is this: if two persons have been given a thing separately and neither possesses it, the cause of the one who takes possession by suing is better; but if one possesses it, he always wins: l. siue autem 9, §si duobus, 4, de publiciana in rem actione; l. si ea res 31, §vlt., de actionibus empti. Therefore Bulgarus is rightly rebuked. The reasoning here is: the cause of the possessor is always stronger, even if he did not take possession first; the cause of the claimant is not stronger unless he took possession. In this matter Accursius has erred. Accursius: For it is not the example that is rebuked but the reasoning. The reasoning is about the one who sued first: by the right of taking possession he is the stronger or first, and so the cause of the plaintiff is the stronger. Finally, the cause of the one who takes possession is stronger even if he sues; the earlier possessor is stronger even if he did not begin to sue. Cuia in Recit.

units.la: Ad Leg. 126. De eo, qui pretium numerauit. 2. De acquisitione liberti. 3. De pe- titore & possessore.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 126. Concerning the one who paid the price. 2. Concerning the acquisition of a freedman. 3. Concerning the claimant and the possessor.

units.la: NEmo praedo est, qui pretium numerauit. §.
units.tr: NNo one is a robber who has paid the price. §.

units.la: 1. Locupletior non est factus, qui libertum acquisierit. §. 2. Cum de lucro duorum quaeritur, melior est causa possidentis.
units.tr: 1. He who has acquired a freedman is not made richer. §. 2. When the question concerns the gain of two parties, the cause of the possessor is the better.

units.la: In hac L. proponuntur tres sententiæ, quæ omnes pertinent ad petitionem hæreditatis. Prima est, Nemo prædo, &c. Petitione hæreditatis tenetur, qui pro hærede vel possessore possidet. Prædo est, qui rem invasit, & cum rogatur, cur possideat, dicit, quia possideo. Quæritur, an videatur prædo esse is, qui sciens emit alienam hæreditatem? Minime: quia nemo prædo est, qui pretium numerat de suo. Est quidem malæ fidei possessor & emptor, sed non etiam prædo, ideo, ut prædo non tenetur actione directa, sed tenetur ut emptor vniuersi iuris. l. 13. §. si quis sciens de pet. hared.
units.tr: In this law three opinions are set out, all of which pertain to the petition for an inheritance. The first is: no one is a robber who pays the price, etc. He who possesses as heir or as possessor is liable to the petition for an inheritance. A robber is one who has seized a thing and, when asked why he possesses it, says, "Because I possess it." The question is whether a person who knowingly buys another's inheritance is to be regarded as a robber. Not at all: for no one is a robber who pays the price out of his own money. He is indeed a possessor and buyer in bad faith, but not also a robber; therefore, as a robber, he is not liable to a direct action, but is liable as a buyer of universal right: l. 13, §si quis sciens, de petitione hereditatis.

units.la: Ad §. Locupletior.
units.tr: On §. Locupletior.

units.la: Secunda sententia etiam pertinet ad petitionem hæreditatis, de qua factum est nobile SCtum authore Hadriano. Eo SCto eo usque tenetur quis, quo locupletior factus est. Finge, rem hereditariam vendidit Titius bona fide & distraxit, pretiumque accepit, an restituero cogitur, quod ex distractione consecutus est? Sic sane, si habet penes se: sed si perdiderit, non tenetenetur, quia locupletior factus non est leg. sed verum 14. l. sed & si 25. §. consuluit. ii. de petit. hared. An etiam videtur locupletior factus, si rem hereditariam alienauit, non vendidit? Videtur locupletior factus, cum donando, naturalem obligationem quaesierit. Sed haec obligatio pro nihilo habetur, quia actionem non parit. Ideo ille non est locupletior factus, qui naturalem quaesiuit obligationem. Non etiam locupletior est factus, qui manumittendo libertum acquisierit. Itaque aestimatio patronatus non venit in diuitias, nec patronus est locupletior, argumento l. naturalis 5. §. vlt. de praescript. verb. si conuenit inter nos, ut seruum tuum manumitteres & ego meum manumitterem; Ego meum manumisi, tu tuum non manumisisti. Ego habeo actionem praescriptis verbis, in quantum interest, me seruum habuisse, quem manumisi, nec deducitur quod libertum habeo. Nam id in aestimationem venire non potest. Manumisi seruum, nec videor locupletior factus. sic l. 2. quib. ad lib. proclam. non lic. haeres ex dolo defuncti nihil videtur consecuturus, qui libertum est adeptus: ideo eius rei nulla aestimatio fieri potest.
units.tr: The second opinion also concerns the petition of inheritance, on which the famous senatus consultum was made under the authority of Hadrian. By that senatus consultum a person is liable only so far as he has been made richer. Suppose a man sold the hereditary property in good faith, disposed of it, and received the price. Is he compelled to restore what he obtained from the disposal? Certainly, if he still has it in his possession. But if he has lost it, he is not liable, because he has not become richer. leg. sed verum 14. l. sed & si 25. §. consuluit. ii. de petit. hared. Is he also seen as made richer if he alienated the hereditary thing rather than sold it? He is seen as made richer when, by giving it away, he has acquired a natural obligation. But this obligation is counted as nothing, because it does not give rise to an action. Therefore the man who acquired only a natural obligation has not become richer. Nor is he made richer who acquires a freedman by manumitting. Thus the estimated value of the patronage does not count as wealth, and the patron is not richer, by the argument of l. naturalis 5. §. vlt. de praescript. verb. If it was agreed between us that you would manumit your slave and I would manumit mine, and I manumitted mine but you did not manumit yours, I have an action praescriptis verbis for the extent of my interest, namely that I had the slave whom I manumitted; and what I have as a freedman is not deducted, for that cannot enter the estimate. I manumitted a slave, and I do not seem to have become richer. sic l. 2. quib. ad lib. proclam. non lic. An heir who has obtained a freedman through the deceit of the deceased seems to gain nothing; therefore no estimate of that thing can be made.

units.la: Ad §. Cum de lucro.
units.tr: On §. Cum de lucro.

units.la: Tertia sententia pertinet quoque ad petitionem hereditatis. Omne lucrum praedoni auferrauferturin petitione bonorum. l.28. de petit. hered. hoc ita; si petitor hereditatis de damno contendat. Cæterum si tam petitor quam possessor contendat de lucro, & neuter sit hæres; potior possessor est. l.33. & l.98. sup. h.tit. (Quiac. in Recit. posth.).
units.tr: The third opinion also concerns the petition of inheritance. All gain is to be taken away from the possessor in a petition of goods. l.28. de petit. hered. This holds if the petitioner of the inheritance contends about loss. But if both the petitioner and the possessor contend about gain, and neither is the heir, the possessor has the stronger claim. l.33. & l.98. sup. h.tit. (Cuiac. in Recit. posth.).

units.la: Ad Leg. 127. De hærede conuento in id, quod ad eum peruenit.
units.tr: On Leg. 127. On the heir sued for what has come to him.

units.la: Cum Prætor in hæredem dat actionem, quatenus ad eum peruenit, sufficit, si vel momento ad eum peruenit ex dolo defuncti. In articulo, l.ult. C. de offic. Comitis sacri palat. De momento dixi ad l.ult. in f. C. de bon. quæ liberis. Gothofr.
units.tr: Since the Praetor gives an action against the heir so far as the property has come to him, it is enough if it came to him even for a moment, through the fraud of the deceased. On the article, l.ult. C. de offic. Comitis sacri palat. I have spoken about "a moment" on l.ult. in f. C. de bon. quæ liberis. Gothofredus.

units.la: Hæc lex etiam est ex tractatu, de petitione hereditatis. In illo tractatu, verbum, peruenisse, relatum ad bonæ fidei possessorem, sic accipitur: si etiam duret bonæ fidei possessor. Nam non sufficit, peruenisse semel. Bonæ fidei possessor restituit petitori hereditatis, quod ad eum peruenit ex venditione rerum hærehæreditariarum, sed necesse est, vt duret & manserit pecunia. l.utrum 23. de petit.hæred. In edictis, quibus scilic. Prætor pollicetur, actionem in hæreditatem peruenisse, vel momento sufficit.l.videamus 17. quod metus causa. Sed si ipse hæres perdiderit & consumpserit: non si res perierit naturaliter ante litem contestatam. Nam si naturaliter interierit, hæres non tenetur; Quod longe secus est in petitione hæreditatis, qua agitur cum bonæ fidei possessore. Nam bonæ fidei possessor non tenetur, siue rem consumpserit, siue perierit naturaliter ante litem contestatam. Post litem contestatam bonæ fidei possessor tenetur, si rem consumpserit, & spectatur tempus rei iudicatæ. Et hæc differentia edictorum & sententiarum est maxime notanda: quod diligenter fecit Bulg. Cuiac. in Recit. posthum.
units.tr: This law also comes from the treatise on the petition of inheritance. In that treatise, the word "has come" (peruenisse), as applied to the possessor in good faith, is understood thus: if the possessor in good faith still holds it. For it is not enough that it came once. A possessor in good faith restores to the petitioner of the inheritance what came to him from the sale of hereditary things, but it is necessary that the money lasts and remains. l.utrum 23. de petit.hæred. In the edicts, by which the Praetor promises an action on what has come into the inheritance, a moment suffices. l.videamus 17. quod metus causa. But if the heir himself has lost and spent it, the position differs from the case where the thing perished naturally before litis contestatio. For if it perished naturally, the heir is not liable. It is quite otherwise in the petition of inheritance, which is brought against a possessor in good faith. For a possessor in good faith is not liable, whether he has consumed the thing or it has perished naturally before litis contestatio. After litis contestatio, a possessor in good faith is liable if he has consumed the thing, and the time of the judgment is considered. This difference between edicts and sentences is most worth noting, and Bulgarus did well to observe it carefully. Cuiac. in Recit. posthum.

units.la: Ad Leg. 128. De petitore & possessore. De successore.
units.tr: On Leg. 128. On the petitioner and the possessor. On the successor.

units.la: IN pari causa possessor potior haberi debet. §. Hi qui in vniuersum ius succedunt, heredis loco habentur.
units.tr: In an equal case the possessor ought to be held the stronger. §. Those who succeed to the whole right are held in the place of the heir.

units.la: In pari] extit. de publiciana in rem actione.
units.tr: In equal case (see the extract on the Publician action in rem).

units.la: Hi qui] vt fiscus: is enim hæredis loco habetur. l.3. sup. soluto l.2. C. ad L. Iul. de vi. l.4. Cod. de bon. proscript. Goth.
units.tr: Those who] as the fiscus: for it is held in the place of the heir. l.3. sup. soluto l.2. C. ad L. Iul. de vi. l.4. Cod. de bon. proscript. Goth.

units.la: In vniuersum ius] l.60. sup. eod. l.194. inf. eod. l.9. §.12. sup. de hæred. instit. 2. Eclog. 3. c.126. Gothof.
units.tr: In the whole right] l.60. sup. eod. l.194. inf. eod. l.9. §.12. sup. de hæred. instit. 2. Eclog. 3. c.126. Gothof.

units.la: Principium huius legis iunctum est l.33. & ibi explicatum.
units.tr: The beginning of this law is joined to l.33., and is explained there.

units.la: Ad §. Hi qui in vniuersum.
units.tr: On the paragraph "Hi qui in universum"

units.la: L. Item videndum 18.§. Licet autem 13. de hæred. petit. eadem est conditio bonorum possessoris, hoc est, qui se existimat iustum esse possessorem, igitur hæredum loco sunt, qui in vniuersum ius quocunque modo succedunt. Cuiac. in Recit. posthum. op.
units.tr: Law "Item videndum" 18, §. "Licet autem" 13, de hæreditatis petitione: the condition of a possessor of goods is the same, that is, one who thinks himself to be the rightful possessor; therefore those who succeed in universal right in whatever manner stand in the place of heirs. Cuiacius, in Recitationes posthumas.

units.la: Ad Leg. 129. Qui suum recipit. Principale & accessorium.
units.tr: On Law 129. "Qui suum recipit." Principal and accessory.

units.la: NIhil dolo creditor facit, qui suum recipit. §. Cum principalis causa non consistit, nec ea quidem, quæ sequuntur, locum habent.
units.tr: Nothing is done by the creditor with fraud who recovers what is his own. §. When the principal cause does not subsist, neither do those things which follow it have any place.

units.la: Qui suum] l.55. sup. eod. v. l.26. sup. de damno.
units.tr: "Qui suum": law 55 above, same title; cf. law 26 above, de damno.

units.la: Principium huius legis explicatum est sup. in l.Culpa caret 5o.hoc tit.
units.tr: The beginning of this law has been explained above, at law "Culpa caret," 50, in this title.

units.la: Ad §. Cum principalis causa.
units.tr: On the paragraph "Cum principalis causa."

units.la: Huius sententiae innumera sunt exempla. Liberato reo, liberatur fideiussor: fideiussio est accessio. Si non liberatur fideiussor, ergo nec reus, cum fideiussor aduersus reum regressum habeat. Sublata actione personali, tollitur hypothecaria. l.debitor.59.ad SC.Trebell. Legato seruo cum peculio, si seruus legatus extinguitur, etiam peculium extinguitur: est enim accessio. Rupto testamento principali, hoc est, paterno rumpitur pupillare. §. liberis. Instit. de vulg. & pupill. substit. Praeterea si inutilis est principalis obligatio, sequens quoque inutilis erit.l.75.de verb.oblig. Repetitur eadem regula in l.cum principalis 178.in sin.hoc tit. sed additur tamen, plerunque, ut intelligatur, non esse perpetuum, quod apparet ex l.1.& 2.C.de luit.pign. Finge, vnus est debitor pignoratitius, qui decedit, duobus relictis hæredibus. In eos duplex est actio, principalis siue personalis & hypothecaria. Principali tamen ex parte tenentur, pro parte scil. hæreditaria ex L.12. tabul. actione vero hypothecaria in solidum tenentur; quia indiuisa est pignoris causa. Si igitur vnus ex illis debitum soluerit pro parte hæreditaria; non tenetur in solidum actione personali: hypothecaria tamen in solidum tenetur: quia non est satisfactum creditori in solidum. Ergo in cuius persona sublata est actio principalis, non est sublata hypothecaria. Cuiac. in Recit. posthum.
units.tr: There are countless examples of this principle. When the debtor is released, the surety is released: suretyship is an accessory. If the surety is not released, neither is the debtor, since the surety has a right of recourse against the debtor. When the personal action is removed, the hypothecary action is removed too: law "debitor" 59, ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum. When a slave is bequeathed with his peculium, if the bequeathed slave is extinguished, the peculium is extinguished too, for it is an accessory. When the principal will is broken, that is, the father's, the pupillary substitution is broken with it: §. "liberis," Institutes, de vulgari et pupillari substitutione. Moreover, if the principal obligation is void, the following one will also be void: law 75, de verborum obligationibus. The same rule is repeated in law "cum principalis" 178, at the end of this title, but it is added that this is usually so, so that it is understood not to be perpetual, as appears from laws 1 and 2, C., de luitione pignoris. Suppose there is one pledge debtor, who dies leaving two heirs. Against them there is a double action, the principal or personal, and the hypothecary. They are liable for the principal, indeed, in respect of the part of the inheritance, by the Law of the Twelve Tables; but they are liable for the hypothecary action for the whole, because the cause of the pledge is undivided. If therefore one of them pays the debt for his hereditary share, he is not liable for the whole by the personal action; yet he is liable for the whole by the hypothecary action, because the creditor has not been satisfied in full. Therefore, in whose person the principal action has been removed, the hypothecary action has not been removed. Cuiacius, in Recitationes posthumas.

units.la: Ad Leg.130. De concurrentibus actionibus.
units.tr: On Law 130. "On concurrent actions."

units.la: NVnquam actiones, præsertim pœnales, de eadem re concurrentes, alia aliam consumit.
units.tr: Never do actions, especially penal ones, concurring concerning the same matter, one consume another.

units.la: Nunquam ] ex tit. ad Leg. Aquil. Pac. §. vlt. Insitit si quadrupes. l. 60. sup. de obligat. v. Hotom. 27. illustr. Gothofr.
units.tr: "Never": from the title on the Lex Aquilia, Pauli §. last, Institutes "si quadrupes"; law 60 above, de obligationibus; cf. Hotomanus, Illustrations 27; Gothofredus.

units.la: Pœnales ] & personales v. l. 43. sup. eod.
units.tr: "Penal": and personal; cf. law 43 above, same title.

units.la: De eadem re ] non ex diuersis causis & tributis: tunc enim ne electione quidem vnius, altera tollitur. l.12. §.1. sup. de acquir. possess. l.32. l.34. sup. de oblig. l.2. sup. de priu. delict. l.1. sup. arbor. furt. caes. L.1. sup. vi bon. rapt. Goth.
units.tr: "Concerning the same matter": not arising from different causes and grounds; for then, not even by the choice of one is the other removed. Laws 12 §1 above, de acquirenda possessione; laws 32 and 34 above, de obligationibus; law 2 above, de privato delicto; law 1 above, arborum furtim caesarum; law 1 above, vi bonorum raptorum; Gothofredus.

units.la: Consumit ]non concursu, sed electione. l. 3. in sin. l. 6. §. 4. §. familia. l. 9. §. 1. ṡ de tributoria. l. 10. in sin. sup. de act. empti. l. 25. §. 5. sup. locati. l. 53. sup. de obligat. & merito, est enim iniquum, ut quis bis idem consequatur. v. leg. 57. sup. eod. Goth.
units.tr: "Consumes": not by concurrence but by choice; laws 3 at the end; 6 §4 and §familia; 9 §1, de tributoria; 10 at the end, above, de actione empti; 25 §5 above, locati; 53 above, de obligationibus. And rightly, for it is unfair that someone should obtain the same thing twice; cf. law 57 above, same title; Gothofredus.

units.la: Hæc regula pertinet ad tractatum de actionibus & l. siquis egerit. 88. de furt. Repetitur autem in l. pen. de oblig. & act. quanquam est varietas inscriptionum. Sed huius l. inscriptio est melior. In altera l. ait Vlp. de eadem pecunia: quæ lectio non est mutanda : nam ita est in libris Basilicon. Rei appellatio latior est, quam pecuniæ, ut apparet ex l. 5. de verb. sign. Vnde apparet, eandem rem non accipi hic pro eodem facto. Imo secundum l. nunquam. 2. de privat. delict. locus est huic regulæ, si plures actiones competant, ex pluribus factis, licet sint de eodem corpore. Earum actionum altera non consumit alteram: ut si vnus occiderit hominem, & eundem furatus sit, duo sunt facta, hoc est, actiones: agitur enim ex L. Aquil. & furti. Altera alteram non consumit, hoc est, ex vtraque actione solidum consequitur: vtrumque punitur, furtum, & cædes. Ponuntur alia exempla in l. nunquam. Eodem modo eiusdem rei & pecuniæ nomine ex diversis factis tenetur quis actione furti manifesti, & nec manifesti. l. vulgaris 21. de furtis. Item si tutor in tutela gerenda aliquid abstulerit, vel auerterit ex bonis pupilli, qui li, qui per se poenam meretur. Sed quid si surandi animo auerterit & surripuerit: Duo facta, & duae obligationes esse intelliguntur, & alia aliam non tollit. Igitur agi potest & furti, & tutelae distractionis. l. 1. §. in tutela 21. l. 2. de tut. & rat. distrah. Item si quis feram bestiam ibi habeat, qua vulgo iter fieri solet, & fera bestia transeunti noceat; duo facta sunt, hoc est, duae actiones. Quia ibi habuit feram bestiam, est Aedilitia actio in duplum. Quia autem fera nocuit, est actio, si quadrupes pauperiem fecisse dicatur. §. vlt. Instit. si quadrupes, &c. Igitur quoties ex pluribus factis plures sunt actiones, una non minuit aliam, utraque competit in solidum, sine ulla distinctione. Poenales actiones hic vocat, non tantum mere poenales, sed etiam mixtas. l. si is 71. de furt. Actio furti significat condictionem furtiuam, ut & in l. 9. de in lit. iur. secundum eam l. 71. si concurrat cum actione commodati condictio, altera alteram consumit, ipso iure, vel per exceptionem. Ipso iure, si prius actum sit condictione. Per exceptionem, si prius actum sit commodati, quae est bonae fidei. Nam si postea agatur condictione, opponitur exceptio l. 2. de rescind. vend. Igitur actiones rei persecutoriae de eadem re concurrentes altera alteram consumit, nisi scilicet quid sit pluris in altera l. praedia 28. de aed. empt. l. si quis 41. & l. seq. & l. sed si ex causa 47. pro soœͤ. Rursus huic regulæ locus est, siue plures actiones poenales ex pluribus factis descendant, siue ex vno facto sint plures actiones poenales, vt si quid publicanus non iure abstulerit: nam tenetur edicto de publicanis in duplum, & actione furti, vel bonorum raptorum. Nam raptor est fur quidam improbior. l.2. vi bon. rapt. Et si quis rem alienam rapuerit, etiam tenetur actione furti, & vi bonorum raptorum. l.1. vi bon. rapt. Si quis alienum seruum verberauerit: si quis furtim alias arbores caeciderit: tenetur, nempe L. Aquilia, & arborum furtim caesarum. l.1. arb. furt. caes. Item si quis alienam ancillam adulteram flagitauerit: is tenetur iniuriarum, & serui corrupti. l. 6. ad L. Iul. de adulter. His omnibus casibus ex vno facto, & vna obligatione sunt plures actiones poenales. Sed dubitatum fuit, An omnibus vti liceat? quod constat ex l.cum ex vno 32. de oblig. & act. d. l.1. arb. furt. caes. Dicta l. cum ex vno, ait: post magnas varietates obtinuit, omnibus licere vti. Sed obiter notandum in l. plura, rem non ita accipi, vt hic ait. Plura delicta in vna re. Vbi rem accipimus non pro corpore & pecunia eadem, sed de eodem facto & crimine l. senatus 14. de accus. Plura delicta plures pariunt actiones. Notandum, aliud esse plura delicta ex vno facto, quia tunc plures sunt actiones: sed tunc non esse omnibus utendum. Itaque l. plura nihil pertinet ad hanc regulam. Sed excusari potest aliqua ratione l. cum ex uno. Hoc enim innuit, omnibus actionibus experiri licet, si prius leui quis usus sit. Nam quod pluris est in altera, peti potest: ut si egerit cum raptore furti in duplum, qui tenetur etiam vi bonorum raptorum in quadruplum; superest actio vi bonorum raptorum: leg. si quis egerit 88. de furtis. Actio quæ est leuior, delibat, & diminuit, & ad aliquid consumit actionem grauiorem, nempe vi bonorum raptorum. Non omnibus uti licet, si prius egit graviore actione, ut in hoc exemplo. Si enim priore actione grauauit reū, & prius egerit vi bonorum raptorum; consumitur actio furti. Denique in multis aliis exemplis locum habet, ut in exemplo arborum furtim cæsarum: l. 2. arb. furt. cæs. l. quoties 41. de oblig. & act. Sed in ea lege quoties, legendum pro id consequatur; nihil consequatur. Nam cum in uno facto sunt plures actiones pœnales, una peracta, superest altera, si quid habeat pluris: sed si habeat minus, vel tantundem, nihil consequitur. Restat ex iis, quæ diximus rei persecutoria, persecutoriam solui pœnali actione: pœnalem ex uno facto, vel omnino, vel ad aliquid. Quid dicemus, si actio rei persecutoria cum actione pœnali concurrat? Actio pœnalis aut est mere pœnalis, aut mixta. Rursus actio mixta vel est arbitraria, vel non. Arbitrariæ tratiæ actionis natura est, vt euitetur re restituta. Actio quod metus causa in quadruplum, est arbitraria: re restituta euitatur pœna quadrupli, aut tripli; quia mixta est. l. metum. 9. §. licet. 6. quod metus causa. Nunc dicemus, mere pœnales si concurrant cum actione rei persecutoria, altera alteram non tollit, vt condictio furtiua non tollit actionem furtiuam. l. 7. §. 1. de condict. furt. actio furti non tollit actionem pro socio & locati: & econtra. l. rei communis 45. pro socio. l. si locatum 42. locati. Per actionem mixtam omnino tollitur actio rei persecutoria. Nam qui agit mixta, rem est consecutus. Per rei persecutionem tollitur etiam mixta arbitraria, vt per actionem in rem restitutoriam, vel per actionem de dolo malo, tollitur actio, Quod metus causa. l. 9. §. licet 6. quod met. causa. & l. si cum 14. §. eum qui 13. eod. tit. Eadem ratione, vt puto, per actionem tutelæ, vel per condictionem furtiuam, tollitur actio, de Rationibus distrahendis, mixta arbitraria. l. 1. §. in tutela. 21. l. 2. §. 1. de tut. & rat. distrah. Per actionem autem rei persecutoriam non omnino tollitur actio mixta, non arbitraria: quia in id superest, quod amplius est in ea. Per condictionem furtiuam non tollitur actio L. Aquiliæ. l. qui seruum 34. §. vlt. de oblig. & act. l. 2. §. quæsitum. 3. de priuat. delict. Per actionem commodati, non tollitur actio L. Aquiliæ d. §. vlt. in quo §. abundabant duæ negationes, quarum ego vnam sustuli, alteram sustulerunt Pandectæ Florentinæ. Species est. Is cui rem commodaui, eam deteriorem fecit, tenetur commodati & L. Aquiliæ. Si prius egero actione L. Aquiliæ, consumitur commodati actio: sed si prius egero commodati, an remanet Aquilia? Ita, & recte sic Florentinæ. Et subducto simplo, quod sum consecutus, in reliquum locum habet actio L. Aquiliæ. Itaque etiam in specie l. si colonus 9. arb. furt. caes. est actio locati, & arborum furtim cæsarum mixta, & in specie l. si vulnerauerit 43. locati. vbi est actio locati & L. Aquiliæ: quibus locis satis esse dicitur, vna actione vti: intellige, si prius egerit mixta. l. vnde quaeritur 7. l. in rebus 18. §. 1. commod. sic in l. hæredem 5. de calumniat. dum l. ait; alterutram actionem sufficere: ita accipe, vt si prius egero in quadruplum ex illo edicto de calumniatoribus, quod tibi pecuniam dedi, ne me vexares & negotium facesseres, postea non agam condictione ob turpem causam. Et si prius egero condictione ob turpem causam, non agam in quadruplum, sed in triplum tantum. Actio illa ex edicto est in quadruplum mixta, si ego dedi, ne negotium fieret: sed si dedi, ne alteri fieret, tunc est mere poenalis, ideo tunc non consumitur per condictionem ob turpem causam: quinimo, cum ego dedi, ne negotium Titio fieret, mihi competit actio ob turpem causam. Titio vero cum competit actio in quadruplum, nec altera alteram tollit. l. si quis ab alio. 7. cod. tit. Huic sententiae, Quod videlicet rei persecutoria non tollat mere poenalem, vel contra; obstat l. 3. §. vlt. Naut. caup. stab. ubi dicitur, si actum sit actione de recepto, non posse agi furti actione, quae est mere poenalis. Respondeo: Si idem in eundem habeat actionem rei persecutoriam, & mere poenalem; altera alteram non tollit: sed si idem in unum rei persecutoriam, in alterum mere poenalem habeat, ut vector, qui in exercitorem actionem habet de recepto, & in furem furti: hic sane vector, si elegerit exercitorem & egerit cum eo de recepto, non potest postea agere furti, & transire ad furem. Sed non ideo fur exuitur poena: nam aequum est, ut exercitor, cuius periculo res fuit, in furem habeat actionem furti. At si vector elegerit furem, exercitor de recepto liberatur. Idem seruatur in actione in duplum, quae est ex quali maleficio exercitoris. l. licet. 6. §. possumus 4. cod. tit. Restat hanc regulam habere locum, si sint actiones plures plurium factorum, licet sint de eadem re vel pecunia. Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: This rule belongs to the treatise on actions. It is repeated in l. pen. de oblig. & act., although the inscriptions vary. The inscription of this law is the better one. In the other, l. ait Vlp. de eadem pecunia: the reading should not be changed, for it is so in the Basilica. The term res (thing) is wider than pecunia (money), as appears from ex l. 5. de verb. sign. Hence it is clear that "the same thing" is not taken here to mean "the same act." Indeed, according to l. nunquam. 2. de privat. delict., this rule applies when several actions arise from several acts, even if they concern the same body. One of these actions does not consume the other. For example, if one man kills a person and also steals from him, there are two acts, that is, two actions: he is sued under the Lex Aquilia and for theft. One action does not consume the other; from each action he recovers the whole, and he is punished for both the theft and the homicide. Other examples are given in l. nunquam. In the same way, for the same thing and the same money, a person is liable to the action for manifest theft and to the action for non-manifest theft, arising from different acts: l. vulgaris 21. de furtis. Likewise, if a guardian in administering the guardianship takes or diverts something from the goods of his ward, he deserves a penalty on account of that act alone. But what if he diverts and removes the goods with intent to steal? Then there are understood to be two acts and two obligations, and one does not cancel the other. Therefore an action both for theft and for the wrongful diversion of accounts may be brought: l. 1. §. in tutela 21. l. 2. de tut. & rat. distrah. Likewise, if someone keeps a wild beast where people commonly pass, and the beast harms a passer-by, there are two acts, that is, two actions. Because he kept the wild beast there, there is the aedilician action for double damages. Because the beast did the harm, there is the action, if it is said that a quadruped has caused damage: §. vlt. Instit. si quadrupes, &c. Therefore, whenever several actions arise from several acts, one does not diminish another; each is available for the whole, without any distinction. Here he calls them penal actions, not only purely penal but also mixed: l. si is 71. de furt. The action for theft means the condiction for stolen goods, as also in l. 9. de in lit. iur. According to that law, l. 71., if a condiction concurs with the action of loan for use, one consumes the other, either ipso iure or by exception. Ipso iure, if the condiction was brought first. By exception, if the action of loan for use, which is of good faith, was brought first. For if afterwards the condiction is brought, the exception is raised: l. 2. de rescind. vend. Therefore, actions for recovering a thing concurring concerning the same thing consume one another, unless, of course, there is something more in one: l. praedia 28. de aed. empt. l. si quis 41. & l. seq. & l. sed si ex causa 47. pro soœͤ. Again, this rule applies whether several penal actions arise from several acts, or from one act there are several penal actions, as when a tax-farmer has taken something without right. For he is liable under the edict concerning tax-farmers for double damages, and to the action for theft or for goods seized by violence. For a robber is a kind of more wicked thief: l.2. vi bon. rapt. And if someone seizes another's property, he is liable also to the action for theft and to the action for goods seized by violence: l.1. vi bon. rapt. If someone beats another's slave, or secretly cuts down another's trees, he is liable under the Lex Aquilia and for trees cut secretly: l.1. arb. furt. caes.
