Likewise, if someone solicits another's maidservant to adultery, he is liable for injury and for corrupting a slave: l. 6. ad L. Iul. de adulter. In all these cases, from one act and one obligation there are several penal actions. But it has been doubted whether it is lawful to use all of them. This is established by l. cum ex vno 32. de oblig. & act. d. l.1. arb. furt. caes. The law cum ex vno says that, after great disputes, it was settled that it is lawful to use all of them. But it should be noted in passing that in l. plura the thing is not taken as this law says: "several offences in one thing." Here we take "thing" not for the same body or money, but for the same act and crime: l. senatus 14. de accus. Several offences produce several actions. It should be noted that it is one thing for several offences to arise from one act, because then there are several actions, but then it is not lawful to use all of them. So l. plura has nothing to do with this rule. But l. cum ex uno can be excused on some ground. For it implies that one may bring all the actions, if one has first used a lighter one. For what is more in another can be sought: for example, if one has sued a robber for theft for double damages, who is also liable for goods seized by violence for fourfold damages, the action for goods seized by violence remains: leg. si quis egerit 88. de furtis. The lighter action takes away and diminishes, and in some respect consumes, the heavier action, namely the action for goods seized by violence. It is not lawful to use all of them if one first brought the heavier action, as in this example. For if by the earlier action one has burdened the defendant, and has first sued for goods seized by violence, the action for theft is consumed. Finally, this rule applies in many other examples, as in the example of trees secretly cut: l. 2. arb. furt. cæs. l. quoties 41. de oblig. & act. But in that law quoties one should read, instead of id consequatur, nihil consequatur (he obtains nothing). For when in one act there are several penal actions, once one has been pursued, the other remains, if it has something more; but if it has less, or the same amount, he obtains nothing. There remains from what we have said that a recovery action is discharged by a penal action, and a penal action from one act is discharged either wholly or in part. What shall we say if a recovery action concurs with a penal action? A penal action is either purely penal or mixed. Again, a mixed action is either arbitrary or not. The nature of an arbitrary action is that it is avoided by restoring the thing. The action quod metus causa for fourfold damages is arbitrary: by restoring the thing, the penalty of fourfold or threefold is avoided, because it is mixed: l. metum. 9. §. licet. 6. quod metus causa. Now we say that if purely penal actions concur with a recovery action, one does not cancel the other; as the condiction for stolen goods does not cancel the action for theft: l. 7. §. 1. de condict. furt. The action for theft does not cancel the action on partnership or the action of hire, and conversely: l. rei communis 45. pro socio. l. si locatum 42. locati. By a mixed action a recovery action is wholly cancelled, for one who sues by a mixed action has already obtained the thing. By recovery of the thing even a mixed arbitrary action is cancelled, as by the action for restoration of the thing, or by the action for fraud, the action quod metus causa is cancelled: l. 9. §. licet 6. quod met. causa. & l. si cum 14. §. eum qui 13. eod. tit. By the same reasoning, I think, by the action of guardianship, or by the condiction for stolen goods, the mixed arbitrary action for the wrongful diversion of accounts is cancelled: l. 1. §. in tutela. 21. l. 2. §. 1. de tut. & rat. distrah. But by a recovery action a mixed, non-arbitrary action is not wholly cancelled, because what is more in it remains. By the condiction for stolen goods the action of the Lex Aquilia is not cancelled: l. qui seruum 34. §. vlt. de oblig. & act. l. 2. §. quæsitum. 3. de priuat. delict. By the action of loan for use the action of the Lex Aquilia is not cancelled: d. §. vlt. In that §. there were two negatives, of which I have removed one, and the Florentine Pandects have removed the other. The case is this: one to whom I lent a thing has made it worse; he is liable under the loan for use and the Lex Aquilia. If I first sue under the Lex Aquilia, the action of loan for use is consumed; but if I first sue under the loan for use, does the Aquilian action remain? Yes, and rightly so, as the Florentine text has it. And when the simple amount that I have recovered is deducted, the action of the Lex Aquilia holds for the remainder. Therefore also in the case of l. si colonus 9. arb. furt. caes., there is the action of hire, and the mixed action for trees secretly cut; and in the case of l. si vulnerauerit 43. locati., where there is the action of hire and the Lex Aquilia: in these places it is said that it is enough to use one action, namely if one has first brought the mixed one: l. vnde quaeritur 7. l. in rebus 18. §. 1. commod. So too in l. hæredem 5. de calumniat., where the law says that either action is enough, understand it thus: if I first sue for fourfold damages under that edict on calumniators, because I gave you money so that you would not harass me and make trouble, I shall afterwards not sue by the condiction for a dishonourable cause. And if I first sue by the condiction for a dishonourable cause, I shall not sue for fourfold damages, but only for threefold. That action under the edict is mixed, for fourfold damages, if I gave money that the business should not be done; but if I gave it that the business should not be done for another, then it is purely penal, and therefore then it is not consumed by the condiction for a dishonourable cause. Indeed, when I gave it that the business should not be done for Titius, I have the action for a dishonourable cause; but Titius has the action for fourfold damages, and neither cancels the other: l. si quis ab alio. 7. cod. tit. This opinion, namely that a recovery action does not cancel a purely penal action, or the reverse, is opposed by l. 3. §. vlt. Naut. caup. stab., where it is said that if the action on the deposit of goods has been brought, one cannot bring the action for theft, which is purely penal. I reply: if the same person has against the same both a recovery action and a purely penal action, one does not cancel the other; but if against one he has a recovery action, and against another a purely penal action, as a passenger who has an action against the shipowner on the deposit of goods, and against the thief an action for theft: here, if the passenger has chosen the shipowner and has sued him on the deposit, he cannot afterwards bring the action for theft and turn to the thief. But the thief is not thereby freed from punishment; for it is fair that the shipowner, at whose risk the goods were, should have the action for theft against the thief. But if the passenger has chosen the thief, the shipowner is released from the action on the deposit. The same rule is observed in the action for double damages, which arises from a wrongful act of the shipowner: l. licet. 6. §. possumus 4. cod. tit. It remains that this rule applies if there are several actions arising from several acts, even if they concern the same thing or money. Cuiac. in Recit.

units.la: Ad Leg. 131. De eo qui dolo desiit possidere.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 131. Concerning one who has ceased to possess through fraud.

units.la: QVi dolo desierit possidere, pro possidente damnatur, quia pro possessione dolus est.
units.tr: One who has ceased to possess through fraud is condemned as if he were still in possession, because fraud stands in place of possession.

units.la: Nec enim potest fieri cessio, sicut nec ei, qui possidet. Vide Dynum ad d. c. 36. de reg. in 6. nu. 2. Goth.
units.tr: Nor indeed can a cession be made by him, just as it cannot be made by one who is in possession. See Dynus on c. 36, de reg. in 6, n. 2. Goth.

units.la: Qua actione tenetur, qui possidet, eadem tenetur, qui dolo possidere desiit, nec seid-circo circo actione exuit possessor, si dolo desiit possidere. Huic sententiae locus est in petitione hereditatis, & in rei vindicatione & inactione ad exhibendum, & in noxalibus actionibus, & in interdictis: Quorum legatorum l.1. quor. bon. de libero homine exhibendo l.1. de li. hom. exhib. Ne quid in loco publico l.2. §. hoc interdicto. ne quid in loco publ. Ex quo loco sumpta est l. parem 150. inf. hoc tit. vbi eadem regula repetitur. Cuiac. in Recit. oper. posth.
units.tr: The one who has ceased to possess through fraud is bound by the same action as the one who possesses, and the possessor is not freed from the action merely because he has ceased to possess through fraud. This opinion holds in the petition of inheritance, in the action for recovery of a thing, in the action for production, in noxal actions and in the interdicts. Of these, the interdict quorum bonorum (l.1. quor. bon.), the interdict for producing a free man (l.1. de li. hom. exhib.), and the interdict ne quid in loco publico (l.2. §. hoc interdicto. ne quid in loco publ.) are examples. This rule was taken from the place where l. parem 150. inf. hoc tit. repeats the same principle. Cuiac. in Recit. oper. posth.

units.la: Ad Leg. 132. De imperitia.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 132. Concerning want of skill.

units.la: IMperitia culpae annumeratur. Imperitia l.6. §.7. sup. de offic. praesid. l.28. §. 29. sup. ad L. Aquil. l.9. §. 5. l. 13. §. 5. sup. locati. §. 7. Institut. de L. Aquil. 2. Eclog. 3. capit. 135. Gothofr.
units.tr: Want of skill is counted as fault. Want of skill: l.6. §.7. sup. de offic. praesid. l.28. §. 29. sup. ad L. Aquil. l.9. §. 5. l. 13. §. 5. sup. locati. §. 7. Institut. de L. Aquil. 2. Eclog. 3. capit. 135. Gothofr.

units.la: Annumeratur regulariter, at non in mensore. l.1. §.1. sup. si mensor, &c. Goth.
units.tr: Is counted as a rule, but not in the case of a surveyor. l.1. §.1. sup. si mensor, &c. Goth.

units.la: Vide de imperitia quaedam sup. in l. 108.
units.tr: On want of skill, see some points above on l. 108.

units.la: Ad Leg. 133. De servis.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 133. Concerning slaves.

units.la: MElior conditio nostra per seruos fieri potest, deterior non potest.
units.tr: Our condition can be made better through slaves, but it cannot be made worse.

units.la: Deterior l.28, inf. sup. de pact. l.19. sup. mandati. l. 122. §. 1. sup. de verb. oblig. l. 2. §. 1. sup. de pol‑licit. l. 3. C. de pactis l. vlt. C. de acquir. possess.
units.tr: Deterior: see the law 28, below, and the law 19 of the title on the pact, the law 19 on mandate, the law 122 §1 on the verb of obligation, the law 2 §1 on promises, the law 3 of the Code on pacts, and the last law of the Code on acquiring possession.

units.la: nisi dominus delictum à seruo committi sciuerit, nec prohibuerit. vide Paulum 5. sentent. 12. §. vlt. Goth.
units.tr: unless the master knew that a wrong was being committed by the slave and did not forbid it. See Paulus, Sent. 5.12 §. last. Goth.

units.la: Et hæc lex iam supra aliquot locis satis expli‑ cata est.
units.tr: This law has already been explained sufficiently in several places above.

units.la: Ad Leg. 134. Quomodo creditores frau- dantur. De delicto.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 134. How creditors are defrauded. Concerning wrongdoing.

units.la: NOn fraudantur creditores, cum quid non acquiritur à debitore: sed cum quid de bonis deminuitur. §. Nemo ex suo delicto me‑ liorem suam conditionem facere potest.
units.tr: Creditors are not defrauded when nothing is acquired by the debtor, but only when something is diminished from his goods. §. No one can make his own condition better through his own wrongdoing.

units.la: excipe l. 25. §. 8. sup. de hæred. petit. l. 2. §. 5. sup. de hæreditate vendita. l. 64. §. 7. ̄soluto l. 1. §. 12. sup. si quis omissa causa. adde l. 78. sup. eodem.
units.tr: Except D. 6.1.25.8 (above, de haeredis petitione); D. 18.4.2.5 (above, de hereditate vendita); D. 39.5.64.7 (sol.); D. 3.1.1.12 (above, si quis omissa causa); add D. 6.1.78 (above, the same title); D. 17.2.68 (in fine, above, pro socio); D. 24.1.5.13 (above, de donationibus inter virum et uxorem); D. 1.7.1.23 (above, de decollatione... ); D. 42.8.6 (above, quae in fraudem creditorum); Goth.

units.la: puta de patrimonio. l. 5. §. 13. sup. de donat. inter virum & vx. Goth.
units.tr: That is, concerning the patrimony. l. 5. §. 13. sup. de donat. inter virum & uxorem. Goth.

units.la: Meliorem ]est enim iniquum, vt dolus proprius alteri noceatl.39.l.49.sup.eod.leg.155.inf. eod. Gothofr.
units.tr: Meliorem] for it is unjust that one's own fraud should harm another. l.39. l.49. sup. eod. leg. 155. inf. eod. Gothofr.

units.la: Pertinet hæc L. ad actionem Paulianam, qua creditores gesta fraudationis causa rescindunt, & reuocant. Nam est ei locus, si debitor ex bonis suis deminuerit aliquid, vel si delabi de re iam quæsita passus est, si seruitutem amittat non vtendo. Non est ei locus, si occasione acquirendi non vtatur, vel si legatum non agnoscat.l. 5.qua in fraud.credit.
units.tr: This law relates to the Pauline action, by which creditors rescind and revoke transactions done for the purpose of fraud. For it applies if the debtor has diminished something from his goods, or if he has allowed something already acquired to slip away, as when he loses a servitude by not using it. It does not apply if he fails to take advantage of an opportunity to acquire, or if he does not accept a legacy. l. 5. qua in fraud. credit.

units.la: Ad §. Nemo ex suo.
units.tr: On the §. Nemo ex suo.

units.la: Huius §. exemplum sume ex leg.si ab hostibus 10. §. 1. solut. matrim. sciendum est, dotem adventitiam, mortua in matrimonio vxore, cedere lucro viri, & hoc iure nostro comprobari potest.l.15. de fundo dot. leg.Celsus 22. de relig. & sumptib. fun. l. mulier. 20. de condit. instit. l.sed & si post. 23. de cuict. l. 5. de bon. damnat. l. unic. C.si aduersus dot. Species eius haec est: Mortua vxore, cedebat dos lucro mariti: sed ipse maritus occidit vxorem: tum haeredibus vxoris repetitio dotis dabitur, non viro, quia non est æquum, eum suo delicto dotem lucrari. Nemo enim ex suo delicto meliorem suam condiditionem facere potest. Cuiac. in Recitat. oper. posthum.
units.tr: For an example of this §, take the law si ab hostibus 10. §. 1. solut. matrim. It must be known that an adventitious dowry, when the wife has died during the marriage, falls to the husband's gain, and this can be confirmed by our law. l.15. de fundo dot. leg. Celsus 22. de relig. & sumptib. fun. l. mulier 20. de condit. instit. l. sed & si post 23. de cuict. l. 5. de bon. damnat. l. unic. C. si adversus dot. The case is this: the wife having died, the dowry passed to the husband's gain; but the husband himself killed the wife. Then the recovery of the dowry will be given to the wife's heirs, not to the husband, because it is not fair that he should gain the dowry by his own wrongdoing. For no one can make his own condition better through his own wrongdoing. Cuiac. in Recitat. oper. posthum.

units.la: Ad Leg. 135. Quæ dari nequeunt, vel in rerum natura non sunt.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 135. Things which cannot be given, or which do not exist in nature.

units.la: EA, quæ dari impossibilia sunt, vel quæ in rerum natura non sunt, pro non adiectis habentur.
units.tr: Those things which are impossible to give, or which do not exist in nature, are held as if they had not been added.

units.la: Sumatur exemplum ex leg. si ita stipulatus 97. de verborum oblig. species est. Stipulatus sum, Tesisti. Hæc est una stipulatio. Subieci alteram; Nisi sistas, hippocentaurum dari vel hominem liberum. Hæc adiectio pro non scripta est. Inutilis adiectio non vitiat utilem stipulationem, licet liber homo dari non possit. l. liber homo eod. tit. veluti nec hippocentaurus. Igitur hæ adiectiones inutiles sunt, & pro non adiectis habentur, salua manente principali obligatione, cui sunt adiectæ. Cuia. in Recit. oper. posth.
units.tr: Let an example be taken from the law si ita stipulatus 97, de verborum oblig. The case is this. I stipulated, "Will you appear?" That is one stipulation. I added another: "Unless you appear, a hippocentaur or a free man shall be given." This addition is held as not written. A useless addition does not vitiate a useful stipulation, even though a free man cannot be given, as the law liber homo in the same title says, and likewise a hippocentaur cannot be given. Therefore these additions are useless and are held as not added, the principal obligation to which they were attached remaining in force. Cuia. in Recit. oper. posth.

units.la: Ad Leg. 136. De bona fide possidenti- s. Et de veritate.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 136. Concerning the possessor in good faith. And concerning truth.

units.la: BOna fides tantundem possidenti præbet, quantum veritas, quoties lex impedimento non est.
units.tr: Good faith gives the possessor as much as truth does, whenever the law is no obstacle.

units.la: Legis huius exemplum tale sumamus. Sicut domino datur vindicatio rei, ita & bonae fidei possessori, cui tantum bona fides praestat, quantum veritas, hoc est, dominium. Sed bonae fidei possessori datur vindicatio Publiciana, quarum actionum eadem est potestas. Sicut verum est, possessorem teneri vindicatione directa; eum, qui dolo desiit possidere, utili. Sed parvum est discrimen: ideoque non male dicebamus supra in l. 131. dolum pro possessione esse: Datur autem bonae fidei possessori vindicatio, quae dicitur Publiciana, in iis rebus, quae usucapi possunt, vel etiam in iis, quae licet usucapi non possint, tamen longo tempore acquiri possunt; ut in praediis vectigalibus l. cum sponsus 12. §. in vectigalibus 2. de Public. in rem act. In aliis autem rebus, quae usucapi non possunt, Publiciana usucapionem non habet, ut in re furtiva. Rei furtivae possessionem si quis nactus sit bona fide, & amiserit, non habet Publicianam: quia nec rem usu suam facere potest. Lex enim 12. tabularum est impedimento, hoc est, inhibet usucapionem rei furtivae. Praeterea publiciana actione tantum tenetur, qui usucapere, vel longo tempore ac-netur, quirere potest. d. l. cum sponsus 12. §. si res 4. & l. sive autem 9. §. vlt. de public. in rem act. Et hoc est, quod ait haec lex, Impedimento non esse. Rei furtiuae vindicationem bonae fidei possessor non habet: rei tamen dominus eam habet. Sic non tantum valet bona fides, quantum veritas. Sed hoc etiam exemplum apponatur. Sicut res surrepta domino non ante potest vsucapi, quam sit reuersa ad dominum: sic res surrepta bonae fidei possessori, non potest vsucapi, antequam sit reuersa ad bonae fidei possessorem. l. 4 §. si pupillus de vsucap. l. qui fundum §. si tutor. pro emptore. Nam in iis locis, pupillus non accipitur pro domino, cum res propria pupilli non possit vsucapi: sed accipitur pro bonae fidei possessore. Res autem aliena, quam pupillus bona fide possidet, potest vsucapi. Sic igitur tantum praestat, quantum veritas. Sic non est mirum, si dominus saepe in libris nostris pro bonae fidei possessore accipiatur. Cuia. in Recit. posthum.
units.tr: Let us take the following example of this law. Just as the owner is given an action to recover the thing, so too the possessor in good faith, to whom good faith gives as much as truth does, that is, ownership. But the possessor in good faith is given the Publician action, and the power of these actions is the same. Just as it is true that the possessor is bound by the direct action for recovery, so the one who ceased to possess through fraud is bound by the useful action. But the difference is slight, and so we were not wrong to say above, on law 131, that fraud stands in place of possession. The possessor in good faith is given the action for recovery called Publician in those things which can be acquired by usucapion, or even in those which, although they cannot be acquired by usucapion, can nevertheless be acquired over a long time, as in lands subject to tribute: law cum sponsus 12, §. in vectigalibus 2, de Public. in rem act. But in other things which cannot be acquired by usucapion, the Publician action has no usucapion, as in the case of stolen property. If anyone has obtained possession of stolen property in good faith and has lost it, he does not have the Publician action, because he cannot make the thing his own by use. For the law of the Twelve Tables is an impediment, that is, it forbids the usucapion of stolen property. Moreover, one is bound only by the Publician action who can acquire by usucapion or over a long time. d. l. cum sponsus 12, §. si res 4, & l. sive autem 9, §. vlt. de public. in rem act. And this is what this law means by "not being an impediment." The possessor in good faith does not have the action for recovery of stolen property, but the owner of the thing has it. Thus good faith does not give as much as truth does. But let this example also be set down. Just as a thing taken from its owner cannot be acquired by usucapion before it has returned to the owner, so a thing taken from a possessor in good faith cannot be acquired by usucapion before it has returned to the possessor in good faith. l. 4, §. si pupillus de vsucap. l. qui fundum, §. si tutor. pro emptore. For in those passages "pupil" is not taken to mean the owner, since the pupil's own property cannot be acquired by usucapion, but is taken to mean the possessor in good faith. But another's property which the pupil possesses in good faith can be acquired by usucapion. Thus good faith gives only as much as truth does. Hence it is no wonder that in our books the owner is often taken to mean the possessor in good faith. Cuia. in Recit. posthum.

units.la: Ad Leg. 137. Quis sit bonae fidei possessor?
units.tr: Ad Leg. 137. Who is a possessor in good faith?

units.la: QVi authore Iudice comparauit, bonae fidei possessor est.
units.tr: One who has acquired with a judge as his authority is a possessor in good faith.

units.la: Qui] ex tit. de religios. leg. at si quis §. sed si adita.
units.tr: Qui] from tit. de religios. leg. at si quis §. sed si adita.

units.la: Authore] 2. Eclog. 3. c. 134. l. 167. in sin. inf. eod. l. 11. sup. de acquir. possess. secus si mala fide.
units.tr: Authore: 2 Eclog. 3, c. 134; l. 167, in sin., inf. eod.; l. 11, sup. de acquir. possess. Otherwise if in bad faith.

units.la: c. {*}qui contra 82. de reg. in 6. ubi vide Dynum. l. 27. sup. de contrahenda empt. Goth.
units.tr: c. qui contra 82, de reg. in 6, where see Dynus; l. 27, sup. de contrahenda empt. Goth.

units.la: Regulæ huius exemplum sumamus ex l. & si quis 14. §. 1. de relig. & sumptib. fun. cuius species est. Non est, unde defunctus funeretur, & nondum adiit hæres: res tamen quædam apparent, quæ quibusdam legatæ sunt: res illæ vendi iubentur prætore authore, ut ex hac venditione funus comparetur. Melius est, ut de suo funus comparetur, quam ut quidam legata consequantur. Quod si venditis rebus legatis ob causam funeris, hæres postea adeat, & conueniatur à legatariis, an auferre potest res legatas emptori? Minime; nec rescinditur venditio facta Prætore authore: sed debet hæres legatariis satisfacere, si potest, hoc est, si bona sufficiant. Legatariis autem non tenetur hæres supra vires hereditarias, imo nec supra dodrantem & Legem Falcidiam, & deducitæs alienum, antequam legata præstentur. Igitur recte ait: si potest hæres, debet indemnem reddere hæreditatem. Sed si non potest, melius est, legatarium non lucrari, quam emptorem in damno versari. Igitur non rescinditur venditio facta Prætore authore. Sic missio facta Prætore authore, non continetur interdicto, Quorum legatorum. l. 1. §. quæsitum eod. Eo interdicto tenetur legatarius qui occupauit; qui occupauit rem legatam, non amittit legatum propterea, sed rem, quam occupauit debet restituere haeredi. Sed quid, si legatarius missus sit in possessionem, legati seruandi causa, cum ei non caueretur, an tenetur hoc interdicto? Minime: qui authorem praetorem habet, nisi haeres offerat cautionem legati nomine: nam tunc credere debet. Iuste possidet, qui authore praetore possidet. l. iuste. de acquir. possess. l. electio §. vlt. de nox. act. Cuiac. in Recitat. posthum.
units.tr: For the example of this rule let us take the law & si quis 14, §. 1, de relig. & sumptib. fun., the case of which is this. A dead man has no means to pay for his funeral, and the heir has not yet entered on the inheritance. However, some goods are found which have been bequeathed to certain persons. Those goods are ordered to be sold by the praetor's authority, so that the funeral may be paid for from that sale. It is better that the funeral be paid for from the dead man's own goods than that certain legatees should receive their legacies. But if, after the goods bequeathed have been sold for the funeral, the heir later enters on the inheritance and is sued by the legatees, can he take back the bequeathed goods from the buyer? Not at all; the sale made by the praetor's authority is not rescinded. But the heir ought to satisfy the legatees, if he can, that is, if the goods suffice. Yet the heir is not bound to the legatees beyond the strength of the inheritance, nor even beyond three-quarters of it under the Falcidian law, and the debts of the estate are deducted before the legacies are paid. Therefore it is rightly said: "If the heir can, he must restore the inheritance unimpaired." But if he cannot, it is better that the legatee gain nothing than that the buyer be left at a loss. Therefore the sale made by the praetor's authority is not rescinded. Likewise, a putting into possession made by the praetor's authority is not covered by the interdict Quorum legatorum, l. 1, §. quaesitum, eod. By that interdict the legatee is bound who took possession of the bequeathed thing; one who has taken possession of a bequeathed thing does not thereby lose the legacy, but must restore to the heir the thing he has taken. But what if the legatee was put into possession for the preservation of the legacy, and security was not given to him: is he bound by this interdict? Not at all: one who has the praetor as his authority is not bound, unless the heir offers security in respect of the legacy, for then the legatee ought to trust him. He possesses rightfully who possesses with the praetor as his authority. l. iuste. de acquir. possess. l. electio, §. vlt. de nox. act. Cuiac. in Recitat. posthum.

units.la: Ad Leg. 138. De aditione continuanda. De æstimatione delicti.
units.tr: On Law 138. On the continuation of acceptance. On the estimation of a delict.

units.la: OMnis haereditas, quamuis postea adeatur, tamen cum tempore mortis continuatur. §. Nunquam crescit ex postfacto praeteriti delicti æstimatio.
units.tr: Every inheritance, although it is accepted later, nevertheless continues from the time of death. §. Nothing increases from the later estimation of a past delict.

units.la: Continuatur] l. 193. inf. eod. l. 54. sup. de acquir. haered. l. 28. §. 4. sup. de stipul. seru. Goth.
units.tr: Continuatur] see l. 193 below in this title; l. 54 above, on the acquisition of inheritances; l. 28 §. 4 above, on stipulations concerning slaves. Goth.

units.la: Ex postfacto] l. 9. sup. de furtis.
units.tr: Ex postfacto] l. 9 above, on thefts.

units.la: Sensus regulae est, Haeres, qui adit haereditatem, videtur haeres extitisse ex tempore mortis defuncti: acquisitio & aditio retrotrahuntur, & iunguntur tempora aditionis & mortis, l. haeres 54. de acquir. haered. l. omnia fere iura inf. hoc tit. Iura haeredum accipe actiue & passiue. Effectus regulae duplex est, in l. si ex re 38. §. vlt. de stipul. seru. Vnus est ex iure ciuili: seruum haeredireditarium ante aditam hæreditatem recte stipulari hæredi futuro. Nam etiamsi postea adeat, retrotrahitur aditio, & videtur fuisse dominus stipulationis tempore. Alter effectus est ex iure pontificio: Hæredis familiam ex tempore mortis esse funestam. Ergo expiandam quibusdam piaculis. Est & alius effectus in l. si exheredatus 10. de SCto Syllan. Filio exhæredato occiso, & post mortem destituto testamento, hoc est, repudiata hæreditate ab hærede scripto, de familia quæstio habetur, quasi domino occiso: Nam videtur retro hæres extitisse mortis tempore. Male Accurs. & cæteri confundunt cum hac regula illam, quæ dictat, Hæreditatem esse dominam, & vicem defuncti sustinere. l. non minus 31. de instit. hared. l. hereditas 61. de acquir. dom. l. denique 13. §. quæsitum 5. quod vi aut clam. l. 1. §. 1. si quis exteft. hæres extitisse. quasi utriusque regulæ eadem vis atque potestas sit: quod adeo alienum a vero est, ut una potius alteram subvertat, quod liquebit hoc modo. Sciendum est, seruum alienum non posse hæredem institui, nisi ipsius dominus possit instituí hæres, & cum eo sit testamenti factio. Instituitur seruus hereditarius iacente hereditate: cum eius domino fuit testamenti factio, cum hærede futuro non est testamenti factio. Hic seruus, si secundum regulam nostram videtur retrotracta aditio hæreditas reditareditatis fuisse, non est vtiliter institutus. Sed si constituas, hereditatem iacentem pro domino, heres erit vtiliter institutus. Et est verius, vtiliter institutum esse, quia cum defuncto, quem hereditas repræsentat, fuit testamenti factio. Sic in hac specie prævalet hæc regula, Hereditatem dominam esse: qua de causa recte additur fere in l. omnis 193. hoc tit. sed hoc loco non admodum bene Interpretes tradunt, eum articulum additum propter l. vsusfructus 26. de stipul. serv. quod seruus hereditarius non posset vsumfructum stipulari. Nam illa est potius exceptio huius regulæ, qua dicitur, Hereditatem dominam esse. d. l. hereditas 61. de acquir. domin. sed cum confundunt regulam, confundunt omnes exceptiones.
units.tr: The sense of the rule is this: an heir who accepts an inheritance is deemed to have been heir from the time of the deceased's death. Acceptance and acquisition are carried back, and the time of acceptance is joined to the time of death: l. haeres 54 on the acquisition of inheritances; l. omnia fere iura below in this title. Take the rights of heirs both actively and passively. The effect of the rule is twofold, as in l. si ex re 38 §. last, on stipulations concerning slaves. One effect belongs to the civil law: a hereditary slave may validly stipulate for a future heir before the inheritance is accepted. For even if the heir accepts afterwards, the acceptance is carried back, and the heir is taken to have been owner at the time of the stipulation. The other effect belongs to the pontifical law: the household of an heir is deemed unclean from the time of death, and so must be purified by certain expiatory rites. There is also another effect, in l. si exheredatus 10 de SC. Syllaniano: when a disinherited son has been killed, and the will has afterwards been set aside, that is, the inheritance has been renounced by the heir named in the will, an inquiry into the household is held, as if the owner had been killed. For the heir is taken to have existed retroactively at the time of death. Accursius and the others wrongly confuse with this rule that other rule which lays down that an inheritance is an owner and takes the place of the deceased: l. non minus 31 de institutionibus heredum; l. hereditas 61 de acquirendo dominio; l. denique 13 §. quaesitum 5 quod vi aut clam; l. 1 §. 1 si quis exteft.; "heir" having existed. It is as if both rules had the same force and power. That is so far from the truth that one rather overturns the other, as will become clear in this way. It must be known that another's slave cannot be instituted heir unless his owner could be instituted heir and has testamentary capacity with him. A hereditary slave is instituted while the inheritance lies unaccepted: the owner has testamentary capacity with the deceased, but there is no testamentary capacity with the future heir. If, according to our rule, acceptance is carried back, this slave, who would then be the slave of the inheritance, has not been validly instituted. But if you hold that the unaccepted inheritance stands in place of the owner, he will be validly instituted heir. And it is truer that he is validly instituted, because the testamentary capacity was with the deceased, whom the inheritance represents. So in this case the rule "the inheritance is the owner" prevails, and for that reason the words are rightly added in l. omnis 193 of this title. But here the commentators do not very well explain that this clause was added on account of l. usufructus 26 on stipulations concerning slaves, because a hereditary slave could not stipulate for a usufruct. For that is rather an exception to this rule, which says that the inheritance is the owner: d. l. hereditas 61 on the acquisition of ownership. But those who confuse the rule confuse all its exceptions as well.

units.la: Ad §. Nunquam crescit.
units.tr: On §. Nunquam crescit.

units.la: Exemplum sumatur ex l. sed si surripuit 28. de furt. si debitor surripuerit Chirographum suo creditori, actione furti in tantum tenetur, quantum interest creditoris, non esse surreptum Chirographum: quæ pœna dupli non crescit, etsi debitor id postea deleat: delendo nihil ad pœnam adiicit, quamuis delendo rursus furtum facere videatur; delet enim animo lucri faciendi. Sed ex post facto, delicti præteriti æstimatio nunquam crescit, sicut assidue rem surreptam contrectando, nihil adiicio ad pœnam. l. 9. de furt. Cuj. in Recit. posth.
units.tr: Take the example from l. sed si surripuit 28 on thefts. If a debtor has stolen his creditor's written acknowledgment of debt, he is liable in an action for theft only to the extent of the creditor's interest in the document not having been stolen. The penalty of double does not increase if the debtor afterwards destroys it: by destroying it he adds nothing to the penalty, although by destroying it he seems again to commit theft, for he destroys it with the intent of gaining. But by a later act the estimation of a past delict never increases, just as by handling the stolen thing again and again I add nothing to the penalty. l. 9 on thefts. Cuj. in Recit. posth.

units.la: Ad Leg. 139. De actionibus perpetuandis. De eo quod auferri potest.
units.tr: On Law 139. On perpetuating actions. On what can be taken away.

units.la: OMnes actiones, quæ morte aut tempore pereunt, semel inclusæ iudicio saluæ permanent. §. Non videtur perfecte cuiusq; id esse, quod ex casu auferri potest.
units.tr: All actions which perish by death or by lapse of time, once included in a judgment, remain safe. §. It does not seem that anything is perfectly a person's if it can be taken away by chance.

units.la: Inclusæ ] id est, contestatę v. l. 58. sup. de oblig. l. vlt. sup. de præscript. 30. annor. Goth.
units.tr: Inclusae] that is, contested (litis contestatae). See l. 58 above on obligations; l. last above on prescription of thirty years. Goth.

units.la: Principium huius Legis expositum est supra in l. 86. Cuiac.
units.tr: The beginning of this law was explained above, in l. 86. Cuiac.

units.la: Ad §. Non videtur.
units.tr: On §. Non videtur.

units.la: Vtamur exemplo l. cum quis 38. §. qui hominem debet solut. Qui promisit hominem generaliter, debet certum hominem dare, hoc est, persecte accipientis facere. Nam in stipulationibus qui promittit, se daturum, perfecte eius facere, promittit. Finge: soluens Stichum statuliberum, hoc est, cuius de libertate disputatur, non liberatur: quia ex causa auferri stipulatori potest, hoc est, ex euentu conditionis, & existente conditione. Quo sensu dicimus, casu militiæ, aut ex casu militiæ deberi: Mortuo militte, hæredem militis teneri. Sic ex casu dorem deberi, vel non deberi, hoc est, in casum diuortii vel tit. vel mortis uxoris. Ait haec lex: perfecte, quod l. Neratius 63. de condict. indebiti dixit, in plenum, id veteres etiam dixerunt in plenum. Sic etiam si promissor rem pignori obligatam non liberat. l. si rem meam 20. de solut. Ergo is, qui statuliberum soluit, videtur perfecte eius non secisse. Ideoque soluendo eum, non liberatur, qui soluere debuit rem, quae eius fuit ad plenum. Caeterum eum potest vendicare & alienare: & fundo pignori obligato, potest imponere seruitutem, etsi obligatus sit Fisco: leg. plerumque 205. h.t. cum qua iunge l. alienato 67. de contrahend. empt. l. non ideo 66. de rei vindic. seruus legatus sub conditione, non est haeredis persecte, quia ex causa auferri potest. Sed recte vindicabitur, ab haerede interim, imo & alienabitur: frustra tamen. Nam existente conditione, legatario vindicatio competit. l. sed to 69. §. si seruum 1. de legat. 1. frustra etiam manumittet. l. seritus 3. de manumiss. Idemque hodie est in legatis & fideicommissis conditionalibus. l. ult. C. communia de legat. Cuin Retit. posth.
units.tr: Let us use the example of l. cum quis 38 §. qui hominem debet, on payment. One who has promised a man in general terms must give a definite man, that is, must make him wholly the recipient's. For in stipulations one who promises that he will give promises to make it wholly the other's. Suppose someone pays a statuliber slave, that is, one whose freedom is in dispute: he is not discharged, because the thing can be taken away from the stipulator by chance, that is, by the outcome of a condition, and while the condition is pending. In this sense we say that something is owed by a chance of military service, or from the chance of military service: if the soldier dies, the soldier's heir is bound. So a dowry is owed or not owed by a chance, that is, in the event of divorce or of the wife's death. This law says "perfectly," which l. Neratius 63 on the condictio of what is not owed called "in full," and which the ancients also called "in full." So too, if the promisor does not free a thing pledged as security. l. si rem meam 20 on payment. Therefore he who pays a statuliber is not seen to have made the slave wholly the other's. So one who pays him is not discharged, if he was bound to pay a thing that was wholly his. Otherwise the owner may claim and alienate him, and may impose a servitude on a field pledged as security, even if he is bound to the Treasury: l. plerumque 205 in this title; with which join l. alienato 67 on contracting sales, and l. non ideo 66 on the vindication of a thing. A slave bequeathed under a condition is not wholly the heir's, because he can be taken away by chance. But meanwhile he may rightly be vindicated by the heir, indeed even alienated, but to no effect. For when the condition is fulfilled, the legatee has the right of vindication: l. sed to 69 §. si servum 1 on legacies, book 1. Likewise, if he manumits him, it is in vain: l. servus 3 on manumission. And the same holds today for conditional legacies and fideicommissa: l. ult. C. communia de legatis. Cuj. in Recit. posth.

units.la: Ad Leg. 140. De absentia Reipub. causa.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 140. Concerning the absence of one who is away for the sake of the commonwealth.

units.la: ABsentia eius, qui Reipublicae causa abest, neque ei, neque alii damnosa esse debet.
units.tr: The absence of a man who is away on public business ought to harm neither him nor anyone else.

units.la: Qui] 2. ecl. 3. cap. 137. l. 22. §. 1. sup. ex quibus causis maiores.
units.tr: Qui] 2 ecl. 3 cap. 137; l. 22 §. 1 sup. ex quibus causis maiores.

units.la: Abest] seruus abesse ita non potest. l. ult. inf. cod. Vulgaris est interpretatio, hanc legem esse rationem dandæ actionis rescissoriæ, & restitutoriæ, non tantum absentibus, sed etiam contra absentes, vt dicitur nominatim leg.1.in princip.ex quib.caus.maior.Cuia.in Recit.
units.tr: Abest] A slave cannot be absent in this way. l. ult. inf. cod. The common interpretation is that this law gives the reason for granting the rescissory and restitutory action, not only for the absent but also against the absent, as is stated by name in leg. 1 in princip. ex quib. caus. maior. Cuia. in Recit.

units.la: Ad Leg.141. De iure singulari. De hærede.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 141. Concerning singular law. Concerning an heir.

units.la: QVod contra rationem iuris receptum est, non est producendum ad consequentia.
units.tr: What has been received contrary to the reason of law is not to be extended to consequences.

units.la: Vni duo prosolido hæredes esse non possunt.
units.tr: Two heirs cannot be heirs of the whole of one estate.

units.la: Quod ] ex tract.de usur, vid. etiam l.quod vero de legibus. Pac.
units.tr: Quod] From the treatise on usury; see also l. quod vero de legibus. Pacius.

units.la: Contra ] l.14.l.15.sup.de legib.cap.quod ob gratiam 61.de regulis in 6. καὶ ᾳ ὁ ἰκανὰς 2.ecl.3.cap.138. Gothofr.
units.tr: Contra] l. 14, l. 15 sup. de legib.; cap. quod ob gratiam 61 de regulis in 6; [καὶ ᾳ ὁ ἰκανὰς] 2 ecl. 3 cap. 138. Gothofredus.

units.la: Consequentia ] Cōsequentias vulgat. εἰς ὅμοια. 2.ecl.3.cap.138. similia.
units.tr: Consequentia] The common reading is "consequentias"; [εἰς ὅμοια] 2 ecl. 3 cap. 138, "similia" (like cases).

units.la: Solido ] Duorum in solidum dominium esse non potest, l.5.§.vlt.sup.Commodati. l.3 §.5.sup. de acquir.possess. l.19.sup.de precario. Goth.
units.tr: Solido] Ownership of one thing in full cannot belong to two persons; l. 5 §. vlt. sup. Commodati; l. 3 §. 5 sup. de acquir. possess.; l. 19 sup. de precario. Gothofredus.

units.la: Contra rationem iuris receptum esse dicimus, quod est receptum iure singulari, necessitatis, vel vtilitatis gratia, quod est receptum contra ius commune, iure singulari, fauore libertatis. Receptum est, libertatem fideicommissariam à filio relictam, cum erit quatuordecim annorum, & defuncto ante eam ætatem, ab hærede filii præstituta die debetur. Quod est contra rationem iuris. Nam videtur defecisse conditio libertatis, quia non peruenit ad eam ætatem: hoc igitur non porrigemus ad certa fideicommissa. l. fideicommissaria 23. §. etiam 3. de fideicommiss. libert. Item iure singulari receptum est, ut mutuum contrahatur, si à debitore meo mea voluntate pecuniam acceperis. l. singularia 15. de reb. cred. l. qui negotia. 34. mandati. quod etiam est contra rationem iuris, quæ exigit in mutuo, ut mea pecunia fiat tua, pecunia autem mihi debita, non est mea. Vlpianus tamen in l. rogasti. 11. de reb. cred. trahit id ad consequentiam: Si pecuniam mihi debitam tibi traditam volo, quod refellit Africanus in d.l. qui negotia. Quia quod benigne receptum est, non est producendum ad consequentiā. Id benigne receptum in priore specie tantum, non est igitur producendum ad aliam speciem. Ius ciuile producitur facile ad consequentiam, quod in paribus causis æquitas paria iura desiderat. l. non possunt 12. cum leg. seq. de legibus. at ius singulare non producitur ad consequentiam; hinc quæ à pari ex iure singulari ducuntur argumenta, vitiosa sunt, licet videantur ex arte profecta. Quæ regula repetitur in l. quod vero 14. de legibus. Et idem est sensus l. quæ propter 162. inf. eod. tit. Necessitati quandoque succumbimus. l. penult. §. vlt. de excusat. tut. Et propter necessitatem quandoque recedimus à ratione iuris, quod non debet trahi ad consequentias, sed id ad suam speciem coangustare debemus, etiamsi euidenter similitudo ad alia porrigi postulet. Et in d. l. quæ propter 162. Accursius recte citat l. item quamuis 10. §. 1. & penult. comm. diuid. Quæ lex ostendit, propter necessitatem, tollendæ scil. controuersiæ causa vsum nudum rei communis vni totum adiudicari, quia non diuiditur vsus, ita tamen vt is mercedem præstet alteri pro sua parte, qui & ipse hoc modo videbitur vti, mercedem percipiendo: quia plus videtur facere, imo frui mercedem suscipiendo; Hæc autem iuris ratio non permittit. Igitur vsus neque vendi, neque locari poterit ab vsuario: vti tamen poterit, non compendium, aut lucrum facere. Igitur non videtur iudex communi diuidundo, qui debuit diuidere, vni totum adiudicare vsum potuisse; sed propter necessitatem hoc à Prætore comprobabitur, & is emendabit, hoc est, supplebit.
units.tr: We say that what is received contrary to the reason of law is what is received by a singular law, for the sake of necessity or usefulness, and what is received against the common law, by a singular law, out of favour to liberty. It is received that a fideicommissary freedom left by a son, when he reaches fourteen years of age, is due, if he dies before that age, by the heir's appointed day. This is contrary to the reason of law, for the condition of freedom seems to have failed, since he did not reach that age. We therefore will not extend this to other fideicommissa. l. fideicommissaria 23 §. etiam 3 de fideicommiss. libert. Likewise it is received by a singular law that a loan is contracted if you receive money from my debtor with my consent. l. singularia 15 de reb. cred.; l. qui negotia 34 mandati. This too is contrary to the reason of law, which requires for a loan that my money become yours, whereas money owed to me is not mine. Ulpian, however, in l. rogasti 11 de reb. cred., draws this into a consequence: if I want money owed to me to be handed over to you, which Africanus refutes in d. l. qui negotia. For what has been received kindly is not to be extended to consequences. That was received kindly only in the former case, so it is not to be extended to another case. Civil law is easily extended to consequences, because in equal cases equity requires equal rights. l. non possunt 12 cum leg. seq. de legibus. But singular law is not extended to consequences; hence arguments drawn from singular law by analogy are faulty, although they may seem to proceed from skill. This rule is repeated in l. quod vero 14 de legibus. And the same sense is in l. quae propter 162 inf. eod. tit. We sometimes yield to necessity. l. penult. §. vlt. de excusat. tut. And on account of necessity we sometimes depart from the reason of law, which ought not to be drawn into consequences, but which we ought to confine to its own case, even if a clear likeness seems to call for it to be extended elsewhere. And in d. l. quae propter 162. Accursius rightly cites l. item quamuis 10 §. 1 & penult. comm. divid. That law shows that, on account of necessity, namely to end a dispute, the bare use of a common thing is wholly adjudged to one party, since use is not divided; yet on condition that he pays the other a share of the hire, which he too will seem to be using by receiving the hire. For he seems to do more, indeed to enjoy the thing, by taking the hire; but the reason of law does not allow this. So the user can neither sell nor let out the use, though he may use the thing without making gain or profit. Therefore the judge who was to divide the common thing, and who ought to have divided it, does not seem to have been able to adjudge the whole use to one party; but on account of necessity the praetor approves this, and he will amend it, that is, supply what is lacking.

units.la: Ad §. Vni duo, &c.
units.tr: Ad §. Vni duo, &c.

units.la: Posterior sententia legis est, vni duo pro solido hæredes esse non possunt, hoc est, non sunt duo hæredes vnius hominis, vnius rei, vnius hæreditatis, quia vnius hominis duæ hæredireditates esse non possunt. l. Iurisperitos 30. de excusat.tut. Vnius autem rei non possunt esse duo domini in solidum. l.5. §. si duobus commod. l.penult. §.1. de castr.pecul. Ergo vnius hominis duo haeredes esse non possunt in solidum; sed sunt haeredes pro partibus singulis, si nullae sunt partes adscriptae. l.quoties 9. §. haeredes 12. de haered.instit.Cui.in Recit.posthum.
units.tr: The latter part of the law is "two heirs cannot be heirs of the whole of one estate", that is, there are not two heirs of one man, of one thing, of one inheritance, because two inheritances of one man cannot exist. l. Iurisperitos 30 de excusat. tut. Now two persons cannot be full owners of one thing; l. 5 §. si duobus commod.; l. penult. §. 1 de castr. pecul. Therefore two heirs cannot be heirs of one man in full; but they are heirs in single shares, if no shares are assigned. l. quoties 9 §. haeredes 12 de haered. instit. Cuiacius in Recit. posthum.

units.la: Ad Leg. 142. De eo qui tacet.
units.tr: On Leg. 142: On One Who Keeps Silent

units.la: QVi tacet, non utique fatetur; sed tamen verum est, eum non negare.
units.tr: He who keeps silent does not, of course, confess; yet it is true that he does not deny.

units.la: Tacet] c.is qui tacet 44. de reg. in 6.2. ecl.3. cap.139. Nazianzenus ἡ τῷ σιωπὴν συγκαταθέσιν εἶναι δοκεῖ τῆς ἡσυχίας. V. Cuiac. 16. obser. vlt. Consentit, qui non repugnat. l.12. sup. de sponsalib. 4. Harmen. non tamen consentit continuo, qui exceptione vtitur. l.8. sup. de except. Consentimus aut expresse, aut tacite, hinc illa velle, non nolle. l.4. sup. eod. Goth.
units.tr: Keeps silent: c. "is qui tacet" 44, de reg. in 6; 2 Eccl. 3, c. 139. Nazianzen: "Silence is thought to be a tacit assent of quietness" [ἡ τῷ σιωπὴν συγκαταθέσιν εἶναι δοκεῖ τῆς ἡσυχίας]. See Cuiacius, 16 Obs. ult. He who does not resist consents. l. 12 sup. de sponsalibus; 4 Harmen. Yet he who uses an exception does not consent at once: l. 8 sup. de except. We consent either expressly or tacitly; hence "he wills those things" rather than "he refuses them." l. 4 sup. eod.; Goth.

units.la: Fatetur unde Cic. in Catil. quid expectas, inquit, loquentium auctoritatem, quorum voluntatem tacitorum perspicis? Pac. h. Vel eo ipso quod tacet, nec roganti aut loquenti contradicit. Got.
units.tr: Confesses: whence Cicero in the Catilinarian orations: "What do you expect," he says, "the authority of speakers, whose wishes you perceive from the silent?" Pac. h. Or because by the very fact that he is silent he neither contradicts the one asking nor the one speaking. Got.

units.la: Negare quia non palam contradicit.
units.tr: Deny: because he does not openly contradict.

units.la: Effectus est huius regulae coniunctae cum l. 1. de confess. Confessus pro iudicato habetur.
units.tr: The effect of this rule, taken together with l. 1 de confessis: "He who confesses is held as having been adjudged."

units.la: Confessus est, qui confitetur, vel cum, vel sine interrogatione, qui confitetur in iure; vel in iudicio, confessus ergo pro iudicato est. Ergo non tenetur propria quadam actione; quod Paulus tradit secundo Sententiarum lib. sed tenetur ea actione, de qua confessus est. Quod si confessus sit, se occidisse, tenebitur actione legis Aquiliæ, quæ vocatur confessoria: cuius hoc est proprium, ut non agatur rei iudicandæ causa, cum iudicata æstimetur, sed æstimandæ. l. inde Neratius 23. §. vlt. l. proinde 25. ad L. Aquil. Ersciendum est, eam actionem Legis Aquil. in confitentem esse in simplum; in negantem in dupluin. Quod si quis tacuerit, an is, qui tacet, consentire videtur? Minime; ideoque nec tenetur actione confessoria, nec inficiatoria, quasi videatur negare; nam videtur negasse. Quamobrem ob taciturnitatem actio Legis Aquiliæ non crescit in duplum: Idemque dicendum est in cæteris actionibus, quæ inficiatione non solent crescere. Cæterum, qui tacet, nec pro confesso, nec pro inficiante habetur. Confessus pro iudicato habetur, si diserte confessus est. Inficiator in duplum damnatur, si palam inficiatus sit; Huic regulæ locus non est in edicto. De interrogationibus in iure faciendis; qui titulus hoc ipso distat à titulo de confessis, quod titulus de confessis pertineat ad eos, qui ultro fatentur, titulus vero, De interroterrogationibus ad eos, qui interrogati à Prætore, vel aduersario, instante Prætore, coguntur respondere. Hi ex confessione sua, vel mendacio tenentur actione interrogatoria; si confitentur, constat eos teneri, si negant falso, hanc mendacii pœnam ferunt, vt in solidum teneantur.l. de ætate 11. §. si cum esset 2. l. si seruus 16. de interrogat. in iur. faciend. Quid dicemus, si interrogatus à Prætore, tacuerit? Hic etiam tenetur in solidum, quasi contumax; quia, qui non respondet, contumax est, hoc est, Prætoris auctoritatem spernit, ideoque contumaciæ pœnam feret; vt si negasset, d. l. de ætate. §. qui tacuit 4. & §. nihil interest 6. d. tit. ul. l. non solum 39. de procurator. Contumax est, qui prætori non respondet, & superbus est, qui alii non respondet. Eadem ratione in cessione in iure tacens neganti comparatur. Gaius 2. Instit. Est & alia differentia inter titulum de confessis, & titulum de interrog. in iure faciend. Nam ille pertinet ad eos, qui veluti conuenti incerti condictione fatentur se debere; qui conuenti actione Leg. Aquil. fatentur, se occidisse, vel vulnerasse; Qui conuenti rei vindicatione fa-centur, rem suam non esse: Hic vero pertinet ad eos, qui fatentur; vt qui fatetur, se hæredem esse ex semisse; qua ex re actor cognoscit, se tantum agere pro semisse, & vero necesse est, vt actor de eo certior etur ne incidat in periculum plus petitionis, qua de causa interrogationes & responsiones in iis causis sunt necessariæ; Tacens est contumax, & habetur pro negante, & tenetur in solidum. Itaque hæc regula non pertinet ad tit. de interrogat. in iure faciend. sed ad tit de confessis. ex quo confessus habetur pro iudicato, sed si propalam sit confessus, non si tacuerit; Nam etsi habeatur pro confesso, qui mortem sibi conscivit, aut actori pretium dedit; tamen non habetur pro damnato. l. eius 29. de iure fisci. l. qui rei postulat. 3. de bon. eorum, qui ante sentent. Alia quæstio est, an, qui tacet, consentire videatur? Idem non est tacere & consentire; In superiore quæstione taciturnitas, modo negationem, modo confessionem imitatur, & in tit. de interrogat. modo nullum consensum, modo neutrum. l. item quæritur. 13. §. ult. locati. In hac autem quæstione consensum imitatur taciturnitas, in iis scil. causis, in quibus voluntas exquisita non requiritur. l. 3. & 4. sup. h. tit. Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: He is a confessor who confesses, whether on questioning or without it, who confesses in court (in iure), or in trial (in iudicio); the confessed man is therefore held as adjudged. He is therefore not bound by a special action of his own, as Paulus teaches in the second book of the Sentences; but he is bound by the action concerning which he has confessed. If he has confessed that he killed someone, he will be bound by the action of the Lex Aquilia, which is called "confessoria"; and it is peculiar to this action that it is brought not for the sake of adjudicating the matter, since it is already judged, but for the sake of assessing the damages. l. inde Neratius 23 §. ult.; l. proinde 25 ad L. Aquil. It must be noted that this action under the Lex Aquilia against one who confesses is for single damages; against one who denies it is for double. But if someone has kept silent, does he who keeps silent seem to consent? Certainly not; and therefore he is bound neither by the confessory nor by the denial action (inficiatoria), as if he seemed to deny; for he is held to have denied. For that reason the action under the Lex Aquilia does not increase to double on account of silence; and the same must be said of the other actions, which do not usually increase by denial. Otherwise, he who keeps silent is held neither as confessing nor as denying. One who has confessed expressly is held as adjudged. A denier is condemned to double if he has denied openly; this rule has no place in the edict. Concerning questions to be put in court (de interrogationibus in iure faciendis): this title differs from the title de confessis in that the latter concerns those who confess of their own accord, whereas the title "de interrogationibus" concerns those who, questioned by the praetor or by the adversary, under the praetor's insistence, are compelled to answer. These are bound by an action on interrogation, on the basis of their confession or their lie; if they confess, it is clear they are bound; if they deny falsely, they suffer this penalty of falsehood, that they are bound for the whole amount. l. de aetate 11 §. si cum esset 2; l. si servus 16 de interrogat. in iure faciend. What shall we say if, when questioned by the praetor, he has kept silent? Here too he is bound for the whole amount, as one in contempt; for he who does not answer is contumacious, that is, he spurns the authority of the praetor, and therefore he shall suffer the penalty of contumacy, just as if he had denied. d. l. de aetate §. qui tacuit 4; and §. nihil interest 6; d. tit. ult.; l. non solum 39 de procurator. He who does not answer the praetor is contumacious, and he who does not answer another is proud. For the same reason, in cession in court, one who keeps silent is compared to one who denies. Gaius, 2 Institutes. There is also another difference between the title de confessis and the title de interrogationibus in iure faciendis. For the former concerns those who, as if sued in an action for an uncertain sum (condictio), confess that they owe; who, sued under the action of the Lex Aquilia, confess that they killed or wounded; who, sued in a vindication action, confess that the thing is not theirs. The latter, however, concerns those who confess, as one who confesses that he is heir to a half share, whereby the plaintiff learns that he is suing only for a half share; and it is necessary that the plaintiff be informed of this, lest he fall into the danger of claiming too much; for which reason questions and answers are necessary in such cases. He who keeps silent is contumacious, is held as denying, and is bound for the whole amount. Thus this rule does not pertain to the title de interrogationibus in iure faciendis, but to the title de confessis, by which one who has confessed is held as adjudged; but only if he has confessed openly, not if he has kept silent. For although one who has taken his own life, or has paid a price to the plaintiff, is held as having confessed, he is nonetheless not held as condemned. l. eius 29 de iure fisci; l. qui rei postulat 3 de bon. eorum qui ante sentent. Another question is whether he who keeps silent seems to consent. To keep silent and to consent are not the same thing. In the former question, silence sometimes imitates denial, sometimes confession; and in the title de interrogationibus, sometimes no consent, sometimes neither. l. item quaeritur 13 §. ult. locati. In this question, however, silence imitates consent, namely in those cases in which an express will is not required. l. 3 and 4 sup. h. tit.; Cuiac. in Recit.

units.la: Ad Leg. 143. De contrahentibus & eorum successoribus.
units.tr: On Law 143. On contracting parties and their successors.

units.la: Quod ipsis, qui contraxerunt, obstat, & successoribus eorum obstabit.
units.tr: What binds those who contracted will also bind their successors.

units.la: Successoribus] l. 52. §. 1. sup. de pact. l. 37. sup. de acquir. hered. hinc illa regula, Resoluto iure dantis, resoluitur ius accipientis & habentis ab eo causam. v. l. 2. C. pignus pignori. adde l. 160. in sin. inf. eod. Gothof. Explicationem huius legis vide sup. in l. 54. vbi dixi. Cuiac.
units.tr: Successors] Law 52, §1, above, de pactis; law 37, above, de acquirenda hereditate. Hence that rule: when the right of the giver is dissolved, the right of the recipient, and of the one who has his title from him, is dissolved. See law 2 C., pignus pignori. Add law 160 at the end, below, same title. Gothofredus. For the explanation of this law see above on law 54, where I said so. Cujacius.

units.la: Ad Leg. 144. De licito & honesto: De tempore in stipulationibus spectando.
units.tr: On Law 144. On the lawful and the honourable: On the time to be considered in stipulations.

units.la: NOn omne, quod licet, honestum est.
units.tr: Not everything that is lawful is honourable.

units.la: §. In stipulationibus id tempus spectatur, quo contrahimus.
units.tr: §. In stipulations, the time at which we contract is considered.

units.la: Coniunge l. si filiusfam. 68. de verb. obligat. Pac.
units.tr: Compare the law si filiusfam. 68, de verborum obligationibus. Pacius.

units.la: l. 197. 2. Ecl. 3. c. 140. Exemplum vide in l. 14. §. 2. sup. de ritu. Goth.
units.tr: Law 197, §2, Ecl. 3, c. 140. For an example see on law 14, §2, above, de ritu nuptiarum. Gothofredus.

units.la: i. impunitum legibus: Cum Iulia Nouerca Bassiani ei sinum nudasset, vellem, inquit, si liceret, at illa, si libet licet, an nescis Imperatorem leges dare, non accipere.
units.tr: That is, unpunished by the laws: when Julia Noverca had exposed her breast to Bassianus, he said, "I would, if it were permitted." But she replied, "If you wish, it is permitted. Or do you not know that the emperor gives laws, and does not receive them?"

units.la: Exemp. vide in l. 27. in sin. sup. de hered. petit. l. 1. in sin. sup. de periculo. tanta est honesti ratio; hinc turpis persona, vide l. 27. sup. de inofficioso. Conditio. l. 112. §. 3. sup. de legat. 1. L. 63. §. 7. sup. ad Trebell. Vita. l. 43. §. 5. sup. de ritu. arbiter. l. 9. §. 3. sup. de arbitr. turpiter datum, sup. de condict. ob turp. Gothof.
units.tr: For examples see the end of law 27, above, de hereditatis petitione; law 1, at the end, above, de periculo. So great is the reason of honour. Hence a disgraceful person: see law 27, above, de inofficioso testamento; law 112, §3, above, de legatis 1; law 63, §7, above, ad Trebellianum; law 43, §5, above, de ritu arbitri; law 9, §3, above, de arbitris; turpiter datum, above, de condictione ob turpem causam. Gothofredus.

units.la: Vel vtile πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν, ἀλλ' οὐ πάντα συμφέρει· πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν, ἀλλ' οὐ πάντα οἰκοδομεῖ. I. Corint. 10. 10. verf.23. & cap.6. verf.12. & Siracus cap.37. verf.31. οὐ γὰρ πάντα πᾶσι συμφέρει, ἡ οὐ πᾶσα ψυχὴ ἐν παντὶ δόκιμεῖ. Goth.
units.tr: Or useful: "All things are lawful for me, but not all things are advantageous; all things are lawful for me, but not all things build up." 1 Cor. 10.23, and ch. 6.12, and Sirach ch. 37.31: "For not all things are good for all, nor is every soul approved in everything." [πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν, ἀλλ' οὐ πάντα συμφέρει· πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν, ἀλλ' οὐ πάντα οἰκοδομεῖ. 1 Cor. 10.23; οὐ γὰρ πάντα πᾶσι συμφέρει, ἡ οὐ πᾶσα ψυχὴ ἐν παντὶ δόκιμεῖ. Sirach 37.31.] Gothofredus.

units.la: Stipulationibus] l.18.sup.eod.vide l.78.in sin. sup.de verb.ob. Licet habere concubinam, sed non honestum est, L. probrum 41. de ritu nupt. licet dare meretrici, sed non honestum est. l.4. §.1. de condict. ob turp.caus. hæc non prohibentur ob solam causam honestatis. Quædam tamen sunt, quæ prohibentur ob solam honestatis rationem; eo referenda est regula; Non omne, quod licet, honestum est: hoc est, non non omne, quod licet, est permittendum. Nam in nuptiis naturale ius & pudor spectatur, non ciuile ius leg. adoptiuus 14. §.2. de ritu nupt. Boni mores, non leges: quod honestum est, non quod licet. l.197. inf. hoc tit. semper in coniunctionibus, hoc est in nuptiis. Post diuortium ab vxore ex alio suscepta filiam mihi ducere licet, sed non est honestum. Ergo ab eiusmodi nuptiis abstinendum est. §.si vxor. Instit. de nuptiis. Male Bulgarus: licere contrahentibus se inuicem decipere, non tamen decere. Nam honestum est cum dicatur, licere naturaliter. Item si pretio 22. §.vlt. & l.seq. locati. Vendere licet pluris, si possum, Bulgarus tamen non debuit dicere, decipere; nam significat dolum, sed circumuenire, circumscribere, quo significatur fraus, quæ est in re ipsa;
units.tr: Stipulations] law 18, above, same title; see law 78 at the end, above, de verborum obligationibus. It is lawful to keep a concubine, but it is not honourable: L. probrum 41 de ritu nupt. It is lawful to give to a prostitute, but it is not honourable: l.4. §.1. de condict. ob turp. caus. These things are not forbidden for the sole reason of honour. Some things, however, are forbidden for the sole reason of honour, and to these the rule belongs: Not everything that is lawful is honourable; that is, not everything that is lawful is to be permitted. For in marriages natural law and modesty are considered, not civil law: leg. adoptivus 14, §2, de ritu nupt. Good morals, not laws: what is honourable, not what is lawful. l.197. inf. hoc tit. always in connections, that is, in marriages. After divorce from a wife, by whom I had a daughter from another marriage, it is lawful for me to marry her daughter, but it is not honourable. Therefore one must abstain from such marriages. §. si vxor, Instit. de nuptiis. Bulgarus is wrong in saying that contracting parties may lawfully deceive each other, but it is not seemly. For what is honourable is said to be lawful by nature. Item si pretio 22 §.vlt. and l.seq. locati. It is lawful to sell for more, if I can. Yet Bulgarus ought not to have said decipere, for that signifies deceit, but circumvenire, circumscribere, which signify a fraud that lies in the thing itself.

units.la: Dolus debet abesse in contractu: non licet mihi dolo te inducere, ut mihi vendas minoris, sed detracto dolo, possunt se circumscribere contrahentes. Redeamus ad nuptias: licet ducere consobrinam, vel defunctæ vxoris sororem, honestum tamen non est. Ergo inhibendum, sic pleraque, quæ iure ciuili licent, iure Prætorio emendantur, quasi minus honesta, ut licet rem meam vendere, etiamsi fraudentur creditores: & tamen rescinditur venditio iure Prætorio. Licet vsucapere rem absentis metus causa, & vero res mea fit vsucapione: rescinditur tamen vsucapio ex iure Prætorio, ex tit. quib. ex caus. maior.
units.tr: Fraud must be absent from the contract: it is not lawful for me to induce you by deceit to sell to me for less, but with the deceit removed, contracting parties may circumvent one another. Let us return to marriages: it is lawful to marry a first cousin, or the sister of a deceased wife, yet it is not honourable. Therefore it must be prohibited. So many things that are lawful by civil law are corrected by praetorian law, as being less honourable: as it is lawful to sell my own property even if creditors are defrauded, yet the sale is rescinded by praetorian law. It is lawful to usucapt the property of an absent person through fear, and indeed the thing becomes mine by usucaption, yet the usucaption is rescinded by praetorian law, ex tit. quib. ex caus. maior.

units.la: Ad §. In stipulationibus, &c.
units.tr: On §. In stipulations, etc.

units.la: Quæ ad hunc §. spectant tradita sunt sup. in l. 13. & l. 115. Cui. in Recit.
units.tr: What pertains to this §. has been set out above on law 13 and law 115. Cujacius in Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg. 145. An quis fraudari dicatur.
units.tr: On Law 145. Whether someone is said to defraud.

units.la: Nemo videtur fraudare eos, qui sciunt & consentiunt.
units.tr: No one is thought to defraud those who know and consent.

units.la: Nemo ] Ex tit. qua in fraud. Creditorum.
units.tr: Nemo] From the title quae in fraudem creditorum.

units.la: Sciunt ] c. scienti & consentienti 27. de reg. in 6. 2. ecl. 3. c. 41. l. 1. in sin. sup. de act. empt. l. 24. §. 9. sup. de edilitio. l. 1. §. 3. sup. depositi l. 1. in sin. sup. quod falso tutore: & hæc quidem locum habere existi existimo, in sciente simul, & consentiente. Gothofr.
units.tr: Sciunt] c. scienti & consentienti 27, de reg. iur. in 6; 2 Ecl. 3, c. 41; l. 1, in fine, sup. de act. empt.; l. 24, §. 9, sup. de aedilicio; l. 1, §. 3, sup. depositi; l. 1, in fine, sup. quod falso tutore: and I think these things hold indeed where one knows and consents at the same time. Gothofredus.

units.la: Consentiunt] l.11. sup. si quid in fraud. patroni, & volunt l. 11. in sin. sup. de in ius vocando l. 1. § 5. sup. de iniuriis. l. 8. § 5. sup. de aqua pluv. l. 3. § 5. sup. de homine libero, voluisse intelligitur, qui adversus se aliquid scripsit, leg. 8. § 6. supr. eod. Gothofr.
units.tr: Consentiunt] l.11. sup. si quid in fraudem patroni; and volunt, l. 11, in fine, sup. de in ius vocando; l. 1, §5, sup. de iniuriis; l. 8, §5, sup. de aqua pluv.; l. 3, §5, sup. de homine libero: he is understood to have wished who wrote something against himself, l. 8, §6, sup. eod. Gothofredus.

units.la: Pertinet ad actionem Paulianam, & est remedium ex leg. 6. § praterea, quae in fraud. cred. & locum habetur in actionibus, Pauliana, Fabiana, & Calusiana. Si quid libertus gesserit consentiente patrono, non est satis, scire, sed consentire est necesse. leg. non videtur si quid in fraud. patroni. leg. 9. de aq. pluv. arc. Cuiac. in Recitat.
units.tr: It pertains to the Pauline action, and is a remedy from law 6, §praeterea, quae in fraud. cred. and it holds in the actions Pauliana, Fabiana, and Calusiana. If a freedman has done something with the patron consenting, it is not enough to know; consent is necessary. Law non videtur, si quid in fraud. patroni; law 9, de aq. pluv. arc. Cujacius in Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg. 146. De eo quod quis egit ante libertatem.
units.tr: On Law 146. On what a person did before becoming free.

units.la: Quod quis, dum servus est, egit, proficere libero facto non potest.
units.tr: Whatever a person did while he was a slave cannot benefit him once he is free.

units.la: Proficere] l. 98. § vlt. de solut. Et nocere vide leg. 1. & passim tit. Codicis an servus ex suo facto. Gothofr.
units.tr: To benefit] See law 98, last §, de solutionibus. And for "to harm", see law 1 and passim in the Code title whether a slave is liable for his own act. Gothofredus.

units.la: Ait proficere; addatur, vel nocere, quod servus egit in seruitute, id post libertatem neque prodest ei, neque nocet, ut si seruus ante conditionem libertatis existens, pactus sit cum credicreditoribus hæreditariis, pactum non prodest; ideo non datur exceptio pacti, sed doli, l. Iurisgent. 7. §. penult. de pact. Eadem regula constituitur in filiofamilias. Nam quod ante manumissionem egit, nihil prodest, vel nocet. Verbum egit refertur ad contractum & pactum. Nam ex delicto in seruitute commisso seruus tenetur. Sed de hac regula & eius vitiis est tit. Cod. an seruus post manumiss. pro suo facto teneatur. Cuia. in Recit.
units.tr: It says "to benefit"; add "or to harm". What a slave did while in servitude neither benefits nor harms him after he is freed. For example, if a slave, while still a slave and before the condition of liberty was fulfilled, made a pact with the creditors of an inheritance, the pact does not benefit him; so no exception of pact is given to him, only an exception of fraud, law Iuris gentium 7, penultimate §, de pactis. The same rule holds for a son under paternal power, since what he did before manumission benefits or harms him not at all. The word "did" refers to contracts and pacts, for a slave is liable for a delict committed in servitude. But on this rule and its exceptions see the title in the Code whether a slave after manumission is liable for his own act. Cuiacius, in Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg. 147. De generalibus & specialibus.
units.tr: On Law 147. On general and special things.

units.la: SEmper specialia generalibus insunt. Specialia ] v. l. 80. l. 113. sup. eod. 2. ecl. 3. cap. 141. species inest suo generi, inest, id est, comprehenditur c. generi per speciem derogatur 34. de reg. in 6. Goth.
units.tr: Specials are always contained in generals. Specials] See law 80, law 113 above, Eclogue 2, Eclogue 3, chapter 141. A species is contained in its genus, that is, is comprehended. The genus is derogated by the species, 34, de regulis iuris in 6. Gothofredus.

units.la: Vide sup. in l. 110. vbi tractatum est quod huc pertinet. Cuiac.
units.tr: See above at law 110, where the matter pertinent here is treated. Cuiacius.

units.la: Ad Leg. 148. De eo, cuius effectus omnibus prodest.
units.tr: On Law 148. On that whose effect benefits all.

units.la: CVius effectus omnibus prodest, eius & partes ad vniuersos pertinent. Cuius ] ex tit. de reb. auth. iud. possid.
units.tr: Whose effect benefits all, of that its parts also pertain to all. Whose] from the title on things to be possessed by authority of the judge.

units.la: Eius ] Qui omnibus prospicit, nullos excipit, hinc, qui totum restituere tenetur vindicanti, nullam partem retinere debet.adde l. 67. sup. de rei vind. Qui totum alienat, nullam partem retinet. l. 25. sup. de vsur. Qui omnes seruos legat, nullum excipit. l. 52. sup. de leg. Goth.
units.tr: What] He who looks after all excepts none; hence one who is bound to restore the whole to a claimant ought to retain no part. Add law 67 above, de rei vindicatione. He who alienates the whole retains no part, law 25 above, de usuris. He who bequeaths all the slaves excepts none, law 52 above, de legatis. Gothofredus.

units.la: Hinc colligunt, idem ius esse in parte quod in toto arg. l. 82. supr. de acq. hared. cuius reg. 4. except. vid. hic apud Dec. Nihil eorum quæ tradunt Interpretes, conuenit huic regulæ: Nos vtamur hoc exemplo, vno creditore misso in possessionem rei seruandæ causa, vel possidere iusso, eius rei efsectus omnibus prodest. Nam missio possessionis fit in rem, non in personam, & possidere iussus, possidet omnibus. l. is qui §. si plures. vt in possess. leg. caus. leg. cum vnus 12. de rebus aut. iud. possid. Creditor fructus restituere debet l. Prætor 9. §. his verbis 3. l. creditor 14. d. tit. Cum igitur effectus rei eius prosit omnibus, impensæ etiam pertinent ad omnes: hoc est, si vnus missus sit, & impenderit necessaria, vt si fulcierit ædificia, ad omnes pertinet, quia commune negocium gessit. d.l. Prætor 9. §. generaliter, 4. d. tit. cuius rei pars est, vt communiter omnia onera sustineant. Cui. in Recit.
units.tr: Hence they conclude that the same right holds in a part as in the whole, by argument from law 82 above, de acquirenda hereditate; the 4th exception of this rule; see here Decius. None of what the commentators teach agrees with this rule. Let us use this example: one creditor is put in possession to preserve the thing, or is ordered to possess it, and the effect of that thing benefits all. For possession is granted in respect of the thing, not the person, and one ordered to possess, possesses for all: law "is who", §"if several", de possessione legatorum causa; law "since one", 12, de rebus auctoritate iudicis possidendis. The creditor must restore the fruits: law Praetor 9, §"by these words" 3; law creditor 14 of this title. Therefore, since the effect of the thing benefits all, the expenses also pertain to all. That is, if one was put in possession and has spent on necessary things, such as shoring up buildings, it pertains to all, because he managed a common affair: the same law Praetor 9, §"generally" 4, of this title. Part of this is that all bear the burdens in common. Cuiacius, in Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg. 149. De lucro ex persona alterius.
units.tr: On Law 149. On profit from another's person.

units.la: EX qua persona quis lucrum capit, eius factum præstare debet.
units.tr: A person from whose person one gains profit must make good that person's act.

units.la: Lucrum ] l. 10. sup. eod. l. 10. sup. si quis omissa causa l. 13. §. 1. sup. de acq. possess. l. 14. sup. de rei vindicat.
units.tr: Profit] law 10 above, same title; law 10 above, si quis omissa causa; law 13, §1 above, de acquirenda possessione; law 14 above, de rei vindicatione.

units.la: Debet ] Excipe donatarios, l. 15. C. de donat. & eos qui succedunt facto inuentario, necenim factum defuncti praestant. Decius hic nn. 2. Gothofr.
units.tr: Must] Except donees, law 15 of the Code, de donationibus, and those who succeed by making an inventory, for they do not answer for the deed of the deceased. Decius here, n. 2. Gothofredus.

units.la: Eadem est sententia huius legis, quae superioris. Factum scilicet defuncti l. si Titio 22. de pignor. l. 3. & l. 5. de rei non alienan. l. cum autem fundi 52. De rei abeo delit. caus. Vt si defunctus rem haeredi obligauerit, id pignus tanquam alienum non valet, sed cum dominus rei haeres extiterit, eam habere debet. Aliud exemplum petitur est ex lege si non solum 10. si quis omiss. caus. Cuiac. in Recitat.
units.tr: The sense of this law is the same as that of the previous one: namely, the deed of the deceased. Law "si Titio" 22, de pignoribus; law 3 and law 5, de rei non alienanda; law "cum autem fundi" 52, de rei vindicatione delictorum causa. For example, if the deceased pledged a thing to his heir, that pledge is not valid, as being another's property; but when the heir has become owner of the thing, he ought to hold it. Another example is taken from the law "si non solum", 10, si quis omissa causa. Cuiacius, in Recitationes.

units.la: Ad Leg. 150. De eo qui possidet, vel habet, aut dolo desiit possidere, vel habere.
units.tr: On Law 150. On one who possesses or holds, or by fraud has ceased to possess or hold.

units.la: PArem esse conditionem oportet eius, qui quid possideat, vel habeat: atque eius, cuius dolo malo factum sit, quo minus possideret vel haberet.
units.tr: The condition ought to be equal for the one who possesses or holds something and for the one by whose fraud it came about that he did not possess or hold.

units.la: Parem ] Ex tractatu interdictorum.
units.tr: Equal] From the treatise on interdicts.

units.la: Cuius dolo malo ] vid. l. 131. sup. eod. l. 2. §. 42. sup. ne quid in loco publico.
units.tr: By whose fraud] See law 131 above, same title; law 2, §42 above, ne quid in loco publico.

units.la: Haec lex iam explicata est supra l. 131 Cuiac.
units.tr: This law has already been explained above at law 131. Cuiacius.

units.la: Ad Leg. 151. De damno.
units.tr: Ad Leg. 151. On Damage.

units.la: NEMO damnum facit, nisi qui id fecit, quod facere ius non habet.
units.tr: No one causes damage unless he does what he has no right to do.

units.la: Ex tit. ne quid in loco publico, vbi mentio fit damni.
units.tr: From the title ne quid in loco publico, where damage is mentioned.

units.la: Quod facere ius non habet ] Damnum dare est iniuriam facere. l. 1. §. 10. 11. sup. ne quid in loco publico. vi facit, qui facit iniuriam. l. 73. §. 2. sup. eod. vim non facit, qui suo iure vtitur. l. 155. inf. eod. qui iniuria quid facit, punitur: è contra, factum legitime, poenam non meretur. l. 6. C. de adulteriis. vid. Goth.
units.tr: What he has no right to do] To cause damage is to do an injury. l. 1. §. 10. 11. sup. ne quid in loco publico. He does violence who does an injury. l. 73. §. 2. sup. eod. He does no violence who uses his own right. l. 155. inf. eod. Whoever does something by injury is punished; conversely, an act done lawfully does not deserve punishment. l. 6. C. de adulteriis. See Goth.

units.la: Pertinere videtur haec regula ad legem Aquiliam. Nam etsi damnum facere dicamus aliquando pro pati, tamen hoc loco dare intelligitur. l. 30. ad leg. Aquiliam. Is porro videtur damnum facere, hoc est dare, qui id facit, quod facere ius non habet: vt si quid violentius secerit magistratus aduersus se defendentem acrius: vel qui suam attrectantem vxorem occiderit, non tenetur l. Aquilia. Et hoc in l. Aquilia est euidentissimum: cum sit additum, contra ius. Et cum actio legis Aquiliae sit iniuria damni dati, proprie tamen, sicut superior regula, pertinet ad interdictum, ne quid in loco publico. Cuia. in Recit. hic. terrogationibus ad eos, qui interrogati à Prætore, vel aduersario, instante Prætore, coguntur respondere. Hi ex confessione sua, vel mendacio tenentur actione interrogatoria; si confitentur, constat eos teneri, si negant falso, hanc mendacii poenam ferunt, vt in solidum teneantur.l. de aetate 11. §. si cum esset 2. l. si seruus 16. de interrogat. in iur. faciend. Quid dicemus, si interrogatus à Prætore, tacuerit? Hic etiam tenetur in solidum, quasi contumax; quia, qui non respondet, contumax est, hoc est, Prætoris auctoritatem spernit, ideoque contumaciæ poenam ferer, vt si negasset, d. l. de aetate. §. qui tacuit 4. & §. nihil interest 6. d. tit. l. non solum 39. de procurator.
