units.tr: By the law of nature it is fair that no one be made richer to the detriment and injury of another.

units.la: Hac ratione haeredes ex delicto defunctorum tenentur: & praedo, si utiles & necessarias fecerit impensas, earum ratio habetur officio iudicis, vel exceptione doli vel condictione certi; haec enim est omnium condictionum causa. Cuiac.
units.tr: By this reasoning heirs are liable for the delicts of the deceased; and a possessor in bad faith, if he has made useful and necessary expenses, has them taken into account by the office of the judge, or by the exception of fraud, or by the condictio certi, for this is the cause of all condictions. Cuiac.

units.la: Ad Leg. 207. De re iudicata.
units.tr: On Law 207. On a thing adjudged.

units.la: REs iudicata pro veritate accipitur. Iudicata] l. 25. in f. sup. de statu hom.
units.tr: A thing adjudged is taken for truth. Iudicata] law 25 at the end, above, de statu hom.

units.la: Reperita est ex l. ingenuum de stat. hom. Res iudicata ingenuum facit, ingenuus est, quem esse ingenuum iudicatum est; patronus est, quem esse patronum pronunciatum est. l. si iu-ramento de iure patronatus. Suus est, quem suum esse pronunciatum est. l. 3. de lib. agnosc. Res au-tem iudicata non tollit naturalem obligationem. l. Iulianus de condict. indeb. & nunquam possessori parit actionem l. 7. de pignor. Idem dici etiam potest de sententia arbitri, vt pro veritate habeatur; Sed excipiendi sunt duo casus, quibus sententia eius ius non facit; Si colluserit praeses, & si condemnatus sit ex edicto peremptorio. Cuiac. in Recit.
units.tr: Taken from law ingenuum de stat. hom. A thing adjudged makes a man free: he is free whom it has been adjudged to be free; he is a patron whom it has been pronounced to be a patron (law si iuramento de iure patronatus). He is one's own whom it has been pronounced to be one's own (law 3 de lib. agnosc.). But a thing adjudged does not remove a natural obligation (law Iulianus de condict. indeb.), and never gives an action to a possessor (law 7 de pignor.). The same can also be said of the sentence of an arbiter, that it be held as truth. But two cases must be excepted, in which his sentence does not make law: if the praeses has colluded, and if he was condemned by a peremptory edict. Cuiac. in Recit.

units.la: Ad Leg. 208. Desinere habere.
units.tr: On Law 208. On ceasing to have.

units.la: NOn potest videri desisse habere, qui nunquam habuit.
units.tr: One cannot be seen to have ceased to have what he never had.

units.la: Qui] l. 82. l. 174. sup. desisse non videtur quod nec incepit. l. 5. sup. de iniusto l. 96. in princ. & §. 1. sup. de condit. & demonstr. l. 13 sup. de suis l. 116. sup. de verb. oblig. l. 19. sup. quemadmodum servitutes amittuntur. Goth.
units.tr: He who] l. 82. l. 174. sup. it does not seem to have ceased, which never began. l. 5. sup. on an unjust will. l. 96. in princ. & §. 1. sup. on conditions and demonstrations. l. 13 sup. on heirs of one's own. l. 116. sup. on verbal obligations. l. 19. sup. in what ways servitudes are lost. Goth.

units.la: Et ideo non tenetur, qui non potuerit immissum habere, interdicto; Ne quid in loco pu-blico, blico, fœmina non desiit suos habere hæredes. l. nulla de suis & legit. hared. quod proprie ad hanc regulam pertinere puto, quod similitudo inscriptionis ad l. Iul. & Papiam facit, & ideo qui desinit suos habere capite minutos, non amittit ius legitimæ successionis. Cuiac.
units.tr: And therefore one who could not have had an immission is not bound by the interdict "Ne quid in loco publico"; a woman has not ceased to have her heirs (suos). Law nulla de suis et legit. hared., which I think properly pertains to this rule, since the similarity of the inscription relates to the lex Iulia and Papia; and therefore one who ceases to have his heirs by capitis deminutio does not lose the right of legitimate succession. Cuiac.

units.la: Ad Leg. 209. De seruitute.
units.tr: On Law 209. On Slavery.

units.la: SEruitutem mortalitati fere comparamus. Seruitutem ] & manumissionem v. leg. 92. sup. de solut.
units.tr: We compare slavery almost to mortality. Seruitutem ] see on manumission, law 92 above, under de solutionibus.

units.tr: Mortality ] see law 59 in the section de conditionibus et demonstrationibus. See above on law 39. Cuiac.

units.la: Ad Leg. 210. De institutione.
units.tr: On Law 210. On Institution.

units.la: QVæ ab initio inutilis fuit institutio, ex post facto convalescere non potest.
units.tr: An institution that was invalid from the beginning cannot be made valid afterwards.

units.la: Ab initio ] v. l. 29. sup. eod.
units.tr: From the beginning ] see law 29 above, under the same title.

units.la: Ex post facto ] id est, tractu temporis. Docui in l. 29. sup. vbi vide.
units.tr: Afterwards ] that is, with the passage of time. I explained this on law 29 above, where see.

units.la: Ad Leg. 211. De servo & absentia Reip. causa.
units.tr: On Law 211. On the Slave and Absence for the Sake of the Commonwealth.

units.la: SErvus reipub. causa abesse non potest.
units.tr: A slave cannot be absent for the sake of the commonwealth.

units.la: Seruus ] adde l. 140. sup. eod.
units.tr: Slave ] add law 140 above, under the same title.

units.la: Repetita est ex l. si quis seruum 7. si quis caut. in iud. sistend. causs. fact. non obtemper. Et hanc non esse vltimam suspicabar, quod in Florentino libro imperfecta sit, sed Basilix̃ libri vltimam esse, testantur. Cuiac.
units.tr: This is repeated from the law si quis seruum 7, si quis caut. in iud. sistend. causs. fact. non obtemper. I suspected this was not the last, since it is incomplete in the Florentine book, but the Basilica books attest that it is the last. Cuiac.

units.la: INSTITVTIO- NES CAII, VNA CVM NOTIS SVCCINCTIS ac selectis optimorum Iuris- consultorum.
units.tr: THE INSTITUTES OF GAIUS, WITH SHORT NOTES AND SELECTED PASSAGES FROM THE BEST JURISTS.

units.la: Tit. I. De Libertatibus servorum.
units.tr: Title 1. On the Liberty of Slaves.

units.la: Aij Institutionum liber primus dicit, omnes homines, aut liberos esse, aut seruos. Sed ex ipsis, qui liberi sunt, alios esse ingenuos, alios libertinos. Ingenuos, qui ingenui nati sunt: Libertinos, qui pro iusta seruitute manumissi, liberi fiunt. Ingenuorum omnium unus status est. Libertorum vero ideo non unus est, quia tria sunt genera libertorum; quia Liberti aut cives Romani sunt, aut Latini, aut Dediticii. Tamen qui cives Romani sunt, qui Latini, qui Dediticii, breuiter explanandum est. Cives Romani sunt, qui in his tribus modis, id est, testamento, aut in Ecclesia, aut ante Consulem fuerint manumissi. Latini sunt, qui aut per epistolam, aut inter amicos, aut convivii adhibitione manumittuntur.
units.tr: The first book of the Institutes says that all men are either free or slaves. But among those who are free, some are freeborn (ingenui) and some are freedmen (libertini). The freeborn are those born free; the freedmen are those who become free by manumission from lawful slavery. All the freeborn share one status. The freedmen, however, do not share one status, because there are three kinds of freedmen: they are either Roman citizens, or Latins, or Dediticii. We must briefly explain what Roman citizens, Latins and Dediticii are. Roman citizens are those manumitted in one of three ways: by will, in the church, or before the consul. Latins are those manumitted by letter, among friends, or by admission to a dinner table.

units.la: Dediticii vero sunt, qui post admissa crimina suppliciis subditi, & publice pro criminibus cæsi sunt: aut in quorum facie vel corpore quæcunque indicia aut igne, aut ferro impressa sunt, & ita impressa sunt, ut deleri non possint. hij si manumissi fuerint, Dediticii appellantur. Sed inter hæc tria genera libertorum ideo cives Romani meliorem statum habent: quia & testamenta facere, & ex testamento quibuscunque personis succedere possunt. Nam & Latini, & Dediticii nec testamenta condere, nec sibi ex testamento aliorum aliquid dimissum possunt vllatenus vindicare. Tamen Latini certis rebus priuilegia ciuium Romanorum Libertorum consequi possunt: Dediticii vero nulla ratione possunt ad ciuium Romanorum Libertorum beneficium peruenire. Nam Latini patronorum beneficio, id est, si iterum ab ipsis aut testamento, aut in Ecclesia, aut ante Consulem manumittantur, ciuium Romanorum priuilegia consequuntur. Non tamen omnes domini seruos suos manumittere possunt. Nam si aliquis multa debita habeat, cuius substantia à creditoribus teneatur obnoxia, si in fraudem creditoris sui seruos suos manumittere voluerit, collata manumissio non valet. Aut si libertus ciuis Romanus filios liberos non habuerit, & in fraudem patroni sui seruos suos manumittat, similiter data manumissio missio non valet. Præterea minor quicunque viginti annorum dominus, seruo suo libertatem dare non potest, nisi forte tantum minor manumissor, cui pater suus & mater à patrono donati sunt, eosdem manumittat, aut certe pædagogum, aut collactaneum manumittat. Nam quamliber dominus, id est, quatuordecim annos egressus, testamentum facere possit, & hæredem instituere, & legata relinquere, libertatem tamen seruis non potest in hac ætate conferre.
units.tr: The Dediticii are those who, after committing crimes, were handed over to punishments and publicly beaten for their crimes; or those on whose face or body some marks were branded with fire or iron, and so branded that they cannot be erased. If such persons are manumitted, they are called Dediticii. Among these three kinds of freedmen, Roman citizens have the better status, because they can both make wills and succeed by will to any persons whatever. For Latins and Dediticii can neither make wills nor claim for themselves anything left to them by the will of others. Yet Latins can obtain the privileges of Roman citizen freedmen in certain matters; Dediticii, however, can in no way attain the benefit of Roman citizen freedmen. For Latins, by the favour of their patrons, that is, if they are manumitted again by those same patrons by will, in the church, or before the consul, they obtain the privileges of Roman citizens. Yet not all masters can manumit their slaves. For if someone has many debts, and his property is liable to his creditors, and he wishes to manumit his slaves to the creditor's fraud, the manumission made is not valid. Or if a freedman who is a Roman citizen has no free children, and manumits his slaves to the fraud of his patron, the manumission given is likewise not valid. Moreover, any master under twenty years of age cannot give liberty to his slave, unless perhaps a master under age manumits those whose father and mother were given to him by his patron, or manumits his tutor or his foster-brother. For any master, that is, one who has passed fourteen years, can make a will, institute an heir and leave legacies, but he cannot confer liberty on slaves at this age.

units.tr: All men.

units.la: §. 2. Ciues Romani sunt, qui his tribus modis, id est, testamento, aut in Ecclesia, aut ante consulem fuerint manumissi.
units.tr: §. 2. Roman citizens are those manumitted in these three ways, that is, by will, in the church, or before the consul.

units.tr: By will

units.tr: Or in the church

units.tr: Before the consul, or by the adsertor (torem), or by the rod (vindicta). See the notes to Ulpian, the passage cited, §. 7.

units.la: §. 3. Latini sunt, qui aut per epistolam, aut inter amicos, aut conuiuii adhibitione manumittuntur.
units.tr: §. 3. Latins are those manumitted by letter, among friends, or by admission to a dinner table.

units.la: §. 4. Dedititii vero sunt, qui post admissa crimina suppliciis subditi, & publice pro criminibus caesi sunt: aut in quorum facie vel corpore quaecunque indicia aut igne aut ferro impressa sunt, & ita impressa sunt, vt deleri non possint. ii si manumissi fuerint, Dedititicii appellantur.

The Dediticii, however, are those who, after committing crimes, were handed over to punishments and publicly beaten for their crimes; or on whose face or body some marks were impressed with fire or iron, and so impressed that they cannot be erased. If such persons are manumitted, they are called Dediticii.

units.la: cf. Festus in voce subuerbustae. ce subuerbustam. Tertullianus in libro de Pallio, subuerbustos in liberalibus, intelligit autem ἀνυμφίας. vid. Goth. hic.
units.tr: Compare Festus on the word subverbustae, and subverbustam. Tertullian, in his book De Pallio, understands subverbustos in the sense of unwedded [ἀνυμφίας] among the liberal (free) ones. See Gothofredus here.

units.la: §. 5. Sed inter hæc triagenera libertorum, ideo ciues Romani meliorem statū habent: quia & testamenta facere, & ex testamento quibuscunq; personis succedere possunt. Nā & Latini, & Dediticii, nec testamēta condere, nec sibi ex testamento aliorū aliquid dimissum possunt vlla tenus vindicare. Tamen Latini certis rebus priuilegia ciuium Romanorum libertorū consequi possunt: Dediticii vero nulla ratione possunt ad ciuium Romanorum Libertorum beneficium peruenire. Nam Latini Patronorum beneficio, id est, si iterum ab ipsis, aut testaméto, aut in ecclesia, aut ante consulem manumittantur, ciuium Romanorum priuilegia consequuntur.
units.tr: §. 5. But among these three kinds of freedmen, Roman citizens have the better status, because they can both make wills and succeed by will to any persons whatever. For Latins and Dediticii can neither make wills nor claim for themselves anything left to them by the will of others. Yet Latins can obtain the privileges of Roman citizen freedmen in certain matters; Dediticii, however, can in no way attain the benefit of Roman citizen freedmen. For Latins, by the favour of their patrons, that is, if they are manumitted again by those same patrons, by will, in the church, or before the consul, they obtain the privileges of Roman citizens.

units.la: Testamenta condere ] vid. §. 4. Inst. de success. libertor.
units.tr: To make wills: see §. 4 of the Institutes, On the Succession of Freedmen.

units.la: Certis rebus ] de quibus vid. sup. Vlpian. 3.
units.tr: Certain matters: of which see above, Ulpian 3.

units.la: Si iterum ab ipsis ] 3. Vlpiani 4.
units.tr: If again by them: Ulpian, book 3, §. 4.

units.la: Aut in ecclesia ] Cuiac. lib. 7. observat. cap. 15. Priscianum lib. 6. allegat ex fide manuscriptorum (quod hac in parte Priscianus valde corruptus sit) Caius inquit in primo Instit. Adhibitis non minus quinque testibus puberibus, item libripende. In eodem, qui libram æneam tenet, qui appellatur libripens, &c. Quæ cum non ita sint in Caij institutionibus, quae vulgo circumferuntur, apparet interpretationem Aniani ad illas eam esse, non ipsum Caij contextum, quod & argumento manumissionis factae in ecclesia, quam manumissioni censu factae substituit Anianus: Et adfiliatorum appellationis, qua etiam utitur in l. 2. C. Theod. de legitim. haered. & multis aliis comprobari potest. Haec Cuiac. Pacius hic.
units.tr: Or in the church: Cuiacius, book 7 of the Observations, chapter 15, cites Priscian book 6 from the testimony of the manuscripts (since Priscian is badly corrupted in this part): Gaius says in the first book of the Institutes: with not fewer than five adult witnesses, likewise the libripens. In the same place: he who holds the bronze scale, who is called the libripens, etc. Since these things are not so in the Institutes of Gaius that are commonly circulated, it appears that the interpretation of Anianus on them is what is meant, not the actual text of Gaius; this can also be shown from the account of manumission made in the church, which Anianus substituted for manumission made by the census, and from the term for those adopted into sonship, which he also uses in law 2 of the Theodosian Code, On Legitimate Heirs, and from many other things. So Cuiacius. Pacius here.

units.la: §. 6. Non tamen omnes domini servos suos manumittere possunt. Nam si aliquis multa debita habeat, cuius substantia a creditoribus teneatur obnoxia, si in fraudem creditoris sui servos suos manumittere voluerit, collata manumissio non valet.
units.tr: §. 6. Yet not all masters can manumit their slaves. For if someone has many debts, and his property is liable to his creditors, and he wishes to manumit his slaves to the fraud of his creditor, the manumission made is not valid.

units.la: Obnoxia] Nec sit solvendo. vid. Ulpian. 1. §. 14. vid. Inst. quib. ex causs. manumitt. non licet. leg. 10. l. 16. ff. qui & a quib. manum. liberi non fiant.
units.tr: Liable: that is, when he is not able to pay. See Ulpian 1, §. 14; see the Institutes, by what causes manumission is not permitted; law 10, law 16 of the Digest, by whom and to whom manumitted children do not become free.

units.la: §. 7. Aut si libertus civis Romanus filios liberos non habuerit, & in fraudem Patroni sui servos suos manumittat, similiter data manumissio non valet.
units.tr: §. 7. Or if a freedman who is a Roman citizen has no free children, and manumits his slaves to the fraud of his patron, the manumission given is likewise not valid.

units.la: In fraudem patroni sui] vid. Gothofr. in notis ad. Ulpian. 1. §. 15.
units.tr: To the fraud of his patron: see Gothofredus in the notes to Ulpian 1, §. 15.

units.la: §. 8. Praeterea minor quicunque viginti annorum dominus, servo suo libertatem dare non potest, nisi forte tantum minor manumissor, cui pater suus & mater a patrono donati sunt, eosdem manumittat, aut certe paedagogum, aut collactaneum manumittat. mittat. Nam quamliber dominus, id est, quatuordecim annos egressus, testamentum facere possit, & hæredem instituere, & legata relinquere, libertatem tamen seruis non potest in hac ætate conferre.
units.tr: §. 8. Moreover, any master under twenty years of age cannot give liberty to his slave, unless perhaps a master under age manumits those whose father and mother were given to him by his patron, or manumits his tutor or his foster-brother. For any master, that is, one who has passed fourteen years, can make a will, institute an heir and leave legacies, but he cannot confer liberty on slaves at this age.

units.la: Tit. II. De numero seruorum testamento manumittendorum.
units.tr: Title II. On the number of slaves who may be manumitted by will.

units.la: CONstitutum est, quantum seruorum numerum testamento, de quanta familia liceat manumittri, hoc ordine: vt si quis duos seruos habet, ambos manumittere possit: qui vero tres, duos testamento manumittat. Qui quatuor, similiter duos. Qui sex, tres. Qui octo, quatuor. Qui decem, quinque. Qui vndecim, duodecim, tredecim, quatuordecim, quindecim, sedecim, decem & septem: similiter quinque. Qui decem & octo, sex. Et ab hoc numero vsque ad triginta, tertiam partem manumittere liceat. Qui amplius quam triginta habuerit, vsque ad centum, quartam partem de numero seruorum manumittere poterit.
units.tr: It is laid down, as to how many slaves, out of how large a household, may be manumitted by will, in this order. If someone has two slaves, he may manumit both. He who has three may manumit two by will; he who has four, likewise two; he who has six, three; he who has eight, four; he who has ten, five; he who has eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen or seventeen, likewise five; he who has eighteen, six. From this number up to thirty, it is lawful to manumit a third part. He who has had more than thirty, up to a hundred, may manumit a fourth part of his slaves.

units.la: Qui vero plures quam centum habuerit, quintam partem manumittere potest. Sed & hoc statutum est, ut de qualibet grandi familia, nulli amplius, quam centum testamento manumittere liceat. Nam qui voluerit aut in Ecclesia, aut ante Consulem, aut inter amicos, aut per epistolam manumittere, potest his manumissionibus omnem familiam iugo servitutis absoluere. Nam si aliquis testamento plures manumittere voluerit, quam continet numerus supradictus, ordo servandus est: ut illis tantum libertas valeat, qui prius manumissi sunt, usque ad illum numerum, quem explanatio continet superius comprehensa. Qui vero postea supra constitutum numerum manumissi leguntur, integre in servitute eos certum est permanere. Quod si non nominatim servi, vel ancillae in testamento manumittantur, sed confuse omnes servos suos, vel ancillas is qui testamentum facit, liberos facere voluerit, nulli penitus firma esse iubetur hoc ordine data libertas, sed omnes in servili conditione, qui hoc ordine manumissi sunt, permanebunt. Nam & si ita in testamento servorum manumissio adscripta fuerit, id est, in circulo, ut qui prior, qui posterior nominatus sit, non possit agnosci, nulli ex his libertatem valere manifestum est, si agnosci non poterit qui prior, qui posterior manumissus fuerit. Nam si aliquis in ægriægritudine constitutus, in fraudem huius legis facere noluerit testamentum, sed epistolis, aut quibuscunque aliis rebus seruis suis pluribus quam per testamentum licet, conferre voluerit libertates, & sub tempore mortis hoc fecerit, hii qui prius manumissi fuerunt, vsque ad numerum superius constitutum, liberi erunt. Qui vero post statutum numerum manumissi fuerint, serui sine dubio permanebunt: nam si incolumis quoscunque diuerso rempore manumisit, inter eos qui per testamentum manumissi sunt, nullatenus computentur.
units.tr: He who has more than a hundred may manumit a fifth part. But it has also been established that, out of any large household, no more than a hundred may be manumitted by will. For he who wishes to manumit in the church, before the consul, among friends, or by letter, can by these manumissions release his whole household from the yoke of servitude. But if anyone by will wishes to manumit more than the number above contains, the order must be observed: freedom is valid only for those who were manumitted first, up to the number set out in the explanation above. Those who are named as manumitted beyond the number fixed above will certainly remain in servitude in full. But if slaves or maidservants are not manumitted by name in the will, and the one making the will wishes to make all his slaves or maidservants free in a general way, the freedom given in this manner is ordered to be valid for no one at all; all who would be manumitted in this way will remain in servile condition. For even if the manumission of slaves is written into the will in such a way, in a circle, that it cannot be recognized which was named first and which later, it is plain that freedom is valid for none of them, if it cannot be known which was manumitted first and which later. For if someone, being sick, is unwilling to make a will in fraud of this law, but wishes to confer freedom on more slaves than the will allows, by letters or by any other means, and does this at the time of death, those who were manumitted first, up to the number fixed above, will be free. Those who were manumitted after the fixed number will undoubtedly remain slaves. For if, while in health, he manumitted anyone at a different time, they are not to be counted among those manumitted by will.

units.la: De numero ] vid. l. 5. ff. qui testam.
units.tr: On the number] see Digest, law 5, qui testam.

units.la: §. 1. Constitutum est, quantū seruorum numerū testamento de quàtafamilia liceat manumitti, hoc ordine, vt si quis duos seruos habet, ambos manumittere possit. Qui vero tres, duos testamento manumittat. Qui quatuor, similiter duos. Qui sex, tres: Qui octo, quatuor. Qui decem, quinque: Qui vndecim, duodecim, tredecim, quatuordecim, quindecim, sedecim decem & septem; similiter quinque. Qui decem & octo, sex. & ab hoc numero vsque ad triginta, tertiam partem manumittere liceat. Qui amplius quam triginta habuerit, vsque ad centum, quartam partem de numero seruorum manumittere potest. Qui vero plures quam centum habuerit, quintam partem manumittere potest. Sed & hoc statutum est, vt de
units.tr: §. 1. It is laid down, as to how many slaves, out of how large a household, may be manumitted by will, in this order. If someone has two slaves, he may manumit both. He who has three may manumit two by will; he who has four, likewise two; he who has six, three; he who has eight, four; he who has ten, five; he who has eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen or seventeen, likewise five; he who has eighteen, six. From this number up to thirty, it is lawful to manumit a third part. He who has had more than thirty, up to a hundred, may manumit a fourth part of his slaves. He who has had more than a hundred may manumit a fifth part.

units.la: Sed & hoc statutum est, vt de qualibet grandi familia, nulli amplius quam centum testamento manumittere liceat.
units.tr: But it has also been established that, out of any large household, no more than a hundred may be manumitted by will.

units.la: Hoc ordine]
units.tr: In this order]

units.la: Quam centum]
units.tr: Quam centum] than a hundred

units.la: §. 2. Nam qui voluerit aut in ecclesia, aut ante consulem, aut inter amicos, aut per epistolam manumittere, potest his manumissionibus omnem familiam iugo seruitutis absoluere.
units.tr: §. 2. For he who wishes to manumit in the church, before the consul, among friends, or by letter, can by these manumissions release his whole household from the yoke of servitude.

units.la: §. 3. Nam si aliquis testamento plures manumittere voluerit, quã continet numerus supra scriptus, ordo seruandus est: vt illis tantum libertas valeat, qui prius manumissi sunt vsque ad illum numerum, quem explanatio continet superius comprehensa. Qui vero postea supra constitutum numerum manumissi leguntur, integre in seruitute eos, certum est, permanere. Quod si non nominatim serui, vel ancillae in testamento manumittantur, sed confuse omnes seruos suos, vel ancillas, is, qui testamentum facit, liberos facere voluerit, nulli penitus firma esse iubetur hoc ordine data libertas, sed omnes in seruili conditione, qui hoc ordine manumissi sunt, permanebunt. Nam etsi ita in testamento seruorum manumissio adscripta fuerit, id est, in circulo, vt qui prior, qui posterior nominatus sit, non possit agnosci, nulli ex his libertatem valere manifestum est, si agnosci non potest, qui prior, qui posterior manumissus fuerit.
units.tr: §. 3. For if anyone by will wishes to manumit more than the number written above, the order must be observed: freedom is valid only for those who were manumitted first, up to the number set out in the explanation above. Those who are named as manumitted beyond the number fixed above will certainly remain in servitude in full. But if slaves or maidservants are not manumitted by name in the will, and the one making the will wishes to make all his slaves or maidservants free in a general way, the freedom given in this manner is ordered to be valid for no one at all; all who would be manumitted in this way will remain in servile condition. For even if the manumission of slaves is written into the will in such a way, in a circle, that it cannot be recognized which was named first and which later, it is plain that freedom is valid for none of them, if it cannot be known which was manumitted first and which later.

units.la: §. 4. Nam si aliquis in aegritudine constitutus in fraude huius legis facere noluerit testamentum, sed epistolis, aut quibuscunque aliis rebus seruis suis pluribus, quam per testamentum licet, conferre voluerit libertates, & sub tempore mortis hoc fecerit, ii qui prius manumissi fuerunt, vsque ad numerum superius constitutum, liberi erunt. Qui vero post statutum numerum manumissi fuerint, serui sine dubio permanebunt.
units.tr: §. 4. For if someone, being sick, is unwilling to make a will in fraud of this law, but wishes to confer freedom on more slaves than the will allows, by letters or by any other means, and does this at the time of death, those who were manumitted first, up to the number fixed above, will be free. Those who were manumitted after the fixed number will undoubtedly remain slaves.

units.la: Sed Epistolis ] Epistola manumittere quis servum potest, ut & Codicillis. Paul. 4. sent. 14. §. 2.
units.tr: But by letters ] A slave may be manumitted by letter, as also by codicils. Paul, Sentences 4, 14, §. 2.

units.la: §. 5. Nam si incolumis quoscunque diverso tempore manumisit: inter eos, qui per testamentum manumissi sunt, nullatenus computentur.
units.tr: §. 5. For if, while in health, he manumitted anyone at a different time, they are not to be counted among those manumitted by will.

units.la: Tit. III. De iure personarum.
units.tr: Title III. On the Law of Persons.

units.la: ALiquae personae sui iuris sunt, aliquae alieno iuri subiectae sunt. Itaque cum ostenditur, quae personae alieno iuri subiectae sint, tunc evidenter agnoscitur quae sui iuris sint. In potestate itaque dominorum sunt servi, quam potestatem omnes gentes habere certum est: sed distringendi in servos dominis pro sua potestate permittitur, occidendi tantum servos suos domini licentiam non habebunt: nisi forte servus dum pro culpae modo caeditur, casu forsitan moriatur. Nam si servus dignum morte crimen admiserit, iis iudicibus, quibus publici officii potestas commissa est, tradendus est, ut pro suo crimine puniatur. In potestate etiam patrum sunt filii, ex legitimo matrimonio procreati.
units.tr: Some persons are their own masters (sui iuris), others are subject to the authority of another (alieno iuri subiectae). Therefore, when it is shown which persons are subject to another's authority, it is clearly recognised which are their own masters. Slaves are thus in the power of their masters, a power which all nations are known to possess; but masters are permitted to inflict blows on their slaves within the bounds of their authority, though masters shall not have licence to kill their own slaves; except perhaps where a slave, while being beaten in proportion to his fault, happens by chance to die. For if a slave has committed a crime deserving death, he is to be handed over to those judges to whom the power of public office has been entrusted, so that he may be punished for his crime. Children begotten in lawful marriage are also in the power of their fathers.

units.la: §. 1. Aliquae personae sui iuris sunt, aliquae alieno iuri subiectae sunt. Itaque cum ostenditur, quae personae alieno iuri subiectae sint, tunc evidenter agnoscitur, quae sui iuris sint.
units.tr: §. 1. Some persons are their own masters, others are subject to the authority of another. Therefore, when it is shown which persons are subject to another's authority, it is clearly recognised which are their own masters.

units.la: In potestate itaque dominorum sunt serui, quam potestatem omnes gentes habere, certum est: sed distringendi in seruos dominis pro sua potestate permittitur, occidendi tantum seruos suos domini licentiam non habebunt: nisi forte seruus, dum pro culpae modo cæditur, casu forsitan moriatur. Nam si seruus dignum morte crimen admiserit, iis iudicibus, quibus publici officii potestas commissa est, tradendus est, ut pro suo crimine puniatur.
units.tr: Slaves are thus in the power of their masters, a power which all nations are known to possess; but masters are permitted to inflict blows on their slaves within the bounds of their authority, though masters shall not have licence to kill their own slaves; except perhaps where a slave, while being beaten in proportion to his fault, happens by chance to die. For if a slave has committed a crime deserving death, he is to be handed over to those judges to whom the power of public office has been entrusted, so that he may be punished for his crime.

units.la: In potestate etiam patrum sunt filii, ex legitimo matrimonio procreati.
units.tr: Children begotten in lawful marriage are also in the power of their fathers.

units.la: Tit. IV. De Matrimoniis.
units.tr: Title IV. On Marriages.

units.la: LEgitimæ sunt nuptiæ; si Romanus Romanam nuptiis intervenientibus, vel consensu ducat vxorem. Sed non omnes personas vxores ducere licet: quia nec patri filiam, nec filio matrem, nec auo neptem, nec nepoti auiam. Quod non solum de personis, quae nobis propinquitate coniunctae sunt, sed etiam de adoptiuis, hoc est, adsiliatis iussum est observari. Nam etsi per emancipationem adoptio dissoluatur, nuptias tamen inter has personas semper constat illicitas. Inter fratrem quoque & sororem, siue eodem patre ac matre nati fuerint, siue diuersis matribus aut patribus, matrimonia esse non possunt. Inter adoptiuos etiam fratres illicita sunt coniugia, nisi forte adoptio emancipatione fuerit dissoluta: nam si emancipatio intervenerit, nuptiae inter huiusmodi fratres licito contrahuntur. Fratris quoque & sororis filiam vxorem ducere non licet: sororem quoque patris ac matris vxores accipere non licet: genero quoque socrum suam: nec socero nurum vxorem accipere licet, neque vitrico priuignam, neque priuigno nouercam.
units.tr: Marriage is lawful when a Roman man takes a Roman woman as his wife, with the nuptial ceremony intervening, or by consent alone. But it is not lawful for all persons to take wives: a man may not marry his daughter, nor a son his mother, nor a grandfather his granddaughter, nor a grandson his grandmother. This has been ordered to be observed not only of persons joined to us by kinship, but also of adoptive persons, that is, those made sons by adoption. For although adoption is dissolved by emancipation, marriage between these persons is always held to be unlawful. Marriages also cannot exist between brother and sister, whether they were born of the same father and mother or of different mothers or fathers. Marriages between adoptive brothers are likewise unlawful, unless perhaps the adoption was dissolved by emancipation; for if emancipation has intervened, marriages between such brothers are lawfully contracted. Nor is it lawful to take as wife the daughter of a brother or of a sister, nor the sister of one's father or mother. A man may not take his mother-in-law as wife, nor may a father-in-law take his daughter-in-law, nor a stepfather his stepdaughter, nor a stepson his stepmother.

units.la: Fratres enim amitinos vel consobrinos in matrimonium iungi nulla ratione permittitur. Sed nec vni viro duas sorores vxores habere: nec vni mulieri duobus fratribus iungi permittitur. Quod si quis incestas vel nesarias, id est, quae sunt superius comprehensae, nuptias inierit, nec vxorem habere videtur, nec filios. Nam hii qui ex huiusmodi conceptione prione nati fuerint, quamliber matrem videantur habere, patrem vero nullatenus habere censentur, & tanquam si de adulterio concepti fuerint computantur: qui spurii appellantur, hoc est, sine patre filii. Regula iuris hoc continet, ut qui legitime concipiuntur, tempore conceptionis statum sumant: qui vero non de legitimo matrimonio concipiuntur, statum sumant eo tempore quo nascuntur. Ac proinde legitima coniunctione conceptus, etiamsi mater eius statum mutet, id est, si ancilla fiat, ille, qui legitime conceptus est, ingenuus nascitur. nam qui non legitimo matrimonio concipitur, si mater eius ex ancilla dum praegnans est, libera facta fuerit, liber nascetur: si vero ex ingenua ancilla praegnans facta fuerit, seruus nascetur: quia non legitime, sed vulgo conceptus est.
units.tr: For it is by no means permitted to join in marriage paternal or maternal cousins. Nor is it permitted for one man to have two sisters as wives, nor for one woman to be joined to two brothers. If anyone enters into incestuous or nefarious marriages, that is, those listed above, he is held to have neither wife nor children. For those born of such a union, although they may seem to have a mother, are held to have no father at all, and are reckoned as if conceived in adultery: they are called spurii, that is, sons without a father. The rule of law holds that those who are lawfully conceived take their status at the time of conception, but those who are not conceived in lawful marriage take their status at the time they are born. And so, when the conception was lawful, the child is born free even if the mother changes her status, that is, if she becomes a slave; he who was lawfully conceived is born free. But he who is not conceived in lawful marriage will be born free if his mother, being a slave while pregnant, was made free; but if she was a free woman while pregnant and afterwards became a slave, he will be born a slave, because he was conceived not lawfully but casually.

units.la: §.4. Fratris quoque & sororis filiam vxorem ducere non licet.

units.la: §. 9. Quod si quis incestas vel nefarias, id est, quæ sunt superius comprehensæ, nuptias inierit, nec vxorem habere videtur, nec filios. Nam ii, qui ex huiusmodi conceptione nati fuerint, quamlibet matrem videantur habere, patrem vero nullatenus habere censentur, & tanquam si de adulterio concepti fuerint, computantur: qui spurii appellantur, hoc est, sine patre filii.
units.tr: §.9. If anyone enters into incestuous or nefarious marriages, that is, those described above, he is held to have neither wife nor children. For those born of such a conception, although they may seem to have a mother, are held to have no father at all, and are reckoned as if conceived in adultery: they are called spurii, that is, sons without a father.

units.la: §. 10. Regula iuris hoc continet, vt qui legitime concipiuntur, tempore conceptionis statum sumant: qui vero non de legitimo matrimonio concipiuntur, statum sumant eo tempore, quo nascuntur. Ac proinde legitima coniunctione conceptus, etiamsi mater eius statum mutet, id est, si ancilla fiat: ille, qui legitime conceptus est, ingenuus nascitur, nam qui non legitimo matrimonio concipitur, si mater eius ex ancilla dum prægnans est, libera facta fuerit, liber nascetur: si vero ex ingenua ancilla prægnans facta fuerit, seruus nascetur: quia non legitime, sed vulgo conceptus est.
units.tr: §.10. The rule of law holds that those who are lawfully conceived take their status at the time of conception, but those who are not conceived in lawful marriage take their status at the time they are born. And so, when the conception was lawful, the child is born free even if the mother changes her status, that is, if she becomes a slave. For he who is not conceived in lawful marriage will be born free if his mother, being a slave while pregnant, was made free; but if she was free while pregnant and afterwards became a slave, he will be born a slave, because he was conceived not lawfully but casually.

units.la: Tit. V. De Adoptionibus.
units.tr: Title V. On Adoptions.

units.la: ADoptio naturæ similitudo est, vt aliquis filium habere possit, quem non generauerit. Et ipsa adoptio duobus modis fit: vna, quæ adrogatio dicitur: alia, quæ adoptio. Adrogatio est, quando aliquis patrem non habens adoptatur, & ipse se in potestatem adoptiui patris dat. Et ideo adrogatio dicitur, quia & ille qui adoptat interrogatur, vtrum illum quem adoptat filium habere velit: & ille, qui adoptatur, interrogatur, vtrum id fieri velit. Illa vero alia adoptio est, vbi quis patrem habens, ab alio patre adoptatur: & ita ille, qui adoptatur, de certi patris potestate discedit, & in adoptiui patris incipit esse potestate. Nam & fœminæ adoptari possunt, vt loco filiarum adoptiuis patribus habeantur: fœminæ vero adoptare non possunt, quia nec filios ex se natos in potestate habent. Spadones autem qui generare non possunt, adoptare possunt. Et licet filios generare non possint, quos adoptauerunt filios habere possunt. Si quis vero filios habens se dederit adoptandum, non solum ipse ipse in patris adoptiui potestatem redigitur, sed & filii eius, si tamen auum paternum non habuerint, in adoptiui patris transeunt potestatem, tanquam nepotes.
units.tr: Adoption is a likeness of nature, so that a man may have a son whom he did not beget. Adoption itself takes place in two ways: one is called adrogation, the other adoption. Adrogation is when a man who has no father is adopted, and he himself gives himself into the power of the adoptive father. It is called adrogation because both the one who adopts is asked whether he wishes to have as his son the one whom he adopts, and the one who is adopted is asked whether he wishes this to happen. The other kind of adoption is when a man who has a father is adopted by another father; thus the one who is adopted departs from the power of his certain father and begins to be in the power of his adoptive father. For women too can be adopted, so that they may be held by adoptive fathers in the place of daughters; but women cannot adopt, because they do not even have in their power the sons born from themselves. Eunuchs, however, who cannot beget, can adopt; and although they cannot beget sons, those whom they have adopted they can have as sons.

units.la: Tit. VI. Quibus modis filii exeunt de potestate patris.
units.tr: Title 6. By what means sons go out from the power of their father.

units.la: Filii qui in potestate patris sunt, mortuo patre sui iuris fiunt. Sed si hic filius, qui morte patris sui iuris effectus est, filios habeat, in eius post patris sui obitum erunt filii potestate. Nam te. Nam si pater moriatur, & avus paternus vivat nepos ex filio sui iuris esse non potest: quia in avi remanet potestate, qui avo mortuo sui iuris efficitur. Item si moriatur pater, & relinquat filium emancipatum, & ex eodem filio emancipato nepotes, tunc nepotes liberi & sui iuris erunt, & in patris emancipati potestatem non veniunt. Item de potestate patris exeunt filii, si pater eorum in exilium missus fuerit: quia non potest filium civem Romanum in potestate habere homo peregrinae conditionis effectus. Item filius si vivo patre in exilium missus fuerit, in potestate patris civis Romanus esse non potest, quia similiter peregrinae conditionis factus cognoscitur. Item si ab hostibus pater captus sit, in potestate quamdiu apud hostes fuerit, filios non habebit: Sed si de captivitate evaserit, iure postliminii omnem, sicuti in aliis rebus, ita & in filios recipit potestatem. Si vero pater, qui ab hostibus captus est, in captivitate moriatur, ab eo tempore, quo ab hostibus captus est, filii sui iuris effecti intelliguntur. Item per emancipationem filii sui iuris efficiuntur. Sed filius masculus tribus emancipationibus de potestate patris exit, sui iuris efficitur. Mancipatio autem, hoc est, manus traditio quaedam similitudo venditionis est: quia & in emancipationibus praeter illum, hoc est, certum patrem, alius pateradhibetur, qui fiduciarius nominatur. Ergo iste naturalis pater filium suum fiduciario patri mancipat, hoc est, manu tradit: a quo fiduciario patre naturalis pater vnum aut duos nummos, quasi in similitudinem prætii accipit, & iterum eum acceptis nummis fiduciario patri tradit. Hoc secundo & tertio fit, & sic de patris potestate exit. Quæ tamen mancipatio solebat ante Præsidem fieri, modo ante Curiam facienda est, vbi quinque testes cives Romani in præsenti erunt, & pro illo, qui Libripens appellatur, id est, stateram tenens. & qui Antestatus appellatur, alii duo, vt septem testium numerus impleatur: tamen cum tertio manciparus fuerit filius a patre naturali fiduciario patri, hoc agere debet naturalis pater, vt ei a fiduciario patre remancipetur, & a naturali patre manumittatur: vt si filius ille mortuus fuerit, ei in hæreditate naturalis pater, non fiduciarius succedat. Fœminæ, vel nepotes masculi ex filio, vna emancipatione de patris vel aui exeunt potestate, & sui iuris efficiuntur. Et hii ipsi quamlibet vna mancipatione de patris vel aui potestate exeant, nisi a patre remancipati fuerint, & a naturali patre manumissi, succedere eis naturalis pater non poteft, nisi fiduciarius a quo manumissi sunt. nam si remancipatum sibi naturalis pater vel auus manumiserit, ipse eis in hæreditate succedit. Quod si habeat quis filium, & ex eo nepotes, & voluerit filium emancipare, & nepotes in sua potestate retinere, in arbitrio eius est: aut si voluerit nepotes emancipare, & filium in sua potestate retinere; & hoc ei pro iuris ordine licere manifestum est. Quod non solum de nepotibus, sed & de pronepotibus similiter facere potest.
units.tr: Sons who are in their father's power become sui iuris on the father's death. But if this son, who became sui iuris by his father's death, has sons, they will be under the power of him, their grandfather's successor. For if the father dies while the paternal grandfather is alive, the grandson cannot become sui iuris through the son, because he remains in the grandfather's power and becomes sui iuris only when the grandfather dies. Likewise, if the father dies and leaves an emancipated son, and the grandsons by that emancipated son, then the grandsons are free and sui iuris and do not fall under the power of their emancipated father. Sons also go out from their father's power if he is sent into exile, because a man who has become of foreign status cannot hold a son who is a Roman citizen in his power. Likewise, if a son is sent into exile while his father is living, he cannot be a Roman citizen in his father's power, because he is recognised as having become of foreign status in the same way. Likewise, if the father is captured by enemies, he will not have his sons in his power for as long as he is among the enemy. But if he escapes from captivity, by the right of postliminy he recovers power over his sons as well as over other things. If, however, the father who was captured by enemies dies in captivity, his sons are understood to have become sui iuris from the time he was captured. Sons also become sui iuris by emancipation. A son is released from his father's power and becomes sui iuris by three emancipations. Mancipation, that is, the transfer by hand, is a kind of likeness of sale: in emancipations, besides that one definite father, another father is also called in, who is named the fiduciary. The natural father therefore mancipates, that is, hands over, his son to the fiduciary father, and from that fiduciary father the natural father receives one or two coins, as a kind of likeness of a price, and then hands the son back to the fiduciary father once the coins have been received. This is done a second and a third time, and in this way the son goes out from the father's power. This mancipation used to take place before the governor, but it must now be done before the Curia, where five Roman citizens are present, together with the one called Libripens, that is, the one holding the scales, and the one called Antestatus, and two others, so that the number of seven witnesses is complete. However, when the son has been mancipated the third time by the natural father to the fiduciary father, the natural father must take care to have him remancipated to himself by the fiduciary father and manumitted by the natural father, so that if that son dies, the natural father, and not the fiduciary, succeeds him in the inheritance. Women, or male grandsons through a son, go out from the power of their father or grandfather by one emancipation and become sui iuris. And however many times such persons are mancipated, unless they have been remancipated by the father and manumitted by the natural father, the natural father cannot succeed them, except the fiduciary by whom they were manumitted. For if the natural father or grandfather has manumitted one who was remancipated to him, he himself succeeds in the inheritance. If someone has a son and grandsons through that son, and wishes to emancipate the son but keep the grandsons in his power, it is for him to decide. Or if he wishes to emancipate the grandsons and keep the son in his power, it is plainly permitted to him by the order of law. This he can do not only with grandsons but likewise with great-grandsons.

This mancipation used to take place before the governor, but it must now be done before the Curia, where five Roman citizens are present, together with the one called Libripens, that is, the one holding the scales, and the one called Antestatus, and two others, so that the number of seven witnesses is complete. Fœminæ, vel nepotes masculi ex filio, vna emancipatione de patris vel aui exeunt potestate, & sui iuris efficiuntur. Et il-li ipsi, quamlibet vna mancipatio de patris vel aui potestate exeant, nisi à patre remancipati fuerint, & à naturali patre manumissi, succedere eius naturalis pater non potest, nisi fiduciarius, à quo manumissi sunt. nam si remancipatum sibi naturalis pater vel auus manumiserit, ipse eis in hæreditate succedit. Quod si habeat quis filium & ex eo nepotes, & voluerit filium emancipare, & nepotes in sua potestate retinere, in arbitrio eius est: aut si voluerit nepotes emancipare, & filium in sua potestate retinere,& hoc ei pro iuris ordine licere manifestum est. units.tr: Pater captus sit] Ulpian, 10, §1, §5. ...in the inheritance the natural father, not the fiduciary father, succeeds to him. Women, or grandsons through a son, leave the power of their father or grandfather by a single emancipation and become sui iuris. And those same persons, however many mancipations they leave their father's or grandfather's power by, cannot be succeeded to by their natural father unless they have been remancipated to him and manumitted by their natural father; then they are succeeded by the fiduciary father from whom they were manumitted. For if the natural father or grandfather has had them remancipated to himself and manumitted them, he himself succeeds them in the inheritance. But if someone has a son and grandsons by him, and wishes to emancipate the son while keeping the grandsons in his power, or to emancipate the grandsons while keeping the son in his power, it is in his discretion; and it is clear that this is permitted by the order of law. This may be done similarly not only for grandsons but also for great-grandsons.

units.tr: Similitudo venditionis est] Mancipation is a likeness of sale. To be mancipated three times, therefore, is to be sold three times; a threefold mancipation is a threefold sale.

units.la: Et in emancipationibus. Huiusmodi vēditiones liberarum personarum figuratæ l. 6. C. de emancip. liber. & imaginariæ dicuntur §. 6. Olim parentibus licuit filios quoque interficere. vid. Goth. ad l. 11 in sin. ff. de liberis. ad l. ult. C. de patria potestate. Hodie vetitum est, ne quis filios vendat, donet, vel pignoret. l. 1. l. 2. C. de patrib. qui filios distraxerunt. vetitum est etiam ne interficiat d. leg. ultim. Gothofred.
units.tr: Et in emancipationibus. Such sales of free persons are called feigned and imaginary (Code, on the emancipation of free persons; Inst. 1, 12, §6, on the ways in which patria potestas is dissolved), empty formalities (said law 6), and ancient (said §6), since they were not carried out without injuries and slaps (Novel 81). This was received from the Twelve Tables: if a father sold his son three times, the son should be free from his father (Ulpian 10, §1). It is likewise known to have been changed under the laws of Romulus (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, 12: "Formerly parents were also permitted to kill their sons"). See Gothofredus on Dig. 11 at the end, De liberis; on the last law of the Code, De patria potestate. Today it is forbidden for anyone to sell, give or pledge his sons (Code 1 and 2, on parents who have alienated their sons); it is also forbidden to kill them (said last law, Gothofredus).

units.tr: Fiduciario patre] A fiduciary father.

units.la: Hoc secundo & tertio fit ] ne id ita intelligas, quasi trinæ illæ venditiones fierent vno & eodem tempore : cum singulis diebus, adhibitis testibus fieri possent, vel eodem die, vel intermisso. Paul. 2. sentent. 25. § 2. adeo vt filius, ex prima secundave mancipatione manumissus reuersus in patriam potestatem adgnasceretur suus hæres. Vlpian. tit. 23. §. 3. vid. Goth. hic.
units.tr: Hoc secundo & tertio fit] Do not understand this as though those three sales took place at one and the same time, since they could be made on successive days, with witnesses present, or on the same day or at an interval. Paul, Sentences 2, 25, §2; so that a son, manumitted after the first or second mancipation and returned to his father's power, becomes a sui heres by agnation (Ulpian, title 23, §3). See Gothofredus here.

units.tr: Fœminæ] See Gothofredus on Ulpian 10, §1 at the end.

units.la: Tit. VII. De Tutelis.
units.tr: Tit. VII. On Guardians.

units.la: TVtores aut legitimi sunt, aut testamentarii. Legitimi sunt, qui pupillo per virilem sexum propinquitate coniunguntur: & qui proximior fuerit de agnatis, ad ipsum legitima tutela pertinet: quia is qui proximus fuerit ad tutelam, ipse proximus est ad hæreditatem. Testamentarij sunt, quos patres aut aui paterni in testamento suo tutores filiis, aut nepotibus delegauerint. Quod si nec testamentarius tutor fuerit, nec legitimus, tunc inquisitione iudicis pupillis tutores dantur.
units.tr: Guardians are either legitimate or testamentary. Legitimate guardians are those who are joined to the ward through a male line of kinship; and the nearest of the agnates has the legitimate guardianship, because the person who is nearest to the guardianship is also nearest to the inheritance. Testamentary guardians are those whom fathers, or paternal grandfathers, have appointed in their wills as guardians for their sons or grandsons. But if there is neither a testamentary nor a legitimate guardian, then guardians are given to the wards by the judge's inquiry.

units.la: PEraćtis pupillaribus annis, quibus tutores absoluuntur, ad curatores ratio minorum incipit pertinere: Sub curatore sunt minores ætate, maiores euersores, insani. Hii qui minores sunt, vsque ad viginti & quinque annos completos sub curatore sunt. Qui vero euersores, aut insani sunt, omni tempore vitæ suæ sub curatore esse iubentur; quia substantiam suam rationabiliter gubernare non possunt.
units.tr: When the years of wardship, after which guardians are released, have passed, the oversight of minors begins to belong to curators. Under curators are minors by age, prodigals, and the insane. Those who are minors are under a curator until they have completed twenty-five years. But those who are prodigals or insane are ordered to be under a curator for the whole of their lives, because they cannot manage their property reasonably.

units.la: CAius superiori commentario de iure per-sonarum aliqua disputauit. Nunc in hoc commentario de rebus iterum tractat. Omnes itaque res aut nostri iuris sunt, aut diuini, aut publici. Nostri iuris sunt, quæ in proprietate nostra esse noscuntur. Diuini iuris sunt ecclesiæ, id est, templa Dei, vel ea patrimonia, ac substantiæ, quæ ad Ecclesiastica iura pertinent. Publici iuris sunt muri, fora, portæ, theatra, circus, arena, quæ Antiqui sancta appellauerunt, pro eo quod exinde tolli aliquid aut contingi non liceret: sed hæc omnia in nullius bonis sunt, ideo publici iuris esse dicuntur. Sed & res hereditariæ antequam aliquis hæres existat, id est, quando dubitatur, utrum scriptus, an legitimus hæres succedere debeat, in nullius bonis esse videntur. Præterea quædam res corporales sunt, quædam incorporales. Corporales sunt, quæ manu tangi possunt: velut ager, mancipium, vestis, aurum, argentum, & hiis similia. Incorporales sunt, quæ tangi non possunt: qualia sunt ea, quæ non in corpore, sed in iure consistunt, sicut est hereditas, & obligationes diuersis contractibus scriptæ. Et licet hæreditas, vel emptio, aut diuersi contractus res corporales in se habeant, iustamen ipsius hæreditatis vel emptionis, aliorumque contractuum incorporale est. Incorporalia etiam sunt iura prædiorum vrbanorum vel rusticorum. Prædiorum vrbanorum iura sunt, stillicidia, fenestræ, cloacæ, altius erigendæ domus, aut non erigendæ, & luminum; vt ita quis fabricet, vt vicinæ domui lumen non tollat. Prædiorum vero rusticorum iura sunt, via vel iter, per quod pecus aut animalia debent ambulare vel ad aquam duci, & aquæ ductus, quæ similiter incorporalia sunt. Hæc iura tamen rusticorum prædiorum Seruitutes appellantur. Item regulariter constitutum est, vt superposita inferioribus cedant: Vt si quis in solo nostro sine nostro permissu domum ædificauerit, ad eum cuius terra est, domus ædificata pertineat. Vel si aliquis in agro nostro arbores, aut vineas, vel plantas quascunque posuerit, similiter superficies solo cedat. Vel si messem in campo seminauerit, omnia hæc quæ in terram alienam iactantur, domino terræ acquiruntur. Quod & de chartis & pergamenis, si in alienis scribat, licet aureis vel argenteis literis, similiter eius est scriptura, cuius charta aut pergamenum fuerit. Quod & de tabula, hoc est, si aliquis in tabula mea picturam fecerit, obseruatur: quia statutum est, vt tabulæ pictura cedat. Quod si quis ex vuis meis vinum, aut spicis frumentum, aut ex oliuis oleum fecerit, eius vinum, triticum, vel oleum est, cuius spicæ, aut vuæ, aut oliuæ fuerint. Si quis etiam ex tabulis alienis nauem aut armarium, aut quodcunque ad vsum pertinens, fecerit, simili ratione eius erunt quæ facta fuerint, de cuius ligno facta probantur. Similiter etiam, si ex lana vel lino vestimenta fecerit, eius erunt vestimenta, cuius lana vel linum fuisse probabitur. Sed in hiis omnibus superius comprehensis, quicunque in terra aliena aliquid posuerit, aut ædificauerit, aut horum quæ dicta sunt, aliquid fecerit, illis qui aliena præsumpserunt hoc competit, vt expensas vel impendia, quæ in hiis fecerint, à dominis qui rem factam vendicant, recipere possint. Acquiritur autem nobis non solum per nosmetipsos, sed & per eos qui in potestate nostra sunt, sicut filii vel serui: quia quicquid hiis à qualibet persona donatum, vel venditum fuerit, aut heredes fuerint instituti, id patribus & dominis sine aliqua dubitatione conquiritur: præter eos filios, quibus per leges castrense peculium habere permissum est. Hii vero serui qui in vsufructu nostro, & in proprietate alterius sunt, hoc tantum vsufructuario acquirere possunt, quod opere aut manibus suis fecerint, aut de mercedibus operis sui acceperint. Nam si eis aut hereditas, aut legatum dimittatur, aut donationis aliquid conferatur; hoc proprietario domino, non vsufructuario acquiritur.
units.tr: Gaius, in the earlier commentary, discussed some matters concerning the law of persons. Now, in this commentary, he treats again of things. All things, therefore, are either of our law, or of divine law, or of public law. Those things are of our law which are known to be in our ownership. Those things are of divine law which belong to the Church, that is, the temples of God, or those endowments and goods which pertain to ecclesiastical rights. Those things are of public law which are walls, fora, gates, theatres, circuses, and arenas, which the ancients called sacred, because it was not lawful to remove anything from them or to touch them. But all these things are among no one's goods, and for that reason they are said to be of public law. Yet also inheritances, before anyone becomes heir, that is, while it is uncertain whether the instituted or the legal heir ought to succeed, seem to be among no one's goods. Furthermore, some things are corporeal, and some incorporeal. Corporeal things are those that can be touched by the hand: such as a field, a slave, a garment, gold, silver, and things like these. Incorporeal things are those that cannot be touched: such as those which consist not in a body but in law, like an inheritance and obligations written down in various contracts. And although an inheritance, or a purchase, or various contracts, have corporeal things within them, yet the right of the inheritance itself, or of the purchase, and of the other contracts, is incorporeal. Incorporeal, too, are the rights of urban or rural estates. The rights of urban estates are: the right of eaves dripping, windows, drains, the right to build a house higher or not to build it higher, and rights of light, so that one may build in such a way as not to take light from a neighbouring house. The rights of rural estates, however, are the right of way or passage along which cattle or animals must walk or be led to water, and the right of conducting water, which likewise are incorporeal. These rights of rural estates, however, are called easements. Likewise it is a general rule that things built upon things below yield to them: so that if anyone builds a house on our ground without our permission, the built house belongs to him whose land it is. Or if anyone has planted trees, vines, or any plants in our field, the surface likewise yields to the soil. Or if he has sown a crop in a field, all these things that are put into another's land become acquired by the owner of the land. This is also so with papers and parchments: if someone writes on those of another, even in golden or silver letters, the writing likewise belongs to him whose paper or parchment it is. The same is observed with a panel, that is, if someone has painted a picture on my panel, because it is established that the painting yields to the panel. But if someone has made wine from my grapes, or grain from my ears of corn, or oil from my olives, the wine, wheat, or oil belongs to him whose ears, grapes, or olives they were. If someone has also made a ship, or a chest, or anything for use, out of another's boards, by the same reasoning they will belong to him whose wood the things made are shown to be made of. Similarly, if he has made garments from another's wool or flax, the garments will belong to him whose wool or flax it is proved to have been. But in all those cases comprised above, whoever has placed something in another's land, or built, or done any of the things that have been mentioned, those who presumed to use another's property have this claim, that they may recover from the owners who claim the made thing the expenses or outlays that they have incurred on these matters. Moreover, we acquire not only through ourselves, but also through those who are in our power, such as sons or slaves: because whatever is given or sold to them by any person, or whatever they are instituted heirs to, is acquired for fathers and masters without any doubt, except for those sons to whom it is permitted by law to have a military property. But those slaves who are in our usufruct and in another's ownership can acquire for the usufructuary only what they have done by their work or hands, or have received from the wages of their labour. For if an inheritance or legacy is left to them, or something is conferred by gift, this is acquired for the owner of the property, not for the usufructuary.

units.la: §. 5. Incorporalia etiam sunt iura prædiorum urbanorum, vel rusticorum. Prædiorum urbanorum iura sunt stillicidia, fenestræ, cloacæ, altius erigendæ domus aut non erigendæ, & luminum: ut ita quis fabricet, ut vicinæ domui lumen non tollat. Prædiorum vero rusticorum iura sunt, via, vel iter, per quod pecus vel animalia debent ambulare, vel ad aquam duci, & aquæ ductus, quæ similiter incorporalia sunt. Hæc iura tamen rusticorum prædiorum servitutes appellantur.
units.tr: §. 5. Rights over urban and rural estates are also incorporeal. The rights over urban estates are gutters, windows, drains, raising a house or not raising it higher, and rights of light, so that a man builds in such a way as not to take light from a neighbouring house. The rights over rural estates are a road or path along which cattle or animals must walk or be led to water, and a right of water-course, which are likewise incorporeal. These rights over rural estates, however, are called servitudes.

units.la: §. 6. Item regulariter constitutum est, ut superposita inferioribus cedant: ut si quis in solo nostro sine nostro permissu domum ædificauerit, ad eum, cuius terra est, domus ædificata pertineat. Vel si aliquis in agro nostro arbores, aut vineas, vel plantas quascunque posuerit, similiter superficies solo cedat. Vel si messem in campo seminauerit, omnia hæc, quæ in terram alienam iactantur, domino terræ adquiruntur. Quod & de chartis, & pergamenis, si in alienis scribat, licet aureis vel argenteis literis, sin autem eius est scriptura, cuius charta aut pergamenum fuerit. Quod & de tabula, hoc est, si aliquis in tabula mea picturam fecerit, observatur: quia statutum est, ut tabulæ pictura cedat.
units.tr: §. 6. It is also a general rule that things lying on top give way to things below. So if someone builds a house on our ground without our permission, the built house belongs to the owner of the land. Or if someone plants trees, vines or any plants whatever in our field, the surface likewise goes with the soil. Or if he sows a crop in a field, all these things that are put into another's ground are acquired by the owner of the land. The same applies to paper and parchment: if someone writes on another's, even in gold or silver letters, the writing belongs to the owner of the paper or parchment. The same holds for a panel, that is, if someone paints a picture on my panel, because it is established that the picture goes with the panel.

units.la: §.7. Quod si quis ex vuis meis vinum, aut spicis frumentum, aut ex oliuis, oleum fecerit: eius vinum, triticum, vel oleum est, cuius spicæ, aut vuæ, aut oliuæ fuerint. Si quis etiam ex tabulis alienis, nauem aut armarium, aut quodcunque ad vsum pertinens, fecerit, simili ratione eius erunt; quæ facta fuerint, de cuius ligno facta probantur. Similiter etiam si ex lana vel lino vestimenta fecerit, eius erunt vestimenta, cuius lana, vel linum fuisse probabitur.
units.tr: §.7. But if someone makes wine from my grapes, or grain from my ears of corn, or oil from my olives, the wine, wheat or oil belongs to the owner of the ears, grapes or olives. Likewise, if someone makes from another's planks a ship, a cabinet, or anything for use, these things belong to the owner of the wood from which they are proved to have been made. Similarly, if someone makes clothing from wool or flax, the clothing belongs to the owner of the wool or flax, as it is shown to have been.

But in all the cases mentioned above, whoever has put something, or built something, on another's land, or has made any of the things just described, the persons who have presumed to act on what belongs to others have this right: that they may recover from the owners, who claim the thing made, the expenses or outlays they have incurred on them.

units.la: §. 9. Acquiritur autem nobis non solum per nosmetipsos, sed & per eos, qui in potestate nostra sunt. Sicut filii vel serui: Quia, quicquid iis à qualibet persona donatum, vel venditum fuerit, aut hæredes fuerint instituti, id patribus & dominis sine aliqua dubitatione conquiritur: præter eos filios, quibus per leges castrense peculium habere permissum est. Hi vero serui, qui in usufructu nostro, & in proprietate alterius sunt, hoc tantum usufructuario acquirere possunt, quod opere aut manibus suis fecerint, aut de mercedibus operis sui acceperint. Nam si eis aut hereditas, aut legatum dimittatur, aut donationis aliquid conferatur, hoc proprietario domino, non usufructuario adquiritur.
units.tr: §. 9. We acquire not only through ourselves but also through those who are in our power, such as sons or slaves. For whatever is given or sold to them by any person, or whatever they are instituted heirs to, is without any doubt acquired for their fathers and masters, except for those sons to whom the laws allow a military peculium. Those slaves, however, who are in our usufruct and in another's ownership, can acquire for the usufructuary only what they have done by their work or their hands, or have received from the wages of their labour. For if an inheritance or a legacy is left to them, or something is conferred by gift, this is acquired for the owner of the property, not for the usufructuary.

units.la: PEr vniuersitatem, hoc est, omnia simul bona acquirimus hereditate, emptione, adoptione: quia is quem adoptauerimus, si sine patre est, cum omnibus bonis suis ad nos transit. Id quoque statutum est, quod non omnibus liceat facere testamentum. Sicut hij sunt, qui sui iuris non sunt, & alieno iuri subiecti sunt, hoc est, filii tam ex nobis nati, quam adoptiui. Item testamenta facere non possunt impuberes, id est, minores 14. annorum, aut puellæ 12. Item & hii qui furiosi, id est, mente insani fuerint, non possunt facere testamenta. Sed hij qui insani sunt: si interualla ipsius insaniæ habent, per interualla quibus sani sunt, possunt facere testamenta.
units.tr: We acquire the whole estate, that is, all goods at once, by inheritance, purchase, or adoption, because a person we have adopted, if he has no father, passes to us together with all his goods. It is also established that not everyone may make a will. Those who are not independent in law but subject to another's authority cannot make one: such are sons, both those born of us and those adopted. Likewise, those below the age of puberty, that is, boys under 14 years of age and girls under 12, cannot make wills. Likewise, those who are mad, that is, insane in mind, cannot make wills. But those who are insane, if they have intervals of lucidity, may make wills during the intervals in which they are sane.

units.la: §. 1. Per vniuersitatem, hoc est, omnia simul bona acquirimus hæreditate, emptione, adoptione, quia is, quem adoptauerimus, si sine patre est, cum omnibus bonis suis ad nos transit.
units.tr: §. 1. By universal succession we acquire all goods at once, that is, by inheritance, purchase or adoption; for when we adopt someone who is without a father, he passes over to us together with all his goods.

units.la: §. 2. Id quoque statutum est, quod non omnibus liceat facere testamentum. Sicut ii sunt, qui sui iuris non sunt, & alieno iuri subiecti sunt, hoc est, filij tam ex nobis nati, quam adoptiui.
units.tr: §. 2. It has also been laid down that not everyone may make a will: namely, those who are not their own masters (sui iuris) but are subject to another's authority, that is, children, whether born to us or adopted.

units.la: Qui sui iuris non est] Qui sui iuris non est, testari non potest.
units.tr: One who is not his own master] One who is not his own master cannot make a will.

For soldiers may make wills concerning their military property (peculium castrense). Paul, book 3, 4, §. 3.

units.la: §. 3. Item testamenta facere non possunt impubes puberes, id est, minores quatuordecim annorum, aut puellæ 12.
units.tr: §. 3. Likewise, those who are below puberty (impubes) cannot make wills, that is, minors under fourteen years of age, or girls under twelve.

units.la: §. 4. Item & ii, qui furiosi, id est, mente insani fuerint, non possunt facere testamenta.
units.tr: §. 4. Likewise, those who are mad (furiosi), that is, have been out of their minds, cannot make wills.

units.la: §. 5. Sed ii qui insani sunt, si interualla ipsius insaniæ habent, per interualla, quibus sani sunt, possunt facere testamenta.
units.tr: §. 5. But those who are insane, if they have lucid intervals of their insanity, may make wills during the intervals in which they are sane.

units.la: Tit. III. De Exheredatione liberorum.
units.tr: Tit. III. On the Disinheritance of Children.

units.la: IS qui filium in potestate habet, curam agere debet, ut testamentum faciens, masculum filium aut nominatim heredem instituat, aut nominatim exheredet. Nam si masculum filium in testamento præterierit, non valebit testamentum: si vero filiam præterierit, non rumpit testamentum filia prætermissa, sed inter fratres suos, legitimo stante testamento, suam sicut alij fratres consequitur portionem. Si vero testamento extranei heredes scripti fuerint, stante testamento filia medietatem heredit-ditatis
units.tr: A man who has a son in his power should take care, when making his will, either to institute his male son as heir by name or to disinherit him by name. For if he passes over a male son in the will, the will will not be valid. But if he passes over a daughter, the daughter who was passed over does not break the will; with the will standing, she receives her portion among her brothers, as the other brothers do. But if outside heirs have been written into the will, then with the will standing the daughter acquires half of the inheritance.

units.la: Ddd 2 ... ditatis acquirit. Nam si facto testamento, in quo filius masculus praetermissus est, euenerit, ut viuente adhuc patre filius qui praetermissus est moriatur, sic quoque quamlibet filius ille mortuus fuerit, testamentum quod factum est non valebit. Posthumorum duo genera sunt: quia Posthumi appellantur hij, qui post patris mortem de vxore nati fuerint: & illi qui post testamentum factum nascuntur. Et ideo nisi is qui testamentum facit, in ipso testamento comprehenderit: Quicunque filius aut filia mihi natus, natave fuerit, heres mihi sit: aut certe dicat, heres sit, valere eius non potest testamentum: quia sicut superius iam dictum est, legitime concepti pro natis habeantur. Nisi quod melior conditio est posthumae quam natae: quia nata, si praetermissa fuerit, non rumpit testamentum: posthuma vero, sicut masculus, testamentum rumpit.
units.tr: ...half of the inheritance. For if, after the will is made in which the male son was passed over, it happens that the son who was passed over dies while his father is still alive, then, however that son died, the will that was made will not be valid. There are two kinds of posthumous children. Those are called posthumi who are born of the wife after the father's death, and also those who are born after the will is made. Therefore, unless the testator has included in the will itself: Whatever son or daughter is born to me, let him or her be my heir, or at least says let him be heir, his will cannot be valid; because, as has already been said above, those lawfully conceived are regarded as born. Except that the position of a posthumous daughter is better than that of a born daughter: for a born daughter, if passed over, does not break the will; a posthumous daughter, like a male, does break it.

units.la: Si quis post factum testamentum adoptauerit apud populum illum qui sui iuris est, hoc est, qui patrem non habet, aut apud Praetorem illum adoptauerit qui in potestate patris est, quasi ei filius natus sit, ita eius rumpitur testamentum: posteriore quoque testamento, quod iure factum est, id quod iure factum ante fuerat, rumpitur. Quod si facto posteriore testamento heres scriptus, aut ante aditionem hereditatis moriatur, aut viuo testatore defecerit, aut conditio possibilis, sub qua heres institutus est, impleta non fuerit, is qui testamentum fecit intestatus mori videtur: quia testamentum quod prius fecerat, testamento posteriore rescissum est, & quod posterius factum est, hiis rebus, quas diximus, infirmatur. Alio quoque modo testamenta iure facta infirmantur, si aliquis post factum testamentum capite minuatur, id est, aut ab hostibus capiatur, aut pro crimine in exilium deputetur. Similiter & si qui adoptatus fuerit, testamentum quod antequam adoptaretur fecerat, non valebit.
units.tr: If anyone, after making a will, adopts before that people which is sui iuris, that is, which has no father, or adopts before that praetor who is in his father's power, as if a son had been born to him, his will is thereby broken. A later will, made lawfully, also breaks an earlier lawful will. But if, after the later will is made, the heir written in it either dies before accepting the inheritance, or fails while the testator is alive, or the possible condition under which he was instituted is not fulfilled, the man who made the will is considered to have died intestate. For the will he had made earlier was rescinded by the later will, and what was made later is invalidated by the circumstances we have mentioned. Lawfully made wills are also invalidated in another way: if someone, after making a will, suffers loss of status, that is, is captured by enemies or condemned to exile for a crime. Similarly, if someone has been adopted, the will he made before his adoption will not be valid.

units.la: Heredes autem sui sunt, aut necessarii, aut extranei. Sui heredes appellantur, filii aut nepotes ex filiis masculis, quos in potestate aut vel pater habet. Necessarii sunt heredes servi qui cum libertate heredes instituuntur. Necessarii ideo, quia aut velint aut nolint, necesse est eis heredes esse. Nam qui creditoribus renentur obnoxii, & putant se non tantum in substantia, quantum in debitis relinquere, ipsi servos suos manumittunt, & heredes necessarios faciunt, ut quo magis heres quam dominus infamiam incurrat, cum res eius, id est, hereditas domini pro debitis venditur, & creditoribus datur. Extranei sunt, qui nullo propinquitatis gradu testatori iunguntur, sed eos quicunque pro arbitrio suo scribit heredes.
units.tr: Heirs are either sui heredes, necessarii, or extranei. Sui heredes are called sons, or grandsons through male sons, whom the father has in his power. Necessarii are slave heirs who are instituted heirs together with their freedom. They are called necessary because, whether they wish it or not, they must be heirs. For those who are bound by debts to creditors, and think they will leave not as much in substance as in debts, manumit their own slaves and make them necessary heirs, so that the infamy falls on the heir rather than the master: the master's property, that is, the inheritance, is sold for debts and given to the creditors. Extranei are those who are joined to the testator by no degree of kinship, but whom he writes as heirs at his own discretion.

units.la: De exhaeredatione] vid. 2. inst. 13.

units.la: §. 1. Is, qui filium in potestate habet, curam agere debet, vt testamentum faciens, masculum filium, aut nominatim haeredem instituat, aut nominatim exhaeredet. Nam si masculum filium in testamento praeterierit, non valebit testamentum.

units.la: §. 2. Si vero filiam praeterierit, non rumpit testamentum filia praetermissa, sed inter fratres suos, legitimo stante testamento, suam, sicut alii fratres, consequitur portionem. Si vero testamento extranei haeredes scripti fuerint, stante testamento, filia medietatem haereditatis acquirit. Nam, si facto testamento, in quo filius masculus praetermissus est, euenerit, vt viuente adhuc patre, filius, qui praetermissus est moriatur, sic quoque quamlibet filius ille mortuus fuerit, testamentum, quod factum est, non valebit.
units.tr: §. 2. But if he passes over a daughter, the daughter who was passed over does not break the will; with the will standing, she receives her portion among her brothers, as the other brothers do. But if outside heirs have been written into the will, then with the will standing the daughter acquires half of the inheritance. For if, after the will is made in which the male son was passed over, it happens that the son who was passed over dies while his father is still alive, then, however that son died, the will that was made will not be valid.

units.la: Si vero filiam] Filiae quondam poterant praeteriri à patre Inst. cod. vers. sed nonnita de filiabus. 22. Ulpian. 16. 20.
units.tr: But if he passes over a daughter: daughters could once be passed over by the father. Inst. cod. vers. sed nonnita de filiabus. 22. Ulpian. 16. 20.
