Nisi, quod melior conditio est posthumæ, quam natæ: quia nata si prætermissa fuerit, non rumpit testamentum: posthuma vero, sicut masculus, testamentum rumpit.
units.tr: §. 3. There are two kinds of posthumous children. Those are called posthumi who are born of the wife after the father's death, and also those who are born after the will is made. Therefore, unless the testator has included in the will itself: Whatever son or daughter is born to me, let him or her be my heir; or at least says, let him be disinherited; his will cannot be valid, because, as has already been said above, those lawfully conceived are regarded as born. Except that the position of a posthumous daughter is better than that of a born daughter: for a born daughter, if passed over, does not break the will; a posthumous daughter, like a male, does break it.

units.la: Posthumorum alii viuo patre post testamentum nascuntur: alii post mortem: utrique sæpe post testamentum.
units.tr: Of posthumous children, some are born after the will while the father is alive, others after his death; both often occur after the will.

units.la: §. 7. Hæredes autem sui sunt, aut necessarii, aut extranei. Sui hæredes appellantur filii aut nepotes ex filiis masculis, quos in potestate avus vel pater habet. Extranei sunt, qui nullo propinquitatis gradu testatori iunguntur, sed eos quicunque pro arbitrio suo scribit hæredes.
units.tr: §. 7. Heirs are either heirs of the body (sui), necessary heirs, or external heirs. Heirs of the body are called the sons or grandsons through male sons, whom the grandfather or father holds in his power. Necessary heirs are slaves who are instituted as heirs together with their freedom. They are called necessary because it is necessary for them to be heirs, whether they wish it or not. For those who are bound as debtors to creditors, and think that they will leave behind not so much property as debts, free their slaves and make them necessary heirs, so that the heir, rather than the master, incurs the disgrace, since the master's property, that is, his inheritance, is sold to pay the debts and given to the creditors. External heirs are those who are joined to the testator by no degree of kinship, but whom he names as heirs at his own discretion.

units.la: Tit. IV. De Substitutionibus & de faciendis secundis tabulis.
units.tr: Title IV. On Substitutions and on Making Second Wills.

units.la: SVbstitutio est, quæ post institutionem à testatore fieri solet, id est, secundi hæredis appellatio. Et duæ sunt, quarum una vulgaris dicitur, alia pupillaris. Vulgaris dicitur, Ille hæres mihi esto: siue hoc filio siue extraneo. Quod si hæreditatem meam adire noluerit, illum substituo, ad quem hereditas mea debeat pertinere. Pupillaris substitutio filiis tantummodo impuberibus dari potest, quæ ita fit: Ille filius meus, si intra pubertatem decesserit, illum ei substituo. Sed pupillaris substitutio ita secreta esse debet, vt ad notitiam substituti peruenire non possit, ne vitæ pupilli aliquas substitutus insidias moliatur. Nam in extrema pagina testamenti fieri debet, vt pars illa in qua substitutio pupillaris scripta est, quandiu pupillus annos pubertatis egrediatur, obsignata permaneat, & prior pars testamenti, in qua hæres scriptus est, referatur. Hoc etiam & de donis fieri potest: Nam si extraneus hæres scriptus sit, etsi aliquem substituere non possumus, vt si hæres exiterit, & intra aliquod tempus mortuus fuerit, alius ei hæres sit, potest tamen per fideicommissum missum obligari, vt alii, rogatus à testatore, hæreditatem aut integram, aut pro parte restituat.
units.tr: Substitution is what is usually made by the testator after the institution, that is, the naming of a second heir. There are two kinds: one is called vulgar, the other pupillary. The vulgar form is: Let such a one be my heir, whether this is a son or a stranger. But if he is unwilling to take up my inheritance, I substitute such a one, to whom my inheritance ought to pass. A pupillary substitution can be given only to sons who are still under puberty, and it is made thus: If that son of mine dies before puberty, I substitute such a one for him. But a pupillary substitution must be kept so secret that it cannot come to the knowledge of the substitute, lest the substitute plot against the life of the ward. For it ought to be written on the last page of the will, so that the part in which the pupillary substitution is written stays sealed for as long as the ward has not reached the years of puberty, and the earlier part of the will, in which the heir is named, is shown. This can also be done with gifts. For if a stranger has been named heir, although we cannot substitute anyone for him, as in: if he becomes heir and dies within some period, another is to be his heir, he may nevertheless be bound by a trust, so that he, being asked by the testator, shall hand over the inheritance either whole or in part to another.

units.la: §. 1. Substitutio est, quæ post institutionem à testatore fieri solet, id est, secundi hæredis appellatio. Et duæ sunt, quarum una vulgaris dicitur, alia pupillaris.
units.tr: §1. A substitution is what is usually made by the testator after the institution, that is, the naming of a second heir. There are two kinds: one is called vulgar, the other pupillary.

units.la: Secundi hæredis] substitutio, secundi hæredis appellatio: substituitur etiam tertio gradu. Paul.3.sent.4.§.17.22. Ulpian.33.
units.tr: Second heir] a substitution, the naming of a second heir; one may also be substituted in the third degree. Paul, Sent. 3.4.17–22; Ulpian 33.

units.la: Duæ sunt] duplex substitutio.
units.tr: There are two kinds] a twofold substitution.

units.la: §. 2. Vulgaris dicitur; ille hæres mihi esto: sive hoc filio, sive extraneo, quod si hæreditatem meam adire nolueris, illum substituo, ad quem hæreditas mea debebat pertinere.
units.tr: §2. The vulgar form is: Let such a one be my heir, whether this is a son or a stranger; but if you are unwilling to take up my inheritance, I substitute such a one, to whom my inheritance ought to have passed.

units.la: Vulgaris dicitur] vid. Inst. de vulgari.
units.tr: The vulgar form] see Inst. on the vulgar substitution.

units.la: §. 3. Pupillaris substitutio filiis tantummodo impuberibus dari potest, quæ ita fit: Ille filius meus, si intra pubertatem decesserit, illum ei substituo. Sed pupillaris substitutio ita secreta esse debet, vt ad noritiam substituti pervenire non possit, ne vitæ pupilli aliquas substitutus insidias moliatur. Nam in extrema pagina testamenti fieri debet, vt pars illa, in qua substitutio pupillaris scripta est, quamdiu pupillus annos pubertatis egrediatur, obsignata per-ta perta permaneat, & prior pars testamenti, in qua hæres scriptus est, referatur. Hoc etiam & de donis fieri poterit.
units.tr: §3. A pupillary substitution can be given only to sons who are still under puberty, and it is made thus: If that son of mine dies before puberty, I substitute such a one for him. But a pupillary substitution must be kept so secret that it cannot come to the knowledge of the substitute, lest the substitute plot against the life of the ward. For it ought to be written on the last page of the will, so that the part in which the pupillary substitution is written stays sealed for as long as the ward has not passed the years of puberty, and the earlier part of the will, in which the heir is named, is shown. This can also be done with gifts.

units.la: vid.Inst.de pupillari.
units.tr: See Inst. on the pupillary substitution.

units.la: Si intra pubertatem l.1.§.1.Inst.de vulgar. & pupillar. post pubertatem filio miles potest substituere. l.15.ff.de vulgari.
units.tr: If before puberty: Dig. 1.1.§1 Inst. on the vulgar and pupillary substitution. After puberty a soldier can substitute for his son: Dig. 15 on the vulgar substitution.

units.la: Secreta esse debet vid. §. 3. Institut. de pupillari.
units.tr: It ought to be kept secret: see §3 of the Inst. on the pupillary substitution.

units.la: In extrema pagina testamenti Inferioribus partibus d.§.3. ima cera. Sueton.
units.tr: On the last page of the will: on the lower parts, §3 above, the lowest part of the wax. Suetonius.

units.la: De donis eisdem paginis. ita legitur à quibusdam.
units.tr: With gifts: on the same pages; so some read it.

units.la: §. 4. Nam si extraneus hæres scriptus sit, & si aliquem substituere non possumus, ut si hæres extiterit, & intra aliquod tempus mortuus fuerit, alius ei hæres sit, poterit tamen per fideicommissum obligari, ut alii, rogatus à testatore, hæreditatem aut integram, aut pro parte restituat.
units.tr: §4. For if a stranger has been named heir, and although we cannot substitute anyone for him, as in: if he becomes heir and dies within some period, another is to be his heir, he may nevertheless be bound by a trust, so that he, being asked by the testator, shall hand over the inheritance either whole or in part to another.

units.la: Extraneus hæres §.9.Inst.de pupillari.
units.tr: A stranger heir: §9 of the Inst. on the pupillary substitution.

units.la: Non possumus Fallit hæc sententia in milite.
units.tr: We cannot substitute: This rule does not apply to a soldier.

units.la: Tit. V. De Legatis.
units.tr: Title V. On Legacies.

units.la: LEgatorum genera sunt quatuor, vendicationis, damnationis, sinendi modo, & præceptionis. Vendicationis legatum est, si testator sic locutus fuerit: Illum servum tibi do, aut legato: Vel go : Vel, illam rem tibi præsume, habe, vendica. Quod post mortem testatoris statim legatarius non expectato herede, sibi præsumit. Quam si præsumpserit, nec pro præsumpto legato ab herede potest calumniam sustinere, nec si aliena res fuerit, quæ legata est, legatarius hoc poterit ab herede repetere. Si per vendicationem una res multis legata sit, & singuli hanc ipsam rem præsumere velint, æquales singuli de re legata capiant portiones.
units.tr: There are four kinds of legacy: by vindication, by damnation, by permission (sinendi modo), and by preception. A legacy by vindication is made when the testator speaks thus: I give or bequeath that slave to you; or Take that thing for yourself, claim it, vindicate it. The legatee claims it at once after the testator's death, without waiting for the heir. If he has claimed it, he cannot be sued by the heir over the legacy he has claimed, and if the thing bequeathed was another's, the legatee cannot demand it back from the heir. If one thing is bequeathed by vindication to several people and each wishes to claim that same thing, each takes an equal share of the bequeathed thing.

units.la: Per damnationem isto ordine legatum dimittitur, ut testator in testamento scribat : Tu heres meus illi hoc da : aut, Illud illi ab herede meo dari inbeo. In quo genere legati, etiam alienæ res per legatum dimitti possunt. Et necesse est heredi aut redimere eam rem, quæ iuris alieni est, & legatario tradere, aut si is cuius est res vendere noluerit, quantum res illa valebit, legatario in pretio compensare. Sed si testator rem alienam quasi suam credens, per hoc genus legatum reliquerit, legatarius hoc ab herede petere non potest : & inutile est legatum. Nam si sciens alienam esse, per legatum dederit, necesse est ab herede aut ipsam rem, aut æstimationem rei in pretio legatario dari. Cæterum inter damnationis legatum & vendicationis hoc interest, quod per vendicationem res aliena relinqui non potest: per damnationem eo pacto, quo superius comprehensum est, potest. Illæ etiam res, quæ in rerum natura non sunt, per damnationem legato dimitti possunt, velut si ita testator in testamento scribat: Fructus qui ex illo agro nati fuerint, aut id quod ex illa ancilla natum fuerit. quod in legato vendicationis fieri non potest: quia non potest hæc legatarius testatore mortuo continuo vendicare. Inter legatum vendicationis & damnationis ista similitudo est, quod legatum vendicationis, sive damnationis, si coniunctim, id est, duobus aut pluribus vna res in legato dimissa fuerit, in utroque legato simul ab omnibus præsumatur: Inter legatum vendicationis, & damnationis ista distantia est, ut si disiunctim, id est, singulis quæcunque res per legatum damnationis relicta fuerit, singulis integra debeatur: Id est, ut unus rem ipsam accipiat, alii æstimationem rei ipsius in pretio ab herede percipiant. Sinendi modo hæc legati verba sunt: Ille heres meus rem illam illum permitte præsumere & sibi habere. Nam & propriam rem testator & heredes sui, & [alienam] per sinendi legatum relinquere poterit. In quo legato non quidem heres legatario rem quæ relicta est iubetur tradere, sed vendicanti legatario non permittitur prohibere. Præceptionis vero legatum non nisi uni ex heredibus dari potest, ut aliquid ei ex hereditate præcipuum relinquatur, etsi aut coniunctim, id est, multis aut
units.tr: A legacy by damnation is bequeathed in this form, when the testator writes in his will: You, my heir, give this to him; or, I order that this be given to him by my heir. In this kind of legacy, even another's property can be bequeathed. The heir must either buy the thing, which belongs to another, and hand it over to the legatee, or, if its owner is unwilling to sell, pay the legatee in money the value that thing would have. But if the testator, believing the thing another's to be his own, leaves it by this kind of legacy, the legatee cannot demand it from the heir, and the legacy is void. For if he knew it was another's and gave it by legacy, the heir must give the legatee either the thing itself or its value in money. Otherwise, the difference between a legacy by damnation and one by vindication is this: another's property cannot be left by vindication, but it can be left by damnation in the manner stated above. Things that do not yet exist in nature can also be bequeathed by damnation, as when the testator writes in his will: The fruits that shall be produced from that field, or whatever shall be born of that slave-girl. This cannot be done with a legacy by vindication, because the legatee cannot claim such things immediately upon the testator's death. The similarity between a legacy by vindication and one by damnation is this: if a legacy by vindication or by damnation is made jointly, that is, if one thing is bequeathed to two or more, it is claimed by all of them together under either kind of legacy. The difference between a legacy by vindication and one by damnation is this: if it is made severally, that is, if whatever thing is left by a legacy of damnation is left to each separately, each is owed the whole. That is, one person receives the thing itself, while the others receive from the heir the value of that same thing in money. The words of a legacy by permission are these: Let my heir permit that man to claim that thing and keep it for himself. For the testator can leave by permission legacy both his own property, and that of his heir, and [another's]. In this kind of legacy the heir is not ordered to hand over the thing bequeathed, but he is not allowed to prevent the legatee who claims it.

units.la: [Note: the bracketed word "alienam" appears in square brackets in the print.] aut disiunctim singulis relinquatur, omnibus una res tantum quæ nominata est debetur, non uni res, & alii æstimatio, sicut in legato damnationis est constitutum.
units.tr: Preceptive legacy, on the other hand, can be given only to one of the heirs, so that something is left to him from the inheritance as a preferred share. Even if it is left jointly, that is, to several, or severally, to each, only the one thing that is named is owed to all. It is not one thing to one and an estimated value to another, as is established for a legacy of damnation.

units.la: §. 1. Legatorum genera sunt quatuor: vindicationis, damnationis, sinendi modo, & præceptionis.
units.tr: §1. There are four kinds of legacy: by vindication, by damnation, by permission, and by preception.

units.la: §. 2. Vendicationis legatum est, si testator sic locutus fuerit: illum servuum tibi do, aut lego: vel, illam rem tibi præsume, habe, vendica. Quod post mortem testatoris statim legatarius, non expectato hærede, sibi præsumit. Quam si præsumserit, nec pro præsumto legato ab hærede poterit calumniam sustinere, nec si aliena res fuerit, quæ legata est, legatarius hoc poterit ab hærede repetere. Si per vindicationem una res multis legata sit, & singuli hanc ipsam rem præsumere velint, æquales singuli de re legata capiant portiones. Habe, vendica ] inde legatum per vindicationem dictum.
units.tr: §2. A legacy by vindication is made when the testator speaks thus: I give or bequeath that slave to you; or Take that thing for yourself, claim it, vindicate it. The legatee claims it at once after the testator's death, without waiting for the heir. If he has claimed it, he cannot be sued by the heir over the legacy he has claimed, and if the thing bequeathed was another's, the legatee cannot demand it back from the heir. If one thing is bequeathed by vindication to several people and each wishes to claim that same thing, each takes an equal share of the bequeathed thing. Habe, vendica: hence the legacy is called one by vindication.

units.la: §. 3. Per damnationem isto ordine legatum dimittitur, vt testator in testamento scribat: Tu, haeres meus, illi hoc da: aut, illud illi ab haerede meo dari iubeo. In quo genere legati etiam alienae res per legatum dimitti possunt. Et necesse est haeredi, aut redimere eam rem, quae iuris alieni est, & legatario tradere, aut si is, cuius est res, vendere noluerit, quantum res illa valebit, legatario in precio compensare. Sed si testator rem alienam, quasi suam credens, per hoc genus legatum reliquerit, legatarius hoc ab haerede petere non potest: & inutile est legatum. Nam si sciens alienam esse, per legatum dederit, necesse est, ab haerede aut ipsam rem, aut aestimationem rei in precio legatario dari.
units.tr: §3. A legacy by damnation is bequeathed in this form, when the testator writes in his will: You, my heir, give this to him; or, I order that this be given to him by my heir. In this kind of legacy even another's property can be bequeathed. The heir must either buy the thing, which belongs to another, and hand it over to the legatee, or, if its owner is unwilling to sell, pay the legatee in money the value that thing would have. But if the testator, believing the thing another's to be his own, leaves it by this kind of legacy, the legatee cannot demand it from the heir, and the legacy is void. For if he knew it was another's and gave it by legacy, the heir must give the legatee either the thing itself or its value in money.

units.la: Per damnationem] vid. 24. Vlpian. 1.
units.tr: Per damnationem: see Ulpian, book 24, 1.

units.la: Dari iubeo ] alias formulas aptiores vid. apud 24. Vlpian. 4. & §. 1. in sin. Inst. de legat. Paul. 3. sent. 6. §. 6.
units.tr: Dari iubeo: for other, more suitable forms see Ulpian, book 24, 4, and the end of §1 of the Institutes on legacies; Paulus, Sentences 3, 6, §6.

units.la: Alienae res ] 24. Vlpian. 8.
units.tr: Alienae res: Ulpian, book 24, 8.

units.la: §. 4. Caeterum inter damnationis legatum, & vendicationis hoc interest, quod per vendicationem res aliena relinqui non potest: per damnationem eo pacto, quo superius comprehensum est, potest. Illae etiam res, quae in rerum natura non sunt, per damnationem legato dimitti possunt, velut, si ita testator in testamento scribat: Fructus qui ex illo agro nati fuerint, aut, id quod ex illa ancilla natum fuerit. quod in legato vendicationis fieri non potest: quia non potest hæc legatarius testatore mortuo continuo vendicare.
units.tr: §4. Otherwise, the difference between a legacy by damnation and one by vindication is this: another's property cannot be left by vindication, but it can be left by damnation in the manner stated above. Things that do not yet exist in nature can also be bequeathed by damnation, as when the testator writes in his will: The fruits that shall be produced from that field, or whatever shall be born of that slave-girl. This cannot be done with a legacy by vindication, because the legatee cannot claim such things immediately upon the testator's death.

units.la: Res aliena relinqui per damnationem res aliena relinqui potest: per vindicationem non potest. vid. 2. Vlpian. 7. Huc etiam pertinet, per damnationem rem creditori obligatam legari posse à sciente testatore. Paul. 3. sentent. 6. §. 8. Gothofr.
units.tr: Res aliena relinqui: another's property can be left by damnation but not by vindication: see Ulpian, book 2, 7. To this also belongs the point that a thing pledged to a creditor can be bequeathed by a testator who knows it; Paulus, Sentences 3, 6, §8; Gothofredus.

units.la: Quæ in rerum natura Quæ in rerum natura non sunt, legare possumus per damnationem, non per vindicationem.
units.tr: Quae in rerum natura: Things that do not yet exist in nature we can bequeath by damnation, not by vindication.

units.la: §. 5. Inter legatum vendicationis & damnationis ista similitudo est, quod legatum vendicationis, sive damnationis, si coniunctim, id est, duobus aut pluribus una res in legato dimissa fuerit, in utroque legato simul ab omnibus præsumatur.
units.tr: §5. The similarity between a legacy by vindication and one by damnation is this: if a legacy by vindication or by damnation is made jointly, that is, if one thing is bequeathed to two or more, it is claimed by all of them together under either kind of legacy.

units.la: Similitudo est] 24. Vlpian. 13. in princ.
units.tr: Similitudo est: Ulpian, book 24, 13, at the beginning.

units.la: Si coniunctim Coniunctim legare possumus, per damnationem & vindicationem.
units.tr: Si coniunctim: We can bequeath jointly, by damnation and by vindication.

units.la: §. 6. Inter legatum vendicationis, & damnationis ista distantia est, ut si disiunctim, id est, singulis quæcunque res per legatum damnationis relicta fuerit, singulis integra debeatur, id est, vt vnus rem ipsam accipiat, alii æstimationem rei ipsius in precio ab hærede percipiant.
units.tr: §6. The difference between a legacy by vindication and one by damnation is this: if it is made severally, that is, if whatever thing is left by a legacy of damnation is left to each separately, each is owed the whole. That is, one person receives the thing itself, while the others receive from the heir the value of that same thing in money.

units.la: §. 7. Sinendi modo hæc legati verba sunt: Ille hæres meus rem illam, illum permittre præsumere, & sibi habere. Nam & propriam rem testator, & hæredis sui, & (alienam) per sinendi legatum relinquere potest. In quo legato, non quidem hæres legatario rem, quæ relicta est, iubetur tradere, sed vendicanti legatario non permittitur prohibere.
units.tr: §7. The words of a legacy by permission are these: Let my heir permit that man to claim that thing and keep it for himself. For the testator can leave by permission legacy both his own property, and that of his heir, and (another's). In this kind of legacy the heir is not ordered to hand over the thing bequeathed, but he is not allowed to prevent the legatee who claims it.

units.la: §. 8. Præceptionis vero legatum, non, nisi vni ex hæredibus dari potest, vt aliquid ei ex hæreditate præcipuum relinquatur, & si aut coniunctim, id est, multis, aut disiunctim singulis relinquatur, omnibus vna res tantum, quæ nominata est, debetur, non vnires, & alii æstimatio, sicut in legato damnationis est constitutum.
units.tr: §. 8. A legacy of preception may be given only to one of the heirs, so that something is left to him from the inheritance as a special portion. And if it is left either jointly, that is, to several, or severally to each, only the one thing that is named is owed to all; it is not owed as separate things, and the estimated value goes to another, just as has been established for the legacy of damnation.

units.la: Tit. VI. De Lege Falcidia.
units.tr: Tit. VI. On the Falcidian Law

units.la: (drop-initial)LEge Falcidia constitutum est: quicunque heres fuerit institutus, quartam partem totius hereditatis habeat. Quod si testator hereditatem suam legatis exinanierit, hoc statutum est, ut Falcidiam sibi de imminutione legatorum heres retineat, constante nihilominus testamento. Hîc de Pauli sententiis addendum.
units.tr: (drop-initial)BY the Falcidian law it was established that whoever is instituted heir shall have a fourth part of the whole inheritance. But if the testator has drained his estate by legacies, it was decreed that the heir retains the Falcidian portion for himself from the reduction of the legacies, the will nevertheless remaining valid. Here something is to be added from the Sentences of Paul.

units.la: Lege Falcidia constitutum est: quicunque heres fuerit institutus, quartam partem totius hereditatis habeat. Quod si testator hereditatem suam legatis exinanierit, hoc statutum est, ut Falcidiam, sibi de imminutione legatorum hæres retineat; constante nihilominus testamento. Hîc de Paul. sent. addendum.
units.tr: By the Falcidian law it was established that whoever is instituted heir shall have a fourth part of the whole inheritance. But if the testator has drained his estate by legacies, it was decreed that the heir retains the Falcidian portion for himself from the reduction of the legacies, the will nevertheless remaining valid. Here something is to be added from the Sentences of Paul.

units.la: Tit. VII. De Fideicommissis.
units.tr: Title VII. On Fideicommissa.

units.la: POtest aliquis recto iure heredem instituere: & rogare eum, vt hereditatem suam, aut omnem, aut ex parte alii per fideicommissum reddat. Nam si heredem directo iure non instituerit, fideicommissarius non potest ad alium acceptam hereditatem transmittere. Sed in hac quoque re hoc obseruandum est, quod de Falcidia supra iam dictum est, vt heres institutus etiamsi omnem hereditatem alii restituere iussus sit, ita hereditatem alii restituat, vt quartam sibi ex ipsa hereditate retineat. Et singulae quaecunque res per fideicommissum dimitti possunt, hoc est, fundus, aut domus, aut mancipium, aut argentum. Ab ipso fideicommissario alteri fideicommissum dimitti potest. Et a legatario, licet legatum dimitti non possit, fideicommissum potest. Et non solum propriae res a testatore per fideicommissum dimitti possunt, sed etiam ipsius heredis, aut legatarii, aut cuiuslibet extranei, ne legatarius cui per testamentum parum dimissum est, plus alii per fideicommissum quam id quod consequitur reddere iubeatur. Cum autem aliena res per fideicommissum relinquitur, necesse est heredi, vel legatario, rem illam quae per fideicommissum est relicta, aut redimere, & fideicommissario dare, aut pretium eiusdem rei, quantum æstimata fuerit, fideicommissario numerare, sicut in damnationis legato fieri diximus. Libertates etiam seruis per fideicommissum dari possunt, vt heres vel legatarius ea mancipia manumittant, quæ testator ab hiis vt manumitterent, sperauit. Nec interest, vtrum hoc testator de suis seruis, an de ipsius heredis vel legatarii, aut de alienis fieri iubeat. Quod si de alienis fecerit, similiter cogitur heres emere ipsum seruum & manumittere. Sed si illum dominus suus noluerit vendere, perit per fideicommissum data libertas: quia in hac re heres æstimationem in pretio dare non cogitur: sed cum per fideicommissum libertas datur, is qui manumissus fuerit, non testatoris, sed heredis libertus est. Præterea inter fideicommissa & legata sunt quædam distantiæ. Fideicommissum ad eum, cui aliquid commissum est, herede mortuo poterit peruenire, si talis fuerit conditio testamenti: nam legatum ita relinqui non potest. Item legatum per codicillum relictum non valet, nisi codicilli testamento fuerint confirmati: fideicommissum vero etiam si testamento codicilli non fuerint confirmati, nihilominus debetur. Item, per legatarium legatum alteri relinqui non potest, sed fideicommissum potest. Item per legatum seruo alieno directa libertas dari non potest, per fideicommissum potest. Item per codi-
units.tr: A person may rightly institute an heir and ask him to hand over his inheritance, whether the whole or a part of it, to another by fideicommissum. For if he has not instituted the heir by direct right, the fideicommissary cannot pass the inheritance he has received on to another. But in this matter too, what was said above about the Falcidian portion must be observed: an heir instituted, even if ordered to restore the whole inheritance to another, should so restore it that he keeps for himself a quarter of the inheritance itself. Any single things whatever can be left by fideicommissum: an estate, a house, a slave, or silver. A fideicommissum can be left by the fideicommissary himself to another. And although a legacy cannot be left by a legatee, a fideicommissum can. Not only the testator's own things can be left by fideicommissum, but also those of the heir, or of a legatee, or of any outsider, so that a legatee to whom little has been left by the will is not ordered to hand over to another by fideicommissum more than what he receives. When, however, another's thing is left by fideicommissum, the heir or legatee must either buy that thing, which has been left by fideicommissum, and give it to the fideicommissary, or pay the fideicommissary the assessed value of the same thing, just as we said is done in the case of a legacy per damnationem. Liberty too can be given to slaves by fideicommissum, so that the heir or legatee manumits those slaves whom the testator hoped they would manumit. It makes no difference whether the testator orders this to be done with his own slaves, or with those of the heir or legatee, or with those of others. If he orders it with another's slaves, the heir is likewise compelled to buy the slave himself and manumit him. But if the owner is unwilling to sell him, the liberty given by fideicommissum perishes, because in this matter the heir is not compelled to pay the estimated price. But when liberty is given by fideicommissum, the person manumitted is freedman not of the testator but of the heir. Moreover, there are certain differences between fideicommissa and legacies. A fideicommissum can reach the person to whom something has been entrusted after the heir's death, if the will is so worded; a legacy cannot be left in this way. Likewise, a legacy left by codicil is not valid unless the codicils have been confirmed by the will; but a fideicommissum is owed even if the codicils have not been confirmed by the will. Likewise, a legacy cannot be left to another by a legatee, but a fideicommissum can. Likewise, direct liberty cannot be given to another's slave by a legacy, but it can by fideicommissum. Likewise, by codi-

units.la: Ec 3 codicillos nemo heres instituì potest, quamuis testamento confirmati sint: sed is qui testamento heres fuerit institutus, potest per codicillum rogari, ut hereditatem, quae ei data est, alii totam vel pro parte restituat: quod validum est, etiamsi codicilli testamento non fuerint confirmati. Item quamuis non possimus post mortem eius quem heredem instituimus, alium ei substituere, tamen per fideicommissum rogare eum possumus, ut cum moriatur, alii eam hereditatem vel totam, vel pro parte restituat. Et quia, sicut superius dictum est, etiam post mortem heredis fideicommissum ei cui relictum est, dari potest: quod hoc ordine fit, ut testator scribat: Illum heredem instituo, & volo, ut quum mortuus fuerit, ad illum hereditas mea pertineat. Praeterea & in hocalia fideicommissorum & legatorum conditio est, quia fideicommissa, si tardius quam scriptum est soluta fuerint, usurae & fructus debentur: legatorum vero usurae non debentur, sed ex mora solutionis, si per damnationem relicta fuerint, duplicantur.
units.tr: By codicils no one can be instituted heir, even if they have been confirmed by the will; but a person who has been instituted heir by the will can be asked by codicil to restore the inheritance given to him, whether wholly or in part, to another, and this is valid even if the codicils have not been confirmed by the will. Likewise, although we cannot substitute another heir for the one we have instituted after his death, we can nevertheless ask him by fideicommissum to restore that inheritance, whether wholly or in part, to another when he dies. And because, as said above, a fideicommissum can be given to the one to whom it is left even after the death of the heir, this is done in the following way: the testator writes, I institute that man as heir, and I wish that, when he has died, my inheritance should pass to that other man. Moreover, there is another difference between fideicommissa and legacies in this respect: if fideicommissa are paid later than the date written, interest and fruits are owed; but interest is not owed on legacies, though for a delay in payment, if they were left per damnationem, they are doubled.

units.la: Vid. 15. Ulp. 4. Paul. sent. 1. de fideicommissariis hereditatibus. 2. Instit. 23. de singulis rebus per fideicommissum relictis. 2. Instit. 24.
units.tr: See 15 Ulpian 4 Paul, Sentences 1, on fideicommissary inheritances. 2 Institutes 23, on single things left by fideicommissum. 2 Institutes 24.

units.la: Potest aliquis recto iure heredem instituere: & rogare eum, ut hereditatem suam, aut omnem, aut ex parte alii per fideicommissum reddat. Nam si heredem directo iure non instituerit, fideicommissarius non potest ad alium acceptam hereditatem transmittere. Sed in hac quoque re hoc observandum est, quod de Falcidia supra iam dictum est, vt heres institutus etiamsi omnem hereditatem alii restituere iussus sit, ita hereditatem alii restituat, vt quartam sibi ex ipsa hereditate retineat.
units.tr: A person may rightly institute an heir and ask him to hand over his inheritance, whether the whole or a part of it, to another by fideicommissum. For if he has not instituted the heir by direct right, the fideicommissary cannot pass the inheritance he has received on to another. But in this matter too, what was said above about the Falcidian portion must be observed: an heir instituted, even if ordered to restore the whole inheritance to another, should so restore it that he keeps for himself a quarter of the inheritance itself.

units.la: Recto iure ] §. 2. Inst. de fideicommiss. hereditatibus.
units.tr: Rightly: §2 Institutes, on fideicommissary inheritances.

units.la: Quartam sibi ] de quarta Trebellianica vid. §. 4. Inst. de fideicommiss. hared. & ad SC. Trebel. l. 1. §. 2. ff. ad Trebel.
units.tr: A quarter for himself: on the Trebellian quarter, see §4 Institutes, on fideicommissary inheritances, and on the Senatus consultum Trebellianum, law 1 §2 Digest, on the Trebellian senatus consultum.

units.la: §. 2. Et singulae quaecunq; res, per fideicommissum dimitti possunt, hoc est, fundus, aut domus, aut mancipium, aut argentum.
units.tr: §2. Any single things whatever can be left by fideicommissum: an estate, a house, a slave, or silver.

units.la: Singulae quaecunque res ] Inst. de singulis rebus per fideicommissum.
units.tr: Any single things whatever: Institutes, on single things left by fideicommissum.

units.la: Per fideicommissum ] & legatum 24. Vlp. 25.
units.tr: By fideicommissum: and by legacy; 24 Ulpian 25.

units.la: §. 3. Ab ipso fideicommissario alteri fideicommissum dimitti potest.
units.tr: §3. A fideicommissum can be left by the fideicommissary himself to another.

units.la: Fideicommissario alteri ] sic à posthumo herede instituto fideicommissum relinqui potest. Paul. 4. sent. 1. §. 2. ab Imperatore herede instituto. §. 3. ibi. a surdo vel muto. §. 4. ibid. at non ab uxore, cui vir dotem praelegauit. §. 1. ibid.
units.tr: To another fideicommissary: so a fideicommissum can be left by a posthumous heir who has been instituted. Paul, Sentences 4, 1 §2; by an heir instituted by the Emperor; §3 there, by a deaf or dumb person; §4 ibid., but not by a wife to whom her husband has prelegated a dowry; §1 ibid.

units.la: Dimitti potest ] quamuis à legatario olim legari non poterat vid. §. 4. inf. eod.
units.tr: Can be left: although formerly it could not be left by a legatee; see §4 below, same title.

units.la: §.4. Et à legatario licet legatum dimitti non possit, fideicommissum potest.
units.tr: §4. And although a legacy cannot be left by a legatee, a fideicommissum can.

units.la: §.5. Et non solum propriæ res à testatore per fideicommissum dimitti possunt, sed etiam ipsius hæredis, aut legatarii, aut cuiuslibet extranei.
units.tr: §5. Not only the testator's own things can be left by fideicommissum, but also those of the heir, or of a legatee, or of any outsider.

units.la: §.6. Ne legatarius, cui per testamentum parum dimissum est, plus alii per fideicommissum, quam id quod consequitur, reddere iubeatur.
units.tr: §6. So that a legatee to whom little has been left by the will is not ordered to hand over to another by fideicommissum more than what he receives.

units.la: §.7. Cum autem aliena res per fideicommissum relinquitur, necesse est hæredi, vel legatario, rem illam, quæ per fideicommissum est relicta, aut redimere, & fideicommissario dare, aut pretium eiusdem rei, quantum æstimata fuerit, fideicommissario numerare, sicut in damnationis legato fieri diximus.
units.tr: §7. When, however, another's thing is left by fideicommissum, the heir or legatee must either buy that thing, which has been left by fideicommissum, and give it to the fideicommissary, or pay the fideicommissary the assessed value of the same thing, just as we said is done in the case of a legacy per damnationem.

units.la: §. 8. Libertates etiam servis per fideicommissum dari possunt, ut hæres vel legatarius ea mancipia manumittant quæ testator ab iis, vt manumitterent, sperauit. Nec interest, vtrum hoc testator de suis seruis, an de ipsius hæredis vel legatarii, aut de alienis fieri iubeat. Quod si de alienis fecerit, similiter cogitur hæres emere ipsum seruum, & manumittere. Sed si illum dominus suus noluerit vendere, perit per fideicommissum data libertas: quia in hac re hæres æstimationem in pretio dare non cogitur. Sed cum per fideicommissum libertas datur, is, qui manumissus fuerit, non testatoris, sed hæredis libertus est.
units.tr: §8. Liberty too can be given to slaves by fideicommissum, so that the heir or legatee manumits those slaves whom the testator hoped they would manumit. It makes no difference whether the testator orders this to be done with his own slaves, or with those of the heir or legatee, or with those of others. If he orders it with another's slaves, the heir is likewise compelled to buy the slave himself and manumit him. But if the owner is unwilling to sell him, the liberty given by fideicommissum perishes, because in this matter the heir is not compelled to pay the estimated price. But when liberty is given by fideicommissum, the person manumitted is freedman not of the testator but of the heir.

units.la: Vlp. 18. §. 2. Inst. de singulis reb. per fideicom. l. 12. §. 1. ff. de fideicom. hared.
units.tr: Ulpian 18. §2 Institutes, on single things left by fideicommissum. Law 12 §1 Digest, on fideicommissary inheritances.

units.la: §. 9. Præterea inter fideicommissa & legata sunt quædam distantiæ. Fideicommissum ad eum, cui aliquid commissum, hærede mortuo, poterit peruenire, si talis fuerit conditio testamenti: nam legatum ita relinqui non potest. Item legatum per codicillum relictum non valet, nisi codicilli testamento fuerint confirmati: fideicommissum vero etiam, si testamento codicilli non fuerint confirmati, nihilominus debetur. Item per legatarium legatum alteri relinqui non potest, sed fideicommissum potest. Item per legatum seruo alieno directa libertas dari non potest, per fideicommissum potest. Item per codicillos nemo hæres instituí potest, quamuis testamento confirmati sint: sed is, qui testamento hæres fuerit institutus, potest per codicillum regari, vt hæreditatem, quæ ei data est, alii totam, vel pro parte restituat, quod validum est, etiamsi codicilli testamento non fuerint confirmati.
units.tr: §9. Moreover, there are certain differences between fideicommissa and legacies. A fideicommissum can reach the person to whom something has been entrusted, after the heir's death, if the will is so worded; a legacy cannot be left in this way. Likewise, a legacy left by codicil is not valid unless the codicils have been confirmed by the will; but a fideicommissum is owed even if the codicils have not been confirmed by the will. Likewise, a legacy cannot be left to another by a legatee, but a fideicommissum can. Likewise, direct liberty cannot be given to another's slave by a legacy, but it can by fideicommissum. Likewise, no one can be instituted heir by codicils, even if they have been confirmed by the will; but a person who has been instituted heir by the will can be asked by codicil to restore the inheritance given to him, wholly or in part, to another, and this is valid even if the codicils have not been confirmed by the will.

units.la: Item quamuis non possimus post mortem eius quem hæredem instituimus, alium ei substituere, tamen per fideicommissum rogare eum possumus, vt, cum moriatur, alii eam hæreditatem vel totam, vel pro parte restituat. Et quia, sicut superius dictum est, etiam post mortem hæredis fideicommissum ei, cui relictum est, dari potest: quod hoc ordine fit, vt testator scribat: illum hæredem instituo, & volo, vt cum mortuus fuerit, ad illum hæreditas mea pertineat.
units.tr: Likewise, although we cannot substitute another heir after the death of the person whom we have instituted as heir, we can nevertheless request him by fideicommissum that, when he dies, he restore that inheritance, whether wholly or in part, to another. And since, as was said above, a fideicommissum can also be given after the death of the heir to the person to whom it is left, this is done in this way: the testator writes, "I institute that man as heir, and I wish that, when he has died, my inheritance pass to that other."

units.la: Præterea & in hoc alia fideicommissorum & legatorum conditio est, quia fideicommissa, si tardius quam scriptum est, soluta fuerint, usuræ & fructus debentur: Legatorum vero usuræ non debentur, sed ex mora solutionis, si per damnationem relicta fuerint, duplicantur.
units.tr: Moreover, there is another difference between fideicommissa and legacies in this respect: if fideicommissa are paid later than the writing provides, interest and fruits are owed. But interest is not owed on legacies; if they were left per damnationem and payment is delayed, they are doubled.

units.la: Distantia] Differentiæ fideicommissi & legati, hodie legata fideicommissis exæquantur. vid. l. 1 ff. de legat. 1.
units.tr: The difference: the differences between fideicommissum and legacy. Nowadays legacies are placed on the same footing as fideicommissa. See l. 1 ff. de legat. 1.

units.la: Mortuo] Prima differentia.
units.tr: After death: the first difference.

units.la: Item legatum] Secunda differentia 25. Vlp. §. 8. in sin.
units.tr: Likewise a legacy: the second difference, Ulpian 25, §8 at the end.

units.la: Etiam si] d. §. 8. Paul. 4. sent. 1. §. 10. Item per legatarium ] Tertia differentia. Item per legatum ] Quarta differentia. Item per codicillos ] Quinta differentia. Nemo] l.10. ff. de codicillis § 2. Inst. de codicill. l.27. in sin. ff. de cond. inst. Potest per codicillum] §.2. Inst. de codicill. Item quamuis ] Sexta differentia. Post mortem eius ] 24. Vlpian. 16. Paul. 3. sent. 6. §.5. Praeterea & ] Septima differentia. Vsuræ & fructus ] vid. C. de usuris & fructib. legatorum.
units.tr: Even if: the same §8; Paul, Sentences 4, 1, §10. Likewise through a legatee: the third difference. Likewise through a legacy: the fourth difference. Likewise through codicils: the fifth difference. No one: l. 10 ff. de codicillis §2; Inst. de codicillis; l. 27 at the end ff. de condit. et demonstr. Can through a codicil: Inst. de codicillis §2. Likewise, although: the sixth difference. After the death of that person: Ulpian 24; Paul, Sentences 3, 6, §5. Moreover: the seventh difference. Interest and fruits: see C. de usuris et fructibus legatorum.

units.la: Tit. VIII. De Int- estatorum Hereditatibus.
units.tr: Title VIII. Of the Inheritances of Those Who Die Intestate.

units.la: INtestatorum hereditates primù ad suos heredes pertinent. Sui autem heredes appellantur, filius filia, nepos neptis, pronepos proneptis ex nepote: quia omnes per virilem sexum descendentes, sui vocantur. Naturales sunt hæ personæ, ac adoptivæ. Adoptivorum enim comparatione legitimi naturales appellantur. Sed ita nepos vel neptis ex filio suo sui heredes sunt; si pater eorum de potestate patris, aut morte aut emancipatione discesserit: nam si eo tempore, quo aliquis moritur, filium in potestate habeat, & ex eo nepotes, illi vivo patre suo, & in potestate aui constituto, sui heredes auo esse non possunt. Similiter posthumi, qui si viuo patre nati fuissent, in potestate eius futuri erant, sui heredes sunt. Si quando aliquis moritur, & reliquerit filium, aut filiam, & ex alio filio mortuo nepotes, neptesve, filii vel nepotes ex filio defuncto, patri vel auo hac ratione succedunt, vt filius vel filia suas partes, & nepotes ex filio portionem, quam pater eorum erat habituru s, accipiant. Quia regulariter constitutum est, vt inter suos proximior longiore gradu positos non excludat, & non in capita, sed in stirpem diuidatur hereditas. Item si quis moriens filium non relinquat, sed ex duobus masculis filiis dimittat nepotes, hoc est, ex uno filio unum, vel duos nepotes, ex altero tres aut quatuor, similiter, sicut superius dictum est, in stirpem, non in capita hereditas diuidatur, hoc modo vt illi duo nepotes ex uno filio medietatem percipiant, & illi quatuor ex alio filio aliam medietatem: hoc est, vt tales accipiant portiones, quales patres eorum si vixissent, habituri erant. Si defuerint heredes sui, tunc hereditas defuncti pertinet ad agnatos. Agnati enim sunt per virilem sexum defuncto propinquitate coniuncti, id est, consanguinei fratres, hoc est, de uno patre nati. Nec disputari potest, si de diuersis matribus nascantur uno patre geniti sunt. Item patruus, id est, frater patris, ... ter patris, fratris sui filio agnatus est: ipso modo sunt fratres patrueles, hoc est, qui de singulis germanis nati sunt. Hoc ordine agnoscitur qui sint agnati, sicut supra diximus, per virilem sexum propinquitate coniuncti. Non tamen omnibus simul agnatis lex hereditatem propinqui intestati dat, sed hiis qui defuncto mortis suae tempore proximiores inveniuntur. In foeminis vero alia conditio est: quia inter foeminas sola tantum soror consanguinea habetur agnata, ut germano suo defuncto, ab intestato ei agnationis iure succedat. Reliquae foeminae, hoc est amitae, id est, patris soror, vel fratris filia, nec in capiendis hereditatibus propinquorum legitimae sunt, nec masculis propinquis agnationis iure succedunt. Ipsarum vero hereditates ad masculos propinquos agnationis conditione perveniunt. Regulariter constitutum est, ut inter agnatos proximior posteriorem excludat, & inter eos non in stirpem, sed in capita, ab intestato dividatur hereditas. Nam inter suos, sicut superius diximus, alia ratio est, ut proximior posteriorem non excludat, & semper hereditas in stirpem non in capita dividatur. Nam si quis moriens dimittat germanum, & ex altero germano filios, germanus frater quia gradu proximior est, solus succedit, fratris filii non succedunt. Item si moriatur quis, & de duobus germanis fratribus bus dimittat filios duntaxat masculos, ex uno fratre dimiserit duos, ex alio quatuor, similiter masculos: omnes quidem fratrum filii patruo suo ab intestato succedunt, sed non in stirpes, sed in capita: ita ut illi duo ex una parte alio accipiant portiones, & illi quatuor ex alio accipiant quatuor portiones. Nam si sorores habuerint, in patrui hereditatem non veniunt; sicut nec sororis filii in avunculi hereditate succedunt. Nam & hoc regulare est, ut cognati tunc intestatorum propinquorum hereditates capiant, quando aut sui, aut agnati defuerint.
units.tr: The inheritances of those who die intestate first pass to their own heirs (sui heredes). Those are called their own heirs who are sons, daughters, grandsons, granddaughters, and great-grandchildren through a grandson, because all who descend through the male line are called "own." These persons are natural, as well as adoptive. For in comparison with adopted children, the others are called natural lawful heirs. But a grandson or granddaughter through a son is an own heir only if their father has passed out of the power of his father, either by death or by emancipation. For if, at the time someone dies, a son is still in his power and has children by him, those grandchildren cannot be own heirs to their grandfather while their father lives and is under the grandfather's power. Likewise, posthumous children, who would have been under their father's power had they been born while he was alive, are own heirs. If someone dies and leaves a son or daughter, and grandchildren or granddaughters by a son who has died, the sons or grandsons through the deceased son succeed in this way: the son or daughter takes their own share, and the grandchildren through the son take the portion their father would have had. This is because it is a general rule that a nearer heir among one's own does not exclude one placed at a more remote degree, and the inheritance is divided not by heads but by stocks. Likewise, if someone dies leaving no son, but leaves grandchildren by two sons, that is, one or two grandchildren by one son and three or four by the other, the inheritance is divided, as said above, by stocks and not by heads, so that those two grandchildren by one son receive a half, and those four by the other son receive the other half. That is, they take such portions as their fathers would have had had they lived. If there are no own heirs, the inheritance of the deceased passes to the agnates. For agnates are those joined to the deceased by kinship through the male line, that is, brothers of the full blood, namely born of one father. Nor can it be disputed that those born of one father are agnates even if they have different mothers. Likewise a paternal uncle, that is, a brother of the father, is agnate to the son of his own brother; in the same way, paternal cousins are those born of two full brothers. In this order, the agnates are recognised, as we said above, as those joined by kinship through the male line. Yet the law does not give the inheritance of an intestate relative to all agnates at once, but to those who are found nearest at the time of the deceased's death. With women the situation is different: among women only a sister of the full blood is counted an agnate, so that on the death of her brother she succeeds him by right of agnation when he dies intestate. The other women, that is, a paternal aunt (the sister of the father) or the daughter of a brother, are neither lawful heirs in taking the inheritances of relatives, nor do they succeed male relatives by right of agnation. Their inheritances, however, pass to male relatives on the condition of agnation. It is a general rule that among agnates the nearer excludes the more remote, and among them the inheritance of one who dies intestate is divided not by stocks but by heads. For among one's own heirs, as we said above, the rule is different: the nearer does not exclude the more remote, and the inheritance is always divided by stocks, not by heads. For if someone dies leaving a brother of the full blood, and sons by another brother, the brother, being nearer in degree, succeeds alone; the sons of the brother do not succeed. Likewise, if someone dies leaving male sons by two full brothers, two by one brother and four by the other, all the sons of the brothers succeed their uncle intestate, but not by stocks, rather by heads, so that those two from one side take their portions, and those four from the other side take their four portions. But if the deceased left sisters, the sons of brothers do not come into the inheritance of their paternal uncle; nor do the sons of a sister succeed to the inheritance of their maternal uncle. For it is also a general rule that cognates take the inheritances of intestate relatives only when there are no own heirs or agnates.

units.la: De hereditatibus, quae ab intestato 3. Inst. 1. de legitimis heredibus. 26. Ulp. de intestatorum successione. Paul. 4. sent. 8.
units.tr: On inheritances which pass by intestacy: Inst. 3, tit. 1, on lawful heirs; Ulp. 26, on the succession of intestates; Paul. Sent. 4, 8.

units.la: Intestatorum hereditates primum ad suos heredes pertinent. Sui autem heredes appellantur, filius, filia, nepos neptis, pronepos proneptis, ex nepote: quia omnes per virilem descendens sui vocantur. Naturales sunt hae personae, ac adoptiuae. Adoptiuorum enim comparatione legitimi naturales appellantur. Sed ita nepos vel neptis ex filio suo sui heredes sunt, si pater eorum de potestate patris aut morte, aut emancipatione discesserit: nam si eo tempore, quo aliquis moritur filium in potestate habeat, & ex eo nepotes, illi vivo patre suo, & in potestate avi constituto, sui heredes avo esse non possunt.
units.tr: The inheritances of those who die intestate first pass to their own heirs. Those are called own heirs who are sons, daughters, grandsons, granddaughters, and great-grandchildren through a grandson, because all who descend through the male line are called "own." These persons are natural, as well as adoptive. For in comparison with adopted children, the others are called natural. But a grandson or granddaughter through a son is an own heir only if their father has passed out of the power of his father, either by death or by emancipation. For if, at the time someone dies, a son is still in his power and has children by him, those grandchildren cannot be own heirs to their grandfather while their father lives and is under the grandfather's power.

units.la: Ad suos hæredes ] vid. 26. Vlp. 1. §. Inst. de hæred. quæ ab intest.
units.tr: To their own heirs: see Ulp. 26, 1; Inst. on heirs who take on intestacy, §.

units.la: Suiautem hæredes ] §. 2. Inst. eod.
units.tr: But own heirs: Inst. ibid., §. 2.

units.la: Naturales sunt ] Naturales, legitimati, sui esse possunt. dict. §. 2. verf. nec interest. verf. quibus.
units.tr: Natural: natural children and legitimated children can be own heirs. Ibid., §. 2, verb. "nor does it matter," verb. "by whom."

units.la: Possunt ] d. §. 2. verf. nam si per id tempus.
units.tr: They can: ibid., §. 2, verb. "for if at that time."

units.la: §. 2. Similiter posthumi, qui si viuo patre nati fuissent, in potestate eius futuri erant, sui hæredes sunt.
units.tr: §. 2. Likewise posthumous children, who would have been under their father's power had they been born while he was alive, are own heirs.

units.la: Posthumi ] d. §. 2. verf. posthumi.
units.tr: Posthumous: ibid., §. 2, verb. "posthumous."

units.la: §. 3. Si quando aliquis moritur, & reliquerit filium, aut filiam & ex alio filio mortuo nepotes; neptesve: filii vel nepotes ex filio defuncto, patri vel avo hac ratione succedunt, ut filius vel filia suas partes, & nepotes ex filio portionem, quam pater eorum erat habiturus, accipiant: quia regulariter constitutum est, ut inter suos proximior, longiore gradu positos non excludat: & non in capita, sed in stirpem dividatur hæreditas. Item, si quis moriens filium non relinquat, sed & duobus masculis filiis dimittat nepotes, hoc est, ex uno filio unum vel duos nepotes, ex altero tres aut quatuor: similiter sicut superius dictum est, in stirpem, non in capita hæreditas dividatur. Hoc modo ut illi duo nepotes ex uno filio medietatem percipiant, & illi quatuor ex alio filio aliam medietatem: hoc est, ut tales accipiant portiones, quales patres eorum si vixissent habituri erant.
units.tr: §. 3. If someone dies and leaves a son or daughter, and grandchildren or granddaughters by a son who has died, the sons or grandsons through the deceased son succeed in this way: the son or daughter takes their own share, and the grandchildren through the son take the portion their father would have had. This is because it is a general rule that a nearer heir among one's own does not exclude one placed at a more remote degree, and the inheritance is divided not by heads but by stocks. Likewise, if someone dies leaving no son, but leaves grandchildren by two sons, that is, one or two grandchildren by one son and three or four by the other, the inheritance is divided, as said above, by stocks and not by heads, so that those two grandchildren by one son receive a half, and those four by the other son receive the other half. That is, they take such portions as their fathers would have had had they lived.

units.la: Ea successio in stirpes dicitur. 26. Vlpian. 2. §. 6. Instit. de hæreditatibus, quæ ab intestato.
units.tr: This succession is called succession by stocks. Ulp. 26; Inst. 2, §. 6, on inheritances which pass by intestacy.

units.la: Nepotes ex filio, patris sui locum repræsentant, siue concurrant cum suis patruis. §. 3. sup. siue plures inter se, vt hic inter fratrum filios non eadem est successio, concurrunt enim inter se non in stirpes, sed in capita. vid. Nouel. 118. c. 3. in sin.
units.tr: Grandchildren through a son represent the place of their father, whether they compete with their paternal uncles, §. 3, above, or with one another, as here among the sons of brothers, where the succession is not the same; for they compete among themselves not by stocks but by heads. See Novel. 118, c. 3, at the end.

units.la: §. 4. Si defuerint hæredes sui, tunc hæreditas defuncti pertinet ad agnatos: Agnati enim sunt per virilem sexum defuncto propinquitate coniuncti, id est, consanguinei fratres, hoc est, vno patre nati. Nec disputari potest, si de diuersis matribus nascantur, qui vno patre geniti sunt. Item patruus, id est, frater patris, fratris sui filio agnatus est. Ipso modo sunt fratres patrueles, hoc est, qui de singulis germanis nati sunt. Hoc ordine agnoscitur, qui sint agnati, sicut supra diximus, per virilem sexum propinquitate coniuncti.
units.tr: §. 4. If there are no own heirs, the inheritance of the deceased passes to the agnates. For agnates are those joined to the deceased by kinship through the male line, that is, brothers of the full blood, namely born of one father. Nor can it be disputed that those born of one father are agnates even if they have different mothers. Likewise a paternal uncle, that is, a brother of the father, is agnate to the son of his own brother. In the same way, paternal cousins are those born of two full brothers. In this order, the agnates are recognised, as we said above, as those joined by kinship through the male line.

units.la: post suos, agnati succedunt.
units.tr: after their own (sui), the agnates succeed.

units.la: quinam agnati.
units.tr: Who the agnates are.

units.la: consanguinei fratres, de vno patre nati: de vno, id est, eodem.
units.tr: Brothers of the full blood (consanguinei fratres), born of one father: "of one," that is, of the same.

units.la: Ex eodem patre, licet diuersis matribus geniti agnati inter se.
units.tr: Those born of the same father, though by different mothers, are agnates to one another.

units.la: patruus patris frater.
units.tr: A paternal uncle (patruus) is the father's brother.

units.la: fratres patrueles duorum fratrum filii. l.1.§.6.ff. de gradibus.
units.tr: Paternal cousins (fratres patrueles) are the sons of two brothers. l.1.§.6.ff. de gradibus.

units.la: §. 5. Non tamen omnibus simul agnatis lex hæreditatem propinqui intestati dat, sed iis, qui defuncto mortis suæ tempore proximiores inueniuntur:
units.tr: §. 5. Yet the law does not give the inheritance of an intestate relative to all the agnates at once, but to those who are found nearest at the time of the deceased's death.

units.la: §. 6. Instit. de legitima agnat. successi.
units.tr: §. 6. Instit. de legitima agnat. successi.

units.la: §. 6. In fœminis vero alia conditio est: quia inter fœminas sola tantum soror consanguinea habetur agnata, vt germano suo defuncto, ab intestato ei agnationis iure succedat. Reliquæ fœminæ, hoc est, amitæ, id est, patris soror, vel fratris filia; nec in capiendis hæreditatibus propinquorum legitimæ sunt, nec masculis propinquis agnationis iure succedunt. Ipsarum vero hereditates ad masculos propinquos agnationis conditione perueniunt.
units.tr: §. 6. With women, however, the situation is different: among women, only a sister of the full blood is counted as an agnate, so that on the death of her brother she succeeds to him intestate by right of agnation. The other women, namely aunts (amitae), that is, the father's sisters, or a brother's daughter, are not lawful heirs of relatives in taking inheritances, nor do they succeed male relatives by right of agnation. Their inheritances, however, pass to male relatives by the condition of agnation.

units.la: 26. Vlp.6. Paul.4. sent.§.3.
units.tr: 26. Vlp.6. Paul.4. sent.§.3.

units.la: §.7. Regulariter constitutum est, vt inter agnatos proximior posteriore excludat, & inter eos non in stirpem, sed in capita ab intestato diuidatur hæreditas. Nam inter suos, sicut superius diximus, alia ratio est, vt proximior posteriorem non excludat, & semper hæreditas in stirpem, non in capita diuidatur. Nam si quis moriens dimittat germanũ, & ex altero filio germano filios: germanus frater, quia gradu proximior est, solus succedit, fratris filii non succedunt. Item si moriatur quis, & de duobus germanis fratribus dimittat filios duntaxat masculos, ex vno fratre dimiserit duos, ex alio quatuor, similiter masculos: omnes quidem fratrum filii patruo suo ab intestato succedunt, sed non in stirpes, sed in capita: ita vt illi duo ex vna parte duas accipiant portiones, & illi quatuor ex alio accipiant quatuor portiones. Nam si sorores habuerint, in patrui hæreditatem non veniunt, sicut nec sorores filii in auunculi hæreditate succedunt.
units.tr: §.7. It has been established as a general rule that among agnates the nearer excludes the more remote, and that among them the inheritance on intestacy is divided not by stocks (in stirpem) but by heads (in capita). For among the sui, as we said above, the rule is different: the nearer does not exclude the more remote, and the inheritance is always divided by stocks, not by heads. For if someone dies leaving one full brother, and sons of another full brother, the brother, being nearer in degree, succeeds alone; the sons of the brother do not succeed. Likewise, if someone dies and leaves only male sons of two full brothers, two from one brother and four from the other, all the sons of the brothers succeed their uncle intestate, but not by stocks, rather by heads, so that those two take two shares from one side, and those four take four shares from the other. For if they have sisters, they do not come into the inheritance of the uncle, just as sisters' sons do not succeed in the inheritance of their maternal uncle.

units.la: Proximior posteriorem
units.tr: Proximior posteriorem

units.la: Non excludat inter suos proximiores non excludunt posteriores.
units.tr: Non excludat the nearer among the sui do not exclude the more remote.

units.la: In stirpem inter suos diuiditur hæreditas in stirpes.
units.tr: In stirpem among the sui the inheritance is divided by stocks.

units.la: Non succedunt Hodie succedunt.
units.tr: Non succedunt Today they do succeed.

units.la: Sed in capita Fratrum filii inter se succedunt in capita: qua de re vide ad Vlpianum 26. §. 4. & ad Nouel. 118. c. 3. in f. Goth.
units.tr: Sed in capita The sons of brothers succeed one another by heads: on this matter see on Ulpian 26 §. 4, and on Novel 118, c. 3, at the end, Gothofredus.

units.la: §. 8. Nam & hoc regulare est, vt cognati tunc intestatorum propinquorum hæreditates capiant, quando aut sui, aut agnati defuerint.
units.tr: §. 8. For this too is a general rule: cognates take the inheritances of intestate relatives only when there are either sui or agnates lacking.

units.la: Quando aut sui post suos & agnatos succedunt agnati. Hodie sublata est differentia agnatorum & cognatorum. Nouel. 118. c. 4.
units.tr: Quando aut sui after the sui and agnates, the cognates succeed. Today the distinction between agnates and cognates has been abolished. Novel 118, c. 4.

units.la: Tit. IX. De Obligationibus.
units.tr: Tit. IX. On Obligations.

units.la: OBligatio in duas species diuiditur. Nam omnes obligationes aut ex contractu nascuntur, aut ex culpa. Quae ex contractu nascuntur, quatuor genera sunt, quae singula hoc ordine distinguuntur. Aut enim re contrahitur obligatio, aut verbis, aut literis, aut consensu. Re contrahitur, quoties aliqua cuicunque mutuo dantur, quae in his rebus contingunt, quae pondere, numero, mensura continentur: hoc est, si pecunia numeretur, vel frumentum detur, vinum, aut oleum, aut aes, ferrum, argentum, vel aurum. Quae omnia numerando, aut pensando, aut metiendo; ad hoc damus ut eorum fiant qui ea accipiunt, & ad nos statuto tempore, non ipse res, sed aliae eius naturae, quales datae sunt, atque ipsius ponderis, numeri, vel mensurae reddantur. Propter quod Mutuum appellatum est, quasi a me tibi ita datum sit, ut ex meo tuum fieret. Verbis contrahitur obligatio, ex interrogatione dantis, & responsione accipientis, ita ut si ille qui dat, interroget: Hoc mihi dabis? qui accipiet, respondeat: Dabo. Aut in obligatione debitoris, si aliquis fideiussor accedat, ille qui personam fideiussoris tra ri tradit, interroget: Istum fide tua esse iubes? & ille respondeat: Fide mea esse iubeo. hac conditione non solum ille qui debitor est, sed & is qui fideiussor existit, obligantur. Et non solum fideiussor ipse dum viuit, sed & heredes ipsius, si ille defecerit, tenentur obnoxii. Creditor autem, qui pecuniam dedit in potestate habet ad reddendam pecuniam quem velit tenere; vtrum ipsum debitorem, an fideiussorem. Sed si debitorem tenere elegerit, fideiussorem absoluit. Si vero fideiussorem tenuerit, debitorem absoluit. Quia vno electo, quem idoneum creditor iudicat, alterum liberat. Sunt & aliæ obligationes, quæ nulla præcedente interrogatione contrahi possunt, id est, vt si mulier siue sponso vxor futura siue iam marito dotem dicat. Quod tam de mobilibus rebus, quam de fundis fieri potest. Et non solum in hac obligatione ipsa mulier obligabitur, sed & pater eius, & debitor ipsius mulieris, si pecuniam, quam ille debebat sponso creditricis, ipse debitor in dotem dixerit. Hæ tantum tres personæ, nulla interrogatione præcedente possunt dictione dotis legitime obligati. Aliæ vero personæ, si pro muliere dotem marito promiserint, communi iure obligari debent: id est, vt & interrogatæ respondeant, & stipulaæ promittant. Item & alio casu, vno loquente, & sine interrogetione alio promittente, contrahitur obligatio, id est, si libertus patrono aut donum, aut munus, aut operas se daturum esse iuraverit. Exponendum hic quid sit donum, aut munus, vel operæ, in qua re supradicti liberti non tam verborum solemnitate, quam iurisiurandi religione tenentur. Sed nulla altera persona hoc ordine obligari potest. Præterea inutilis est promissio, etiamsi stipulatione interveniente facta sit, si id aliquis daturum se promiserit, quod sui iuris non est: hoc est, si aut ingenuum hominem quasi servum se daturum promittat. Aut si mortuum aliquis, quem viuum credebat, promiserit. Aut locum sacrum, aut sanctum, aut religiosum daturum se quicunque promiserit. Præterea inutilis est promissio, si aliquis rem sub tali conditione promittat, quæ impleri pro rei difficultate non possit. Præterea inutilis est interrogatio & promissio, si ita aliquis interroget debitorem, Post mortem meam vel tuam illud dari spondes? Quod propterea inutile vitium est, quia à persona heredis obligatio incipere non potest. Et ideo nec heredi creditoris sub hac sponsione obligatur debitor, nec debitoris heres creditori tenetur obnoxius. Item inutilis est obligatio si dicat creditor, Pridie quam moriar, dare spondes? Vel interroget debitorem, Pridie quam moriaris: Similiter & hæc stipulatio inutilis iudicatur, quia non potest sciri, quando sit pridie quam aliquis moriatur, nisi postquam mortuus fuerit. Item si pure interroget creditor, & debitor sub conditione promittat. Vel si creditor decem solidos debitorem interroget, & debitor quinque promittat: hoc ordine integrum debitum vacillare cognoscitur. Si quis nobis pecuniam debeat, possumus debitorem nostrum compellere, ut pecuniam quam nobis redditurus erat, alteri se caveat redditurum. Neque potest ei, cui pro nostro debito cavet, de cauto & non numerato, sicut fieri solet, aliquid disputationis afferre, cum id quod a nobis accepit, alteri caverit redditurum. Literis obligatio fit, aut a re in personam, aut a persona in personam. A re in personam, velut si id quod ex emptione aut conductione aut societate debes, alii reddas. A persona in personam, velut si id quod mihi alter debet, alteri personae delegem, ut reddere debeat. Consensu fiunt obligationes, ex emptionibus & venditionibus, locationibus conductionibus, societatibus & mandatis. Quia in eiusmodi rebus consensus magis quam scriptura aliqua aut solemnitas quaeritur. In quibus rebus etiam inter absentes obligatio contrahi potest, quod in aliis rebus fieri non potest. Emptio igitur & venditio contrahitur, cum de pretio inter emptorem & venditorem fuerit definitum, etiamsi pretium non fuerit numeratum, & nec pars pretii aut arrha data fuerit.
units.tr: An obligation is divided into two kinds. For all obligations arise either from contract or from fault. Those which arise from contract are of four kinds, and each of these is distinguished in the following order. An obligation is contracted either by a thing (re), by words (verbis), by writing (literis), or by consent. It is contracted by a thing whenever things are lent to someone, things of the kind that consist of weight, number or measure: that is, if money is counted out, or corn, wine, oil, bronze, iron, silver or gold is handed over. All of these we give by counting, weighing or measuring, so that they become the property of those who receive them, and at an agreed time they are returned to us, not the very same things, but others of the same kind, in the same weight, number or measure as were given. For this reason the transaction is called a loan (mutuum), as if it had been given by me to you so that what was mine became yours. An obligation is contracted by words through a question from the giver and an answer from the receiver, so that if the one who gives asks: Will you give me this? and the one who receives answers: I will give. Or in the obligation of a debtor, if a surety comes forward, the one who hands over the surety's person asks: Do you order that man to be under your faith? and the other answers: I order him to be under my faith. By this agreement not only the debtor but also the one who stands as surety is bound. And not only the surety himself while he lives, but also his heirs, if he has died, are held liable. The creditor who has given the money has it in his power to hold to the repayment whichever he chooses: either the debtor himself or the surety. But if he chooses to hold the debtor, he releases the surety; if he holds the surety, he releases the debtor. For when the one whom the creditor judges fit has been chosen, the other is freed. There are also other obligations which can be contracted with no preceding question, as when a woman, whether betrothed as future wife or already married, promises a dowry to her husband. This can be done with movable goods as well as with lands. And in this obligation not only the woman herself is bound, but also her father, and her debtor, if the debtor himself has promised to the woman's fiancé in respect of the dowry the money which he owed to the creditress. These three persons alone can be lawfully bound by the promise of a dowry without any preceding question. But other persons, if they have promised a dowry to a husband on behalf of a woman, ought to be bound by the common law: that is, they must answer when questioned and promise when asked for a stipulation. Likewise, in another case, an obligation is contracted when one party speaks and the other promises without any question, as when a freedman swears to his patron that he will give a gift, a present or services. Here it should be explained what a gift, a present or services are, in which matter the aforesaid freedmen are bound not so much by the solemnity of the words as by the sanctity of the oath. But no other person can be bound in this way. Moreover, a promise is invalid, even if it was made with a stipulation, if someone promises to give what is not within his own right: that is, if he promises to give a free man as if he were a slave, or if he promises a man who is dead, whom he believed to be alive. Or if anyone promises to give a sacred, holy or religious place. Furthermore, a promise is invalid if someone promises a thing under a condition which, on account of the difficulty of the matter, cannot be fulfilled. Moreover, a question and promise are invalid if someone asks the debtor in this way: Do you promise to give that after my death or yours? This defect makes it invalid because an obligation cannot begin with the person of an heir. Therefore the debtor is not bound to the creditor's heir under this undertaking, nor is the debtor's heir held liable to the creditor. Likewise an obligation is invalid if the creditor says: Do you promise to give on the day before I die? or asks the debtor: On the day before you die? This stipulation too is judged invalid, because it cannot be known which day is the day before a person dies until after he has died. Likewise if the creditor asks purely and the debtor promises under a condition; or if the creditor asks for ten shillings and the debtor promises five: in this way the whole debt is recognised as wavering. If someone owes us money, we can compel our debtor to give security to another person that he will repay the money which he was going to repay to us. Nor can he who receives security from the debtor for our debt raise any dispute about it being secured but not paid, as is usually done, since the debtor has given security to another for repayment of what he received from us. An obligation is made by writing (literis), either from a thing to a person or from a person to a person. From a thing to a person, as when you pay to another what you owe from a purchase, a lease or a partnership. From a person to a person, as when I assign to another person what a second party owes me, so that he must pay it. Obligations are made by consent in purchases and sales, lettings and hirings, partnerships and mandates, because in such matters consent is sought rather than any writing or solemnity. In these matters an obligation can also be contracted between absent parties, which cannot be done in other matters. A purchase and sale is therefore contracted when the price has been settled between buyer and seller, even if the price has not been counted out, and no part of the price or any earnest money has been given.

units.la: [the word "fue-" at the foot of the column is the start of the next page's word: fuerit. Locatio & conductio similí ratione consistunt, vt consensu, etiam verbo definitio inter consentientes firma permaneat. Societatem inire possumus, aut omnium bonorum aut vnius alicuius negotiationis. Et potest ita iniri societas, si tamen hoc inter socios convenit, vt vnus pecuniam det, alter operam suam pro pecunia ponat. Et huius rei definitio etiam verbo inita valet, ita vt quicquid societatis tempore quolibet modo fuerit adquisitum, sociis commune sit. Permanet autem inita societas, quandiu in ipso consensu socii perseverant: quia sicut consensu contrahitur, etiam dissensu soluitur. Dissoluitur ergo societas aut morte vnius socii, aut contraria voluntate, aut capitis deminutione, id est, si vnus ex sociis, sicut frequenter supra diximus, capite fuerit deminutus. Similiter & mandari verbo potest. Et cum verbis mandatum fuerit, obligatio contrahitur. Possumus enim aut nostra negotia, aut aliena cuicunque agenda mandare, dummodo honestum aliquid agi mandemus. Nam si contra mores bonos aliquid mandare voluerimus: hoc est, si cuicunque mandemus, vt alicui furtum faciat, aut homicidium, aut adulterium admittat, in hiis rebus mandati obligatio non contrahitur. Soluitur autem mandatum aut morte, cui mandatum est, aut contraria illius voluntate qui mandauit. Sed is cui mandatur, mandari formam egredi non potest. Aut si egressus fuerit,& mandatori teneatur obnoxius, & quod extra mandatum egit, non præiudicet mandatori.
units.tr: Letting and hiring rest on a similar principle: an agreement between those who consent remains firm by consent, even by word alone. We may enter into a partnership either of all goods or of some one business. A partnership may be entered into in this way, provided that it is agreed between the partners that one shall give money and the other put his labour in return for the money. And an agreement about this matter, even if made by word, is valid, so that whatever is acquired in any way during the partnership is common to the partners. An entered partnership continues as long as the partners persist in the very consent; for just as it is contracted by consent, so it is dissolved by dissent. A partnership is therefore dissolved either by the death of one partner, by a contrary will, or by loss of civil status, that is, if one of the partners has been diminished in status, as we have often said above. Likewise a mandate can be given by word. And when a mandate has been given by words, an obligation is contracted. For we may commission either our own affairs or another's to be done by anyone, provided that we commission something honourable to be done. For if we should wish to commission something contrary to good morals, that is, if we should commission someone to commit theft against another, or murder, or to permit adultery, no obligation of mandate is contracted in these matters. A mandate is dissolved either by the death of the one to whom it was given, or by the contrary will of the one who gave it. But the one to whom the mandate is given cannot go beyond the form of the mandate. Or if he has gone beyond it, he is bound to the mandator, and what he has done beyond the mandate does not prejudice the mandator.
See 3. Inst. 14. 44. ff. 7.

units.la: §. 1. Obligatio in duas species diuiditur. Nam omnes obligationes aut ex contractu nascuntur, aut ex culpa. Quæ ex contractu nascuntur, quatuor genere sunt, quæ singula hoc ordine distinguuntur. Aut enim re contrahitur obligatio, aut verbis, aut literis, aut consensu.
units.tr: §. 1. An obligation is divided into two kinds. For all obligations arise either from contract or from fault. Those which arise from contract are of four kinds, and each of these is distinguished in the following order. An obligation is contracted either by a thing, or by words, or by writing, or by consent.
