Lactantius, 1. What then is the reason that Jupiter, most lecherous among the poets, has ceased to raise children? Was he made a sexagenarian, and did the Lex Papia put a clasp on him? Or did he obtain the right of three children? And in Apuleius, Apologia 2, it was objected in court that Pudentilla had married him, in her sixtieth year of age, for lust. Today a man over sixty may marry a woman under fifty. l. 27, C. de nuptiis; l. 12, C. de legitimis heredibus. Add Suetonius, in Claudius, c. 23. Gothofredus, here.

units.la: Senatusconsulto Claudiano ] Lege, Claudiano, ut sup. Goth. & Cuiac.
units.tr: Senatusconsulto Claudiano] Read, Claudiano, as above. Gothofredus & Cuiacius.

units.la: Dos caduca erit vt in l. si quis officium 38. §. veterem 1. l. dote de ritu nupt.
units.tr: The dowry will be forfeit as in law "if anyone" 38, §. "the old" 1, law "dowry" concerning the rite of marriage.

units.la: Tit. XVII. De Caducis.
units.tr: Title XVII. Of Caduca (Lapsed Bequests)

units.la: QVod quis sibi testamento relictum, ita vt iure ciuili capere possit, aliqua ex causa non ceperit, caducum appellatur, veluti cecidit ab eo: verbi gratia, si cœlibi, vel Latino Iuniano legatum fuerit, nec intra dies centum vel cœlebs legi paruerit, vel Latinus ius Quiritium consequutus sit: aut si ex parte scriptus, vel legatarius ante apertas tabulas decesserit, vel peræger factus sit.
units.tr: What someone has not taken under a will, though it was left to him in such a way that he could take it under civil law, is called caducum (lapsed) for some reason, as if it had fallen away from him. For example, if a legacy was left to an unmarried person or to a Junian Latin, and the unmarried person did not obey the law within a hundred days by marrying, or the Latin did not obtain Roman citizenship; or if someone was instituted heir in part, or a legatee died before the tablets were opened, or became a foreigner (peregrinus).

units.la: Hodie ex constitutione Imperatoris Antonini, omnia caduca fisco vindicantur, seruato iure antiquo liberis & parentibus.
units.tr: Today, by a constitution of the Emperor Antoninus, all caduca are claimed by the treasury (fiscus), though the old right is kept for children and parents.

units.la: Caduca cum suo onere fiunt: ideoque libertates & legata fideicommissa ab eo data, ex cuius persona hereditas caduca facta est, salua sunt: scilicet & legata, & fideicommissa cum suo onere fiunt caduca.
units.tr: Caduca fall together with their burden, so freedoms and legacies or trusts left by the person from whom the inheritance became caducum remain valid. Indeed, legacies and trusts also become caduca together with their burden.

units.la: Eorum quæ in testamentis scribuntur, quædam pro non scriptis sunt, quædam in causa caduci, quædam caduca. Pro non scriptis hæc sunt, quæ incapacibus relinquuntur: quæ non intelliguntur: quæ testamentarius sibi adscribit: quæ sunt captatoria: quæ ei, qui in rebus humanis non est, adscribuntur. Pro non scriptis igitur sunt, quæ in ipso initio deficiunt. In causa caduci sunt, quæ paulo post testamentum viuo testatore deficiunt: vtputa, si legatarius viuo testatore decedat, aut conditione excludatur. Caduca sunt, quæ mortuo testatore deficiunt: vtputa, si hæres vel legatarius ante apertas tabulas decesserit, vel alias incapax factus fuerit. Caduca & in causa caducorum, legibus Iuliis fisco vindicantur: legibus Iustiniani apud hæredem remanent cum onere. Quæ pro non scriptis habentur, & novo & antiquo iure apud hæredem remanent sine onere, Cuiac,& Paci.h.
units.tr: Of the things written in wills, some are regarded as unwritten, some are in the condition of caducum, and some are caduca. These are regarded as unwritten: what is left to incapable persons; what is unintelligible; what the testator adds to himself; what is captatory; and what is assigned to someone who is no longer among the living. Those things are therefore unwritten which fail from the very beginning. Those are in the condition of caducum which fail shortly after the will, while the testator is still alive, for example if the legatee dies while the testator lives, or is excluded by a condition. Those are caduca which fail after the testator's death, for example if the heir or legatee dies before the tablets are opened, or otherwise becomes incapable. Caduca, and things in the condition of caducum, are claimed by the treasury under the Julian laws, but under the laws of Justinian they remain with the heir, with their burden. Things regarded as unwritten remain with the heir without burden under both new and old law. Cuiac. and Pac. ad h.

units.la: Caducis ] 6.C.50.
units.tr: Of caduca ] 6.C.50.

units.la: Veluti cecidit ] Malim veluti ceciderit. Constantinus dixit, cadere in casum. leg.omnes C.d. delat. Cuiac.h.
units.tr: As it fell ] I would prefer veluti ceciderit (as it has fallen). Constantine said cadere in casum (to fall into the case). leg. omnes C. de delat. Cuiac. ad h.

units.la: Veluti cecidit ] Caduca sunt, quæ iure relicta capaci, aliqua ex causa post mortem testatoris ab eo cadunt in fiscum. Capaci dixi, nam quæ incapaci relinquuntur, pro non scriptis habentur.
units.tr: As it fell ] Caduca are those things which, having been validly left to a capable person, fall into the treasury for some reason after the testator's death. I say capable, for things left to an incapable person are regarded as unwritten.

units.la: Si cœlibi vel Latino Iuniano ] Ergo & cum cœlibe & cum Latino testamenti factio est: & hoc de Latino nominatim proditum est in tit. 11.& 20. Nam neque cœlibem lex Iulia, neque Latinum lex Iunia hæredem instituì, aut ei legari quippiam vetat: sed ex ijsdem legibus caduca fiunt ea quæ ipsis relinquuntur, nisi intra centum centum dies hic ciuis Romanus fiat, ille matrimonio iungatur, vt in tit.22. Cuiac.h.
units.tr: If to an unmarried person or a Junian Latin ] Therefore both the unmarried person and the Latin have testamentary capacity. This is stated expressly of the Latin in titles 11 and 20. For the Julian law does not forbid an unmarried person, nor the Junian law a Latin, to be instituted heir or to receive any legacy; but by those same laws the things left to them become caduca, unless within a hundred days this citizen becomes a Roman, or that person marries, as in title 22. Cuiac. ad h.

units.la: Si cœlibi ]1. Sozomen.9.
units.tr: If to an unmarried person] 1. Sozomen. 9.

units.la: Vel Latino ] tit. 11. §.16. tit.20. §. 18. tit.22. §. 3. infr. eod.
units.tr: Or to a Junian Latin] title 11, §. 16; title 20, §. 18; title 22, §. 3, infra eod.

units.la: Pauerit ] id est, nuptias non fecerit.
units.tr: Has not married] that is, has not contracted marriage.

units.la: Ex parte scriptus ] Recte id adiectum est; nam ex parte scriptus, etiam clausis tabulis testamenti, adire hereditatem potest: quatenus lex Papia ius tantum adcrescendi aufert cohaeredibus vel legatariis. Goth.h.
units.tr: Instituted in part] This is rightly added, for a person instituted in part may enter on the inheritance even when the tablets of the will are closed, inasmuch as the Papian law takes away only the right of accrual from co-heirs or legatees. Goth. ad h.

units.la: Peraeger ] malim Peregrinus.
units.tr: Peraeger] I would prefer peregrinus.

units.la: Hodie ex constitutione imp. Antonini ] Imo ex lege Papia. Quamobrem videntur mihi haec esse transposita, atque restituenda in hunc modum, omnia caduca fisco vindicantur, sed seruato iure antiquo liberis & parentibus. Hodie ex constitutione Imp. Antonini, caduca cum suo onere fiunt: & quae sequuntur: vt intelligatur constitutio ea cuius fit mentio in l. licet.de leg.1.l.4. C.ad Treb. Quae enim ille de substitutis, ad coheredes & ad fiscum transferuntur. l.si Titio §. 1. de legat. 2. l. quidam §. quotiens de leg. 1. l. in facto §. ult. de condit. & demonstr. Cuiac. hic.
units.tr: Today by a constitution of the Emperor Antoninus] Rather, it is by the Papian law. Hence these words seem to me to be transposed and should be restored in this way: all caduca are claimed by the treasury, but the old right is kept for children and parents. Today, by a constitution of the Emperor Antoninus, caduca fall together with their burden, and what follows, so that the constitution mentioned in l. licet, de leg. 1; l. 4 C. ad Treb. is understood. For what that law says about substitutes is transferred to co-heirs and to the treasury. l. si Titio §. 1, de legat. 2; l. quidam §. quotiens, de leg. 1; l. in facto §. ult., de condit. et demonstr. Cuiac. hic.

units.la: Fisco vindicantur ] Hodie caducariae leges abrogatae. (C.de caduc. tollen.
units.tr: Are claimed by the treasury] Today the caducary laws have been abrogated. (C. de caduc. tollend.

units.la: Seruato iure ] vid.tit.18.infr.eod.
units.tr: The old right kept] see title 18, infra eod.

units.la: Caduca] Initium huius §. emendatum est §. superiore.
units.tr: Caduca] The beginning of this §. has been corrected, from the preceding §.

units.la: Scilicet & scribendum, sed &. Cuiac.
units.tr: It should be written scilicet & (indeed), but sed &. Cuiac.

units.la: Tit. XVIII. Qui habeant ius antiquum in caducis.
units.tr: Tit. XVIII. Who have the ancient right in caducous property.

units.la: ITem liberis & parentibus testatores vsq; ad tertium gradum lex Papia ius antiquum dedit: vt heredibus illis institutis, quod quis ex eo testamento non capit, ad hos pertineat, aut totum, aut ex parte, prout pertinere possit.
units.tr: Likewise, the Papian law gave the ancient right to testators' children and parents up to the third degree, so that when heirs have been instituted, whatever someone does not take under that will passes to these relatives, either wholly or in part, as far as it can pass.

units.la: Ea quae mortuo testatore deficiunt ex iure antiquo, apud haeredem remanent, post legem Iuliam & Papiam caduca fiunt: ius tamen ea lege antiquum seruatur liberis & parentibus vsque ad tertium gradum. §. & cum lex. Cod. de caduc. tollend. quod & in tit. proximo. & tit. 1. & tit. 35. Vlpian. notat. Inde Celsus in l. pater meus. §. vlt. de legat. 2. Si filio, inquit, haeredi pars eius, a quo nominatim legatum est, accrescit, non praestabit legatum, quod iure antiquo capit. Id vero immixtum portioni haereditatis eo iure capit, quod legem Papiam antecessit, quoniam filius est. Caeterum vt de Iuliano Vlpianus in l. si Titio. ita nos de Celso dicere possumus. Celsus quidem ait legatum non praestari. Sed post constitutionem Seueri & Antonini alio iure vtimur: ac frustra nostri interpretes Celsum, qui Hadriani temporibus floruit vna cum Iu-liano, cum rescripto D. Seueri in concordiam adducere conantur. Cuiac. hic.
units.tr: Those things which fail on the testator's death under the ancient law remain with the heir; after the Julian and Papian laws they become caducous. Yet by that law the ancient right is preserved for children and parents up to the third degree. §. & cum lex. Cod. de caduc. tollend. which also appears in the preceding title. & tit. 1. & tit. 35. Vlpian. notat. Hence Celsus in l. pater meus. §. vlt. de legat. 2. says: "If a son who is heir receives the share of the heir to whom the legacy was expressly given, he will not pay the legacy, which he takes under the ancient law. But what he takes as part of the inheritance under that law, which preceded the Papian law, he takes because he is a son." But just as Ulpian says of Julian in l. si Titio., so we may say of Celsus: Celsus indeed says the legacy is not paid. But after the constitution of Severus and Antoninus we use a different law, and our interpreters vainly try to reconcile Celsus, who flourished in the time of Hadrian along with Julian, with the rescript of the divine Severus. Cuiac. hic.

units.tr: Item liberis] tit.1.§.21.tit.17.§.2.supr.eod.tit. 25.§.17.

units.la: Tit. XIX. De dominiis & adquisition- ibus rerum.
units.tr: Title 19. On the ownership and acquisition of things.

units.la: OMnes res aut mancipi sunt, aut necmancipi. Mancipi res sunt prædia in Italico solo, tam rustica, qualis est fundus: quam vrbana, qualis domus. Item iura prædiorum rusticorum: velut via, iter, actus, & aquæductus. Item serui & quadrupedes, quæ dorso collove domantur, velut boues, muli, equi, asini: cæteræ res necmancipi sunt. Elephanti & cameli, quâuis collo dorsove domentur, necmancipi sunt: quoniam bestiarum numero sunt.
units.tr: All things are either mancipable or non-mancipable. Mancipable things are landed property on Italian soil, both rural, such as a farm, and urban, such as a house. Likewise the rights of rural estates, such as a way, a path, a driveway and an aqueduct. Likewise slaves and those four-footed animals that are broken to the back or the neck, such as oxen, mules, horses and asses. All other things are non-mancipable. Elephants and camels, though broken to neck or back, are non-mancipable, since they belong to the class of wild beasts.

units.la: Singularum rerum dominia nobis adquiruntur, mancipatione, traditione, vsucapione, in iure cessione, adiudicatione, lege.
units.tr: Ownership of individual things is acquired by us through mancipation, delivery, usucaption, cession in court, adjudication, or by law.

units.la: Mancipatio propria species alienationis est, & rerum mancipi: eaque fit certis verbis, libripende, & quinque testibus præsentibus.
units.tr: Mancipation is a particular form of alienation, and of mancipable things. It is effected with set words, with a scale-holder, and five witnesses present.

units.la: Mancipatio locum habet inter cives Romanos, & Latinos Coloniarios, Latinosque Iunianos. tianos, eosque peregrinos quibus commercium datum est.
units.tr: Mancipation takes place between Roman citizens, Latin colonists, Junian Latins, and those foreigners to whom commercium has been granted.

units.la: Commercium est emendi vendendique invicem ius.
units.tr: Commercium is the mutual right of buying and selling.

units.la: Res mobiles non nisi præsentes mancipari possunt, & non plures quam quæ manu capi possunt. Immobiles autem, etiam plures simul, & quæ diversis locis sunt, mancipari possunt.
units.tr: Movable things can be mancipated only when they are present, and not more than can be taken in the hand. Immovable things, however, can be mancipated even several at once, and even those lying in different places.

units.la: Traditio, proprie est alienatio rerum. Nec mancipi rerum dominia, ipsa traditione adprehendimus: scilicet, si ex iusta causa traditæ sunt nobis.
units.tr: Delivery is properly the alienation of things. We acquire ownership of non-mancipable things by delivery itself, namely if they have been delivered to us from a just cause.

units.la: Vsucapione dominia adipiscimur, tam mancipi rerum, quam nec mancipi. Vsucapio est autem dominij adeptio, per continuationem possessionis anni, vel biennij: rerum mobilium anni, immobilium biennij.
units.tr: We acquire ownership by usucaption, both of mancipable and of non-mancipable things. Usucaption is the acquisition of ownership through continuous possession for a year or for two years: of movables for a year, of immovables for two years.

units.la: In iure cessio quoque communis alienatio est, & mancipi rerum, & nec mancipi, quæ fit per tres personas in iure cedentes, vindicantes, addicentes.
units.tr: Cession in court is also a common form of alienation, both of mancipable and of non-mancipable things. It is effected through three persons: the one ceding in court, the one claiming, and the one adjudicating.

units.la: In iure cedit dominus: vindicat is cui ceditur: addicit Prætor.
units.tr: The owner cedes in court; the one to whom it is ceded claims it; the praetor adjudicates.

units.la: In iure cedi res etiam incorporales possunt, velut vsusfructus, & hereditas, & tutela legitima, & libertas.
units.tr: Even incorporeal things can be ceded in court, such as usufruct, an inheritance, legal guardianship, and liberty.

units.la: Hereditas in iure cedītur, vel antequam adcatur, vel posteaquam adita fuerit.
units.tr: An inheritance is ceded in court either before it has been entered upon or after it has been entered upon.

units.la: Antequam adeatur in iure cedi potest legitimo ab herede: posteaquam adita est, tam a legitimo, quam ab eo qui testamento heres scriptus est.
units.tr: Before it is entered upon, it can be ceded in court by the legal heir. After it has been entered upon, it can be ceded by both the legal heir and the one named heir by will.

units.la: Si antequam adeatur hereditas, in iure cessa sit, perinde heres fit cui cessa est, ac si ipse heres legitimus esset. Quod si posteaquam adita fuerit, in iure cessa sit, is cui cessa est permanet heres, & ob id creditoribus defuncti manet obligatus: debita vero pereunt, id est debitores defuncti liberantur.
units.tr: If the inheritance is ceded in court before it is entered upon, the one to whom it is ceded becomes heir just as if he were the legal heir himself. But if it is ceded in court after it has been entered upon, the one to whom it is ceded remains heir, and for that reason remains bound to the creditors of the deceased. The debts, however, perish, that is, the debtors of the deceased are released.

units.la: Res autem corporales, quoties singulae in iure cessae sunt, transeunt ad eum cui cessa est hereditas.
units.tr: Corporeal things, however, whenever they are ceded in court singly, pass to the one to whom the inheritance is ceded.

units.la: Adiudicatione dominia nanciscimur, per formulam Familiae erciscundae, quae locum habet inter coheredes: & per formulam Communi dividundo, cui locus est inter socios: & per formulam Finium regundorum, quae est inter vicinos. Nam si iudex vni ex heredibus aut sociis, aut vicinis rem aliquam adiudicaverit, statim illi adquiritur, sive mancipi, sive nec mancipi sit.
units.tr: We acquire ownership by adjudication: through the formula for dividing an estate, which applies among coheirs; through the formula for dividing a common thing, which applies among partners; and through the formula for fixing boundaries, which applies between neighbours. For if the judge adjudges some thing to one of the heirs, partners or neighbours, it is at once acquired by him, whether it is mancipable or non-mancipable.

units.la: Lege nobis adquiritur, velut caducum vel ereptitium ex lege Papia Popaea: item legatum ex lege duodecim Tabularum, sive mancipi res sint, sive necmancipi.
units.tr: We acquire by law, for example what is caducous or ereptitious under the Lex Papia Poppaea; likewise a legacy under the Law of the Twelve Tables, whether the things are mancipable or non-mancipable.

units.la: Adquiritur autem nobis etiam per eas personas, quas in potestate, manu mancipiove habemus. b mus. Itaque siquidem (mancipio puta) accerint, aut traditum eis sit, vel stipulati fuerint, ad nos pertinet:
units.tr: We also acquire through those persons whom we have in our power, hand or ownership. Therefore, if they receive something (say by mancipation), or it is delivered to them, or they have stipulated for it, it belongs to us.

units.la: Item si heredes instituti sint, legatum ve eis sit: & hereditatem iussu nostro adeuntes nobis adquirunt, & legatum ad nos pertinet.
units.tr: Likewise, if they have been instituted heirs, or a legacy has been left to them, and they enter the inheritance at our command, they acquire it for us, and the legacy belongs to us.

units.la: Si seruus alterius in bonis, alterius ex iure Quiritium sit, ex omnibus causis adquiret ei, cuius in bonis est.
units.tr: If a slave is in the bonis of one person and ex iure Quiritium of another, he acquires for the one in whose bonis he is, in every case.

units.la: Is quem bona fide possidemus, siue liber, siue alienus seruus sit, nobis adquirit ex duabus causis tantum, id est, quod ex re nostra, & quod ex operibus suis adquirit: extra has autem causas, aut sibi adquirit, si liber sit: aut domino, si alienus seruus sit. Eadem sunt & in eo seruo, in quo tantum vsumfructum habemus.
units.tr: A person whom we possess in good faith, whether a free man or another's slave, acquires for us from two causes only: namely, what he acquires from our property and what he acquires from his own work. Outside these causes, he acquires for himself if he is free, or for his owner if he is another's slave. The same holds for a slave in whom we have only usufruct.

units.la: De dominiis ]4i. ff. 1:
units.tr: On ownerships, Dig. 41.1.

units.la: Mancipi sunt ] Tollitur differentia rerum mancipi & nec mancipi tit. Cod. de vsucapione transformanda.
units.tr: Mancipable things: the difference between mancipable and non-mancipable things is removed. Title in the Code, on the transformation of usucaption.

units.la: Mancipi res ]mancipium est, quicquid capi communiter ac domari solet, vt homo, equus, ouis. Bestiæ mancipia sunt, cum primum domari incipiunt. Isidor. Goth. h.
units.tr: A mancipium is whatever is customarily captured and tamed, such as a man, a horse, a sheep. Beasts become mancipia when they first begin to be tamed. Isidore of Gothofredus, here.

units.la: Elephanti & Cameli ]videntur quidem mancipi esse; non sunt tamen: quia feræ bestiæ sunt. l. 2. §. vlt. ad l. Aquil. Isidor. Mancipium, inquit, est, quicquid manu capi subdique potest, vt homo, equus, ouis. Hæc enim animalia statim vt nata sunt ; mancipium esse putantu Nam & ea quæ in bestiarum numero sun tunc videntur mancipium esse , quando capi siue domari cœperunt.Cuiac. hic.
units.tr: Elephants and camels seem indeed to be mancipable, but they are not, because they are wild beasts. Dig. 9.2, last §, on the Lex Aquilia. Isidore says: a mancipium is whatever can be taken and subdued by hand, such as a man, a horse, a sheep. For these animals are regarded as mancipia as soon as they are born. Those which belong to the class of wild beasts seem to be mancipia only when they have begun to be captured or tamed. Cuiacius here.

units.la: adde l. 2. in sin. ff. ad l. Aquiliam.
units.tr: Add Dig. 9.2, at the end, on the Lex Aquilia.

§ 8 below.

units.la: §. 17. infr. eod.
units.tr: § 17 below, same title.

units.la: Species alienationis est eiusque similitudo. Cai. 6. §. 3. unde imaginaria venditio dicitur. Inst. de testam. ordinand. imaginaria causa l. 3. ff. de capite minut.
units.tr: A species of alienation, and a likeness of it. Gaius 6 § 3. Whence it is called an imaginary sale. Inst. on testamentary ordinance. An imaginary cause, Dig. 4.5.3 on loss of status.

units.la: Et rerum particula, & dispungenda.
units.tr: And of things: a particle to be struck out.

units.la: Mancipi. Hac solennitate vtebantur in emancipationibus. d. l. 3. d. §. 3. in testamentis. Inst. de testam. ordinand. in solutionibus. Cicero 2. de legib. & breuiter Boëthius, quamcunque rem lege 12. tabularum aliter quam per hanc solennitatem non potuisse alienari, testatur : adde Contium 1. disput. 2. unde mancipatio inter actus legitimos refertur. l. 77. ff. de reg. iur. Gothofr. hic.
units.tr: Mancipable. This solemnity was used in emancipations. Ibid., law 3, § 3; in wills, Inst. on testamentary ordinance; in payments. Cicero, On the Laws, book 2; and briefly Boethius, who attests that no thing could be alienated under the Twelve Tables except through this solemnity. Add Contius, Disputation 1, chapter 2. Whence mancipation is classed among legal acts. Dig. 50.17.77, on rules of law; Gothofredus here.

units.la: Eaque sit certis verbis exempla sunt in §. praterea quib. modis potest. solu. & §. 1. de testam. ordinand. Pacius hic.
units.tr: "Effected with set words": examples are in the § on what modes of payment; and § 1 on testamentary ordinance. Pacius here.

units.la: Eaque fit certis verbis ] Hæc solennitas fuit verborum. Qui mancipium accipiebat, æs tenens ita dicebat, Hunc ego hominem ex iure Quiritium meum esse aio: isque mihi emptus est hoc æré æneaque libra: deinde æré percutiebat libram, idque ei dabat, à quo mancipium accipiebat.vid. Goth. hic.
units.tr: "Effected with set words": this was a solemnity of words. The one who received the mancipium, holding the bronze, spoke thus: "I say this man is mine by Quiritary right, and he was bought for me with this bronze and this bronze balance." Then he struck the scale with the bronze and gave it to the one from whom he received the mancipium. See Gothofredus here.

units.la: Libripende ] Inst. de testam. ordinand. Libripens libram æneam tenebat.
units.tr: Scale-holder. Inst. on testamentary ordinance. The libripens held the bronze balance.

units.la: Latinos colonarios ] horum exemplo Juniani introducti sunt, ut Iustinianus scribit init. de lat. lib.
units.tr: Latin colonists. On their model the Junian Latins were introduced, as Justinian writes at the beginning of On Latin freedom.

units.la: Latinos colonarios ] Latini libertini ad similitudinem antiquæ Latinitatis (quæ in colonias missa est) videtur esse introducti.l. uni. C. de Lati. libert. Goth. hic.
units.tr: Latin colonists. The Latin freedmen seem to have been introduced in likeness of the ancient Latinity, which was sent out into the colonies. Code, law single, on Latin freedom; Gothofredus here.

units.la: Commercium ] commercium est permutatio.l. ex hoc iure. de inst. & iur. Ex permutatione originem cepit emtio & venditio: in qua etsi utrinque merx non sit, ut in permutatione, sed aliud pretium, aliud merx, de ea tamen commercium dicitur frequentissime: inde & mercari, & promercium, & promercalis res. vide Cuiacium & Pacium hic.
units.tr: Commercium is exchange. Dig. 1.1, law "ex hoc iure," on the Institutes and law. From exchange arose buying and selling. In these, even if the goods are not on both sides as in exchange, but one side is the price and the other the goods, it is very often still called commercium; hence mercari, promercium, and promercalis res. See Cuiacius and Pacius here.

units.la: Quibus commercium ] Peregrinis datur ius commercii.l. 15. ff. de interdict. & releg.
units.tr: Those to whom commercium is granted. Foreigners are given the right of commercium. Dig. 48.22.15, on interdicts and banishment.

units.la: Emendi vendendique ] commercium; ius vendendi, emendi, permutandi.l. 5. ff. de iustitia. Patet tamen interdum latius id vocabulum tempus, sed debuit & vocem hanc, mobilium, circumscribere. Nam idem prorsus est in vsucapionibus rerum immobilium. Scitum plane est huius erroris causam in Tribonianum conferre. Cuiac.
units.tr: Buying and selling: commercium is the right of selling, buying and exchanging. Dig. 1.1.5, on justice. Yet this term sometimes extends more widely, though the word "movable" ought also to be restricted, since it is entirely the same in usucaptions of immovable things. It is plainly a neat point to trace the cause of this error to Tribonian. Cuiacius.

units.la: In iure cessio ] Tribus verbis omne officium praetoris continetur; Do, Dico, Addico. Dat Iudices, Dicitur, Addicit, exempli gratia, in cessionibus. Addicit bona libertatū conseruandarū causa. Unde & in antiquis legibus, Manilia, Peducea, Alliena, Fabia, de finibus agrorum, ita legitur, Deque ea re curatoris, qui hac lege erit, iurisdictio, reciperatorumque datio, addictio esto. Si curator hac lege non erit, tunc quicunque magistratus in ea colonia, municipio, praefectura, foro, conciliabulo, iuridicundo praeerit, magistratus de ea re iurisdictio, iudicisque datio, addictio esto. Cuiac. & Pacius hic.
units.tr: In iure cessio ] The whole office of the praetor is contained in three words: I give, I say, I award (Do, Dico, Addico). He gives judges, he declares the law, he awards, for example in cessions. He awards goods for the sake of preserving freedom. Hence also in the old laws, the Manilian, Peducaean, Allienan and Fabian laws concerning the boundaries of fields, it reads thus: "And concerning that matter, the jurisdiction of the guardian who shall be under this law, and the giving of recuperators, shall be an award. If there is no guardian under this law, then whatever magistrate shall preside in that colony, municipality, prefecture, forum, conciliabulum or jurisdiction, let the jurisdiction over that matter, and the giving of judges, be an award." Cuiacius and Pacius here.

units.la: Per tres personas ] Cessio in iure, seu praesente Praetore, ita fit. Is cui res creditur, rem tenens ita vindicat, hunc ego hominem ex iure Quiritium meum esse aio. Ab his, Praetor interrogat cedentem, an contra vindicet, vel A. F. A. id est, anne fies author. Est enim ita in notis apud Probum A. T. D. Q. C. V. id est, Anne tu dicis qui contra vindicaueris. Quo negante aut tacente, Praetor ei qui vindicasset rem addicebat, idque legis actio vocabatur. Formula addicendi talis esse potuit Q. N. H. E. H. P.
units.tr: Per tres personas ] A cession in law, or in the presence of the praetor, is made thus. The one to whom the thing is conveyed, holding the thing, claims it in this way: "I say that this man is mine by Quiritary right." Then the praetor asks the one ceding whether he will claim it in return, or "A. F. A.", that is, "will you become the surety?" For it is so in the notes of Probus: "A. T. D. Q. C. V.", that is, "Do you say, you who claim in return?" If he denies it or keeps silent, the praetor awarded the thing to the one who had claimed it, and this was called a legal action. The formula of awarding could have been: "Q. N. H. E. H. P. H. P. E. V. A.", that is, "Since you deny, I award this man to the one present and claiming."

units.la: H.P.E.V.A. id est, Quando negas, Hunc ego hominem præsenti & vindicanti addico. Potuit etiam ita concipi, Q.N.A.N.N.H.E.H, P.E.V.A. id est, Quando neque ais neque negas, Hunc ego hominem petenti & vindicanti addico. Hinc constat in rei vindicatione, non satis fuisse, possessorem negare intentionem actoris, sed præterea eum debuisse contra vindicare. argum. §. 2. Institut. de action. ibi, Possessor autem dominum eius se esse dicat. adde Cont. 1. disput. 12. vid. Goth. h.
units.tr: It could also have been phrased thus: "Q. N. A. N. N. H. E. H. P. E. V. A.", that is, "Since you neither say nor deny, I award this man to the one seeking and claiming." Hence it is clear that in a vindication of a thing it was not enough for the possessor to deny the plaintiff's claim, but he had moreover to claim it in return. Compare the argument from §. 2 of the Institutes de actionibus, where it reads: "But the possessor let him say that he is its owner." Add Contius, 1 disputation 12; see Gothofredus here.

units.la: Velut usufructus ] usufructus sive domino cedatur, sive extraneo, cessione finitur. Nam & extraneo cessus, ad proprietatem recurrit. l. si usufructus de iur. dot. nihil vero agitur in persona extranei. Cuiac. & Paci. hic.
units.tr: Velut usufructus ] A usufruct, whether it is ceded to the owner or to a stranger, ends by cession. For even when ceded to a stranger, it returns to the ownership. See l. si usufructus de iure dotium; but nothing is done in the person of the stranger. Cuiacius and Pacius here.

units.la: Er hæreditas ] vid. §. 12. inf. eod.
units.tr: Et hæreditas ] See §. 12 below in this same title.

units.la: Er tutela legitima ] tit. 11. §. 7. sup. eod.
units.tr: Et tutela legitima ] Title 11, §. 7 above in this same title.

units.la: Et libertas ] quæ & cessicia. Fit autem vindicta: cedit libertatem dominus, seruus vindicat: Prætor addicit. Verba domini si requiras, ea fuerunt: Hunc hominem liberum esse volo, Festus in voce, manumitti. Verba Prætoris, φαμὲν τὸν παρόντα ἄνθρωπον εἶναι ἐλεύθερον κ̀ πολίτην Ῥωμαίων. Fragmentum indicis Latinograeci in Bibliotheca regia. Interdum etiam fiebat manumissio, sed & absente Prætore, præsente solo eius lictore. l. 23. ff. de manumiss. vindict. Cuiac. Goth. Pacius hic.
units.tr: Et libertas ] which is also called cessicia. It is done by the rod: the master cedes the liberty, the slave claims it, the praetor awards it. If you ask for the words of the master, they were: "I wish this man to be free," as Festus says under the word manumitti. The words of the praetor were: "We declare this present man to be free and a citizen of Rome" [φαμὲν τὸν παρόντα ἄνθρωπον εἶναι ἐλεύθερον καὶ πολίτην Ῥωμαίων]. A fragment of the Latin-Greek index in the royal library. Sometimes manumission was also done without the praetor, with only his lictor present. l. 23 ff. de manumissionibus vindicta. Cuiacius, Gothofredus, Pacius here.

units.la: Vel antequam adeatur ] vid. §. 13. §. 14. 15. inf. eod.
units.tr: Vel antequam adeatur ] See §. 13 and §§. 14, 15 below in this same title.

units.la: Is cui cessa] Videtur Legendum, is à quo cessa est, quoniam subinfert, Permanet hæres. Atque facit quidem ab hac coniectura ipsa iuris ratio. Ideo enim tenetur creditoribus, quod adeundo cum eis contraxisse videatur. l. 3. in sin. l. 4. quib. ex causis in possess. eat. Ideo ei debitores non tenentur, quod se omni hæredis iure abdicauerit. Sed neque Cessicio hæredi tenentur, quia ei non sunt obligati: attamen emptori hæreditatis vtiles actiones dantur, venditori directæ. leg. emptor. ff. de hared. vend. Aliud ergo est cedere hæreditatem in iure, longe aliud vendere hæreditatem. De cessitia hæreditate in libris Iustiniani mentio, quod sciam, nulla fit. ait Cuiac. & Pacius h.
units.tr: Is cui cessa] It seems one should read "he from whom it is ceded", since it goes on to say "the heir remains". And indeed the reasoning of the law itself supports this conjecture. For he is bound to the creditors because by entering he is seen to have contracted with them, l. 3 in fine, l. 4 quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur. He is not bound to the debtors because he has renounced all the rights of heir. But neither are the debtors bound to the cessionary heir, because they are not obliged to him; yet the buyer of an inheritance is given useful actions, the seller direct ones, l. emptor ff. de hereditate vendita. So it is one thing to cede an inheritance in law, and quite another to sell an inheritance. As far as I know, there is no mention of a cessicia inheritance in the books of Justinian. So say Cuiacius and Pacius here.

units.la: Creditoribus defuncti] Qui debitoris hæreditatem adit, contrahit cum defuncti creditoribus l. 3. in sin. l. 4. quib. ex causs. in possess.
units.tr: Creditoribus defuncti] He who enters the inheritance of a debtor contracts with the creditors of the deceased, l. 3 in fine, l. 4 quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur.

units.la: Res autem corporales ] Dixit de rebus incorporalibus quæ ceduntur in iure, nunc de rebus corporalibus. Quid est igitur, quod ait in extremo huius sententiæ, cui cessa est hæreditas: Malim, cui cessæ sunt. Cuiac. & Pacius h.
units.tr: Res autem corporales ] He spoke of incorporeal things which are ceded in law; now he speaks of corporeal things. What then is the meaning of what he says at the end of this sentence, "to whom the inheritance was ceded"? I would prefer "to whom the inheritances were ceded". Cuiacius and Pacius here.

units.la: Res autem corporales ] Superius dixit de hæreditate, hic de rebus corporalibus; vt hinc colligas, hæreditatem inter res corporales non adnumerari. Hæreditas iuris nomen. l. 119. leg. 178.§.1 ff. de verb. signif. incorporalis, §.2. Inst. de rebus corporal. vid. Goth. h.
units.tr: Res autem corporales ] Above he spoke of an inheritance, here of corporeal things; from this you may infer that an inheritance is not counted among corporeal things. "Inheritance" is a legal term, l. 119, and l. 178 §. 1 ff. de verborum significatione; it is incorporeal, §. 2 Institutes de rebus corporalibus. See Gothofredus here.

units.la: Adiudicatione ] Idem Iustinianus scribit in extremo tit. de off. iudic. l. 11. sin. de iurisd. l. 21. §. 3. de annuis: neq; vero vllus estalius casus, in quo iudicis sententia dominium adquiratur.
units.tr: Adiudicatione ] Justinian writes the same at the end of the title de officio iudicis, l. 11 in fine de iurisdictione, l. 21 §. 3 de annuis: indeed there is no other case in which the sentence of a judge acquires ownership.

units.la: Per formulam ] Nota formulam, id est, actionem, vt tit. 25. §. 12. inf. eod. adiudicationis familiae erciscundae, communi diuidundo, finium regundorum. Goth. h.
units.tr: Per formulam ] Note the formula, that is, the action, as in title 25, §. 12 below in this same title: the award in the action for dividing a family inheritance, for dividing common property, and for fixing boundaries. Gothofredus here.

units.la: Familiae erciscundae ] §. 4. Inst. de off. iud.
units.tr: Familiae erciscundae ] §. 4 Institutes de officio iudicis.

units.la: Communi diuidundo ] §. 5. Institut. de off. iudicis.
units.tr: Communi dividundo ] §. 5 Institutes de officio iudicis.

units.la: Finium regundorum ] §. 6. Inst. eod.
units.tr: Finium regundorum ] §. 6 Institutes eod.

units.la: Velut caducum ] Quid caducum vid. titul. sup. eod.
units.tr: Velut caducum ] For what a caducum is, see the title above in this same title.

units.la: Vel ] Hanc particulam Hotomannus 3. observ. 32. expungit.
units.tr: Vel ] Hotomannus, Observations 3, 32, deletes this particle.

units.la: Ereptitium ] Ereptitium, quod quasi indigno aufertur, vt in l. penult. ff. de iur. fisci. quadrans eripiatur, & in leg. 25. ff. de vi. Haereditas eripietur. Cuiac. 6. observ. 37. & fisco statim ipso iure vindicatur l. 9. l. 18. l. vlt. ff. de his quae vt indignis. Et recte Vlpianus eripiendi verbo potius vsus est, quam auferendi, vt indicaret quasi de manibus auferri quod iam esset acquisitum. l. 4. ff. ne quis eum. vid. Contium 1. disput. 12. sed tamen Hotomannus 3. observat. 32. legit: rectereceptitium. Quod quid sit vide eundem d. loco. Gothofr. hic.
units.tr: Ereptitium ] An ereptitium is what is taken away as from one unworthy, as in l. penult. de iure fisci, where a quarter is snatched away, and in l. 25 de vi, where an inheritance will be snatched away. Cuiacius, Observations 6, 37; and it is claimed by the treasury at once by law itself, l. 9, l. 18, l. ult. de his quae ut indignis. And Ulpian rightly used the word "snatch away" rather than "take away", to show that what has already been acquired is taken, as it were, out of one's hands, l. 4 ff. ne quis eum. See Contius, 1 disputation 12; but Hotomannus, Observations 3, 32, reads recte receptitium. For what this means see the same author in the place cited. Gothofredus here.

units.la: Vel ereptitium ] Nescio quid sit ereptitium; nisi id forsitan sit quod alias in causa caduci esse dicitur. Neque enim id cadit a nobis (quandoquidem vivo testatore deficit) sed hæredi ereptitur: caduca cadunt a nobis ait Cuiac. h.
units.tr: Vel ereptitium ] I do not know what an ereptitium is, unless perhaps it is what elsewhere is said to fall under the case of a caducum. For it does not fall away from us (since it fails while the testator is alive) but is snatched from the heir. Caducum things fall away from us, says Cuiacius here.

units.la: Ex l. Papia Popæa ] Ea lata est de caducis hæreditatibus & legatis, ut Falcidia de modo legatorum.
units.tr: Ex lege Papia Poppaea ] It was passed concerning caducous inheritances and legacies, just as the Falcidian law concerns the limit on legacies.

units.la: Item legatum ] l. 47. in sin. ff. de peculio l. 120. ff. de verb. signif.
units.tr: Item legatum ] l. 47 in fine de peculio, l. 120 de verborum significatione.

units.la: Etiam per eas personas ] vid. Instit. per quas person. cuique adquiratur.
units.tr: Etiam per eas personas ] See Institutes, through what persons a thing is acquired for each.

units.la: Aut traditum ] §. 3. Inst. per quas person. cuique. l. 10. §. 1. ff. de acquir. rerum.
units.tr: Aut traditum ] §. 3 Institutes per quas personas cuique adquiritur; l. 10 §. 1 ff. de acquirenda rerum dominio.

units.la: Stipulati fuerint ] vid. Instit. & ff. de stipulat. servor.
units.tr: Stipulati fuerint ] See Institutes and ff. de stipulatione servorum.

units.la: Hæredes instituti sint ] §. 3. Instit. de hæred. instituendis.
units.tr: Heredes instituti sint ] §. 3 Institutes de heredibus instituendis.

units.la: Legatumve ] d. §. 3. l. 39. §. 1. in sin. l. 89. §. 2. ff. de legat. 1.
units.tr: Legatumve ] The same §. 3; l. 39 §. 1 in fine, l. 89 §. 2 ff. de legatis 1.

units.la: Iussu nostro ] In hæreditate, nihil mutatum: in legato mutatum: cum invito servius acquirat. d. §. 3.
units.tr: Iussu nostro ] In an inheritance nothing is changed; in a legacy it is changed, since a slave acquires even against the will of the master. The same §. 3.

units.la: Alterius in bonis ] Dominus Bonitarius præferetur domino Quiritario, Cuiac.
units.tr: Alterius in bonis ] The bonitary owner is preferred to the Quiritary owner, Cuiacius.

units.la: Alterius in bonis ] id est, Bonitarius. Theoph. Inst. de libert. §. ᾧ τὰς ἔσιν ἕν[?], ὡς εἶπον Φυσικὴ δικαιοσύνη[?],
units.tr: Alterius in bonis ] that is, bonitary. Theophilus, Institutes de libertate §. [The Greek of this note is too garbled in the scan to reproduce reliably; it sets out the natural and the lawful possession, the one called natural, the other, in which the master is the Quiritary owner, called lawful.]

units.la: ἔννομος δὲ ποτεία ἡ ἢ μὲ Φυσικὴ λέγεται in bonis ἐ δεσπότης ϛοντιτάεια, ἡ δὲ ἔννομο λέγεται. Iure Quiritium, ex iure Quiritium. Hæc ille, adde cit. §. 16 sup. eod. Goth.b.
units.tr: [The Greek continuation is likewise corrupt in the scan; it says that lawful possession is what is called natural, and that the in bonis ownership of a master is the lawful one.] By Quiritary law, from Quiritary law. So far he; add the cited §. 16 above in this same title. Gothofredus, b.

units.la: Ex operibus suis ] Alij dicunt ex operis : sed hoc quoque rectum est, vt auctoribus scriptis libris, in §. de his. per quas person. nob. adq. §. item. per quas personas oblig. nob.adq. Er auctoribus Florentinis in l. quod seruus de stip. seru. ait Cuiac. & Pac. hic.
units.tr: Ex operibus suis] Others say "ex operis", but this too is correct, as the written books show, in §. de his, per quas personas nobis adquiritur, and §. item, per quas personas obligatio nobis adquiritur. And the Florentine manuscripts have it so, in l. quod servus de stipulatione servorum; Cuiacius and Pacius say so here.

units.la: Extra has autem ] §. 4. Instit. per quas person. unique adquir.
units.tr: Extra has autem] §. 4, Institutes, per quas personas unicuique adquiritur.

units.la: Tit. XX. De Testamentis.
units.tr: Title XX. On Testaments.

units.la: TEstamentum, est mentis nostræ iusta contestatio, in id solenniter factum, vt post mortem nostram valeat.
units.tr: A testament is a lawful attestation of our mind, solemnly made so that it may be valid after our death.

units.la: Testamentorum genera fuerunt tria: vnum, quod calatis Comitiis, alterum quod in procinctu; tertium quod per æs & libram appellatum est. Illis duobus testamentis abolitis hodie solum in vsu est, quod per æs & libram fit: id est, per mancipationem imaginariam, in quo testamento libripens adhibetur, & familiæ emptor, & non minus quam quinque testes, cum quibus testamenti factio est.
units.tr: There were three kinds of testament: one made at the Calata Assemblies, another in procinctu, and a third called per aes et libram. The first two are abolished, and today only the one made per aes et libram is in use. That is, it is made by an imaginary mancipation, in which a balance-holder (libripens) is present, along with the buyer of the family (emptor familiae) and no fewer than five witnesses, with whom the testator has testamentary capacity.

units.la: Qui in potestate testatoris est, aut familiæ emptoris, testis ad libræ pensa adhiberi non potest. quoniam familiæ mancipatio inter testatorem & familiæ emptorem fit:& ob id domestici testes adhibendi non sunt.
units.tr: A person under the power of the testator or of the buyer of the family cannot be admitted as a witness to the weighing of the bronze. This is because the mancipation of the family takes place between the testator and the buyer of the family, and so household members are not to be admitted as witnesses.

units.la: Filio familiæ emente, pater eius testis esse non potest.
units.tr: If a son under power is the buyer, his father cannot be a witness.

units.la: Ex duobus fratribus qui in eadem patris potestate sunt, alter familiæ emptor, alter testis esse non potest: quoniam quod vnus ex his mancipium accipit, adquirit patri, cui filius suus testis esse non debet:pariter & qui in potestate eius est constitutus. Duo fratres, qui in eiusdem patris potestate sunt, testes vtrique, vel alter testis,alter libripens fieri possunt, alio familiam emente: quoniam nihil nocet ex vna domo plures testes alieno negotio adhiberi.
units.tr: Of two brothers under the same father's power, one cannot be the buyer of the family and the other a witness. This is because whatever one of them takes by mancipation he acquires for the father, and a father's son ought not to be a witness to a transaction that benefits his father. The same holds for anyone else placed under the father's power. But two brothers under the same father's power may both be witnesses, or one a witness and the other the balance-holder, when another man is the buyer of the family, because it does no harm for several witnesses from one household to be admitted to another person's business.

units.la: Mutus, surdus, furiosus, pupillus, fœmina, neque familiæ emptor, neque testis, libripensve fieri potest.
units.tr: A mute person, a deaf person, a madman, a ward, or a woman cannot be the buyer of the family, a witness, or the balance-holder.

units.la: Latinus Iunianus,& familiæ emptor, & testis, & libripens fieri potest: quoniam cum eo testamenti factio est.
units.tr: A Junian Latin may be the buyer of the family, a witness, and the balance-holder, because he has testamentary capacity.

units.la: In testamento, quod per æs & libram fit, duæ res aguntur, familiæ mancipatio, & nuncupatio testamenti. Nuncupatur testamentum in hunc modum: tabulas testamenti testator tenens ita dicit, Hæc vti his tabulis cerisve scripta sunt, ita do, ita lego, ita testor. Itaque vos QuiQuirites testimonium præbitote, quæ nuncupatio & testatio vocatur.
units.tr: In a testament made per aes et libram two things are done: the mancipation of the family and the nuncupation of the testament. The testament is nuncupated in this way: the testator, holding the tablets of the testament, says, "As these things are written in these tablets and wax, so I give, so I bequeath, so I attest. Therefore, you Quirites, bear witness." This is called the nuncupation and attestation.

units.la: Filiusfamiliæ testamentum facere non potest: quoniam nihil suum habet, vt testari de eo possit. Sed Diuus Augustus Marcus constituit, vt filius familiæ miles, de eo peculio quod in castris adquisiuit testamentum facere possit.
units.tr: A son under power cannot make a testament, since he has nothing of his own about which he could make one. But the deified Augustus and Marcus ordained that a son under power who is a soldier may make a testament concerning that property (peculium) which he acquired in camp.

units.la: Qui de statu suo incertus est (facito quod patre peregre mortuo, ignorat se sui iuris esse) testamentum facere non potest.
units.tr: A person who is uncertain of his own status (for example, when his father has died abroad and he does not know that he is sui iuris) cannot make a testament.

units.la: Impubes, licet sui iuris sit, testamentum facere non potest: quoniam nondum plenum iudicium animi habet.
units.tr: A minor, although sui iuris, cannot make a testament, because he does not yet have full judgment of mind.

units.la: Mutus, surdus, furiosus itemque prodigus, cui lege bonis interdictum est, testamentum facere non possunt: mutus, quoniam verba nuncupationis loqui non potest: surdus, quoniam verba familiæ emptoris exaudire non potest: furiosus, quoniam mentem non habet, vt testari de ea re possit: prodigus, quoniam commercium illi interdictum est, & ob familiam mancipare non potest.
units.tr: A mute person, a deaf person, a madman, and likewise a prodigal on whom the law has interdicted his goods cannot make a testament. The mute person cannot speak the words of nuncupation; the deaf person cannot hear the words of the buyer of the family; the madman has no mind with which to attest to the matter; and the prodigal is forbidden commerce and so cannot mancipate for the family.

units.la: Latinus Iunianus, item is qui Dedititiorum numero est, testamentum facere non potest. Latinus quidem, quoniam nominatim lege Iunia prohibitus est: is autem qui Dedititiorum numero est, quoniam nec quasi ciuis Romanus testari potest, cum sit peregrinus: nec quasi peregrinus, quoniam nullius certæ ciuitatis, sciens vt aduersus leges ciuitatis suæ testetur.
units.tr: A Junian Latin, and likewise one who belongs to the class of Dediticii, cannot make a testament. The Latin is forbidden by name under the lex Iunia. The Dediticius cannot testify as a Roman citizen, since he is a foreigner, nor as a foreigner, since he belongs to no certain state; and he would be testifying knowingly against the laws of his own state.

units.la: Fœminæ post duodecimum annum ætatis testamenta facere possunt tutore auctore donec in tutela sint.
units.tr: Women may make testaments after their twelfth year of age, with the authorization of their guardian, for as long as they are under guardianship.

units.la: Seruus publicus prætorisve, parte dimidia testamenti faciendi habet ius.
units.tr: A public slave, or a slave of the praetor, has the right to make half a testament.

units.la: De testamentis ] 2. Instit. 10. adde 4. Paul. sent. 4.
units.tr: On testaments: Inst. 2.10; add Paul. Sent. 4.4.

units.la: Iusta contestatio ] 6. Gell. 12. testatio, Instit. eod. μαρτυρία, Theoph. Inst. de testam. ordin. sententia l. 1. ff. qui testament. βίλησις. 25. Eclog. 1. c. 2. 5. Harmenop. 1. Goth. hic.
units.tr: Lawful attestation ] 6. Gell. 12. attestation, Instit. eod. μαρτυρία [martyria], Theoph. Inst. de testam. ordin. sentence l. 1. ff. qui testament. βούλησις [boulēsis]. 25. Eclog. 1. c. 2. 5. Harmenop. 1. Goth. hic.

units.la: Testamentorum genera ] Iure ciuili. Fuit & quartum, iure prætorio. Est & quintum, iure ciuili, prætorio, & principali, iure permixto. vid. 15. Gell. 27.
units.tr: Kinds of testament: under civil law. There was also a fourth, under praetorian law. There is also a fifth, under civil, praetorian and imperial law together, a mixed kind. See Gell. 15.27.

units.la: Calatis Comitiis ] Comitia Calata, pro collegio pontificum habebantur: aut regis, sacrorum, aut flaminum, inaugurandorum causa. Eorum alia curiatis (quæ per lictorem curiatim Calari, id est, conuocari moris erat) Centuriata per Cornicinem. Calatis etiam sacrorum detestatio & testamenta fieri solebant. Gell. 15. 27. Calata Comitia bis in anno fieri solita scribit, pacis tempore: Calata dici, quod populus ad ea vocetur. Est enim calari πρὸς καλεῖν. Theoph. d. loco. Is autem qui non vniuersum populum, sed partem aliquam adesse iubet, non comitia, sed concilium edere iubet. Centuriata in campo Martio habebantur, non intra pomerium: Illud addendum est ex Lælio Fœlice, Curiata Comitia fuisse; cum ex generibus omnium, suffragium ferretur: Centuriata, cum ex censu & ætate. Tributa, cum ex regionibus & locis. 15. Gell. 27. in sin. videtur tamen Festus in voce centuriata, Centuriata & Curiata confundere; vide Goth. hic. In procinctu ] cum in prælium exituri essent. Inst. eod. §. 1. cum viri ad prælium faciendum in aciem vocabantur 15. Gell. 27. Goth. h. Per æs & libram ] per familiæ emancipationem, cuiæs & libra adhibebatur. 15. Gell. 27. §.
units.tr: Calata Comitia: the Calata Assemblies were held for the college of pontiffs, or for the king of sacred rites or the flamens, for the purpose of inauguration. Some of these were curiate (which, as the lictor used to summon them curiatim, were called calari, that is, convened), and others centuriate, summoned by the cornicen. Sacred detestations and testaments were also customarily made at the Calata Assemblies. Gellius (15.27) writes that the Calata Assemblies were customarily held twice a year in time of peace, and were called Calata because the people are summoned to them, for calari is πρὸς καλεῖν [pros kalein]. Theophilus, loc. cit. But one who orders not the whole people but only some part of it to attend does not convene comitia but a concilium. The centuriate assemblies were held in the Campus Martius, not within the pomerium. It must be added from Lelius Felix that the curiate assemblies were those in which the vote was cast by kinds of people, the centuriate by property assessment and age, and the tribal by districts and places. Gellius 15.27 at the end; yet Festus, under the word centuriata, seems to confuse centuriata with curiata; see Gothofredus here. In procinctu: when men were about to go out to battle; Inst. eod. §1: when men were called into line to fight. Gell. 15.27; Gothofredus here. Per aes et libram: by the emancipation of the family, at which a balance was used.

units.la: 1. Inst. eod. Per emancipationem ] 15. Gell. 27. d. §. 1. Inst. eod. Imaginariam] vid. l. ult. C. de adopt. Quam quinque testes] tit. 19. §. 3. sup. eod. Hodie septem adhibendi §. 3. Inst. eod. Cum quibus ] §. 6. Inst. eod. Qui in potestate ] §. 9. Inst. eod. Ad libram pensa] Lege, aut libripens. Cuiac. Inter testatorem & familiæ emptorem] Et ideo seorsim in tabulis hæres scriptus (plerunque enim cui fit mancipatio, non fit nuncupatio) ad testamentum testis adhiberi potest: at sublata mancipatione, sane creditur hodie, ut recte Iustin. ait in §. sed neque de testam. ordin. totum hoc negocium inter testatorem & hæredem agi. Proinde hæres, aut qui per potestatem hæredi coniunctus est, testis adhiberi non potest. Cuiac. h.
units.tr: Per emancipationem: Gell. 15.27; d. §1 Inst. eod. Imaginariam: see l. ult. C. de adopt. Quinque witnesses: tit. 19 §3 sup. eod. Today seven are to be admitted: §3 Inst. eod. Cum quibus: §6 Inst. eod. Qui in potestate: §9 Inst. eod. "Ad libram pensa": read "aut libripens" (Cujas). Inter testatorem et familiae emptorem: so an heir named separately in the tablets (for usually the one to whom the mancipation is made is not the one who receives the nuncupation) can be admitted as a witness to the testament. But with mancipation abolished, it is indeed now held, as Justinian rightly says in the §sed neque de testam. ordin., that the whole business is conducted between the testator and the heir. Therefore an heir, or one who is joined to the heir by power, cannot be admitted as a witness. Cujas here.

units.la: Inter testatorem ] l. 20. ff. qui testamenta.
units.tr: Inter testatorem: l. 20 ff. qui testamenta.

units.la: Ob id domestici ] vid. l. 20. ff. de testibus l. 3. C. de testam.
units.tr: Ob id domestici: see l. 20 ff. de testibus; l. 3 C. de testam.

units.la: Pater eius ] §. 8. Inst. eod.
units.tr: Pater eius: §8 Inst. eod.

units.la: Duobus fratribus ] d. §. 8.
units.tr: Duobus fratribus: d. §8.

units.la: Pariter & qui in potestate ] Lege, pater & qui in potestate eius est constitutus, & duo fratres, &c. vid. l pater de test. Cuiac. h.
units.tr: Pariter et qui in potestate: read "the father, and whoever is placed under his power, and two brothers," etc. See l. pater de test.; Cujas here.

units.la: Aluo familiam emente ] Duo fratres in alieno testamento testes esse possunt. d. §. 8. inf. l. 22. ff. qui testamenta.
units.tr: Alio familiam emente: two brothers can be witnesses in another's testament. d. §8 inf.; l. 22 ff. qui testamenta.

units.la: Nihil nocet ] d §. 8. inf. l. 17. ff. de testib.
units.tr: Nihil nocet: d. §8 inf.; l. 17 ff. de testib.

units.la: Murus (surdus) ] §. 6. Inst. eod.
units.tr: Mutus (surdus): §6 Inst. eod.

units.la: Furiosus ] d. §. 6. l. 20. §. 4. ff. qui testam.
units.tr: Furiosus: d. §6; l. 20 §4 ff. qui testam.

units.la: Pupillus ] d. l. 3. §. 5. l. 19. in sin. ff. de testam. d. §. 6. Inst. eod.
units.tr: Pupillus: d. l. 3 §5; l. 19 in fin. ff. de testam.; d. §6 Inst. eod.

units.la: Fœmina ] v. leg. 20. §. 6. ff. qui testamenta. l. 18. ff. de testam.
units.tr: Foemina: see l. 20 §6 ff. qui testamenta; l. 18 ff. de testam.

units.la: Familiæ emptor ] id est, hæres.
units.tr: Familiae emptor: that is, the heir.

units.la: Latinus Junianus ] Quoniam commercium habet, ut sup. tit. prox.
units.tr: Latinus Iunianus: because he has commerce, as above in the preceding title.

units.la: Latinus Iunianus ] de quo dictum est tit. 1. §. 5. sup. eod. & tit. 3. sup. eod. tit. 19. §. 4. sup. eod.
units.tr: Latinus Iunianus: of whom it was said in tit. 1 §5 sup. eod., and tit. 3 sup. eod.; tit. 19 §4 sup. eod.

units.la: Dueres ] Quænam agantur in testamento per æs & libram.
units.tr: Dueres: What things are transacted in a will by bronze and scales (per aes et libram).

units.la: Nuncupatur] Formula nuncupationis testa-mentariæ, cui adde l. 58.ff.de hæred.inst.
units.tr: Nuncupatur: The formula of testamentary nuncupation; add l. 58. ff. de hered. inst.

units.la: Testimonium prabitote] Forsitan rectius legeretur, perhibetote: Apuleius lib. 2. Vos in hanc rem, boni Quirites, testimonium perhibetote.
units.tr: Testimonium prabitote: Perhaps it would be more correctly read as "perhibetote." Apuleius, lib. 2: "You, good Quirites, bear witness to this matter."

units.la: Filiusfamiliæ] l.6.l. 16.l.19.ff.qui testam.
units.tr: Filiusfamilias: l. 6, l. 16, l. 19, ff. qui testam.

units.la: Divus Augustus Marcus] iupereft Marcus; §.1.Inst.quib non est permiss.factest.
units.tr: Divus Augustus Marcus: Read "superest Marcus" (Marcus survives); §. 1. Inst. quib. non est permiss. fact. test.

units.la: Miles de eo peculio] l. 6. in sin.ff. de iniusto.l. 22.ff.de testam. militis.
units.tr: Miles de eo peculio: l. 6 in sin. ff. de iniusto; l. 22 ff. de testam. militis.

units.la: Qui de statu] l.14.in sin.l.15 ff. qui testam.l.de statu.de testam.
units.tr: Qui de statu: l. 14 in sin.; l. 15 ff. qui testam.; l. de statu de testam.

units.la: Facere non potest] vid.Nov. Leonis 40.
units.tr: Facere non potest: see Nov. Leonis 40.

units.la: Impubes] §. 1.Inst. quib: non est permiss.l. 5.ff. qui testam.
units.tr: Impubes: §. 1 Inst. quib. non est permiss.; l. 5 ff. qui testam.

units.la: Mutus surdus] surdus mutus ita natus, testamentu facere non pot. Surdus mutus ita factus, testamentu facere potest, si sciat litteras. Æque surdus ita natus aut factus testamentum facere potest: Itemque mutus ita natus aut factus, si sciat litteras. Cæterum hæc est Iustiniani constitutio, ex qua in l.mutu de legat.3. additum est, nisi superueniens morbus ei impedimento sit: l.6.in sin.l.7.ff. eod. §. 3.Instit. quib.non est.l. 16.ff. eod.&c.de his vide Cuiac.& Goth.h.
units.tr: Mutus surdus: A deaf-mute born so cannot make a will. A deaf-mute made so can make a will, if he knows letters. Likewise a deaf man, born or made so, can make a will; and likewise a mute, born or made so, if he knows letters. Moreover, this is Justinian's constitution, to which the phrase was added in l. mutu de legat. 3: unless a supervening illness is an impediment to him. l. 6 in sin.; l. 7 ff. eod.; §. 3 Instit. quib. non est; l. 16 ff. eod., etc.; on these see Cuiacius and Gothofredus here.

units.la: Quoniam Commercium] Quanquam hæc ratio deficit hodie, non tamen habet prodigus testamenti factionem: nimirum quia non tantum tum commercio ei, sed etiam bonis suis interdicitur. Ait enim prætor, vt est in formula interdictionis: OB EAM REM TIBI EA RE COMMERCIOQVE INTERDICO. EA RE, id est, bonis paternis auitisque.vid. Cuiac. h.
units.tr: Quoniam Commercium: Although this reason fails today, a prodigal nonetheless does not lack testamentary capacity, since he is forbidden not only commerce but also his own goods. For the praetor says, as in the formula of interdiction: "FOR THIS REASON I INTERDICT YOU FROM THAT THING AND FROM COMMERCE." "That thing" means paternal and ancestral goods. See Cuiacius here.

units.la: Latinus qui Dediticiorum numero] Hi testari non possunt. v. C. de latin. libert. tit. 22. §. 2. inf. C. de dedit. libertate.
units.tr: Latinus who is among the number of the Dediticii: These cannot make a will. See C. de latin. libert. tit. 22, §. 2; below, C. de dedit. libertate.

units.la: Peregrinus ] Peregrinus testamenti factionem non habet, vt hic: nisi accepto vsu togæ, l. 31, 32. ff. de iur. fisci. de his vid. Goth. h.
units.tr: Peregrinus: A foreigner has no testamentary capacity, as is said here, unless he has received the use of the toga; l. 31, 32 ff. de iur. fisci. On these see Gothofredus here.

units.la: Certæ ciuitatis sciens] Leges, certæ ciuitatis ciuis est: vel certæ ciuitatis sit. Cuiac.
units.tr: Certae civitatis sciens: Read either "is a citizen of a certain state" or "let him be of a certain state." Cuiacius.

units.la: Vt aduersus leges ] Aduersus pro secundum, positum est: vt sit secundum leges. Sic in tit. 28. Bonor. possessio aduersus tabulas; quæ iuxta tabulas in tit. 23. sic in l. naturaliter de vsur. & vsuc. Caius ait, Possessionem non tantum aduersus euim interrumpi qui eripit, sed aduersus omnes: id est, non ei tantum vtilem esse vsurpationem qui eripit; sed etiam omnibus: id quod intelligi potest ex tit. quemad. seruit. amitt. in quo multis in locis ostenditur; [seruitutes vsurpari] per socium; & quemcunque possessorem, per eum etiam qui se suo iure vti non putat. vid. Cuiac. hic.
units.tr: Ut adversus leges: Adversus is used for secundum (according to), as if it said "secundum leges" (according to the laws). So in title 28, "bonorum possessio adversus tabulas" (possession of goods against the tablets), which in title 23 is "iuxta tabulas" (according to the tablets); and so in l. naturaliter de usur. et usuc. Gaius says that possession is interrupted not only against the one who snatches it away, but against everyone; that is, usucaption is not useful only to the one who snatches, but to everyone. This can be understood from title quemad. servit. amitt., in which it is shown in many places that [servitudes are usurped] through a partner and through any possessor, even through one who does not think he is using them by his own right. See Cuiacius here.

units.la: Seruus publicus prætorisve] Legendum, seruis publipublicus P. Romani, cui non absimilis error est in tit. 24. Plus ergo Iuris habent serui publici P. Romani, quam aut ciuitatum, aut priuatorum serui. vid. Cuiac. & Paci. h.
units.tr: Servus publicus praetorisve: Read "servus publicus populi Romani" (a public slave of the Roman people), an error not unlike that in title 24. Public slaves of the Roman people therefore have more right than the slaves of cities or of private persons. See Cuiacius and Pacius here.

units.la: Tit. XXI. Quemadmodum heres institui debeat.
units.tr: Tit. XXI. How an heir ought to be instituted.

units.la: HEres institui recte potest his verbis, Titius heres esto, Titius heres sit, Titium heredem esse iubeo. Illa autem institutio, Heredem instituo, Heredem facio, plerisque improbata est.
units.tr: An heir can validly be instituted by these words: "Let Titius be heir," "Let Titius be heir," "I order Titius to be heir." But the institution, "I institute an heir," "I make an heir," has been disapproved by most.

units.la: Cur hæc Institutio plerisque improbata est, HEREDEM INSTITVO, HEREDEM FACIO? vtrum quia sola lex hæredem Instituit, hæredem facit? an quia hæc verba plerisque videntur non esse directa? Sed hæc verborum solennitas abolita est. l. quoniam C. de testam. vid. Cuiac. & Pac. hoc tit.
units.tr: Why has this institution, "I institute an heir," "I make an heir," been disapproved by most? Is it because only the law institutes an heir and makes an heir, or because these words seem to most not to be direct? But this solemnity of words has been abolished. l. quoniam C. de testam. See Cuiacius and Pacius on this title.

units.la: His verbis] Olim ita ius fuit, Hodie quibufcunque verbis institui potest. l. 15. C. de test.
units.tr: "By these words": formerly the law was such that only certain words were permitted; today an heir may be instituted by whatever words. l. 15. C. de test.

units.la: Tit. XXII. Qui heredes institui possunt.
units.tr: Title XXII. Who may be instituted heirs.

units.la: HEredes institui possunt, qui testamenti factionem cum testatore habent. Dedi-
units.tr: Heirs may be instituted who have testamentary capacity with the testator. Dedi-

units.la: Deditioriorum numero heres instituì non potest, quia peregrinus est.
units.tr: A person of the Dediticii class cannot be instituted heir, because he is a foreigner.

units.la: Cùm quo testamenti factio non est, si quidem mortis testatoris tempore, vel intra diem cretionis ciuis Romanus sit, heres esse potest: quod si Latinus manserit lege Iunia, capere hereditatem prohibetur. Idem iuris est in persona cœlibis propter legem Iuliam.
units.tr: A person with whom there is no testamentary capacity can be heir if, at the time of the testator's death or within the day of cretio, he is a Roman citizen. But if he remains a Latin under the Junian law, he is prohibited from taking the inheritance. The same rule applies to an unmarried person because of the Julian law.

units.la: Incerta persona heres institui non potest, veluti hoc modo: Quisquis primus ad funus meum venerit, heres esto: quoniam certum consilium debet esse testantis.
units.tr: A person who is uncertain cannot be instituted heir, for example in this form: "Whoever comes first to my funeral, let him be heir." For the testator's intention must be certain.

units.la: Nec municipia, nec municipes heredes institui possunt: quoniam incertum corpus est, vt neque cernere vniuersi, neque pro libito de herede cernere possunt, vt heredes fiant. Senatusconsulto tamen concessum est, vt à libertis suis heredes institui possint. Sed fideicommissa hereditas municipibus restitui potest: idque hoc senatusconsulto prospectum est.
units.tr: Neither municipalities nor their members can be instituted heirs, since a corporate body is uncertain, so that neither all the members together can make cretio, nor can one of them make cretio on behalf of the others so as to become heir. By a senatus-consultum, however, it was permitted that heirs might be instituted from among their freedmen. But an inheritance held in trust can be restored to a municipality, and provision for this was made by the same senatus-consultum.

units.la: Deos heredes instituere non possumus præter eos, quos senatusconsulto, constitutionibus Principum instituere concèssum est: sicuti Iouem Tarpeium, Apollinem Didymæum, sicuti Martem in Gallia, Mineruam Meliensem, Herculem Gaditanum, Dianam Ephesiam, matrem deorum Cybelem, eam quæ Smyrnæ colitur, & Cœlestum Salinensem Carthaginis.
units.tr: We cannot institute gods as heirs, except those whom a senatus-consultum or the constitutions of the emperors have allowed us to institute: such as Jupiter Tarpeius, Apollo of Didyma, Mars in Gaul, Minerva of Melia, Hercules of Gades, Diana of Ephesus, the mother of the gods Cybele, the goddess worshipped at Smyrna, and the Heavenly One of Salinae at Carthage.

units.la: Seruos heredes instituere possumus nostros cum libertate: alienos, sine libertate: communes, cum libertate, vel sine libertate.
units.tr: We may institute our own slaves as heirs with freedom, other people's slaves without freedom, and common slaves with or without freedom.

units.la: Eum seruum, qui tantum in bonis nostr est, nec cum libertate heredem instituere possumus, quia Latinitatem consequitur: quod non proficit ad hereditatem capiendam.
units.tr: A slave who belongs to us only in bonis cannot be instituted heir even with freedom, because he attains only Latin status, which does not enable him to take the inheritance.

units.la: Alienos seruos heredes instituere possumus: eos tamen, quorum cum dominis testamenti factionem habemus.
units.tr: We may institute other people's slaves as heirs, but only those with whom we have testamentary capacity through their masters.

units.la: Communis seruus cum libertate recte quidem heres instituitur, quasi proprius pro parte nostra: sine libertate autem, quasi alienus, propter socii partem.
units.tr: A common slave is validly instituted heir with freedom, as our own slave in respect of our share; without freedom, however, he is instituted as another's slave, on account of his co-owner's share.

units.la: Proprius seruus cum libertate heres institutus, siquidem in eadem causa permanserit, ex testamento liber & heres sit, id est, necessarius.
units.tr: A slave of our own instituted heir with freedom, provided he remains in the same condition, becomes free and heir by the will, that is, a necessary heir.

units.la: Quod si ab ipso testatore viuente manumissus, vel alienatus sit suo arbitrio, vel iussu emptoris hereditatem adire potest. Sed si sine libertate sit institutus, omnino non constat institutio.
units.tr: But if he is manumitted or alienated by the testator himself while living, at his own discretion or by the order of the purchaser, he may enter upon the inheritance. But if he has been instituted without freedom, the institution is not valid at all.

units.la: Alienus seruus heres institutus, siquidem in ea causa permanserit, iussu domini debet hereditatem adire. Quod si viuo testatore manumissus, aut alienatus a domino fuerit: aut suo arbitrio, aut iussu emptoris poterit adire hereditatem.
units.tr: A slave of another, instituted heir, provided he remains in the same condition, must enter upon the inheritance by the order of his master. But if he is manumitted or alienated by his master while the testator lives, he may enter upon the inheritance either at his own discretion or by the order of the purchaser.

units.la: Sui heredes instituendi sunt, vel exheredandi. Sui autem heredes sunt liberi quos in potestate habemus, tam naturales, quam adoptiui: item vxor quæ in manu est, & nurus quæ in manu est filii, quem in potestate habemus.
units.tr: Heirs of the body (sui heredes) are to be instituted or disinherited. Now those are heirs of the body who are in our power: children, both natural and adopted; likewise a wife who is in our hand, and a daughter-in-law who is in the hand of a son whom we have in our power.

units.la: Posthumi quoque liberi, id est, qui in vtero sunt, si tales sunt, vt nati in potestate nostra suturi sint, suorum heredum numero sunt.
units.tr: Posthumous children also, that is, those who are in the womb, if they are such that when born they will be in our power, belong to the number of heirs of the body.

units.la: Ex suis heredibus filius quidem neque heres institutus, neque nominatim exheredatus, non potest valere testamentum. Reliquæ vero personæ liberorum, velut filia, nepos, neptis, si præteritæ sint, valet testamentum.
units.tr: Of heirs of the body, a son who is neither instituted heir nor expressly disinherited makes the will invalid. But other children, such as a daughter, grandson or granddaughter, if passed over, do not invalidate the will.

units.la: Scriptis heredibus adcrescunt, suis quidem heredibus in partem virilem: extraneis autem in partem dimidiam.
units.tr: Accrual goes to written heirs: to heirs of the body in an equal share, but to strangers in half a share.

units.la: Posthumi quoque liberi cuiuscunque sexus omissi, quod valuit testamentum agnatione rumpitur.
units.tr: Posthumous children of either sex, if omitted, break the will that would otherwise have been valid, by agnation.

units.la: Eos qui in vtero sunt, si nati sui heredes nobis futuri sunt, possumus instituere heredes: siquidem post mortem nostram nascantur, ex iure ciuili: si vero viuentibus nobis, ex lege Iulia.
units.tr: Those in the womb, if they are to be heirs of the body when born, we may institute as heirs: if they are born after our death, by the civil law; but if they are born while we are living, by the Julian law.

units.la: Filius qui in potestate est, si non instituatur heres, nominatim exheredari debet: reliqui sui heredes vtriusque sexus aut nominatim, aut inter cæteros.
units.tr: A son in power, if he is not instituted heir, must be expressly disinherited; the other heirs of the body of either sex must be disinherited either by name or among the rest.

units.la: Posthumus filius nominatim exheredandus est: filia posthuma, cæteræque posthumæ fœminæ vel nominatim, vel inter cæteros dummodo inter cæteros exheredatis aliquid legetur.
units.tr: A posthumous son must be disinherited by name; a posthumous daughter and other posthumous females may be disinherited either by name or among the rest, provided that something is left by legacy to those disinherited among the rest.

units.la: Nepotes & pronepotes, cæterique masculi posthumi præter filiam, vel nominatim, vel inter cæteros cum adiectione legati sunt exheredandi: sed rutius est tamen nominatim eos exheredari: & id obseruatur magis.
units.tr: Grandchildren and great-grandchildren, and other posthumous males besides a daughter, must be disinherited either by name or among the rest with the addition of a legacy; but it is safer to disinherit them by name, and this is the more usual practice.

units.la: Mancipatos liberos cum iure ciuili neque heredes instituere, neque exheredare necesse sit, tamen prætor iubet, si non instituantur heredes, exheredari masculos omnes nominatim, fœminas vel inter cæteros: alioqui contra tabulas bonorum possessionem eis pollicetur.
units.tr: Children who have been emancipated need not, by the civil law, be either instituted or disinherited; nevertheless the praetor orders that, if they are not instituted heirs, all the males be disinherited by name and the females either by name or among the rest; otherwise he promises them possession of the goods against the tablets.

units.la: Inter necessarios heredes, id est, seruos cum libertate heredes scriptos, & suos scilicet necessarios, id est, libertos qui in potestate sunt, iure ciuili nihil interest (nam utrique etiam inuiti heredes sunt) sed iure prætorio suis & necessariis heredibus abstinere se à parentis hereditate permittitur: necessariis autem tantum heredibus abstinendi potestas non datur.
units.tr: Between necessary heirs, that is, slaves instituted heirs with freedom, and one's own necessary heirs, that is, freedmen who are in power, there is no difference under the civil law, for both are heirs even against their will. But under the praetorian law, heirs of the body and necessary heirs are permitted to abstain from their parent's inheritance; necessary heirs alone are not given the power of abstaining.

units.la: Extraneus heres, siquidem cum cretione sit heres institutus, cernendo fit heres: siue sine cretione, pro herede gerendo.
units.tr: An external heir, if he has been instituted with cretio, becomes heir by making cretio; or if without cretio, by acting as heir.

units.la: Pro herede gerit, qui rebus hereditariis tanquam dominus utitur: velut qui actionem rerum rum hereditariarum facit: aut seruis hereditariis cibaria mandat.
units.tr: A person acts as heir who uses the goods of the inheritance as owner, for example one who brings an action concerning the things of the inheritance, or who orders food for the slaves of the inheritance.

units.la: Cretio est certorum dierum spacium, quod datur instituto heredi ad deliberadum, utrum expediat ei adire hereditatem, necne: velut, Titius heres esto, cernitoque in diebus centum proximis, quibus scieris, poterisque: nisi ita creueris, exheres esto.
units.tr: Cretio is a space of fixed days given to an instituted heir for deliberating whether it is advantageous for him to enter upon the inheritance or not; for example: Titius heres esto, "Let Titius be heir, and let him make cretio within the next hundred days, from the day he knows and is able; unless he makes cretio thus, let him be disinherited."

units.la: Cernere est verba cretionis dicere, ad hunc modum, Cum me Mæuius heredem instituerit, eam hereditatem adeo cernoque.
units.tr: To make cretio is to speak the words of cretio in this form: "Since Maevius has instituted me heir, I take up and accept this inheritance."

units.la: Sine cretione heres institutus, si constituerit, nolle se heredem esse, statim excluditur ab hereditate, & amplius eam adire non potest.
units.tr: A person instituted heir without cretio, if he determines that he does not wish to be heir, is at once excluded from the inheritance and can no longer enter upon it.

units.la: Cum cretione vero heres institutus, sicut cernendo fit heres, ita non aliter excluditur, quam si intra diem cretionis non creuerit: idcoque etiam si constituerit nolle se heredem esse, tamen si supersint dies cretionis, pœnitentia actus, cernendo heres fieri potest.
units.tr: But a person instituted heir with cretio, just as he becomes heir by making cretio, is excluded in no other way than by failing to make cretio within the day of cretio. Therefore, even if he has determined that he does not wish to be heir, yet while days of cretio remain, having changed his mind, he can become heir by making cretio.

units.la: Cretio autem vulgaris dicitur, aut continua. Vulgaris, in qua adiiciuntur hæc verba, Quibus scieris, poterisque. Continua, in qua non adiiciuntur.
units.tr: Cretio is called either ordinary (vulgaris) or continuous (continua). Ordinary is that to which these words are added: "from the day you know and are able." Continuous is that to which they are not added.

units.la: Ei qui vulgarem cretionem habet, dies illi dati computantur, quibus scit se heredem institutum esse, & potuit cernere. Ei vero qui continuam habet cretionem, etiam illi dies conr computantur, quibus ignorauit se heredem institutum, aut sciuit, sed non potuit cer- nere.
units.tr: For a person who has ordinary cretio, the days are counted from the day on which he knows he has been instituted heir and was able to make cretio. But for a person who has continuous cretio, those days are counted during which he was ignorant that he had been instituted heir, or knew it but was unable to make cretio.

units.la: Heredes aut instituti dicuntur, aut substituti: instituti, qui primo gradu scripti sunt: substituti, qui secundo gradu, vel sequentibus.
units.tr: Heirs are called either instituted or substituted: instituted are those written in the first degree; substituted are those written in the second degree or later.

units.la: Heredes scripti sunt, veluti: Titius heres esto, cernitoque in diebus proximis centum quibus scieris, poterisque: nisi ita creueris, exheres esto: tunc Mæuius heres esto, cernitoque in diebus, & reliqua. Similiter & deinceps substitui potest.
units.tr: Heirs are written thus: "Let Titius be heir, and let him make cretio within the next hundred days, from the day he knows and is able; unless he makes cretio thus, let him be disinherited; then let Maevius be heir, and let him make cretio within the days," and so on. In the same way a substitute may be named further down.

units.la: Si sub imperfectam cretionem heres institutus sit, id est, non adiectis his verbis, Si non creueris, exheres esto; sed si ita, si non creueris, tunc Mæuius heres esto: cernendo quidem, su- perior inferiorem excludit: non cernendo autem, sed pro herede gerendo, in partem admittit substitutum. Sed postea Diuus Marcus con- stituit, ut & pro herede gerendo, ex asse fiat he- res. Quod si neque creuerit, neque pro herede gesserit, ipse excluditur, & substitutus ex asse fit heres.
units.tr: If someone is instituted heir under an imperfect cretio, that is, without these words, "If you do not make cretio, let you be disinherited," but thus: "If he does not make cretio, then let Maevius be heir": the first, by making cretio, excludes the second; but if he does not make cretio and yet acts as heir, the substitute is admitted to a share. Afterwards, however, the deified Marcus ordained that even one who acts as heir becomes heir to the whole estate.
